native_language_example: He/She prepared dinner for his/her children.

meaning: to his parents / to her parents.
additional_notes: Uses the preposition+article "a + i" → "ai" to mean "to" (often with verbs like scrivere, chiedere, dire). "suoi" agrees with "genitori" (masculine plural) and can refer to either "his" or "her" depending on context. If you mean "to my parents," say "ai miei genitori."
target_language_example: Devo telefonare ai suoi genitori stasera.
native_language_example: I have to call his/her parents tonight.

meaning: to the children; for the children.
additional_notes: Contraction of "a + i" (= "ai") plus "bambini". Often marks an indirect object with verbs like "piacere" (e.g., "Ai bambini piace..." = "The children like..."). It can also mean "to/for children" in general (intended for them) or "next to children" with "accanto ai bambini".
target_language_example: Ho comprato un libro ai bambini.
native_language_example: I bought a book for the children.

meaning: “the children like” (literally, “to the children it is pleasing”).
additional_notes: Used with piacere to express what someone likes. The person who likes something is introduced with a + the indirect object (ai bambini = to the children), and the thing liked is the grammatical subject: Ai bambini piace + infinitive (piace arrampicarsi) or a singular noun; with plural nouns, use piacciono (Ai bambini piacciono i giochi).
target_language_example: Ai bambini piace giocare al parco.
native_language_example: The children like playing at the park.

additional_notes: Used after the verb "credere" to say you believe in something: "credere a" + noun. Here, "ai" is the contraction of "a" + "i" (plural masculine), because "fantasmi" is plural. Singular: "al fantasma".
target_language_example: Non credo ai fantasmi, ma mi piacciono le storie di paura.
native_language_example: I don’t believe in ghosts, but I like scary stories.

additional_notes: "Ai" = "a" + "i" and is used with a plural masculine noun. It commonly appears with verbs like piacere ("Ai gatti piacciono…" = "Cats like…"), dare ("dare da mangiare ai gatti" = "feed the cats"), and with expressions like "allergico ai gatti" ("allergic to cats"). It can also mark comparison: "preferire i cani ai gatti" = "prefer dogs to cats."
target_language_example: Non avvicinarti: sono allergica ai gatti.
native_language_example: Don’t get close: I’m allergic to cats.

meaning: to my (plural masculine or mixed-gender noun); to my family/parents (when used alone).
additional_notes: Formed by a + i miei. It usually means “to my …” with plural masculine/mixed nouns (ai miei amici, ai miei bambini, ai miei interessi, ai miei messaggi). In some contexts “i miei” can mean “my parents/family,” so ai miei can mean “to my parents/family.” Often used after verbs like pensare a (think about), rispondere a (reply to), piacere a (be liked by), rinunciare a (give up).
target_language_example: Devo telefonare ai miei genitori stasera.
native_language_example: I have to call my parents tonight.

additional_notes: Used to indicate the indirect object (the people something is told/written/asked/given to). It’s the contraction of "a" + "i" → "ai" ("to the"), plus "miei" (my) and "amici" (friends). Often used with verbs like dire (to say/tell), chiedere (to ask), scrivere (to write), dare (to give).
target_language_example: Ho mandato un messaggio ai miei amici.
native_language_example: I sent a message to my friends.

additional_notes: It’s the preposition+article "a" (to) + "i" (the, plural) → "ai" before a plural masculine noun. Used with verbs that take "a" (like chiedere a qualcuno = to ask someone; mentire a qualcuno = to lie to someone) and also in fixed phrases like "grazie a" (thanks to).
target_language_example: Voglio telefonare ai miei genitori stasera.
native_language_example: I want to call my parents tonight.

meaning: to his / to its (masculine plural); to your (formal, "Lei").
additional_notes: "Ai" = "to the" + "suoi" = "his/its" (masculine plural, agreeing with a plural masculine noun like "limiti, tempi, studi, principi, bisogni"). It’s often used with verbs like "rinunciare a" (to give up), "pensare a" (to think about), "rimanere fedele a" (to remain faithful to), or to express suitability: "adatto a" (suitable for). In formal address, "suoi" can also mean "your" (as in "ai suoi bisogni" = "to your needs").
target_language_example: Questo corso è adatto ai suoi obiettivi.
native_language_example: This course is suitable for your goals.

additional_notes: "A" + "i" → "ai" means "to the" (plural). Used with indirect-object verbs like raccontare (tell), insegnare (teach), mostrare (show), and with adjectives like fedele a (faithful to). The possessive "suoi" agrees with "amici" (plural masculine; for female friends you’d usually say "alle sue amiche").
target_language_example: Ho mandato un messaggio ai suoi amici.
native_language_example: I sent a message to his friends.

additional_notes: Indirect object with "a" + "i" (= "ai"), used with verbs like parlare (to speak to), obbedire (to obey), mentire (to lie to), presentare (to introduce to), piacere (to be pleasing to). "Suoi" can mean either "his" or "her" depending on context.
target_language_example: Ha telefonato ai suoi genitori dopo la lezione.
native_language_example: He/She called his/her parents after class.

additional_notes: Formed by combining the preposition "a" (to) + "i tuoi" (your, masculine plural). It’s used before plural nouns like "ai tuoi obiettivi" (to your goals) or "ai tuoi figli" (to your children).
target_language_example: Parla ai tuoi amici con calma.
native_language_example: Talk to your friends calmly.

meaning: like in the old days; like we used to (back then).
additional_notes: Used to refer nostalgically to the past or to doing something the way it was done before. Often appears with "come" ("come ai vecchi tempi" = "like in the old days") or with verbs like "tornare" ("Torniamo ai vecchi tempi" = "Let’s go back to the old days/old ways").
target_language_example: Rivediamoci domani e facciamo una passeggiata, come ai vecchi tempi.
native_language_example: Let’s see each other tomorrow and go for a walk, like in the old days.

meaning: "to your" (addressing more than one person; masculine plural).
additional_notes: It’s the preposition+article "a" + "i" (= "ai") followed by the possessive "vostri" (your, plural). Used before a masculine plural noun: "ai vostri figli" = "to your children/sons". Very common in commands like "Ai vostri posti!" = "To your seats/places!".
target_language_example: Per favore, parlate ai vostri genitori di questa decisione.
native_language_example: Please, talk to your parents about this decision.

meaning: “to your places / take your seats!” (plural, addressing a group).
additional_notes: Used as a command to tell a group to go back to where they should be (their seats, spots, or positions), often by a teacher, organizer, or announcer. You can also hear it in race/sports contexts like “Ai vostri posti, pronti, via!” (“On your marks, get set, go!”).
target_language_example: Signori, ai vostri posti: lo spettacolo sta per cominciare.
native_language_example: Ladies and gentlemen, please take your seats: the show is about to begin.

additional_notes: "Aiutare" means "to help." "Gli altri" means "others" (literally "the others") and refers to other people in general. It’s commonly used after verbs like "piacere" (to like) or expressions like "sentire il bisogno di" (to feel the need to).
target_language_example: Cerco sempre di aiutare gli altri quando posso.
native_language_example: I always try to help others when I can.

additional_notes: Used with the verb pattern **aiutare + [person] + a + infinitive** to say someone helps someone do something. Here **-mi** means “me” ("help **me**"), and **a** introduces the action verb in the infinitive (e.g., *aiutarmi a capire* = “help me understand”). Often translates as “help me to …” or simply “help me …” in English.
target_language_example: Puoi aiutarmi a trovare la stazione?
native_language_example: Can you help me (to) find the station?

additional_notes: "Aiutò" is the passato remoto (simple past) of "aiutare" for he/she. "Sua madre" means “his mother” or “her mother” (Italian "sua" can refer to either; context tells you which). Often followed by "a" + infinitive to say what the help was with: "aiutò sua madre a cucinare" = “helped his/her mother to cook.”
target_language_example: Ieri aiutò sua madre a fare la spesa.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she helped his/her mother do the grocery shopping.

meaning: at work; to work (when going/heading there).
additional_notes: Most often used to say someone is at their workplace ("Sono al lavoro") or going there with verbs like andare/venire ("Vado al lavoro" = “I’m going to work”). It can also mean “while at work” ("al lavoro" = “at work/on the job”).
target_language_example: Oggi sono al lavoro fino alle sei.
native_language_example: Today I’m at work until six.

meaning: to the market; at the market.
additional_notes: "Al" = "a" + "il". With "andare/venire" it usually means "to the market" (destination): "Vado al mercato." With "essere/stare" it means "at the market" (location): "Sono/Sto al mercato." Often followed by what kind of market: "al mercato dei fiori" (flower market).
target_language_example: Domani mattina vado al mercato a comprare la frutta.
native_language_example: Tomorrow morning I'm going to the market to buy fruit.

meaning: at the park; to the park.
additional_notes: "Al" = "a" + "il". With verbs of movement (andare, tornare, venire) it often means "to the park" (destination). With activities happening there (passeggiare, pranzare, ascoltare musica) it often means "at the park" (location).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo al parco dopo scuola.
native_language_example: See you at the park after school.

additional_notes: Used with movement verbs like andare, salire, tornare, seguire to indicate going to/being on the upper floor of a building. Often contrasts with al piano di sotto (“downstairs”).
target_language_example: La camera da letto è al piano di sopra.
native_language_example: The bedroom is upstairs.

meaning: safe; in a safe place/out of danger.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "essere" (to be) to say someone/something is safe or protected ("essere al sicuro"). It can refer to physical safety or being protected from harm/risk, and is often used with time expressions like "per il momento" (for now).
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: i tuoi documenti sono al sicuro qui.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: your documents are safe here.

meaning: to his / to her / to its (to the person’s).
additional_notes: Contraction of "a + il suo". "Suo" agrees with the thing owned (masculine singular noun): e.g., "al suo cane" (to his/her dog), "al suo amico" (to his/her friend). If the owned noun is feminine or plural, it changes: "alla sua...", "ai suoi...", "alle sue...".
target_language_example: Ho lasciato le chiavi al suo collega.
native_language_example: I left the keys with/to his (or her) colleague.

meaning: to the supermarket; at the supermarket.
additional_notes: “Al” = “a” + “il” and is used for masculine singular places. With verbs of movement (andare, guidare) it often means “to the supermarket” (andare al supermercato). With verbs describing location or activities (lavorare, vedere) it often means “at the supermarket” (lavorare al supermercato, vedere qualcuno al supermercato).
target_language_example: Devo andare al supermercato dopo il lavoro.
native_language_example: I have to go to the supermarket after work.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of going/inviting (andare, invitare) to talk about attending a school dance event, often like an American-style prom. "Al" = "a" + "il" (to the).
target_language_example: Mi ha chiesto di andare al ballo studentesco con lui.
native_language_example: He asked me to go to the school dance with him.

meaning: at the bar / at the café.
additional_notes: "Al" = "a" + "il" ("to/at the"). "Bar" in Italian usually means a café/coffee bar (for espresso, snacks), not necessarily a pub. Used for location ("I’m/it’s at the bar") and with verbs of going ("go to the bar").
target_language_example: Ci vediamo al bar alle otto.
native_language_example: See you at the café at eight.

additional_notes: Used for being without light (e.g., a room/street/bridge is dark) and also figuratively for not having information: "lasciare qualcuno al buio" = to keep someone in the dark.
target_language_example: Sono rimasto al buio perché nessuno mi ha detto cosa stava succedendo.
native_language_example: I was kept in the dark because nobody told me what was happening.

additional_notes: Contraction of **a + il = al**. Used to show the indirect object/recipient (e.g., *dare qualcosa al cane* = to give something to the dog) and also after some verbs that take **a** (e.g., *sparare al cane* = to shoot at the dog; *fare un bagno al cane* = to give the dog a bath). Note: Italian **cane** means 'dog' (not an English 'cane' = a walking stick).
target_language_example: Non dare cioccolato al cane.
native_language_example: Don’t give chocolate to the dog.

meaning: in the center; downtown/in the city center.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located or needs to go to the central area of a place (al centro di + city/place = “in the center of…”). It can also refer to a central facility or hub (e.g., a data center, space center).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo al centro alle sei, davanti al teatro.
native_language_example: See you downtown at six, in front of the theater.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a position halfway between the sides/edges of a place or area. It’s often followed by a noun introduced by "del" (di + il): "al centro del fiume" (in the middle of the river), "al centro del campo" (in the center of the field). You can use it with movement/position verbs like "restare", "mettersi", "remare".
target_language_example: Mettiti al centro del ponte e guarda il panorama.
native_language_example: Stand in the middle of the bridge and look at the view.

meaning: to the cinema; at the cinema (movie theater).
additional_notes: Common set phrase with "andare" (to go): "andare al cinema" = to go to the movies. It can also mean being physically inside/at the movie theater, depending on context. "Al" = "a" + "il" (to/at the + masculine singular).
target_language_example: Stasera andiamo al cinema con degli amici.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re going to the movies with some friends.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "andare" (to go): "andare al cinema con lui" = “to go to the cinema with him.” "Al" is the contraction of "a + il" (to + the). In Italian, the subject pronoun is often omitted when it’s clear from the verb (e.g., "Va spesso..." = “(He/She) often goes...” ).
target_language_example: Domani vado al cinema con lui.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going to the cinema with him.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say something is chocolate-flavored or contains chocolate: "latte al cioccolato" (chocolate milk), "torta al cioccolato" (chocolate cake). It’s a common pattern: "al" + ingredient/flavor (e.g., "al limone" = lemon).
target_language_example: Vorrei un gelato al cioccolato, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a chocolate ice cream, please.

meaning: on/at the neck; around the neck.
additional_notes: Used to say where something is or where an injury/attack happens (e.g., "Ho male al collo" = "My neck hurts"). With objects it often means "hanging around the neck" (e.g., a rifle, a camera). You may also see it in the expression "avere la corda al collo" (literally "to have the rope around your neck"), meaning to be in a desperate situation with no way out.
target_language_example: Mi sono messo la sciarpa al collo perché faceva freddo.
native_language_example: I put my scarf around my neck because it was cold.

meaning: at the concert; to the concert.
additional_notes: "Al" = "a" + "il" and is used with masculine singular places/events. With verbs of being/doing something in a place, it often means "at the concert" (e.g., "Sono al concerto"). With verbs of going, it often means "to the concert" (e.g., "Vado al concerto").
target_language_example: Ci vediamo al concerto stasera.
native_language_example: See you at the concert tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is going to a concert happening tonight. Often appears with verbs like “andare” (to go): “Vai al concerto stasera?” “Al” = “a + il” (to the), and “stasera” = “this evening/tonight.”
target_language_example: Io vado al concerto stasera con alcuni amici.
native_language_example: I'm going to the concert tonight with some friends.

meaning: on the contrary; the other way around; inside out/backwards.
additional_notes: Used in a few common ways: (1) as a connector meaning “on the contrary” to correct or oppose what was just said: “..., al contrario.” (2) with “di” to mean “unlike / in contrast to”: “al contrario di …”. (3) to describe something reversed, backwards, or inside out (especially clothing): “il maglione al contrario”.
target_language_example: Pensavo che fosse chiuso; al contrario, è aperto.
native_language_example: I thought it was closed; on the contrary, it’s open.

meaning: aware of; informed about (up to date on).
additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs like essere/tenere/mettere al corrente (di) = “to be/keep/bring someone informed (about).” Also venire al corrente (di) = “to find out / come to know (about).” Often followed by di + noun/infinitive, or ne (meaning “about it/of it”).
target_language_example: Tienimi al corrente delle novità, per favore.
native_language_example: Keep me informed about the news/updates, please.

meaning: (Pasta) cooked so it’s still firm to the bite; “to the tooth.”
additional_notes: Used mainly when talking about how pasta or rice is cooked. It means not too soft/overcooked, with a slight firmness in the center. Common in restaurants and on cooking instructions (e.g., cuocere la pasta al dente).
target_language_example: Vorrei la pasta al dente, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like the pasta al dente (still firm), please.

additional_notes: Used with "di" to specify what something is beyond: "al di là del fiume" (across the river), "al di là della vostra comprensione" (beyond your understanding). It can be literal (a physical other side) or figurative (beyond reason/ability/strength): "al di là della ragione", "al di là delle mie forze". Often appears with nouns and articles (del/degli/della/delle).
target_language_example: Non posso aiutarti: è al di là delle mie competenze.
native_language_example: I can't help you: it's beyond my skills.

meaning: above; over; higher than (often: “more important than”).
additional_notes: Used with di + noun/pronoun: al di sopra di… = “above/over…”. Can be literal (higher than a level/rate) or figurative (beyond/above suspicion; more important than everything). Common fixed phrases: al di sopra di ogni sospetto (“above all suspicion”), al di sopra di tutto (“above everything”).
target_language_example: Per me, la famiglia è al di sopra di tutto.
native_language_example: For me, family is above everything.

additional_notes: Strong exclamation used to show anger, frustration, or to reject someone/something (“Al diavolo questa barba!” = “To hell with this beard!”). With a verb it becomes an insult/command: “Vacci tu al diavolo” (informal “you go to hell”), “Vada al diavolo” (formal “go to hell”). Can also be used on its own as “Al diavolo!” = “Damn it!/To hell with it!”
target_language_example: Al diavolo i problemi, stasera voglio rilassarmi.
native_language_example: To hell with the problems—tonight I want to relax.

meaning: in order to; for the purpose of.
additional_notes: Formal phrase used to introduce a purpose, usually followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., "al fine di evitare..."). Common in writing, instructions, and bureaucratic/legal contexts. In everyday speech, Italians often use "per" or "per (non)" instead.
target_language_example: Al fine di evitare ritardi, arriva con dieci minuti di anticipo.
native_language_example: In order to avoid delays, arrive ten minutes early.

additional_notes: Used to talk about going to the river or being at the river. "Al" is the contraction of "a + il" and often means "to the" (with movement verbs like "andare") or "at the" (with location).
target_language_example: Domani andiamo al fiume a fare un picnic.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going to the river to have a picnic.

additional_notes: Used mainly with cooking to say something is cooked in the oven (not boiled or fried). Common in food names/menus: "pasta al forno" (baked pasta), "patate al forno" (oven-baked potatoes). With verbs: "cuocere/cucinare al forno" = to bake (cook in the oven).
target_language_example: Vorrei le verdure al forno, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like the baked vegetables, please.

meaning: per day; a day (in frequency/rate expressions).
additional_notes: Used to say how much something happens or changes each day (a rate or frequency): amounts earned/spent, time gained/lost, hours studied, doses taken, flights offered, etc. Often follows a number: “due ore al giorno” (two hours a day), “una volta al giorno” (once a day).
target_language_example: Bevo almeno un litro d’acqua al giorno.
native_language_example: I drink at least one liter of water a day.

meaning: at the lake; to the lake.
additional_notes: "Al" = "a" + "il" (to/at the). Use it with "lago" when you mean a location (meeting/parking/fishing at the lake) or destination (going to the lake). For "near the lake" you’ll often see "vicino al lago".
target_language_example: Domani andiamo al lago e facciamo un picnic.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going to the lake and having a picnic.

meaning: at work; to work (going/being at work).
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like essere/andare/tornare: “Sono al lavoro” (I’m at work), “Vado al lavoro” (I’m going to work). It can also mean “on the job / working” in a broader sense (e.g., “mettersi al lavoro” = to get to work). In “interessata al lavoro,” it refers to “the job/work” as an opportunity or position.
target_language_example: Sono al lavoro fino alle sei.
native_language_example: I’m at work until six.

meaning: at the limit; at my/its breaking point.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something has reached (or is very close to) the maximum they can handle—physically, emotionally, or in performance (e.g., a car/tires pushed to the limit). In other contexts, it can also mean “if necessary / at worst” (e.g., “Al limite, ci andiamo domani” = “If necessary, we’ll go tomorrow”).
target_language_example: Oggi sono al limite: ho lavorato tutto il giorno.
native_language_example: Today I'm at my breaking point: I've worked all day.

meaning: to the seaside; at the sea.
additional_notes: Common with verbs of going or being somewhere. Use it when you mean the sea/coast as a place to go or spend time: andare al mare (go to the beach/seaside), essere/vivere vicino al mare (be/live near the sea). Can also be used more literally as “at sea” in comparisons (e.g., a lake that looks like the sea).
target_language_example: Domenica andiamo al mare se fa bel tempo.
native_language_example: On Sunday we're going to the seaside if the weather is nice.

meaning: at most; at the most / to the fullest (maximum).
additional_notes: Most often means an upper limit: “no more than” (Al massimo, una decina; Una dozzina al massimo). It can also mean “at your best / at full strength” when followed by a noun phrase like “al massimo delle mie/ tue forze” (“to the fullest of my/your strength”) or “al massimo della mia innocenza” (“at the height of my innocence”). In encouragement, “Dai, al massimo!” means “Come on, give it your all!”
target_language_example: Possiamo aspettare al massimo dieci minuti, poi andiamo.
native_language_example: We can wait at most ten minutes, then we’ll go.

meaning: in the morning; in the mornings.
additional_notes: Used to say when something happens during the morning. It can mean a specific morning (e.g., today) or mornings in general, depending on context. Similar to "di mattina".
target_language_example: Al mattino bevo sempre un caffè.
native_language_example: In the morning I always drink a coffee.

meaning: as best as possible; at one’s best.
additional_notes: Used to say you’ll do something in the best possible way (often: “al meglio delle mie/tue/sue capacità” = “to the best of my/your/his abilities”). With “essere (non) al meglio” it means to be (not) in top form / not feeling your best.
target_language_example: Oggi non sono al meglio, ma farò del mio meglio.
native_language_example: Today I’m not at my best, but I’ll do my best.

meaning: to the market; at the market.
additional_notes: "Al" = "a" + "il" (to/at the). Use it with places you go to or are located at: "vado al mercato" (I’m going to the market), "sono al mercato" (I’m at the market). Often refers to an open-air food market, but can also mean a general marketplace.
target_language_example: Siamo al mercato a comprare frutta e verdura.
native_language_example: We’re at the market buying fruit and vegetables.

meaning: on the black market (illegally, outside official channels).
additional_notes: Used to say something is bought/sold illegally or unofficially, often to avoid taxes or because it’s restricted. Common with verbs like comprare/vendere/trovare: “comprare al mercato nero”.
target_language_example: Non comprare biglietti al mercato nero.
native_language_example: Don’t buy tickets on the black market.

additional_notes: Used with numbers or frequency expressions to say how often something happens or how much is earned/paid each month (e.g., "due/tre volte al mese", "X euro al mese"). Common in contexts like salary, rent, subscriptions, and habits.
target_language_example: Pago 700 euro al mese di affitto.
native_language_example: I pay 700 euros a month in rent.

meaning: 'to my' / 'at my' (before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Contraction of "a" + "il mio". Used with verbs that take the preposition "a" (e.g., aggiungere qualcosa al mio cibo = add something to my food). It’s followed by a masculine singular noun (al mio cappello, al mio compleanno). For feminine singular, use "alla mia"; for plural, "ai miei" (m.) / "alle mie" (f.).
target_language_example: Devo parlare al mio insegnante.
native_language_example: I have to talk to my teacher.

additional_notes: Contraction of "a" + "il" = "al". Used when "amico" is an indirect object after verbs like "piacere" (Lei piace al mio amico = My friend likes her) or with expressions like "capitare" (È capitato al mio amico = It happened to my friend). Also used in phrases like "sparare a" (to shoot at) and with possession like "appartenere a" (belongs to). For a female friend: "alla mia amica".
target_language_example: Ho dato le chiavi al mio amico.
native_language_example: I gave the keys to my friend.

additional_notes: “Al” = “a” + “il” and often means “to” (sometimes “at/on”) with an indirect object. Use it with verbs like piacere (Piace al mio cane = My dog likes it) and with actions directed toward someone/something (Ha tirato un sasso al mio cane? = threw a stone at my dog).
target_language_example: Ho comprato un gioco al mio cane.
native_language_example: I bought a toy for my dog.

additional_notes: Means “to/at my plan” and is used after verbs/adjectives that take the preposition “a” (e.g., essere favorevole/contrario a, rinunciare a). It’s “a + il” → “al”, plus “mio” (my) + “piano” (plan). In some contexts, “piano” can also mean “floor/level” (e.g., al mio piano = on my floor), but in these examples it clearly means “plan.”
target_language_example: Sono favorevole al mio piano, ma devo spiegartelo meglio.
native_language_example: I’m in favor of my plan, but I have to explain it to you better.

meaning: in my place; instead of me.
additional_notes: Used to say someone takes your place or does something for you ("Andrai al mio posto?" = will you go instead of me?). It can also mean being in the same situation as you, often with the subjunctive/conditional: "Se fossi al mio posto..." = if you were in my place. It can also be literal for returning to your seat/spot: "Sono tornato al mio posto."
target_language_example: Puoi parlare tu al mio posto, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you speak in my place (instead of me), please?

meaning: at the moment; currently; for now.
additional_notes: Used to say something is true right now (and may change later). Common in updates/status reports: “al momento non c’è…”, “al momento va bene così”. Often interchangeable with “per ora” (for now).
target_language_example: Al momento non ho tempo, ti richiamo più tardi.
native_language_example: At the moment I don’t have time; I’ll call you back later.

meaning: at the right time; just in time.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens at the perfect time for a situation. Very common with verbs like arrivare (“to arrive”) and with the phrase “nel posto giusto, al momento giusto” (“in the right place at the right time”). “Proprio al momento giusto” adds emphasis (“exactly/just at the right time”).
target_language_example: Se mi chiami al momento giusto, posso passarti a prendere.
native_language_example: If you call me at the right time, I can pick you up.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the world in general (people/things “in the world”) or for emphasis in phrases like "che abbia al mondo" (= “that I have in the whole world”). Also appears in fixed expressions like "in cima al mondo" (“on top of the world”), where "al mondo" is part of the idiom.
target_language_example: È la cosa più bella al mondo.
native_language_example: It’s the most beautiful thing in the world.

meaning: to the shop/store; at the shop/store.
additional_notes: "Al" = "a" + "il" (to/at the). With movement verbs like "andare" it usually means "to the shop" (destination). With actions done there (e.g., buying), it often means "at the shop" (location).
target_language_example: Devo andare al negozio a comprare il pane.
native_language_example: I have to go to the store to buy bread.

additional_notes: It’s the contraction of **a + il nostro**. Use it before a **masculine singular noun**: *al nostro problema/progetto/club*. The exact meaning depends on context: **to our** (destination/recipient: *partecipare al nostro progetto*), **at our** (location/time: *al nostro risveglio*), or in transitions like *al nostro prossimo argomento* (“to our next topic”). Other forms: **alla nostra** (fem. sing.), **ai nostri** (masc. plural), **alle nostre** (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Benvenuti al nostro ristorante!
native_language_example: Welcome to our restaurant!

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "unirsi" (to join) or "unire" (to add/attach) to indicate joining/being added to your group. "al" = "a" (to) + "il" (the); "nostro" changes to match the noun (here: "gruppo" is masculine singular).
target_language_example: Vuoi unirti al nostro gruppo?
native_language_example: Do you want to join our group?

meaning: at the park / to the park.
additional_notes: `Al` = `a` + `il` (“to/at the”). With motion verbs (e.g., *andare*) it often means “to the park”; with staying/meeting verbs (e.g., *incontrare*, *essere*) it often means “at the park.”
target_language_example: Ci vediamo al parco alle cinque.
native_language_example: See you at the park at five.

additional_notes: Used to say you are at the park (al parco) together with another person (con + name/pronoun). "Al" = "a" + "il" (to/at the). Often used with verbs like andare (to go) or essere/vedere (to be/see).
target_language_example: Domani vado al parco con i miei amici.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going to the park with my friends.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like “stare” or “andare”: “stare/andare al passo” = to keep up, to match the pace. Common expression: “stare al passo coi/con i tempi” = to keep up with the times (stay up to date). Can also be used as an instruction: “Stai/State al passo!” = “Keep up!”
target_language_example: Devo studiare di più per stare al passo con la classe.
native_language_example: I have to study more to keep up with the class.

meaning: for the worst; for the worst-case scenario.
additional_notes: Used almost always after verbs like essere pronto/preparato (“to be ready/prepared”), meaning you should expect that the worst might happen. Often appears in the phrase "prepararsi al peggio" (“prepare for the worst”).
target_language_example: Porta un ombrello: prepariamoci al peggio.
native_language_example: Bring an umbrella: let’s prepare for the worst.

additional_notes: “Al” = a + il (“to the / at the”). With **piano** it most commonly means a building **floor/level**: *Sono arrivato al piano sbagliato* (“I arrived on the wrong floor”). But **piano** can also mean **plan**, especially with verbs like *pensare* / *parlare* / *dire* + *a*: *Stavo pensando al piano* (“I was thinking about the plan”). Usually the context makes it clear which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: L’ufficio è al secondo piano.
native_language_example: The office is on the second floor.

al piano che ha presentato alla riunione

target_language_multi_word_term: al piano che ha presentato alla riunione
meaning: "to/for the plan that he/she presented at the meeting."
additional_notes: "Al" = "a" + "il" (to/at the). "Il piano" means "the plan." "Che ha presentato" is a relative clause meaning "that (he/she) presented." "Alla riunione" = "a" + "la" (at the meeting). Often used after phrases like "essere favorevole/contrario a" (to be in favor of/against).
target_language_example: Siete favorevoli al piano che ha presentato alla riunione?
native_language_example: Are you in favor of the plan that he presented at the meeting?

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is on the upper floor in a building. With verbs of movement it often means “upstairs” (going up), and with “essere” it often means “upstairs” (located there).
target_language_example: Il bagno è al piano di sopra.
native_language_example: The bathroom is upstairs.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone/something is on a lower floor inside a building. Often answers “Where?” (Dov’è?) and can be used with verbs like essere (to be), vivere (to live), andare/venire (to go/come). Related phrase: al piano di sopra = upstairs/on the floor above.
target_language_example: Il bagno è al piano di sotto.
native_language_example: The bathroom is downstairs.

meaning: as soon as possible; as quickly as you can.
additional_notes: Used to express urgency about doing something quickly or without delay. Often follows the verb (e.g., "rispondere/arrivare/tornare al più presto") or is used alone as a short answer meaning “ASAP.” Slightly more formal than "il prima possibile," but both are common.
target_language_example: Mi mandi i documenti al più presto, per favore.
native_language_example: Please send me the documents as soon as possible.

meaning: instead of; in someone’s place (in their situation).
additional_notes: Used mainly in two patterns: (1) **al posto di + noun/pronoun** = “instead of” (Al posto del latte = instead of milk). (2) **al posto mio/tuo/suo…** = “in my/your/his… place,” meaning “if I were you / in your situation.” Often used with articles (al posto del/dello/della/dei/degli/delle).
target_language_example: Prendo un tè al posto del caffè; al posto tuo, andrei a casa.
native_language_example: I’ll have tea instead of coffee; if I were you, I’d go home.

meaning: instead of; in place of; taking someone/something’s place.
additional_notes: Used with a noun or pronoun to say that one person/thing replaces another: "Sono andato al posto di mio padre" = “I went in my father’s place.” With places/positions it can mean “to/at the position of”: "al posto di comando" = “at/to the command post.”
target_language_example: Puoi venire tu al posto di Marco oggi?
native_language_example: Can you come in Marco’s place today?

meaning: "to the first" / "on the first (time/round)"; also "in first place" (with *posto*).
additional_notes: Common patterns: **al primo che + verb** = “to the first person who …” (e.g., *al primo che arriva*). With nouns like **giro** it means “on the first round/lap/try” (*al primo giro*). With **posto** it forms **al primo posto** = “in first place / first priority”.
target_language_example: Dai questo premio al primo che finisce la gara.
native_language_example: Give this prize to the first person who finishes the race.

meaning: on the first floor; to the first floor.
additional_notes: Used to say where something is located ("on the first floor") or where you’re going ("to the first floor"), often in buildings, elevators, hotels, etc. In Italy, "primo piano" is typically the floor above the ground floor ("piano terra").
target_language_example: L’ufficio è al primo piano, prenda l’ascensore.
native_language_example: The office is on the first floor; take the elevator.

meaning: to the point; to the main issue (also: to the point that).
additional_notes: Common in set phrases like "arrivare al punto" / "venire al punto" / "andare dritto al punto" = "to get to the point" (stop talking around it and address the main issue). With "al punto che" it can mean "to the point that" to introduce a result or consequence: "...al punto che non dormivo" = "...to the point that I wasn’t sleeping."
target_language_example: Ok, andiamo al punto: quanto costa?
native_language_example: OK, let’s get to the point: how much does it cost?

meaning: in a safe place; under shelter (out of danger).
additional_notes: Often used with "mettere" (to put) or "mettersi" (to get) + "al riparo": "Mettete i camion al riparo" = put the trucks somewhere protected (e.g., from weather or damage); "Mettetevi al riparo!" = get to safety / take cover. Can refer to protection from danger (explosion, gunfire, etc.) or from the elements (rain, wind).
target_language_example: Quando ha iniziato a grandinare, ci siamo messi al riparo sotto un portico.
native_language_example: When it started hailing, we took shelter under a porch.

meaning: at the restaurant; to the restaurant.
additional_notes: Used to say where you are/where something happens ("at the restaurant") or where you are going ("to the restaurant") depending on the verb and context. "Al" = "a" + "il" (to/at + the).
target_language_example: Stasera andiamo al ristorante con i miei amici.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re going to the restaurant with my friends.

meaning: (of meat) rare; cooked so it’s still very red inside.
additional_notes: Used mainly when ordering or describing how meat (especially steak) is cooked. Often appears after the food: “bistecca/carne al sangue”. You may also see it in combinations like “media-al sangue” (medium-rare).
target_language_example: Per favore, una bistecca al sangue.
native_language_example: A rare steak, please.

meaning: safe; in a safe place; out of danger.
additional_notes: Used with "essere" to say someone is safe ("Siamo al sicuro?"). Also common with "tenere" to mean "to keep (someone/something) safe" ("tenere al sicuro"). Refers to being protected or not in danger, physically or emotionally.
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: qui sei al sicuro.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you’re safe here.

additional_notes: Used to say you are safe in this place. Very common with the verb "sentirsi" ("mi sento al sicuro qui" = "I feel safe here"). You can add intensifiers like "più" (safer), "molto" (very), or "piuttosto" (quite).
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: siamo al sicuro qui.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we’re safe here.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is exposed to direct sunlight (e.g., lying/sitting outside, leaving something where the sun hits it). In scientific/astronomy contexts it can also mean literally “around the Sun” (il sole = the Sun).
target_language_example: Non lasciare la crema al sole.
native_language_example: Don’t leave the cream in the sun.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens in the typical/normal way, often with a tone of routine or mild annoyance. Common with verbs like essere, fare, arrivare, and expressions like “come al solito” (“as usual”).
target_language_example: Come al solito, sei in ritardo.
native_language_example: As usual, you're late.

additional_notes: Contraction of "a + il suo". It’s used before a masculine singular noun ("al suo studio", "al suo sogno"). Italian possessives agree with the thing owned (studio/sogno), not with the owner. For feminine singular you’ll see "alla sua"; for plural "ai suoi" (masc.) / "alle sue" (fem.).
target_language_example: Ha parlato al suo medico ieri.
native_language_example: He/she talked to his/her doctor yesterday.

additional_notes: “Al” = “a + il” (“to the”). “Suo” means “his/her/its” and agrees with the noun (cane = masculine singular), not with the owner. So “al suo cane” can mean “to his dog” or “to her dog,” depending on context. Common after verbs like dare (to give), insegnare (to teach), lanciare (to throw).
target_language_example: Ha dato un biscotto al suo cane.
native_language_example: He/She gave a biscuit to his/her dog.

additional_notes: Literally "to the his/her teacher" (a + il = al). Use it after verbs like chiedere (to ask) and prestare attenzione (to pay attention): chiedere qualcosa al suo insegnante = to ask his/her teacher something. "Suo" agrees with what is owned (insegnante), not with the owner; in these examples it can mean either "his" or "her" depending on context.
target_language_example: Puoi chiedere al suo insegnante se c’è un compito per domani?
native_language_example: Can you ask his/her teacher if there’s homework for tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to say someone is/was attending a wedding. "al" = "a" + "il" (to/at the), and "suo" means "his" or "her" depending on context. You can also say "al mio matrimonio" (at my wedding), "al tuo matrimonio" (at your wedding), etc.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo al suo matrimonio sabato.
native_language_example: See you at his/her wedding on Saturday.

meaning: in his/her place; instead of him/her.
additional_notes: Used to talk about what you would do if you were someone else (“If you were in his/her shoes…”). It can also be a polite instruction meaning “go back to your seat/place.” Changes with the person: al mio posto (in my place), al tuo posto (in your place), al loro posto (in their place).
target_language_example: Al tuo posto, chiamerei subito il medico.
native_language_example: If I were you, I’d call the doctor right away.

meaning: at the supermarket; to the supermarket.
additional_notes: "Al" = "a" + "il". With verbs of motion (andare, venire, tornare) it often means "to the supermarket" (Andiamo al supermercato). With verbs describing location or actions happening there (essere, comprare, lavorare), it means "at the supermarket" (Sono/Compro al supermercato). You can add an adjective or specify which one: "al supermercato asiatico", "al supermercato dove vado".
target_language_example: Devo andare al supermercato dopo il lavoro.
native_language_example: I have to go to the supermarket after work.

meaning: at the table; (with motion) to the table.
additional_notes: "Al" = "a" + "il". Used to say someone/something is positioned at a table (often sitting and eating/working): "Sono seduto al tavolo." With verbs of movement like "tornare/andare", it can mean "to the table": "Torna al tavolo." Often interchangeable with "al tavolo" vs "a tavola" ("a tavola" focuses more on mealtime: "Siamo a tavola").
target_language_example: Puoi venire al tavolo? La cena è pronta.
native_language_example: Can you come to the table? Dinner is ready.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is speaking using the telephone or that something happened via a phone call. Often with verbs like parlare (to speak), rispondere (to answer), stare/essere (to be), passare tempo (to spend time).
target_language_example: Scusa, ero al telefono con mia madre.
native_language_example: Sorry, I was on the phone with my mom.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is in a building (rooms, offices, etc.). "al" = "a + il" and can mean "on the" (location) or "to the" (direction) depending on the verb: "La mia camera è al terzo piano" (is on), "Vada al terzo piano" (go to). Note: in Italy, the ground floor is often "piano terra"; "primo piano" is typically one level above the ground floor.
target_language_example: L’ufficio del dottore è al terzo piano.
native_language_example: The doctor’s office is on the third floor.

meaning: "to your" / "at your" / "for your" (to a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Contraction of "a + il tuo". It’s used before a masculine singular noun (e.g., al tuo lavoro = to/for your job; al tuo giudizio = to your judgment). The exact English preposition depends on the verb or context (pensare a = think about; tornare a = return to; dovuto a = due to). Not used before vowel sounds: use "al tuo" vs. "al tuo amico"? → actually "al tuo amico" is fine because "amico" starts with a vowel but doesn't require "all'"; "all'" is used with the article "l'" (e.g., "all'amico" / "al tuo amico").
target_language_example: Puoi rispondere al tuo insegnante domani.
native_language_example: You can reply to your teacher tomorrow.

meaning: in your place; if I were you.
additional_notes: Used either literally (someone replaces you in a role/seat/job: “io al tuo posto”) or figuratively to give advice/opinion: “Al tuo posto, farei…” (= If I were you, I’d…). In commands it can mean “stay in your place / stay in your lane”: “Stai al tuo posto.”
target_language_example: Al tuo posto, parlerei con il capo domani.
native_language_example: If I were you, I’d talk to the boss tomorrow.

additional_notes: Common idiom used with “essere” (e.g., “sono al verde”) to say you have no money left. It’s fairly informal. Note: in other contexts, “al verde” can also literally mean “to green” (e.g., a traffic light changing “dal rosso al verde”).
target_language_example: Dopo aver pagato l'affitto, sono al verde.
native_language_example: After paying the rent, I'm broke.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is driving (in control of the car). Common in warnings and rules: “Non bere al volante” = “Don’t drink and drive.” You can also use it to comment on someone’s driving ability: “Sei bravo/pessimo al volante.”
target_language_example: Non usare il telefono al volante.
native_language_example: Don’t use your phone while driving.

meaning: quickly; on the fly; in a flash.
additional_notes: Used to say something is done very fast or with no preparation. Common with verbs like fare/prendere/andare/salire/saltare “al volo” (= quickly, at the last second). In “furti al volo” it means quick grab-and-run thefts (snatch theft). In “prendere la palla al volo” it can mean literally “catch the ball in mid-air,” and also figuratively “pick up an opportunity/idea immediately.”
target_language_example: Te lo spiego al volo e poi andiamo.
native_language_example: I’ll explain it to you quickly and then we’ll go.

meaning: "to your" / "at your" (addressing more than one person, or formal "your").
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: **al vostro + noun** (e.g., *al vostro capo* = to your boss). It’s made of **a + il = al** plus **vostro**. The exact meaning can be “to your” or “at your” depending on the verb/context. Related forms: **alla vostra** (feminine singular), **ai vostri** (masculine plural), **alle vostre** (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Posso parlare al vostro medico?
native_language_example: Can I speak to your doctor?

additional_notes: Used for the decorated tree people put up during Christmas. With an indefinite article it’s “un albero di Natale”; with a possessive it’s “il mio/suo albero di Natale”.
target_language_example: Quest'anno compriamo un albero di Natale vero.
native_language_example: This year we’re buying a real Christmas tree.

meaning: “any place to” (in negative sentences: “no place to”).
additional_notes: Used with a following infinitive (e.g., dormire, nascondersi) to mean “a place where/in which to do something.” It’s very common in negative phrases like “non ho alcun posto in cui…” = “I don’t have anywhere to…”. Similar alternatives: “nessun posto dove…”, “non ho un posto dove…”.
target_language_example: Non abbiamo alcun posto in cui sederci.
native_language_example: We don’t have anywhere to sit.

additional_notes: Used almost always in negative statements (often with “non”) to say something is meaningless or doesn’t make sense: “non ha alcun senso” = “it makes no sense / there’s no point.” “Alcun” is like “any” and is common in negatives; in positive sentences you usually use “qualche” instead.
target_language_example: Questa regola non ha alcun senso.
native_language_example: This rule makes no sense.

additional_notes: Plural phrase using the feminine plural of “alcuno/a” + “cose.” Used when you refer to an unspecified number of things. Often followed by “di” + noun (“alcune cose della vita” = “some things in life”) or by a relative clause (“alcune cose che posso fare…” = “some things I can do…”).
target_language_example: Vorrei dirti alcune cose importanti.
native_language_example: I’d like to tell you some important things.

additional_notes: Used when you mean an unspecified number of questions (more than one). Often appears with verbs like fare (to ask) or rispondere a (to answer): fare alcune domande = to ask some questions; rispondere ad alcune domande = to answer some questions.
target_language_example: Vorrei fare alcune domande prima di iniziare.
native_language_example: I’d like to ask a few questions before we start.

meaning: some people (a certain number, not all).
additional_notes: Used to talk generally about an unspecified group of people. Often followed by a verb in the plural (e.g., credono, vogliono). You can change gender/number: "alcuni" (some, masculine/mixed) + "persone" (people) stays feminine plural; e.g., "alcune persone" is always feminine because "persone" is feminine.
target_language_example: Alcune persone preferiscono lavorare da sole.
native_language_example: Some people prefer to work alone.

meaning: at the library; to the library.
additional_notes: "Alla" = "a" + "la" (to/at + the). Use it with verbs of going/moving (andare, tornare) to mean "to the library" and with location/stay verbs (essere, lavorare, conoscere qualcuno) to mean "at the library."
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alla biblioteca domani pomeriggio.
native_language_example: See you at the library tomorrow afternoon.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of going or coming (andare/venire) to mean “to the party,” and with verbs describing what happens there (divertirsi, ballare, parlare) to mean “at the party.” It’s the contraction of a + la (to/at + the) + festa.
target_language_example: Vieni alla festa sabato sera?
native_language_example: Are you coming to the party on Saturday night?

meaning: "to my question" / "to my request" (i.e., as a reply to what I asked).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like "rispondere" (to answer): "rispondere alla mia domanda" = "to answer my question." "Alla" is the combination of "a" + "la" and here means "to" (to the question). You can change "mia" to match who asked: "alla tua domanda" (to your question), "alla sua domanda" (to his/her question).
target_language_example: Puoi rispondere alla mia domanda, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you answer my question, please?

meaning: to the mosque; at the mosque.
additional_notes: Means “a + la moschea” (to/at the mosque). With movement verbs like andare/portare it usually means “to the mosque” (going/taking someone there). With essere/stare it can mean “at the mosque” (being there): “Sono alla moschea.”
target_language_example: Domani vado alla moschea con un amico.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going to the mosque with a friend.

additional_notes: Contraction of "a" + "la" + "sua". Used before a feminine singular noun (e.g., "alla sua famiglia" = to his/her family, "alla sua chiamata" = to his/her call). "Sua" can mean either "his" or "her"—the context tells you which. With masculine singular you’d use "al suo"; with feminine plural "alle sue"; with masculine plural "ai suoi".
target_language_example: Ho risposto alla sua email subito.
native_language_example: I replied to his/her email right away.

additional_notes: Means “to the party” (motion: inviting/going) or “at the party” (location: being/having fun), depending on the verb and context. The structure is a + la = alla (“to/at the”), sua = “his/her” (possessive), festa = “party.” Often the gender of the owner is understood from context; if needed you can clarify with “la sua festa” (her) vs “la sua festa” (his) still looks the same, or use a name: “alla festa di Maria.”
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alla sua festa sabato sera.
native_language_example: See you at his/her party Saturday night.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is at their desk (often at work) or does something there. "alla" = "a" + "la" (at the). "sua" agrees with the desk (scrivania, feminine), and can change depending on the person: alla mia scrivania (at my desk), alla tua scrivania (at your desk), alla loro scrivania (at their desk). Sometimes you may also hear "alla scrivania" without the possessive if it’s clear whose desk it is.
target_language_example: Sono alla sua scrivania e sto finendo il rapporto.
native_language_example: I'm at his/her desk and I'm finishing the report.

meaning: to the library; at the library.
additional_notes: "Alla" = "a" + "la" (to/at the). Use it with verbs of going/returning (and sometimes access) to indicate destination ("to the library") or location ("at the library"), depending on context.
target_language_example: Domani vado alla biblioteca per studiare.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going to the library to study.

additional_notes: A place phrase. "alla" = "a" + "la" and can mean "to the" (movement: invitate/i... alla...) or "at the" (location: si sono incontrati... alla...). "della" = "di" + "la" meaning "of the" (the library belonging to the mosque).
target_language_example: Domani ci vediamo alla biblioteca della moschea alle cinque.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’ll meet at the mosque’s library at five.

additional_notes: Contraction of "a + la". Commonly used with verbs like "rispondere" (to answer): "rispondere alla domanda" = "to answer the question". Also used to refer to a specific question already mentioned (e.g., on a form, website, or in a conversation).
target_language_example: Puoi rispondere alla domanda, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you answer the question, please?

additional_notes: As an interjection, “Alla faccia!” expresses surprise, admiration, or sometimes sarcasm (tone and context matter). In other contexts it can be literal, meaning something happened or was done to someone’s face: “Che ti è successo alla faccia?” = “What happened to your face?” You may also hear “Alla faccia sua!” as an exclamation directed at someone (often meaning “Yeah, right—look at him/her!” or “Well, would you look at that!” depending on tone).
target_language_example: Alla faccia, che bella macchina!
native_language_example: Wow, what a nice car!

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens or where someone is. It’s the combination of "a" + "la" (= "alla") + "festa" (party). Common with verbs like "essere" (to be), "vedersi" (to see each other/meet), "bere" (to drink), and "partecipare" (to participate/attend).
target_language_example: Ci incontriamo alla festa alle nove.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at the party at nine.

additional_notes: Used with events/holidays to say you’re going to or you are at a specific party. It combines: a + la = alla (“to the/at the”) + festa (“party”) + di (“of/for”). In English you usually translate it as “the … party” rather than literally “the party of …”.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alla festa di compleanno di Marco.
native_language_example: See you at Marco’s birthday party.

meaning: in the end; eventually; at the end (of).
additional_notes: Often used to talk about the final outcome after some time or uncertainty: "Alla fine ci sei riuscito!" = "In the end you managed it!". With "di" it can mean a literal end point in time or a sequence: "alla fine di maggio" = "at the end of May". In questions it can mean "so, in the end...?" (asking what finally happened).
target_language_example: Alla fine abbiamo deciso di restare a casa.
native_language_example: In the end we decided to stay home.

additional_notes: Used to indicate the end point of a time period or event (alla fine del mese/discorso) or the end of a place/route (alla fine del corridoio). It’s followed by a masculine singular noun introduced by “del” (= di + il). For feminine singular you use “alla fine della…”, and for plural “alla fine dei/degli/delle…”.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alla fine del corso.
native_language_example: See you at the end of the course.

meaning: at the ends of the earth; in a very remote place.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a place is extremely far away or hard to reach (often exaggerating). It can be literal (a very remote location) or figurative (“in the middle of nowhere”). Often used with verbs like andare/essere (to go/be).
target_language_example: Il ristorante è buonissimo, ma è proprio alla fine del mondo.
native_language_example: The restaurant is amazing, but it’s really in the middle of nowhere.

additional_notes: Used to say what happens when something finishes. It’s followed by a feminine singular noun (la giornata, la discussione, la riunione). With masculine nouns you use "alla fine del" (e.g., alla fine del film).
target_language_example: Alla fine della lezione facciamo un ripasso veloce.
native_language_example: At the end of the lesson we do a quick review.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of position or movement: “essere/stare alla finestra” = to be at the window; “andare/correre alla finestra” = to go to the window. In requests you’ll often see “vicino alla finestra” (“near the window”).
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere un tavolo vicino alla finestra?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have a table near the window?

additional_notes: Formed by **a + la = alla** plus **gente** (“people”). Used to show who something is directed to (an indirect object): *parlare alla gente* (“to talk to people”), *insegnare ... alla gente* (“to teach ... to people”). With words like **davanti**, it can mean “in front of people” (*davanti alla gente*).
target_language_example: Non dire queste cose alla gente.
native_language_example: Don’t say these things to people.

meaning: really well; great; in a big way.
additional_notes: Used to say something is going very well or will turn out great (often like “great!” / “awesome!”). It can also mean doing something on a grand scale or making a strong, impressive exit (e.g., “leave in style”). Common in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: L’esame è andato alla grande!
native_language_example: The exam went really well!

meaning: literally; word for word; exactly (to the letter).
additional_notes: Used when something is understood in the most literal sense or followed very precisely: *prendere alla lettera* (to take literally), *seguire/rispettare alla lettera* (to follow exactly). In some contexts *alla lettera* can also simply mean “to the letter” in the non-idiomatic sense (e.g., *rispondere alla lettera* = “to reply to the letter”).
target_language_example: Segui le istruzioni alla lettera.
native_language_example: Follow the instructions exactly.

meaning: “to my / at my” (used with a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Contraction of “a + la” (= “to/at the”) + “mia” (= “my”). You’ll see it before feminine singular nouns: alla mia festa (to/at my party), alla mia casa (to my house). In phrases like “alla mia portata” it means “within my reach/ability.”
target_language_example: Stasera puoi venire alla mia casa?
native_language_example: Can you come to my house tonight?

additional_notes: Used mainly after verbs like rispondere (to answer): rispondere alla mia domanda = “to answer my question.” The preposition “a” + “la” becomes “alla.” “Domanda” is usually a question (not “demand” in the English sense).
target_language_example: Puoi rispondere alla mia domanda, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you answer my question, please?

additional_notes: Used to describe people, clothes, objects, or ideas that follow current trends. Often with verbs like essere (è alla moda), tornare (tornare alla moda = to come back into fashion), or restare (restare alla moda = to stay fashionable). Can also be used sarcastically to criticize something as “trendy.”
target_language_example: Quel ristorante è molto alla moda, ma è caro.
native_language_example: That restaurant is very fashionable, but it’s expensive.

additional_notes: Usually means someone is led/sent toward dying (often figuratively or dramatically): *condurre alla morte* “to lead to death,” *mandare alla morte* “to send to their death.” With *pensare a*, it can also mean “to think about death” (*pensare alla morte*).
target_language_example: Non voglio mandarti alla morte per una causa persa.
native_language_example: I don’t want to send you to your death for a lost cause.

meaning: to the mosque; at the mosque.
additional_notes: "Alla" = "a" + "la" and is used with feminine singular places. With motion verbs (andare/venire/ritornare) it usually means "to the mosque"; with stative context it can mean "at the mosque."
target_language_example: Domani vado alla moschea con un amico.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going to the mosque with a friend.

additional_notes: Combination of **a** (“to/at”) + **la** (“the”) + **nostra** (“our”, feminine singular). Used before a feminine singular noun: **alla nostra casa** (to our house), **alla nostra età** (at our age), **alla nostra tavola** (at our table). The same pattern exists with other forms: **al nostro** (to our, masculine singular), **ai nostri / alle nostre** (to our, plural).
target_language_example: Non avvicinarti alla nostra macchina!
native_language_example: Don’t come near our car!

additional_notes: Used to talk about the worst-case scenario, often to reassure someone that there’s a fallback plan. It’s similar in meaning to "nel peggiore dei casi" (more formal). You’ll often see it with a verb like "andare" (to go): "Alla peggio, andiamo a casa".
target_language_example: Alla peggio, prendiamo un taxi.
native_language_example: At worst, we’ll take a taxi.

additional_notes: Used as an adverbial phrase to say something works/goes extremely well, with no problems (common with verbs like funzionare, andare). In "La ripetizione porta alla perfezione", it means "to perfection" (practice leads to perfection).
target_language_example: Il test è andato alla perfezione, non c’erano errori.
native_language_example: The test went perfectly; there were no mistakes.

meaning: at the door; to the door.
additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns: a + la = alla. Very common in phrases like "bussare alla porta" (to knock on the door) and with motion/delivery verbs like "andare/portare alla porta" (to go/bring to the door). Often followed by a specification: "alla porta della camera" (at the bedroom door).
target_language_example: Ho lasciato il pacco alla porta.
native_language_example: I left the package at the door.

meaning: on the radio; on the radio station (heard/broadcast via radio).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like sentire (to hear), ascoltare (to listen), dire (to say), passare/trasmettere (to play/broadcast) to indicate something was heard or broadcast via radio. Literally 'at the radio', but in English it’s usually 'on the radio'.
target_language_example: L'ho ascoltata alla radio stamattina.
native_language_example: I heard it on the radio this morning.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone is/was/will be present at a meeting. It’s made of a + la (“to/at the” + feminine singular), and riunione means “meeting” (a gathering). Often goes with essere/stare (“to be”) and presente (“present”).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alla riunione di domani.
native_language_example: See you at tomorrow’s meeting.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done or oriented in the opposite direction/way than normal. Common with verbs like leggere (to read), scrivere (to write), fare (to do), mettere (to put), and can refer both to physical orientation (upside down) and to a process/order done in reverse.
target_language_example: Hai messo la maglietta alla rovescia.
native_language_example: You put your T-shirt on inside out/backwards.

meaning: “Cheers!” (a toast) / “to (your) health”; also “to health” in general.
additional_notes: Used in two main ways: (1) as a toast when clinking glasses: “Alla salute!” or “Alla salute di tutti” (“To everyone’s health”). (2) In phrases like “fa bene/male alla salute” meaning “is good/bad for your health.” Often includes a possessive: “alla tua/vostra salute” (“to your health”).
target_language_example: Allora, alla salute!
native_language_example: So, cheers!

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency or how often something happens within a week (often with numbers: “una volta alla settimana”, “tre volte alla settimana”). It’s also used to say how many regular activities you have each week: “quattro lezioni alla settimana”.
target_language_example: Vado in palestra due volte alla settimana.
native_language_example: I go to the gym twice a week.

additional_notes: Used especially with verbs like "cogliere" (to catch) or "prendere" (to take) to mean someone is surprised and not ready to react ("cogliere/prendere qualcuno alla sprovvista" = to catch someone off guard). Often follows the verb: "mi ha colto alla sprovvista". Agreement note: "colto" (male) / "colta" (female) agrees with the person being caught off guard.
target_language_example: La domanda mi ha preso alla sprovvista.
native_language_example: The question caught me off guard.

meaning: at the train station; to the train station.
additional_notes: "Alla" = "a" + "la" (to/at + the). With places, it can mean either being there (at) or going there (to), depending on the verb and context: "Ci vediamo alla stazione" (meet at) vs. "Come arrivare alla stazione?" (how to get to). Often used with "vicino alla stazione" = "near the station."
target_language_example: Andiamo alla stazione a prendere il treno.
native_language_example: Let’s go to the station to catch the train.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a destination or location. It combines the preposition + article "a" + "la" → "alla" ("to the/at the"), with "stazione degli autobus" (bus station). Often used with verbs of movement like "andare" (to go).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alla stazione degli autobus alle otto.
native_language_example: See you at the bus station at eight.

additional_notes: Used to say you are at (or arrived at) a specific train/metro station. It’s a + la = alla, and it’s typically followed by the station name: alla stazione di Osaka, alla stazione di Shibuya. Common with verbs like essere (to be), arrivare (to arrive), andare (to go), incontrare/imbattersi (to meet/run into).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alla stazione di Milano Centrale alle 8.
native_language_example: See you at Milan Central Station at 8.

additional_notes: Combination of the preposition+article “a + la” → “alla” (“to the”) + the possessive “sua” (“his/her/its”). It’s used before a feminine singular noun: “alla sua dieta” = “to his/her diet”, “alla sua condizione” = “to his condition” (condizione is feminine in Italian). The possessive agrees with the thing owned (sua/sue vs suo/suoi), not with the owner.
target_language_example: Non dare ascolto alla sua storia.
native_language_example: Don’t listen to his/her story.

additional_notes: Means going/being/participating at someone else’s party. It’s made of: a + la = alla (“to the/at the”) + sua (“his/her”) + festa (“party”). Note: sua can mean “his” or “her” (the owner is understood from context), while festa is feminine, so it stays sua (not suo). Common with verbs like andare (to go), essere (to be), invitare (to invite), partecipare (to participate), divertirsi (to have fun).
target_language_example: Non posso venire alla sua festa stasera.
native_language_example: I can’t come to his/her party tonight.

additional_notes: Uses "a" + "la" → "alla" to mean being at a place. "Sua" agrees with "scrivania" (feminine singular) and can mean either his or her depending on context. Often used for where someone is working, studying, eating, etc., typically at a desk (home or office).
target_language_example: Se hai bisogno di lui, è alla sua scrivania.
native_language_example: If you need him, he's at his desk.

additional_notes: Common in spoken Italian to urge someone to do something immediately (“E alla svelta!” = “And make it quick!”). It can also describe doing something quickly (e.g., falling asleep). Often overlaps with "presto" and "in fretta".
target_language_example: Finisci i compiti alla svelta, poi usciamo.
native_language_example: Finish your homework quickly, then we’ll go out.

additional_notes: Contraction of **a + la tua**. It’s used before a **feminine singular noun**: *alla tua casa* (to your house), *alla tua destra* (to your right), *alla tua auto* (at/to your car). In a different context, **Alla tua!** can also be a toast meaning “To you!/Cheers!”, short for *alla tua salute*.
target_language_example: Puoi lasciare il pacco alla tua porta?
native_language_example: Can you leave the package at your door?

meaning: 'at the sight of' (when seeing something triggers a reaction).
additional_notes: Used with a noun (often with a reaction like being scared, shouting, crying, etc.). It’s a fixed expression meaning “upon seeing” or “as soon as (someone) saw”. The article changes with the noun: alla vista del (di + il), alla vista dello (di + lo), alla vista della (di + la), alla vista dei/degli/delle.
target_language_example: Alla vista del sangue, mi sono sentito male.
native_language_example: At the sight of blood, I felt sick.

meaning: at a time; one by one.
additional_notes: Used to say you should do something in separate turns or small batches, often with numbers (e.g., "tre alla volta" = three at a time) or with "uno" ("uno alla volta" = one at a time / one by one). Common for instructions like entering, speaking, taking items, or increasing something gradually.
target_language_example: Parlate uno alla volta, per favore.
native_language_example: Speak one at a time, please.

meaning: toward; on the way to; headed for.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (especially "andare", "partire", "mettersi") to say you are setting off in the direction of a place. Common in writing and news-style Italian; in everyday speech you can often say "verso" instead.
target_language_example: Siamo partiti alla volta di Firenze alle sette.
native_language_example: We left for Florence at seven.

meaning: at the party; to the party.
additional_notes: “Alla” = “a + la” and can mean either “to the” (movement/direction: andare/venire/essere diretto) or “at the” (location: essere/incontrarsi). “Festa” means “party,” and you’ll also often specify whose party: “alla festa di Mary” = “to/at Mary’s party.”
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alla festa stasera?
native_language_example: See you at the party tonight?

additional_notes: Contraction of "a + la mia". Used before a feminine singular noun (e.g., "alla mia macchina" = "to my car", "alla mia salute" = "to my health" in a toast). It can express direction/relationship ("to"), adaptation/connection ("to"), or be used in set phrases like toasts.
target_language_example: Non toccare alla mia borsa!
native_language_example: Don’t touch my bag!

additional_notes: Used after verbs of going/coming/inviting (e.g., venire/andare/invitare) to say someone should come/go to your party. "Alla" = "a" + "la" (to the), and it agrees with the feminine noun "festa". Formal invitation: "Venga alla mia festa" (Lei form).
target_language_example: Ti va di venire alla mia festa sabato sera?
native_language_example: Do you feel like coming to my party on Saturday evening?

additional_notes: Used after verbs like consegnare (hand over/turn in), denunciare (report), portare (take/bring) to indicate that someone/something is handed over, reported, or taken to the police. It can also refer to going to the police station (e.g., “alla polizia più vicina”).
target_language_example: Dobbiamo andare alla polizia per denunciare il furto.
native_language_example: We have to go to the police to report the theft.

meaning: at the station; to the station.
additional_notes: "Alla" = "a" (to/at) + "la" (the). With motion verbs like "portare" (to take/bring), "accompagnare" (to accompany), "andare" (to go), it usually means "to the station" (destination). In other contexts it can mean "at the station" (location), e.g., something happened there.
target_language_example: Possiamo incontrarci alla stazione alle otto?
native_language_example: Can we meet at the station at eight?

meaning: to/at his or her (feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (or an implied one): alla sua professoressa = “to/in front of his/her teacher”; alla sua partenza = “at his/her departure.” It’s the combination a + la (“to the/at the”) + sua (“his/her”). Note: in very formal Italian, Sua (capital S) can mean “Your” (formal), e.g., alla Sua attenzione.
target_language_example: Non ho potuto partecipare alla sua festa.
native_language_example: I couldn’t attend his/her party.

additional_notes: Contraction of **a + la tua** (“to/at the your”, feminine singular). Used before a feminine singular noun: **alla tua festa** = “at your party”, **alla tua mamma** = “to your mom”. For masculine singular you usually use **al tuo** (a + il tuo).
target_language_example: Puoi dirlo alla tua amica?
native_language_example: Can you tell it to your friend?

additional_notes: Used to say the time something happens. It’s the preposition “a” + the plural article “le” (for ore, “hours”): “alle” = “at the”. Common with verbs like partire (to leave) and essere (to be).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alle otto davanti al cinema.
native_language_example: See you at eight in front of the movie theater.

additional_notes: Used to say the exact time something happens. "Alle" = "a" + "le" (at the + plural), used with most clock times: alle due, alle sette, alle 9. With 1 o’clock you usually say "all’una" (singular). You can add parts of the day like "domattina" (tomorrow morning) or "di sera" (in the evening).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alle sei davanti alla stazione.
native_language_example: See you at six in front of the station.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. It’s the preposition “a” + the plural article “le” because “ore” (hours) is understood: “alle sette (ore)”. For 1 o’clock you usually say “all’una” (not *alle una*).
target_language_example: Il treno parte alle sette e dieci.
native_language_example: The train leaves at 7:10.

meaning: in high school (during your high school years).
additional_notes: Short for "alle scuole superiori" (Italy’s upper secondary school). Used to talk about a time in your life: meeting someone, what you were like, what happened back then. Often with verbs like "essere" or "conoscere": "Ero... alle superiori", "L’ho conosciuto alle superiori".
target_language_example: Ci siamo conosciuti alle superiori.
native_language_example: We met in high school.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. It’s the preposition "a" + the feminine plural article "le" (because "ore" = hours is feminine), so you say "alle" for most clock times: "alle cinque", "alle sei". For a time range, you can use "dalle ... alle ..." (from ... to ...).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alle sei davanti alla stazione.
native_language_example: See you at six in front of the station.

meaning: in high school (attending upper secondary school).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like essere/andare/fare to say someone is/was in high school. It refers to the school level (le scuole superiori) and is common when talking about a period in someone’s life. Often used in the past: "Quando ero alle superiori..."
target_language_example: Quando ero alle superiori, studiavo inglese tutti i giorni.
native_language_example: When I was in high school, I studied English every day.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. It’s made of a (to/at) + le (the, plural) → alle + dieci (ten). It can refer to 10:00 in the morning or at night; the context (e.g., going to bed) makes it clear.
target_language_example: L’appuntamento è alle dieci.
native_language_example: The appointment is at ten o’clock.

additional_notes: Used with feminine plural nouns (e.g., figlie, labbra, aspettative). It’s the preposition + article + possessive: a + le + mie = alle mie. Often translates naturally as “to my” or “at my,” depending on the verb (e.g., piacere: “to my daughters”).
target_language_example: Non dare retta alle mie amiche, stanno scherzando.
native_language_example: Don’t listen to my (female) friends; they’re joking.

additional_notes: Used to say what time something happens. With most clock times in Italian you use "alle" + the hour (e.g., alle due, alle nove). For 1 o’clock, Italian usually uses the singular: "all’una".
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alle nove davanti alla stazione.
native_language_example: See you at nine in front of the station.

meaning: "at the gates/door"; imminent or just outside/nearby.
additional_notes: Used literally for being at/near an entrance (alle porte di servizio = at the service doors). Very commonly used figuratively with events or situations to mean they’re about to happen soon: "L’autunno è alle porte" = autumn is just around the corner. Can also suggest a threat is very close: "Il nemico è alle porte".
target_language_example: Gli esami sono alle porte, devo studiare di più.
native_language_example: The exams are just around the corner, I need to study more.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. "Alle" = "a" (at) + "le" (the, feminine plural), because "ore" (hours) is implied: "alle (ore) sei". For 1 o’clock you usually say "all’una" (singular), not *alle uno*.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alle sei davanti alla stazione.
native_language_example: See you at six in front of the station.

additional_notes: Used to say the time something happens. With clock times, Italian uses "a" + the plural article ("le") for most hours: "alle" + hour (alle due, alle sette). For 1 o’clock, it’s singular: "all’una". You can use it with or without "a casa" depending on context ("tornerà alle sette" = he/she will be back at seven).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alle sette davanti al cinema.
native_language_example: See you at seven in front of the movie theater.

meaning: behind (someone); left behind; off (someone else’s support).
