additional_notes: Used to suggest or decide to leave and go back home. Andiamo is the “we” form of andare (“to go”), and it’s often used like English “let’s …”. You can add allora (“then”), via! (“come on!”), or say it firmly as an instruction.
target_language_example: È tardi: andiamo a casa.
native_language_example: It’s late: let’s go home.

additional_notes: Used to suggest doing something together (literally “we go to see”). Often means going to look at something or going to check what’s happening: “Andiamo a vedere che succede” = “Let’s go see what’s going on.”
target_language_example: Non so se il negozio è aperto: andiamo a vedere.
native_language_example: I don’t know if the shop is open—let’s go check.

additional_notes: "Andiamo" is "we go" and is commonly used as "let’s go". Adding "via" emphasizes leaving/going away (often from a place). Very common with "da qui" (from here) or "di lì" (from there).
target_language_example: È tardi, andiamo via.
native_language_example: It’s late, let’s leave.

meaning: 'he/she/it will go to' (future of andare) + a; also used for 'will go to (do something)' before an infinitive.
additional_notes: "Andrà" is the 3rd person singular future of "andare" (to go): *andrà a Roma* = "he/she will go to Rome." Use **a** before a place (cities) or before an infinitive: *andrà a trovare suo zio* = "he/she will go to visit his/her uncle." You may also see the idiom **andrà a finire che...** meaning "it will end up that..." / "it’ll turn out that..."
target_language_example: Domani andrà a Milano per lavoro.
native_language_example: Tomorrow he/she will go to Milan for work.

meaning: "it will be fine / it will work (be OK)."
additional_notes: Future tense of andare + bene. Used (1) to reassure someone: "Tutto andrà bene" = "Everything will be fine," and (2) to say something will be suitable/acceptable for a purpose: "Questo/questa andrà bene?" = "Will this work / Is this OK?" You can also use it about time plans: "Ogni giorno andrà bene" = "Any day will be fine."
target_language_example: Va bene anche domani, ma se preferisci sabato, andrà bene lo stesso.
native_language_example: Tomorrow is fine too, but if you prefer Saturday, that will be fine as well.

meaning: “Everything will be fine / it’ll all be okay.”
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or express optimism about the future. It’s the future tense of “andare” (“to go”): literally “everything will go well,” but it’s usually translated as “everything will be fine/okay.” Often said as encouragement (“Avanti, andrà tutto bene”) or with “penso/credo” (“I think/I believe everything will be fine”).
target_language_example: Tranquillo: andrà tutto bene, ci penso io.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everything will be fine, I’ll take care of it.

additional_notes: Uses the passato remoto form of “andare” (andò = he/she went). Common in storytelling, books, news reports, and in some regions of Italy for past events. It’s followed by “a” before a destination (a Boston, a Kyoto) or a place like “a letto” (to bed).
target_language_example: Ieri sera andò a casa molto tardi.
native_language_example: Last night he/she went home very late.

additional_notes: Past historic (passato remoto) of "andare a casa" (to go home). Common in written narratives and storytelling; in everyday conversation many speakers use "è andato/a a casa" instead. The subject is usually understood from context (e.g., Tom, he, she).
target_language_example: Dopo la riunione, andò a casa subito.
native_language_example: After the meeting, he/she went home right away.

additional_notes: Passato remoto (simple past) of “andare a letto” = “to go to bed,” often used in storytelling, books, or to talk about a completed action in the past (especially in some regions). With a time: “andò a letto alle dieci” = “went to bed at ten.” Note: “andare a letto con qualcuno” can also mean “to sleep with someone” (often implying sex), depending on context.
target_language_example: Dopo cena, andò a letto presto.
native_language_example: After dinner, he/she went to bed early.

additional_notes: Past tense using the passato remoto of andare (andò = “he/she went”), common in written storytelling and in some regions when speaking. Used literally for going/attending school; it can be expanded (e.g., “andò a scuola di legge” = “he went to law school”).
target_language_example: Da bambino, Marco andò a scuola in centro.
native_language_example: As a child, Marco went to school downtown.

additional_notes: "Andò" is the passato remoto (remote past) of "andare" and is common in stories, news, and historical narration (especially in central/southern Italy). In everyday conversation, people often use "è andato/a" instead. "Al" = "a" + "il" and is used with masculine singular places: "andò al museo", "andò al lavoro".
target_language_example: Ieri Marco andò al cinema con gli amici.
native_language_example: Yesterday Marco went to the cinema with friends.

meaning: “he/she went to (into)” (past tense of andare + in).
additional_notes: Used to say someone went to a place in the past. It’s the passato remoto form of “andare” (andò = he/she went), common in storytelling and in some regions; in everyday speech you often hear “è andato/a in…”. Use “in” especially with countries/continents (in Italia, in America), cities as “in città”, and certain places like “in una moschea”.
target_language_example: Ieri andò in Francia per lavoro.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she went to France for work.

additional_notes: Used for the ring given when a couple gets engaged. Often appears with possessives (il mio/il suo anello di fidanzamento) and verbs like dare (to give), comprare (to buy), perdere (to lose), portare (to wear).
target_language_example: Ha comprato un anello di fidanzamento per la sua ragazza.
native_language_example: He bought an engagement ring for his girlfriend.

additional_notes: Used to talk about animals kept as companions in a home (e.g., a dog, cat, rabbit, parrot). In questions you’ll often hear: "Che tipo di animale domestico...?" (What kind of pet...?) and "Hai un animale domestico?" (Do you have a pet?). Plural: "animali domestici".
target_language_example: Abbiamo due animali domestici: un cane e un gatto.
native_language_example: We have two pets: a dog and a cat.

additional_notes: Used to talk about animals kept at home (like cats and dogs). In signs and rules (e.g., hotels, apartments), it often means “pets are allowed/not allowed.” Singular: "animale domestico".
target_language_example: In questo appartamento sono ammessi gli animali domestici.
native_language_example: Pets are allowed in this apartment.

meaning: "... years ago" (a number of years in the past).
additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It usually comes after the time expression: "cinque anni fa" (five years ago), "molti anni fa" (many years ago), "un paio di anni fa" (a couple of years ago). You can also use it without a number to mean "years ago" or "a long time ago": "È successo anni fa."
target_language_example: Ho studiato italiano dieci anni fa.
native_language_example: I studied Italian ten years ago.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages. It follows a number: “(qualcuno) ha X anni in più di me” = “(someone) is X years older than me.” You can swap “me” with another person: “di te” (than you), “di lui” (than him), “di lei” (than her), “di noi” (than us).
target_language_example: Mia sorella ha tre anni in più di me.
native_language_example: My sister is three years older than me.

meaning: “opened the” (past participle + feminine singular “the”), used with a verb like “ho”.
additional_notes: You’ll most often see this as part of the passato prossimo: (io) ho aperto la finestra / la borsa / la busta (“I opened the window/bag/envelope”). “Aperto” agrees in gender/number only in some cases (e.g., with certain pronouns), but with a noun after it you normally keep “aperto”. It can also be used figuratively: “mi ha aperto la mente” = “it opened my mind.”
target_language_example: Ho aperto la porta perché faceva caldo.
native_language_example: I opened the door because it was hot.

additional_notes: Usually used with the helping verb **avere** to make the past tense: **ho aperto la porta** = “I opened the door / I have opened the door.” You can add details like **lentamente** (slowly) or **per qualcuno** (for someone): **Ho aperto la porta per Tom** = “I opened the door for Tom.”
target_language_example: Ho aperto la porta e sono entrato.
native_language_example: I opened the door and went in.

additional_notes: Used with the passato prossimo (present perfect) of aprire: ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno aperto la scatola. Note: with avere, the past participle usually stays the same (aperto); it doesn’t change to match “scatola” unless a direct-object pronoun comes before the verb (e.g., L’ho aperta = “I opened it”).
target_language_example: Hai aperto la scatola prima di arrivare a casa?
native_language_example: Did you open the box before getting home?

additional_notes: Used to say who owns something. It’s the 3rd-person singular of the verb “appartenere” + “a” (to): appartiene a Tom = it belongs to Tom. You can replace the person with an indirect pronoun: appartiene a me/te/lui/lei/noi/voi/loro.
target_language_example: Questa borsa appartiene a me.
native_language_example: This bag belongs to me.

meaning: “belongs to her” or “belongs to you (formal, to a woman)”.
additional_notes: From the verb *appartenere* (“to belong to”). *Lei* can mean “her” or formal “you” (used with strangers or in polite situations); if addressing a man formally, you still say *Lei* (same word). Often used to talk about ownership of objects: *Questo/Questa ... appartiene a lei?* = “Does this ... belong to her/you (formal)?”
target_language_example: Mi scusi, questa borsa appartiene a lei?
native_language_example: Excuse me, does this bag belong to you?

additional_notes: Used to say that something is your property/possession. "Appartiene" is the 3rd person singular of "appartenere" (to belong), so it matches singular things: "questo/quella cassa/questa automobile". For plural, use "appartengono a me" (they belong to me). Often you can also just say "È mio/a" (it’s mine) depending on the noun’s gender.
target_language_example: Scusi, questo zaino appartiene a me.
native_language_example: Excuse me, this backpack belongs to me.

additional_notes: Used with essere (to be): “essere appassionato/a di + noun” to say someone is very interested in something (music, sports, art, etc.). It agrees with the person: appassionato (male), appassionata (female), appassionati/appassionate (plural).
target_language_example: Sono appassionata di fotografia.
native_language_example: I’m passionate about photography.

additional_notes: Used with the verb essere (e.g., sono/sei/è appena arrivato) to say someone arrived a moment ago. The adverb appena means “just/barely,” and the past participle arrivato agrees with the person (appena arrivata for a woman; appena arrivati/arrivate for plural). Often used as a quick update when you’ve just gotten somewhere.
target_language_example: Scusa il ritardo: sono appena arrivato alla stazione.
native_language_example: Sorry I'm late: I just arrived at the station.

additional_notes: Used to say someone arrived too late and the train has already left. "Appena" means "just" (a moment ago), and "perdere il treno" literally "to lose the train" but in English we say "miss the train." It can also be used figuratively to mean "miss an opportunity," though here it’s literal.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ho appena perso il treno e devo aspettare il prossimo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I just missed the train and I have to wait for the next one.

additional_notes: A common pattern with the passato prossimo: "ho appena venduto" = "I’ve just sold". It’s usually followed by a noun like "auto/macchina/automobile" (car). "Gli" or "le" can be added to mean "to him" or "to her": "Gli/Le ho appena venduto la mia auto". The past participle is "venduto" (used with "avere": ho/hai/ha venduto).
target_language_example: Gli ho appena venduto la mia moto.
native_language_example: I just sold my motorcycle to him.

meaning: “I appreciate your …” (polite way to show gratitude/value).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to say you value something about the other person. It’s common in polite or semi-formal Italian (work, customer service, emails). The possessive must agree with the noun: **la tua** (feminine singular), **il tuo** (masculine singular), **le tue** (feminine plural), **i tuoi** (masculine plural).
target_language_example: Apprezzo la tua pazienza.
native_language_example: I appreciate your patience.

meaning: "I appreciate your..." (formal/polite, addressing more than one person).
additional_notes: Used to thank people in a formal tone. "Vostra" is the polite plural form of "your" (to a group, e.g., customers, colleagues, an audience). It is typically followed by a noun like "comprensione" (understanding), "pazienza" (patience), "fiducia" (trust), "cooperazione" (cooperation). For one person formally, you usually say "Apprezzo la Sua..."; informally to one person: "Apprezzo la tua...".
target_language_example: Apprezzo la vostra disponibilità a aiutarmi.
native_language_example: I appreciate your willingness to help me.

meaning: "open the door" (formal) / "that you open the door" (subjunctive).
additional_notes: "Apra" is the formal command (Lei form) of "aprire" used in polite requests: "Per favore, apra la porta." It can also appear after verbs like "volere che..." or expressions like "a meno che... non..." where Italian often uses the subjunctive: "vogliamo che tu apra la porta" = "we want you to open the door." With "tu" the informal command is "apri la porta!".
target_language_example: Mi scusi, apra la porta, per favore.
native_language_example: Excuse me, please open the door.

meaning: "Open your eyes"; also "wake up / face reality".
additional_notes: Imperative (tu form) of "aprire" + "gli occhi". It can be a literal command (e.g., after someone has their eyes closed) or a figurative one meaning "stop being naive" or "realize what’s really going on." Often said with urgency or frustration; adding a name makes it more direct ("Apri gli occhi, Diane").
target_language_example: Apri gli occhi: ti sta mentendo.
native_language_example: Open your eyes: he’s lying to you.

meaning: “open the …” (to one person), before a feminine singular noun.
additional_notes: It’s the tu imperative of aprire (“to open”) + la (“the”, feminine singular). You use it when telling one person to open something feminine: apri la porta (the door), apri la finestra (the window). With a masculine noun, use apri il / apri lo (e.g., apri il libro).
target_language_example: Apri la porta, per favore.
native_language_example: Open the door, please.

additional_notes: Imperative (tu) form of "aprire" + "la bocca". Used to tell one person to open their mouth, e.g., at the dentist/doctor, when feeding someone, or when asking someone to speak/sing. For a more polite request, you can add "per favore/per piacere" (as in the examples).
target_language_example: Dal dentista: apri la bocca, per favore.
native_language_example: At the dentist: open your mouth, please.

additional_notes: A direct command using the tu form of aprire (apri). Use it with friends, family, kids, or someone you address as tu. To be more polite, add per favore or per piacere. With Lei (formal), you would say: "Apra la porta".
target_language_example: Scusa, apri la porta un attimo?
native_language_example: Sorry, can you open the door for a moment?

meaning: to open one’s mouth; (often) to speak / say something.
additional_notes: Often used to mean “to speak,” especially in negative forms like “non ha aperto bocca” = “he/she didn’t say a word.” You can also use it literally when talking about opening your mouth (e.g., at the dentist).
target_language_example: Non ha aperto bocca per tutta la riunione.
native_language_example: He/She didn’t say a word during the whole meeting.

meaning: to open your eyes; (figuratively) to realize / wake up to the truth.
additional_notes: Often used in the imperative (Apri gli occhi! / Devi aprire gli occhi.) either literally (open your eyes now) or figuratively to tell someone to stop being naive and notice what’s really happening. With "adesso" it’s typically literal: "Puoi aprire gli occhi adesso!"
target_language_example: Apri gli occhi: non ti sta dicendo la verità.
native_language_example: Open your eyes: he’s not telling you the truth.

meaning: to open fire; to start shooting.
additional_notes: Used mainly in military/police or news contexts to mean starting to shoot with guns. It can also be used more broadly to mean starting an attack or hostilities (rarely metaphorical in everyday conversation).
target_language_example: I soldati hanno aperto il fuoco contro il nemico.
native_language_example: The soldiers opened fire on the enemy.

meaning: “to open the …” (and by extension: “to kick off/start” an event).
additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns (la bottiglia, la porta, la finestra, la serata, etc.). Literally means “to open,” but with events like *la serata* it can mean “to open/kick off” (e.g., be the first act). For masculine nouns you use *aprire il/lo* (e.g., *aprire il vino*).
target_language_example: Puoi aprire la finestra, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you open the window, please?

additional_notes: Used for physically opening a window to let in air/light. Common with modal verbs like dovere (devo/deve) and with instructions using di + infinitive (mi ha detto di aprire...). You can also use the polite request: Può aprire la finestra?
target_language_example: Puoi aprire la finestra, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you open the window, please?

additional_notes: Used for physically opening a door (by turning the handle, pushing/pulling, etc.). You’ll often see it with modal verbs like riuscire a (to manage to) or with requests like Puoi aprire la porta? (Can you open the door?).
target_language_example: Puoi aprire la porta, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you open the door, please?

additional_notes: Used for physically opening a box/container (e.g., a package). In many situations Italian also uses the shorter phrase "aprire la scatola" simply meaning "open the box"; you can add an object pronoun if needed (e.g., "Aprila!" = "Open it!").
target_language_example: Puoi aprire la scatola, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you open the box, please?

meaning: to open the doors; (figuratively) to open up opportunities / allow access.
additional_notes: Literal: opening actual doors (e.g., a building, shop, or venue). Figurative: giving someone access, permission, or a chance to do something (similar to English “open doors”). Often used with "a" + person/thing: "aprire le porte a qualcuno/a qualcosa" = "to open the door to someone/something."
target_language_example: Questo corso può aprire le porte a molte opportunità di lavoro.
native_language_example: This course can open the door to many job opportunities.

meaning: "Open your eyes" (often: "wake up" / "realize what's really going on").
additional_notes: Imperative plural: said to more than one person (voi). It can be literal (stop keeping your eyes closed) or figurative, meaning “pay attention,” “stop being naive,” or “face reality.” Tone depends on context; it can sound like a strong warning or reprimand.
target_language_example: Apri gli occhi: ti sta mentendo.
native_language_example: Open your eyes: he/she is lying to you.

meaning: “open the door” (command to more than one person, or formal ‘you’).
additional_notes: Imperative of aprire used for: (1) talking to a group (“you all”), or (2) formal/polite ‘you’ to one person (Lei). Often said urgently with subito (“right now”) or softened with per piacere (“please”). Negative command: Non aprite la porta! = “Don’t open the door!”
target_language_example: Scusate, aprite la porta, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you open the door, please?

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun after it (la bocca, la lettera, la scatola). Aprì is the passato remoto (simple past), common in stories, news reports, and in some regions of Italy; in everyday conversation people often use the passato prossimo instead (ha aperto la...).
target_language_example: Aprì la porta e guardò fuori.
native_language_example: He/She opened the door and looked outside.

additional_notes: "Aprì" is the passato remoto of "aprire" (to open), used especially in narratives and (in many regions) for actions completed in the distant past. In everyday conversation many Italians often use passato prossimo instead: "ha aperto la porta". It can also appear with an indirect object: "aprì la porta a Maria" = he/she opened the door for Mary (or opened the door to Mary).
target_language_example: Quando suonarono, aprì la porta e salutò tutti.
native_language_example: When they rang the doorbell, he/she opened the door and greeted everyone.

additional_notes: General term for a weapon that shoots bullets using gunpowder/explosive force (e.g., a pistol or rifle). Often used in formal contexts like police reports or medical/legal descriptions (e.g., "ferite da arma da fuoco" = gunshot wounds).
target_language_example: La polizia ha trovato un’arma da fuoco nell’auto.
native_language_example: The police found a firearm in the car.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "essere" (e.g., "sono/è arrabbiata con...") to say you’re mad at a person. "Arrabbiata" is feminine singular; the masculine form is "arrabbiato" (e.g., "Sono arrabbiato con te"). You can also use it with pronouns: "con me/te/lui/lei/noi/voi/loro".
target_language_example: Non sono arrabbiata con te, solo stanca.
native_language_example: I'm not angry with you, just tired.

meaning: angry with me (said about a woman).
additional_notes: Uses the adjective “arrabbiato/a” (“angry”) + “con” (“with”) to say someone is angry with someone else: “arrabbiata con me/te/lui/lei…”. “Arrabbiata” agrees with a feminine subject; for a man, use “arrabbiato con me”. You can intensify it with “molto” (very): “molto arrabbiata con me”.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace: sei arrabbiata con me?
native_language_example: I’m sorry: are you angry with me?

additional_notes: Used with a person you’re angry at: arrabbiato con + [person]. It agrees with who is angry: arrabbiato (male), arrabbiata (female), arrabbiati/arrabbiate (plural). Often used with essere: Sono arrabbiato/a con te.
target_language_example: Non sono arrabbiata con te, sono solo stanca.
native_language_example: I’m not angry with you, I’m just tired.

additional_notes: "Arrabbiato" means "angry" (male speaker or referring to a man). "Con lei" means "with her" (formal "lei" can also mean "with you" when addressing someone politely). For a woman, use "arrabbiata con lei".
target_language_example: Perché sei arrabbiato con lei?
native_language_example: Why are you angry with her?

additional_notes: "Arrabbiato" is the masculine singular form (for a man). For a woman, use "arrabbiata": "Sono arrabbiata con lui." The person you’re angry with is introduced by "con" + pronoun/name: "arrabbiato con me/te/lei/loro", "arrabbiato con Marco". Common question: "Perché sei arrabbiato con lui?" = "Why are you angry with him?"
target_language_example: Non sono più arrabbiato con lui.
native_language_example: I’m not angry with him anymore.

additional_notes: Use **essere arrabbiato/a con [someone]** to say you’re angry *with* someone. Change the ending for gender/number: **arrabbiato** (male), **arrabbiata** (female), **arrabbiati/e** (plural). The pronoun can change too: **con te** (with you), **con lui/lei** (with him/her), **con noi/voi** (with us/you all), **con loro** (with them). You can add a reason with **per**: *arrabbiato con me per...* (“angry with me for...”).
target_language_example: Sei ancora arrabbiato con me?
native_language_example: Are you still angry with me?

additional_notes: Reflexive verb: "arrampicarsi" = "to climb" (by gripping/using hands and feet). "Sugli" is "su + gli" and means "on/onto the"; used with plural masculine "alberi" (trees). Often used with "piacere" (e.g., "Mi piace arrampicarmi sugli alberi").
target_language_example: Da piccolo mi piaceva arrampicarmi sugli alberi nel parco.
native_language_example: When I was little, I liked climbing trees in the park.

additional_notes: From the verb *arrivare* (“to arrive”) + *a casa* (“home”). Used to say someone reaches home, often in the present tense to describe a routine or something scheduled (also common with future meaning). You can change the subject: *arrivo a casa* (I get home), *arrivi a casa* (you get home), *arrivano a casa* (they get home).
target_language_example: Quando arriva a casa, mi chiama.
native_language_example: When she gets home, she calls me.

meaning: to get home; to arrive home.
additional_notes: Used for reaching your home (or the place you’re staying). Common in questions about how/when you’ll get home (e.g., in macchina/on foot/by bus) and with time expressions (e.g., tardi, alle otto).
target_language_example: Sono arrivato/a a casa alle nove.
native_language_example: I got home at nine.

additional_notes: Past participle of arrivare (“to arrive”) + qui (“here”). Used with the auxiliary essere: sono arrivato/a qui (I arrived here), è arrivato/a qui (he/she arrived here). The ending agrees with the subject: arrivato (male), arrivata (female). Often used with time expressions like ieri, tre giorni fa, appena.
target_language_example: Siamo arrivati qui alle otto di sera.
native_language_example: We arrived here at eight in the evening.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato remoto) of "arrivare a casa" (to arrive home). Common in narratives, books, news reports, or storytelling; in everyday conversation Italians often use "è arrivato/a a casa" (passato prossimo) instead. "Arrivò" agrees with the subject only by context (it can mean he or she).
target_language_example: Quando arrivò a casa, trovò un messaggio sul tavolo.
native_language_example: When he/she got home, he/she found a message on the table.

additional_notes: Refers to fighting disciplines (e.g., karate, judo, taekwondo, kung fu) practiced for sport, self-defense, training, or tradition. Often used with verbs like praticare (to practice) and fare (to do): “Pratico/Faccio arti marziali.”
target_language_example: Da bambino praticavo arti marziali due volte a settimana.
native_language_example: As a kid, I practiced martial arts twice a week.

additional_notes: "Ascoltando" is the gerund of "ascoltare" and expresses an action in progress (often with "stare": "sto/stiamo/stanno ascoltando..."). "La radio" can mean the radio device or radio programs in general. Used for present ongoing actions ("stanno/stiamo...") and past ongoing actions ("stava/stavano/stavate...").
target_language_example: Sto ascoltando la radio mentre cucino.
native_language_example: I’m listening to the radio while I cook.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase. Use it after verbs like piacere (Mi piace ascoltare la musica) or amare (Amo ascoltare la musica). You can add a genre after musica (musica pop/rock/jazz) or use soprattutto (“especially”) to say your favorite type.
target_language_example: Mi piace ascoltare la musica mentre studio.
native_language_example: I like listening to music while I study.

additional_notes: A literal phrase: ascoltare = “to listen (to)”, sette = “seven”, persone = “people.” Often used with contemporaneamente (“at the same time”) or alla volta (“at once”) to emphasize multitasking or handling multiple people speaking.
target_language_example: Non riesco ad ascoltare sette persone contemporaneamente: parlate uno alla volta.
native_language_example: I can't listen to seven people at the same time: speak one at a time.

additional_notes: Repetition of the imperative aspetta (“wait”) to sound more urgent or to interrupt and get someone to pause. Very common in spoken Italian; often followed by a short request like solo un attimo/un minuto/un secondo, or by a correction/added thought (e.g., “ascolta…”).
target_language_example: Aspetta, aspetta: ho dimenticato le chiavi!
native_language_example: Wait, wait—I forgot the keys!

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to pause briefly while you do something or think. Common in spoken Italian; you can also hear it repeated for emphasis (“Aspetta un attimo, aspetta”) or used as a quick interruption (“Aspetta un attimo!”).
target_language_example: Aspetta un attimo, devo rispondere a questo messaggio.
native_language_example: Wait a moment, I have to reply to this message.

additional_notes: Used to say something can be delayed and dealt with tomorrow. Often appears with "può" (it can) or "riesci/riesce/riuscite" (can you/he/she/you all manage) to ask someone to be patient or postpone an action.
target_language_example: Possiamo aspettare fino a domani e decidere con calma.
native_language_example: We can wait until tomorrow and decide calmly.

additional_notes: Used when you ask/tell someone to stay in the car and wait (often while you go do something quickly). Very common with the pattern: dire a qualcuno di aspettare in macchina (to tell someone to wait in the car).
target_language_example: Aspettami in macchina, torno subito.
native_language_example: Wait for me in the car, I’ll be right back.

meaning: “waited a long time” / “waited for a long time”.
additional_notes: Past participle of aspettare (“to wait”) used with the auxiliary avere (ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/hanno aspettato). Often followed by a direct object (e.g., “ti/lo/lei”) to say who was waited for: Ti ho aspettato a lungo = “I waited for you a long time.”
target_language_example: Abbiamo aspettato a lungo, ma il treno non è arrivato.
native_language_example: We waited a long time, but the train didn’t arrive.

additional_notes: Used mainly with the verb essere (or sometimes stare) to say someone did not go to school: “Sono/ero/è assente da scuola.” You can add a reason with “per” or “per via di” (e.g., “per via della malattia” = due to illness).
target_language_example: Oggi Giulia è assente da scuola perché ha la febbre.
native_language_example: Today Giulia is absent from school because she has a fever.

additional_notes: Used to say you are with someone (same place, doing an activity, living/working) or doing something jointly. It’s a common variant of "insieme a" (same meaning). Often followed by a person/pronoun: "assieme a me/te/lui/lei/noi/voi/loro" or a noun: "assieme a Maria".
target_language_example: Stasera vado al cinema assieme a un amico.
native_language_example: Tonight I'm going to the movies together with a friend.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something looks similar to someone/something else. It’s the verb assomigliare (to resemble) + a (to). Common pattern: [subject] assomiglia a + person/thing (e.g., Mia sorella assomiglia a mia madre).
target_language_example: Questo bambino assomiglia molto a suo padre.
native_language_example: This child looks a lot like his father.

meaning: (He/She) looks like his/her mother; (he/she) resembles his/her mother.
additional_notes: Used to say someone has a similar appearance or similar traits to their mother. Italian often drops the subject pronoun, so it can mean “he resembles…” or “she resembles…” depending on context. You can change the possessive: “assomiglia a mia madre” (resembles my mother), “assomiglia a tua madre” (your mother), etc. With specific people you can also say: “Marco assomiglia a sua madre.”
target_language_example: Secondo me, Giulia assomiglia a sua madre.
native_language_example: In my opinion, Giulia looks like her mother.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is similar to their father in appearance, personality, or other traits. The verb is "assomigliare a" (to resemble), so you can swap in other people: "assomiglia a sua madre" (he looks like his mother), "assomiglio a mio padre" (I look like my father).
target_language_example: Secondo me, Marco assomiglia a suo padre, soprattutto negli occhi.
native_language_example: In my opinion, Marco looks like his father, especially in the eyes.

meaning: “I look like my father” / “I resemble my father.”
additional_notes: "Assomigliare a" means "to resemble" someone (in appearance, character, etc.) and takes the preposition "a" + a person. The verb changes with the subject: (io) assomiglio, (tu) assomigli, (lui/lei) assomiglia, (noi) assomigliamo, (voi) assomigliate, (loro) assomigliano. You can swap in other people: "assomiglio a mia madre", "assomigli a tuo fratello".
target_language_example: Da piccolo assomigliavo molto a mio padre.
native_language_example: When I was little, I looked a lot like my father.

additional_notes: Used mainly with the verbs **fare attenzione a** (= to be careful to/about) and **prestare attenzione a** (= to pay attention to). It can be followed by **a + infinitive** (e.g. *attenzione a non cadere* = be careful not to fall) or by **a + noun/pronoun/person** (e.g. *attenzione a Tom* = attention to Tom).
target_language_example: Fai attenzione a dove metti le chiavi.
native_language_example: Be careful where you put the keys.

meaning: 'be careful not to' / 'watch out not to'.
additional_notes: Used to warn someone to avoid an action or mistake. It often follows (fare) attenzione: "Fai/Fate attenzione a non + infinitive". The subject of the infinitive is usually the same person being warned.
target_language_example: Fai attenzione a non dimenticare il passaporto.
native_language_example: Be careful not to forget your passport.

additional_notes: Used to warn or advise someone to listen carefully and take someone’s words seriously. It often appears with commands like "Fai/Fate attenzione..." (informal you / you all) or more formal forms like "Presti attenzione...". "Quello che dice" means “what he/she says”; you can add a name (e.g., Tom) or change "dice" to match the person (dico/dici/dicono).
target_language_example: Fai attenzione a quello che dice il medico.
native_language_example: Pay attention to what the doctor says.

additional_notes: Often used with the verb fare (“to do”): fare attività fisica = “to do physical activity / to exercise.” You can add più (“more”) to talk about increasing exercise: fare più attività fisica. Common in health/doctor’s advice and general fitness contexts.
target_language_example: Cerco di fare attività fisica tre volte a settimana.
native_language_example: I try to do physical activity three times a week.

additional_notes: Used for position or movement near/around a person or thing: "attorno a lei" = "around her". It can also mean "around" in the sense of approximately with times: "attorno a mezzanotte" = "around midnight". In some contexts it implies being nearby or hanging around someone/somewhere.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo attorno alle otto?
native_language_example: Shall we meet around eight?

additional_notes: Uses the gerund (attraversando = “crossing/while crossing”) to describe an action in progress, often with mentre (“while”). The verb is attraversare (“to cross”), and la strada can mean “the street” or “the road,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Stai attento: una macchina sta arrivando mentre stai attraversando la strada.
native_language_example: Be careful: a car is coming while you’re crossing the street.

additional_notes: “Attraversare” means “to cross,” and “a nuoto” means “by swimming” (i.e., swimming rather than using a bridge or boat). It’s often used with verbs like “provare a” (to try to) and “riuscire a” (to manage to).
target_language_example: Non è sicuro attraversare a nuoto il fiume qui.
native_language_example: It’s not safe to swim across the river here.

additional_notes: Literally “to cross the river by swimming.” Uses the verb *attraversare* (to cross) + *il fiume* (the river) + *a nuoto* (“by swimming / swimming”). You can swap *il fiume* for other places: *attraversare il lago a nuoto* (swim across the lake).
target_language_example: Non è sicuro attraversare il fiume a nuoto qui.
native_language_example: It’s not safe to swim across the river here.

additional_notes: Used for going from one side of a street/road to the other (on foot or generally). Often appears after verbs like "guardare" (to look) or with warnings like "È pericoloso..." (It’s dangerous...). In Italian, "strada" can mean both "street" and "road" depending on context.
target_language_example: Scusi, dov’è l’attraversamento pedonale per attraversare la strada?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the crosswalk to cross the street?

additional_notes: Past participle of "attraversare" (to cross) used with the auxiliary "avere" (e.g., "ho/ha attraversato la strada"). It can refer to crossing at a crosswalk or just in general; if you want to specify “outside the crosswalk,” you can say "fuori dalle strisce".
target_language_example: Scusi, ho attraversato la strada per arrivare qui.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I crossed the street to get here.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun (il). It can mean moving from one side to the other ("through the desert/country"), looking through something ("through the microscope"), or indicating a means/channel ("through mutual respect", "through the Quran", "transmitted through a kiss"). For feminine singular use "attraverso la"; for plural "attraverso i/le".
target_language_example: Ho imparato l'italiano attraverso il lavoro.
native_language_example: I learned Italian through work.

additional_notes: Attraverso means “through” (looking/seeing via something). Il suo means “his” (also used for “its”), and microscopio is “microscope.” It’s used to say you observe something using the microscope as the means/instrument: guardare (qualcosa) attraverso il suo microscopio.
target_language_example: Ha osservato il campione attraverso il suo microscopio.
native_language_example: He observed the sample through his microscope.

meaning: back and forth; to and fro.
additional_notes: Used to describe repeated movement in one direction and then the opposite (walking, carrying something, going between places). Often used with verbs like camminare/andare (to walk/go) or portare (to carry/bring). It can describe pacing (e.g., in a room) or going back and forth over time.
target_language_example: Ho passato la mattina ad andare avanti e indietro tra casa e l’ufficio.
native_language_example: I spent the morning going back and forth between home and the office.

meaning: “Come on, come on!” / “Go on!” (to encourage someone or urge them to hurry).
additional_notes: Used as an exclamation to push someone to move faster, keep going, or continue what they’re doing. It can sound encouraging (“go on!”) or impatient (“hurry up!”), depending on tone. Often followed by a name or a compliment like "bravo!".
target_language_example: Avanti, avanti, sbrigati: siamo in ritardo!
native_language_example: Come on, come on, hurry up: we’re late!

additional_notes:
Used with the verb phrase "stare avendo" (present continuous) or "stavamo avendo" (past continuous) to describe an ongoing difficulty. Often followed by:
- "a" + infinitive: "avere dei problemi a perdere peso" = to have trouble losing weight
- "con" + person/thing: "avere dei problemi con Tom" = to have problems with Tom
- a place/context: "avere dei problemi qui / a scuola" = to be having problems here / at school
target_language_example: Sto avendo dei problemi a capire questa lezione.
native_language_example: I'm having trouble understanding this lesson.

meaning: entitled to; having the right to.
additional_notes: Used in formal/official contexts (laws, benefits, tickets, discounts) to indicate a person who qualifies for something: "gli aventi diritto" = "those who are entitled/eligible". It often appears with "a" + noun/infinitive (e.g., "avente diritto al rimborso").
target_language_example: Il rimborso è riservato agli aventi diritto.
native_language_example: The refund is reserved for those who are entitled to it.

aver detto una cosa del genere

target_language_multi_word_term: aver detto una cosa del genere
meaning: to have said something like that / such a thing.
additional_notes: Used (often with disbelief or denial) to refer to a statement considered shocking, inappropriate, or hard to believe. Common after verbs like "negare" (to deny): "negare di aver detto una cosa del genere" = "to deny having said such a thing." "del genere" means "of that kind / like that."
target_language_example: Non posso credere di aver detto una cosa del genere.
native_language_example: I can't believe I said something like that.

meaning: “to have done” (past infinitive, used after modal/auxiliary verbs).
additional_notes: It’s the past infinitive of **fare**: **avere + fatto**. Very common after modal verbs like **dovere/potere/volere** to talk about a past action in an uncertain, hypothetical, or regretful way: **devi/potrebbe/non può/vorrei aver fatto...** = “you must have done / might have done / can’t have done / I wish I had done...”.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace non aver fatto in tempo a chiamarti.
native_language_example: I’m sorry I didn’t manage to call you in time.

additional_notes: Perfect infinitive (aver + past participle) used after verbs like dovere/potere to talk about a possible past mistake: e.g., “Devo aver fatto un errore” = “I must have made a mistake,” “Posso aver fatto un errore” = “I may have made a mistake.” Often followed by “da qualche parte” (“somewhere”).
target_language_example: Mi sa che devo aver fatto un errore.
native_language_example: I think I must have made a mistake.

additional_notes: Used after a verb like confessare/negare (to confess/deny) with di + infinitive in the past: confessare/negare di aver rubato i soldi. It’s the past infinitive of rubare (to steal) and refers to an action completed before the main verb or before now.
target_language_example: Ha negato di aver rubato i soldi.
native_language_example: He/She denied having stolen the money.

meaning: "to have found" (to have already found something).
additional_notes: This is the passato infinito of "trovare". It’s used to talk about a completed action in an infinitive clause, often after words like "per" (for), "di" (to/of), "senza" (without): e.g., "Grazie per aver trovato tempo" = "Thanks for finding/making time." It can also be negated: "non aver trovato" = "not to have found."
target_language_example: Sono felice di aver trovato un appartamento vicino al lavoro.
native_language_example: I’m happy to have found an apartment near work.

additional_notes: Used after another verb (often with di) to report or refer to a completed action in the past: dice di aver visto..., pensavo di aver visto..., dopo aver visto.... In speech you may also hear the longer form "avere visto".
target_language_example: Sono felice di aver visto Roma di notte.
native_language_example: I’m happy to have seen Rome at night.

meaning: to need (something); to be in need of.
additional_notes: Used to express necessity or need. It’s the infinitive form (often after verbs like pensare di, dire di, potere): “Penso di aver bisogno di riposo.” Conjugated form is “avere bisogno di” (ho bisogno di…, hai bisogno di…). It’s followed by a noun or pronoun: “Ho bisogno di aiuto / di te”.
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di parlare con te.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you.

additional_notes: Used with "di" to say what you’re afraid of: "aver paura di" + noun/pronoun ("aver paura delle api" = to be afraid of bees). You can also use "di cui" to mean "to be afraid of" in a more general way ("niente di cui aver paura" = nothing to be afraid of). Often appears in the negative as encouragement: "non aver paura" = don’t be afraid.
target_language_example: Non aver paura: sono qui con te.
native_language_example: Don’t be afraid: I’m here with you.

additional_notes: Used to say you have enough free time to date or be in a relationship. In the examples, “una” is completed by a feminine noun like “fidanzata” (girlfriend/fiancée), “morosa” (girlfriend, more informal/regional), or “ragazza” (girl/girlfriend). It can also work more generally as “avere tempo per + [someone/something]” = “to have time for…”.
target_language_example: In questo periodo non ho tempo per una ragazza: lavoro troppo.
native_language_example: Right now I don’t have time for a girlfriend: I work too much.

additional_notes: Infinitive perfect: avere + past participle (mentito). Used after prepositions like "per" to explain the reason/cause of something (e.g., "punito per avere mentito" = punished for having lied). It agrees with the subject only in context (punito/punita), not in the phrase itself.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace per avere mentito.
native_language_example: I'm sorry for having lied.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" + past participle "perso" to say someone has lost something. "Il suo" is a possessive meaning “his” (or sometimes “its”/formal “your”), and it must match the noun that follows: il suo treno (his train), la sua borsa (his bag), i suoi documenti (his documents), le sue chiavi (his keys). In real sentences, a noun usually follows "il suo" (e.g., "avere perso il suo treno").
target_language_example: Credo che abbia perso il suo telefono.
native_language_example: I think he lost his phone.

meaning: to have to do with; to be related to.
additional_notes: Used with a subject + conjugated form of avere + a che fare con + noun/pronoun. Often used to say something is (or isn’t) connected to something else: "Non ho niente a che fare con..." (= I have nothing to do with...). It can also mean "to deal with" someone/something in the sense of having dealings/contacts with them.
target_language_example: Questo problema ha a che fare con il lavoro.
native_language_example: This problem has to do with work.

additional_notes: Used to express necessity. Conjugate avere (ho, hai, ha, abbiamo, avete, hanno) + bisogno + di + noun/infinitive: "Ho bisogno di acqua" (I need water), "Ho bisogno di dormire" (I need to sleep). With a person as the object, Italian typically uses a pronoun + aiutare: "Ho bisogno di aiutarlo/la" (I need to help him/her) or "Ho bisogno del suo aiuto" (I need his/her help).
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di parlare con te.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you.

additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase "avere bisogno di" (literally "to have need of") + a noun. Very common to say what you need. You can change it by person/tense: "Ho bisogno di aiuto" (I need help), "Hai bisogno di aiuto?" (Do you need help?), "Aveva bisogno di aiuto" (He/She needed help).
target_language_example: Hai bisogno di aiuto con i compiti?
native_language_example: Do you need help with your homework?

additional_notes: Usually followed by di + noun/pronoun: avere cura di qualcuno/qualcosa (“to take care of someone/something”). It focuses on responsibility, attention, and caring (family, children, animals, possessions). Similar in meaning to prendersi cura di, often interchangeable.
target_language_example: Puoi avere cura del gatto mentre sono via?
native_language_example: Can you take care of the cat while I’m away?

meaning: to have children (to be a parent / to have kids).
additional_notes: Used when talking about having children in general—often about plans or desire to become a parent. It can also mean already being a parent (“Ho due figli” = “I have two children”), but in questions like “Vuoi/Vorresti avere dei figli?” it usually means “Do you want to have kids (someday)?”
target_language_example: Non so se voglio avere dei figli.
native_language_example: I don't know if I want to have kids.

meaning: to have an effect; to work (e.g., a medicine or remedy).
additional_notes: Used to say that something produces a result or works as intended. Often followed by “su” + person/thing affected: “avere effetto su di me/su qualcosa”. For medicines, Italians also commonly say “fare effetto” (same idea, often more natural in everyday speech).
target_language_example: Questo farmaco non ha effetto su di me.
native_language_example: This medicine doesn’t work on me.

additional_notes: Italian uses “avere” (to have) + a noun for many physical feelings/needs: avere fame (hungry), avere sete (thirsty), avere sonno (sleepy). You can say it about yourself (“Ho fame”) or with an infinitive after another verb (“Sembra avere fame” = “He seems to be hungry”).
target_language_example: Ho fame: possiamo mangiare qualcosa?
native_language_example: I’m hungry: can we eat something?

additional_notes: Literally “to have cold.” In Italian you use avere (to have) + a feeling: avere caldo (to be hot), avere fame (to be hungry), avere sete (to be thirsty). Conjugate avere: ho freddo (I’m cold), hai freddo (you’re cold), ha freddo (he/she is cold), abbiamo freddo (we’re cold), avete freddo (you all are cold), hanno freddo (they’re cold).
target_language_example: Ho freddo: puoi chiudere la finestra?
native_language_example: I’m cold—can you close the window?

additional_notes: Used especially in announcements, schedules, and formal writing to say when an event, meeting, ceremony, or process starts. It commonly appears with a time or date (e.g., "alle 9", "il 3 maggio"). Similar in meaning to "iniziare" / "cominciare" but more formal.
target_language_example: La conferenza avrà inizio alle nove.
native_language_example: The conference will begin at nine.

meaning: to have your hands tied (to be unable to act).
additional_notes: An idiom used when you can’t do what you want because of rules, lack of authority, a promise, or circumstances. Often followed by a reason: "Ho le mani legate: non posso..."
target_language_example: Vorrei aiutarti, ma ho le mani legate: non posso decidere io.
native_language_example: I’d like to help you, but my hands are tied: it’s not up to me.

additional_notes: Used mainly in formal or written Italian (news, notices, official communication) to say that an event happens. It’s commonly followed by a time or place expression: “La riunione avrà luogo domani” (time) / “avrà luogo a Roma” (place).
target_language_example: La conferenza avrà luogo venerdì alle 18 in sala A.
native_language_example: The conference will take place on Friday at 6 p.m. in room A.

additional_notes: In Italian you say you "have" hunger (avere fame), not "are" hungry. "Molta" intensifies it: very/really hungry. Often used with modal verbs like dovere (must) or in the past with avere/cominciare a (to start).
target_language_example: Dopo la palestra ho molta fame.
native_language_example: After the gym I’m very hungry.

avere nulla a che fare con

target_language_multi_word_term: avere nulla a che fare con
meaning: to have nothing to do with; to not want to be involved with.
additional_notes: Used to say you want no relationship, contact, or involvement with someone/something. Commonly used with a person (con lei/te/voi), but it can also be used with things or situations (con questa storia). Often appears with negation: non voglio avere nulla a che fare con...
target_language_example: Non voglio avere nulla a che fare con questo problema.
native_language_example: I don't want to have anything to do with this problem.

meaning: to be afraid; to be scared.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "avere" (to have) + "paura" (fear). Often followed by "di" or "del/della" + noun ("avere paura del buio" = to be afraid of the dark) or "di" + infinitive ("avere paura di parlare" = to be afraid to speak). You can ask "Perché hai paura?" (Why are you afraid?) or reassure someone with "Non avere paura" (Don’t be afraid).
target_language_example: Ho paura di volare, quindi prendo il treno.
native_language_example: I'm afraid of flying, so I take the train.

meaning: to keep in mind; to be aware of.
additional_notes: Used to say you remember something and are considering it while deciding or acting. Often followed by a clause with “che” (e.g., “Abbi presente che…” = “Keep in mind that…”).
target_language_example: Abbi presente che domani i negozi sono chiusi.
native_language_example: Keep in mind that the shops are closed tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s opinion/statement is correct: “Hai ragione” = “You’re right.” Often appears with modal verbs: “potresti avere ragione” = “you might be right.” The opposite is “avere torto” (to be wrong). Although it literally looks like “to have reason,” in English the natural translation is usually “to be right.”
target_language_example: Mi sa che hai ragione.
native_language_example: I think you’re right.

meaning: to make sense; to be meaningful.
additional_notes: Used to say something is logical, understandable, or worthwhile. Often in questions/negatives: “Ha senso?” (Does it make sense?), “Non ha senso” (It doesn’t make sense). You can also use it about usefulness: “Non ha senso farlo” (There’s no point in doing it).
target_language_example: Non ha senso discutere adesso: ne parliamo domani.
native_language_example: It doesn’t make sense to argue now: we’ll talk about it tomorrow.

additional_notes: In Italian you literally say “to have thirst” (avere + sete). Very common in everyday situations: Ho sete. / Hai sete? You can add intensity: avere molta sete (very thirsty), avere poca sete (a little thirsty).
target_language_example: Dopo la corsa ho sete: posso avere un bicchiere d’acqua?
native_language_example: After the run I’m thirsty: can I have a glass of water?

meaning: to be sleepy; to feel like sleeping.
additional_notes: Used with the verb avere (“to have”) to describe a state: Ho sonno (I’m sleepy). You can also specify degree: Ho molto/poco sonno (I’m very/a little sleepy), or ask: Hai sonno? (Are you sleepy?).
target_language_example: Scusa, ho sonno: vado a letto presto stasera.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m sleepy: I’m going to bed early tonight.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb avere and followed by the noun successo. It can refer to achieving a goal (Il piano è destinato ad avere successo) or being generally successful in life/work. Common with verbs like sperare di (to hope to), augurare di (to wish to), and expressions like essere destinato a (to be destined to).
target_language_example: Se lavori con costanza, puoi avere successo.
native_language_example: If you work consistently, you can succeed.

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s opinion, judgment, or statement is incorrect. Often contrasts with "avere ragione" (to be right). You can use it with different tenses and modals: "può avere torto" (may be wrong), "potrebbe avere torto" (might be wrong), "sapevo di avere torto" (I knew I was wrong).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, credo di avere torto.
native_language_example: Sorry, I think I’m wrong.

meaning: "to have a" (with a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have) plus the masculine singular indefinite article "un" before a noun: "avere un cane" = to have a dog. With some masculine nouns you use "uno" instead (e.g., "avere uno zaino", "avere uno studente", "avere uno psicologo"), and with feminine nouns you use "una" ("avere una sorella").
target_language_example: Vorrei avere un cane.
native_language_example: I’d like to have a dog.

meaning: to have a/an (before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns: avere una visione (a vision), una teoria (a theory), una tazza (a cup), una fine (an end), una moglie (a wife). In conversation it can be a request/question: “Potrei avere una…?” = “Could I have a…?”. Compare: avere un (masculine), avere un’ (before a vowel).
target_language_example: Posso avere una bottiglia d’acqua, per favore?
native_language_example: Can I have a bottle of water, please?

additional_notes: Past infinitive of "fare" ("avere" + past participle "fatto") with the direct object pronoun "lo" (= "it"). Used to say that an action was completed before another action/time, often after verbs like "dire", "essere felice", "pentirsi", etc.: "Disse di averlo fatto" = "He said he had done it."
target_language_example: Mi dispiace di averlo fatto.
native_language_example: I'm sorry I did it.

additional_notes: Used after expressions of thought/opinion like “pensavo che…” (“I thought that…”). “Avesse” is the imperfect subjunctive of “avere” and is common in reported thoughts about an uncertain or assumed situation in the past. “Una partita di calcio” means “a soccer match” (Italian “calcio” = soccer).
target_language_example: Pensavo che Luca avesse una partita di calcio domenica.
native_language_example: I thought Luca had a soccer match on Sunday.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of comprare: avete (you have) + comprato (bought). Used with “you” plural (you all) or polite/formal “you” (Lei/Loro, depending on context). In questions, intonation or context can make it mean “Did you buy…?”
target_language_example: Avete comprato anche il pane?
native_language_example: Did you buy bread too?

meaning: "you met" / "have you met" (you plural or polite).
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of *conoscere* with **voi** (you all) or formal **Lei** (you). It’s used when asking or saying when/where you first met someone: *Dove avete conosciuto…?* In some contexts it can also mean “got to know” someone, but in questions like these it usually means “met.”
target_language_example: Dove avete conosciuto Laura?
native_language_example: Where did you meet Laura?

meaning: "you gave" / "you have given" (to give — 2nd person plural or formal).
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of the verb "dare" (to give): "voi/Lei (pl.) avete dato". Used with a direct object (Avete dato una chiave), often with an indirect object introduced by "a" (Avete dato una chiave a qualcuno; Avete dato loro quel cane). Common pattern: "dare da mangiare" = "to feed" (literally “to give to eat”). Another common use is "dare del/della + insult/label" = "to call someone ..." (Mi avete dato della codarda = You called me a coward).
target_language_example: Mi avete dato un consiglio molto utile.
native_language_example: You gave me very useful advice.

meaning: "have you decided to" (you plural or formal "you").
additional_notes: "Avete" is the present of *avere* used to form the past tense (*passato prossimo*) with *decidere*: *avete deciso* = "you have decided". It’s used to ask or state a decision made in the past that matters now, and it’s followed by *di* + infinitive: *avete deciso di andare/tornare...* It can address more than one person (you all) or one person formally (Lei/voi style, less common today).
target_language_example: Avete deciso di restare a casa stasera?
native_language_example: Have you decided to stay home tonight?

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "dire" for "voi". Used when addressing more than one person, or one person in a formal/plural address (e.g., in some regions/contexts). Often followed by: "a" + person (avete detto a Tom…), a direct object pronoun (me lo avete detto = you told it to me), or an indirect object pronoun (gli/le/ci avete detto… = you told him/her/us…).
target_language_example: Mi avete detto la verità?
native_language_example: Did you tell me the truth?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "dire" in the passato prossimo: "avete detto" = "you (plural or formal) said/told". It’s typically followed by "a" + a person (the indirect object): "Avete detto a Tom…?" = "Did you tell Tom…?" You can then add what was told (often with a clause or a pronoun like "cosa", "quello che").
target_language_example: Avete detto a Maria che domani non veniamo?
native_language_example: Did you tell Maria that we’re not coming tomorrow?

meaning: "you said that" (addressing more than one person).
additional_notes: Uses passato prossimo of dire: "avete detto" = "you (plural) said" / "you have said." It’s followed by "che" to introduce what was said. "Avete" is the voi form, used when speaking to a group (not the polite singular "Lei," which would be "ha detto che").
target_language_example: Avete detto che la riunione iniziava alle tre, giusto?
native_language_example: You said that the meeting started at three, right?

additional_notes: Past tense of "fare" addressed to "voi" (you all) or formal "you" in some contexts. It’s used to talk about actions completed in the past ("You did...") or with a link to the present ("You have done..."). Often followed by a noun (avete fatto i compiti = you did the homework) or by something/anything/nothing (avete fatto qualcosa/niente). In questions it’s very common: "Perché avete fatto...?" = "Why did you do...?"
target_language_example: Avete fatto una prenotazione per stasera?
native_language_example: Did you make a reservation for tonight?

additional_notes: "Avete" is the present tense of "avere" used to form the passato prossimo with "giocato" (= played). It addresses "you" plural (voi) or can be used as a polite/formal "you" in some contexts. "A tennis" is used with the verb "giocare" to mean playing a sport/game (giocare a + sport).
target_language_example: Avete giocato a tennis questa settimana?
native_language_example: Have you played tennis this week?

additional_notes: Used with "voi" (you plural), either to address more than one person or, in some regions, as a polite form. It commonly appears in questions about whether something has been done yet (e.g., "Avete già + past participle?"). For one person formally, you’d usually say "Ha già..." (Lei). Word order can change with pronouns: "L’avete già trovata?" = "Have you already found her/it?"
target_language_example: Avete già finito di mangiare?
native_language_example: Have you already finished eating?

meaning: "have you ever" / "have you ever (not)" (you plural or formal).
additional_notes: Used in questions (and sometimes negative statements) with the present perfect to ask about life experience up to now. It refers to "you" as voi (plural) or as formal "you" (e.g., to one person in polite speech). With negation: "non avete mai..." = "you have never..." / "you never...".
target_language_example: Avete mai visitato Roma?
native_language_example: Have you ever visited Rome?

meaning: “Have you ever eaten…?” (asking about someone’s past experience).
additional_notes: Used to ask one or more people (voi) if they have ever eaten/tried something at any point in their life. It uses the present perfect (avere + mangiato) and often introduces a food you’re curious about: Avete mai mangiato + [food]? You can answer with: Sì, l’ho mangiato / No, non l’ho mai mangiato.
target_language_example: Avete mai mangiato il sushi?
native_language_example: Have you ever eaten sushi?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (voi) or to be polite/formal with one person (Lei) if they have ever heard something or someone before. Often followed by an infinitive (sentito + suonare/cantare...) or by a noun (sentito questa parola).
target_language_example: Avete mai sentito parlare di questa città?
native_language_example: Have you ever heard of this city?

meaning: "Have you ever seen...?" (asking if someone has ever seen something at any time).
additional_notes: "Avete" is the 2nd person plural (voi) of "avere" in the present tense, used for addressing multiple people or as a polite/formal "you". It’s typically followed by a person/thing + an infinitive ("Avete mai visto Tom ballare?") or a noun ("Avete mai visto un orso?"). Often used with "prima" to mean "before" ("... prima?").
target_language_example: Avete mai visto questo film?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen this movie?

meaning: "Have you ever seen a …?" (to more than one person).
additional_notes: Used to ask a group (or one person politely with "voi") if they have ever seen something. "mai" = "ever" and usually goes between the auxiliary and the past participle: "avete mai visto…?" Change the article as needed: "un" (masc. singular), "uno" (before s+consonant, z, gn, etc.), "una" (fem. singular). With one person informally: "Hai mai visto un/una…?".
target_language_example: Avete mai visto una lucertola così grande?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen a lizard this big?

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "mangiare" for "voi" (2nd-person plural). Use it when talking to more than one person: "Avete mangiato?" = "Have you eaten?" In a statement it means "You ate..." / "You have eaten...". (In some contexts "voi" can be used as a polite form, but the most common polite singular is "Lei ha mangiato".)
target_language_example: Avete mangiato qualcosa oggi?
native_language_example: Have you eaten anything today?

meaning: "have you spoken/talked with" (you plural or formal).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has talked with a person (con + name/pronoun). It’s the present perfect of parlare: avete parlato = “you have spoken / did you speak?”. Often followed by a topic: a riguardo (“about it”), di... (“about...”), or ne (“about it”) as in “Ne avete parlato con loro?”.
target_language_example: Avete parlato con il medico di questa cosa?
native_language_example: Have you spoken with the doctor about this?

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "prendere" used with "avere": "voi" + "avete" + past participle "preso". Used for many meanings of "prendere": taking (medicine, an object), getting/buying something ("Dove avete preso...?" = Where did you get it?), and in set phrases like "prendere parte" (to take part/participate). Word order changes with questions: "Avete preso...?" = Have you taken...?.
target_language_example: Avete preso i biglietti online?
native_language_example: Did you get the tickets online?

meaning: "have you heard" / "did you hear" (you all / formal you).
additional_notes: Second-person plural of "sentire" (to hear). It can mean literally hearing a sound/words, or more generally "to hear about" news (often with "di": "Avete sentito di...?" = "Have you heard about ...?"). Used for speaking to a group, or as the polite/formal "you" in some regions/contexts.
target_language_example: Avete sentito che domani scioperano i treni?
native_language_example: Have you heard that the trains are on strike tomorrow?

additional_notes: Second-person plural of the passato prossimo of trovare (“to find”). Used when speaking to more than one person (voi) or as a polite/formal “you” (especially in some regions) to ask if someone has found something, like a job.
target_language_example: Avete trovato una soluzione?
native_language_example: Have you found a solution?

additional_notes: Past tense of vedere (to see). Used with voi (you all) or as the polite form for addressing one person (like English “you” but formal). Often used in questions to ask if someone has seen a person/thing, or has watched something (a show, a movie). The object can be a noun (Avete visto Tom?), a pronoun (Lo avete visto?), or a whole clause (È questo quello che avete visto?).
target_language_example: Avete visto il mio telefono da qualche parte?
native_language_example: Have you (all) seen my phone anywhere?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (voi) if they have seen something, using the past tense (passato prossimo) of vedere: avete visto = “you have seen / did you see”. It’s often followed by a masculine singular noun with il (il film, il giardino). Before a vowel, il becomes l’: Avete visto l’aereo? In some regions/older usage, voi can also be a very formal singular “you,” but standard polite singular is Lei (Ha visto...?).
target_language_example: Scusate, avete visto il mio zaino?
native_language_example: Excuse me, have you seen my backpack?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (voi) if they’ve seen something that belongs to you. Very common when you’ve lost an object or can’t find it. Agree the ending with the noun you’re looking for: il mio (masc. singular), la mia (fem. singular), i miei (masc. plural), le mie (fem. plural). In informal singular you’d say: Hai visto il mio ...?
target_language_example: Scusate, avete visto il mio zaino?
native_language_example: Excuse me, have you seen my backpack?

meaning: "Have you seen this?" (speaking to more than one person).
additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people whether they have seen something/someone. It uses the plural "voi" form: "avete visto" = "have you seen". "Questo" means "this" (masculine singular) and can be followed by a noun (e.g., "questo documento") or used alone. For a single person you’d say: "Hai visto questo?" For feminine: "avete visto questa ...?"
target_language_example: Scusate, avete visto questo passaporto?
native_language_example: Excuse me, have you seen this passport?

additional_notes: "Avete" is the present tense of *avere* (to have) for *voi* (you all). "Avere bisogno (di)" is the common way to say "to need" in Italian, usually followed by **di + noun** (Avete bisogno di aiuto?) or **di + infinitive** (Avete bisogno di parlare?). Often used in questions and offers of help.
target_language_example: Avete bisogno di aiuto?
native_language_example: Do you (all) need help?

additional_notes: Form of "avere bisogno di" (to need). "Avete" is for "you" plural (you all) or formal "you" (e.g., speaking to customers). It’s followed by "di" + an infinitive (Avete bisogno di aggiornare…) or "di" + a noun with an article (Avete bisogno di un dizionario?). In questions, intonation or a question mark makes it “Do you need…?”
target_language_example: Avete bisogno di aiuto con la prenotazione?
native_language_example: Do you need help with the booking?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has certain items or people (e.g., in a shop, hotel, restaurant, or talking to a family). "Avete" is 2nd-person plural (you all) and is also used as the polite/formal "you" in some regions. "Dei" is a partitive meaning "some/any" before a masculine plural noun; the feminine plural form is "delle" (Avete delle camere?), and for plural nouns starting with s+consonant, z, ps, gn, etc., it becomes "degli" (Avete degli asciugamani?). Often in English it translates as "any" in questions.
target_language_example: Scusi, avete dei biglietti per oggi?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you have any tickets for today?

meaning: “do you (plural/formal) intend to…?” / “are you planning to…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s intention or plan. It’s the verb phrase "avere intenzione di" (to intend/plan to) conjugated for "voi" (you all) or formal "you" in some contexts, followed by an infinitive (e.g., cominciare, ritornare).
target_language_example: Avete intenzione di venire con noi domani?
native_language_example: Are you planning to come with us tomorrow?

meaning: 'are you afraid of' / 'are you scared to'.
additional_notes: Used when speaking to more than one person ("voi"), asking if they’re afraid of someone/something or afraid to do something. If it’s followed by a verb, use "di" + infinitive: "Avete paura di dirlo?" (= Are you afraid to say it?). If it’s followed by a noun/pronoun, it means "afraid of": "Avete paura di me?" (= Are you afraid of me?).
target_language_example: Avete paura di fare una domanda?
native_language_example: Are you afraid to ask a question?

meaning: “you have a …” / “do you have a …?” (to a group).
additional_notes: "Avete" is the 2nd-person plural of "avere" (to have), used when speaking to two or more people ("you all"). With rising intonation or a question mark, it’s a common way to ask if someone has something available: "Avete un…?" = “Do you have a…?”. "Un" is the masculine singular article (“a/an”); for feminine you use "una" (e.g., "Avete una penna?").
target_language_example: Scusi, avete un tavolo libero?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you have a free table?

additional_notes: Used to challenge or question whether the people you’re speaking to (voi) object to someone/something, or have an issue with it. Can refer to people (con lui/lei/loro/me) or things/ideas (con questo, con quello che...). In speech it can sound confrontational depending on tone; for one person you’d say “Hai un problema con…?” and more formal/plural “Ha/Avete un problema con…?”.
target_language_example: Avete un problema con questa soluzione?
native_language_example: Do you have a problem with this solution?

meaning: "do you have a…?" / "you have a…" (addressing you-plural or polite).
additional_notes: From the verb "avere" (to have). "Avete" is 2nd-person plural: used when speaking to more than one person (you all), and also commonly as a polite/formal way to address one person (e.g., a customer, receptionist, waiter). "Una" is "a" for feminine singular nouns, so it’s followed by a feminine noun (e.g., una prenotazione, una stanza).
target_language_example: Scusi, avete una penna?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you have a pen?

additional_notes:
Imperfetto of “avere bisogno (di)” = “to need”. Used for an ongoing need in the past, a habitual need, or to describe a past situation/background. It’s followed by:
- di + noun/pronoun: “Aveva bisogno di lei.” = “He/She needed her.”
- di + infinitive (often passive): “Il bagno aveva bisogno di essere pulito.” = “The bathroom needed to be cleaned.”
target_language_example: Da piccolo, aveva bisogno di dormire presto.
native_language_example: When he was little, he needed to go to sleep early.

additional_notes: Imperfect past of “avere bisogno di” (to need). Used for an ongoing situation in the past, a repeated past need, or to set background (“he/she needed…”). Follow with a noun/pronoun (aveva bisogno di lei/noi) or an infinitive, often passive: “aveva bisogno di essere + past participle” (needed to be cleaned/done).
target_language_example: Quando ero bambino, avevo bisogno di più tempo per fare i compiti.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I needed more time to do homework.

additional_notes: Imperfetto of "avere bisogno di" (to need): "aveva bisogno" = "he/she used to need" or "he/she needed" (ongoing situation in the past). "Di" + a noun tells what is needed: "di soldi" = "(some) money" (not specific bills/coins). Often used with a subject (lui/lei/Tom) or after "che" in reported speech: "mi ha detto che aveva bisogno di soldi".
target_language_example: Quando ha perso il lavoro, aveva bisogno di soldi.
native_language_example: When he lost his job, he needed money.

meaning: he/she needed space (time/room away from someone or something).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of "avere bisogno di" (to need): "aveva bisogno di" = "he/she needed" or "he/she was in need of". "Spazio" can mean physical room or, very often, emotional/personal space (especially in relationships). You can change the subject: "Lui/Lei aveva bisogno di spazio".
target_language_example: Dopo la discussione, mi ha detto che aveva bisogno di spazio.
native_language_example: After the argument, he/she told me that he/she needed space.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of "avere" (to have): "aveva" = "he/she had" or "he/she was having" in the past. "Dei" often means "some" (unspecified amount). Used for practical difficulties (e.g., at work) or personal/relationship issues ("con lei/lui" = "with her/him").
target_language_example: Pensavo che avesse dei problemi a casa.
native_language_example: I thought he/she was having some problems at home.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **avere** (“to have”) with **fame** (“hunger”) to talk about being hungry. **Aveva** is the **imperfetto** (imperfect past) form of *avere* for **lui/lei** (“he/she”), often used for background situations or ongoing states in the past (e.g., *stamattina* = “this morning”).
target_language_example: Dopo la passeggiata, aveva fame e ha mangiato un panino.
native_language_example: After the walk, he was hungry and ate a sandwich.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (aveva) to describe an ongoing emotional state in the past. You can change the subject and tense: ho il cuore infranto (I’m heartbroken), aveva il cuore infranto (he/she was heartbroken). Common in serious or emotional contexts (breakups, loss, disappointment).
target_language_example: Dopo la rottura, aveva il cuore infranto e non voleva uscire.
native_language_example: After the breakup, he was heartbroken and didn’t want to go out.

meaning: he/she intended to; was planning to.
additional_notes: Imperfect past of "avere intenzione di" (“to intend/plan to”), used to talk about someone’s intention in the past (often a plan that was in progress, not yet completed, or later changed). Followed by an infinitive: "aveva intenzione di + verb".
target_language_example: Avevo intenzione di chiamarti ieri, ma poi mi sono dimenticato.
native_language_example: I was planning to call you yesterday, but then I forgot.

additional_notes: Uses the expression "avere nostalgia di" + a person/place/thing to say you miss it. "Casa" here means “home.” "Aveva" is the imperfect tense (“he/she used to have / was having”), often used for an ongoing feeling in the past.
target_language_example: Quando era all’estero, aveva nostalgia di casa.
native_language_example: When he was abroad, he was homesick.

additional_notes: Imperfect past of "avere paura" (to be afraid). Used to describe an ongoing state in the past or background context. Often followed by "di" + noun/infinitive (e.g., "aveva paura di cadere") or "del/della" + noun (="di" + "il/la").
target_language_example: Da bambino aveva paura del buio.
native_language_example: As a child, he was afraid of the dark.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of "avere paura di" (to be afraid of / to be afraid to do). Use "aveva paura di" to talk about a past, ongoing state of fear. It can be followed by an infinitive to mean “was afraid to (do something)” (e.g., "andare", "dire"), or by a noun/pronoun to mean “was afraid of (someone/something)" (e.g., "di Sami").
target_language_example: Da bambino, aveva paura di dormire da solo.
native_language_example: As a child, he was afraid to sleep alone.

additional_notes: From the expression **avere ragione** (“to be right”). **Aveva** is the imperfect tense of *avere* and often corresponds to “was”/“used to be” right in the past, depending on context. You can add **riguardo a / su** to say “about” someone/something: *aveva ragione su di lei* = “he was right about her.” Note: **avere ragione di + infinitive** means “to have reason to…”: *Non aveva ragione di essere arrabbiato* = “He had no reason to be angry.”
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, avevi ragione tu.
native_language_example: Sorry, you were right.

additional_notes: "Avere torto" means "to be wrong". "Aveva" is the imperfect past tense (used for an ongoing state in the past or background information), often translated as "was" or "used to be". You can also ask "Chi aveva torto?" = "Who was wrong?"
target_language_example: Pensavo che fosse colpa mia, ma avevo torto.
native_language_example: I thought it was my fault, but I was wrong.

additional_notes: Imperfetto of "avere" + "un". Used to say someone/something had (or used to have) something in the past, often describing a state or ongoing situation/background: "Aveva un problema" (He/She had a problem), "Il latte aveva un cattivo sapore" (The milk had a bad taste). "Aveva" can mean he, she, or it depending on context; with feminine nouns it becomes "aveva una".
target_language_example: Da bambino aveva un cane.
native_language_example: As a child, he had a dog.

additional_notes: Used when talking about (usually criminal) investigations to say someone could prove they were elsewhere at the time.
