You can change the verb/person: ho un alibi (I have an alibi), hai un alibi? (Do you have an alibi?), aveva un alibi? (Did he/she have an alibi?). Often followed by a time expression: per quella notte / per ieri sera.
target_language_example: Non poteva essere lui: aveva un alibi per quella sera.
native_language_example: It couldn’t have been him: he had an alibi for that evening.

meaning: "he/she had a problem with the …" (an issue with …; sometimes also "had a problem with …" meaning addiction).
additional_notes: Imperfetto of "avere" (aveva) is used for a past ongoing/background situation: "he/she used to have" or "he/she had". The article changes with the noun: con la (feminine singular), con il (masculine singular), con l’ (before a vowel), con i/gli/le (plural). With things like "la macchina/l’automobile" it usually means a mechanical/technical issue; with "la droga" it can mean drug addiction.
target_language_example: Aveva un problema con la sua carta di credito.
native_language_example: He/She had a problem with his/her credit card.

additional_notes: From avere (to have) in the imperfetto: aveva = “he/she had / used to have / was having.” It’s followed by a feminine singular noun with una (“a”). The subject is often understood from context (e.g., Tom aveva una… = “Tom had a…”).
target_language_example: Quando era piccolo, aveva una bicicletta rossa.
native_language_example: When he was little, he had a red bike.

additional_notes: "Avere una cotta per [persona]" means to have a (usually romantic) crush on someone, often used for a teenage-style or not-yet-serious attraction. "Aveva" is the imperfect past (he/she had/used to have), so it describes an ongoing feeling in the past; in the present you’ll often hear "ha una cotta per".
target_language_example: Da adolescente, avevo una cotta per il mio compagno di classe.
native_language_example: As a teenager, I had a crush on my classmate.

additional_notes: Past tense (imperfetto) of "avere voglia di". Used to express a desire or mood to do something at that time (often ongoing, repeated, or background in a story). Followed by an infinitive verb: "aveva voglia di + verb" (e.g., "aveva voglia di dormire").
target_language_example: Ieri sera avevo voglia di restare a casa.
native_language_example: Last night I felt like staying home.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of "avere bisogno di" (to need). Used for an ongoing/continuous need in the past or to describe a situation in the past ("we needed..."). It’s followed by a noun or a pronoun: "...di informazioni", "...di lei/te".
target_language_example: Avevamo bisogno di aiuto, ma non sapevamo a chi chiedere.
native_language_example: We needed help, but we didn’t know who to ask.

additional_notes: Past tense (imperfetto) of “avere bisogno di” = “to need.” Used for ongoing/repeated need in the past, or to describe a past situation/background. Structure: avere bisogno di + noun (avevano bisogno di aiuto/denaro) or + pronoun (avevano bisogno di voi).
target_language_example: Quando erano piccoli, avevano bisogno di molta attenzione.
native_language_example: When they were little, they needed a lot of attention.

meaning: “you had said that …” (talking about what someone previously said).
additional_notes: Used to remind someone of a past statement or to point out what they previously claimed. It’s the past perfect of dire: avevi detto = “you had said/told”. Often followed by che + a clause. In questions/negatives (Non avevi detto che…?) it can mean “Didn’t you say that…?”
target_language_example: Avevi detto che saresti arrivato alle otto.
native_language_example: You had said you would arrive at eight.

meaning: "you were right" (informal singular), in the past.
additional_notes: Used to tell one person (tu) that they were correct about something, often after you realize it later. Common with prepositions: avevi ragione a + infinitive ("you were right to..."); avevi ragione riguardo a / su ("you were right about..."). In the plural/formal you’d say: avevate ragione (you all were right) / aveva ragione (he/she was right) / aveva ragione (Lei was right).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace: avevi ragione su tutto.
native_language_example: I’m sorry: you were right about everything.

additional_notes: Past perfect of dire (“to say/tell”): avevo detto = “I had said/I had told.” Used for something you said before another past moment. Often appears in questions like Che ti avevo detto? (“What did I tell you?”) and with di + infinitive to report an instruction: Vi avevo detto di restare… (“I had told you to stay…”). The person you told can be shown with an indirect object pronoun: ti/le/vi avevo detto (“I told you/her/you all”).
target_language_example: Te l’avevo detto di non toccarlo.
native_language_example: I told you not to touch it.

meaning: “I had said that / I had told (you) that.”
additional_notes: Uses the trapassato prossimo (pluperfect) of dire (“to say/tell”) to refer to something you said earlier, often to remind someone or complain. Very common in rhetorical questions like “Non ti/vi avevo detto che...?” = “Didn’t I tell you that...?” The “you” is usually understood from context or made explicit with ti (to you, informal singular) or vi (to you, plural/formal).
target_language_example: Te l’avevo detto che sarebbe successo.
native_language_example: I told you it would happen.

additional_notes: Used to remind someone of an earlier instruction or suggestion. Literally “I had said to…”, followed by an infinitive (e.g., fare, restare, prendere). The pronoun can change: ti/vi avevo detto di… = “I had told you (sing./plural) to…”. Often has a reproachful tone in context (“I told you to…”).
target_language_example: Ti avevo detto di non uscire senza chiavi.
native_language_example: I had told you not to go out without keys.

additional_notes: Used to remind someone of a previous warning/instruction, often with an annoyed or reproachful tone. It’s the imperfetto of avere + past participle (ho detto) to mean “I had said/told,” followed by di non + infinitive: "Avevo detto di non + verb". You can change the object: "ti/le/vi avevo detto di non…" = "I had told you/her/you (plural) not to…".
target_language_example: Ti avevo detto di non aprire quella porta!
native_language_example: I had told you not to open that door!

meaning: “I had never seen” (used with non… mai).
additional_notes: It’s the trapassato prossimo of vedere (“to see”) in the 1st person singular: avevo visto = “I had seen.” With non… mai it becomes “I had never seen.” Often followed by prima (“before”) for emphasis: Non avevo mai visto… prima = “I’d never seen… before.”
target_language_example: Non avevo mai visto una città così grande.
native_language_example: I had never seen such a big city.

additional_notes: Past tense (imperfetto) of "avere bisogno di" + noun/infinitive, used to say you needed something (often as background, ongoing, or not tied to one single moment). "Di" is required: avevo bisogno di cibo / di dormire. Common variants: "ho bisogno di" (I need), "avevi/aveva/avevamo... bisogno di".
target_language_example: Ieri avevo bisogno di dormire presto.
native_language_example: Yesterday I needed to go to sleep early.

meaning: I was planning to / I meant to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to say you had an intention in the past, often something you planned but may not have done. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., andare, chiamare, aiutare). Note the tense: "avevo" is imperfect, so it often implies an ongoing intention or background plan.
target_language_example: Avevo intenzione di studiare, ma poi mi sono addormentato.
native_language_example: I was planning to study, but then I fell asleep.

meaning: "I was afraid of" / "I was afraid to".
additional_notes: Imperfetto of "avere paura" (to be afraid), used to describe an ongoing or habitual fear in the past. Use "di" + noun (avevo paura di mio padre = I was afraid of my father) or "di" + infinitive (avevo paura di prendere un raffreddore = I was afraid of catching a cold).
target_language_example: Da bambino avevo paura di parlare in classe.
native_language_example: As a child, I was afraid to speak in class.

additional_notes: Imperfetto of the expression "avere ragione" (to be right). Used to say you were correct about something in the past, often with emphasis like "E avevo ragione io" = "And I was the one who was right." You can add what you were right about with "su" (e.g., "Avevo ragione su di te").
target_language_example: Te l’avevo detto: avevo ragione.
native_language_example: I told you: I was right.

meaning: "I felt like" / "I wanted to" (in the past).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a desire/urge you had at a particular moment in the past. It’s often closer to “I felt like…” than a firm plan. The verb after di stays in the infinitive (di parlare, di urlare). Related forms: ho voglia di (present), avevi voglia di (you had), aveva voglia di (he/she had), avevamo voglia di (we had).
target_language_example: Ieri sera avevo voglia di restare a casa.
native_language_example: Last night I felt like staying at home.

meaning: “should have” / “ought to have” (past advice or criticism).
additional_notes: Conditional perfect of dovere (“to have to / must”). Used to say someone didn’t do something in the past but it would have been the right thing to do: Avrebbe dovuto + infinitive. Often implies regret, reproach, or a missed obligation (“he should have… but he didn’t”).
target_language_example: Avresti dovuto chiamarmi prima di partire.
native_language_example: You should have called me before leaving.

additional_notes: Conditional perfect of dovere + essere: expresses regret, criticism, or an expectation that didn’t happen in the past. Used with a noun/adjective ("avrebbe dovuto essere un problema" = it should have been a problem) or with a past participle to form the passive ("avrebbe dovuto essere fatto/preso/punito" = should have been done/taken/punished). Often implies "but it wasn’t / didn’t happen".
target_language_example: La riunione avrebbe dovuto essere ieri, ma è stata rimandata.
native_language_example: The meeting should have been yesterday, but it was postponed.

meaning: “would have done / would do” (conditional past of “fare”).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that was expected, hypothetical, or reported as something someone said they would do. It’s the conditional past of fare: avrebbe (he/she/it would have) + fatto (done/made). Often appears in indirect speech after a past verb (e.g., disse che avrebbe fatto...), and with expressions like “avrebbe fatto meglio a...” = “he/she would have been better off (to)...”. It can also mean “it would be (weather)” in phrases like “avrebbe fatto freddo” = “it would be cold.”
target_language_example: Non sapevo cosa avrebbe fatto al mio posto.
native_language_example: I didn’t know what he/she would have done in my place.

meaning: “could have / would have been able to” (conditional past of potere).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a possibility or ability in the past seen from a hypothetical/conditional point of view. Common in regrets/criticism (“He could have told me”) and in imagined outcomes (“She could have caught a cold”). Often followed by an infinitive: avrebbe potuto dire/fare/andare. Negative: non avrebbe potuto (“couldn’t have / wouldn’t have been able to”).
target_language_example: Avrei voluto chiamarti, ma non avrei potuto farlo.
native_language_example: I wanted to call you, but I couldn’t have done it.

meaning: “I should have” / “I ought to have” (in hindsight).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something you now think was the right thing to do, but you didn’t do it. It’s the conditional past of dovere (“to have to / should”), often followed by an infinitive: avrei dovuto + dire/fare/andare… Negative: non avrei dovuto (“I shouldn’t have”). Questions are common for second-guessing: Non avrei dovuto dirlo? (“Shouldn’t I have told him/it?”).
target_language_example: Avrei dovuto studiare di più per l’esame.
native_language_example: I should have studied more for the exam.

meaning: "I should have done" / "I was supposed to do" (but didn’t).
additional_notes: This is the conditional past of *dovere* + *fare*. It’s used to talk about a missed duty/expectation, often with regret or criticism. You can change the subject: *avresti dovuto fare* (you should have done), *avrebbe dovuto fare* (he/she should have done), *avremmo dovuto fare* (we should have done). Often followed by what you should have done: *Avrei dovuto fare di più* (I should have done more).
target_language_example: Avrei dovuto fare una domanda prima di firmare.
native_language_example: I should have asked a question before signing.

additional_notes: Used with the conditional of avere (avrei) plus mai (“ever”). Very commonly appears with non to express something you would never do or would never have done: Non lo avrei mai fatto. In past contexts it often corresponds to English “would never have …”. The verb after it is typically a past participle (avrei mai dimenticato/a, avrei mai dato, etc.).
target_language_example: Non l’avrei mai detto a nessuno.
native_language_example: I would never have told anyone.

additional_notes: Used with the conditional perfect (avrei dovuto + infinitive) to say you regret a past action or decision. It often appears with a negative: non avrei mai dovuto + infinitive = 'I should never have (done something)'.
target_language_example: Non avrei mai dovuto accettare quell'offerta.
native_language_example: I should never have accepted that offer.

meaning: “I could have” / “I would have been able to.”
additional_notes: Conditional perfect of potere (“can/to be able to”), used for past possibilities or abilities (often hypothetical or unreal). Common in “how could I have…?” questions (Come avrei potuto…?). Often appears in conditional sentences with se (“if”): Se + imperfect subjunctive …, avrei potuto + infinitive (“If…, I could have / would have been able to …”).
target_language_example: Avrei potuto aiutarti, ma non lo sapevo.
native_language_example: I could have helped you, but I didn’t know.

meaning: "I would have liked" / "I would have wanted".
additional_notes: Past conditional of "volere" (io). Used to express a wish or preference about the past (often with regret: you wanted something but it didn’t happen). Common patterns: (1) "avrei voluto" + infinitive: "Avrei voluto venire." (2) "avrei voluto che" + subjunctive (often past subjunctive for past events): "Avrei voluto che tu fossi venuto." It can also sound softer/more polite than a direct "volevo" in some contexts.
target_language_example: Avrei voluto chiamarti ieri, ma ero troppo stanco.
native_language_example: I would have liked to call you yesterday, but I was too tired.

meaning: "you should have" / "you ought to have" (talking about something in the past).
additional_notes: This is the conditional perfect of "dovere" ("to have to / must"). It’s used to say what someone was expected to do in the past, often with a tone of advice, criticism, or regret. "Avreste" is 2nd person plural ("you all"), and it can also be used as a polite form in some contexts.
target_language_example: Avreste dovuto dirmelo prima.
native_language_example: You should have told me earlier.

meaning: “you should have” / “you ought to have” (but you didn’t).
additional_notes: Conditional perfect of dovere: avresti (you would have) + dovuto (had to/should). Used to express regret, criticism, or advice about a past action not done. Usually followed by an infinitive: Avresti dovuto + verbo (es. dire, fare, rifiutare).
target_language_example: Avresti dovuto chiamarmi prima di uscire.
native_language_example: You should have called me before going out.

meaning: “you could have” (past possibility/ability; often implying regret or criticism).
additional_notes: Formed by the conditional of avere (avresti) + past participle potuto. Used to talk about something someone had the chance/ability to do in the past but didn’t: Avresti potuto dirlo = “You could have said it.” It can sound like a reproach (“you should have”) depending on tone/context. Commonly followed by an infinitive: avresti potuto fare/chiedere/dire…
target_language_example: Avresti potuto avvisarmi prima.
native_language_example: You could have warned me earlier.

additional_notes: Future tense of avere successo (“to succeed”). Used after a subject (explicit or implied): Tom avrà successo = “Tom will succeed.” It can also refer to things (an idea, a plan, a business): Il progetto avrà successo = “The project will be a success.”
target_language_example: Sono sicuro che la tua idea avrà successo.
native_language_example: I’m sure your idea will succeed.

meaning: had some problems; had trouble (doing something).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have) to say you experienced difficulties. Often followed by "a" + infinitive: "abbiamo avuto dei problemi a entrare" = "we had trouble getting in." The "dei" means "some" (not specific problems).
target_language_example: Ho avuto dei problemi a trovare parcheggio.
native_language_example: I had trouble finding parking.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase used with the verb "avere" in the passato prossimo: "ha avuto successo" (he/she/it was successful), "hanno avuto successo" (they were successful). Common with people, projects, plans, missions, etc.: "La missione ha avuto successo."
target_language_example: Il progetto ha avuto successo grazie al tuo aiuto.
native_language_example: The project was successful thanks to your help.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" to talk about having/experiencing something in the past (events/conditions like "un ictus", "un crollo nervoso", or situations like "un esame", "un test") or to say you possessed something (e.g., "avere un pianoforte"). You’ll also see it inside longer forms like "aver avuto" = "to have had" (e.g., "Vorrei aver avuto..." = "I wish I had had...").
target_language_example: Ho avuto un problema con la macchina ieri.
native_language_example: I had a problem with the car yesterday.

additional_notes: Past tense of "avere un incidente" (to have an accident). Very common for traffic accidents (car/bike), but it can also mean any kind of accident. Often used with an implied subject: "(Lui/Lei) ha avuto un incidente". Note: Italian "incidente" often means "accident"; it looks like English "incident" but is usually more serious/accidental than the general English word.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ho avuto un incidente e arrivo in ritardo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I had an accident and I’m arriving late.

meaning: “had a” / “have had a” (past of avere + a feminine noun).
additional_notes: This is the past participle of **avere** (“to have”) used in the **passato prossimo**: *ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno avuto una...*. It’s followed by a **feminine singular noun** (e.g., *una bambina, una cotta, una morosa, una chiacchierata, una esperienza*). It’s used for many meanings of “have”: having an experience (*ho avuto un’esperienza*), having a chat (*abbiamo avuto una chiacchierata*), having a crush (*ha avuto una cotta*), and having a baby (*hanno avuto una bambina*). The participle **avuto** does **not** change for gender/number when used with *avere*.
target_language_example: Ho avuto una giornata davvero difficile.
native_language_example: I had a really difficult day.

additional_notes: Used when you hear knocking and refer to an unknown person/people at the door. Literally: "they knock at the door." It’s the 3rd person plural present of *bussare* (to knock). Often appears like a stage direction in scripts or subtitles before someone speaks from outside.
target_language_example: Bussano alla porta: vai tu ad aprire?
native_language_example: They’re knocking at the door—will you go open it?

additional_notes: A sharp warning in the imperative (from **badare a** = “to pay attention to / to watch out for”). Used to tell someone to speak more respectfully or stop being rude; often said in an angry or threatening tone. You can also say **bada a come parli con me** (“watch how you talk to me”).
target_language_example: Ehi, bada a come parli con mia sorella.
native_language_example: Hey, watch how you talk to my sister.

additional_notes: Used in legal/courtroom contexts to indicate the place where a witness sits/stands to give testimony. Often used with "essere/salire/andare/ritornare sul banco dei testimoni" (to be/take the stand/return to the stand). Note: "banco" can look like English "bank," but here it means a bench/stand.
target_language_example: Il testimone è salito al banco dei testimoni per rispondere alle domande.
native_language_example: The witness took the stand to answer the questions.

meaning: “red flag”; also the “red flag” signal (e.g., in racing) meaning stop/danger.
additional_notes: Literally “red flag.” Used both figuratively (a warning sign/problem) and literally as a signal, especially in sports like motor racing (“Bandiera rossa!” = the session/race is stopped). In contexts like “Vedo un commissario con una bandiera rossa,” it refers to an official holding a physical red flag.
target_language_example: Bandiera rossa: la gara è stata sospesa per un incidente.
native_language_example: Red flag: the race was stopped because of an accident.

meaning: a rowboat; a boat you row with oars.
additional_notes: Used for a small boat propelled by rowing (using oars), not a motorboat or sailboat. Often appears after verbs like andare in (to go by) or avere (to have).
target_language_example: Siamo andati al lago in barca a remi.
native_language_example: We went to the lake in a rowboat.

additional_notes: Used for a small, packaged snack bar made with oats/granola (often with nuts, honey, or chocolate). In Italian you may also hear “barretta ai cereali” (cereal/grain bar).
target_language_example: Per colazione prendo una barretta di granola e un caffè.
native_language_example: For breakfast I have a granola bar and a coffee.

additional_notes: A simple time expression: "dopo la scuola" = "after school." Often used with "giocare a" (to play): "giocare a baseball dopo la scuola". You can swap in other activities: "calcio dopo la scuola", "studio dopo la scuola".
target_language_example: Di solito gioco a baseball dopo la scuola.
native_language_example: I usually play baseball after school.

meaning: "enough with" / "stop with" (used to tell someone to stop doing or saying something).
additional_notes: Used before a noun or noun phrase to express annoyance or impatience and demand that something stop: "Basta con le scuse!" = "Enough with the excuses!" You can also say just "Basta!" (“Enough!”). Common in spoken Italian, often in arguments or complaints.
target_language_example: Basta con queste lamentele: troviamo una soluzione.
native_language_example: Enough with these complaints—let’s find a solution.

meaning: "as long as" / "provided that"; also "all you have to do is".
additional_notes: Introduces a condition that is enough to make something acceptable or true. Very common in spoken Italian. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive (e.g., "basta che tu venga" = "as long as you come"), though in informal speech you may also hear the indicative.
target_language_example: Puoi prendere la mia macchina, basta che me la riporti stasera.
native_language_example: You can take my car, as long as you bring it back tonight.

additional_notes: Literally “to hit/strike on a machine.” Used mainly for typing on a typewriter (today you’ll more often hear “digitare” or “scrivere al computer” for typing on a computer). Often appears with “saper/capere” to ask if someone can type (e.g., “Sa battere a macchina?”).
target_language_example: Non so battere a macchina, ma so scrivere al computer.
native_language_example: I can’t type on a typewriter, but I can type on a computer.

additional_notes: Used in medical/health contexts to talk about the heart’s beating, especially whether it’s regular/irregular or present. Common with verbs like “sentire” (to feel/hear) and adjectives like “regolare” (regular). In everyday Italian you may also hear “battito del cuore.”
target_language_example: Il medico controlla il battito cardiaco e la pressione.
native_language_example: The doctor checks the heartbeat and blood pressure.

additional_notes: An English loanword used in Italian for the sport played on sand. Typically used with "giocare a" (to play): "Gioco a beach volley". It’s usually masculine: "il beach volley".
target_language_example: D'estate giochiamo a beach volley in spiaggia.
native_language_example: In summer we play beach volleyball at the beach.

meaning: "Well then," / "Well, so…" (reacting and drawing a conclusion).
additional_notes: Common conversational filler used at the start of a reply to show you’re reacting to what was just said (surprise, acceptance, mild disagreement) and often to introduce a conclusion or next step. As a question ("Beh, allora?") it can mean "Well, then?" / "So?"—asking what happens next, sometimes with impatience.
target_language_example: Beh, allora andiamo: è tardi.
native_language_example: Well then, let’s go: it’s late.

meaning: "Well, I..." (used to introduce what you’re about to say).
additional_notes: Used as a conversational opener before giving your opinion, reacting, hesitating, or slightly changing topic. Often followed by a statement about yourself ("io..."). In writing it’s usually followed by a comma: "Beh, io...".
target_language_example: Beh, io non so cosa dire.
native_language_example: Well, I don’t know what to say.

meaning: "Well, (no/not…)"—used to introduce a negative reply or disagreement.
additional_notes: “Beh” is a very common spoken interjection (like “well…”). With “non” it often softens or sets up a correction, refusal, or negative opinion. It’s typical in conversation and can sound a bit informal/colloquial.
target_language_example: Beh, non sono d'accordo.
native_language_example: Well, I don't agree.

additional_notes: "Bei" is the plural of "bel" (meaning "beautiful/nice") and is used before a plural noun (like "fiori"). It’s an adjective + noun phrase used to compliment flowers, often with "molti" (many) or in phrases like "grazie per...".
target_language_example: Ho comprato dei bei fiori per tua madre.
native_language_example: I bought some beautiful flowers for your mother.

meaning: “Nice shot!” / “Good one!” (a great move, hit, or success).
additional_notes: Used to congratulate someone after a good action (a shot in sports, a clever idea, a successful attempt). Literally “nice hit/blow,” and it can also describe an achievement or a well-executed move: *È stato un bel colpo* = “That was quite a feat / a great success.”
target_language_example: Bel colpo! Hai risolto il problema in un attimo.
native_language_example: Good one! You solved the problem in no time.

meaning: “nice place” (sometimes used sarcastically, depending on tone/context).
additional_notes: Bel is the shortened form of bello used before a masculine singular noun (bel posto = bello posto). Often used to praise a location (“Che bel posto!”), and it can also be ironic when followed by something negative (e.g., “Bel posto di merda.”). Common pattern: bel posto per + infinitive = “a nice place to + verb” (e.g., bel posto per fare il bagno).
target_language_example: Che bel posto! Ci torniamo domani?
native_language_example: What a nice place! Shall we come back tomorrow?

additional_notes: "Bel" is the shortened form of "bello" used before a noun (like "un bel regalo"). It’s a common, neutral way to say something is a good/nice present.
target_language_example: Questo è proprio un bel regalo, grazie!
native_language_example: This is a really nice gift, thank you!

meaning: a nice smile; a lovely smile.
additional_notes: "Bel" is the shortened form of "bello" used before a noun (especially masculine singular) to compliment someone or something. In "un bel sorriso," it’s a common, friendly way to say someone has an attractive/pleasant smile.
target_language_example: Hai proprio un bel sorriso.
native_language_example: You really have a lovely smile.

meaning: a good impression; to come across well.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like fare/farsi ("fare bella figura", "fare una bella figura") meaning to look good, impress others, or behave appropriately in a situation. It can be said seriously (hoping to impress) or sarcastically when things go badly ("che bella figura stiamo facendo!").
target_language_example: Con quel discorso hai fatto davvero bella figura.
native_language_example: With that speech you really made a good impression.

ben al di sotto della media questo

target_language_multi_word_term: ben al di sotto della media
additional_notes: Used to say something (often grades, results, performance) is noticeably lower than the usual/expected level. "Ben" intensifies the comparison (more than just "al di sotto della media" = below average). Often followed by a time period like "questo semestre/trimestre" (this semester/term).
target_language_example: La mia prestazione è stata ben al di sotto della media quest'anno.
native_language_example: My performance was well below average this year.

additional_notes: Used to congratulate or praise someone for something they did (often as an exclamation on its own: “Ben fatto!”). You can intensify it with “molto”: “Molto ben fatto.” As an adjective describing a noun, it can agree in gender/number (ben fatto, ben fatta, ben fatti, ben fatte), but as a standalone compliment it’s commonly kept as “Ben fatto!”
target_language_example: Ben fatto! Hai fatto un ottimo lavoro.
native_language_example: Well done! You did a great job.

additional_notes: Usually written as one word: "benvenuto". It agrees with the person/people welcomed: "benvenuta" (female), "benvenuti" (plural masc./mixed), "benvenute" (plural fem.). Used as an exclamation ("Benvenuto!") or in phrases like "Sei il benvenuto" = "You’re welcome here / You’re welcome (to come)."
target_language_example: Benvenuti a casa mia!
native_language_example: Welcome to my home!

additional_notes: Used when something is OK/going well, then you add a problem, limitation, or unexpected detail. Often follows phrases like "sto bene" (I’m fine) or "va bene" (it’s OK): "Sto bene, ma…" = “I’m fine, but…”. Punctuation can vary ("bene ma", "bene, ma").
target_language_example: Sto bene, ma oggi preferisco restare a casa.
native_language_example: I’m fine, but today I’d rather stay home.

additional_notes: Used at the end of a statement to check or confirm something you believe is true, similar to an English tag question. Literally it’s “well, true?”, but it’s normally translated as “right?” / “isn’t it?” / “didn’t you?” depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Domani ci vediamo alle 10, bene, vero?
native_language_example: We’re seeing each other tomorrow at 10, right?

additional_notes: Used to say someone plays tennis well. Commonly appears with the verb "giocare" (to play): "giocare bene a tennis" = "to play tennis well". You can also use the same pattern with other sports: "bene a calcio" (well at soccer), "bene a basket" (well at basketball).
target_language_example: Lei gioca bene a tennis, ma io gioco meglio a calcio.
native_language_example: She plays tennis well, but I play soccer better.

additional_notes: Used after a verb (often "parlare") to say you do something well in French: "parlare bene il francese" = "to speak French well". You can also intensify it with "così" (so) or "davvero" (really): "parlare così/davvero bene il francese".
target_language_example: Parlo bene il francese, ma non lo scrivo molto bene.
native_language_example: I speak French well, but I don’t write it very well.

meaning: “Okay, then,” / “Well, then,” (used to move things along or conclude).
additional_notes: Common conversational connector. Use it to react to what was just said and then state your next action, decision, or question. Often followed by what you’ll do next (Bene, allora vado…) or by a prompt (Bene, allora cosa facciamo?). Commas are common in writing; intonation carries the meaning in speech.
target_language_example: Bene, allora ci vediamo domani alle otto.
native_language_example: Okay, then, see you tomorrow at eight.

meaning: "Alright, alright" / "Good, good" (often said with emphasis, sometimes teasing or ironic).
additional_notes: Repeating *bene* adds emphasis. It can signal approval or that you’re acknowledging what someone said and moving on (like “okay then”). Depending on tone, it can also sound ironic/skeptical—similar to English “well, well” or “alright, alright.”
target_language_example: Bene, bene, allora ci vediamo domani.
native_language_example: Alright, alright—then I’ll see you tomorrow.

additional_notes: "Bere" means "to drink." In "bere del vino," "del" = "some" (partitive: di + il), so it often means drinking an unspecified amount of wine. Common in offers/questions: "Vuole/Volete bere del vino?" You can also say "bere vino" more generally ("drink wine" in general).
target_language_example: Stasera possiamo bere del vino a casa mia.
native_language_example: Tonight we can drink some wine at my place.

meaning: to drink something (often: to have something to drink).
additional_notes: Common, polite everyday phrase used when offering or suggesting a drink. "Qualcosa" means "something" and can be followed by an adjective or "di + adjective" to specify what kind: "qualcosa di fresco" = "something cold/refreshing". Often used with "vuoi/vuole" (do you want?) or "vieni" (do you want to come?) to invite someone for a drink.
target_language_example: Dopo la passeggiata, andiamo a bere qualcosa?
native_language_example: After the walk, shall we go have something to drink?

additional_notes: Used when offering someone a choice of drink. Often appears in questions with different levels of politeness: “Vuoi…?” (informal singular), “Vuole…?” (formal singular), “Volete…?” (plural), “Vorrebbe/Vorreste…?” (more polite: “would you like…?”).
target_language_example: Dopo pranzo, preferisci bere tè o caffè?
native_language_example: After lunch, do you prefer to drink tea or coffee?

additional_notes: Common idiom used to describe someone who drinks a lot (usually alcohol). You can change the verb for different subjects/tense: "bevono come una spugna" (they drink like a sponge), "beveva come una spugna" (used to drink/was drinking heavily).
target_language_example: Non uscire con lui: beve come una spugna.
native_language_example: Don’t go out with him: he drinks like a fish.

additional_notes: Often used with forms of "stare" to make the present or past continuous: "sto/stai/sta... bevendo del latte" = "I am/you are/he is... drinking (some) milk"; "stavo..." = "I was...". "Del" is a partitive article meaning "some" (not necessarily all the milk). You can also say "bevendo latte" (more general) or "bevendo il latte" (the milk, specific).
target_language_example: Scusa, non posso parlare: sto bevendo del latte.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t talk: I’m drinking some milk.

additional_notes: Used with the passato prossimo of bere (“to drink”): ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno + bevuto. "Del" means “some” (an unspecified amount), so "ho bevuto del caffè" = “I drank some coffee / I had some coffee.” You can also say "ho bevuto caffè" (more general: “I drank coffee”).
target_language_example: Non ho bevuto del caffè oggi.
native_language_example: I didn’t drink any coffee today.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase used with "avere" to form the passato prossimo of "bere" (to drink): ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno bevuto. "Del tè" means "some tea" (partitive "del" = di + il) and is often used when the exact amount isn’t specified. In questions, word order can stay the same ("Avete bevuto del tè?").
target_language_example: Ho bevuto del tè dopo cena.
native_language_example: I drank some tea after dinner.

meaning: "a glass of" (also: "a drinking glass made of").
additional_notes: Used to talk about a serving in a glass: un bicchiere di acqua/birra/vino/vodka. With a material, it means the glass is made of that material: un bicchiere di plastica (= a plastic cup/glass).
target_language_example: Vorrei un bicchiere di acqua, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a glass of water, please.

additional_notes: Used to refer to beer served in a glass (not a bottle or a can). In bars/restaurants you can ask for it with: “Un bicchiere di birra, per favore.” “Bicchiere” = glass; “di birra” = of beer.
target_language_example: Scusi, mi porta un bicchiere di birra, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you bring me a glass of beer, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask for, offer, or talk about a serving of milk in a glass. Common with quantities like "un" (a) or "un altro" (another): "un bicchiere di latte", "un altro bicchiere di latte".
target_language_example: Vorrei un bicchiere di latte, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a glass of milk, please.

additional_notes: Used to order wine or refer to one serving of wine in a glass. Common patterns: “Potrei avere un bicchiere di vino?” (Could I have a glass of wine?) and “finire/riempire/mettere giù il bicchiere di vino” (finish/fill/put down the glass of wine).
target_language_example: Vorrei un bicchiere di vino rosso, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a glass of red wine, please.

additional_notes: Used for a card with your name and contact details, especially in professional contexts. Often with verbs like avere/dare/lasciare (to have/give/leave) and with possessives: il mio biglietto da visita (my business card). Figuratively, it can mean a “calling card” or something that represents you/your work (e.g., È il nostro biglietto da visita = It’s our calling card).
target_language_example: Le lascio il mio biglietto da visita.
native_language_example: I’ll leave you my business card.

additional_notes: Used to order beer politely in a bar/restaurant. Often said as a short order: “Una birra, per favore.” You can also use it after a fuller request (e.g., “Posso avere una birra, per favore?”). Note the polite forms with staff: “Mi dia…” (more formal) or “Dammi…” (informal).
target_language_example: Scusi, una birra, per favore.
native_language_example: Excuse me, a beer, please.

additional_notes: Used to order beer politely in a bar or restaurant. Often shortened to "Una birra, per piacere." You can swap in quantities: "Due birre, per piacere" (two beers) or "Un'altra birra, per piacere" (another beer).
target_language_example: Scusi, una birra alla spina, per piacere.
native_language_example: Excuse me, a draft beer, please.

additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase "avere bisogno di" (= "to need"). "Del" = "di + il" (“of the”), and "suo" agrees with the thing owned ("aiuto"), not with the person who owns it. In context, "suo" can mean “his” or “her”; Italian often relies on context to clarify. You can also say "ho bisogno del tuo aiuto" (“I need your help”).
target_language_example: Ho bisogno del suo aiuto per compilare questo modulo.
native_language_example: I need his/her help to fill out this form.

additional_notes: Used with the expression "avere bisogno di" (to need). "del" = "di" + "il" and is used before a masculine singular noun (il computer, il denaro, il telefono, il diario, il libro). With other nouns you change the article: "dello" (lo), "dell'" (l'), "della" (la), "dei" (i), "degli" (gli), "delle" (le).
target_language_example: Ho bisogno del passaporto per viaggiare.
native_language_example: I need the passport to travel.

additional_notes: Used with the structure "avere bisogno di" + noun/pronoun: "(avere) bisogno del mio aiuto" = "(to) need my help." "del" is the contraction of "di + il". You’ll often see it after "ha/hai/aveva/avete bisogno..." and in questions like "Perché hai bisogno del mio aiuto?"
target_language_example: Se hai bisogno del mio aiuto, dimmelo.
native_language_example: If you need my help, tell me.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere bisogno di + [noun]" = "to need + [noun]". Here: "(avere) bisogno del nostro aiuto" = "(to) need our help". You can add "ancora" to mean "still": "Hai ancora bisogno del nostro aiuto?". With people: "ho bisogno del tuo/suo/nostro aiuto" = "I need your/his/her/our help".
target_language_example: Se hai bisogno del nostro aiuto, chiamaci.
native_language_example: If you need our help, call us.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" ("avere bisogno di..." = "to need..."). "Suo" here is the formal/polite form meaning "your" (to one person you address with Lei). In context it often appears as "(avere) bisogno del suo aiuto" = "(to) need your help."
target_language_example: Mi scusi, ho bisogno del suo aiuto.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need your help.

additional_notes: Used after the verb "avere" (to have): "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo bisogno del tuo aiuto" = "I/you/he/she/we need your help." You can put it in the future with "avrò bisogno..." (I will need...), or make it negative: "non ho più bisogno del tuo aiuto" = "I don't need your help anymore."
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma ho bisogno del tuo aiuto oggi.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, but I need your help today.

additional_notes: "Avere bisogno di" means “to need.” "Del" = "di" + "il" (“of the”), and "vostro" is the formal/plural way to say “your” (to one person politely, or to more than one person). Very common with different tenses: "ho/avrò/abbiamo bisogno del vostro aiuto".
target_language_example: Scusi, ho bisogno del vostro aiuto per compilare questo modulo.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need your help to fill out this form.

additional_notes: Used with forms of avere (ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno) to express necessity: avere bisogno di + noun (need for something) or avere bisogno di + infinitive (need to do something). Often strengthened with adverbs like veramente (really) or urgentemente (urgently).
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di parlare con te.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere": "avere bisogno di" + noun = "to need" + noun. You can change the subject: "Ho/Hai/Ha/Abbiamo/Avete/Hanno bisogno di acqua". Common in practical situations (asking if someone needs water, talking about animals/plants needing water).
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di acqua, per favore.
native_language_example: I need water, please.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere bisogno di aiuto" = "to need help." You can change the verb for tense/person: "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/hanno bisogno di aiuto" (present), "avevo/avevi/aveva... bisogno di aiuto" (past/imperfect). Often used to offer or ask for assistance: "Hai bisogno di aiuto?"
target_language_example: Scusa, ho bisogno di aiuto con questo modulo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I need help with this form.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere": "avere bisogno di + infinitive" = "to need to + verb". It often implies necessity/requirement rather than desire. Common negatives: "non ho bisogno di andare" (I don’t need to go) and questions like "Perché avevi bisogno di andare?" (Why did you need to go?).
target_language_example: Non ho bisogno di andare al supermercato oggi.
native_language_example: I don’t need to go to the supermarket today.

meaning: need food / in need of food.
additional_notes: Used after forms of "avere" (to have): "(io) ho bisogno di cibo" = "I need food". You can intensify it with an adverb like "disperatamente" (desperately). Often appears in lists: "bisogno di cibo e acqua" (need food and water).
target_language_example: Dopo il viaggio, avevamo bisogno di cibo e acqua.
native_language_example: After the trip, we needed food and water.

additional_notes: Used to say you need money (often for a purpose). Most commonly with “avere bisogno di (qualcosa)” (to need something): “Ho bisogno di denaro.” You can also say “sentire il bisogno di…” to express feeling a need, though with money it can sound more emphatic or less common than “avere bisogno di”.
target_language_example: Se hai bisogno di denaro, posso aiutarti.
native_language_example: If you need money, I can help you.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere bisogno di dormire" = "to need to sleep." Often refers to being tired and needing rest; you can add "di più" (more) to say you need more sleep.
target_language_example: Dopo il viaggio, ho bisogno di dormire un po'.
native_language_example: After the trip, I need to sleep a bit.

meaning: "need to be" (followed by an adjective or past participle).
additional_notes: Used with forms of "avere" (e.g., "ho/hai/ha bisogno di essere...") to say that someone/something needs to be in a certain state or needs an action done to them: "ha bisogno di essere riparato" = "it needs to be repaired"; "ho bisogno di essere da solo" = "I need to be alone".
target_language_example: La porta ha bisogno di essere chiusa.
native_language_example: The door needs to be closed.

additional_notes: Used with the verb avere: (io) ho bisogno di…, (tu) hai bisogno di…, (lui/lei) ha bisogno di…. It’s followed by an infinitive. With fare it often means “to do” in a general sense (fare una domanda = ask a question / make a request, fare un bagno = take a bath). In negatives, non hai bisogno di… means “you don’t need to…”.
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di fare una pausa.
native_language_example: I need to take a break.

meaning: 'need to do it' / 'need to do that'.
additional_notes: Used after forms of "avere bisogno" (to need): "(io) ho bisogno di farlo", "(lui/lei) ha bisogno di farlo", "(voi) avevate bisogno di farlo". "Farlo" = "fare" (to do/make) + "lo" (it), referring back to something already known from context. Often followed by a reason: "Ho bisogno di farlo perché..."
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di farlo oggi, altrimenti è troppo tardi.
native_language_example: I need to do it today, otherwise it's too late.

additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase **avere bisogno di** (“to need”): *ho bisogno di lei* = “I need her.” **Lei** can mean “her,” and it can also be the polite/formal “you” depending on context; in these examples it means “her.”
target_language_example: Non posso farlo da solo: ho bisogno di lei.
native_language_example: I can’t do it alone: I need her.

additional_notes: Used after expressions like "avere bisogno di" (to need) or "c’è bisogno di" (there is a need for). With people, Italian uses "di" + stressed pronoun: "di me" (me), "di te" (you), "di lui/lei" (him/her), etc. Example: "Hai bisogno di me?" = "Do you need me?"
target_language_example: Se hai bisogno di me, chiamami subito.
native_language_example: If you need me, call me right away.

additional_notes: Used after avere bisogno di (“to need”): avere bisogno di più + noun = “to need more + noun.” Common with uncountable nouns (burro) and abstract nouns (pratica, potere). In speech you may also hear: Mi serve di più… (“I need more…”).
target_language_example: Abbiamo bisogno di più tempo.
native_language_example: We need more time.

meaning: need money / be in need of money.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere bisogno di soldi" = "to need money". You can add a time word like "ora/adesso" (now) or a reason with "per" + infinitive: "Ho bisogno di soldi per...".
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di soldi per pagare l'affitto.
native_language_example: I need money to pay the rent.

meaning: need space (room), or need personal space/time alone.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere bisogno di + noun" = "to need + noun". "Spazio" can mean physical room (more space in a house, car, suitcase, etc.) or emotional/personal space (some time alone or distance in a relationship). Often heard as "Ho bisogno di spazio".
target_language_example: Dopo una giornata lunga, ho bisogno di spazio.
native_language_example: After a long day, I need some space.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere bisogno di te" = "to need you." It can express practical need (help, support) or emotional need depending on context. The subject changes the verb form (ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno) but "di te" stays the same.
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di te adesso.
native_language_example: I need you right now.

additional_notes: Used after forms of "avere" (to have): "avere bisogno di un + noun" = "to need a + (masculine singular) noun". Use "di una" for feminine singular (e.g., "bisogno di una mano"), "di" + plural article for plural ("dei/degli/delle").
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di un biglietto per domani.
native_language_example: I need a ticket for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used after forms of "avere" (to have): "ho/hai/ha bisogno di un abbraccio" = "I/you/he/she need(s) a hug." Often appears with intensifiers like "solo/solamente/soltanto/semplicemente" (“just/simply”) to emphasize that a hug is all someone needs.
target_language_example: Dopo quella brutta giornata, ho bisogno di un abbraccio.
native_language_example: After that bad day, I need a hug.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone for help politely. Often said as: “Avrei bisogno di un favore” (“I’d need a favor / Could you do me a favor?”). You can add “Ti” for clarity: “Avrei bisogno di un favore, ti va?”
target_language_example: Scusa, avrei bisogno di un favore: puoi accompagnarmi alla stazione?
native_language_example: Sorry, I need a favor: can you take me to the station?

bisogno di un passaggio a casa

target_language_multi_word_term: bisogno di un passaggio a casa
additional_notes: Used with forms of "avere bisogno di" (to need) + "un passaggio" (a lift/ride, usually by car) + "a casa" (home). Common when offering or asking if someone still needs a ride home: "Hai/Ha/Avete ancora bisogno di un passaggio a casa?".
target_language_example: Se vuoi, ti do un passaggio: hai bisogno di un passaggio a casa?
native_language_example: If you want, I can give you a ride: do you need a ride home?

additional_notes: Used with forms of the verb "avere" (to have): "avere bisogno di" = "to need". "Una" agrees with a feminine singular noun that follows (e.g., una ricetta, una forchetta, una scorta). For a masculine noun use "bisogno di un" (e.g., un medico) or "bisogno di uno" (e.g., uno zaino). Common tenses: "ho bisogno di una..." (I need a...), "avrò bisogno di una..." (I will need a...), "avrai bisogno di una..." (you will need a...).
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di una prenotazione per entrare?
native_language_example: Do I need a reservation to get in?

additional_notes: Used after forms of "avere" (to have): "ho/ha/abbiamo/avevano bisogno di voi" = "I have/he/she has/we have/we had need of you." "voi" is used for more than one person (“you all”) and also as a polite form in some contexts (less common than "Lei"). Often strengthened with "non": "Non ho bisogno di voi!" = "I don't need you!"
target_language_example: Abbiamo bisogno di voi per finire questo lavoro.
native_language_example: We need you (all) to finish this work.

meaning: (with a) full mouth; mouth full (of food).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like avere (“to have”) and phrases like a bocca piena (“with your mouth full”), often in polite warnings/commands: Non parlare a bocca piena. Can also take di + noun to say what the mouth is full of: la bocca piena di....
target_language_example: Scusi, non riesco a rispondere: ho la bocca piena.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t answer: my mouth is full.

additional_notes: Used for money or funding awarded to someone to study (often based on merit, need, or sports). Common with verbs like ricevere/ottenere/avere una borsa di studio, and you can add the field or destination: una borsa di studio di calcio; una borsa di studio per la Germania.
target_language_example: Ha ricevuto una borsa di studio per studiare all’università.
native_language_example: He/She received a scholarship to study at university.

additional_notes: Used to describe a bag by its color. Often heard in questions to identify who a bag belongs to (è tua? = is it yours?; è sua? = is it his/hers?).
target_language_example: Scusi, questa borsa nera è sua?
native_language_example: Excuse me, is this black bag yours?

meaning: "a bottle of" (a bottle containing a drink or other liquid).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the container/quantity: bottiglia di + noun (e.g., bottiglia di vino, bottiglia di latte, bottiglia di profumo). You can add amounts like una mezza bottiglia di (half a bottle of).
target_language_example: Vorrei una bottiglia di acqua, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a bottle of water, please.

additional_notes: Used to refer to one specific bottle of champagne. Very common in requests with "aprire" (to open): "Aprire una bottiglia di champagne" = "to open a bottle of champagne". You can swap in other drinks: "una bottiglia di vino" (a bottle of wine), "una bottiglia d’acqua" (a bottle of water).
target_language_example: Porto una bottiglia di champagne per festeggiare.
native_language_example: I’m bringing a bottle of champagne to celebrate.

additional_notes: Used when buying, recommending, or bringing wine. The partitive structure “di” indicates the contents: a bottle containing wine. You’ll often hear it with an adjective (e.g., “una buona/bella bottiglia di vino”) or in questions in shops/restaurants (“Quale bottiglia di vino consiglia?”).
target_language_example: Per la cena ho comprato una bottiglia di vino rosso.
native_language_example: For dinner I bought a bottle of red wine.

additional_notes: Used when talking about a quantity of beer measured in bottles, often with a number (e.g., due/tre/quattro bottiglie di birra). Singular: una bottiglia di birra.
target_language_example: Per la festa abbiamo comprato sei bottiglie di birra.
native_language_example: For the party we bought six bottles of beer.

additional_notes: Used to count wine by the bottle. With numbers: "due/tre bottiglie di vino". Singular is "una bottiglia di vino" (a bottle of wine). In shops or restaurants you might also hear "una bottiglia di vino rosso/bianco" (red/white wine).
target_language_example: Vorrei due bottiglie di vino, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like two bottles of wine, please.

meaning: right arm; (figurative) right-hand man/most trusted assistant.
additional_notes: Literally “right arm” (braccio = arm, destro = right). Used both for the physical body part (Alza il braccio destro) and figuratively to mean someone’s main helper or trusted aide (Essere il braccio destro di qualcuno). Agreement: braccio destro / braccia destre (fem. plural in Italian), but the adjective stays masculine singular with the singular noun: il suo braccio destro.
target_language_example: Giulia è il braccio destro del direttore.
native_language_example: Giulia is the director’s right-hand woman (most trusted assistant).

meaning: good at playing tennis (said about a female).
additional_notes: Used to say someone has skill at an activity: essere bravo/brava a + infinitive. Here brava agrees with a female subject (lei/Yumi); for a male you’d say bravo. You can turn it into a question with intonation or a question mark.
target_language_example: Mia sorella è brava a giocare a tennis.
native_language_example: My sister is good at playing tennis.

meaning: a good/nice person (usually said about a woman).
additional_notes: "Brava" agrees with the person being described (brava = feminine; bravo = masculine). In this context, bravo/brava means "good/kind/decent" rather than "brave" (so it’s not about courage). Often used as a compliment: "Che brava persona!" = "What a nice person!"
target_language_example: Giulia è una brava persona: aiuta sempre gli altri.
native_language_example: Giulia is a good person: she always helps others.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is skilled at something. Common patterns: (1) "essere bravo/a a" + infinitive: "Sono bravo a cucinare" (I’m good at cooking). (2) "essere bravo/a a" + noun (often a sport/activity): "È bravo a calcio / a rugby" (He’s good at soccer/rugby). Agree "bravo" with the person: "bravo" (male), "brava" (female).
target_language_example: Mia sorella è molto brava a parlare in pubblico.
native_language_example: My sister is very good at speaking in public.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has ability/skill in the French language. "Bravo" changes to match the person: bravo (male), brava (female), bravi (mixed/plural), brave (female plural). Often used with other subjects too: "bravo in matematica" = good at math.
target_language_example: Mia sorella è brava in francese, ma io sono bravo in inglese.
native_language_example: My sister is good at French, but I’m good at English.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "essere" to say someone has skill in a subject: "essere bravo/a in + subject". "Bravo" agrees with the person (bravo = male, brava = female). You can add intensifiers like "davvero" (really) or "molto" (very).
target_language_example: Mia sorella è molto brava in matematica.
native_language_example: My sister is very good at math.

meaning: "good boy" / "good guy" (a nice, well-behaved young man).
additional_notes: Used to praise a boy/young man for being kind, well-mannered, or doing the right thing. Often used with "un" (un bravo ragazzo) to describe someone: "Tom era un bravo ragazzo." "Bravo" changes with gender/number (bravo ragazzo, brava ragazza, bravi ragazzi, brave ragazze).
target_language_example: È un bravo ragazzo: aiuta sempre i suoi amici.
native_language_example: He’s a good guy: he always helps his friends.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or talk about unpleasant information. Often said with verbs like avere/portare/dare (“to have/bring/give”) and with per to say who the news is for (e.g., brutte notizie per lui).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma ho brutte notizie per te.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, but I have bad news for you.

meaning: A very offensive insult: “you/that bastard” / “you son of a bitch.”
additional_notes: Extremely vulgar and aggressive. Used to insult someone directly ("Tu, brutto figlio di puttana!") or to curse about someone/thing ("Questo brutto figlio di puttana!"). In real life, avoid it unless you fully understand the consequences (it can provoke a serious conflict).
target_language_example: Quel brutto figlio di puttana mi ha imbrogliato!
native_language_example: That bastard screwed me over!

additional_notes: A common Christmas greeting used from the holiday season through Christmas Day. You can say it when you meet someone, in messages/cards, or as a toast. Often written with a capital N (Buon Natale).
target_language_example: Ti auguro un buon Natale e un felice anno nuovo!
native_language_example: I wish you a Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year!

additional_notes: Used as a New Year’s greeting, often expanded to “Buon anno nuovo!” You can say it when greeting someone around New Year’s Day or in messages/cards. In other contexts it can also be literal (“a good year”), as in “È stato un buon anno.”
target_language_example: Auguri e buon anno!
native_language_example: Best wishes and Happy New Year!

additional_notes: Used as a polite wish before someone starts eating (said by the host, server, or anyone at the table). You can also say it on its own: “Buon appetito!” Note: in sentences like “ha un buon appetito,” it means “to have a good appetite” (to be hungry / eat well), not the mealtime wish.
target_language_example: Il pranzo è pronto: buon appetito!
native_language_example: Lunch is ready: enjoy your meal!

additional_notes: Used as a birthday greeting. Often followed by the person’s name or said on its own. You may also see the same idea as “Tanti auguri!” (more general: “best wishes”).
target_language_example: Buon compleanno! Ti auguro una bellissima giornata.
native_language_example: Happy birthday! I wish you a wonderful day.

additional_notes: Used as a friendly wish when someone is about to do something enjoyable (a party, trip, show, night out). It can be casual on its own (“Buon divertimento!”) or more formal with a polite phrase like “Le auguro buon divertimento” (“I wish you have fun”). Similar structure to “buona notte/buon viaggio/buon appetito.”
target_language_example: Vai al concerto stasera? Buon divertimento!
native_language_example: Are you going to the concert tonight? Have fun!

additional_notes: A polite, standard greeting used during the daytime, especially in the morning and early afternoon. Often written as one word: "buongiorno". You can use it when greeting someone directly (e.g., with a name or a friendly term like "vicino" = neighbor).
target_language_example: Buon giorno, come sta?
native_language_example: Good morning, how are you?

meaning: "Good work" / "have a good day at work"; also "a good job" (employment).
additional_notes: Used as a greeting/wish to someone who is about to work or is working (like saying “Have a good shift” / “Have a good one at work”). It can also describe employment: “un buon lavoro” = “a good job” (a good position). Agreement: buon lavoro (masc. sing.); but with the article it’s “un buon lavoro”.
target_language_example: Buon lavoro! Ci vediamo stasera.
native_language_example: Have a good day at work! See you tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say something (or someone) smells pleasant. Often said as an exclamation: "Che buon odore!" = "That smells so good!". With people, it usually refers to perfume/soap ("Hai un buon odore" = "You smell nice").
target_language_example: Che buon odore in cucina!
native_language_example: It smells so good in the kitchen!

additional_notes: A polite greeting used from early afternoon until early evening (after lunch, before "buona sera"). Often followed by "a tutti" (everyone) or used when addressing a group (e.g., "signore e signori").
target_language_example: Buon pomeriggio, come posso aiutarla?
native_language_example: Good afternoon, how can I help you?

additional_notes: Often used with "avere": "(qualcosa) ha un buon sapore" = “(something) tastes good.” It’s common for food/drinks ("Queste mele hanno un buon sapore"), but can also describe how someone’s breath/mouth tastes (e.g., after not smoking).
target_language_example: Questo tè ha un buon sapore, anche senza zucchero.
native_language_example: This tea tastes good, even without sugar.

additional_notes: Used to talk about practical, reasonable thinking. Often appears with verbs like avere (to have), mancare (to lack), or expressions like un briciolo di (a bit of): avere buon senso, manca il buon senso, senza un briciolo di buon senso.
target_language_example: Serve un po' di buon senso per risolvere questo problema.
native_language_example: It takes a bit of common sense to solve this problem.

additional_notes: Used to say someone feels cheerful/positive. Common in phrases like “essere di buon umore” (to be in a good mood) and “mettere di buon umore” (to put someone in a good mood).
target_language_example: Oggi sono di buon umore.
native_language_example: Today I’m in a good mood.

additional_notes: Used to wish someone well before they leave on a trip or journey. You can say it directly (“Buon viaggio!”) or with verbs like augurare/fare: “Ti auguro buon viaggio” (I wish you a good trip), “Fai buon viaggio” (have a good trip).
target_language_example: Domani parti per Milano? Buon viaggio!
native_language_example: Are you leaving for Milan tomorrow? Have a good trip!

additional_notes: Used to wish someone well before an exam, job, trip, or any challenging situation. Often followed by “con/col + noun” (Buona fortuna con l’esame!) or used on its own as an exclamation. Can be formal (con il suo...) or informal (con il tuo...).
target_language_example: Hai un colloquio domani? Buona fortuna!
native_language_example: Do you have an interview tomorrow? Good luck!

additional_notes: Used as a polite greeting or, more commonly, as a farewell (like “Have a good day”). It can also be used literally to describe that today is a good day (often with “una”: “una buona giornata”). As a greeting, it’s more formal than “ciao” and similar in tone to “buona giornata, signore/signora”.
target_language_example: Grazie per l’aiuto, buona giornata!
native_language_example: Thanks for the help, have a good day!

additional_notes: Used to say something is a good suggestion/plan (È una buona idea?) or to agree with someone’s proposal (Sì, buona idea.). Often used with the article: una buona idea (“a good idea”).
target_language_example: Andiamo in treno: è una buona idea.
native_language_example: Let’s go by train: it’s a good idea.

meaning: Good night (said when going to sleep).
additional_notes: Used as a nighttime farewell, typically when you or the other person is going to bed. You can say it to one person or a group (e.g., family, kids). Often contrasted with "buona sera" (good evening), which is used earlier in the evening.
target_language_example: È tardi, vado a dormire: buona notte!
native_language_example: It’s late, I’m going to sleep: good night!

meaning: a good opinion of; to think well of (someone).
additional_notes: Used with the verb avere: "avere una buona opinione di qualcuno" = to have a positive view of someone. Often followed by pronouns: di me/te/lui/lei/noi/voi/loro.
target_language_example: Spero che tu abbia una buona opinione di me.
native_language_example: I hope you have a good opinion of me.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is healthy or in good condition. Common with the verb essere: “essere in buona salute” (to be in good health), and also as an adjective phrase with di: “essere di buona salute” (to be in good health).
target_language_example: Sono in buona salute, grazie.
native_language_example: I'm in good health, thanks.

additional_notes: A polite greeting used from late afternoon through the evening. Common in both formal and neutral situations, often followed by a name or title (e.g., "Buona sera, signora"). It can also be used when entering a place (shops, restaurants) or starting a conversation.
target_language_example: Buona sera, avete un tavolo per due?
native_language_example: Good evening, do you have a table for two?

additional_notes: Plural feminine form. Use it when the friends are women/girls (or an all-female group): "Siamo buone amiche" = "We’re good friends." For a mixed group or male friends, use "buoni amici"; for two women, you can also say "due buone amiche".
target_language_example: Siamo buone amiche da tanti anni.
native_language_example: We’ve been good friends for many years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone being well-mannered (or ironically, if their actions contradict it). Often appears with verbs like "avere" (to have): "Ha delle buone maniere". You can also use it when talking about teaching etiquette to children.
target_language_example: Cerchiamo di usare buone maniere a tavola, per favore.
native_language_example: Let’s try to use good manners at the table, please.

additional_notes: Common way to announce or introduce something positive. Often used after verbs like avere/portare (to have/bring): “Ho delle buone notizie (per te/voi)” = “I have good news (for you).” Can also stand alone as an announcement: “Buone notizie!” Note: “notizia” is singular; “notizie” is plural.
target_language_example: Ho buone notizie per te: domani non lavoriamo.
native_language_example: I have good news for you: we’re not working tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say two or more people have a friendly relationship. Often with "essere" (to be) or "diventare" (to become): "Siamo buoni amici" = "We’re good friends." You can add "dei" before it when it follows "sono" to mean "some"/"(they are) good friends of yours": "Sono dei tuoi buoni amici."
target_language_example: Siamo buoni amici da molti anni.
native_language_example: We’ve been good friends for many years.

additional_notes: A strong insult used to say someone is lazy, incompetent, or worthless. It’s often said with "essere" (e.g., "Sei/Lui è buono a nulla"). Can also be used as a noun insult: "un/una buono/a a nulla" (plural: "buoni a nulla"). Avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Non ascoltarlo: ti chiama "buono a nulla" solo per offenderti.
native_language_example: Don’t listen to him: he calls you a “good-for-nothing” just to insult you.

additional_notes: Common food item. You can also say “burro d’arachidi” (with d’ before a vowel) in normal speech/writing. Often used with verbs like “comprare” (to buy), “mangiare” (to eat), or “spalmare” (to spread) and with “su” + food: “spalmare il burro di arachidi sul pane” (to spread peanut butter on bread).
target_language_example: Vorrei un panino con burro di arachidi e marmellata.
native_language_example: I’d like a sandwich with peanut butter and jam.

meaning: butter in blocks/loaves (solid butter sold as a lump, not spreadable butter).
additional_notes: "Pane" (plural "pani") can mean a loaf or a block. In shopping/food contexts, "burro in pani" refers to butter sold in solid blocks (similar to "burro in panetti"). You might see it when talking about finding/buying butter or when it’s hard to find in a certain area.
target_language_example: Al supermercato ho trovato solo burro in pani, non quello spalmabile.
native_language_example: At the supermarket I only found butter in blocks, not the spreadable kind.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "bussare" (to knock) + "a" + a surface/object. It can be literal (someone knocks at a door) or used when you’re about to ask to enter: "Posso bussare alla porta?". Often followed by whose door it is: "bussare alla porta di qualcuno".
target_language_example: Prima di entrare, bussa alla porta.
native_language_example: Before coming in, knock on the door.

meaning: to throw to the ground; to knock down.
additional_notes: Used for physically tossing or dropping something onto the ground (intentionally or accidentally). It can also mean to knock someone/something down (e.g., in a fight, an accident, or strong wind). Often interchangeable with "buttare per terra" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ha buttato a terra il bicchiere e si è rotto.
native_language_example: He/She threw the glass on the ground and it broke.

meaning: to throw out; to kick out (expel).
additional_notes: Used both literally (remove and throw something outside) and figuratively (force a person to leave a place, e.g., a bar/club). Often followed by what is removed ("buttare fuori la spazzatura") or by a person + da ("buttare fuori qualcuno dal locale"). Related noun: "il buttafuori" = the bouncer.
target_language_example: Hanno buttato fuori un cliente dal bar perché faceva troppo rumore.
native_language_example: They kicked a customer out of the bar because he was making too much noise.

meaning: to knock down/demolish; (figurative) to bring down, discourage.
additional_notes: Often used for tearing down something physically (a wall, a house, a building): “buttare giù la parete/la casa”. With a person as the object, it’s figurative: “Non farti buttare giù” = don’t let it/get it bring you down. Very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Hanno deciso di buttare giù il muro per allargare la stanza.
native_language_example: They decided to knock down the wall to make the room bigger.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrasal verb. Use it literally for getting rid of something (trash, unwanted items): “buttare via le budella” = throw away the guts. Figuratively it means “to waste,” especially with time or opportunities: “buttare via il tempo” = waste time. Often used in the negative as advice/warnings: “Non buttare via…”
target_language_example: Non buttare via i biglietti: ci servono per entrare.
native_language_example: Don’t throw away the tickets: we need them to get in.

additional_notes: Used for a public booth/box where you can make phone calls. In modern Italy they’re less common because of mobile phones, but you may still see them (often containing a public payphone). Typically feminine: una cabina telefonica; plural: cabine telefoniche.
target_language_example: Scusi, c'è una cabina telefonica qui vicino?
native_language_example: Excuse me, is there a phone booth nearby?

additional_notes: Refers to a person who tracks down and captures fugitives for a reward (a "taglia"). Used in news, films, and historical/Western contexts; in everyday conversation it’s less common.
target_language_example: Nel film, il cacciatore di taglie dà la caccia a un criminale per la ricompensa.
native_language_example: In the movie, the bounty hunter hunts a criminal for the reward.

additional_notes: Used to politely order a coffee (usually an espresso) in a bar/café or restaurant. You can add a quantity (Un caffè / Due caffè / Tre caffè) or address the waiter first (Cameriere, …).
target_language_example: Un caffè, per favore, e un bicchiere d’acqua.
native_language_example: A coffee, please, and a glass of water.

additional_notes: Used to order coffee politely (at a bar/café or restaurant). Often preceded by a quantity: "Un caffè, per piacere" (one coffee), "Due caffè, per piacere" (two coffees). You can also use it for different types of coffee: "Un caffè lungo/cappuccino/decaffeinato, per piacere". In Italian, "un caffè" usually means an espresso.
target_language_example: Un caffè decaffeinato, per piacere.
native_language_example: A decaf coffee, please.

additional_notes: Used when ordering or describing how you take your coffee. Often contrasted with “senza zucchero” (without sugar). You can also specify the amount: “poco zucchero” (a little sugar), “molto zucchero” (a lot of sugar).
target_language_example: Vorrei un caffè con lo zucchero, grazie.
native_language_example: I'd like a coffee with sugar, thanks.

additional_notes: Used when stating a preference or ordering coffee without adding sugar. You can also hear it as a request: “Un caffè senza zucchero, per favore.”
target_language_example: Per me un caffè senza zucchero, grazie.
native_language_example: An unsweetened coffee for me, please.

additional_notes: Used in the passive voice to say that someone received a kick from a horse. The agent is introduced by “da” (= by): “(Lei) è stata calciata da un cavallo” (she was kicked by a horse). You may also see past historic “fu” or “venne” instead of “è stata,” especially in writing.
target_language_example: Il contadino è stato calciato da un cavallo e ha chiamato l’ambulanza.
native_language_example: The farmer was kicked by a horse and called an ambulance.

additional_notes: A common, neutral term used in news, science, and everyday conversation to talk about long-term changes in Earth’s climate (often linked to global warming) and their impacts. Often used with verbs like essere (è reale/è un problema), causare, ridurre, combattere, affrontare, and with nouns like effetti, cause, conseguenze.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo ridurre le emissioni per combattere il cambiamento climatico.
native_language_example: We need to reduce emissions to fight climate change.

additional_notes: Used when you want to move the conversation to a different topic, often to avoid something uncomfortable. Common with verbs like cercare/provare a (to try to), essere bravo/a a (to be good at), and in commands like Smettila/La smetta di cambiare argomento (Stop changing the subject).
target_language_example: Possiamo cambiare argomento?
native_language_example: Can we change the subject?

additional_notes: Used when someone decides differently after thinking again or being persuaded. Often appears with "fare" (to make someone change their mind): "Mi hai fatto cambiare idea" = "You made me change my mind."
target_language_example: Ho cambiato idea: andiamo a casa.
native_language_example: I changed my mind: let's go home.

additional_notes: Used when someone has to do something differently than originally intended. "Il suo" can mean "his" or "her" depending on context (e.g., Mary/Tom). In Italian you can also say "cambiare i suoi piani" for "change his/her plans" (plural). Note: "piano" here means "plan," not the musical instrument.
target_language_example: A causa della pioggia, Maria ha dovuto cambiare il suo piano.
native_language_example: Because of the rain, Maria had to change her plan.

meaning: to change things (to improve a situation).
additional_notes: Used when talking about changing a situation, how things work, or the current state of affairs—often with the idea of making an improvement. Common in motivational or problem-solving contexts ("We have to change things").
target_language_example: Non mi piace questa situazione: voglio cambiare le cose.
native_language_example: I don’t like this situation: I want to change things.

additional_notes: Past participle used with avere in the common phrase cambiare idea (“to change one’s mind”): ho/hai/ha cambiato idea, etc. The “one’s” is understood from the subject, so you usually don’t add a possessive (not *la mia idea*). Often used to say you decided differently after thinking more.
target_language_example: Scusa, ho cambiato idea: vengo con te.
native_language_example: Sorry, I changed my mind: I’m coming with you.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "cambiare" in the passato prossimo to say someone has had a big, positive (or sometimes negative) impact on your life. Very common pattern: "(Tu/Lui/Lei/Voi) mi hai/ha/avete cambiato la vita" = "You/He/She/You all changed my life." You can also change the pronoun: "ti/ci/gli/le" depending on who is affected.
target_language_example: Grazie di tutto: mi hai cambiato la vita.
native_language_example: Thanks for everything: you changed my life.

additional_notes: The room where you sleep. Very common in housing contexts (hotel, apartment). Often used with possessives: "la mia camera da letto" (my bedroom). You can also say "una camera da letto" when describing a home: "un appartamento con due camere da letto" (a two-bedroom apartment).
target_language_example: L'appartamento ha due camere da letto.
native_language_example: The apartment has two bedrooms.

additional_notes: Plural of "camera da letto" (bedroom). Used when describing a house/apartment by number of bedrooms: "una casa con tre camere da letto" = "a three-bedroom house." "Camera" alone can mean "room" or (in hotels) "(hotel) room," so add "da letto" to specify it’s a bedroom.
target_language_example: L'appartamento ha due camere da letto e un soggiorno.
native_language_example: The apartment has two bedrooms and a living room.

additional_notes: Used for someone who has won a world championship title in a sport or competition. You can specify how many times with numbers: "tre volte campione del mondo" (three-time world champion), "sette volte" (seven-time). Feminine: "campionessa del mondo".
target_language_example: Lei è stata campionessa del mondo nel 2022.
native_language_example: She was world champion in 2022.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the area where people play golf. Often with possessives/articles: il/un campo da golf; il mio campo da golf. In commands you might hear: Vada via/Se ne vada dal campo da golf! (“Go away/Leave the golf course!”).
target_language_example: Domani giochiamo a golf in un campo da golf vicino alla città.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re playing golf at a golf course near the city.

additional_notes: Used literally for an area with landmines, and very commonly as a metaphor for a situation full of hidden dangers where one wrong move can cause big problems (e.g., relationships, politics, a tense conversation).
