additional_notes: Means either (1) being physically lost (“We got lost in the fog”) or (2) missing something that happened (“Did we miss something?”). In questions you’ll often hear: “Che/ Cosa ci siamo persi?” = “What did we miss?” and “Ci siamo persi qualcosa?” = “Did we miss something?”.
target_language_example: Scusa, siamo arrivati tardi: ci siamo persi l’inizio del film.
native_language_example: Sorry, we arrived late: we missed the beginning of the movie.

additional_notes: From the verb "sposarsi" (to get married). It uses the auxiliary "essere" ("siamo") and the past participle agrees with the subject: "ci siamo sposati" (two or more males or mixed group), "ci siamo sposate" (all females). "Ci" here means "each other" (the two of us). You can add time expressions: "ci siamo sposati tre anni fa" (we got married three years ago).
target_language_example: Ci siamo sposati l'anno scorso in Comune.
native_language_example: We got married last year at city hall.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "trasferirsi" = "to move/relocate" (change home/city). "Ci" is the reflexive pronoun (like "ourselves"), used because "trasferirsi" is reflexive. It’s often followed by a place with "a" (city) or "in" (house/building/country/region): "Ci siamo trasferiti a New York" / "Ci siamo trasferiti in una nuova casa". You may also see "qui/qua" to mean "here."
target_language_example: Ci siamo trasferiti a Milano per lavoro.
native_language_example: We moved to Milan for work.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the reflexive verb vedersi (“to see each other / to meet”). Used for two-way meetings/encounters: Ci siamo visti due volte (“We met twice”). Often appears with time expressions (per cinque ore, a distanza di settimane) or in phrases like la prima volta che ci siamo visti (“the first time we met”).
target_language_example: Ci siamo visti ieri sera per un caffè.
native_language_example: We met last night for a coffee.

additional_notes: Form of the verb phrase “esserci” (to be there / there to be) in the present subjunctive: “(che) ci siano…”. It’s commonly used after expressions like “credo/penso/spero che…” and in indirect questions like “quanti… pensi che ci siano…?”.
target_language_example: Penso che ci siano abbastanza posti per tutti.
native_language_example: I think there are enough seats for everyone.

additional_notes: Past tense of "esserci" ("to be there", used like English "there is/there are"). It agrees with what follows: use "ci sono state" with feminine plural nouns (e.g., proteste, eccezioni). With masculine plural you use "ci sono stati". It can also mean "they (fem. pl.) were there" depending on context (e.g., "Ci sono state tutte" = "They were all there").
target_language_example: Ieri ci sono state molte persone alla riunione.
native_language_example: Yesterday there were many people at the meeting.

meaning: "there were" / "there have been" (past tense: something happened/existed).
additional_notes: Past form of "ci sono" used with masculine plural nouns (or mixed-gender groups): "ci sono stati incidenti" = "there were accidents." For feminine plural, it becomes "ci sono state" (e.g., "ci sono state molte proteste"). Often used in news/reporting about events, problems, or results (incidents, arrests, damages).
target_language_example: Ci sono stati molti ritardi oggi.
native_language_example: There were a lot of delays today.

meaning: "it took" (past tense, used mainly with a plural feminine noun like 'ore').
additional_notes: This is the past tense of the verb "volerci" (to be needed / to take [time]). It’s used to say how long something took. The verb agrees with what follows: "ci sono volute tre ore" (hours = feminine plural). You can add the person with an indirect object pronoun: "mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli ci sono volute..." = "it took me/you/him/her/us/you/them...". For singular you often see "ci è voluto" (e.g., "Ci è voluto un minuto").
target_language_example: Per arrivare in centro, mi ci sono volute due ore.
native_language_example: To get downtown, it took me two hours.

additional_notes: Used with a time expression to say how long something took. It’s the past tense of “ci vogliono” and agrees with what is “needed”: plural with plural things (e.g., anni, giorni: “ci sono voluti…”), singular with singular (e.g., un giorno: “ci è voluto…”). Often appears as “(mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi) ci sono voluti…” to mean “it took me/you/him/her/us/you all…”.
target_language_example: Ci sono volute due ore per arrivare.
native_language_example: It took two hours to get there.

additional_notes: Used to say that something exists or is present somewhere. Common with numbers and quantities: "Ci sono cinque persone" = "There are five people." Often followed by a place phrase: "ci sono ... sul tavolo / in città / in questa stanza". Singular form: "c'è" = "there is".
target_language_example: Ci sono molti ristoranti vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: There are many restaurants near the station.

additional_notes: Used to say that some unspecified number of things exists/is present somewhere. It’s the plural form of "c’è" (there is). Usually followed by a plural noun: "Ci sono alcuni libri...". In everyday speech, Italians often drop "alcuni" and just say "Ci sono libri..." (= There are books / There are some books).
target_language_example: Ci sono alcuni posti liberi vicino alla finestra.
native_language_example: There are some free seats near the window.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "esserci" (there is/are) to say that additional items/people exist or are available. "Altre" agrees with a feminine plural noun (e.g., case, opzioni). With masculine plural nouns, use "ci sono altri". In questions, intonation (or a question mark in writing) makes it mean "are there...?"; in negatives: "non ci sono altre ..." = "there aren’t any other ...".
target_language_example: Ci sono altre domande?
native_language_example: Are there other questions?

meaning: "there are other things" / "there are more things."
additional_notes:
Used to say that more items, issues, or tasks exist beyond what’s already being discussed. Often followed by extra information, e.g.:
- "ci sono altre cose da + infinitive" = "there are other things to + verb" (Ci sono altre cose da imparare.)
- "ci sono altre cose a cui + verb" = "there are other things to/that + verb" (Ci sono altre cose a cui pensare.)
You can also say "Ci sono altre cose." on its own to mean "There are other things."
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: ci sono altre cose da fare oggi.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there are other things to do today.

additional_notes: Used to say that additional people/things exist, or to ask if more are available. It’s often followed by a plural noun ("Ci sono altri pazienti?") or by a number ("Ci sono altri due..."). In questions it can mean "Are there any others?"
target_language_example: Ci sono altri posti liberi?
native_language_example: Are there any other free seats?

additional_notes: Used to add extra items or people to a list (something exists in addition to what was just mentioned). It’s built from: "ci sono" = "there are" + "anche" = "also/too". It’s typically followed by a plural noun: "Ci sono anche dei/delle..."; with a definite article for specific things: "Ci sono anche le mie...".
target_language_example: In questo quartiere ci sono anche molti parchi.
native_language_example: In this neighborhood there are also many parks.

additional_notes: Used with plural nouns to say something continues to exist or remains unsolved/uncompleted. It’s the plural form of "c’è ancora" (there is still). "ci" is part of the expression "ci sono" = "there are"; "ancora" means "still/yet".
target_language_example: Ci sono ancora due posti liberi.
native_language_example: There are still two free seats.

additional_notes: Used to say that five of something exist/are present. "Ci sono" is the plural form of "esserci" (= to be there), so it’s used with plural nouns (persone, penne, ecc.). You can add a place word like "qui/qua" (here) before or after: "Qui/Qua ci sono cinque...".
target_language_example: In frigo ci sono cinque uova.
native_language_example: There are five eggs in the fridge.

additional_notes: Used to say that some people/things exist or are present. "Ci sono" = "there are" (plural). "degli" is an indefinite article meaning "some" before a masculine plural noun (e.g., degli orsi, degli aggiornamenti, degli elementi). In questions, it asks if some exist/are present: "Ci sono degli ...?"
target_language_example: Ci sono degli ristoranti aperti vicino a qui?
native_language_example: Are there some restaurants open near here?

additional_notes: Used to say that some things exist/are available/present. "Ci sono" = "there are"; "dei" is an indefinite plural article meaning "some" (often before a masculine plural noun, e.g., "dei film", "dei suggerimenti"). In questions, it often means "Are there any…?".
target_language_example: Ci sono dei ristoranti aperti vicino a qui?
native_language_example: Are there any restaurants open near here?

additional_notes: Used with plural nouns to say that some things/people exist or are present. Often starts a statement or a question: "Ci sono delle…?" = "Are there any…?" (expecting a plural answer). "Delle" is an indefinite plural article (roughly “some”).
target_language_example: Scusa, ci sono delle sedie libere qui?
native_language_example: Excuse me, are there any free chairs here?

additional_notes: Used to say that people exist/are present in a place or in general. "Ci sono" = "there are"; "delle" is a partitive article meaning “some.” Often followed by a place ("a scuola") or a relative clause ("che...") to describe which people.
target_language_example: Ci sono delle persone fuori che ti stanno aspettando.
native_language_example: There are some people outside who are waiting for you.

additional_notes: Used to say that two of something exist/are present. It’s the plural form of "c’è" (there is), using "sono" because the thing that exists is plural. Often followed by a plural noun: "Ci sono due finestre" (There are two windows).
target_language_example: In cucina ci sono due sedie.
native_language_example: There are two chairs in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Used to say that certain people/things exist or are present. It’s the plural of “c’è” and uses masculine plural “i” before a noun (e.g., “i fantasmi”, “i tuoi”). For feminine plural, use “ci sono le …”. Word order can vary, but the idea is “there are …”.
target_language_example: In cucina ci sono i bicchieri.
native_language_example: In the kitchen there are the glasses.

additional_notes: Used to say that things exist/are present in a place: "ci sono" = "there are" (plural of "c'è"), and "in" introduces the location (in/inside). Very common in questions with "quanti/quante" (how many): "Quante città ci sono in America?"
target_language_example: Quanti supermercati ci sono in questa città?
native_language_example: How many supermarkets are there in this city?

meaning: 'there are (in this …)' (used to ask or say how many are inside something).
additional_notes: "Ci sono" is the Italian way to say "there are" (plural of "c'è" = "there is"). "In questo" means "in this" + a masculine singular noun (e.g., in questo albergo/album/ospedale). For feminine singular nouns use "in questa" (e.g., in questa casa). Often used with "Quanti/Quante … ci sono in questo/questa …?" to ask "How many … are there in this …?"
target_language_example: Quanti negozi ci sono in questo centro commerciale?
native_language_example: How many shops are there in this mall?

meaning: "I'm here" / "I've got this" (reassuring: you can count on me).
additional_notes: Used to comfort or reassure someone, often implying support, protection, or taking responsibility. It can stand alone (Ci sono io.) or be followed by “con te” (ci sono io con te = I’m here with you / I’m here for you). In context it can also mean “I’ll take care of it.”
target_language_example: Non ti preoccupare: ci sono io.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’m here (I’ve got this).

additional_notes: Used to say that many things exist/are present. It’s the plural of "c’è" and matches feminine plural nouns (molte frasi, molte stanze). With masculine plural nouns, use "ci sono molti" (molti libri). Often followed by a noun; you can add a place: "In Italia/Nella città ci sono molte...".
target_language_example: Qui ci sono molte opzioni vegetariane.
native_language_example: There are many vegetarian options here.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a list of questions, topics, or things you want to do/say. It’s built from: "ci sono" = "there are" + "molte cose" = "many things" + "che" = "that/which". Often followed by a verb like "voglio chiedere" (I want to ask) or "voglio insegnare" (I want to teach). You can change "molte" to "tante" (more conversational) or to another quantity ("alcune", "due", etc.).
target_language_example: Ci sono molte cose che voglio dirti prima di partire.
native_language_example: There are many things I want to tell you before leaving.

additional_notes: Uses "ci sono" (there are) to say that many people are present/exist in a place or situation. Often followed by a place (e.g., "in Europa") or used alone to mean a place is crowded.
target_language_example: In questa stanza ci sono molte persone, facciamo silenzio.
native_language_example: In this room there are many people, let’s be quiet.

additional_notes: Used to say that many people/things exist or are present. It’s the plural form of "c’è" (there is). Usually followed by a plural noun: "Ci sono molti modi" (There are many ways).
target_language_example: Ci sono molti ristoranti in questa zona.
native_language_example: There are many restaurants in this area.

additional_notes: Uses **ci sono** (“there are”) to state the existence/presence of something in a place. **Molti** agrees with the plural noun (**alberi**). Often followed by a location phrase (e.g., *nel parco*, *in questa foresta*) or a relative clause (*che crescono…*).
target_language_example: In questo quartiere ci sono molti alberi e l’aria è più fresca.
native_language_example: In this neighborhood there are many trees and the air is cooler.

additional_notes: Uses **ci sono** (plural of **c’è**) to say that something exists/is present somewhere. Often followed by extra details like adjectives (**alti**, **moderni**) and a place (**qui intorno**, **in quella città**).
target_language_example: In centro ci sono molti edifici storici.
native_language_example: Downtown there are many historic buildings.

additional_notes: Used to say that many books exist/are present in a place. "Ci sono" is the plural form of "c’è" (there is/there are) and is followed by a plural noun. You can add a location with "in" or "nella/nella mia" + place (e.g., "in questa biblioteca", "nella mia stanza").
target_language_example: Ci sono molti libri sul tavolo.
native_language_example: There are many books on the table.

additional_notes: Used with *ci sono* (“there are”) to say that problems/issues exist, or in questions to ask if something is wrong. Often followed by *di* + noun (e.g., *problemi di comunicazione* = communication problems) or *con* + noun (e.g., *problemi con la macchina* = problems with the car). In questions, intonation or a question mark makes it “Are there any problems?”
target_language_example: Se ci sono problemi con l’ordine, dimmelo subito.
native_language_example: If there are any problems with the order, tell me right away.

additional_notes: Used to say that the number/amount is limited (and often less than expected). It’s made of: "ci sono" = "there are" + "solo" = "only", and it’s followed by a plural noun or a quantity (e.g., "poche", a number).
target_language_example: Ci sono solo due sedie in cucina.
native_language_example: There are only two chairs in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Used to say that three people/things exist or are present somewhere. It’s the plural form of “esserci” (to be there): “c’è” = “there is” (singular), “ci sono” = “there are” (plural). You can swap out “tre” for any other number (e.g., “ci sono due…”, “ci sono quattro…”).
target_language_example: In frigo ci sono tre uova.
native_language_example: There are three eggs in the fridge.

additional_notes: Used to say an excessive number of things/people are present. It’s the plural form of "c’è / ci sono" + "troppe" (feminine plural), so it’s followed by a feminine plural noun: "ci sono troppe persone/cose/domande". For masculine plural nouns, use "ci sono troppi" (e.g., "ci sono troppi problemi").
target_language_example: Non possiamo entrare: ci sono troppe persone.
native_language_example: We can’t go in: there are too many people.

additional_notes: Used to complain or comment that an excessive number of something (plural) is present. It’s made of: "ci sono" = "there are" + "troppi" = "too many" (masculine plural). Change "troppi" to match what follows: feminine plural "troppe" (Ci sono troppe persone), singular "troppo/troppa" with an uncountable noun (C’è troppo rumore / C’è troppa gente).
target_language_example: Ci sono troppi autobus in centro oggi.
native_language_example: There are too many buses downtown today.

meaning: "there are lots of / a ton of".
additional_notes: Very common, fairly informal way to say there are many of something. It’s built from "ci sono" (there are) + "un sacco di" (a lot of). Usually followed by a plural noun ("Ci sono un sacco di persone"), but it can also be used with uncountable nouns ("Ci sono un sacco di traffico / di gente"). More neutral alternatives: "ci sono molti/e" or "ci sono tanti/e".
target_language_example: Ci sono un sacco di cose da fare oggi.
native_language_example: There are lots of things to do today.

meaning: "is" (with "ci" = "us" or "there"), often used to form the continuous tense.
additional_notes: "Ci" is a pronoun that can mean "us" or "there" depending on context. "Sta" is from "stare" (he/she/it is). Very common in the present continuous: "stare" + gerund (e.g., "sta seguendo" = "is following"). So "ci sta seguendo" means "he/she is following us" (here "ci" = "us").
target_language_example: Ci sta aspettando fuori.
native_language_example: He/She is waiting for us outside.

additional_notes: Uses the present progressive: "stare" + gerund ("sta guardando" = "is watching"). "Ci" here means "us" (object pronoun): "watching us". The subject is understood from context (he/she/it), e.g., "Tom ci sta guardando" = "Tom is watching us."
target_language_example: Non parlare così forte: ci sta guardando.
native_language_example: Don’t talk so loudly: he’s watching us.

meaning: "we are" (used to form the present continuous: "we’re …-ing").
additional_notes: Used with a gerund (verb ending in -ando/-endo) to mean “we are doing something right now”: *stiamo + gerund* = “we’re …-ing”. The pronoun *ci* can mean “us/ourselves” or “each other” (reciprocal), depending on the verb (e.g., *ci stiamo incontrando* = “we’re meeting (each other)”). Sometimes *ci* can also refer to “there/here” in other contexts, but in many everyday sentences it’s part of the verb phrase.
target_language_example: Ci stiamo preparando per uscire.
native_language_example: We’re getting ready to go out.

additional_notes: "Ci" replaces a previously mentioned place or destination (like "there"), and sometimes an activity/event you’re going to (like "to it"). It’s very common in spoken Italian when the destination is understood from context. Negative: "non ci vado" = "I’m not going (there)."
target_language_example: Hai voglia di andare al cinema? Sì, ci vado volentieri.
native_language_example: Do you feel like going to the cinema? Yes, I’ll gladly go.

additional_notes: Common farewell or plan-confirming phrase (often like “See you!”). It can be used with a time or place: ci vediamo domani (see you tomorrow), ci vediamo alla stazione (see you at the station), ci vediamo tra poco (see you soon). It can also be negated to mean it’s better not to meet: È meglio se non ci vediamo (It’s better if we don’t see each other).
target_language_example: Ok, allora ci vediamo alle otto davanti al cinema.
native_language_example: Okay, then see you at eight in front of the movie theater.

additional_notes: A very common way to say goodbye while agreeing to meet again the next day. Literally “we see each other tomorrow,” but it functions like English “see you tomorrow.” You can add a place/time: “Ci vediamo domani a scuola/in ufficio.”
target_language_example: Va bene, ci vediamo domani alle otto.
native_language_example: Alright, see you tomorrow at eight.

additional_notes: Common, friendly way to say goodbye when you expect to meet again later (today or soon). Literally "we see each other later"; the pronoun "ci" means "each other/us". Often used on its own or with a time/place: "Ci vediamo dopo alla festa" (see you later at the party).
target_language_example: Devo andare adesso: ci vediamo dopo!
native_language_example: I have to go now: see you later!

additional_notes: Used mainly with time expressions, especially in questions like: "Quanto tempo pensa/pensi/pensate che ci voglia per andare da [place A] a [place B]?". "ci voglia" is the subjunctive form (from "ci vuole" = "it takes"), commonly triggered by verbs of opinion like "pensare" (pensa/pensi/pensate) and by indirect questions.
target_language_example: Quanto tempo pensi che ci voglia per andare da Roma a Firenze?
native_language_example: How long do you think it takes to go from Rome to Florence?

additional_notes: Future tense of "ci vuole" (from "volerci"), used to say how much time (or sometimes effort) something will require. Often followed by a time expression ("un minuto", "molto tempo") or by "per" + infinitive: "Ci vorrà tempo per...". You can negate it: "Non ci vorrà tanto" = "It won’t take long".
target_language_example: Per arrivare in centro, ci vorrà circa mezz’ora.
native_language_example: To get downtown, it will take about half an hour.

additional_notes: Impersonal use of "volere" with "ci" to say that something is necessary or that a certain amount of time/effort is required. Common patterns: "Ci vuole + noun" (Ci vuole pazienza. = You need patience.), "Ci vuole + time" (Ci vuole un attimo. = It takes a moment.), "Quanto tempo ci vuole per..." (How long does it take to...?). Plural: "ci vogliono" (Ci vogliono due ore. = It takes two hours.)
target_language_example: Per arrivare in centro, ci vuole mezz'ora a piedi.
native_language_example: To get downtown, it takes half an hour on foot.

additional_notes: Common greeting + the verb “to be” (sono = “I am”). Often used to introduce yourself (“Ciao, sono Marco”), identify yourself on the phone or at the door (“Ciao, sono io!”), or announce you’ve returned (“Ciao, sono tornato/a”). “Ciao” is informal; in more formal situations use “Buongiorno/Salve, sono …”.
target_language_example: Ciao, sono Laura. Piacere!
native_language_example: Hi, I’m Laura. Nice to meet you!

additional_notes: A very informal, often playful way to say goodbye (sometimes used to quickly end a chat/call). Tone depends on context: it can sound friendly with friends/family, but it can also be dismissive or rude if said sharply or paired with an insult.
target_language_example: Devo andare, ciao ciao!
native_language_example: I have to go, bye-bye!

additional_notes: Used to talk about Chinese cuisine in general, whether you’re eating it, cooking it, or ordering it. Often appears with verbs like mangiare (to eat), cucinare (to cook), and ordinare (to order). You may also hear/see "ristorante cinese" (Chinese restaurant).
target_language_example: Stasera ordiniamo cibo cinese.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re ordering Chinese food.

additional_notes: Used to talk about Japanese cuisine in general or to identify whether a dish/restaurant is Japanese. In questions, you’ll often hear it with "che tipo/i di" (what kind(s) of): "Che tipo di cibo giapponese...?"
target_language_example: Stasera mangiamo cibo giapponese.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re eating Japanese food.

meaning: halal food (food prepared according to Islamic rules).
additional_notes: Used to ask for or describe food that meets halal dietary requirements. You might see it on menus or use it when ordering: "Avete cibo halal?" or "Servite cibo halal?".
target_language_example: Scusi, avete cibo halal?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you have halal food?

additional_notes: Common in advice or warnings about unhealthy eating (often with verbs like mangiare “to eat”, smettere di “to stop”, or essere dipendente da “to be addicted to”). You can also say "junk food" as "cibo junk" in informal contexts, but "cibo spazzatura" is the standard Italian phrase.
target_language_example: Cerco di evitare il cibo spazzatura durante la settimana.
native_language_example: I try to avoid junk food during the week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the highest point of a mountain. Often appears with prepositions like “in cima alla montagna” (at the top of the mountain) and with verbs like “raggiungere” (to reach). “Cima” can also mean the top of other things (e.g., “la cima dell’albero” = the top of the tree).
target_language_example: Dopo tre ore di cammino, siamo arrivati in cima alla montagna.
native_language_example: After three hours of walking, we arrived at the top of the mountain.

additional_notes: Used when you clink glasses before drinking. You can say it on its own (often with an exclamation mark) or with someone’s name (e.g., “Cin cin, Marco!”). It’s casual and friendly; also sometimes written with a hyphen: “cin-cin”.
target_language_example: Cin cin, ragazzi!
native_language_example: Cheers, guys!

meaning: five years (or: at five years old).
additional_notes: Used for duration ("per cinque anni" = for five years), age ("a cinque anni" / "quando avevo cinque anni" = at age five / when I was five), and in the pattern "Sono cinque anni che..." meaning "It’s been five years since...".
target_language_example: Sono cinque anni che vivo in Italia.
native_language_example: I’ve been living in Italy for five years.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened five years in the past. Typically goes at the end of the sentence (e.g., “Ho iniziato a lavorare qui cinque anni fa.”). You can replace the number for other time spans: “due anni fa” (two years ago), “dieci anni fa” (ten years ago).
target_language_example: Mi sono trasferito a Roma cinque anni fa.
native_language_example: I moved to Rome five years ago.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an amount of money in US dollars. In Italian you often say the number first, then the currency: "cinque dollari". In questions it commonly appears with "hai... ?" (Do you have...?).
target_language_example: Mi presti cinque dollari, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you lend me five dollars, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration or time remaining. Often followed by “di + noun” to mean “five days of …” (e.g., “cinque giorni di vacanza”), or used with verbs like “durare” (to last) and “restare” (to remain).
target_language_example: Mi mancano cinque giorni per finire il progetto.
native_language_example: I have five days left to finish the project.

additional_notes: Used for duration or time remaining ("for/in five minutes"), and very commonly as a rough estimate ("just a few minutes"). It can refer to having a bit of time available ("Hai cinque minuti?" = “Do you have five minutes?”), distance on foot ("Sono cinque minuti a piedi" = “It’s a five-minute walk”), or a time offset ("cinque minuti prima" = “five minutes earlier”; "fra cinque minuti" = “in five minutes”).
target_language_example: Aspettami cinque minuti, per favore.
native_language_example: Wait for me five minutes, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration of time (how long something lasts). Common with "per" (for): "per cinque ore" = "for five hours". In the pattern "Sono cinque ore che...", it means "It’s been five hours since..." / "...has been ... for five hours."
target_language_example: Ho aspettato per cinque ore.
native_language_example: I waited for five hours.

additional_notes: Used for the car’s safety belt (and sometimes other safety belts). Common in travel/driving contexts and in safety instructions: "Metta/Metti la cintura di sicurezza" (Put on your seat belt), "Allacci la cintura" (Fasten your seat belt).
target_language_example: Per favore, allaccia la cintura di sicurezza.
native_language_example: Please, fasten your seat belt.

additional_notes: A common drink, especially in autumn/winter. In Italy it’s often thicker than American-style hot cocoa. You’ll hear it with an article: "una cioccolata calda" (a hot chocolate) or with partitive "della cioccolata calda" (some hot chocolate). "Qui fanno una cioccolata calda..." means “they make/serve a hot chocolate here.”
target_language_example: Prendo una cioccolata calda, per favore.
native_language_example: I’ll have a hot chocolate, please.

meaning: about his/her age; roughly the same age.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is approximately the same age as another person. "la sua" means "his" or "her" depending on who you’re talking about (e.g., "circa la mia età" = about my age; "circa la tua età" = about your age).
target_language_example: Cerco qualcuno circa la mia età.
native_language_example: I’m looking for someone about my age.

meaning: about how many hours per day
additional_notes: Used to ask for an approximate amount of time spent on something each day. It often appears in questions, with the activity verb placed at the end (e.g., studiare, lavorare). You can use it with different subjects: tu/Lei/voi, etc.
target_language_example: Circa quante ore al giorno lavori?
native_language_example: About how many hours per day do you work?

meaning: a vicious cycle; a self-reinforcing negative loop.
additional_notes: Used for a situation where one problem causes another, which then makes the first problem worse (e.g., stress → poor sleep → more stress). Common verbs: entrare in/iniziare un circolo vizioso (to get into/start one), uscire da un circolo vizioso (to get out of one), spezzare/interrompere un circolo vizioso (to break one).
target_language_example: Se rimandi sempre, entri in un circolo vizioso di ansia e ritardi.
native_language_example: If you always procrastinate, you get into a vicious cycle of anxiety and delays.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an idea or thing, meaning “the thing that…”. Common in more formal or written Italian; in everyday speech people often use “quello che” instead. It’s followed by a verb clause: “Ciò che dici è vero” = “What you say is true.”
target_language_example: Non capisco ciò che hai detto.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what you said.

meaning: 'what he/she says' (the thing that he/she says).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the content of someone’s words. "Ciò che" means "what/that which" and "dice" is "says" (present tense of dire). Often followed by a person’s name (e.g., "ciò che dice Tom") or understood from context.
target_language_example: Non credere a tutto ciò che dice.
native_language_example: Don’t believe everything he/she says.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause referring to an action or statement. “Ciò che” means “what / that which,” and “ha” is “has” (3rd person singular of avere), often used with a past participle in the passato prossimo: ciò che ha detto (what he/she said), ciò che ha fatto (what he/she did). The subject (he/she/it) is understood from context.
target_language_example: Non capisco ciò che ha scritto.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what he/she wrote.

additional_notes: Uses "ciò che" (= "what/that which") + past tense "ha detto" (has said/said). It refers back to a statement already made. The person who spoke is understood from context (he, she, you, a named person: "ciò che ha detto Mary"). Often followed by opinions or evaluations: "è sbagliato", "è contrario ai fatti", "ci ha convinti".
target_language_example: Mi dispiace per ciò che ha detto ieri.
native_language_example: I'm sorry about what you said yesterday.

meaning: what he/she did; what (someone) has done.
additional_notes: Used to refer back to an action already mentioned or understood from context. "Ciò che" = "what/that which"; "ha fatto" is the passato prossimo of "fare" and agrees with the subject (e.g., "ciò che hai fatto" = what you did/you’ve done; "ciò che hanno fatto" = what they did).
target_language_example: Non riesco a credere a ciò che ha fatto ieri.
native_language_example: I can’t believe what he did yesterday.

additional_notes: Uses the pronoun phrase "ciò che" (= “what / that which”) + "hai detto" (past: “you said/you have said”). It can act as the subject or object of the sentence: "Ciò che hai detto mi ha convinto" (“What you said convinced me”).
target_language_example: Non ho capito ciò che hai detto.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what you said.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to the content of your earlier words (a specific statement or message). Common after verbs like avere dubbi (to have doubts), rimpiangere (to regret), capire (to understand), ricordare (to remember). The pronoun "ciò che" means "what/that which" and is slightly more formal than "quello che" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace per ciò che ho detto ieri.
native_language_example: I'm sorry for what I said yesterday.

meaning: "what I want" / "the thing that I want".
additional_notes: Uses the relative expression "ciò che" (“what/that which”) + "voglio" (“I want”) to refer to a desired thing or action. Often followed by a verb in the infinitive (e.g., "Questo è ciò che voglio fare") or by a noun phrase (e.g., "Ciò che voglio è un computer nuovo"). A common alternative is "quello che voglio" with a very similar meaning.
target_language_example: Dimmi ciò che vuoi davvero.
native_language_example: Tell me what you really want.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific thing (or things) that someone wanted. It’s built from "ciò che" (= "what/that which") + "voleva" (imperfect of "volere", "to want"). The subject is implied by context (he/she).
target_language_example: Ho trovato ciò che voleva Luca.
native_language_example: I found what Luca wanted.

additional_notes: Uses "ciò che" (= “what/that which”) to refer to an unspecified thing or action. "Vuole" can refer to he or she (Italian often relies on context for the subject). If you need to be explicit, you can say: "ciò che lui vuole" / "ciò che lei vuole".
target_language_example: Non posso darti ciò che vuole.
native_language_example: I can't give him/her what he/she wants.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective or phrase to refer to “the thing(s) that are …”: ciò che è giusto (what is right), ciò che è richiesto (what is required), ciò che è tuo (what is yours). It’s fairly formal and close to “quello che è,” but “ciò” sounds more abstract/general. Often appears in set expressions like Riprendersi ciò che è suo (“to take back what is his”).
target_language_example: Ho imparato a riconoscere ciò che è davvero importante.
native_language_example: I learned to recognize what is really important.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a thing (or things) needed, talked about, etc., where Italian requires "di" after the verb/adjective (e.g., avere bisogno di). Very common in sentences like "Ciò di cui ho bisogno è..." = "What I need is...". Often followed by a verb: "ciò di cui avevo bisogno".
target_language_example: Non ho ancora trovato ciò di cui ho bisogno.
native_language_example: I still haven’t found what I need.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a hairstyle where the hair is tied back in a tail. Often used with the verb avere (to have): “Ha una coda di cavallo.” It can also be used as a suggestion or question: “Coda di cavallo oggi?”
target_language_example: Mi piace portare i capelli a coda di cavallo quando fa caldo.
native_language_example: I like wearing my hair in a ponytail when it’s hot.

meaning: No way / Yeah right (strong, vulgar denial).
additional_notes: Very vulgar expression used to strongly reject something or to say you absolutely won’t do something. Often appears as “Col cazzo che …” meaning “No way that … / As if …” It can also be used sarcastically to contradict a statement (like “Sure he is… not!”). Avoid in polite settings.
target_language_example: Col cazzo che vengo alla festa dopo quello che hai detto.
native_language_example: No way I’m coming to the party after what you said.

additional_notes: Contraction of “con il tempo.” Used to say that something changes or happens gradually as time passes (often with verbs like abituarsi, smettere, migliorare, risolversi). Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis: “Col tempo, …”.
target_language_example: Col tempo, imparerai a parlare italiano più facilmente.
native_language_example: Over time, you’ll learn to speak Italian more easily.

additional_notes: Used to talk about having breakfast earlier today, often with the verb "fare": "fare colazione" = "to have breakfast". You can ask in different levels of formality ("Hai..." informal singular, "Lei ha..." formal singular, "Voi avete..." plural).
target_language_example: Ho fatto colazione questa mattina alle sette.
native_language_example: I had breakfast this morning at seven.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for the hobby/collection of postage stamps. Often used with possessives (la mia/ la sua collezione di francobolli) and verbs like avere (to have), mostrare (to show), essere fiero/orgoglioso di (to be proud of).
target_language_example: Da bambino, ho iniziato una collezione di francobolli con mio nonno.
native_language_example: As a child, I started a stamp collection with my grandfather.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of people defined by what follows in the relative clause (che + verb). It’s a more formal/plural way to say "those who"; for women only you can also hear "coloro che" used, but the explicitly feminine form is "coloro" is masculine plural/mixed, while "coloro" often covers mixed groups in Italian.
target_language_example: Coloro che parlano inglese possono aiutarmi?
native_language_example: Those who speak English, can you help me?

additional_notes: Used to accept responsibility or deny it. Common patterns: "È colpa mia" = "It’s my fault"; "Non è colpa mia" = "It’s not my fault"; also with other possessives: "colpa tua" (your fault), "colpa sua" (his/her fault). Often follows "è/non è" and can be emphasized with "tutta": "È tutta colpa mia" (It’s all my fault).
target_language_example: Scusa, è colpa mia se siamo in ritardo.
native_language_example: Sorry, it’s my fault if we’re late.

meaning: his/her fault; blame belongs to him/her.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is responsible for a mistake/problem. Common patterns: "È (tutta) colpa sua" = "It’s (all) his/her fault" and "Non è stata colpa sua" = "It wasn’t his/her fault." With "per colpa sua" it means "because of him/her" (often negative consequences). "Sua" agrees with the feminine noun "colpa"; you can also say "colpa mia/tua/nostra/vostra/loro".
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma è colpa sua se siamo in ritardo.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but it’s his/her fault if we’re late.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone is responsible for something bad that happened. Most common pattern: “È (tutta) colpa tua” = “It’s (all) your fault.” With prepositions: “per colpa tua” = “because of you / due to you” (usually negative). You can soften it with “Non è colpa tua” = “It’s not your fault.”
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, è stata colpa tua, ma possiamo rimediare.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, it was your fault, but we can fix it.

additional_notes: Used (often with the verb essere/venire/fu) to describe someone being hit by lightning. You may also see the plural: "colpito da un fulmine" (masc.), "colpita da un fulmine" (fem.), "colpiti/colpite da un fulmine" (plural).
target_language_example: Durante il temporale, un albero è stato colpito da un fulmine.
native_language_example: During the storm, a tree was struck by lightning.

meaning: "a blow/hit of"; used in many set phrases (e.g., a cough, a gunshot, a coup).
additional_notes: Literally “a blow of,” but in practice it’s a very common pattern used to form nouns meaning a single impact/sudden event or a specific kind of “strike”: colpo di tosse (a cough), colpo di pistola (a gunshot), colpo di martello (a hammer blow), colpo di Stato (a coup d’état), colpo di fantasia (a burst/flash of imagination). The exact English translation depends on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Ho sentito un colpo di pistola in lontananza.
native_language_example: I heard a gunshot in the distance.

meaning: a stroke of luck; a lucky break.
additional_notes: Used to talk about an unexpected positive event that happens by chance. Very common with exclamations like “Che colpo di fortuna!” and with “per un colpo di fortuna” (thanks to luck / by a lucky chance) or “sperare in un colpo di fortuna” (to hope for a lucky break).
target_language_example: Abbiamo trovato un tavolo libero all’ultimo minuto: che colpo di fortuna!
native_language_example: We found a free table at the last minute: what a stroke of luck!

meaning: a coup (d’état); an attempt to overthrow a government by force.
additional_notes: Used in political/historical contexts to describe a sudden, usually illegal takeover of power (often by the military or a faction within the state). In Italian it’s commonly used with verbs like "organizzare" (to organize), "fare" (to do/carry out), "eseguire" (to execute/carry out).
target_language_example: Temono un colpo di stato dopo le proteste.
native_language_example: They fear a coup after the protests.

additional_notes: Used for an everyday knife used to prepare food. Common with verbs like avere (to have), servire (to need), prendere/prendi/prendete (to take). The pattern “da + noun” often means “for + purpose” (here: for the kitchen/for cooking).
target_language_example: Puoi passarmi il coltello da cucina, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you pass me the kitchen knife, please?

additional_notes: Formal, written-style way to refer to a person identified by a relative clause (che + verb). It’s masculine singular; feminine is **colei che**, plural **coloro che**. In everyday speech you often use **chi** (“whoever/the one who”) instead.
target_language_example: Colui che ha trovato le chiavi è già uscito.
native_language_example: The one who found the keys has already gone out.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens in the typical/normal way, often implying “no surprise.” Common in everyday speech and can sound mildly ironic depending on tone. Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence: "Come al solito, ..." / "..., come al solito."
target_language_example: Come al solito, sei in ritardo.
native_language_example: As usual, you're late.

meaning: “like you” (formal) / “like her”; also used in comparisons (“as … as you/her”).
additional_notes: “Lei” (capital L) is the polite/formal way to say “you” in Italian. So “come lei” often means “like you” when speaking politely to someone. With “lei” (lowercase), it can mean “like her” (referring to a woman). It’s also common in comparisons: “È alto come lei” = “He is as tall as you/her.”
target_language_example: Non conosco nessuno come lei.
native_language_example: I don’t know anyone like you. (formal)

meaning: 'like him' (in the same way / similar to him).
additional_notes: Used to compare a person’s behavior, character, or situation to a specific male person already mentioned (lui = him). Often follows nouns or verbs: “persone come lui” = “people like him,” “diventare come lui” = “to become like him,” “finire come lui” = “to end up like him.”
target_language_example: Non voglio diventare come lui.
native_language_example: I don’t want to become like him.

additional_notes: Used to compare someone/something to yourself. With adjectives it often means “as + adjective + as me” (e.g., alto come me = as tall as me). With nouns/plurals it means “people like me / those like me” (quelli come me).
target_language_example: Nessuno capisce questa situazione come me.
native_language_example: No one understands this situation like I do.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is attending/acting in an official role on behalf of your company. It often follows verbs like partecipare (to take part), andare (to go), intervenire (to speak/attend), or essere presente (to be present).
target_language_example: Sono qui come nostro rappresentante aziendale per discutere il contratto.
native_language_example: I’m here as our company representative to discuss the contract.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the same as it used to be, often after a change or problem: "tutto come prima" = "everything back to normal." In negative form it’s common in emotional contexts: "non è più come prima" = "it’s not like it was anymore."
target_language_example: Dopo la lite, voglio che tra noi sia tutto come prima.
native_language_example: After the argument, I want everything between us to be like before.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the same as it normally is (often with a positive or negative tone). It can appear at the start of a sentence (“Come sempre, ...”) or after an adjective (“Incantevole come sempre”).
target_language_example: Sei in ritardo come sempre!
native_language_example: You’re late as always!

meaning: like her mother; as her mother (did).
additional_notes: Used to compare someone to her mother, in looks, personality, skills, etc. It can mean (1) “like her mother” (similar to her), or (2) “as her mother (did/was)” when talking about a role or situation that repeats. Note: Italian come usually means “like/as,” not English “come.”
target_language_example: Parla piano, come sua madre.
native_language_example: She speaks softly, like her mother.

additional_notes: Used to compare someone to his father (similarity in job, behavior, etc.). With verbs like "chiamarsi" or "essere chiamato", it can mean "(to be) named like his father" (e.g., having the same name).
target_language_example: Luca parla inglese come suo padre.
native_language_example: Luca speaks English like his father.

additional_notes: Used to compare someone/something to the person you’re talking to. It often follows a noun (e.g., persone come te = people like you). Variants: come me (like me), come lui/lei (like him/her), come voi (like you, plural/formal), come loro (like them).
target_language_example: Non conosco nessuno come te.
native_language_example: I don’t know anyone like you.

meaning: like everyone else; like all the others.
additional_notes: Used to compare someone/something to the rest of a group, meaning “in the same way as the others” or “normally/typically.” Common with verbs like essere (“to be”), fare (“to do”), and iniziare (“to start”): *essere/fare/iniziare come tutti gli altri*. It can sound neutral (“normally”) or express frustration about not being normal/treated the same. In sentence 7, *di merda* is very vulgar slang (“like crap”).
target_language_example: Voglio essere trattato come tutti gli altri.
native_language_example: I want to be treated like everyone else.

meaning: "like a" / "as a" (to compare someone or something to something else).
additional_notes: Used to make comparisons and similes: verb + come un + noun (e.g., "corre come un razzo" = "runs like a rocket"). It can also express how you interpret something: "lo prendo come un complimento" (“I take it as a compliment”). Note: Italian "come" often means “like/as,” not English “come.”
target_language_example: Dorme come un bambino quando è stanco.
native_language_example: He sleeps like a baby when he’s tired.

meaning: like a child; like a little kid.
additional_notes: Used to compare someone’s behavior to a child’s, often to criticize them for being immature. It can also describe being treated in an overly protective or patronizing way ("He treats me like a child").
target_language_example: Non parlarmi così: non sono come un bambino!
native_language_example: Don’t talk to me like that: I’m not like a child!

meaning: “like a dog” (often: in a miserable/undignified way).
additional_notes: Used as a comparison, often with a negative or harsh tone. It can mean being treated badly (“ammazzarlo come un cane” = kill him like a dog), being left completely alone (“finirai solo come un cane”), or doing something in a rough/uncomfortable way (“ho dormito come un cane” = I slept terribly). In literal contexts it can also simply mean “like a dog” (e.g., “abbaiare come un cane” = bark like a dog).
target_language_example: Dopo il viaggio ho dormito come un cane.
native_language_example: After the trip I slept terribly.

meaning: like a horse; (figuratively) very fast/strong, or eating a lot.
additional_notes: Used with verbs and adjectives to intensify a comparison: correre come un cavallo (run very fast), essere forte come un cavallo (very strong), mangiare come un cavallo (eat a lot). Literally means “like a horse,” and it can be complimentary (strong/fast) or just descriptive (eats a lot).
target_language_example: Dopo l’allenamento ho mangiato come un cavallo.
native_language_example: After training I ate a ton.

meaning: “like a pig” (used to say someone eats greedily, sweats a lot, or bleeds heavily).
additional_notes: A strong, often rude/impolite comparison. Common with verbs like "mangiare" (to eat), "sudare" (to sweat), and "sanguinare" (to bleed). Used for emphasis, usually in informal speech.
target_language_example: Dopo la corsa, sudavo come un maiale.
native_language_example: After the run, I was sweating like a pig.

meaning: "like a" / "as a" (used to make a comparison).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun in comparisons or to describe someone/something in terms of another thing (often in similes): "X è/era ... come una ...". With masculine nouns you use "come un" (or "come uno" before s+consonant, z, gn, ps, etc.).
target_language_example: È testarda come una mula.
native_language_example: She’s as stubborn as a mule.

meaning: like a little girl; like a child (often implying childish behavior).
additional_notes: Used to compare someone’s behavior or feelings to those of a child. It can be neutral (feeling inexperienced or vulnerable) or critical/teasing (acting immature, crying, being treated as if you’re not grown up). Often used with verbs like "comportarsi" (behave), "piangere" (cry), "sentirsi" (feel), and "trattare" (treat).
target_language_example: Non trattarmi come una bambina: posso farlo da sola.
native_language_example: Don’t treat me like a child: I can do it myself.

meaning: like a sponge; (especially) drinking a lot.
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like "bere" to mean someone drinks heavily (often alcohol). It’s a colorful, colloquial comparison: they "absorb" drinks like a sponge.
target_language_example: Ieri sera ha bevuto come una spugna.
native_language_example: Last night he drank like a sponge.

additional_notes: Used with the plural/formal “voi” to compare or say someone is similar to the people you’re speaking to. With nouns/pronouns it often means “people like you” (persone come voi). With adjectives/adverbs it makes comparisons: “intelligente/alto/ricca come voi” = “as smart/tall/rich as you (all)”.
target_language_example: Non conosco molte persone come voi.
native_language_example: I don’t know many people like you (all).

meaning: "how did you" / "how have you" (you plural or formal).
additional_notes: Used to ask how someone did something. "Avete" is the verb "avere" (you have) used as an auxiliary in the passato prossimo (e.g., "Come avete risolto...?" = "How did you solve...?"), or as the main verb "have" depending on context. It addresses more than one person (voi) or can be used as a polite/formal "you" in some contexts.
target_language_example: Come avete trovato questo ristorante?
native_language_example: How did you find this restaurant?

meaning: “how …” with ci = “to us / there / in it” (depends on context).
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask the way something happens/works. The pronoun **ci** can mean **“us”** (e.g., *come ci dividiamo…* = “how do we divide it between us?”) or **“there / in it / about it”** (very common with verbs like *arrivare, andare, riuscire*). You’ll often see it as **come ci si …** (impersonal “how can one … / how do you … in general?”).
target_language_example: Scusa, come ci arrivo al museo?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how do I get to the museum?

meaning: "how does it feel?" / "how do you feel?"
additional_notes: Uses the impersonal "si" ("one/people"), so it’s a general question about the feeling or experience of a situation. Often followed by "a + infinitive" (Come ci si sente a essere...?) or "in + noun" (Come ci si sente in libertà?). You can also use it on its own to ask someone for their reaction: "Quindi, come ci si sente?"
target_language_example: Come ci si sente a vivere da soli?
native_language_example: How does it feel to live alone?

additional_notes: Used to ask how something is possible or how someone is able to do something (often with surprise, disbelief, or criticism). Structure: "Come fa a" + infinitive (e.g., come fa a dormire = how does he/she manage to sleep). You can add the subject after "fa": "Come fa Sam a…?".
target_language_example: Come fai a ricordarti tutti questi nomi?
native_language_example: How do you manage to remember all these names?

additional_notes: Used to question how someone knows something or how they could be sure. It’s built with "come" (how) + "fa" (does) + "a" + infinitive: "sapere" (to know). Often changes person: "come fai a sapere...?" (you), "come fa a sapere...?" (he/she/you formal), "come fate a sapere...?" (you all).
target_language_example: Come fai a sapere che è vero?
native_language_example: How do you know it’s true?

meaning: “How do I…?” / “How can I…?” (how to do something).
additional_notes: Used to ask for instructions or the way to do something: Come faccio a + infinitive (come faccio a pagare? = how can I pay?). It can also express difficulty or impossibility depending on tone/context (“How am I supposed to…?”).
target_language_example: Scusa, come faccio a arrivare alla stazione?
native_language_example: Sorry, how do I get to the station?

meaning: “How do you manage to…?” / “How can you…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask how someone is able to do something, often with surprise, disbelief, or curiosity. It’s built from come (how) + fai (you do/make) + a + infinitive: “Come fai a saperlo?” = “How do you know?” In everyday speech it can sound a bit challenging depending on tone.
target_language_example: Come fai a ricordarti tutti questi nomi?
native_language_example: How do you manage to remember all these names?

meaning: "How do you know (that)?" / "How did you find out?"
additional_notes: Used to ask how someone knows some information. Often followed by **che + clause** (Come fai a sapere che…?) or by a noun phrase (Come fai a sapere il mio nome?). **fai** is the informal singular “you” (tu).
target_language_example: Come fai a sapere dove abito?
native_language_example: How do you know where I live?

additional_notes: Used to ask how someone found out some information, often with surprise or suspicion. It’s built from: come = how, fai = you do/you manage, a + sapere = to know, lo = it/that. You can add emphasis with a subject (e.g., “Tu come fai a saperlo?” = “How do you know that, you?”).
target_language_example: Come fai a saperlo? Non te l’ho mai detto.
native_language_example: How do you know that? I never told you.

meaning: “how it works” / “how it works (how it functions).”
additional_notes: Used to ask for or explain the way something works. Often followed by a noun (e.g., come funziona la lavastoviglie) or by “questo/quella cosa” (“this/that”). It can also be used in questions (“Come funziona?”) or embedded in a longer sentence (“Spiegami come funziona”).
target_language_example: Puoi mostrarmi come funziona questa app?
native_language_example: Can you show me how this app works?

additional_notes: Used in indirect questions after verbs like sapere (to know), capire (to understand), or spiegare (to explain): “Sai come funziona il sistema?” = “Do you know how the system works?” Word order stays like a normal question (come funziona...), even though it’s inside a longer sentence.
target_language_example: Non capisco come funziona il sistema.
native_language_example: I don’t understand how the system works.

additional_notes: Used to ask for an explanation of how a device works. Often appears inside a longer question with verbs like spiegare (“to explain”), e.g. Puoi/Può spiegare…?. Puoi is informal (to a friend), while Può is formal/polite (to a stranger).
target_language_example: Non capisco: come funziona questa macchina?
native_language_example: I don’t understand: how does this machine work?

meaning: “How did you do it?” / “How did (someone) manage to…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask about the way or method someone achieved something, often with surprise or disbelief. It’s usually followed by “a” + infinitive: “Come ha fatto a trovare…?” (How did you manage to find…?). You can also use it alone (“Come ha fatto?”) meaning “How did you do it?” In informal speech you’ll also hear “Com’è che ha fatto…?” or with “hai” for “you” singular informal: “Come hai fatto a…?”
target_language_example: Come ha fatto a finire il lavoro così presto?
native_language_example: How did you manage to finish the work so early?

additional_notes: Used to ask how someone was able to do something, often with surprise, curiosity, or disbelief. It’s built with the passato prossimo (ha fatto) + infinitive: "Come ha fatto a trovare…?" = "How did you/he manage to find…?" You can change the auxiliary for other persons: "Come hai fatto a…?" (you), "Come hanno fatto a…?" (they).
target_language_example: Come ha fatto a arrivare qui così presto?
native_language_example: How did he manage to get here so early?

meaning: "How did you..." / "How have you..." (asking about method or way).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to ask how someone did something. It’s literally “how + you have,” using the auxiliary verb *avere* for many past tenses (e.g., *passato prossimo*): *Come hai fatto?* = “How did you do it?” In some contexts it can mean “What did you say?” when followed by *detto?* (*Come hai detto?*).
target_language_example: Come hai fatto a imparare l’italiano così in fretta?
native_language_example: How did you manage to learn Italian so quickly?

meaning: "How did you do it?" / "How did you manage?"
additional_notes: Used to ask how someone achieved something, often with **a + infinitive**: *Come hai fatto a capirlo?* (= How did you manage to understand it?). Depending on tone, it can express surprise or disbelief: *Aspetta, come hai fatto?* It can also be used more generally to mean “How did you manage (to cope)?” in a situation.
target_language_example: Come hai fatto a finire così in fretta?
native_language_example: How did you manage to finish so quickly?

meaning: “How did you manage to…?” / “How did you (ever) …?”
additional_notes: Used to ask how someone achieved something, often with surprise, curiosity, or disbelief. It’s typically followed by an infinitive: “Come hai fatto a + infinitive?” (e.g., “Come hai fatto a saperlo?”). You can change the subject/person: “Come avete fatto a…?” (you all), “Come ha fatto a…?” (he/she), “Come hanno fatto a…?” (they).
target_language_example: Come hai fatto a trovare questo posto senza GPS?
native_language_example: How did you manage to find this place without GPS?

meaning: “how could you…?” (expresses shock, disappointment, or reproach).
additional_notes: Used to criticize or show disbelief about something someone did or didn’t do. It’s the past tense of "potere" (to be able to), addressed to "tu". You can use it alone (“Come hai potuto?”) or followed by an infinitive (“Come hai potuto fare/dire/permettere…?”).
target_language_example: Come hai potuto dirmi una cosa del genere?
native_language_example: How could you tell me something like that?

additional_notes: Used when the direct object is the pronoun “la” (= her / it, feminine singular) and it comes before the verb. The full meaning depends on the verb that follows: e.g. “Come la descriverebbe?” = “How would you describe her?”; “Come la pago?” = “How do I pay for it?” (often implying “how can I pay it” / “what method can I use?”). “La” can refer to a woman (“her”) or to a feminine noun like “la multa” (the fine), “la bolletta” (the bill), etc.
target_language_example: Come la posso aiutare?
native_language_example: How can I help you?

additional_notes: Used to ask how someone does something or how someone knows something. "Come" means "how" and "lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" (a thing/idea) or "him" (a man). It commonly appears before verbs like conoscere (to know/meet), sapere (to know a fact), fare (to do/make): "Come lo conosci?" = "How do you know him?" / "How did you meet him?"
target_language_example: Come lo dici in italiano?
native_language_example: How do you say it in Italian?

meaning: "How did you know that...?" (spoken to more than one person).
additional_notes: Used to ask a group how they found out some information. "lo" refers to the fact/information, "sapevate" is past tense (imperfect) of "sapere" for "voi" (you plural). Often followed by a full clause with "che". For one person you’d say: "Come lo sapevi che...?"
target_language_example: Come lo sapevate che oggi era il mio compleanno?
native_language_example: How did you (all) know that today was my birthday?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason behind something, usually when you find it unexpected. It’s close to English “How come…?” and is common in spoken Italian. You can use it with normal word order (no inversion): “Come mai sei qui?”
target_language_example: Come mai non vieni alla festa stasera?
native_language_example: How come you’re not coming to the party tonight?

additional_notes: Used to express doubt or skepticism about someone’s reliability or honesty. It’s a question with the reflexive verb fidarsi di (“to trust”), followed by the person you’re talking about (di te/di lui/di lei/di loro/di voi). You can also use it with names or nouns: “Come mi posso fidare di Marco?” / “...di questa azienda?”
target_language_example: Hai mentito una volta: come mi posso fidare di te adesso?
native_language_example: You lied once: how can I trust you now?

additional_notes: Used as a short reply to confirm something (“Of course!”), but very often said with a certain tone to express disbelief or sarcasm (“Yeah, right”). Meaning depends heavily on intonation and context; in writing it can be ambiguous. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: —Hai davvero finito in dieci minuti? —Come no!
native_language_example: —Did you really finish in ten minutes? —Yeah, right!

additional_notes: Strong, accusatory phrase used to express shock or anger at someone’s behavior. Often followed by an infinitive: “Come osi dirmelo?” (How dare you tell me that?). “Osi” is the 2nd-person singular (tu) present of the verb “osare” (to dare), and “tu” can be added for emphasis: “Come osi, tu?”
target_language_example: Come osi parlare così a mia sorella?
native_language_example: How dare you talk to my sister like that?

meaning: "How can I...?" (asking for instructions or possibility).
additional_notes: Used to ask for help or advice on how to do something. It’s often followed by an infinitive (come posso fare/andare/pagare...) or by a verb phrase like "fare per" + infinitive. In polite requests you can also use "Come posso..." at the start of a question.
target_language_example: Scusi, come posso arrivare alla stazione da qui?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how can I get to the station from here?

meaning: 'how can you be so…?' (addressed to more than one person, or formal 'you')
additional_notes: Used to express surprise, disbelief, or criticism about someone’s behavior or attitude. It’s followed by an adjective (e.g., crudeli, ciechi/e, pessimisti, sicuri/e). Uses the 'voi' form: potete = 'you (plural/formal) can', essere = 'to be', così = 'so/this'.
target_language_example: Come potete essere così tranquilli dopo quello che è successo?
native_language_example: How can you be so calm after what happened?

meaning: “how can you…?” (often expressing disbelief or criticism).
additional_notes: Used to question someone’s ability or decision: *Come* = “how”, *puoi* = “can you”. Very common in emotional or rhetorical questions, often implying “I can’t believe you did that” / “How could you?”. Followed by an infinitive (*come puoi dirlo?*) or by a noun phrase (*come puoi chiamare questo…?*).
target_language_example: Come puoi pensare una cosa del genere?
native_language_example: How can you think such a thing?

additional_notes: Used to ask how something is possible or how something could happen. It can express surprise, disbelief, or criticism depending on tone. The verb changes with the subject: come posso (how can I), come puoi (how can you), come può (how can he/she/it), come possiamo (how can we), etc.
target_language_example: Come può funzionare senza elettricità?
native_language_example: How can it work without electricity?

meaning: “how you are”; also used in exclamations (“how … you are!”) and in questions like “how did you …?”
additional_notes:
- **With an adjective**, it’s often an **exclamation** showing surprise/admiration: *Come sei bello!* = “How handsome you are!” / “You’re so handsome!”
- **With a past participle** (e.g., *entrato, arrivato*), it asks **how someone managed/did something**: *Come sei entrato?* = “How did you get in?”
- Not to confuse with **come stai?** = “How are you?” (health/feeling).
target_language_example: Come sei cambiato in questi anni!
native_language_example: How you’ve changed in these years! / You’ve changed so much!

additional_notes: Used with an impersonal verb form ("si"), common in questions about procedures, rules, or the correct way to do/say something. Often followed by a verb in the 3rd-person singular: "Come si fa...?" = "How do you do it? / How is it done?"
target_language_example: Scusi, come si dice "thank you" in italiano?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how do you say "thank you" in Italian?

additional_notes: Used to ask the name of a person, animal, place, or thing. Often followed by the noun you’re asking about (e.g., "Come si chiama questa pianta?"). For a person you can also use "Come ti chiami?" (What’s your name?).
target_language_example: Scusi, come si chiama questa strada?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what is this street called?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the name/word for something you’re pointing at. Literally “how is this called,” but the natural English meaning is “What is this called?” You can add a category or language: “Come si chiama questo in inglese?” (“What is this called in English?”). For feminine nouns, use “questa”: “Come si chiama questa pianta?”
target_language_example: Scusa, come si chiama questo in italiano?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what is this called in Italian?

meaning: “What was it called?” / “What was his/her name?”
additional_notes: Used to ask for the name of a person, animal, place, or thing in the past, or when you can’t remember the name. It’s the imperfect past of "chiamarsi" (to be called). Often the subject is added (e.g., "Come si chiamava tua moglie?") but it can also stand alone ("Come si chiamava?"). For the present, you use "come si chiama?".
target_language_example: Scusa, come si chiamava quel ristorante vicino alla stazione?
native_language_example: Sorry, what was that restaurant near the station called?

meaning: “how do you do it?” / “how is it done?” (how to do something).
additional_notes: Used to ask for instructions or the method for doing something. Often followed by “a + infinitive” (Come si fa a capire? = How do you manage to understand?) or with a direct object (Come si fa il pane? = How do you make bread?). By itself (Come si fa?) it means “How do you do it?” / “How are we supposed to do this?”. In phrases like “E ora come si fa?” it means “So what do we do now?”; and “Ma come si fa?!” can express disbelief/complaint (“How can you do that?!”).
target_language_example: Scusa, come si fa a comprare i biglietti online?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how do you buy tickets online?

meaning: "how do you/does one" (how to do something).
additional_notes: Used to ask about the way to do something or how something is possible. Very common in questions. Often followed by an infinitive: "Come si fa a + verb" (e.g., "come si fa a sapere..."). Literally "how is it done to...", but in English it’s usually "How do you...?" / "How can someone...?"
target_language_example: Scusa, come si fa a comprare i biglietti online?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how do you buy the tickets online?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone about their physical or emotional state. Often followed by time words like oggi (today) or ora (now). With a topic it means “How do you feel about …?” / “What’s your opinion/feeling about …?” (e.g., come si sente riguardo a…). Uses the formal Lei form (si sente) when speaking politely to one person; for informal “you,” use come ti senti?
target_language_example: Come si sente dopo l’operazione?
native_language_example: How do you feel after the operation?

come si usa questa macchina fotografica

target_language_multi_word_term: come si usa questa macchina fotografica
additional_notes: A common question to ask for instructions. “Come si usa…?” = “How do you use…?” The “si” makes it impersonal/passive-like (literally “how is this used”). You can swap in another object: “Come si usa questa stampante?” (printer). In conversation, it’s often used after “Sai/Sa/Sapete…”: “Sai come si usa…?” = “Do you know how to use…?” (tu/Lei/voi).
target_language_example: Scusi, come si usa questa macchina fotografica?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how do you use this camera?

meaning: "How is it going?" / "How is it going so far?"
additional_notes: Used to ask how something is progressing (work, a party, a weekend, a situation). You can add a topic with "con" or by naming it directly: "Come sta andando con il progetto?" / "Come sta andando la festa?". With an adjective/adverb like "bene", "male", or "veloce", it asks about the way something is going: "Come sta andando (così) veloce il treno!" = "How fast the train is going!" (often an exclamation).
target_language_example: Ciao! Come sta andando il corso di italiano?
native_language_example: Hi! How is your Italian course going?

additional_notes: Uses the formal pronoun “Lei” (3rd person singular), so it’s polite and common with strangers, customers, older people, or in professional settings. With a name it often means “How is [name]?” (asking about someone’s condition). Informal version: “Come stai?”
target_language_example: Buongiorno, signora Rossi: come sta oggi?
native_language_example: Good morning, Mrs. Rossi: how are you today?

additional_notes: A common greeting/question using the informal "tu" form. Use with friends, family, kids, or people your age. For a more formal/polite version use "Come sta?" With friends you can add follow-ups like "Tutto a posto?" (= “Everything okay?”). Common replies: "Bene, grazie"; "Così così"; "Non c’è male"; "Male".
target_language_example: Ciao! Come stai?
native_language_example: Hi! How are you?

additional_notes: Used at the start of questions where the action or experience is about the person addressed (ti = “you” as an object/reflexive). Common patterns: come ti chiami? (“what’s your name?”), come ti trovi…? (“how are you finding…/getting on…?”), come ti va/vanno…? (“how’s it going/ how are things going?”), come ti sei…? (“how did you…?”). Note that Italian come means “how,” not English “come.”
target_language_example: Come ti chiami?
native_language_example: What's your name?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s name when speaking to one person you address as tu. Neutral and common in everyday situations (meeting someone, talking to a child, etc.). For a more formal/polite version (Lei), use: Come si chiama?
target_language_example: Piacere, come ti chiami?
native_language_example: Nice to meet you—what’s your name?

meaning: “How do you feel?” (asking about someone’s physical or emotional state).
additional_notes: Used to check in on someone’s wellbeing. You can add a time word like oggi (today), adesso/in questo momento (right now). Often followed by an adjective: Mi sento bene/male/stanco(a) (I feel good/bad/tired).
target_language_example: Ehi, come ti senti dopo l’esame?
native_language_example: Hey, how do you feel after the exam?

meaning: How’s it going? / How is it going?
additional_notes: Used to ask how someone is doing or how something is going (health, a situation, progress). Very common in greetings: “Ciao, come va?” It can be followed by the topic: “Come va la gamba/la schiena?” = “How’s your leg/back?” Often answered with “Bene”, “Così così” (so-so), “Non c’è male” (not bad), “Male” (bad).
target_language_example: Ciao! Come va il lavoro?
native_language_example: Hi! How’s work going?

meaning: “How is the … going/doing?” (asking about a specific thing).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (la + noun) to ask how something is going or how someone/something is doing: "Come va la salute?" = “How’s your health?” For masculine nouns, use "come va il …?" or more commonly "come va …?" without the article. It’s a common, neutral way to check on a situation, activity, or condition.
target_language_example: Ciao! Come va la giornata?
native_language_example: Hi! How’s your day going?

additional_notes: Common way to ask generally how life, work, or a situation is progressing. You can add a place ("... a Washington?") or a topic/relationship ("... tra te e Tom?"). Often used as a friendly check-in, but it can also be used in business contexts.
target_language_example: Ciao! Come vanno le cose in ufficio?
native_language_example: Hi! How are things going at the office?

additional_notes: “Come” means “how” (not English “come”). “Vi” is the object/reflexive pronoun for “you” (plural) and is also used as the polite form in some contexts. It’s used to ask how something happens to/for you, or how you do something: e.g., come vi chiamate? (what are your names?), come vi conoscete? (how do you know each other?), come vi è piaciuta…? (how did you like…?).
target_language_example: Come vi siete conosciuti?
native_language_example: How did you meet (each other)?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (or to speak formally to one person) for their opinion or feelings about someone or something. It uses the reflexive verb "sentirsi" (to feel) and is followed by "riguardo a" + a noun/pronoun (or sometimes an infinitive/idea). Singular informal is "Come ti senti riguardo a...?" and formal singular is also "Come si sente riguardo a...?".
target_language_example: Come vi sentite riguardo a questa decisione?
native_language_example: How do you feel about this decision?

additional_notes: Uses the verb *conoscersi* (“to meet/get to know each other”) in the *passato prossimo*: *vi siete conosciuti* = “you (plural) met each other.” Common when asking about the story of how two people first met. *Vi* is the reflexive pronoun (“each other”). Agreement can change: *conosciute* for an all-female group (or two women).
target_language_example: Come vi siete conosciuti voi due?
native_language_example: How did you two meet?

additional_notes: Used to say something is happening in the normal/typical way, often with a tone of resignation, mild complaint, or irony (e.g., someone is late again). It can stand alone as a short comment: "Come al solito."
target_language_example: Ha dimenticato le chiavi come al solito.
native_language_example: He forgot his keys as usual.

meaning: how to get (there); directions on how to arrive.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like dire/dirmi (to tell me) or sapere (to know) to ask for or give directions. It’s often followed by a + place name (a Shinjuku) or by a + article for common places (alla banca, al municipio). You can also add da qui (“from here”).
target_language_example: Scusi, mi può dire come arrivare alla stazione da qui?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you tell me how to get to the station from here?

meaning: how to get to the station.
additional_notes: Used to ask for directions. Often follows polite phrases like “Mi può/potete dire…?” (Can you tell me…?) or “Mi potrebbe dire…?” (Could you tell me…?). “Alla stazione” is usually understood as the train station; you can also say “alla stazione ferroviaria” to be extra clear.
target_language_example: Scusi, mi può dire come arrivare alla stazione?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you tell me how to get to the station?

additional_notes: Used when asking for directions. Often comes after a verb like sapere (“to know”): *Sa/Sai/Sapete come arrivare allo zoo?* (“Do you know how to get to the zoo?”). *allo zoo* = *a + lo zoo* (“to the zoo”).
target_language_example: Scusi, mi può dire come arrivare allo zoo?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you tell me how to get to the zoo?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the feeling/experience of a situation, often meaning “what it’s like (to be in that position).” The "ci" is impersonal here (similar to English “you”/“one”), and "si sente" comes from "sentirsi" (to feel). Common after verbs like "sapere" (to know), "immaginare" (to imagine), and "vedere" (to see/notice).
target_language_example: Non puoi capire come ci si sente dopo una giornata così.
native_language_example: You can’t understand what it feels like after a day like that.

come eliminare il mio account di

target_language_multi_word_term: come eliminare il mio account di
additional_notes: Used to ask for instructions on deleting your account on a specific service/platform. It’s usually followed by the service name (e.g., Facebook, Instagram). In requests you may see polite forms like dimmi (informal, to one person), ditemi (informal, to multiple people), or mi dica (formal).
target_language_example: Scusi, può dirmi come eliminare il mio account di Instagram?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you tell me how to delete my Instagram account?

additional_notes: Used after verbs like sapere (to know) to say someone knows the way/method to fix computers. It’s an infinitive phrase: come (how) + riparare (to repair) + i computer (computers). In Italian, computer is often invariable: i computer (plural) and il computer (singular).
target_language_example: Non so come riparare i computer, ma posso provarci.
native_language_example: I don’t know how to repair computers, but I can try.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the method/steps for solving something. It often follows verbs like capire (to understand), scoprire (to find out/discover), and dire (to tell): e.g., Capisco/Ho capito come risolvere il problema; Dimmi come risolvere il problema. You can swap il problema for another noun: come risolvere questo esercizio (how to solve this exercise).
target_language_example: Non so come risolvere il problema.
native_language_example: I don't know how to solve the problem.
