The article changes with gender/number: essere un insegnante (male or generic), essere un’insegnante (female), essere insegnanti (plural, no article). Often follows verbs like piacere (to like), volere (to want), and sapere (to know).
target_language_example: Da grande voglio essere un insegnante.
native_language_example: When I grow up, I want to be a teacher.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun after the verb essere (“to be”), especially for jobs/roles/identities: essere una dentista / una professoressa. For masculine nouns you usually use essere un (or uno before s+consonant, z, gn, ps, etc.): essere un medico, essere uno studente. The article (una/un/uno) agrees with the gender and number of the noun, not the person.
target_language_example: Da grande vuole essere una veterinaria.
native_language_example: When she grows up, she wants to be a veterinarian.

additional_notes: Used to talk about humans in general, often in a neutral, scientific, or emphatic way (more formal than just "persona"). Plural: "esseri umani". Often used in contrast with animals, monsters, robots, etc., or to stress someone’s dignity ("treated you like a human being").
target_language_example: Non è un animale: è un essere umano.
native_language_example: It’s not an animal: it’s a human being.

additional_notes: Used to say you are physically together with someone, accompanying them, or spending time with them. It can also imply being with someone in a relationship depending on context (e.g., “Voglio essere con te”). Often followed by a person: “essere con te/lui/lei/loro”.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, stasera non posso essere con voi.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't be with you all tonight.

additional_notes: Used to talk about being in her company (spending time together) and, depending on context, it can also imply being romantically together. "Lei" means "her" and can also be the formal "you"—but in these examples it clearly means "her".
target_language_example: Voglio essere con lei stasera.
native_language_example: I want to be with her tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you are in his company/presence (spending time together). In many contexts it can also imply being together as a couple, but often it’s simply about being with someone physically or socially. In the negative it can mean you can’t join him (e.g., because you’re busy).
target_language_example: Vorrei essere con lui stasera, ma devo studiare.
native_language_example: I’d like to be with him tonight, but I have to study.

additional_notes: Common, neutral term for people as a species (often used when contrasting humans with animals, aliens, robots, etc.). Singular: "essere umano" (a human being).
target_language_example: Dobbiamo rispettare tutti gli esseri umani.
native_language_example: We must respect all human beings.

additional_notes: Used to say a pain hasn’t gone away yet. It usually appears with an indirect object pronoun to show who feels the pain: mi fa ancora male (it still hurts me), ti fa ancora male? (does it still hurt you?), gli/le fa ancora male (it still hurts him/her). Often followed by the body part: Mi fa ancora male la schiena.
target_language_example: Mi fa ancora male il ginocchio.
native_language_example: My knee still hurts.

additional_notes: Used with the verb fare (fa = “it does/makes”) to say something benefits someone’s health or well-being. Often used with a dative pronoun: mi fa bene (it’s good for me), ti fa bene (good for you), gli/le fa bene (good for him/her), ci fa bene (good for us), vi fa bene (good for you all), gli fa bene (good for them). You can also specify what it’s good for with a + noun: fa bene alla salute (it’s good for your health). The negative is non fa bene (it’s not good for you).
target_language_example: Una passeggiata dopo cena ti fa bene.
native_language_example: A walk after dinner is good for you.

additional_notes: Used with the verb fare (“to do/make”) to describe weather and temperature: fa caldo (it’s hot), fa bello (nice weather), fa brutto (bad weather). You can turn it into a question: Fa freddo? (“Is it cold?”) and refer to another time/place: Domani fa freddo. / Lì fa freddo.
target_language_example: Fuori fa freddo, meglio mettere una sciarpa.
native_language_example: It’s cold outside, better to put on a scarf.

meaning: "It doesn't matter" / "it's all the same"; also "(to) do the same".
additional_notes: Very common in spoken Italian. Used impersonally to say something makes no difference: "Fa lo stesso!" = "No problem / Never mind." With a subject, it can mean "to do the same (thing)": "Lui fa lo stesso" = "He does the same." Often followed by "se..." (if...): "Fa lo stesso se..." = "Does it matter if...?"
target_language_example: Non posso venire stasera; fa lo stesso, ci vediamo domani.
native_language_example: I can't come tonight; it doesn't matter, I'll see you tomorrow.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **fare male** (“to hurt”). It’s often used **impersonally**: **Mi fa male la schiena** = “My back hurts” (literally “It hurts my back”). You can also say **Fa male!** on its own as an exclamation when something is painful.
target_language_example: Ahi, mi fa male la testa.
native_language_example: Ouch, my head hurts.

additional_notes: Used with the verb fare + male. It can mean physical pain (Ti fa male la testa? = Does your head hurt?) or emotional harm (Mi fa male quando dici così = It hurts me when you say that). With an indirect object pronoun (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli): Mi fa male = It hurts me. With reflexive: farsi male = to get hurt/injure oneself (Nessuno si fa male = Nobody gets hurt). You can also specify what hurts: Mi fa male la schiena = My back hurts.
target_language_example: Mi fa male la gola, posso avere una pastiglia?
native_language_example: My throat hurts—can I have a lozenge?

additional_notes: Used to say something belongs to a group, whole, process, agreement, job, etc. It’s from the verb phrase "fare parte di" (to be part of). With a noun that has an article you often see: "fa parte del" (= di + il), "della" (= di + la), "dei" (= di + i), "delle" (= di + le).
target_language_example: Anche sbagliare fa parte del processo di imparare.
native_language_example: Making mistakes is also part of the learning process.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **fare parte di** (“to be part of”). **Fa parte della** is 3rd-person singular present (“it/he/she is part of the”) and is used to say something is included in, belongs to, or is a normal/expected element of something (e.g., *fa parte della vita* = “it’s part of life”). Also appears with other forms: *faccio parte di* (I’m part of), *fanno parte di* (they’re part of), etc.
target_language_example: Questo documento fa parte della domanda.
native_language_example: This document is part of the application.

meaning: "makes (someone) think that" / "what makes you think that".
additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason or evidence behind someone’s belief. It often appears in questions like “Cosa ti/Le/vi fa pensare che...?” (“What makes you think that...?”). After “che” you typically use the subjunctive when reporting a belief (e.g., “sia”, “abbia”).
target_language_example: Cosa ti fa pensare che lui sia arrabbiato?
native_language_example: What makes you think he’s angry?

fa pensare che io lo abbia scritto

target_language_multi_word_term: fa pensare che io lo abbia scritto
meaning: "makes you think that I wrote it."
additional_notes: Used in questions like "Che cosa/Cosa (ti/le/vi) fa pensare che…?" to ask what evidence or reason leads someone to believe something. The structure is: (Che cosa/Cosa) + indirect object pronoun (ti = you informal singular, le = you formal singular, vi = you plural) + fa pensare + che + clause. After "fa pensare che" Italian commonly uses the subjunctive (here: "io lo abbia scritto" = "that I wrote it").
target_language_example: Che cosa ti fa pensare che io lo abbia scritto?
native_language_example: What makes you think I wrote it?

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli or a + name): "Mi fa piacere" = "I’m glad / That’s nice". Often followed by a clause with che + subjunctive/indicative ("Mi fa piacere che tu sia qui"), or by an infinitive ("Mi fa piacere essere qui"). Literally it’s "it makes (someone) pleasure", but the natural English is "it makes me happy/pleased" or simply "I’m glad".
target_language_example: Mi fa piacere che tu sia venuto oggi.
native_language_example: I’m glad you came today.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does whatever is necessary/possible or what they’re told/believe is right. It’s the 3rd-person singular of *fare* (“to do/make”) + *quello che* (“what/that which”). You can change the verb for other people: *faccio quello che…* (I do what…), *fai quello che…* (you do what…), *fanno quello che…* (they do what…).
target_language_example: Lei fa quello che può per aiutare la sua famiglia.
native_language_example: She does what she can to help her family.

additional_notes: Used to say something is really unpleasant, bad quality, or gross. It can describe situations (Fa schifo avere il raffreddore.) or things/skills (La mia grammatica fa schifo.). Common in spoken Italian and quite rude/strong; use with friends, avoid in formal contexts. Literally “it makes disgust.”
target_language_example: Oggi il tempo fa schifo: piove sempre.
native_language_example: The weather sucks today: it’s always raining.

meaning: "(he/she) always does"; "(he/she) does what (he/she) usually does".
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s habitual behavior. It often appears in phrases like “fa quello che fa sempre” (“does what he/she always does”). The subject is understood from context (lui/lei).
target_language_example: Quando c’è un problema, lei fa sempre la stessa cosa: chiama sua madre.
native_language_example: When there’s a problem, she always does the same thing: she calls her mom.

additional_notes: Used with an object pronoun to say how someone/something affects your feelings: mi fa sentire (makes me feel), ti fa sentire (makes you feel), ci fa sentire (makes us feel). Common patterns: "fa sentire + adjective" (fa sentire meglio = makes you feel better; fa sentire al sicuro = makes you feel safe) and "fa sentire + a + noun/pronoun" (fa sentire tutti a loro agio = makes everyone feel comfortable).
target_language_example: Questa musica mi fa sentire tranquillo.
native_language_example: This music makes me feel calm.

additional_notes: Used for meeting, speaking, or confronting someone directly, in the same place (not by phone/text). It can also emphasize a direct confrontation ("a face-to-face battle"). Often used with verbs like incontrarsi (to meet), parlare (to talk), and affrontare (to face/confront).
target_language_example: Preferisco dirglielo faccia a faccia, non per messaggio.
native_language_example: I’d rather tell him/her face to face, not by message.

additional_notes: Used to criticize someone for being bold in an inappropriate way—having the “nerve” to do/say something. Often appears in exclamations ("Che faccia tosta!") or with verbs like "avere" ("avere la faccia tosta di + infinitive" = "to have the nerve to...").
target_language_example: Ha la faccia tosta di chiedermi un favore dopo quello che ha fatto.
native_language_example: He has the nerve to ask me a favor after what he did.

additional_notes: Imperative used to warn someone politely or in formal situations (Lei form). Often followed by “a/ai/alle” to say what to watch out for: “Faccia attenzione ai borseggiatori.” Less formal: “Fai attenzione.”
target_language_example: Faccia attenzione quando attraversa la strada.
native_language_example: Be careful when you cross the street.

additional_notes: Formal/polite command using the "Lei" form (third-person singular): faccia (from fare) + del suo meglio (“your best”). Often used alone as encouragement, or followed by "per" + someone/goal: "Faccia del suo meglio per loro." You can also hear it with calming phrases like "Stia calmo/a e faccia del suo meglio" (“Stay calm and do your best”).
target_language_example: Faccia del suo meglio durante l’esame.
native_language_example: Do your best during the exam.

meaning: "let’s end it / let’s be done with it."
additional_notes: Used to stop an argument or wrap up an unpleasant/annoying situation, often with impatience or urgency (like “enough—let’s just finish this”). Literally it refers to “making it finished,” but it’s an idiomatic set phrase. You may also hear the singular command: “Falla finita!” (“Cut it out/Stop it!”).
target_language_example: Dai, facciamola finita: dimmi la verità e basta.
native_language_example: Come on, let’s be done with it: just tell me the truth.

meaning: "I struggle to" / "I find it hard to" (do something).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb (e.g., capire, parlare, riconoscerti) to say something is difficult for you. You can change the verb to match the subject: faccio (I), fai (you), fa (he/she), facciamo (we), fate (you all), fanno (they).
target_language_example: Oggi faccio fatica a concentrarmi.
native_language_example: Today I’m having trouble concentrating.

additional_notes:
From "fare vedere" (= to show). Very common when offering to show something or demonstrate how something works. It’s usually used with object pronouns:
- ti faccio vedere = I’ll show you (singular informal)
- vi faccio vedere = I’ll show you (plural / formal)
- le faccio vedere = I’ll show you (formal “you”, to a woman)
- te lo / ve lo faccio vedere = I’ll show it to you.
Can also sound emphatic in phrases like "Te lo faccio vedere io!" ("I’LL show you!" / "I’ll take care of it and show you").
target_language_example: Aspetta un attimo: ti faccio vedere come si usa.
native_language_example: Wait a moment: I’ll show you how to use it.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to say something is easy to do: “è facile da + infinitive” (è facile da capire = it’s easy to understand). With “non” it means “not easy to…”. It can also be intensified with words like “abbastanza” (enough/quite) or “molto” (very).
target_language_example: Questo esercizio è facile da finire in dieci minuti.
native_language_example: This exercise is easy to finish in ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used to say something is not difficult for you personally. Often followed by an infinitive ("È facile per me capire") or used with a noun/subject ("La matematica è facile per me"). You can add intensifiers like "troppo" (too) or comparisons like "più" (easier).
target_language_example: Non è facile per me parlare in pubblico.
native_language_example: It’s not easy for me to speak in public.

additional_notes: Imperative (informal 'tu' form) used to warn someone or tell them to watch out, often followed by "a" + person/thing ("Fai attenzione a..." = "Be careful with / watch out for..."). Can also be used alone as a warning: "Fai attenzione!"
target_language_example: Fai attenzione a non scivolare sul pavimento bagnato.
native_language_example: Be careful not to slip on the wet floor.

additional_notes: Used to warn someone or tell them to watch out for something/someone. Follow it with a noun/pronoun (Fai attenzione a Tom), with "ciò/quel che/quello che" + clause (Fai attenzione a ciò che dice), or with "a" + infinitive, often negative, to mean "be careful not to..." (Fai attenzione a non scivolare!).
target_language_example: Fai attenzione a dove metti i piedi.
native_language_example: Watch where you step.

additional_notes: Imperative phrase using tu (informal singular) to encourage or instruct someone to try as hard as they can. Often followed by per + infinitive (e.g., fai del tuo meglio per arrivare in tempo). The polite/formal version is: Faccia del suo meglio.
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: fai del tuo meglio e andrà bene.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: do your best and it will be fine.

meaning: Go ahead; feel free (to do it).
additional_notes: Used to give someone permission or encouragement to proceed. Often said on its own as a friendly reply (similar to “sure, go ahead”). You can add what you’re allowing: “Fai pure e mangia quanto ti pare” = “Go ahead and eat as much as you like.”
target_language_example: Se vuoi usare il mio telefono, fai pure.
native_language_example: If you want to use my phone, go ahead.

meaning: “do what …” (you do what you have to/like/can/etc.).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to do the thing that follows in the next clause (often with a verb like devi fare = “have to do”, ami = “love”, riesci = “can manage”, ti viene meglio = “you’re best at”). In polite form you’d say: faccia quello che… (formal) or fate quello che… (to more than one person).
target_language_example: Fai quello che puoi e poi riposati.
native_language_example: Do what you can and then rest.

meaning: "(you) are doing here" (used in questions like "What are you doing here?").
additional_notes: Used almost always in questions, often with **che cosa/che**: *Che cosa fai qui?* = “What are you doing here?” It can sound surprised, suspicious, or just curious depending on tone. Very common spoken variant: **Che ci fai qui?** (literally “What are you doing here?” with **ci** = “here/there” used in everyday Italian).
target_language_example: Scusa, che cosa fai qui a quest’ora?
native_language_example: Sorry, what are you doing here at this time?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to do something for you. It’s very common in spoken Italian and is often followed by “e + verb” (e.g., “Fammi un favore e…”). You can also say it on its own to introduce a request; adding “per favore” makes it more polite.
target_language_example: Fammi un favore e chiudi la finestra, per favore.
native_language_example: Do me a favor and close the window, please.

additional_notes: Imperative made from "fare" + "mi" ("fammi" = "make me") + "vedere" ("see"), used to ask someone to show you something or allow you to look (e.g., instructions, an object, someone’s hands). It can also be used alone (“Fammi vedere.”) meaning “Let me see” before you check something yourself. Add "per favore" to make it more polite.
target_language_example: Fammi vedere il biglietto, per favore.
native_language_example: Show me the ticket, please.

meaning: to suck; to be terrible (very vulgar).
additional_notes: Very informal and offensive slang. Often used as "fa cagare" ("it sucks") or "mi fa cagare" ("I think it’s disgusting / I hate it"). Use with close friends only, or avoid in polite/company settings.
target_language_example: Questo film fa cagare.
native_language_example: This movie sucks.

meaning: to make (someone) understand; to get (something) across.
additional_notes: Used when you cause someone to understand something, often with an object pronoun: �Te lo devo far capire� = �Do I have to make you understand it?�. Very common as the reflexive form �farsi capire� = �to make yourself understood� (e.g., �Ti devi far capire!� = �You have to make yourself understood!�). It can also mean �to avoid letting others understand/realize�: �per non far capire che...� = �so as not to let (people) realize that...�.
target_language_example: Devo fartelo capire con calma, altrimenti non cambier�ai idea.
native_language_example: I have to make you understand it calmly, otherwise you won�ai change your mind.

additional_notes:
Used with an object to mean “to make something/someone known” (e.g., a product, an idea, an artist). It can also mean “to introduce someone (to someone else)”: 
- far conoscere qualcuno a qualcuno = to introduce someone to someone
- far conoscere qualcosa a qualcuno = to let someone know about something / to make something known to someone
target_language_example: Ti farò conoscere i miei amici stasera.
native_language_example: I’ll introduce you to my friends tonight.

meaning: to point out; to bring to someone’s attention.
additional_notes: Used when you want to highlight or emphasize a fact, detail, or problem (often politely or formally). Structure: "far notare (a qualcuno) (che) ..." or "far notare qualcosa". In the past: "ho fatto notare...".
target_language_example: Vorrei farle notare che la data sul documento è sbagliata.
native_language_example: I’d like to point out that the date on the document is wrong.

meaning: to be part of (something); to belong to.
additional_notes: Used with "di" or "del/della/dei/delle" to say you are part of a group, team, family, organization, etc.: "far parte di una squadra". You’ll also see "entrare a far parte" = "to join / to become part of".
target_language_example: Sono felice di far parte di questo progetto.
native_language_example: I’m happy to be part of this project.

additional_notes: Uses the causative verb pattern: fare + infinitive. Common with people (far partire qualcuno = to send someone off / make someone leave) and with activities or projects (far partire un progetto/una campagna = to start/kick off). With machines, you’ll more often hear "far partire" meaning “to get it started,” though "avviare" is also common.
target_language_example: Domani dobbiamo far partire il progetto.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we have to get the project started.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object to say something makes a person think or reconsider: "Mi fa pensare" = "It makes me think." It can also mean "to suggest/bring to mind" when something reminds you of something else: "Mi fa pensare a..." = "It makes me think of..."
target_language_example: Questa notizia mi fa pensare che dobbiamo cambiare piano.
native_language_example: This news makes me think we need to change plans.

meaning: to blow up / set off (an explosion); also: to ruin/cause to fail.
additional_notes: Literally means “to make (something) jump,” but very often it means to detonate something (“far saltare un palazzo / una torre”). You’ll also see it with “in aria” (“far saltare in aria”) = “to blow up into the air.” Figuratively, it can mean to make a plan, deal, or cover fail (“far saltare un piano / la copertura”).
target_language_example: Se continui a parlare, farai saltare tutto il piano.
native_language_example: If you keep talking, you’ll ruin the whole plan.

additional_notes: Used when you ask or promise to give information/updates. Often appears with an indirect object (the person you inform): “fammi sapere” = “let me know”, “ti faccio sapere” = “I’ll let you know”, “faccelo sapere” = “let us know”. You can also add “a + person” (e.g., “far sapere a Marco”).
target_language_example: Ti faccio sapere domani.
native_language_example: I’ll let you know tomorrow.

meaning: to show; to let someone see; to demonstrate.
additional_notes: Common patterns: **far vedere qualcosa a qualcuno** = “show something to someone” (Puoi far vedere a Mary come si usa…); **far vedere che + clause** = “show that…” (far vedere che non stiamo a guardare). With **farsi vedere** it means “to show up / to be seen” (Non si è mai voluto far vedere? = “Hasn’t he ever wanted to show up / be seen?”). **Per far vedere** can also mean “just to show (for appearances / to make a point)”.
target_language_example: Mi puoi far vedere dov'è la fermata dell'autobus?
native_language_example: Can you show me where the bus stop is?

meaning: to do without; to manage without.
additional_notes: Often used with **ne** (= “of it/of them”) and/or **di + noun/pronoun**: *non ne posso fare a meno* (“I can’t do without it”), *posso fare a meno di lui* (“I can do without him”). Very common in the negative (*non…*) to mean “can’t live without / can’t stop.”
target_language_example: Non posso fare a meno del caffè la mattina.
native_language_example: I can’t do without coffee in the morning.

meaning: to be unable to stop yourself from (doing something); to not be able to do without.
additional_notes: Usually used in negative forms (non posso/non potevo fare a meno di + infinitive) to say you can’t help doing something (often an emotion or reaction). It can also mean “to do without” in other contexts (e.g., Posso fare a meno del dessert = I can do without dessert), but in the examples it means “can’t help (doing).”
target_language_example: Non posso fare a meno di ridere quando lo sento parlare.
native_language_example: I can’t help laughing when I hear him talk.

meaning: to go shopping; to shop (buy things).
additional_notes: Common everyday expression meaning to buy items, often in stores or at a mall. You can use it with places ("fare acquisti al mercato / in centro") or with someone ("fare acquisti con un amico"). Often used with "andare a" to mean "to go shopping" ("andare a fare acquisti").
target_language_example: Domani andiamo a fare acquisti in centro.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going shopping downtown.

meaning: to do business; to make deals.
additional_notes: Used for conducting business in general or making commercial deals with someone. Often followed by “con” + person/company: “fare affari con qualcuno” = “to do business with someone.” It can sound a bit firm in questions like “Vuoi fare affari o no?”
target_language_example: Preferisco fare affari con aziende locali.
native_language_example: I prefer to do business with local companies.

additional_notes: Used for starting a friendship or getting to know someone, often with "con" + person: "fare amicizia con qualcuno". You can also say "fare amicizia" in general (make friends) without naming the person.
target_language_example: È difficile fare amicizia in una nuova città, ma ci provo.
native_language_example: It's hard to make friends in a new city, but I'm trying.

meaning: to make friends with; to become friends with.
additional_notes: Used with the preposition "con" + a person or group (e.g., "con Nancy", "con gli altri bambini"). It often implies starting a friendship (getting to know someone and becoming friendly), and it’s common with verbs like "volere", "cercare di", "provare a", "trovare difficile".
target_language_example: Ho fatto amicizia con i miei vicini durante la festa.
native_language_example: I made friends with my neighbors during the party.

meaning: to pay attention; to be careful.
additional_notes: Common warning/advice phrase. Often used as "fare attenzione a + infinitive" (be careful to do something) or "fare attenzione a + noun" (watch out for something). You can also say "Fai/Fate attenzione!" as an imperative meaning "Be careful! / Watch out!".
target_language_example: Fai attenzione a non scivolare sul pavimento bagnato.
native_language_example: Be careful not to slip on the wet floor.

meaning: to do well; to be good for (someone).
additional_notes:
Common uses:
- "Fare bene (a fare qualcosa)" = to do well (to do something): "Hai fatto bene a chiamarmi" (You did the right thing to call me).
- "Fa bene" (impersonal) = it’s good/beneficial (often for health): "Camminare fa bene" (Walking is good for you).
- "Fa bene a + person" = it does (someone) good: "Ti fa bene riposare" (Resting does you good).
target_language_example: Hai fatto bene a portare l’ombrello.
native_language_example: You did well/right to bring the umbrella.

meaning: to advance in your career; to get ahead (at work).
additional_notes: Used about professional ambition and moving up (getting promotions, more status/power). It can be neutral ("I want to advance") or negative/accusatory depending on context (e.g., implying someone is using others or unfair methods to get ahead).
target_language_example: Lavora tanto perché vuole fare carriera.
native_language_example: He works a lot because he wants to advance in his career.

meaning: to make a mess; to cause a loud commotion (make a fuss).
additional_notes: Informal expression used when someone is being noisy, creating chaos, or causing trouble (at home, in public, at work, etc.). Often said as a warning or complaint: “Non fare casino!” = “Don’t make a mess / Don’t make so much noise.”
target_language_example: Ragazzi, non fate casino: i vicini stanno dormendo.
native_language_example: Guys, don’t make so much noise: the neighbors are sleeping.

additional_notes: Most often used as **fare caso a + noun/pronoun** (“to notice/pay attention to”): *Non fare caso a quello che dice* = “Don’t pay attention to what he says.” It can also mean “to care/mind” (often in negatives): *Non ne faccio caso* = “I don’t mind / I don’t pay it any attention.”
target_language_example: Scusa, non ho fatto caso al tuo messaggio.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t notice your message.

meaning: to sue; to file a lawsuit.
additional_notes: Used in legal contexts meaning to start legal action against someone/something. Often followed by “a” + person/organization (fare causa a qualcuno) or “contro” (fare causa contro qualcuno). You may also see “fare causa per…” (to sue over/for…).
target_language_example: Vuole fare causa al suo ex datore di lavoro.
native_language_example: He/She wants to sue their former employer.

meaning: to gesture/signal (to someone); to briefly mention.
additional_notes:
Often used with "a" + person/thing. 
- "fare cenno a qualcuno" = to signal to someone (with a hand gesture, nod, etc.).
- "fare cenno a qualcosa" = to make a brief reference to something (mention it without details).
target_language_example: Mi ha fatto cenno di avvicinarmi.
native_language_example: He/She signaled to me to come closer.

meaning: to impress (someone); to make an impression.
additional_notes: Used when someone is trying to seem attractive, cool, or capable to influence someone’s opinion (often in a romantic or show-off context). It’s followed by “su” + person: “fare colpo su di me/te/lei/lui”.
target_language_example: Ha comprato un vestito elegante per fare colpo su di lei.
native_language_example: He bought an elegant outfit to impress her.

meaning: to be convenient / to work for someone (be handy).
additional_notes: Used with an indirect object (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi) to say something is convenient for someone: “Mi fa comodo” = “It works for me / It’s convenient for me.” Common in questions when arranging plans: “Ti fa comodo domani?” = “Does tomorrow work for you?” It doesn’t mean “to make (someone) comfortable” in a literal sense.
target_language_example: Ti fa comodo se ci vediamo alle 18?
native_language_example: Does it work for you if we meet at 6?

meaning: to do with; to deal with (something).
additional_notes: Used with an object (fare con + noun/pronoun) to ask or say what action you will take regarding something/someone. Common in questions like “Che/Cosa devo fare con…?” (“What should I do with…?”). Often implies deciding how to use, handle, or get rid of something. Note: “Che/Cosa c’entra con…?” is different and means “What does it have to do with…?”
target_language_example: Che dobbiamo fare con questi vecchi vestiti?
native_language_example: What should we do with these old clothes?

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object pronoun to say who gets hurt: "mi fare del male" (hurt me), "ti" (you), "gli/le" (him/her), "ci" (us), "vi" (you all), "gli" (them). It can mean physical injury or emotional harm. In many contexts it implies intentional harm ("do harm"), but it can also be accidental depending on context.
target_language_example: Non voglio farti del male, voglio solo parlarne.
native_language_example: I don’t want to hurt you; I just want to talk about it.

additional_notes: Used to say you will try as hard as you can. Often comes after verbs like cercare di / provare a / promettere di (to try to / to promise to): “Ho cercato di fare del mio meglio.” You can change the possessive to match the person: fare del tuo meglio (your best), del suo meglio (his/her best), del nostro meglio (our best), del loro meglio (their best).
target_language_example: Farò del mio meglio per arrivare in orario.
native_language_example: I’ll do my best to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to say someone will try as hard as they can. The possessive changes with the subject: fare del mio meglio (my best), del tuo meglio (your best), del suo meglio (his/her/their best), del nostro/vostro/loro meglio.
target_language_example: Farò del mio meglio per arrivare in tempo.
native_language_example: I’ll do my best to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used for causing physical or emotional harm. With an indirect object pronoun it means “hurt someone”: fare del male a qualcuno / fargli(le) del male (e.g., Non ti voglio fare del male = I don’t want to hurt you). Without an object it can mean “do harm” in general.
target_language_example: Non voglio farti del male, voglio solo parlare.
native_language_example: I don't want to hurt you; I just want to talk.

additional_notes: Used when someone causes physical or emotional pain to a person. The person who is hurt comes after "a" (often as "a + name" or "a + article": "a Tom", "a un bambino"). In the negative, it often expresses intention: "Non voglio fare del male a..." = "I don’t want to hurt...".
target_language_example: Non volevo fare del male a nessuno.
native_language_example: I didn’t mean to hurt anyone.

meaning: to go for walks; to take walks.
additional_notes: Common way to talk about walking for pleasure/exercise. Often used with "andare a" (e.g., "andare a fare delle passeggiate" = to go for a walk / go walking). You can add who you walk with using "con" (with) or "da solo/a" (alone). "delle" is an indefinite plural (some), so it can be translated as “go for (some) walks.”
target_language_example: Nel weekend mi piace fare delle passeggiate nel parco.
native_language_example: On the weekend I like to go for walks in the park.

meaning: to do better; to do a better job (than this).
additional_notes: Used to say someone could have performed better, or to challenge/encourage them to improve. Often appears in negative statements/questions (Non poteva fare di meglio; Non sai fare di meglio?) or as encouragement (Puoi fare di meglio; So che puoi fare di meglio).
target_language_example: Dai, riprova: puoi fare di meglio.
native_language_example: Come on, try again: you can do better.

meaning: to do more; to do more than you’re doing now.
additional_notes: Used when you want to express that more effort/action is needed or desired. Often follows verbs like "volere" (to want) or expressions like "dovremmo" (we should): "voglio fare di più", "dovremmo fare di più". It can be general (more in life/work) or about a specific situation (help more, contribute more).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, posso fare di più per aiutarti.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I can do more to help you.

meaning: to do anything / to do everything possible.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is capable of doing almost anything, or that they will make every effort to achieve something (often followed by "per" + infinitive: "fare di tutto per convincerla"). Depending on context it can suggest determination ("do everything possible") or unpredictability ("could do anything").
target_language_example: Farò di tutto per arrivare in tempo.
native_language_example: I’ll do everything possible to arrive on time.

meaning: to have an effect; to work (e.g., medicine).
additional_notes: Often used with indirect objects: "fare effetto a + person" (have an effect on someone). With medicines you’ll hear "Mi fa effetto" = "It’s working on me" / "It’s taking effect." It can also mean "to make someone feel uneasy/shocked" depending on context (e.g., "Il sangue mi fa effetto" = "Blood makes me feel squeamish").
target_language_example: Questo antidolorifico mi fa effetto dopo dieci minuti.
native_language_example: This painkiller works for me after ten minutes.

meaning: to party; to celebrate (have fun at a party).
additional_notes: Used for going out or getting together to celebrate and have fun (often with music, drinks, friends). Common with verbs like "andare a fare festa" (go party) or invitations like "Venite a fare festa!".
target_language_example: Stasera facciamo festa per il tuo compleanno!
native_language_example: Tonight we’re partying to celebrate your birthday!

meaning: to pretend; to act as if (something were true).
additional_notes: Used with **di + infinitive**: *fare finta di non capire* = “pretend not to understand.” You can also use it with **che + clause**: *fa finta che vada tutto bene* = “he/she pretends that everything is fine.” Often implies you’re deliberately hiding the truth or not reacting on purpose.
target_language_example: Ho fatto finta di non sentire la domanda.
native_language_example: I pretended not to hear the question.

meaning: To pretend nothing happened; to act as if you didn’t notice.
additional_notes: Used when someone ignores something obvious or awkward on purpose (e.g., a mistake, an argument, an embarrassing moment). It’s common in everyday Italian and can describe either your own behavior or someone else’s.
target_language_example: Ho visto tutto, ma ho fatto finta di niente.
native_language_example: I saw everything, but I pretended nothing happened.

meaning: to get rid of; to finish off (also: slang ‘to kill’).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken Italian. Often means to eliminate/remove something or someone (‘get rid of’), to defeat/knock out, or to consume all of something (‘finish off’ food). In crime/action contexts it can mean ‘to kill’. Used with a direct object: fare fuori qualcuno/qualcosa.
target_language_example: Hanno fatto fuori tutti i biscotti in cinque minuti.
native_language_example: They finished off all the cookies in five minutes.

additional_notes: Used with "fare" (to do/make) + "i compiti" (homework). Often refers to school homework: "Devo fare i compiti" (I have to do homework). You can specify the subject: "fare i compiti di matematica" (do math homework).
target_language_example: Non posso uscire: devo fare i compiti.
native_language_example: I can’t go out: I have to do my homework.

meaning: to do the math; to calculate; (also) to settle accounts.
additional_notes: Used for calculating numbers, totals, or expenses (e.g., budgeting). In everyday Italian it can also mean “to settle up/pay what’s owed.” Very common in the set phrase “fare i conti con …” = “to deal with / to reckon with …”.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo fare i conti e vedere quanto spendiamo al mese.
native_language_example: We need to do the math and see how much we spend per month.

additional_notes: Used for school homework. The possessive changes with the person: fare i miei compiti (my), i tuoi (your), i suoi (his/her), i nostri (our), i vostri (your plural), i loro (their). Very often you’ll see it after "di" (e.g., dimenticarsi/scordarsi di fare i suoi compiti = to forget to do his/her homework) or in causative phrases with "fare" (far fare i suoi compiti a qualcuno = to make/let someone do his/her homework).
target_language_example: Mi sono dimenticato di fare i miei compiti ieri sera.
native_language_example: I forgot to do my homework last night.

meaning: to be / act as / play (a role); to act like (someone/something).
additional_notes: Used with a noun: **fare il + job/role** = “to be/serve as” (often about what you do or want to do): *fare il portiere* = “to be a goalkeeper/do the goalkeeper’s job.” With a negative noun it can mean “to act like”: *fare il cretino* = “to act like an idiot / fool around.”
target_language_example: Da piccolo volevo fare il medico, ma poi ho cambiato idea.
native_language_example: When I was little I wanted to be a doctor, but then I changed my mind.

meaning: to take a bath; to go for a swim (go in the water).
additional_notes: Commonly used for bathing at home (in a bathtub) and for swimming/bathing in the sea, lake, river, or pool: *andare a fare il bagno* = “go for a swim/go in the water.” In the plural, *fare il bagno* can also mean “use the bathroom” in some contexts, but the examples here are about bathing/swimming.
target_language_example: Dopo pranzo andiamo a fare il bagno al mare.
native_language_example: After lunch we’re going for a swim at the sea.

meaning: to do the laundry; to wash clothes.
additional_notes: A very common everyday phrase. "Il bucato" refers to the laundry (the clothes to be washed, or the washing). Used with "fare" (to do/make): *Devo fare il bucato* = “I have to do the laundry.”
target_language_example: Oggi non posso uscire: devo fare il bucato.
native_language_example: I can’t go out today: I have to do the laundry.

meaning: (vulgar) to kick someone’s ass; also: to work very hard (reflexive: farsi il culo).
additional_notes:
Very vulgar/strong. Most often used as:
- "fare il culo a qualcuno" = to beat up / thoroughly defeat someone (in sports, competition, arguments).
- "farsi il culo" = to bust your ass, work extremely hard (often to reach a goal). Not appropriate in polite conversation; use neutral alternatives like "lavorare duramente" (work hard) or "sconfiggere" (defeat).
target_language_example: Per questo esame mi sono fatto il culo per settimane.
native_language_example: I busted my ass for weeks for this exam.

meaning: to do the dirty work (an unpleasant or ethically questionable task for someone else).
additional_notes: Used when someone is made to handle the unpleasant, risky, or morally dubious part of a situation so others don’t have to. Often appears after verbs like lasciare (to let) or far(e) (to make/let), as in “Lascia che lo faccia lui” / “Lascialo fare…”.
target_language_example: Non voglio fare il lavoro sporco per loro.
native_language_example: I don’t want to do the dirty work for them.

additional_notes: Used literally to say you are doing your job. Very common in a firm/defensive tone to tell someone not to interfere or tell you what to do (often with verbs like “fammi…” = “let me…”, or “non dirmi come…” = “don’t tell me how…”). The possessive can change: fare il tuo/suo/nostro lavoro = to do your/his-her/our job.
target_language_example: Per favore, lasciami fare il mio lavoro.
native_language_example: Please, let me do my job.

meaning: to fill up (a tank), e.g., get a full tank of gas.
additional_notes: Most commonly used for vehicles at a gas station: “fare il pieno di benzina/diesel” (fill up with gas/diesel). Can also be used more generally to mean “stock up” or “get a full load,” but the default meaning is “fill the tank.”
target_language_example: Prima di partire, dobbiamo fare il pieno di benzina.
native_language_example: Before leaving, we need to fill up with gas.

meaning: to cheer for; to support (a team/person).
additional_notes: Used especially for sports to say you’re rooting for a team or athlete: “Fare il tifo per + team/person” (e.g., “Faccio il tifo per il Milan”). You can also use it more generally to mean “to root for” someone in a competition or challenge.
target_language_example: Stasera faccio il tifo per la nazionale italiana.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m cheering for the Italian national team.

meaning: to make an impression; to shock/creep someone out.
additional_notes: Used to describe a strong effect on someone. Often appears with an indirect object: “Mi fa impressione…” = “It makes an impression on me / It freaks me out.” Commonly used for things that feel disturbing (e.g., blood, injuries), but it can also be positive in some contexts (“mi fai impressione” can mean “you impress me”).
target_language_example: Mi fa impressione vedere il sangue.
native_language_example: Seeing blood freaks me out.

meaning: to make sure; to arrange (so that).
additional_notes: Often followed by **che** + subjunctive to express ensuring a result: **fare in modo che + (congiuntivo)**. You can also see **fare in modo di + infinitive** (more formal/less common) meaning “to manage/arrange to do.”
target_language_example: Faccio in modo che tu abbia tutto il necessario.
native_language_example: I’ll make sure you have everything you need.

meaning: to break in; to burst/storm in (suddenly enter, often by force).
additional_notes: Used for a sudden, often forceful entry into a place. Common with police (e.g., into an apartment) or with criminals who break into a building. It can also be used more generally for someone who suddenly enters a room unexpectedly.
target_language_example: La polizia ha fatto irruzione nell'appartamento alle sei del mattino.
native_language_example: The police broke into the apartment at six in the morning.

meaning: to act as / play the role of; to work as (a job).
additional_notes: Used with a noun (often a role or profession): fare la spia = “to be/act as a spy, to rat someone out”; fare la domestica = “to work as a maid/housekeeper.” It often implies behaving like that person or doing that kind of work, sometimes temporarily or unwillingly. The article changes with gender/number: fare il cuoco, fare la segretaria, fare i babysitter.
target_language_example: In questo film faccio la guida turistica.
native_language_example: In this movie I play a tour guide.

meaning: to poop; to do a poo (childish).
additional_notes: A very common, kid-friendly/euphemistic way to say someone needs to poop (often used with children, pets, or in a playful tone). In more neutral/adult contexts you’ll more often hear "andare in bagno" (to go to the bathroom) or the more direct verb "defecare" (formal/medical).
target_language_example: Devo fare la cacca, dov’è il bagno?
native_language_example: I need to poop—where’s the bathroom?

meaning: to do the accounting; to keep the books.
additional_notes: Used for handling a business’s financial records (recording income/expenses, invoices, etc.). You can use it with "potere" (can) or "sapere" (know how to) to ask if someone is able/qualified to do accounting.
target_language_example: Chi fa la contabilità in questa azienda?
native_language_example: Who does the accounting in this company?

additional_notes: Used when talking about making the morally correct or responsible choice (even if it’s difficult or has negative consequences). Often follows verbs like volere (to want), cercare (to try), dovere (to have to): “Volevo/Stavo cercando di fare la cosa giusta.”
target_language_example: Non è facile, ma dobbiamo fare la cosa giusta.
native_language_example: It’s not easy, but we have to do the right thing.

meaning: to make a difference; to matter.
additional_notes: Used to say something has an important effect or impact. Common patterns: “Può fare la differenza” (it can make a difference), “Questo fa la differenza” (this is what makes the difference), and with negation “non fa (alcuna) differenza” (it doesn’t make any difference).
target_language_example: Anche un piccolo gesto può fare la differenza.
native_language_example: Even a small gesture can make a difference.

additional_notes: Common, mild/euphemistic way to talk about urinating (often used with kids, but also casually among adults). You can use it with "devo" (I need to), "vado a" (I’m going to), or as a question: "Devi fare la pipì?".
target_language_example: Scusa, devo fare la pipì: dov'è il bagno?
native_language_example: Sorry, I need to pee—where’s the bathroom?

meaning: to do the grocery shopping; to go shopping for groceries.
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase meaning to buy food and household necessities (usually at the supermarket). Often used with "andare a" (to go) or "stare andando a" (to be going): "Vado a fare la spesa" = "I'm going grocery shopping."
target_language_example: Dopo il lavoro devo fare la spesa.
native_language_example: After work I have to do the grocery shopping.

meaning: to make room; to clear the way.
additional_notes: Used when you want people/objects to move aside so someone/something can pass. Very common in the imperative: «Fate largo!» (“Make way!”). Often also used reflexively as «farsi largo» = to make your way through a crowd (sometimes by pushing a bit).
target_language_example: Fate largo, per favore: devo passare.
native_language_example: Make way, please: I need to get through.

additional_notes: A very common, general phrase used to talk about actions in a broad way. Often followed by an adverb or expression that explains *how* someone does things: **da solo** (alone), **a modo suo** (his/her own way), **bene/male** (well/badly), **diversamente** (differently), **come vuoi tu** (the way you want). You’ll also see it in **il modo di fare le cose** (“the way of doing things”).
target_language_example: Cerco sempre di fare le cose con calma.
native_language_example: I always try to do things calmly.

meaning: to pay the price; suffer the consequences (often unfairly).
additional_notes: Most commonly used as **farne le spese** (= “to end up paying the price for it”), where **ne** means “of it/for it.” Example pattern: **Qualcuno ne fa le spese** = “Someone suffers the consequences.” Not to be confused with **fare la spesa** (singular), which means “to do the grocery shopping.”
target_language_example: Alla fine ne ha fatto le spese Marco, anche se non c’entrava nulla.
native_language_example: In the end Marco paid the price, even though he had nothing to do with it.

meaning: to teach (a class); to give a lesson/lecture.
additional_notes: Used mainly with the teacher/professor as the subject. Common in school/university contexts. You can add a time or place: “fare lezione alle 9”, “fare lezione in aula 3”.
target_language_example: Oggi il professore fa lezione dalle 10 alle 12.
native_language_example: Today the professor teaches from 10 to 12.

meaning: to shed light on; to clarify (a situation).
additional_notes: Often used figuratively with “su” (“fare luce su…” = “to shed light on…”), especially about explaining something unclear or investigating what really happened. It can also be literal (“turn on/bring some light”), but the most common everyday use is “clarify.”
target_language_example: Dobbiamo fare luce su quello che è successo ieri.
native_language_example: We need to shed light on what happened yesterday.

additional_notes: Common in everyday speech. After negation it often becomes "non fare niente" (= "not do anything" / "do nothing"). You can also use it as an infinitive phrase, like in the example: "Fare niente è...".
target_language_example: Oggi voglio solo fare niente.
native_language_example: Today I just want to do nothing.

meaning: to do nothing; to be unable to do anything.
additional_notes: Often used either literally (not doing any activity) or to express powerlessness: "non posso/non possiamo fare nulla" = "there’s nothing I/we can do." It’s also common with "lasciare" (to let): "non lasci mai fare nulla a nessuno" = "you never let anyone do anything."
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma non posso fare nulla per cambiare la situazione.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but there’s nothing I can do to change the situation.

additional_notes: Often used as **fare pace con qualcuno** (“to make peace with someone”) after an argument. You’ll also very commonly hear **fare la pace** with the same meaning. Note: Italian **pace** means “peace,” so it’s a false friend with English “pace.”
target_language_example: Dopo la lite, hanno deciso di fare pace.
native_language_example: After the argument, they decided to make peace.

meaning: to be pleased / to be glad; to be a pleasure (for someone).
additional_notes: Most often used with an indirect object pronoun: *mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi fa piacere* = “I’m/you’re/he’s/she’s/we’re/you’re glad” or “it’s a pleasure for me/you/etc.” Common in polite invitations/requests: *Mi farebbe piacere...* (“I’d be happy if... / I’d be pleased to...”).
target_language_example: Mi fa piacere conoscerti.
native_language_example: Nice to meet you (I’m glad to meet you).

meaning: to make room (for someone/something); to move over.
additional_notes: Used when you want someone to create space (e.g., on a seat, in a line, on a shelf). Often followed by "a" + person/thing: "Fare posto a qualcuno" = make room for someone. You can also hear it as an instruction: "Fai posto!" = Move over!/Make room!
target_language_example: Scusa, puoi fare posto a questa valigia?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you make room for this suitcase?

meaning: to put pressure on; to pressure someone.
additional_notes: Often used with **su** + person/thing: **fare pressione su qualcuno** (to pressure someone) or **fare pressione sul governo** (to put pressure on the government). You may also hear it in the negative as a request: **Non farmi pressione** (“Don’t pressure me”).
target_language_example: Non farmi pressione: decido io.
native_language_example: Don’t pressure me: I’ll decide.

meaning: to make (something) your own; to adopt/take on (an idea, suggestion).
additional_notes: Used mainly with ideas, opinions, advice, or goals: “fare propria un’idea/una proposta/una causa” = to adopt it and treat it as your own. It takes a direct object (often after the verb): “Ho fatto mia la tua proposta.” In the plural: “fare proprie (le idee)”.
target_language_example: Ho fatto mia la tua idea e l’ho proposta in riunione.
native_language_example: I made your idea my own and brought it up in the meeting.

additional_notes: Used with the verb fare (“to do/make”) + qualcosa (“something”). It often implies taking some action, sometimes because it’s necessary (e.g., devo/ dovrebbe fare qualcosa = “I have to / should do something”). You can also use it to suggest an activity: Vuoi fare qualcosa stasera?
target_language_example: Dobbiamo fare qualcosa per risolvere il problema.
native_language_example: We have to do something to solve the problem.

meaning: to do (or make) something + adjective (e.g., “something big/fun/interesting”).
additional_notes: Common pattern: "fare qualcosa di" + adjective, especially after verbs like potere/volere (posso/voglio/potremmo). The "di" links "qualcosa" to an adjective: "qualcosa di grande" = "something big" (not *"something of big"* in English). You can swap the adjective: qualcosa di divertente / utile / nuovo / speciale.
target_language_example: Stasera vorrei fare qualcosa di diverso.
native_language_example: Tonight I’d like to do something different.

additional_notes: Used when offering, suggesting, or asking if there’s any action you can take to help someone. Often appears with modal verbs like possiamo (we can), dovremmo (we should), riusciamo a (can we manage to), vorrei poter (I’d like to be able to).
target_language_example: Se vuoi, posso fare qualcosa per aiutare con la spesa.
native_language_example: If you want, I can do something to help with the grocery shopping.

meaning: to do anything; to do whatever (it takes).
additional_notes: Used to express no limits on what someone can/will do. Often followed by "per..." to mean “do anything for...” (Io farei qualsiasi cosa per te). In negative or limiting contexts, it can mean “to do anything at all”: "troppo stanco per fare qualsiasi cosa" = “too tired to do anything.”
target_language_example: Farebbe qualsiasi cosa pur di ottenere quel lavoro.
native_language_example: He/She would do anything to get that job.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re willing or able to do any action, often with “per …” to show the purpose (e.g., per te = for you). “Qualunque” can also appear as “qualsiasi” with a very similar meaning.
target_language_example: Farebbe qualunque cosa per aiutare la sua famiglia.
native_language_example: He/She would do anything to help his/her family.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause specifying what someone does/has to do/can do/wants to do: fare quello che devo/posso/voglio. Often followed by another verb (usually in the present or past) that gives the action or requirement.
target_language_example: Non posso fare quello che vuoi oggi.
native_language_example: I can’t do what you want today.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific action or task that’s clear from context (instructions, something just mentioned, a job/task, or an activity someone likes/hates). You can replace questo with other demonstratives: fare quello = “to do that.”
target_language_example: Non posso fare questo oggi; lo farò domani.
native_language_example: I can’t do this today; I’ll do it tomorrow.

meaning: to report (to a superior); to make a report.
additional_notes: Common in military/police/formal hierarchies. Often used as an order or duty: "(Devo) fare rapporto" = "I have to report"; "fare rapporto a [someone]" = "report to [someone]". Note: "rapporto" can also mean "relationship" in other contexts, but here it means a (formal) report.
target_language_example: Dopo l’incidente devo fare rapporto al comandante.
native_language_example: After the incident I have to report to the commander.

meaning: to refer to; to make reference to.
additional_notes: Often used in more formal Italian (documents, emails, explanations). Common pattern: "fare riferimento a + noun/pronoun" (e.g., "fare riferimento a questo punto" = "refer to this point"). Can also be used without "a" when the object follows directly (e.g., "fare riferimento al contratto" / "fare riferimento alle regole").
target_language_example: Nel modulo devi fare riferimento al numero d’ordine.
native_language_example: On the form you have to refer to the order number.

meaning: to be disgusting; to suck (be really bad).
additional_notes: Common, informal expression. Used both literally for something gross (food, smells, mess) and figuratively to say something is terrible (a movie, a job, the weather). Often appears as “Che schifo!” (“How disgusting!”) or “Fa schifo.” (“It sucks/It’s disgusting.”).
target_language_example: Questo pesce fa schifo, non lo mangio.
native_language_example: This fish is disgusting—I’m not eating it.

additional_notes: Common, informal everyday phrase (often used especially for clothes or leisure shopping). It’s usually used with verbs like andare/venire: “andare a fare shopping” = “to go shopping.”
target_language_example: Sabato pomeriggio andiamo a fare shopping in centro.
native_language_example: On Saturday afternoon we’re going shopping downtown.

meaning: to be quiet; to keep silent.
additional_notes: Used to ask or tell someone to stop talking or making noise. Very common with "Devi fare silenzio" (You must be quiet) and as a request with "Per favore" (e.g., "Per favore, fai silenzio"). It can also be used after verbs like "chiedere" (to ask) or "dire/segno di" (to tell/signal) + "di fare silenzio".
target_language_example: Per favore, fai silenzio: il bambino sta dormendo.
native_language_example: Please be quiet: the baby is sleeping.

meaning: to get ahead; to make progress (in life/career).
additional_notes: Often used to say someone is becoming successful or advancing: "Ha fatto strada" = "He/She’s come a long way." In more literal contexts it can also mean to cover distance while traveling (similar to "fare molta strada" = "to go a long way"). Related phrase: "farsi strada" means "to make your way (through a crowd)" / "to push through."
target_language_example: Con questo lavoro, Marta ha fatto strada in pochi anni.
native_language_example: With this job, Marta got ahead in just a few years.

additional_notes: Used when someone handles all the work without help, either by choice ("I want to") or out of necessity ("I’ll have to"). It agrees with the subject: a woman would usually say "fare tutto da sola". Common with verbs like "dovere" (to have to) and "volere" (to want to).
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: posso fare tutto da solo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I can do everything by myself.

meaning: 'to do' / 'to make' (something), used before a singular masculine noun.
additional_notes: Very common structure: fare un + noun (e.g., fare un turno = do a shift; fare un discorso = give/make a speech; fare un passo = take a step). The exact English verb often changes depending on the noun (do/make/give/take). You may also see it in the causative form farsi fare un + noun (literally “to have a … done for oneself”), e.g., farsi fare un ritratto = to have a portrait made.
target_language_example: Devo fare un passo indietro e pensarci bene.
native_language_example: I need to take a step back and think about it carefully.

meaning: to go for a walk/ride; to take a quick trip around.
additional_notes: Used for a short, casual outing (often with no fixed destination): a walk around the neighborhood, a drive, a bike ride, etc. It can also mean “to take someone for a spin/ride” (far fare un giro a qualcuno). In invitations you’ll often hear: “Ti va di fare un giro?” = “Do you feel like going for a walk/going out for a bit?”
target_language_example: Dopo cena facciamo un giro in centro?
native_language_example: After dinner, shall we go for a walk downtown?

additional_notes: Common with verbs of going: "andare a fare un picnic" (to go have a picnic). It’s also used to talk about the plan or the day being good for it: "una bella giornata per fare un picnic". "Picnic" is a borrowed word in Italian and is invariable (il picnic / i picnic).
target_language_example: Se c’è bel tempo, domenica facciamo un picnic al parco.
native_language_example: If the weather is nice, on Sunday we’ll have a picnic in the park.

meaning: “to do / to have a …” (used before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with an activity/event noun to say you do it once: fare una telefonata (make a phone call), fare una nuotata (go for a swim), fare una visita (pay a visit), fare una spedizione (go on an expedition). The noun that follows is usually feminine singular (una). For masculine nouns you use “fare un …”.
target_language_example: Vado a fare una passeggiata.
native_language_example: I’m going to go for a walk.

meaning: to do something; to do a thing.
additional_notes: A very common, general way to talk about doing an action when you don’t specify exactly what. Often followed by an adjective or description (e.g., “una cosa così folle” = “something so crazy”). In the causative form “far(e) fare una cosa a qualcuno,” it means “to make/let someone do something.” Depending on context, it can also refer to a specific activity (even an implied one).
target_language_example: Non voglio fare una cosa di cui poi mi pento.
native_language_example: I don’t want to do something I’ll regret later.

meaning: to do something like that (that kind of thing).
additional_notes: Used to refer to an action of that type, often with surprise, disapproval, or emphasis (e.g., “How could you do such a thing?”). Literally it’s “to do a thing of the kind.” It can refer to something just mentioned or understood from context.
target_language_example: Non posso credere che tu abbia fatto una cosa del genere!
native_language_example: I can’t believe you did something like that!

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase using fare (“to do/make”) + una doccia (“a shower”). Used with andare a + infinitive to mean “go take a shower” (e.g., Andate/Vada a fare una doccia!). You can add bisogno di (“need to”) or proprio (“really”) to emphasize: Ho (proprio) bisogno di fare una doccia.
target_language_example: Dopo la palestra, devo fare una doccia.
native_language_example: After the gym, I have to take a shower.

additional_notes: Used in polite contexts (class, meetings, interviews) when you want permission or to announce that you have a question. Very common with phrases like "Posso fare una domanda?" or "Vorrei fare una domanda.".
target_language_example: Scusi, posso fare una domanda?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I ask a question?

meaning: to go for a walk; to take a walk.
additional_notes: Common, everyday phrase for walking for pleasure or exercise. Often used with "andare a" (to go to) + infinitive: "andare a fare una passeggiata" = "to go for a walk." You can also invite someone with "Vuoi/Volete fare una passeggiata?".
target_language_example: Dopo cena facciamo una passeggiata in centro.
native_language_example: After dinner, we'll go for a walk downtown.

meaning: to go for a walk in the park.
additional_notes: Literally “to do a walk at the park,” but in natural English it’s “to go for a walk.” Very common with andare: “andare a fare una passeggiata (al parco)”. Can be used as an invitation (Vorresti/Vorreste…?) or as a suggestion/command (Vada a…). Past forms agree with who is walking: “siamo andati” (mixed/men) vs “siamo andate” (all women).
target_language_example: Dopo pranzo andiamo a fare una passeggiata al parco?
native_language_example: After lunch, shall we go for a walk in the park?

additional_notes: Used when you stop an activity for a short rest. Very common with verbs like dovere/potere/volere (e.g., Dovremmo fare una pausa. / Vuole fare una pausa?). You can specify the type of break: una pausa caffè = a coffee break.
target_language_example: Dopo due ore di lavoro, facciamo una pausa.
native_language_example: After two hours of work, let's take a break.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase meaning “to place a call.” You can use it with verbs like dovere (devo fare una telefonata = I have to make a call) or volere (vorrei fare una telefonata = I’d like to make a call). Also used when asking where you can call: Dove si può fare una telefonata?
target_language_example: Posso fare una telefonata veloce?
native_language_example: Can I make a quick phone call?

meaning: 'to do is to wait' / 'all you can do is wait.'
additional_notes: Used after expressions like Tutto ciò che... / Tutto quello che... to say there’s no other action possible: the only option is to wait (often with a sense of resignation). Common patterns: Tutto ciò che devi fare è aspettare...; Tutto quello che possiamo fare è aspettare che + subjunctive (e.g., che arrivi, che risponda).
target_language_example: A questo punto, tutto quello che possiamo fare è aspettare notizie.
native_language_example: At this point, all we can do is wait for news.

additional_notes: From **fare del male (a qualcuno)** = “to hurt someone / to do harm to someone.” **Farei** is the conditional (“I would do”), and **mai** with a negative (e.g., **non**) means “never.” Often you’ll see pronouns inserted: **Non le farei mai del male** = “I would never hurt her,” or with **a + person**: **Non farei mai del male a Tom** = “I would never hurt Tom.”
target_language_example: Non ti farei mai del male, fidati.
native_language_example: I would never hurt you—trust me.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of fare (farei = “I would do”) to express willingness/hypothetical readiness to do whatever is needed for someone. Typically followed by an indirect object pronoun or noun (per te, per lui, per Maria).
target_language_example: Farei qualsiasi cosa per aiutarti.
native_language_example: I would do anything to help you.

meaning: "I would do anything for" / "I would do anything to (achieve...)".
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of fare (farei = “I would do”) to express willingness or strong intention. With a person (per te/lui/loro) it means you’d do anything for them; with an infinitive goal (per ottenere...) it means you’d do anything to achieve it.
target_language_example: Farei qualunque cosa per aiutarti.
native_language_example: I would do anything to help you.

meaning: “we’ll do everything we can / we’ll do our best.”
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone that you will make a maximum effort to help or achieve something. It’s future tense of “fare” (to do/make): “faremo” = “we will do,” and “tutto il possibile” = “everything possible.” Often appears with phrases like “Puoi/Potete star certo/i che…” (“You can be sure that…”).
target_language_example: Non ti preoccupare: faremo tutto il possibile per risolvere il problema.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we’ll do everything we can to solve the problem.

additional_notes: Used to give strong advice or a warning. It’s the conditional of fare meglio (“to do better”) + a + infinitive: faresti meglio a + verb (e.g., faresti meglio a chiamare…). You can make it negative with non: faresti meglio a non + infinitive. Often sounds like “You should really…”.
target_language_example: Faresti meglio a prendere un taxi, è tardi.
native_language_example: You’d better take a taxi; it’s late.

meaning: to hurt him; to do him harm.
additional_notes: "Fare del male" means "to hurt" / "to harm." "Gli" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to him" (sometimes also "to them" in some contexts). You’ll often see it after another verb (e.g., "non voglio fargli del male" = "I don’t want to hurt him"). You can swap the pronoun: "farle del male" (hurt her), "farvi del male" (hurt you all), etc.
target_language_example: Non voglio fargli del male, voglio solo parlare.
native_language_example: I don’t want to hurt him; I just want to talk.

meaning: “to make a long story short”; “in short.”
additional_notes: Used to summarize and skip details, often introduced as "Per farla breve," at the start of a sentence. "La" refers to the story/situation being talked about (understood from context). Common in both spoken and written Italian; slightly informal but widely acceptable.
target_language_example: Per farla breve, abbiamo perso il treno e siamo tornati a casa.
native_language_example: To make a long story short, we missed the train and went back home.

meaning: to put an end to it; to stop it (sometimes: to end it all / kill oneself).
additional_notes: Used when someone wants to end a situation once and for all. Often appears as “farla finita con + [someone/something]” (= to be done with someone/something: break up, quit, cut ties). In questions/exclamations like “Volete farla finita?” it means “Will you stop it?” In some contexts it’s a euphemism for suicide (“end it all”), so the meaning depends strongly on the situation and tone.
target_language_example: Basta litigare: facciamola finita.
native_language_example: Stop arguing—let’s put an end to it.

meaning: to hurt her; to harm her.
additional_notes: Used when the object is a woman/girl: le = “to her” (indirect object) and del male = “harm”. Often appears with verbs like volere (to want), cercare (to try), o avere intenzione di (to intend to): “Non voglio farle del male” = “I don’t want to hurt her.” For a man you’d say fargli del male; for you (formal) farLe del male.
target_language_example: Non voglio farle del male.
native_language_example: I don't want to hurt her.

meaning: to do it by herself / on her own.
additional_notes: Used when the subject is a woman/girl ("da sola"). For a man, say "farlo da solo". "Da solo/da sola" emphasizes doing something without help, independently. The "lo" is an object pronoun meaning "it" (the thing/task is understood from context).
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: posso farlo da sola.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I can do it by myself.

meaning: to do it by myself / on my own.
additional_notes: Uses the pronoun "lo" (= it) with "fare" (to do/make). "Da solo" means "alone" in the sense of without help. Change "solo" to match the person: "da sola" (female speaker), "da soli/da sole" (plural). Often used to say you don’t want help or you want independence.
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: posso farlo da solo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I can do it by myself.

additional_notes: Used when asking someone to help you with something. It changes with the person: farmi (do me), farti (do you), fargli/farle (do him/her), farci (do us), farvi (do you all), fargli (do them). Often used with polite forms: “Potrebbe/Può farmi un favore?” (Could you do me a favor?).
target_language_example: Mi puoi fare un favore? Puoi chiudere la finestra, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you do me a favor? Can you close the window, please?

meaning: to step forward; to come forward (volunteer, identify yourself).
additional_notes: Used when asking or ordering someone to move to the front, or to present themselves (e.g., to admit involvement, offer help, or speak up). Often appears as an imperative: "Fatti avanti!" (to one person), "Fatevi avanti!" (to several/formal).
target_language_example: Se qualcuno ha visto qualcosa, si faccia avanti.
native_language_example: If anyone saw something, please come forward.

meaning: to hurt yourself; to get injured.
additional_notes: Commonly used to warn about danger or express concern that someone might be injured. Literally “to do bad to oneself”: the reflexive pronoun (mi/ti/si/ci/vi/si) changes with the subject (e.g., mi faccio male = I hurt myself; si fa male = he/she hurts himself/herself). Often appears with modal verbs like potere/dovere (e.g., potrebbe farsi male = he/she could get hurt).
target_language_example: Attento: potresti farti male!
native_language_example: Careful: you could get hurt!

meaning: to show up / let yourself be seen; (also) to go get checked by a doctor.
additional_notes: Reflexive expression (fare + si + vedere). Often used with negation or stealth contexts: “non farsi vedere (da nessuno)” = “not let anyone see you,” and “senza farsi vedere” = “without being seen / unnoticed.” In advice like “Dovresti/Dovrebbe farsi vedere,” it commonly means “you should go see a doctor (get checked out),” sometimes implying you don’t look well or you’re not acting normally.
target_language_example: Se stai male, dovresti farti vedere da un medico.
native_language_example: If you feel sick, you should go see a doctor.

meaning: to hurt you; to harm you.
additional_notes: Used to say someone will/won’t cause you physical or emotional harm. It’s built from fare (to do/make) + ti (to you) + del male (harm). You can change the pronoun: farmi del male (hurt me), farci del male (hurt us), farle del male (hurt her), farvi del male (hurt you all). Often appears after verbs like voler(e) (to want), poter(e) (can/might), dover(e) (must).
target_language_example: Non voglio farti del male, voglio solo parlare.
native_language_example: I don’t want to hurt you; I just want to talk.

additional_notes: Used to say someone will do everything that is asked/needed. It’s made of: farà (will do) + tutto (everything) + quello che (that which/what). Often followed by a verb in the present tense: “farà tutto quello che le chiedi di fare” = “she’ll do everything you ask her to do.”
target_language_example: Farò tutto quello che posso per aiutarti.
native_language_example: I’ll do everything I can to help you.

additional_notes: Future tense of fare (“to do/make”), used to promise or reassure someone you will try as hard as you can. Often followed by per + infinitive to say what you’ll try to do: “Farò del mio meglio per finire.” You can also say “Farò del mio meglio” on its own.
target_language_example: Farò del mio meglio per arrivare in tempo.
native_language_example: I’ll do my best to arrive on time.

meaning: “I’ll make sure that…” / “I’ll see to it that…”.
additional_notes: Used to promise you will arrange things so that something happens (or doesn’t happen). It’s followed by a clause introduced by che; after che you typically use the subjunctive (e.g., che tu lo ricordi). It’s the future tense of fare in modo che (“to make sure that”).
target_language_example: Farò in modo che tu arrivi in tempo.
native_language_example: I’ll make sure you arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to promise or reassure someone that you’ll do whatever is needed/whatever they want. It’s typically followed by a verb like posso (“I can”) or vuoi/vorrai (“you want / you will want”). The subject is implied (io) and farò is the future tense of fare (“to do/make”).
target_language_example: Farò tutto quello che posso per aiutarti.
native_language_example: I’ll do everything I can to help you.

additional_notes: Used in Italian exactly like in English to refer to quick-service food (e.g., burgers, fries). Usually masculine: "il fast food"; you can also say "del fast food" = "some fast food."
target_language_example: Stasera prendiamo del fast food perché abbiamo poco tempo.
native_language_example: Tonight we’ll get some fast food because we don’t have much time.

additional_notes: Imperative addressed to more than one person ("you" plural) or as a polite form ("Lei"). Often followed by "a" + noun/pronoun: "Fate attenzione al fuoco" (to the fire), "Fate attenzione a loro" (to them). Used as a warning on its own: "Fate attenzione!"
target_language_example: È buio qui: fate attenzione ai gradini.
native_language_example: It’s dark here: be careful on the steps.

additional_notes: Imperative form meaning “make/let me see.” It’s addressed to more than one person (voi) or used as a polite/formal command to one person (Lei). Often followed by a noun (i documenti, le foto) or a clause with “cosa/che” (Fatemi vedere cosa tradurre; Fatemi vedere che cosa avete fatto).
target_language_example: Scusi, fatemi vedere il passaporto, per favore.
native_language_example: Excuse me, show me your passport, please.

meaning: hurt/injured (female speaker), usually in “farsi male” = to hurt oneself.
additional_notes: “Fatta male” is the feminine past participle used with the reflexive verb “farsi male” (to get hurt). You’ll often hear it with “mi/ti/si sono fatta male” (I/you/she got hurt). For a male speaker it’s “fatto male”. It can be followed by a body part with “a/alla/al”: “Mi sono fatta male alla schiena” (I hurt my back).
target_language_example: Mi sono fatta male al ginocchio giocando a calcio.
native_language_example: I hurt my knee playing soccer.

additional_notes: Extremely offensive and vulgar. Used to tell someone off aggressively (often in anger or as a strong dismissal). Avoid in polite conversation; in many contexts it can start a serious confrontation. Literal sense: “get yourself fucked.”
target_language_example: Se non ti va bene, fatti fottere.
native_language_example: If you don’t like it, go fuck yourself.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "fare cadere" = "to make (something) fall" → commonly used to mean "to drop" something by accident. "Fatto" is the past participle, used with "avere" (e.g., "ho/hai/ha fatto cadere..."). "Il" is the masculine singular "the"; it changes with the noun ("la", "lo", "l'", "i", "gli", "le").
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ho fatto cadere il telefono.
native_language_example: Sorry, I dropped the phone.

additional_notes: Used with the verb fare in the passato prossimo: (ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno) fatto colazione = “(I/you/he…) had breakfast.” Often appears with time expressions like stamattina/questa mattina (“this morning”) or ancora (“yet/still”). You’ll also hear: fare colazione (to have breakfast).
target_language_example: Scusa, sono di fretta: ho già fatto colazione.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m in a hurry: I’ve already had breakfast.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb "avere" to say someone acted correctly: "hai fatto la cosa giusta" (you did the right thing), "ha fatto la cosa giusta" (he/she did the right thing), "abbiamo fatto la cosa giusta" (we did the right thing). In formal/standard Italian you typically include the auxiliary (e.g., "hai/ha/hanno fatto la cosa giusta").
target_language_example: Hai fatto la cosa giusta a dire la verità.
native_language_example: You did the right thing by telling the truth.

additional_notes: Used with auxiliary verbs (usually "avere" or "essere") to talk about someone getting hurt or someone hurting someone/something. Common patterns: "fare male a [someone/something]" = to hurt [someone/something] (e.g., "Hai fatto male al fiore?"); "farsi male" = to hurt oneself / get injured (e.g., "Ti sei fatto male?"), and with a body part: "Mi sono fatto male al braccio" = I hurt my arm. "Ti hanno fatto male?" means "Did they hurt you?"
target_language_example: Mi sono fatto male al ginocchio giocando a calcio.
native_language_example: I hurt my knee playing soccer.
