additional_notes: Usually used with **non**: **non ho fatto niente** = “I didn’t do anything.” With **con** it means “do anything with (something)” (e.g., money). In the reflexive form **non si è fatto niente**, it often means “(he/she) didn’t get hurt” (literally “didn’t do anything to himself/herself”).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, oggi non ho fatto niente.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t do anything today.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "avere" in the passato prossimo: "non ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno fatto nulla di male" = "I/you/he… did nothing wrong." The phrase "nulla di male" literally means "nothing bad," and is a common way to say "nothing wrong" after a mistake or accusation.
target_language_example: Tranquillo, non hai fatto nulla di male.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, you didn’t do anything wrong.

additional_notes: Almost always used with a negative: "non ho fatto nulla di sbagliato" (I didn’t do anything wrong) or in the past infinitive after verbs like "dire": "dice di non aver fatto nulla di sbagliato" (he says he didn’t do anything wrong). "Nulla" = nothing, and "di sbagliato" means "wrong" (literally, "of wrong").
target_language_example: Non ho fatto nulla di sbagliato, te lo giuro.
native_language_example: I didn’t do anything wrong, I swear.

additional_notes: Used with essere (e.g., "può essere fatto qualcosa") to talk about taking action in a general or impersonal way, often when you don’t say who will do it. Here fatto is the past participle of fare (to do/make). Note: fatto can also mean "fact" in other contexts (un fatto), but in these sentences it means "done/made."
target_language_example: Dobbiamo vedere se può essere fatto qualcosa oggi.
native_language_example: We have to see if something can be done today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **fare** in the past (often **ho/hai/ha fatto**) to say you did something that has a certain quality: **fatto qualcosa di + adjective** (e.g., *giusto, orribile, avventato, diverso*). In questions, **mai** often appears: *Hai mai fatto qualcosa di…?* = “Have you ever done something…?”
target_language_example: Ho fatto qualcosa di sbagliato?
native_language_example: Did I do something wrong?

additional_notes: Used to ask or suggest that someone has made a mistake or done something bad. It’s built with the past participle "fatto" (from "fare") and usually appears with "avere" (e.g., "hai/avete/abbiamo fatto..."). "Qualcosa di sbagliato" means "something wrong" (literally "something of wrong").
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, credo di aver fatto qualcosa di sbagliato.
native_language_example: Sorry, I think I did something wrong.

additional_notes: Uses the past participle of fare (“to do/make”) with a form of avere (ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno). Often means “did this” or “did this to (someone)” as in: Mi hai fatto questo? (“You did this to me?”). Note: fatto can look like English “fact,” but it means “done/made,” not “fact.”
target_language_example: Non capisco perché hai fatto questo.
native_language_example: I don’t understand why you did this.

meaning: "(you/he) referred to / made reference to my father."
additional_notes: "Fare riferimento a" means "to refer to" or "to mention" someone/something (often as a source of information or as something relevant). Here it’s in the past tense (passato prossimo): ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno fatto riferimento a… You can replace "mio padre" with any person or thing: "al medico", "alla legge", "a questo problema".
target_language_example: Durante la riunione, hanno fatto riferimento a mio padre.
native_language_example: During the meeting, they referred to my father.

meaning: had my/his/her hair cut (got a haircut).
additional_notes: Used with the causative construction "farsi + infinitive" to say you had someone else do something for you (typically a professional). It’s reflexive and changes by person: "mi sono fatto..." (I, male), "mi sono fatta..." (I, female), "si è fatto..." (he), "si è fatta..." (she). In the past tense you’ll often see "mi/ti/si/ci/vi sono" + "fatto/a" + infinitive.
target_language_example: Mi sono fatta tagliare i capelli molto corti dal parrucchiere.
native_language_example: I got my hair cut very short at the hairdresser’s.

additional_notes: Used in the very common pattern **(avere) fatto un/una + noun** to talk about doing/making something: *fare un lavoro* (do a job), *fare un elenco* (make a list), *fare un discorso* (give/make a speech), *fare un favore* (do a favor), *fare un massaggio* (give a massage), *fare un sorriso* (give a smile). The article changes with gender/number: **un** (masc.), **una** (fem.), **un’** (before vowel), **dei/delle** (plural).
target_language_example: Ho fatto una prenotazione per domani sera.
native_language_example: I made a reservation for tomorrow evening.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase from "fare un bagno". It’s often used with the auxiliary "avere" ("ho fatto un bagno" = I took a bath). With a reflexive pronoun ("mi/ti/si") it commonly means the same thing: "mi sono fatto/a un bagno" = I took a bath (lit. "I made myself a bath").
target_language_example: Prima di uscire, mi sono fatto un bagno.
native_language_example: Before going out, I took a bath.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "fare" (to make/do): "fare un errore" = to make a mistake. Often appears with auxiliary "avere" in the passato prossimo: "ho/hai/ha fatto un errore" (I/you/he/she made a mistake). Can also be used after verbs like "credere" or "dire" with "avere": "Credevo che avessi fatto un errore" (I thought you had made a mistake).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ho fatto un errore nel modulo.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, I made a mistake on the form.

meaning: 'made/did a …' (past tense, with a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb *fare* in the past with *avere*: *ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno fatto una + [noun]*. The *una* shows the following noun is feminine singular (e.g., *una promessa, una torta, una scoperta, una proposta, una vacanza, una sosta*). The exact English verb can be “made” or “did” depending on the noun. Note: some fixed expressions with *fare una…* can be slang/vulgar (e.g., *fare una sega*).
target_language_example: Ieri ho fatto una prenotazione per due.
native_language_example: Yesterday I made a reservation for two.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "fare" (to make/do) + "una promessa" (a promise), typically in the past with "avere": "ho/hai/ha fatto una promessa" = "I/you/he/she made a promise." You often add the person with "a" or an indirect object pronoun: "fare una promessa a Maria" / "le ho fatto una promessa" (I made her a promise), "ti ho fatto una promessa" (I made you a promise).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma ho fatto una promessa e devo mantenerla.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but I made a promise and I have to keep it.

additional_notes: Used after a clause like **Quello/Ciò che + [person] ha/hai/avete fatto** (“what [someone] did”). The structure is: **Quello/Ciò che … ha fatto + è stato + adjective**. With a feminine subject (e.g., *la cosa*), you’d say **è stata**.
target_language_example: Quello che avete fatto è stato irresponsabile.
native_language_example: What you did was irresponsible.

meaning: 'the fact that' (used to introduce a clause).
additional_notes: Used mainly in the structure "il fatto che + [verb]" to refer to a specific situation or point as a 'fact'. Very common after verbs/nouns like "accennare a" (mention), "lamentarsi di" (complain about), "dimenticarsi di" (forget), and in statements like "È un fatto che..." (= 'It’s a fact that...'). In Italian it’s common to use the subjunctive after "il fatto che" when it expresses opinion/attitude or is not presented as certain.
target_language_example: Non mi piace il fatto che tu arrivi sempre in ritardo.
native_language_example: I don't like the fact that you always arrive late.

meaning: in favor of or opposed to.
additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s opinion/stance, especially in discussions about plans, projects, proposals, or laws. It agrees in gender/number with the person: a man would say “favorevole o contrario al…”, and for plural “favorevoli o contrari/e a…”. With masculine singular nouns you often see “al” (= a + il); with other nouns you may need different forms like “alla”, “ai”, “alle”.
target_language_example: Siete favorevoli o contrari alla nuova regola?
native_language_example: Are you in favor of or opposed to the new rule?

additional_notes: Used to say someone made their maximum effort to do something. It’s in the passato remoto: fece = “did/made” (remote past), del suo meglio = “his/her best”, per + infinitive = “to” + verb. In everyday speech, many people use the passato prossimo instead: ha fatto del suo meglio per.
target_language_example: Fece del suo meglio per arrivare in tempo.
native_language_example: He did his best to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Uses the verb fare (“to do/make”) in the passato remoto (fece), common in narratives and some regions. Pattern: fare del proprio meglio per + infinitive (“to do one’s best to…”). The possessive changes with the subject: ho fatto del mio meglio, ha fatto del suo meglio, abbiamo fatto del nostro meglio, etc.
target_language_example: Fece del suo meglio per arrivare in tempo.
native_language_example: He/She did his/her best to arrive on time.

additional_notes: “Fece” is the passato remoto (remote past) of “fare” (to do/make). It’s common in written Italian (stories, news, historical narration), especially in some regions; in everyday speech many people use “ha fatto i suoi compiti.” “I suoi” means “his/her” depending on context.
target_language_example: Dopo cena, Luca fece i suoi compiti e poi andò a dormire.
native_language_example: After dinner, Luca did his homework and then went to sleep.

additional_notes: It’s the 3rd-person singular passato remoto of fare + un, common in written stories and narration. It’s often followed by a noun to form an action: fare un salto (stop by briefly), fare un pisolino (take a nap), fare un gesto (make a gesture), fare un sorriso (give a smile). In everyday speech, people often use passato prossimo instead: ha fatto un....
target_language_example: Dopo cena fece una passeggiata nel centro.
native_language_example: After dinner, he/she took a walk in the city center.

meaning: “(he/she/it) made a mistake” / “made an error” (simple past).
additional_notes: “Fece” is the passato remoto of “fare” (to do/make). It’s common in written Italian (stories, history, news reports) to describe a completed action in the past. In everyday conversation, you’ll often hear “ha fatto un errore” instead.
target_language_example: Durante il test, fece un errore e perse punti.
native_language_example: During the test, he made a mistake and lost points.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (una + noun): *fece una lista* (made a list), *fece una smorfia* (made a face), *fece una promessa* (made a promise). **Fece** is the **passato remoto** of *fare* (he/she did/made), common in storytelling, books, and in some regions when talking about the past. In everyday conversation many speakers use *ha fatto una…* instead.
target_language_example: Ieri fece una scelta difficile.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she made a difficult choice.

additional_notes: “Feci” is the passato remoto of “fare” (to do/make). It’s common in storytelling, books, and some regions in the South of Italy; in everyday speech many people would say “ho fatto del mio meglio”. Often followed by “per + infinitive” to say what you tried to do: “feci del mio meglio per aiutare…”
target_language_example: Nonostante la paura, feci del mio meglio per rimanere calmo.
native_language_example: Despite being scared, I did my best to stay calm.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato remoto) of “fare un sogno” = “to have a dream.” It’s mostly used in stories, books, or more literary narration; in everyday conversation people usually say “ho fatto un sogno” (passato prossimo). You can add details with: “strano” (strange), “quel pomeriggio” (that afternoon), “su/di” or “riguardo a” (about).
target_language_example: Ieri notte feci un sogno davvero vivido.
native_language_example: Last night I had a really vivid dream.

additional_notes: Refers to the ring worn to show that someone is married. In Italian, "fede" can also mean "faith," but in this phrase it specifically means a ring; "nuziale" means "wedding/marital." Commonly used with verbs like perdere (to lose), indossare (to wear), togliersi (to take off).
target_language_example: Non trovo la fede nuziale: credo di averla persa.
native_language_example: I can’t find my wedding ring: I think I lost it.

additional_notes: A common New Year’s greeting, used in person, in messages, and on cards around New Year’s Eve/Day. Often written with capitalization: "Felice Anno Nuovo!". A very common alternative is "Buon anno!".
target_language_example: Felice anno nuovo a te e alla tua famiglia!
native_language_example: Happy New Year to you and your family!

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say you’re happy/glad to do something: "felice di + infinitive" (e.g., felice di vedere/andare). It can also be used as a polite phrase when meeting someone: "Felice di conoscerti" = "Nice to meet you".
target_language_example: Siamo felici di aiutarti.
native_language_example: We’re happy to help you.

meaning: happy to be; glad to be.
additional_notes: Used to express satisfaction about being in a certain state or situation. It’s followed by an adjective or noun phrase (e.g., felice di essere libero/vivo) or by a longer description. You can also change the subject: sono/sei/è/siamo/siete felici di essere…
target_language_example: Sono felice di essere qui con voi.
native_language_example: I'm happy to be here with you.

additional_notes: Used to express that someone is glad to be in a place/situation. Common pattern: "felice di" + infinitive (e.g., felice di vederti = happy to see you). "Felice" changes for gender/number: felice (m/f singular), felici (plural). You can intensify it with words like "molto" or "veramente".
target_language_example: Siamo felici di essere qui con voi.
native_language_example: We’re happy to be here with you.

additional_notes: Used to describe two (or more) people who are happy as a couple or as a pair/group. "Assieme" is the same idea as "insieme" (“together”) and is common in everyday speech. You can change the adjective for number/gender (e.g., "felice assieme" for one person, "felici assieme" for plural).
target_language_example: Siete davvero felici assieme.
native_language_example: You are really happy together.

additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like "rimanere/restare" ("to be left/remain") to say someone ended up injured: "è rimasto ferito" (passato prossimo) or "rimase ferito" (remote past, more literary/regional). You can add an adverb for severity, e.g. "gravemente ferito" = "seriously injured". "Incidente stradale" is the standard term for a traffic accident.
target_language_example: Il conducente è rimasto ferito in un incidente stradale, ma non è in pericolo di vita.
native_language_example: The driver was injured in a road accident, but their life is not in danger.

additional_notes: Used as an urgent interruption to make someone stop what they’re doing or to pause the conversation (like “Wait, wait!”). Repeating it more times (“fermo, fermo, fermo!”) adds emphasis and urgency. In speech it often sounds like giving a quick order.
target_language_example: Fermo, fermo! Non toccare quel bottone.
native_language_example: Wait, wait! Don’t touch that button.

additional_notes: Used to name the occasion a party or celebration is for: *festa di Halloween* (Halloween party), *festa di Capodanno* (New Year’s party), *festa di addio* (farewell party), *festa di San Valentino* (Valentine’s party). Often followed by a holiday, event, or time (e.g. *festa di stasera* = tonight’s party).
target_language_example: Stiamo organizzando una festa di compleanno per Marco.
native_language_example: We’re organizing a birthday party for Marco.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a party celebrating someone’s birthday. Often appears with possessives (la mia/tuo/sua festa di compleanno) and common invitation phrases like "Vieni alla mia festa di compleanno?" or "Vuoi venire...?".
target_language_example: Domani facciamo una festa di compleanno per Luca.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re having a birthday party for Luca.

additional_notes: Usually used in the reflexive form **fidarsi di** with a reflexive pronoun: **mi fido di... / ti fidi di... / si fida di... / ci fidiamo di... / vi fidate di... / si fidano di...**. In the past it often appears as **mi sono fidato/a di...** (“I trusted...”).
target_language_example: Non mi fido di quella persona.
native_language_example: I don’t trust that person.

additional_notes: In everyday Italian you usually say it with the reflexive verb: "fidarsi di lei" (or "fidarsi di qualcuno/a"). It’s used when you rely on someone’s honesty, intentions, or ability: "Mi posso fidare di lei?" = “Can I trust her/you?” In the examples with "mi sarei dovuto/a" or "mi sarei potuto/a", it expresses “I should/might have been able to trust her.”
target_language_example: Non riesco a fidarmi di lei dopo quello che è successo.
native_language_example: I can’t trust her after what happened.

additional_notes: In real usage you’ll almost always see it as the reflexive verb **fidarsi di** + person/pronoun: **fidarmi di loro** (to trust them), **ti puoi fidare di loro?** (can you trust them?). It’s commonly used in negative statements and questions when someone is unreliable: **non mi posso più fidare di loro** (I can’t trust them anymore).
target_language_example: Non riesco a fidarmi di loro dopo quello che è successo.
native_language_example: I can’t manage to trust them after what happened.

meaning: to trust him; to rely on him.
additional_notes: In modern Italian you normally use the reflexive form: **fidarsi di** + person (e.g., **fidarsi di lui/lei**, **fidarsi di Marco**). With indirect object pronouns it becomes **fidarsi di me/te/lui/lei/noi/voi/loro**. Often used with modal verbs as in the examples: **potersi fidare di lui** (“to be able to trust him”), **doversi fidare di lui** (“to have to trust him”).
target_language_example: Puoi fidarti di lui: manterrà la promessa.
native_language_example: You can trust him: he’ll keep his promise.

additional_notes: From the verb **fidarsi di** (“to trust”). It almost always takes **di + person**: *Ti fidi di me?* (“Do you trust me?”). **Ti fidi di me** is informal (to one person). The formal/polite version is **Si fidi di me** (used with Lei). You can also say **Non ti fidi di me** (“You don’t trust me”).
target_language_example: Ti prego, fidati di me: andrà tutto bene.
native_language_example: Please, trust me: everything will be fine.

additional_notes: Used with a person, group, or yourself: avere fiducia in qualcuno = to trust someone; perdere fiducia in qualcuno = to lose trust in someone. It can also be used for “confidence in oneself”: fiducia in sé.
target_language_example: Ho fiducia in te, ma ho bisogno che tu sia puntuale.
native_language_example: I trust you, but I need you to be on time.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like avere (to have), perdere (to lose), and mancare di (to lack): "ha fiducia in se stessa" = she’s confident; "ha perso fiducia in se stessa" = she lost confidence in herself. The reflexive part changes with the person: "fiducia in me stesso/a" (in myself), "in te stesso/a" (in yourself), "in se stesso" (in himself).
target_language_example: Dopo l’esame, ha riacquistato fiducia in se stessa.
native_language_example: After the exam, she regained confidence in herself.

meaning: trust in you; confidence in you.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like "avere" (to have): "Ho fiducia in te" = "I trust you / I have confidence in you." Often strengthened with words like "molta" (a lot of) or "completa" (complete). It can also be used as encouragement: "Abbi fiducia in te" = "Have confidence in yourself."
target_language_example: So che puoi farcela: ho fiducia in te.
native_language_example: I know you can do it: I believe in you.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "essere" to say you feel proud about a person or thing (e.g., "fiera di te" = proud of you). The adjective agrees with the subject: "fiero di" (male), "fiera di" (female); plural: "fieri di", "fiere di".
target_language_example: Sono fiera di quello che hai fatto.
native_language_example: I’m proud of what you did.

additional_notes: Used with the verb essere (“to be”): essere fiero/fiera di + person/thing = “to be proud of …”. It agrees with the person who feels proud: fiero (male), fiera (female). You can change the pronoun: fiero di te (proud of you), fiera di lui/lei (proud of him/her), fieri di noi (proud of us), fiere di voi (proud of you all).
target_language_example: Sono fiera di me per quello che ho fatto.
native_language_example: I’m proud of myself for what I did.

additional_notes: Used to express pride about a person, yourself, or something you are/do. It’s followed by a noun/pronoun (fiero di te/lui/lei/sé) or by an infinitive to say what you’re proud of (fiero di essere…, fiero di aver fatto…). "Fiero" agrees with the subject: fiero (m. sing.), fiera (f. sing.), fieri (m. pl.), fiere (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Siamo fieri di te per quello che hai fatto.
native_language_example: We’re proud of you for what you did.

additional_notes: Used to say you feel pride about a woman or girl (lei = “her”). The adjective agrees with the speaker: a man says “sono fiero…”, a woman says “sono fiera…”. You can change the pronoun: “fiero di lui” (proud of him), “fiero di te” (proud of you), “fieri di loro” (proud of them).
target_language_example: Sono fiero di lei per come ha gestito la situazione.
native_language_example: I’m proud of her for how she handled the situation.

additional_notes: Used to express pride in someone’s actions or achievements. It often follows forms of essere (sono fiero di te = I’m proud of you). The adjective agrees with the speaker: fiero (male), fiera (female).
target_language_example: Siamo tutti fieri di te per quello che hai fatto.
native_language_example: We’re all proud of you for what you did.

meaning: "proud of you" (speaking to more than one person, or using polite plural).
additional_notes: Used to express pride about what someone has done. It often appears with the verb essere ("sono/è/sarà... fiero di voi") or sentirsi ("mi sento fiero di voi"). "Fiero" changes for gender/number of the speaker: fiero (male), fiera (female), fieri (plural male/mixed), fiere (plural female).
target_language_example: Sono fiera di voi per il lavoro che avete fatto.
native_language_example: I'm proud of you for the work you did.

additional_notes: Very vulgar/profane. Used to insult a group of people (literally “sons of a prostitute”). Also sometimes used in a rough, joking way among friends, but it’s risky and offensive in most situations. Singular is "figlio di puttana". Often said as an exclamation or shouted at someone.
target_language_example: Muovetevi, figli di puttana!
native_language_example: Move it, you sons of bitches!

meaning: a very vulgar insult (like “son of a bitch”).
additional_notes: Extremely offensive and profane. Literally means “daughter of a prostitute/whore,” but in practice it’s used as a harsh insult or angry outburst toward someone (sometimes also said as an expletive about a situation). Avoid in polite conversation; you may hear it in arguments, movies, or street speech.
target_language_example: Non parlare così: è una figlia di puttana.
native_language_example: Don’t talk like that: she’s a son of a bitch.

additional_notes: Used with a name or noun to say who someone’s father/parent is: "Sono il figlio di James" = "I’m James’s son" / "I’m the son of James." With a noun: "il figlio di un mercante" = "a merchant’s son." Often preceded by the article: "il figlio di...".
target_language_example: Lei è la figlia di Marco?
native_language_example: Is she Marco’s daughter?

additional_notes: Strong profanity used to insult someone, express anger, or threaten them. You may hear it in fights or movies (as in “A terra, figlio di puttana!” = “Get on the ground, you son of a bitch!”). Avoid using it in polite conversation; it can escalate situations quickly.
target_language_example: Quel figlio di puttana mi ha rubato il portafoglio!
native_language_example: That son of a bitch stole my wallet!

additional_notes: Used with essere (e.g., "Sono figlio unico") to say you have no siblings. It agrees with the person: a man says "figlio unico"; a woman says "figlia unica". You may also see it in phrases like "essendo figlio unico" (“being an only child”).
target_language_example: Mia moglie è figlia unica, quindi non ha fratelli né sorelle.
native_language_example: My wife is an only child, so she doesn’t have any brothers or sisters.

meaning: from now on; already (as of now).
additional_notes: Often used to say you’re doing or saying something “already now,” especially in polite/formal language: "La ringrazio fin d'ora" = “Thank you in advance.” It can also mean “as of now / from this moment.” Note: it’s closely related to (and sometimes confused with) "finora" (one word) = “so far / until now.”
target_language_example: La ringrazio fin d'ora per la disponibilità.
native_language_example: Thank you in advance for your availability.

meaning: “up to here / this far”; often “all the way here”.
additional_notes: Used to talk about reaching a place or point: "arrivare/venire fin qui" = to make it (all the way) here. It can also appear in the idiom "Ne ho fin qui (di...)" meaning "I’ve had it up to here (with...)" (more colloquial).
target_language_example: Grazie per essere venuto fin qui per aiutarmi.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming all the way here to help me.

additional_notes: Used to express a limit in time: something continues (or doesn’t happen) up to the moment another event occurs. Very common with the future: *Aspetterò finché non arrivi* (“I’ll wait until you arrive”). Even though Italian uses **non**, it usually doesn’t make the clause negative; it’s part of the structure. Can also appear in the past: *Non l’avevo mai visto finché non sono andato…* (“I had never seen it until I went…”).
target_language_example: Resto qui finché non mi chiami.
native_language_example: I’ll stay here until you call me.

additional_notes: Used to say you will wait or keep doing something up to the moment someone/something arrives. Italian commonly uses **finché non + present tense** (with **non**) even though English usually just says “until … arrives” without a negative.
target_language_example: Resto qui finché non arriva l'autobus.
native_language_example: I’ll stay here until the bus arrives.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to say something ends (time, trip, act, etc.). It’s “fine” + “del” (= di + il). For feminine nouns, use “fine della” (e.g., fine della giornata). Often appears in longer phrases like “alla fine del …” (at the end of …) and “fino alla fine del …” (until the end of …). Note: Italian “fine” means “end,” not English “fine.”
target_language_example: Siamo arrivati alla fine del film.
native_language_example: We arrived at the end of the movie.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to talk about when something finishes (e.g., fine della partita = “the end of the game”). It can also be used as a firm, final statement: “Fine della discussione!” (“End of discussion!”). Note: Italian "fine" means “end,” not English “fine” (= OK / penalty).
target_language_example: Alla fine della lezione, facciamo un ripasso.
native_language_example: At the end of the lesson, we do a review.

additional_notes: The standard Italian word for “weekend.” Often used with articles and prepositions: nel fine settimana / nei fine settimana (“on the weekend / on weekends”), per il fine settimana (“for the weekend”), fino al fine settimana (“until the weekend”). You can also say “Buon fine settimana” as a common greeting/wish.
target_language_example: Andiamo al mare nel fine settimana.
native_language_example: We’re going to the seaside on the weekend.

additional_notes: Literally 'open window' (finestra = window, aperta = open). Common with "con": "dormire con la finestra aperta" = to sleep with the window open.
target_language_example: Non posso dormire con la finestra aperta in inverno.
native_language_example: I can’t sleep with the window open in winter.

additional_notes: Uses the gerund "fingendo" (from "fingere", to pretend) + "di" + an infinitive to describe what someone is pretending to do. Often used with "stare" (e.g., "sta/stava fingendo...") or with verbs like "pensare" in the present subjunctive ("penso che stia fingendo...").
target_language_example: Ha chiuso gli occhi, fingendo di dormire.
native_language_example: He closed his eyes, pretending to be asleep.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "finire" (to finish) + "i miei compiti" (my homework/assignments). Often used with "devo" (I have to) or "devo ancora" (I still have to) to say you haven’t finished yet. "Compiti" usually means school homework; you can specify the subject: "i miei compiti di matematica" (my math homework).
target_language_example: Prima di uscire, devo finire i miei compiti.
native_language_example: Before going out, I have to finish my homework.

meaning: to finish the work (to complete the job/task).
additional_notes: Used for completing a piece of work or a task. Often followed by details like "in tempo" (on time) or "oggi" (today). You can change the object: "finire il compito" (finish the homework/task), "finire il progetto" (finish the project).
target_language_example: Devo finire il lavoro prima di stasera.
native_language_example: I have to finish the work before tonight.

additional_notes: Common spoken imperative used to tell someone to stop doing/saying something annoying or unacceptable. Often said with emphasis or repeated ("Finiscila!"), and can sound quite sharp depending on tone. You can add "dai" to mean "come on" ("Finiscila, dai!") or use "finiscila con + [noun]" to mean "stop with + [that thing]" (e.g., "finiscila con queste scuse" = "stop with these excuses").
target_language_example: Finiscila con le scuse e dimmi la verità.
native_language_example: Stop with the excuses and tell me the truth.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone has stopped/finished an action: finire di + infinitive. Very common in the passato prossimo: (ho/hai/ha) finito di + infinitive (e.g., Ho finito di studiare = I finished studying). In questions it often means “Have you finished … yet?”.
target_language_example: Ho finito di lavorare, possiamo andare.
native_language_example: I’ve finished working; we can go.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "finire" (to finish). In speech you’ll usually say it with an auxiliary verb: "Ho finito i compiti" (I’ve finished my homework), "Hai finito i compiti?" (Have you finished your homework?). With "dopo aver" it means "after finishing": "dopo aver finito i compiti".
target_language_example: Non posso uscire finché non ho finito i compiti.
native_language_example: I can’t go out until I’ve finished my homework.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **finire** in the past: **ho/hai/ha/abbiamo… finito il + noun** = “I/you/he… finished the …” (e.g., *finito il caffè* = finished the coffee). With **essere**, it can mean something has ended: **È finito il tempo!** = “Time’s up!” (here the subject is *il tempo*).
target_language_example: Ho finito il libro ieri sera.
native_language_example: I finished the book last night.

meaning: finished the work; done with work.
additional_notes: Used with the verb finire (“to finish”) + il lavoro (“the work/job”) to say you have completed your work. Very common in questions like Hai finito il lavoro? (“Have you finished work?”). Often takes auxiliary avere in compound tenses: ho/hai/ha finito il lavoro (I/you/he/she finished the work / is done with work).
target_language_example: Ho finito il lavoro, possiamo uscire.
native_language_example: I’m done with work; we can go out.

meaning: up to; until (a time/date); as far as (a place/limit).
additional_notes: Used to mark a limit or endpoint. With places it often means “as far as” (Camminare fino a qui = walk as far as here). With time/dates it means “until” (fino a domattina, fino a ieri, fino a lunedì). It can also mean “up to” with numbers/limits (contare fino a nove = count up to nine).
target_language_example: Resto qui fino a domani.
native_language_example: I’ll stay here until tomorrow.

meaning: all the way home (up to home).
additional_notes: Used after verbs of movement (guidare, camminare, seguire, spingere, ecc.) to show the endpoint: you continue doing the action until you arrive home. It can refer to your home or someone else’s home, depending on context.
target_language_example: Siamo tornati a piedi fino a casa perché non c'erano autobus.
native_language_example: We walked all the way home because there were no buses.

meaning: up to ten (e.g., count to ten).
additional_notes: Used with numbers to mean “up to” that number, very commonly with contare (“to count”): contare fino a dieci = “to count to ten.” It can also mean “as far as ten / no more than ten,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Quando sei arrabbiato, prova a respirare e conta fino a dieci.
native_language_example: When you’re angry, try to breathe and count to ten.

additional_notes: Used to say something will continue up to (and not beyond) tomorrow, or that you should wait/keep/stay until tomorrow. Often follows verbs like aspettare (to wait), restare/rimanere (to stay), and tenere (to keep).
target_language_example: Puoi lasciarlo qui fino a domani.
native_language_example: You can leave it here until tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say something continues and then stops/changes on Monday. It often follows a time expression like "stare" (to stay) or "aspettare" (to wait). You can replace "lunedì" with any day/date: "fino a martedì", "fino al 10".
target_language_example: Resto a casa fino a lunedì.
native_language_example: I’m staying at home until Monday.

meaning: until (when); up to the time that.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a time limit or something that continues up to a certain moment/event. Very often followed by the subjunctive (especially with future/uncertain events) and frequently appears with "non" (e.g., "fino a quando non..."), where "non" is often not negative in meaning but part of the construction meaning “until.” It can also be used in questions: "Fino a quando?" = "Until when?"
target_language_example: Aspettiamo qui fino a quando non arriva l'autobus.
native_language_example: We'll wait here until the bus arrives.

meaning: "until" (up to the moment when something happens).
additional_notes: Used to say that an action continues up to a certain point in time: *fino a quando non + verb*. Italian normally includes **non** here even when English doesn’t use “not” (it’s often called an “expletive non”). Common with the present/past or subjunctive depending on context: *Aspetto fino a quando non arrivi* = “I’ll wait until you arrive.”
target_language_example: Resta qui fino a quando non torno.
native_language_example: Stay here until I come back.

additional_notes: Used to say something continues up to the moment when “we” (noi) do something. Very often it’s followed by a past participle (e.g., "tornate/tornati" = back/returned). In Italian, "fino a quando" is commonly followed by "non" even though it does NOT make the meaning negative (English usually just says “until”). "Siamo" agrees with “we” and is often used with a past participle to form the past tense ("siamo tornate" = we came back, feminine plural).
target_language_example: Aspetta qui fino a quando non siamo pronti.
native_language_example: Wait here until we’re ready.

additional_notes: Used to say something continues up to a late time, or happens late (e.g., sleeping in). Often with verbs like dormire (to sleep), restare/stare (to stay), lavorare (to work). You can add a time reference: fino a tardi la notte = late into the night.
target_language_example: Ieri sera abbiamo parlato fino a tardi.
native_language_example: Last night we talked until late.

meaning: “up to a point; to some extent.”
additional_notes: Used to say something is only partly true/understood/acceptable—there’s a limit (“not completely”). Often follows verbs like capire (to understand) or essere vero (to be true).
target_language_example: Sono d’accordo con te fino a un certo punto, ma non del tutto.
native_language_example: I agree with you up to a point, but not completely.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a time limit: something continues or is true from now (or from another reference time) up to a specific moment already mentioned or understood. In instructions it often means “don’t do anything else before that time” (e.g., wait, keep doing something). It can also mean “up to that moment in the past,” especially with past tenses (e.g., what someone had written up to then).
target_language_example: Non dirlo a nessuno fino ad allora.
native_language_example: Don’t tell anyone until then.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun (a + il → al) after fino a. It indicates an endpoint in space (movement as far as a place: fino al deserto, fino al cancello), time (until a moment/event: fino al secondo tempo), or extent/limit (up to a certain level: fino al liceo). For feminine singular: fino alla; plural: fino ai / fino alle; before vowels: fino all'.
target_language_example: Aspetta fino al ritorno di Marco.
native_language_example: Wait until Marco comes back.

meaning: up to your neck; deeply (in debt/trouble).
additional_notes: Literally “up to the neck.” Often used figuratively to mean being very involved in something or overwhelmed by a bad situation, especially with expressions like “essere nei debiti fino al collo” (deep in debt) or “essere nei guai fino al collo” / “esserci dentro fino al collo” (in serious trouble, in it up to your neck).
target_language_example: Siamo nei guai fino al collo se non consegniamo oggi.
native_language_example: We’re in trouble up to our necks if we don’t deliver today.

meaning: to the bone; through and through (completely).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is total or deep down. Often follows an adjective or description (e.g., "pigro fino al midollo" = lazy to the core, "marcio fino al midollo" = rotten/corrupt to the core). It can also be used more literally for being soaked or wet all the way through: "bagnato fino al midollo" = soaked to the bone.
target_language_example: Dopo la pioggia ero bagnato fino al midollo.
native_language_example: After the rain I was soaked to the bone.

meaning: 'up to' / 'as far as' (to a specific point, place, or limit).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a limit or endpoint in time, space, or extent. It’s the combination of fino a + la, so it’s followed by a feminine singular noun (la biblioteca, la porta, la Luna, la morte). For masculine singular you use fino al; for plural: fino ai / fino alle. Often translates as “until” with time limits (e.g., fino alla fine = until the end) and “as far as” with places.
target_language_example: Restiamo qui fino alla fine del film.
native_language_example: We’ll stay here until the end of the movie.

meaning: until the end; all the way to the end.
additional_notes: Used to say something continues without stopping up to its final point (an activity, a period of time, a text, etc.). Common with verbs like restare (to stay), leggere (to read), aspettare (to wait), andare/seguire (to go/follow). It can also be used emphatically alone: “Fino alla fine!” = “To the very end!”.
target_language_example: Aspettami e poi camminiamo insieme fino alla fine della strada.
native_language_example: Wait for me, and then we’ll walk together to the end of the street.

meaning: until death; to the death (until the very end).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something continues without stopping until a person dies, or that someone will fight/continue with total commitment no matter what. Common with verbs like "combattere" (to fight), "essere fedele" (to be loyal), "seguire" (to follow). Often has a dramatic/serious tone.
target_language_example: Resterò al tuo fianco fino alla morte.
native_language_example: I will stay by your side until death.

meaning: as far as the station / up to the station.
additional_notes: Used to indicate the endpoint of a movement (walking, running, taking a taxi, etc.). "Fino a" = "up to/as far as"; with a feminine singular noun like "stazione" it becomes "fino alla" (a + la). Often answers the question "Fino a dove?" (As far as where?).
target_language_example: Possiamo andare in autobus fino alla stazione, poi camminiamo.
native_language_example: We can go by bus as far as the station, then we’ll walk.

meaning: Usually intended as **fin da**: “since (the very beginning) / from the start.”
additional_notes: **Fino da** is uncommon and is often a typo or mix-up. The standard expression is **fin da** (short for *fino da* in older/less common usage), used with time expressions to mean “right from then/ever since”: **fin da piccolo/a** (since I was little), **fin da subito** (right away/from the start), **fin dal primo giorno** (since the first day). Don’t confuse with **fino a** = “until/up to” (e.g., *fino a domani* = until tomorrow).
target_language_example: Mi piace cucinare fin da bambino.
native_language_example: I’ve liked cooking since I was a child.

meaning: completely; all the way (to the end).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize doing something fully, without holding back, or continuing until the very end. Common with verbs like "andare" (andare fino in fondo = to go all the way/see it through) or to describe someone as totally something ("malvagi fino in fondo" = evil through and through).
target_language_example: Ormai abbiamo iniziato: dobbiamo andare fino in fondo.
native_language_example: We’ve started now: we have to see it through to the end.

meaning: 'pretend to' (usually in the phrase *fare finta di* + infinitive).
additional_notes: Most often used with **fare**: **fare finta di + verb (infinitive)** = “to pretend to + verb.” Common fixed expression: **fare finta di niente** = “to pretend nothing happened / to act like nothing.” You can also use the imperative: **Fai finta di...** = “Pretend to... / Act as if...”.
target_language_example: Ha fatto finta di non sentire la domanda.
native_language_example: He pretended not to hear the question.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "fare": "fare finta di essere + noun/name" = "to pretend to be + noun/name". It can be used for lying/joking or acting (e.g., in a game or story).
target_language_example: Per entrare, ho fatto finta di essere un cliente.
native_language_example: To get in, I pretended to be a customer.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like conoscere (know), sentire (hear), vedere (see), sapere (know) to say someone intentionally ignores something or acts like they don’t know/notice it. Common forms: (fare) finta di non + infinitive (to pretend not to...), ho/hai fatto finta di non..., fa/faceva/fece finta di non...
target_language_example: Ho fatto finta di non sentire il telefono.
native_language_example: I pretended not to hear the phone.

additional_notes: “Finì” is the passato remoto (simple past) of finire (“to finish”), common in written stories and narratives (especially in central/southern Italy). “Il suo” means “his/her” and agrees with the noun that follows (il suo lavoro, il suo pasto, il suo esame). With feminine nouns you’ll see “la sua” (e.g., finì la sua cena). In everyday speech, many speakers often use the passato prossimo instead: “ha finito il suo …”.
target_language_example: Finì il suo lavoro e poi uscì.
native_language_example: He/She finished his/her work and then went out.

additional_notes: Common literal term for a single snowflake. Usually used with an article: un fiocco di neve (a snowflake), il fiocco di neve (the snowflake). Plural: fiocchi di neve.
target_language_example: Ho visto un fiocco di neve posarsi sulla mia mano.
native_language_example: I saw a snowflake land on my hand.

additional_notes: A simple noun phrase: "fiori" (flowers) + "nel" (= in the, contraction of "in" + "il") + "giardino" (garden). Often used after verbs like "ci sono" (there are), "coltivare" (to grow/cultivate), and "contare" (to count).
target_language_example: Ci sono tanti fiori nel giardino in primavera.
native_language_example: There are many flowers in the garden in spring.

additional_notes: Used when someone writes their own name as a signature on a document or form. In real speech it often appears with different possessives depending on the person: firmare il mio nome (my), il tuo nome (your), il suo nome (his/her), il nostro nome (our), il vostro nome (your plural), il loro nome (their). You can also say simply firmare (to sign) when it’s clear what is being signed.
target_language_example: Per favore, firmi il suo nome qui in fondo.
native_language_example: Please sign your name here at the bottom.

meaning: 'signed the contract' (past participle phrase, used with avere).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone has signed a contract. In conversation it often appears after forms of avere to make the passato prossimo: ho/hai/ha/hanno firmato il contratto. You can add time expressions (e.g., a ottobre, ieri, appena).
target_language_example: Non posso iniziare il lavoro finché non ho firmato il contratto.
native_language_example: I can’t start the job until I’ve signed the contract.

additional_notes: Used to refer to one single piece/sheet of paper (often blank), especially for writing or drawing. Common with verbs like "dammi" (give me) and "scrivere" (to write) and in phrases like "un foglio di carta" (a sheet of paper).
target_language_example: Mi serve un foglio di carta per prendere appunti.
native_language_example: I need a sheet of paper to take notes.

additional_notes: Used for the kitchen appliance that heats food with microwaves. Common with the definite article: "il forno a microonde". You can also shorten it to "il microonde" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Puoi scaldare la zuppa nel forno a microonde?
native_language_example: Can you heat up the soup in the microwave?

meaning: to bake a cake (in the oven).
additional_notes: As written, this isn’t a standard Italian phrase. To express this idea, Italian normally uses a verb + "forno": **cuocere al forno una torta** / **cuocere una torta in forno** (“to bake a cake in the oven”). Another common verb is **infornare** (“to put in the oven”): **Inforno una torta**. In your examples, **al forno** = “in the oven / baked,” and **nel forno** = “in the oven (inside the oven).”
target_language_example: Ho cotto al forno una torta di mele.
native_language_example: I baked an apple cake in the oven.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or a hesitant suggestion about leaving or going somewhere. "Forse" = maybe; "dovrei" is the conditional of "dovere" (should/ought to), making it softer and more polite; "andare" = to go. Often followed by where/why you might go (e.g., "a trovare..." = to visit, "ad aiutare..." = to help).
target_language_example: Forse dovrei andare a casa, è tardi.
native_language_example: Maybe I should go home; it’s late.

additional_notes: Used to make a cautious suggestion. "Forse" means "maybe" and "dovremmo" is the conditional of "dovere" ("to have to / should") for "we".
target_language_example: Forse dovremmo chiamare prima di arrivare.
native_language_example: Maybe we should call before arriving.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or a suggestion politely. It’s made of forse (“maybe”) + dovresti (conditional of dovere, “you should/ought to”). Often followed by an infinitive (andare, chiamare, chiedere) or a pronoun attached to it (chiamarlo = “call him”, chiederglielo = “ask it to him”).
target_language_example: Forse dovresti parlarne con il tuo medico.
native_language_example: Maybe you should talk about it with your doctor.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty while negating something (you think something is probably not true, but you’re not sure). Often softens a negative statement or correction: "Forse non ho capito" = “Maybe I didn’t understand.” You’ll commonly see it before a verb: "Forse non è...", "Forse non serve...".
target_language_example: Forse non posso venire stasera.
native_language_example: Maybe I can’t come tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is lucky to be in a situation or state (often with essere + a place/state like qui/qua, nella squadra, vivo, sopravvissuto). Pattern: (essere) fortunato/a + ad essere + [place/state]. You can intensify with molto, davvero, sicuramente, etc. Agreement: fortunato (masc.), fortunata (fem.), fortunati/fortunate (plural).
target_language_example: Siamo fortunati ad essere qui con voi oggi.
native_language_example: We’re lucky to be here with you today.

meaning: "Come on, guys!" / "Let’s go, guys!" (to encourage or hurry people).
additional_notes: Used as an exclamation to push a group to start, move faster, or keep going. Very common in sports and everyday situations. You can also say just “Forza!” or replace “ragazzi” with “ragazze” (girls) or “ragazzi e ragazze” (everyone).
target_language_example: Forza, ragazzi, dobbiamo uscire subito!
native_language_example: Come on, guys, we have to leave right away!

meaning: "was a" (in reported thoughts/opinions: "I thought that he was a...").
additional_notes: Used after expressions like "pensavo/credevo che..." to introduce what someone thought or believed. "Fosse" is the imperfect subjunctive of "essere" and is common in these "che" clauses in Italian. Change "un" to match gender/number: "fosse una" (feminine), "fossero dei/delle" (plural).
target_language_example: Pensavo che Luca fosse un medico.
native_language_example: I thought Luca was a doctor.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like *pensare/credere/sembrare* when reporting a thought/opinion in the past: *pensavo che fosse una…* (“I thought it was a…”). It often corresponds to English “was a,” but Italian uses the subjunctive in these dependent clauses.
target_language_example: Pensavo che fosse una buona soluzione.
native_language_example: I thought it was a good solution.

meaning: 'that you were dead' / 'you were dead' (subjunctive, in reported thoughts/speech).
additional_notes: Used with the imperfect subjunctive of essere (fossi) + morto after verbs like pensare/credere/dire to report what someone thought/said in the past: "Pensavo che fossi morto". Often translated as "(that) you were dead" in English. It can also be used exaggeratingly to mean "I thought something terrible happened to you" when someone hasn’t been in touch.
target_language_example: Non rispondevi da giorni: pensavo che fossi morto!
native_language_example: You hadn’t replied for days—I thought you were dead!

additional_notes: Passive form used to say when/where/by whom a photo was taken. It’s built with essere + past participle (scattata agrees with foto, feminine singular). You can add place/time (a Roma, tre anni fa) or the agent with da (da Tom).
target_language_example: Questa foto è stata scattata durante il viaggio in Italia.
native_language_example: This photo was taken during the trip to Italy.

meaning: "between us" / "among us"; also "between you and me" (keep it secret).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that concerns the people in a group ("among us") or the relationship between two people ("between us"). In the pattern "Che resti/rimanga fra noi", it means “let’s keep this between us” (don’t tell others). Often interchangeable with "tra noi".
target_language_example: Che resti fra noi: domani do le dimissioni.
native_language_example: Keep it between us: tomorrow I’m resigning.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen after a short time (similar to “a moment later” / “shortly”). Often interchangeable with “tra poco”. You can also use it for near-future plans: “Fra poco parto” = “I’m leaving soon.”
target_language_example: Arrivo fra poco, aspettami!
native_language_example: I’ll be there in a little while, wait for me!

additional_notes: Used with verbs like studiare/imparare to say you do French (the language) every day. Word order is typically: verb + language + frequency (e.g., "studio francese ogni giorno").
target_language_example: Studio francese ogni giorno per migliorare.
native_language_example: I study French every day to improve.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that some phrases are in the Berber (Amazigh) language. Italian commonly uses "in" + language to say what language something is written/spoken in: "frasi in italiano", "una parola in inglese". "Berbero" is the adjective/noun meaning "Berber".
target_language_example: Puoi scrivermi alcune frasi in berbero?
native_language_example: Can you write me a few phrases in Berber?

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s siblings. You’ll often hear it with possessives (i miei/tuoi/suoi fratelli e sorelle) or in questions like “Quanti fratelli e sorelle hai/ha?” In everyday Italian, people may also say “fratelli” to mean siblings in general, but “fratelli e sorelle” is explicit about both genders.
target_language_example: Ho due fratelli e una sorella.
native_language_example: I have two brothers and a sister.

additional_notes: Used in questions to ask if someone has any siblings or how many. It literally lists both genders (fratelli = brothers, sorelle = sisters), similar to English “brothers or sisters.” In everyday Italian you may also hear the shorter word “fratelli” used to mean “siblings” in general when the group is mixed.
target_language_example: Hai fratelli o sorelle?
native_language_example: Do you have any brothers or sisters?

additional_notes: Used to say that a man/boy has a twin who is also male. It commonly follows “avere” (to have): “ha un fratello gemello”. For a female twin, use “sorella gemella”; as an adjective it agrees in gender/number (gemello/gemella/gemelli/gemelle).
target_language_example: Non l'ho riconosciuto: era il suo fratello gemello.
native_language_example: I didn’t recognize him: it was his twin brother.

additional_notes: Used to specify the brother who is older (as opposed to a younger brother). It’s common with possessives (mio/tuo/suo) and in comparisons between siblings (identico/diverso dal suo fratello maggiore).
target_language_example: Mio fratello maggiore abita a Milano.
native_language_example: My older brother lives in Milan.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male sibling who is younger than you (or younger than someone else mentioned). Often appears with a possessive: "mio/tuo/suo fratello minore". You can also say "fratellino" as a more affectionate way to say "little/younger brother".
target_language_example: Il mio fratello minore va ancora a scuola.
native_language_example: My younger brother still goes to school.

meaning: (vulgar) “to not give a fuck”; to not care at all.
additional_notes: Very vulgar/strong. Usually used in the negative: “non me ne frega un cazzo” = “I don’t give a fuck.” Often appears with pronouns that show *what* you don’t care about: **non me ne frega un cazzo (di X)** (“I don’t give a fuck about X”), **non te ne frega un cazzo** (“you don’t give a fuck”), **non gliene frega un cazzo** (“he/she doesn’t give a fuck about it/them”). Avoid in polite situations; use neutral alternatives like “non mi importa” or “non me ne frega” (still informal).
target_language_example: A lui non gliene frega un cazzo delle conseguenze.
native_language_example: He doesn’t give a fuck about the consequences.

additional_notes: Used with a person as the subject to say they attend a school regularly. Often followed by the type of school (e.g., scuola elementare = elementary school) or an adjective (scuola pubblica = public school). You can ask where someone attends with: “Dove frequenta la scuola?”
target_language_example: Mia sorella frequenta la scuola vicino a casa.
native_language_example: My sister goes to the school near our house.

additional_notes: More commonly you’ll see the plural "frutti di mare" meaning "seafood" (often mixed seafood, especially shellfish like mussels, clams, shrimp). Used a lot on menus: "spaghetti ai frutti di mare". The singular "frutto di mare" can refer to one item/piece, but in everyday use Italians usually say the plural when talking about seafood in general.
target_language_example: Vorrei gli spaghetti ai frutti di mare, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like spaghetti with seafood, please.

additional_notes: Past tense of "essere in grado di" (to be able to). "Fu" is the passato remoto of "essere" (common in narratives and in some regions instead of "è stato"), and it’s followed by an infinitive: "fu in grado di + [verb]". It often emphasizes having the ability or managing to do something; similar alternatives include "poté" or "riuscì a" (more like "managed to").
target_language_example: Non fu in grado di finire il lavoro in tempo.
native_language_example: He/She wasn’t able to finish the work on time.

meaning: “was killed by a …” (male subject, completed action).
additional_notes: Passive in the passato remoto: fu (past of essere) + ucciso (past participle). Used often in stories, history, or news to describe a completed event. The agent is introduced by da (“by”). Agreement changes with the subject: fu uccisa (female), furono uccisi/e (plural). The article after un changes as needed: da uno, da una, da un’ (e.g., da un uomo; da una tigre; da un’auto).
target_language_example: Il turista fu ucciso da un leone.
native_language_example: The tourist was killed by a lion.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato remoto) of "essere" in the 3rd person singular: "fu" = "was" (often found in written stories, narration, or formal contexts). Common pattern: [infinitive/action] + "fu un errore" ("To do X was a mistake"), e.g., "Venire qui fu un errore".
target_language_example: Dirglielo fu un errore.
native_language_example: Telling him/her was a mistake.

additional_notes: Used to describe a situation, process, or person/thing that is no longer being managed or contained (often getting worse or becoming chaotic). Common with verbs like "essere" (è fuori controllo) and "andare" (andare fuori controllo = to get/go out of control).
target_language_example: La situazione è fuori controllo e dobbiamo chiamare la polizia.
native_language_example: The situation is out of control and we need to call the police.

additional_notes: Used mainly with essere (e.g., è/sono fuori moda) to say that clothes, styles, or trends are no longer fashionable. Opposite: alla moda (“fashionable”). You can intensify it with words like completamente (“completely”) or già (“already”).
target_language_example: Queste scarpe sono fuori moda, ma a me piacciono lo stesso.
native_language_example: These shoes are out of fashion, but I still like them.

meaning: out of service; not working (temporarily unavailable).
additional_notes: Used for people (off duty) and for machines/services (down, broken, or temporarily unavailable). Common on signs or in customer-service contexts: "È fuori servizio" = it’s not operating right now.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, l’ascensore è fuori servizio.
native_language_example: Sorry, the elevator is out of service.

meaning: way off; on the wrong track (about an idea/guess).
additional_notes: Used to say someone’s assumption, opinion, or interpretation is incorrect—often strongly (e.g., "completely/decisamente/totale"). Common with "essere" ("sei/è/siete fuori strada"). Literally it can mean "off the road" too, but in these examples it’s figurative: "wrong" about something.
target_language_example: Se pensi che io sia arrabbiato, sei fuori strada.
native_language_example: If you think I’m angry, you’re way off.

meaning: out of the house; away from home.
additional_notes: Used to say you’re not at home (e.g., you’re at work, school, traveling) or that something happens outside the home. Often used with verbs like essere (to be) or mangiare (to eat): “Sono fuori casa” = “I’m out/away from home”; “mangiare fuori casa” = “to eat out.”
target_language_example: Stasera sono fuori casa, ci sentiamo domani.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m away from home, we’ll talk tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to indicate being outside a place/area (physical movement or position): "Uscite fuori da lì" = "Get out of there." It’s also used more figuratively to mean "excluded/kept out of" a situation: "Lasciatela fuori da questo" = "Leave her out of this."
target_language_example: Per favore, tienimi fuori da questa discussione.
native_language_example: Please keep me out of this discussion.

meaning: out of here; outside (of) this place.
additional_notes: Used to say you want someone/something removed from the current place, often as an order or request. "Qua" is a more conversational form of "qui"; a more neutral alternative is "fuori di qui" or "fuori da qui".
target_language_example: Per favore, lasci la bici fuori da qua.
native_language_example: Please, leave the bike out of here.

meaning: 'out of here' / 'outside from here' (away from this place).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something should be moved or taken to the outside or away from the current place. Very common with verbs like portare (to take/bring), andare (to go), uscire (to go out).
target_language_example: Per favore, portami fuori da qui.
native_language_example: Please, get me out of here.

meaning: “Get the fuck out!” / “Get out of here!” (very vulgar).
additional_notes: A very aggressive, obscene way to tell someone to leave immediately. Often used on its own as a shouted command (“Fuori dai coglioni!”) or with a verb like andare (“Andate fuori dai coglioni!”). Not appropriate in polite conversation; it can easily start a fight.
target_language_example: Fuori dai coglioni, subito!
native_language_example: Get the fuck out, now!

meaning: out of trouble; away from problems.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like stare/restare/tenere/tirare (fuori) dai guai: "stai/resta fuori dai guai" = "stay out of trouble"; "tirare (qualcuno) fuori dai guai" = "get (someone) out of trouble"; "tenere (qualcuno) fuori dai guai" = "keep (someone) out of trouble". "Guai" is plural and means trouble/problems.
target_language_example: Se mi aiuti, riuscirò a restare fuori dai guai.
native_language_example: If you help me, I’ll manage to stay out of trouble.

meaning: “out of the way” / “get out of here!” (often said rudely).
additional_notes: Used as an order to move away and stop being in the way. It can be a strong/impolite way to tell someone to leave or to stay where they won’t bother others. Often used alone as an exclamation (“Fuori dai piedi!”) or with clarifiers like “via da qui!” (“away from here!”).
target_language_example: Per favore, state fuori dai piedi mentre pulisco.
native_language_example: Please, stay out of the way while I clean.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is outside a place or moving out from inside it. It’s the combination of **fuori** + **da** + **il** (so **fuori dal** = **fuori da + il**). Common with places/areas: *fuori dal treno* (out of the train), *fuori dal paese* (outside the town). Also appears with other articles: *fuori dallo* (da + lo), *fuori dalla* (da + la), *fuori dai* (da + i), *fuori dalle* (da + le).
target_language_example: Siamo fuori dal centro adesso.
native_language_example: We’re outside the city center now.

additional_notes: Used to indicate movement from inside to outside or being/ending up outside a place or group. Often follows verbs like tirare (pull), cacciare (kick out), chiudersi (lock oneself out). Before a feminine singular noun you’ll see dalla = di + la (e.g., dalla tasca, dalla tenda); with masculine singular: fuori dal (dal = di + il).
target_language_example: Ho preso il portafoglio fuori dalla borsa.
native_language_example: I took the wallet out of the bag.

meaning: out of the window; outside the window.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like mettere la testa (to stick your head out), guardare (to look), or lanciare/buttare (to throw) to say something is outside the window or goes through/out of it. Often implies movement from inside to outside.
target_language_example: Non sporgerti troppo fuori dalla finestra.
native_language_example: Don’t lean out too far out of the window.

additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns (fuori dalla = fuori da + la). It can mean physically outside a place/area (fuori dalla Cornovaglia, fuori dalla cantina) or figuratively excluded/kept away from something (fuori dalla tua catena di crimini, fuori dalla mia vita). With commands it often means “stay out of …” (Stai fuori dalla cucina).
target_language_example: Tienimi fuori dalla discussione, per favore.
native_language_example: Keep me out of the discussion, please.

meaning: out (through) the window; outside the window.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like guardare (“to look”) or mettere/mise la testa (“to put/stick your head”) to say you’re looking or reaching to the outside from inside a room. Often means looking out from indoors to see what’s happening outside.
target_language_example: C'è molta pioggia fuori dalla finestra.
native_language_example: There’s a lot of rain outside the window.

meaning: “outside my …” / “out of my …” (followed by a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is outside your space, property, area, authority, or ability/reach. It’s commonly followed by a noun like cucina (kitchen), proprietà (property), portata (reach), giurisdizione (jurisdiction). The possessive changes with the noun: fuori dal mio … (masc. sing.), fuori dai miei … (masc. plural), fuori dalle mie … (fem. plural). Often used as an order: “Stai/Stia fuori dalla mia …” = “Stay out of my …”.
target_language_example: Tieni le mani fuori dalla mia borsa.
native_language_example: Keep your hands out of my bag.

additional_notes: Used to say someone should leave your room (“Get out of my room!”) or to describe being locked out (“I locked myself out of my room”). With the verb of motion it often implies “get out/leave”: Vattene fuori dalla mia camera! The verb changes with formality and number: vattene/andatevene (informal), se ne vada (formal).
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato le chiavi e mi sono chiuso fuori dalla mia camera.
native_language_example: I forgot my keys and I locked myself out of my room.

additional_notes: Used with a place (often + a noun like casa) to show movement from inside to outside: "fuori di casa" = "out of the house." It can also appear in fixed expressions like "fuori di sé" (very upset, 'beside oneself') and in commands like "Fuori di qua!" ('Get out of here!'). In everyday Italian you’ll often hear "fuori da" instead of "fuori di" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Sono uscito fuori di casa senza ombrello.
native_language_example: I went out of the house without an umbrella.

additional_notes: Used to say someone should leave this place, often as a command. It can be said alone ("Fuori di qui!") or with an implied verb like "vai" (go) or "portare" (take someone out): "Ti porto fuori di qui" = "I’ll get you out of here." Strong in tone depending on context.
target_language_example: Andiamo fuori di qui, per favore.
native_language_example: Let’s get out of here, please.

meaning: crazy; out of your mind (also: to drive someone crazy).
additional_notes: Commonly used in two ways: (1) essere fuori di testa = to be crazy/out of your mind; (2) andare/fare andare fuori di testa = to go crazy / to drive someone crazy (often because something is very annoying or stressful). In casual speech it can also mean “wild” or “out of control,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Quel rumore mi fa andare fuori di testa.
native_language_example: That noise drives me crazy.

meaning: 'out the trash' (as in “take the trash out”).
additional_notes: Used with the verb portare/mettere: “portare fuori la spazzatura” = to take the trash out (to the bins/outside). Often shortened in speech to “Porta fuori la spazzatura!”
target_language_example: Puoi portare fuori la spazzatura, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you take out the trash, please?

additional_notes: Used to specify the leg on the right side of the body. Often appears with articles and possessives (e.g., "la gamba destra", "la mia gamba destra"). In sports/medical contexts it can also refer to the right leg as the injured/impacted side.
target_language_example: Mi fa male la gamba destra.
native_language_example: My right leg hurts.

additional_notes: Used to specify the left leg (vs. gamba destra). Often appears with body-related verbs and phrases like farsi male a (to hurt), mettersi del ghiaccio su (to put ice on), or in medical contexts (rott[a]=broken, amputata=amputated).
target_language_example: Ho dolore alla gamba sinistra da ieri.
native_language_example: I’ve had pain in my left leg since yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with the verb essere ("to be") to describe a female cat: *La/questa/vostra gatta è...* ("The/this/your cat is..."). *Gatta* is specifically a female cat (male cat = *gatto*). The adjective that follows usually agrees in gender/number: *La gatta è grassa / adorabile / incinta*.
target_language_example: La gatta è stanca oggi.
native_language_example: The (female) cat is tired today.

additional_notes: Used with a plural noun (gatti = cats) + the verb “sono” (they are). Often followed by an adjective or a noun phrase: “I gatti sono diversi” (Cats are different), “I miei gatti sono i miei bambini” (My cats are my babies). In Italian, the subject is often included (I gatti sono...), but it can be omitted if it’s clear from context.
target_language_example: I gatti sono molto curiosi.
native_language_example: Cats are very curious.

additional_notes: Used to describe a cat with an adjective or other description. "È" is the 3rd-person singular of "essere" (to be) and is pronounced like "eh". Common patterns: "Il/Questo gatto è + aggettivo" (Il gatto è grasso. / Questo gatto è adorabile.).
target_language_example: Il gatto è molto affettuoso.
native_language_example: The cat is very affectionate.

additional_notes: Used when ordering or talking about the chocolate flavor of gelato. In Italian, "gelato" is Italian-style ice cream; "al" = "a" + "il" and here means "with/of" a flavor ("gelato al pistacchio", "al limone", etc.).
target_language_example: Per favore, vorrei un gelato al cioccolato.
native_language_example: Please, I’d like a chocolate gelato.

additional_notes: Used to state something about parents. Often preceded by an article or possessive: "I genitori sono..." (The parents are...), "I tuoi genitori sono..." (Your parents are...). "Genitori" is plural; "sono" is the 3rd person plural of "essere" (to be).
target_language_example: I miei genitori sono a casa.
native_language_example: My parents are at home.

additional_notes: Used with a person or pronoun after "con" (e.g., con lui/lei, con tutti) to describe treating someone politely or nicely. It’s common in requests or advice, often in the formal imperative: "Sia gentile con..." = "Please be kind to..."
target_language_example: Per favore, sii gentile con i nuovi colleghi.
native_language_example: Please be kind to the new coworkers.

additional_notes: Used to say someone treats you kindly. You can use it with different tenses (e.g., è stato/era/è sempre stato gentile con me) or as a polite request: "Sia gentile con me" (“Please be kind to me”). "Gentile" can also mean “polite/courteous” depending on context.
target_language_example: Per favore, sii gentile con me.
native_language_example: Please be kind to me.

meaning: "That's very kind of you" / "It's kind of you (to...)" (formal/polite).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone politely or comment on their kindness, often followed by an infinitive: "È gentile da parte sua + fare qualcosa" (e.g., aiutarmi, darmi un passaggio). "Sua" is the formal "your" (to one person). With "da parte sua" you’re referring to the other person’s action/gesture; you can intensify it with "molto".
target_language_example: È molto gentile da parte sua aspettarmi.
native_language_example: It's very kind of you to wait for me.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone or comment positively on their action. Very common with **È (molto) gentile da parte tua + infinitive** (e.g., *aiutarmi*, *dirmelo*) or alone: *È molto gentile da parte tua.* For formal situations, you can say **gentile da parte Sua**.
target_language_example: È davvero gentile da parte tua venire a prendermi alla stazione.
native_language_example: It’s really kind of you to come pick me up at the station.

additional_notes: A polite way to thank or acknowledge someone’s kindness, addressing more than one person (voi) or using formal “you.” Often used with è / è stato / è stato molto, and can be followed by an infinitive: “È stato gentile da parte vostra aiutarmi / di prestarmi…”.
target_language_example: È stato davvero gentile da parte vostra venire fin qui.
native_language_example: It was really kind of you to come all the way here.

meaning: To throw in the towel; to give up.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression (from boxing) used when someone stops trying or surrenders because something is too difficult or they feel they can’t continue. Often used after repeated attempts or setbacks. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Dopo tre tentativi andati male, ho deciso di gettare la spugna.
native_language_example: After three failed attempts, I decided to throw in the towel.

additional_notes: Common idiom meaning to stop trying because you feel you can’t continue or succeed. It’s often used with avere in the passato prossimo: “ho/hai/ha/hanno gettato la spugna”. More generally you may see it in the infinitive form: “gettare la spugna”.
target_language_example: Dopo tre ore a provarci, ho gettato la spugna.
native_language_example: After three hours of trying, I gave up.

additional_notes: Used with the verb giocare + a + sport/game to say someone plays a sport or plays a game: "Gioca a calcio" (He plays soccer), "Gioca a World of Warcraft" (He plays World of Warcraft). For ball sports you’ll often see it with the sport name (calcio, baseball, pallacanestro). You can also specify a place/time: "Dove gioca a…?" (Where does he/she play…?), "gioca a … ogni giorno" (plays … every day).
target_language_example: Mia sorella gioca a tennis il sabato.
native_language_example: My sister plays tennis on Saturdays.

additional_notes: From the verb "giocare" (to play) + "a" + the sport. "Gioca" is the present tense for "lui/lei" (he/she) and also the polite command "Play!" (Lei form) in some contexts. In Italian, you say "giocare a" + sport: "gioca a calcio", "gioca a rugby", etc.
target_language_example: Mio fratello gioca a calcio il sabato.
native_language_example: My brother plays soccer on Saturdays.

additional_notes: "Giocare a" is used for sports and games (gioca a tennis, gioca a calcio, gioca a carte). "Gioca" is the present tense form (he/she plays). You can add an adverb to say how well: "gioca bene/molto bene".
target_language_example: Mio padre gioca a golf una volta alla settimana.
native_language_example: My dad plays golf once a week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a regular habit. The verb is *giocare a* + a sport (e.g., *gioca a tennis*). *Ogni* means “every” and is followed by a time expression, such as *ogni fine settimana* (“every weekend”) or *ogni weekend* (common borrowing).
target_language_example: Mio padre gioca a golf ogni domenica.
native_language_example: My dad plays golf every Sunday.

additional_notes: "Gioca" is the 3rd person singular present of "giocare" (to play). Use it with "a" + a sport (gioca a tennis / a calcio / a basket). To ask a question, you can use rising intonation ("Gioca a tennis?") or add the subject ("Tom gioca a tennis?").
target_language_example: Mia sorella gioca a tennis il sabato mattina.
native_language_example: My sister plays tennis on Saturday morning.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "giocare" + "a" + a sport or game to say what someone is playing. "giocando" is the gerund (like English “playing”), often used with "stare" (e.g., "sto/stavo") to mean “I am/was playing.”
target_language_example: Stiamo giocando a calcio al parco.
native_language_example: We’re playing soccer at the park.

additional_notes: "Giocando" is the gerund of "giocare" (to play), often used with "stare" to form the present/progressive tense ("sto/stai/sta/stiamo/state/stanno + giocando" = "I am/you are/he is/we are/you are/they are playing"). "A pallacanestro" means "basketball" after the verb "giocare" (giocare a + sport).
target_language_example: Stiamo giocando a pallacanestro al parco.
native_language_example: We’re playing basketball at the park.

additional_notes: "Giocando" is the gerund (like English “playing”), used with forms of *stare* to talk about something happening right now or in progress: *sto/stai/sta/stiamo/stanno giocando a tennis* (I am/you are/he/she is/we are/they are playing tennis). You can also use it with *stavo/stavi/stava...* for an action that was in progress in the past.
target_language_example: Stiamo giocando a tennis oggi pomeriggio.
native_language_example: We’re playing tennis this afternoon.

additional_notes: Used with games and sports: giocare a calcio, giocare a tennis, giocare a biliardo, giocare a Scarabeo. It often appears with another verb: andare a giocare a… (go play…), imparare/insegnare a giocare a… (learn/teach to play…).
target_language_example: Vuoi giocare a carte stasera?
native_language_example: Do you want to play cards tonight?

additional_notes: Used with most sports/games in Italian: giocare a + sport/game (giocare a calcio, giocare a tennis). It’s often used to talk about what you like doing (Ti piace…?/Le piace…?) or to suggest an activity (Che ne dici di…?).
target_language_example: Domani giochiamo a badminton al parco.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re playing badminton at the park.

additional_notes: Used with sports that take the preposition "a" in Italian (giocare a + sport). You can suggest it with "Che ne dici di..." (to one person) or "Che ne dite di..." (to more than one person). It also appears after verbs like "guardare" and "vedere" to mean "watch/see someone play baseball" (e.g., "Li abbiamo guardati giocare a baseball").
target_language_example: Domani pomeriggio vuoi giocare a baseball con noi?
native_language_example: Tomorrow afternoon do you want to play baseball with us?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "giocare" + "a" + the sport (giocare a calcio, giocare a tennis). You can say "Mi piace giocare a basket" (I like playing basketball) and ask about ability with "essere bravo/brava a giocare a basket" (to be good at playing basketball).
target_language_example: Nel weekend giochiamo a basket al parco.
native_language_example: On the weekend we play basketball at the park.
