additional_notes: Used with "giocare a" + sport (e.g., giocare a tennis, giocare a basket). In Italian, "calcio" refers to soccer (football).
target_language_example: Il sabato pomeriggio gioco a calcio con i miei amici.
native_language_example: On Saturday afternoon I play soccer with my friends.

additional_notes: Used for playing card games in general (not a specific game): Gioco a carte / Mi piace giocare a carte. With people: giocare a carte con qualcuno (“to play cards with someone”).
target_language_example: Dopo cena ci piace giocare a carte con gli amici.
native_language_example: After dinner we like to play cards with friends.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "giocare" + "a" + a sport/game (giocare a calcio, giocare a tennis). You can add who you play with using "con" (giocare a golf con Maria).
target_language_example: Domani mattina giochiamo a golf con alcuni amici.
native_language_example: Tomorrow morning we’re playing golf with some friends.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "giocare" + "a" + a game (giocare a calcio, giocare a carte, giocare a mahjong). Common in questions about liking or knowing how to play: "Ti piace giocare a…?" / "Sai giocare a…?".
target_language_example: Sai giocare a mahjong o vuoi che ti spieghi le regole?
native_language_example: Do you know how to play mahjong, or do you want me to explain the rules?

giocare a mahjong la scorsa estate

target_language_multi_word_term: giocare a mahjong la scorsa estate
additional_notes: Compositional phrase: giocare a + (game) = “to play (a game)”; la scorsa estate = “last summer” (a past-time expression). Often used with past tenses (e.g., hai giocato…?/sei stata in grado di giocare…?).
target_language_example: Ho iniziato a giocare a mahjong la scorsa estate con i miei amici.
native_language_example: I started playing mahjong last summer with my friends.

additional_notes: Used with sports/games: giocare a + sport (giocare a calcio, giocare a tennis, giocare a pallacanestro). With "piacere": "Mi piace giocare a pallacanestro" = "I like playing basketball". After verbs like "vedere" you can use the infinitive: "Ho visto Tom giocare a pallacanestro" = "I saw Tom play basketball".
target_language_example: Il sabato pomeriggio giochiamo a pallacanestro al parco.
native_language_example: On Saturday afternoon we play basketball at the park.

additional_notes: Use "giocare a" + a sport. "Pallavolo" means volleyball. You can invite someone with "Vieni a giocare a pallavolo (con noi)" (Come play volleyball (with us)).
target_language_example: Domani pomeriggio giochiamo a pallavolo al parco.
native_language_example: Tomorrow afternoon we’re playing volleyball at the park.

additional_notes: Used with sports in Italian: "giocare a + sport" (giocare a calcio, a tennis, a pallavolo). In questions you may see it with "o" to offer a choice: "giocare a pallavolo o a basket?" (play volleyball or basketball?).
target_language_example: Nel weekend giochiamo a pallavolo al parco.
native_language_example: On the weekend we play volleyball at the park.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition “a” after giocare to talk about playing a game/sport: “giocare a + game” (giocare a calcio, giocare a tennis, giocare a scacchi). Often appears with verbs like sapere (“Sai giocare a scacchi?”), volere (“Vuoi giocare a scacchi?”), piacere (“Mi piace giocare a scacchi”), or insegnare (“insegnare a giocare a scacchi”).
target_language_example: La domenica mattina mi piace giocare a scacchi con mio nonno.
native_language_example: On Sunday morning I like to play chess with my grandfather.

additional_notes: "Giocare a" is used with sports and games (giocare a calcio, giocare a carte). With sports you usually don’t use an article: giocare a tennis (not *giocare il tennis*). You can also say "giocare a tennis" to mean playing tennis in general (as a hobby) or at a specific time, depending on context.
target_language_example: Vuoi giocare a tennis con me domani?
native_language_example: Do you want to play tennis with me tomorrow?

additional_notes: Use "giocare a" + sport (giocare a tennis, a calcio, a golf). Add "con" + person to say who you’re playing with: "giocare a tennis con Tom". You can also use it in questions or polite requests: "Vuoi giocare a tennis con me?" / "Potresti giocare a tennis con me?"
target_language_example: Vuoi giocare a tennis con me domani?
native_language_example: Do you want to play tennis with me tomorrow?

additional_notes: "Lei" is the formal/polite third-person pronoun used for “you” (like “with you, ma’am/sir”). In these sentences, "con lei" can mean either “with her” (a woman) or “with you” in a formal register; the intended meaning depends on context and capitalization in writing (Lei = formal you).
target_language_example: Domani vuoi giocare a tennis con lei?
native_language_example: Do you want to play tennis with her/with you (formal) tomorrow?

additional_notes: Uses the verb pattern "giocare a" + sport (giocare a tennis = to play tennis). "Ogni domenica" means "every Sunday" and can be moved around in the sentence (e.g., "Ogni domenica gioco a tennis"). Often appears in polite invitations or suggestions with "Le piacerebbe...?" / "Vorrebbe...?" (formal) or "Ti piacerebbe...?" / "Vorresti...?" (informal).
target_language_example: Vorresti giocare a tennis ogni domenica con noi?
native_language_example: Would you like to play tennis every Sunday with us?

additional_notes: Used to talk about playing together or interacting playfully with a person, animal, or object. It’s followed by the person/thing you play with (giocare con + noun/pronoun). For playing a specific game/sport, Italian often uses "giocare a" (e.g., giocare a calcio).
target_language_example: Vuoi giocare con me dopo scuola?
native_language_example: Do you want to play with me after school?

meaning: to play with words; to be tricky/clever with wording (wordplay).
additional_notes: Used both positively (being witty, making puns) and negatively (being evasive, twisting someone’s words). Very common in the imperative to tell someone to stop: "Smettila/Smettetela di giocare con le parole!" (= Stop playing games with words!).
target_language_example: Non giocare con le parole: dimmi la verità.
native_language_example: Don’t play with words—tell me the truth.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "giocare" with the auxiliary "avere" (e.g., "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno giocato"). It’s followed by "a" before the name of a game or sport: "giocato a Minecraft", "giocato a minigolf". In questions it often appears as "Hai giocato a... ?" / "Avete giocato a... ?".
target_language_example: Hai mai giocato a scacchi?
native_language_example: Have you ever played chess?

additional_notes: Past participle of "giocare" used with "avere" to form the past tense: "ho/abbiamo/hanno giocato" + "a basket" (basketball). Often used with a time expression (e.g., "lunedì", "lo scorso fine settimana").
target_language_example: Ieri ho giocato a basket con mio fratello.
native_language_example: Yesterday I played basketball with my brother.

additional_notes: Past tense with avere: "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno giocato a calcio" = "I/you/he... played soccer." Used to talk about having played soccer at a specific time (often with a time word like "ieri").
target_language_example: Abbiamo giocato a calcio dopo scuola.
native_language_example: We played soccer after school.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary 'avere' to form past tenses: e.g., passato prossimo 'ho/ha/abbiamo giocato a golf' = 'I/he/she/we played golf' (or 'have played golf'). In questions, 'mai' means 'ever' ('Ha mai giocato a golf?' = 'Have you ever played golf?'); with 'non ... mai' it means 'never'.
target_language_example: Hai mai giocato a golf con i tuoi colleghi?
native_language_example: Have you ever played golf with your colleagues?

additional_notes: Used in the passato prossimo with the auxiliary avere (e.g., ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno giocato a tennis). Italian commonly uses “giocare a + sport” (giocare a calcio, giocare a tennis) to say you play a sport.
target_language_example: Ieri ho giocato a tennis con un amico.
native_language_example: Yesterday I played tennis with a friend.

additional_notes: Uses the past tense (passato prossimo) of giocare: (io) ho giocato, (tu) hai giocato, (voi) avete giocato. Giocare takes the auxiliary avere in the passato prossimo. Often you’ll see it with a subject pronoun or an auxiliary verb before it (e.g., ho/hai/avete giocato a tennis ieri).
target_language_example: Ho giocato a tennis ieri pomeriggio.
native_language_example: I played tennis yesterday afternoon.

additional_notes: Used with the verb essere (“to be”) to say someone is/was a baseball player: "È un giocatore di baseball." You can add adjectives like famoso (famous) or migliore (best) before "giocatore" to describe them.
target_language_example: Mio fratello è un giocatore di baseball e si allena ogni giorno.
native_language_example: My brother is a baseball player and he trains every day.

meaning: “(he/she) used to play” / “(he/she) was playing” (a game or sport).
additional_notes: Imperfetto of *giocare a* (“to play” a sport/game). Use it to talk about a habitual action in the past (“used to play”) or an ongoing action in the past (“was playing”). It’s followed by the name of a sport/game: *giocava a tennis*, *giocava a scacchi*.
target_language_example: Da bambino, giocava a calcio tutti i pomeriggi.
native_language_example: As a child, he used to play soccer every afternoon.

meaning: “(he/she) used to play soccer” / “(he/she) was playing soccer”.
additional_notes: Imperfetto of “giocare a calcio” (to play soccer/football). Use it for a repeated/habitual action in the past (“used to play”) or for an ongoing background action (“was playing”) when something else happened. You can add who they played with using “con” (con le sue amiche) and combine sports with “e” (a calcio e a basket).
target_language_example: Da bambino, mio padre giocava a calcio ogni sabato.
native_language_example: As a child, my dad used to play soccer every Saturday.

meaning: “I used to play tennis” / “I was playing tennis.”
additional_notes: "Giocavo" is the imperfetto (imperfect past) of "giocare" and describes a past habit or an ongoing background action. Use it for repeated actions in the past (often with time phrases like "la domenica") or for something that was in progress (often contrasted with a one-time event in the passato prossimo).
target_language_example: Da bambino giocavo a tennis ogni estate.
native_language_example: As a child, I used to play tennis every summer.

additional_notes: "Giocherà" is the 3rd person singular future of "giocare" (to play): he/she will play. Use it to talk about future plans or predictions. For questions, you can add a subject (e.g., "Tom giocherà a tennis?") or just ask "Chi giocherà a tennis?" (Who will play tennis?). For negatives: "Non giocherà a tennis."
target_language_example: Marco giocherà a tennis sabato mattina.
native_language_example: Marco will play tennis on Saturday morning.

additional_notes: "Giochiamo" is the present tense "we" form of giocare (to play). "Spesso" means "often" and usually comes after the verb. "A tennis" is used with the verb giocare to say what sport you play (giocare a + sport). You can add "insieme/assieme" to mean "together" and "noi" to emphasize "we."
target_language_example: Giochiamo spesso a tennis il sabato mattina.
native_language_example: We often play tennis on Saturday morning.

additional_notes: Used to say you play the sport of tennis. It’s formed with the verb giocare (to play) + a + the sport. Note the conjugation: (io) gioco, (tu) giochi, (lui/lei) gioca, (noi) giochiamo, (voi) giocate, (loro) giocano. You often add frequency words like ogni domenica (every Sunday), a volte (sometimes), tutti i giorni (every day), di tanto in tanto / una volta ogni tanto (once in a while).
target_language_example: Non posso uscire stasera: gioco a tennis.
native_language_example: I can’t go out tonight: I’m playing tennis.

additional_notes: Uses the verb pattern **giocare a + sport** (“to play” a sport): *gioco a tennis, giochi a calcio*, etc. **Spesso** means “often” and commonly goes right after the verb (*gioco spesso...*). The subject pronoun **io** is optional in Italian (*[Io] gioco spesso a tennis*).
target_language_example: Gioco spesso a tennis con i miei amici.
native_language_example: I often play tennis with my friends.

meaning: to make fun of me (someone); to mock me (someone).
additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb "prendersi" + "gioco" + "di" + person. It means you’re being laughed at or not taken seriously. Common forms: "Ti stai prendendo gioco di me?" (Are you kidding/mocking me?), "Smettila di prenderti gioco di me" (Stop making fun of me).
target_language_example: Non prenderti gioco di me: sto parlando sul serio.
native_language_example: Don’t make fun of me: I’m being serious.

additional_notes: Used when talking about a joke or clever effect based on similar sounds or double meanings in words. Also used generally for “wordplay” in language, titles, or advertising.
target_language_example: Il titolo è un gioco di parole: fa ridere e fa pensare.
native_language_example: The title is a pun: it makes you laugh and think.

additional_notes: Used to say how many days in the past something happened. It follows a number (e.g., due/cinque/otto giorni fa) or a question word (Quanti giorni fa...?). You can also use it with expressions like meno di (meno di due giorni fa = less than two days ago).
target_language_example: Ci siamo visti tre giorni fa.
native_language_example: We saw each other three days ago.

meaning: day and night; all the time (continuously).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happens continuously or without stopping. Often follows verbs like "studiare" (to study), "lavorare" (to work), "stare di guardia" (to stand guard), or "pensare" (to think). It can be literal (during both day and night) or more general (“nonstop”).
target_language_example: Da quando è nato il bambino, siamo svegli giorno e notte.
native_language_example: Since the baby was born, we’re awake day and night.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause that explains what happens on that day. Often follows a noun like "il giorno" or a specific day/event: "il giorno in cui...", "il venerdì è il giorno in cui...". It works like English "the day when / the day on which".
target_language_example: Lunedì è il giorno in cui ho la lezione di italiano.
native_language_example: Monday is the day when I have my Italian class.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to mean “too young to do something”: "(troppo) giovane per + infinitive" (e.g., "troppo giovane per andare in pensione"). It can also be used with a noun phrase like "per la sua età" to mean “young for his/her age.” Often appears with "sembrare" (to seem) or "essere" (to be).
target_language_example: È troppo giovane per guidare, ma sembra giovane per la sua età.
native_language_example: He’s too young to drive, but he looks young for his age.

meaning: to go/turn around; (figuratively) to beat around the bush / avoid the point.
additional_notes: Used literally for moving around something or someone (e.g., “girare intorno a lui” = move around him). Very commonly used figuratively with topics, words, or questions: “girare intorno al punto/alla questione/alle parole” means to circle around the issue instead of saying it directly (similar to “stop beating around the bush”).
target_language_example: Non girare intorno al punto: dimmi subito la verità.
native_language_example: Don’t beat around the bush—tell me the truth right away.

meaning: to swear not to tell it to (someone).
additional_notes: Used to promise very seriously that you won’t reveal something to a specific person or group. Structure: "giurare di" + infinitive (here: "non dirlo" = “not to say/tell it”) + "a" + person ("a Tom", "a nessuno" = “to nobody”). Very often appears as "far fare" (to make someone do something): "Mi ha fatto giurare di non dirlo a..." = “She made me swear not to tell...”.
target_language_example: Ti giuro di non dirlo a nessuno.
native_language_example: I swear I won’t tell anyone.

meaning: just in time (right before it’s too late).
additional_notes: Used when someone arrives or something happens at exactly the right moment, often at the last possible minute. You can place it after the verb (e.g., "Sono arrivato giusto in tempo") or use it alone as an exclamation ("Giusto in tempo!").
target_language_example: Abbiamo preso l’autobus giusto in tempo.
native_language_example: We caught the bus just in time.

additional_notes: Used to say something has been completed before now. Often answers a suggestion or request: "Non serve, già fatto" = "No need, I’ve already done it." It can refer to a specific task ("Ho già fatto il mio lavoro") or be used alone as a short reply ("Già fatto?").
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: già fatto, ho mandato l’email.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: already done, I sent the email.

additional_notes: Used to say something is completed earlier than expected or by now. Often appears in questions with the passato prossimo of *finire* (e.g., *Hai già finito?* / *Avete già finito?*) and can be followed by *con* + activity or by a direct object (e.g., *finito i compiti*).
target_language_example: Scusi, ha già finito di mangiare?
native_language_example: Excuse me, have you already finished eating?

additional_notes: Used to say someone has finished reading the book earlier than now. Often appears with the passato prossimo: “(avere) già letto” (e.g., “Ho già letto…”). It can also show up with modal verbs (“può/potete avere già letto…”) to express possibility (“may/could have already read…”) or with the subjunctive after expressions like “È possibile che…” (“it’s possible that…”).
target_language_example: Non credo che lui abbia già letto questo libro.
native_language_example: I don’t think he has already read this book.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb (usually "avere") to form the past tense (passato prossimo): "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno già mangiato" = "I/you/he… have already eaten". "Già" (already) usually comes before the past participle "mangiato". Common in questions to check if someone has eaten yet.
target_language_example: Abbiamo già mangiato, grazie.
native_language_example: We’ve already eaten, thanks.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "parlare" in the passato prossimo: "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno già parlato con + person". It means the conversation happened earlier (often before now, or before another event). "Con" here is "with" (talked with someone).
target_language_example: Ho già parlato con il dottore, grazie.
native_language_example: I’ve already spoken with the doctor, thanks.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb (usually “avere”) to form the passato prossimo: “ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno già parlato con lui” = “I/you/he… have already spoken with him.” “Già” means “already” and often implies the action is done sooner than expected. “Con lui” means “with him.”
target_language_example: Ho già parlato con lui, ma non ha risposto.
native_language_example: I’ve already spoken with him, but he didn’t reply.

meaning: 'already been to' (a place), for a female speaker.
additional_notes: Used with the verb essere to say that someone has already visited/been somewhere: "(Lei) è già stata a ...?" / "Sono già stata a ...". Stata is feminine singular (speaking about a woman). For a man, use "già stato a". It’s followed by a place introduced by "a" (e.g., a Roma, a casa, a Parigi).
target_language_example: Sono già stata a Firenze, ma voglio tornarci.
native_language_example: I've already been to Florence, but I want to go back.

additional_notes:
Used when you’re talking about a specific item and you want to say someone already has one. It usually appears with a verb like avere: (tu) Hai già una di quelle? / (lei) Ha già una di quelle. 
- già = already
- una = one (feminine singular)
- di quelle = of those (feminine plural), referring back to something previously mentioned/pointed at.
Change it to match gender/number: già uno di quelli (masc.), già una di questi (these), già uno di quei… (those).
target_language_example: Hai già una di quelle borse?
native_language_example: Do you already have one of those bags?

additional_notes: Used after a number, place, or estimate to mean “more or less” or “in that general area.” Often comes with “o” (“or”): “... o giù di lì” = “... or so / give or take.”
target_language_example: Arrivo alle cinque, o giù di lì.
native_language_example: I’ll arrive at five, or so.

additional_notes: Used with movement verbs (e.g., correre, scendere) to describe going from a higher floor to a lower one via the staircase. Often followed by a destination: "giù per le scale in cantina / nel seminterrato" (down the stairs to the basement).
target_language_example: Siamo scesi giù per le scale in fretta perché eravamo in ritardo.
native_language_example: We went down the stairs quickly because we were late.

additional_notes: An imperative used to tell someone to stop touching or bothering someone/something. Often followed by **da** + noun/pronoun: **Giù le mani da mio figlio!** = “Hands off my son!” It can sound aggressive, especially when combined with swearing or insults.
target_language_example: Giù le mani dal mio telefono!
native_language_example: Hands off my phone!

additional_notes: Used to report a request you made to a man (or to someone addressed as “him”). It’s made of the indirect object pronoun “gli” (= to him) + “chiesi” (past, “I asked”, often in the passato remoto) + “di” + infinitive (what you asked him to do). In everyday conversation many speakers use “gli ho chiesto di …” instead.
target_language_example: Gli chiesi di aspettarmi davanti alla stazione.
native_language_example: I asked him to wait for me in front of the station.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato remoto) of consigliare: consigliò = “he/she advised/recommended.” Gli means “to him.” It’s followed by di + infinitive to say what was recommended: gli consigliò di fare… You’ll often hear the present: gli consiglia di… (“he/she recommends to him to…”).
target_language_example: Il dottore gli consigliò di bere più acqua.
native_language_example: The doctor advised him to drink more water.

additional_notes: Used with the formal command form (Lei): **dia** = “give” (to you/please), and **gli** is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to him” (sometimes “to them” in informal speech, but standard Italian uses **loro** for “to them”). Often used to give instructions politely: *Gli dia questo* = “Please give him this.”
target_language_example: Quando lo vede, gli dia questo messaggio, per favore.
native_language_example: When you see him, please give him this message.

additional_notes: Used to give a polite/formal instruction (Lei form) to someone: dica = "tell" (imperative), gli = "to him". Often followed by che + sentence ("tell him that...") or di + infinitive ("tell him to...").
target_language_example: Gli dica che arrivo tra cinque minuti.
native_language_example: Tell him that I’ll be there in five minutes.

additional_notes: "Gli" means "to him". "Dica" is the formal (Lei) form of "dire" and is used for polite instructions/requests (often after "voglio che...", "è meglio che...", etc.). "Che" introduces what you want to say ("that...").
target_language_example: Per favore, gli dica che arrivo tra cinque minuti.
native_language_example: Please tell him that I’ll arrive in five minutes.

additional_notes: Used when speaking formally (Lei form) to ask someone to tell a third person (gli = “to him”) to do something. "dica" is the formal command (imperative) of dire (“to say/tell”). It’s followed by "di" + infinitive (andare, provare, smettere, venire, etc.).
target_language_example: Gli dica di chiamarmi domani.
native_language_example: Tell him to call me tomorrow.

additional_notes: "Gli" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to him" (sometimes also "to them" in informal usage). "Diede" is the passato remoto (remote past) of "dare" (to give), common in books, storytelling, and some regions; in everyday conversation you’ll more often hear "gli ha dato" (passato prossimo).
target_language_example: Gli diede le chiavi e se ne andò.
native_language_example: He gave him the keys and left.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object pronoun: gli = “to him.” Diedi is the passato remoto of dare (“to give”), common in storytelling and more in southern/central Italy; in everyday speech you’ll often hear gli ho dato (“I gave him / I have given him”). Word order can vary: Gli diedi i soldi / I soldi glieli diedi.
target_language_example: Quando mi chiese aiuto, gli diedi il mio numero di telefono.
native_language_example: When he asked me for help, I gave him my phone number.

additional_notes: “Gli” is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to him” (sometimes also “to them” in informal speech, but here it’s “to him”). “Dissi” is the passato remoto of “dire” (io dissi), commonly used in stories, writing, and in some regions instead of the passato prossimo (“gli ho detto”). Often followed by “che” + a clause.
target_language_example: Gli dissi di aspettarmi fuori.
native_language_example: I told him to wait for me outside.

additional_notes: Used to report what you said to a male person (gli = “to him”). It’s in the past (passato remoto), common in storytelling and written Italian; in everyday conversation many speakers use “gli ho detto che …” instead.
target_language_example: Gli dissi che non potevo venire.
native_language_example: I told him that I couldn’t come.

meaning: “I told him to …” / “I said to him to …”
additional_notes: Used to report what you told a man (or to “him”) in the past. It’s made of: gli = to him, dissi = I said/told (past), di + infinitive = to do something (e.g., di partire = to leave). With “di no” it means “I told him no / I said no to him.”
target_language_example: Gli dissi di aspettare fuori.
native_language_example: I told him to wait outside.

additional_notes:
Used to report giving a negative instruction/advice to a man (or to “him”).
- Gli = “to him” (indirect object pronoun).
- Dissi is the passato remoto of dire (“I said/told”), common in narratives and in some regions; in conversation you may also hear “gli ho detto di non …”.
- Structure: gli + dissi + di non + infinitive (non goes before the infinitive).
target_language_example: Gli dissi di non aprire la porta.
native_language_example: I told him not to open the door.

meaning: "to him" + "(he/she) has" (used before a past participle).
additional_notes: Used with the indirect object pronoun "gli" (= to him) plus the auxiliary "ha" (from "avere") to form the passato prossimo: "gli ha detto" = "he/she told him". The subject is not stated and must be understood from context (he/she/it). Common with verbs like dire (tell), confessare (confess), prestare (lend), dare (give). Note: "gli" can also mean "to them" in everyday speech, but strictly speaking that is "loro".
target_language_example: Gli ha scritto un messaggio ieri sera.
native_language_example: He/She wrote him a message last night.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object pronoun: gli = “to him” (le = “to her”). The structure is: [subject] ha chiesto + a [person]/gli/le + di + infinitive (what you ask them to do). In the examples, the subject is implied (he/she).
target_language_example: Gli ha chiesto di aspettare un momento.
native_language_example: He/She asked him to wait a moment.

additional_notes: Used to report advice given to a male person: **gli** = “to him”, **ha consigliato** = “(he/she) advised / recommended” (passato prossimo), followed by **di + infinitive** to say what he was advised to do. You can change **gli** depending on the person: *mi ha consigliato di* (advised me to), *ti ha consigliato di* (advised you to), *le ha consigliato di* (advised her to).
target_language_example: Il medico gli ha consigliato di dormire di più.
native_language_example: The doctor advised him to sleep more.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "dare" (to give) in the passato prossimo: "ha dato" = "gave/has given". "Gli" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to him" (singular). The subject isn’t stated and is understood from context (lui/lei/Lei, etc.). Often followed by the thing given: "gli ha dato un regalo" = "he/she gave him a gift".
target_language_example: Gli ha dato le chiavi dopo cena.
native_language_example: He/She gave him the keys after dinner.

additional_notes: Made of the indirect object pronoun "gli" (= to him) + "ha detto" (past of "dire"). It’s used to report what someone said to a male person; the subject is often understood from context (he/she/you). In questions, it can mean “did he/she tell him…?” or “have you told him…?”.
target_language_example: Gli ha detto che arriviamo alle otto.
native_language_example: He/She told him that we’re arriving at eight.

meaning: 'he/she told him to' (gave him an instruction).
additional_notes: Used when someone (often implied from context) told a man/someone 'to do' something. Structure: [subject] + ha detto + gli + di + infinitive. 'Gli' = to him; if it’s a woman, you usually use 'le ha detto di' ('told her to'). In questions, word order stays the same: 'Dove gli ha detto di...?'
target_language_example: Il capo gli ha detto di arrivare alle otto.
native_language_example: The boss told him to arrive at eight.

meaning: “(he/she) did/made … for him” or “(it) made/caused him to …”
additional_notes: "Gli" is the indirect object pronoun meaning “to him” (sometimes also “to it,” e.g., to a masculine noun). "Ha fatto" is the passato prossimo of "fare" (“to do/make”). It’s used when someone does something for him (Gli ha fatto una torta. = She made him a cake.) or when something causes an effect on him (Il suo coraggio gli ha fatto guadagnare la fama. = His courage made him gain fame).
target_language_example: La notizia gli ha fatto cambiare idea.
native_language_example: The news made him change his mind.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "sparare". "Gli" literally means “to him,” so "gli ha sparato" often implies “shot at him” (fired a gun in his direction). In everyday Italian it can also be used like “shot him.” The subject (he/she) is not stated and is understood from context.
target_language_example: Quando l’ha visto, gli ha sparato due volte.
native_language_example: When he saw him, he shot at him twice.

meaning: "you have … to him" (used before a past participle).
additional_notes: Made of the indirect object pronoun **gli** (= to him; also used for formal 'to you') + **hai** (= you have). It’s commonly used with the **passato prossimo**: **gli hai detto/parlato/scritto** = “you told/spoke/wrote to him.” The verb often has a direct object after it: **Gli hai detto la verità** = “You told him the truth.”
target_language_example: Gli hai già scritto un messaggio?
native_language_example: Have you already written him a message?

additional_notes: "Gli" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to him" (sometimes also "to them" in informal speech, though standard Italian uses "loro"). "Hai detto" is the passato prossimo of "dire" (to say/tell), used for completed past actions. Often followed by a clause with "che" (Gli hai detto che...?).
target_language_example: Gli hai detto la verità?
native_language_example: Did you tell him the truth?

meaning: "they did to him" / "they made him (do something)".
additional_notes: Literally: "to him" (gli) + "they have" (hanno) + past participle of fare (fatto). Used when someone did something to him (often something negative: Gli hanno fatto del male) or when they made/forced him to do something, especially with another verb in the infinitive: Gli hanno fatto firmare il contratto = "They made him sign the contract." In everyday speech it often translates as simple past in English: "They did..."
target_language_example: È arrabbiato per quello che gli hanno fatto.
native_language_example: He’s angry about what they did to him.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something you did to/for a man (or to “them” in some contexts) in the passato prossimo. “Gli” = “to him” (dative indirect object pronoun), “ho” = “I have” (auxiliary of the present perfect). Common with verbs like prestare (lend), dire (say), dare (give), augurare (wish), fare visita (visit). Example pattern: Gli ho + past participle (e.g., gli ho prestato = I lent him).
target_language_example: Gli ho scritto un messaggio ieri sera.
native_language_example: I wrote him a message last night.

meaning: “I asked him” (literally: “to him I have asked”).
additional_notes: Used when you asked a question or made a request to a male person (“him”). It’s made of the indirect object pronoun gli (“to him”) + ho chiesto (past of chiedere, “I asked / I have asked”). Common patterns: gli ho chiesto aiuto (“I asked him for help”); gli ho chiesto di + infinitive (“I asked him to…”); gli ho chiesto se… (“I asked him if…”).
target_language_example: Gli ho chiesto se poteva venire domani.
native_language_example: I asked him if he could come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report a request you made to a man (or to someone addressed as “lui”). Structure: gli (to him) + ho chiesto (I asked) + di + infinitive (verb in the “to …” form). For a woman, you usually say: “le ho chiesto di …” (“I asked her to …”).
target_language_example: Gli ho chiesto di aspettarmi fuori.
native_language_example: I asked him to wait for me outside.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *dare* (to give) in the *passato prossimo*: *ho dato* = “I gave / I have given.” **Gli** is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to him” (standard Italian; “to her” is usually *le*, though you may sometimes hear *gli* used for a woman in informal speech). It’s followed by what was given: *Gli ho dato la chiave* (“I gave him the key”). With **dare del + insult**, it means “to call someone (a name)”: *Gli ho dato del maiale grasso* (“I called him a fat pig”).
target_language_example: Gli ho dato un regalo per il suo compleanno.
native_language_example: I gave him a gift for his birthday.

meaning: "I gave him a / I gave him an" (past).
additional_notes: Used with the indirect object pronoun "gli" = "to him". It’s the passato prossimo of "dare" (to give): "ho dato" = "I gave / I have given". You normally complete it with a masculine singular noun: "Gli ho dato un regalo." (I gave him a gift.). With some nouns it can mean "gave" in the sense of administering ("un sedativo") or delivering ("un pugno" = a punch).
target_language_example: Gli ho dato un consiglio, ma non mi ha ascoltato.
native_language_example: I gave him some advice, but he didn’t listen to me.

additional_notes: Used to report something you said to a male person (or someone referred to as “him”). It’s the passato prossimo of dire with the indirect object pronoun gli (“to him”): gli + ho detto. Often followed by che + a clause (“I told him that…”) or di + infinitive for instructions (“I told him not to…”).
target_language_example: Gli ho detto che arrivo domani.
native_language_example: I told him that I'm arriving tomorrow.

meaning: "I told him that" / "I said to him that".
additional_notes: Used to report what you told a man (or to "him" in general). "Gli" = "to him" (indirect object pronoun), "ho detto" is past tense (passato prossimo) of "dire" = "to say/tell", and "che" introduces the clause with what you said. In similar sentences, "gli" can change (e.g., "le ho detto che" = I told her that; "ti ho detto che" = I told you that).
target_language_example: Gli ho detto che non posso venire oggi.
native_language_example: I told him that I can’t come today.

additional_notes: Used to report giving someone (gli = “to him”) an instruction/advice: "gli ho detto di" + infinitive (andare, fermarsi, scrivere, ecc.). It’s the passato prossimo of dire (ho detto = “I said/told”). In very informal speech, "gli" is sometimes used to mean “to them,” but in standard Italian it means “to him.”
target_language_example: Gli ho detto di chiamarmi domani.
native_language_example: I told him to call me tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report an instruction you gave to a male person (gli = “to him”). Commonly appears after “quello che/ciò che” (“what”) to mean “what I told him to do.” You can swap the pronoun: le ho detto di fare (to her), gli ho detto di farlo (to do it).
target_language_example: Ha fatto tutto quello che gli ho detto di fare.
native_language_example: He did everything I told him to do.

additional_notes: Used to report that you gave a man a negative instruction/advice. Structure: gli (to him) + ho detto (I said/told) + di non + infinitive (e.g., venire, usare, tornare). For a woman use: “le ho detto di non …”; for plural: “ho detto loro di non …”.
target_language_example: Gli ho detto di non parlare così.
native_language_example: I told him not to talk like that.

meaning: “I did (it) to/for him” / “I made/had him do (something)” (past).
additional_notes: “Gli” means “to him” (indirect object pronoun). “Ho fatto” is the past of “fare” (“I did/made”). Common uses: (1) with a noun: “gli ho fatto una domanda/un favore/visita” = “I asked him a question/did him a favor/visited him”; (2) with an infinitive to mean “make/let someone do”: “gli ho fatto promettere…” = “I made him promise…”; (3) with an infinitive meaning “have/get something done (by someone)”: “gli ho fatto riparare l’orologio” = “I had him/them repair the watch.” Context tells whether it means “made him do” or “had (someone) do.”
target_language_example: Gli ho fatto vedere le foto ieri sera.
native_language_example: I showed him the photos last night.

meaning: 'he likes' (talking about things in the plural).
additional_notes: Used with the verb *piacere* to say what someone likes. *Gli* = “to him,” and *piacciono* is plural to match a plural thing (*i* + plural noun). For a singular thing you say *gli piace il/la...*
target_language_example: Gli piacciono i film d’azione.
native_language_example: He likes action movies.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to express what someone likes. Literally "to him, it is pleasing": gli = "to him" (indirect object), piace = "is pleasing" (3rd person singular). Common patterns: "Gli piace + infinitive" (Gli piace giocare...) and "Gli piace + noun" (Gli piace la pizza). For plural things, use "gli piacciono" (Gli piacciono i film d’azione).
target_language_example: Gli piace ascoltare musica la sera.
native_language_example: He likes listening to music in the evening.

additional_notes: Used with "piacere" to say someone likes something. "Gli" = "to him" (indirect object), and the thing liked is the subject: "Gli piace il reggae" = "He likes reggae". Use "piace" with a singular noun (il tonno, il viola); use "piacciono" with plural nouns (e.g., "Gli piacciono i fiori").
target_language_example: Gli piace il caffè amaro.
native_language_example: He likes bitter coffee.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "piacere" to say what someone likes. "Gli" = "to him". "Piace" is used with singular things; with plural things use "gli piacciono" (e.g., "Gli piacciono i film"). "La" is the feminine singular "the"; it changes with gender/number ("il/lo/l'/i/gli/le").
target_language_example: Gli piace la musica jazz.
native_language_example: He likes jazz music.

meaning: “he liked” / “he used to like” (literally: “it pleased him”).
additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere, which works “backwards” compared to English: the thing liked is the grammatical subject, and the person is an indirect object pronoun. So gli piaceva la pizza = “he liked pizza” (literally “pizza was pleasing to him”). The imperfect (piaceva) often suggests a past habit or a continuing feeling in the past (“used to like”, “liked at the time”).
target_language_example: Da bambino, gli piaceva andare al mare.
native_language_example: As a child, he liked going to the beach.

meaning: he liked it / he enjoyed it (literally: “it pleased him”).
additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere in the past: the thing that is liked is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is an indirect object. So gli = “to him,” and piaciuto agrees with what was liked (e.g., Gli è piaciuto il video; Gli sono piaciuti i video). Often used in questions: Gli è piaciuto? = “Did he like it?”
target_language_example: Gli è piaciuto molto il film.
native_language_example: He really liked the movie.

additional_notes: From the verb "succedere" (to happen). "Gli" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to him". Used to ask about an event or problem involving a man/boy: "Che cosa gli è successo?" = "What happened to him?" For a woman you say "le è successo"; for plural "gli è successo" can also mean "happened to them" (to them = "a loro").
target_language_example: Non so che cosa gli è successo ieri sera.
native_language_example: I don’t know what happened to him last night.

additional_notes: Literally “the affairs.” Most commonly means business or business activities: Come vanno gli affari? (“How’s business?”), Gli affari vanno lenti (“Business is slow”). In expressions like farsi gli affari suoi, it means “mind your own business” (not get involved in other people’s matters). In Gli affari sono affari it means “business is business” (don’t mix business with personal feelings).
target_language_example: In questo periodo, gli affari non vanno molto bene.
native_language_example: These days, business isn’t going very well.

meaning: “Business is business.” (You have to be practical and put business first.)
additional_notes: Used to justify a tough, practical decision, often implying “no hard feelings” or that personal feelings can’t interfere. The verb is plural (“sono”) because “gli affari” is plural (“business matters”), but in English you usually say “Business is business.”
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma devo chiederti il pagamento: gli affari sono affari.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but I have to ask you to pay: business is business.

additional_notes: Plural form of "l'albero" (tree). It uses the masculine plural article "gli" and is used before nouns starting with a vowel (alberi) and also many nouns starting with s+consonant, z, gn, ps, x, y (e.g., gli studenti, gli zaini).
target_language_example: In primavera gli alberi diventano verdi.
native_language_example: In spring the trees turn green.

additional_notes: Plural masculine noun phrase: "gli" is the plural masculine definite article used before words starting with a vowel (like "algerini"). It can refer to a mixed group (men and women) or to Algerian men specifically. Singular: "l’algerino" (male), "l’algerina" (female).
target_language_example: Gli algerini parlano soprattutto arabo e francese.
native_language_example: Algerians mostly speak Arabic and French.

additional_notes: Plural masculine form of "l'altro" used for a group meaning "the others" or "the other ones/people." It often refers to everyone else in a group: "tutti gli altri" = "everyone else," and in comparisons: "più ... di tutti gli altri" = "more ... than all the others." It can refer to mixed-gender groups too (masculine plural as default).
target_language_example: Aspetta qui: parlo con gli altri e poi torno.
native_language_example: Wait here: I’ll talk to the others and then I’ll come back.

additional_notes: Plural masculine form of "l'altro" used as a pronoun meaning "the others" (a group not including the speaker). It can refer to people or things; for a group of only women you can also say "le altre". Common in phrases like "gli altri" = "everyone else" depending on context.
target_language_example: Io sono pronto; gli altri arrivano tra dieci minuti.
native_language_example: I'm ready; the others will arrive in ten minutes.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase: definite article + nationality. Used to talk about Americans in general (as a group). Singular: l’americano / l’americana. You can also use it as an adjective with a noun (e.g., i turisti americani = the American tourists).
target_language_example: Gli americani spesso fanno la mancia al ristorante.
native_language_example: Americans often tip at restaurants.

additional_notes: Plural masculine definite article + noun: "gli" is used before nouns starting with a vowel (amici) and some consonant clusters (e.g., s+consonant). "Gli amici" can refer to a group of male friends or a mixed-gender group; for an all-female group you’d say "le amiche". Often used after "con" (with): "con gli amici".
target_language_example: Stasera esco con gli amici.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m going out with my friends.

additional_notes: "Gli" is the plural masculine definite article used before a vowel (like *animali*) and also before *s* + consonant, *z*, *ps*, *gn*, etc. Used to talk about animals in general or a specific group depending on context.
target_language_example: A casa mia non possiamo avere gli animali.
native_language_example: At my house we can’t have pets/animals.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase with the definite article: "gli" + "anziani". It refers to older people as a group (often with a respectful tone). Singular is "l’anziano" (elderly man/person) and "l’anziana" (elderly woman).
target_language_example: In questo quartiere ci sono molti servizi per gli anziani.
native_language_example: In this neighborhood there are many services for older adults.

additional_notes: Plural of "l’elefante" (the elephant). Used with the verb "piacere" to say someone likes elephants: "Mi piacciono gli elefanti" = "I like elephants" (literally, "Elephants are pleasing to me"). "Gli" is the masculine plural form of "il" (the).
target_language_example: A mio figlio piacciono gli elefanti.
native_language_example: My son likes elephants.

additional_notes: Plural of "l’esame" (exam/test). Used mostly for school or university: "gli esami finali" (final exams). Common verbs: "studiare per gli esami" (to study for exams), "passare/superare gli esami" (to pass exams), "fallire/non passare gli esami" (to fail), "copiare durante gli esami" (to cheat during exams).
target_language_example: Devo studiare per gli esami della prossima settimana.
native_language_example: I have to study for next week’s exams.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase used to talk about humans as a species in a general/neutral way (common in science, news, and formal writing). Often used with general statements: "Gli esseri umani + verb". Singular: "l’essere umano" (a human being).
target_language_example: Gli esseri umani hanno bisogno di acqua per vivere.
native_language_example: Human beings need water to live.

additional_notes: “Hot dog” is an English loanword used in Italian too. In Italian it’s treated as masculine; the plural is usually unchanged (“gli hot dog”). Use “gli” because it’s masculine plural and begins with a vowel sound (“hot…”). In menus or shops you might also see “un hot dog” (one hot dog).
target_language_example: Prendiamo gli hot dog e delle patatine?
native_language_example: Shall we get the hot dogs and some fries?

additional_notes: Plural form of "l’incubo" (a nightmare). Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "Ho gli incubi" = "I have nightmares" (i.e., I’ve been having nightmares). You can ask someone: "Hai gli incubi?" = "Are you having nightmares?"
target_language_example: Da quando ho visto quel film, ho gli incubi.
native_language_example: Since I saw that movie, I’ve been having nightmares.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase with the definite article (gli + inglesi). Used to refer to English people as a group (“the English”). Note: “inglese” can also mean the English language, but in the plural “gli inglesi” almost always refers to people.
target_language_example: Gli inglesi parlano inglese, ma non tutti sono dell’Inghilterra.
native_language_example: The English speak English, but not everyone is from England.

additional_notes: Plural noun with the definite article. Used for insects in general or a specific known group. Singular: "l’insetto" (the insect). You’ll often see it with verbs like "piacere" (to like), "odiare" (to hate), "mangiare" (to eat), "catturare" (to catch).
target_language_example: In estate ci sono molti insetti.
native_language_example: In summer there are many insects.

additional_notes: Plural definite article + noun: gli (the, plural) + italiani (Italians). Used to talk about Italians as a group in general statements (often stereotypes or generalizations), or after come (“like/as”) to mean “like Italians / the Italian way.” It can also mean Italian men specifically, but often it includes Italians in general (mixed group).
target_language_example: Gli italiani spesso fanno una pausa caffè nel pomeriggio.
native_language_example: Italians often take a coffee break in the afternoon.

additional_notes: Plural of "l’occhio". Used for talking about eye color (Hai gli occhi verdi?), physical irritation (mi ha irritato gli occhi), and in common expressions like "aprire gli occhi" = "open your eyes" meaning to stop dreaming/ignoring reality and notice what’s really happening.
target_language_example: Apri gli occhi: non è una buona idea.
native_language_example: Open your eyes: it’s not a good idea.

meaning: 'your eyes open' → stay alert; watch out.
additional_notes: Literally “the eyes open.” Used with verbs like tenere/tieni/tenga (“keep”) to mean paying attention and being ready to notice something (e.g., a taxi, danger, a detail). Very common as an instruction: “Tieni/Tenga gli occhi aperti!” = “Keep your eyes open!”
target_language_example: Tieni gli occhi aperti: potrebbe arrivare il controllore.
native_language_example: Keep your eyes open: the ticket inspector might come by.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s eye color (usually with the verb "avere": "Ho gli occhi blu" = "I have blue eyes"). "Gli" is the plural masculine article for "occhi" (eyes).
target_language_example: Mia sorella ha gli occhi blu.
native_language_example: My sister has blue eyes.

meaning: “(your/the) eyes and …” (used in instructions like “Close your eyes and …”).
additional_notes: Usually follows a form of **chiudere** (“to close”): **Chiudi/Chiuda/Chiudete gli occhi e …** = “Close your eyes and …”. **Gli** means “the” (plural masculine), and **occhi** is plural (“eyes”).
target_language_example: Chiudi gli occhi e fai un respiro profondo.
native_language_example: Close your eyes and take a deep breath.

additional_notes: Plural in Italian: you normally say occhiali (not *occhiale*) to mean a pair of glasses. The article changes with gender/number: *gli occhiali* (the glasses), *degli occhiali* (some glasses), *i miei occhiali* (my glasses). Common with verbs like *mettere* (to put on), *togliere/togliersi* (to take off), *sistemare* (to adjust/straighten).
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato gli occhiali a casa.
native_language_example: I forgot my glasses at home.

additional_notes: Refers to glasses used for reading (often used only when needed). You’ll often see it with reflexive verbs like mettersi/togliersi: “Mettiti gli occhiali da lettura” (Put on your reading glasses), “Si è tolto/a gli occhiali da lettura” (He/She took off their reading glasses).
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato gli occhiali da lettura a casa.
native_language_example: I forgot my reading glasses at home.

additional_notes: Refers to the sunglasses as a specific/plural item: occhiali (glasses) + da sole (for the sun). Often used with verbs like indossare (to wear) and portare (to bring/wear).
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato gli occhiali da sole in macchina.
native_language_example: I forgot my sunglasses in the car.

additional_notes: Plural of "l’ordine". Used especially for commands given by someone in authority (military, police, workplace). Common expressions: "Dare gli ordini" = to give orders; "Seguire/Eseguire gli ordini" = to follow/carry out orders; "Gli ordini sono ordini" = orders are orders (you must obey).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, sto solo eseguendo gli ordini.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m just carrying out orders.

additional_notes: Definite plural form: "gli" + "orsi". Used for bears in general or a specific group of bears. With an adjective, it stays plural (e.g., "gli orsi feriti" = "the injured bears").
target_language_example: Attenzione: gli orsi possono essere pericolosi.
native_language_example: Watch out: bears can be dangerous.

meaning: the guests (male guests or mixed group).
additional_notes: Plural of "l’ospite" (a guest). "Gli" is the plural masculine article used for male or mixed groups. Used for people invited to your home/event, or people staying at a hotel (hotel guests). For an all-female group, you can also say "le ospiti".
target_language_example: Gli ospiti arrivano alle otto, quindi preparo l’aperitivo.
native_language_example: The guests arrive at eight, so I’m preparing appetizers/drinks.

additional_notes: Plural form of "l’ostaggio" (a hostage). Used for people being held against their will (e.g., by terrorists, kidnappers, or criminals). Often appears with verbs like "rilasciare" (to release) and "tenere" (to hold).
target_language_example: La polizia sta cercando di salvare gli ostaggi.
native_language_example: The police are trying to save the hostages.

additional_notes: Plural masculine slang for the police. It’s more like “cops/pigs” than neutral “polizia,” so avoid it in formal/polite situations. Singular: "lo sbirro" (a cop). You’ll often see it in crime movies, street talk, or when someone is angry at the police.
target_language_example: Non parlare così forte: ci sono gli sbirri là fuori.
native_language_example: Don’t talk so loudly: the cops are outside.

additional_notes: Plural masculine form with the definite article "gli". Used for a specific group of squirrels or squirrels in general (as a category), depending on context. Singular: "lo scoiattolo".
target_language_example: Nel parco ci sono gli scoiattoli sugli alberi.
native_language_example: In the park there are squirrels in the trees.

meaning: 'spaghetti' (the pasta), with the plural masculine definite article 'gli' = 'the spaghetti'.
additional_notes: Used to talk about spaghetti in general or specific spaghetti that’s been mentioned. You’ll see 'gli' because 'spaghetti' is masculine plural and starts with 'sp-' (a special consonant cluster). Without the article, you can also say just 'spaghetti' in some contexts (e.g., ordering).
target_language_example: Stasera cucino gli spaghetti al pomodoro.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m making spaghetti with tomato sauce.

gli spaghetti crescono sugli alberi di spaghetti

target_language_multi_word_term: gli spaghetti crescono sugli alberi di spaghetti
meaning: "spaghetti grow on spaghetti trees" (a humorous, absurd claim).
additional_notes: Used as a joke/hoax statement, often after (Lo) sapevi/sapevate/sapeva che...? (“Did you know that...?”). It’s meant to sound like a surprising ‘fun fact,’ but it’s obviously not true.
target_language_example: Non crederci: gli spaghetti crescono sugli alberi di spaghetti è solo uno scherzo.
native_language_example: Don’t believe it: “spaghetti grow on spaghetti trees” is just a joke.

meaning: 'spinach' (plural noun; with the plural masculine article 'gli').
additional_notes: In Italian, spinach is usually said in the plural: (gli) spinaci. Use it after "con" for ingredients (con gli spinaci = with spinach), and as the direct object with verbs like "mangiare" or "odiare".
target_language_example: Non mangio mai gli spinaci, ma li cucino spesso per i miei figli.
native_language_example: I never eat spinach, but I often cook it for my kids.

additional_notes: Used to say two or more people/things are identical or unchanged. It’s the masculine plural form of “lo stesso” and agrees with what it refers to (e.g., “gli stessi problemi” = the same problems). Often intensified with words like “esattamente” (exactly).
target_language_example: Abbiamo scelto gli stessi libri.
native_language_example: We chose the same books.

additional_notes: Plural of "lo stivale" (boot). Used for footwear like winter boots or ski boots. Often appears with verbs like "mettersi" (to put on) and "togliersi" (to take off): "si è messo gli stivali" / "si è tolto gli stivali".
target_language_example: Mi metto gli stivali perché fuori piove.
native_language_example: I’m putting on my boots because it’s raining outside.

additional_notes: Plural masculine form of "lo studente" (student). Used for a group of male students or a mixed-gender group. It’s "gli" because "studenti" starts with s + consonant (st-). For an all-female group: "le studentesse".
target_language_example: Gli studenti sono in classe, ma oggi sono un po' distratti.
native_language_example: The students are in class, but today they’re a bit distracted.

additional_notes: Plural form of the definite article + noun: gli (the, plural masculine, used before vowels and some consonant clusters) + uccelli (birds). Often used to talk about birds in general (“Birds fly…”) or specific birds known from context (“The birds outside…”).
target_language_example: Gli uccelli volano nel cielo.
native_language_example: The birds fly in the sky.

meaning: “the last” (plural masculine), or “the last ones” (the final remaining).
additional_notes: Used with a plural masculine noun (e.g., *gli ultimi posti* = “the last seats/places”). It’s also common in time expressions like *gli ultimi tre anni* (“the last three years”). If the noun is feminine/plural, you’ll see *le ultime*.
target_language_example: Negli ultimi giorni ho lavorato molto.
native_language_example: In the last few days I’ve worked a lot.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase with the definite article (gli = “the”) + umani (“humans”). Often used in general statements about people as a species (especially in science, sci‑fi, or contrasted with animals/aliens). Singular: l’umano / un umano (“a human”).
target_language_example: Gli umani hanno bisogno di acqua per vivere.
native_language_example: Humans need water to live.

additional_notes: Used to say that a group is the only people/animals/things that do something or are in a place. Often followed by: **a + infinitive** (gli unici a fare...) or a relative clause **che...** (gli unici che hanno...). Feminine plural is **le uniche**; singular is **l’unico / l’unica**.
target_language_example: Siamo gli unici a conoscere la risposta.
native_language_example: We’re the only ones who know the answer.

additional_notes: Definite article + plural of uomo (“man”). Used for a specific group of men, or for men in general depending on context. In sentence 3, it refers to a particular group (“Lancer’s men”). Pronunciation note: gli is used before words starting with a vowel (uomo → uomini) and sounds roughly like “lyee”.
target_language_example: Gli uomini sono già qui.
native_language_example: The men are already here.

meaning: 'men are' (talking about men in general or a group of men).
additional_notes: "Gli" is the plural masculine definite article (“the”), and "uomini" means “men.” Used with "sono" (“are”) to make general statements (often stereotypes) or to describe a specific group of men mentioned in context. For generalizations, Italian often uses the definite article ("gli uomini" = “men” in general).
target_language_example: Gli uomini sono tutti uguali?
native_language_example: Are all men the same?

additional_notes: Used when you’re about to tell someone something to another person: glielo = gli (to him / to her / to you formal) + lo (it). So glielo dico literally means “I say it to him/her/you.” Often used emphatically (“Glielo dico!” = “I’m telling you!”) or as a question (“Glielo dico?” = “Should I tell him/her?”). The exact person (him/her/you formal) depends on context.
target_language_example: Va bene, glielo dico subito.
native_language_example: Alright, I’ll tell him/her right away.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an amount or level of something: "alto grado di difficoltà" = “a high degree of difficulty.” With jobs/military it can mean a rank: "il grado di capitano" = “the rank of captain.” Note: in the common expression "essere in grado di" it means “to be able to.”
target_language_example: Che grado di esperienza hai?
native_language_example: What level of experience do you have?

meaning: (usually in the phrase *essere in grado di aiutare*) “to be able to help.”
additional_notes: Most often you’ll see this as **essere in grado di + infinitive** (e.g., *sono in grado di aiutare* = “I’m able to help”). It expresses ability/capability in a slightly more formal way than *potere* (“can”).
target_language_example: Non sono in grado di aiutarti oggi.
native_language_example: I’m not able to help you today.

meaning: the big day; an important/special day.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a long-awaited or very important occasion (often a wedding, but also a graduation, a trip, a major event, etc.). "Gran" is a shortened form of "grande" used before a noun (e.g., "un gran giorno").
target_language_example: Finalmente è arrivato il gran giorno: domani ci sposiamo!
native_language_example: The big day has finally arrived: tomorrow we’re getting married!

additional_notes: Means “a large portion” of something. Often used with a noun: "gran parte del/della/dell'..." (a large part of the...). Can also be used adverbially as "in gran parte" = “largely / for the most part.” "Gran" is a shortened form of "grande" used before some nouns (like "parte").
target_language_example: Ho letto gran parte del libro, ma non tutto.
native_language_example: I read most of the book, but not all of it.

meaning: (the) great love; the love of your life.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a very deep, often life-changing romantic love. It’s often preceded by an article (il/lo/la): "il grande amore" = "true/great love" in a general sense, or "il grande amore della mia vita" = "the love of my life." Can also be used directly to address someone: "Sei il grande amore della mia vita."
target_language_example: Spero di trovare un grande amore un giorno.
native_language_example: I hope to find a great love one day.

meaning: "fat (people) on a plane" / "overweight (people) on a plane".
additional_notes: Literally “fat on a plane.” In the examples it describes people (“tipi/tizi grassi”) and is often used while complaining about having to sit next to two large passengers. In polite speech, consider using less harsh alternatives like “persone in sovrappeso” (overweight people) or “persone robuste” (larger-built people).
target_language_example: Non mi piace quando devo viaggiare accanto a due persone molto robuste su un aereo.
native_language_example: I don’t like it when I have to travel next to two very big people on a plane.

meaning: 'thanks to' / 'because of' (due to someone's help or something's cause).
additional_notes: Used to say that something happened because of a person or thing. Often positive (crediting help: "Grazie a te" = thanks to you), but it can also be neutral/negative (similar to "because of"). Common set phrase: "grazie a Dio" = thank God.
target_language_example: Grazie a te, ho trovato un buon lavoro.
native_language_example: Thanks to you, I found a good job.

additional_notes: Used to express relief or gratitude (often as an exclamation: "Grazie a Dio!"). It can also be used ironically/jokingly, depending on tone and context. Literally "thanks to God"; sometimes followed by a whole sentence: "Grazie a Dio siete tornati" (= Thank God you’re back).
target_language_example: Grazie a Dio, il treno non è in ritardo oggi.
native_language_example: Thank goodness, the train isn’t late today.

additional_notes: Used to show relief that something good happened or something bad didn’t happen. It can start a sentence (Grazie al cielo, ...) or be followed by a clause (Grazie al cielo ho te). In replies, it can stand alone to mean “fortunately not!” (No, grazie al cielo!).
target_language_example: Grazie al cielo sei arrivato in tempo.
native_language_example: Thank goodness you arrived on time.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the person or thing that caused a result. Often positive like “thanks to you,” but it can also be neutral/negative like “because of the rain.” It’s followed by a noun/pronoun (grazie a te/lui/lei) or a name (grazie a Marco).
target_language_example: Siamo arrivati in tempo grazie al tuo aiuto.
native_language_example: We arrived on time thanks to your help.

meaning: "Thanks, but I/we can't" or "Thanks, but no/not…" (polite refusal or correction).
additional_notes: Used to politely decline an offer/invitation or to push back on what someone said. It’s often followed by a verb (e.g., “posso”, “vogliamo”, “è…”) or another phrase to explain the refusal/correction. Similar in tone to “Thanks, but…” in English.
target_language_example: Grazie, ma non posso venire stasera.
native_language_example: Thanks, but I can’t come tonight.

meaning: "thanks for being" / "thank you for being" (followed by a place or a past participle).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for their presence or for having stayed/been somewhere. Very often it’s followed by a past participle to form a completed action with "essere" (e.g., "grazie di essere rimasto/a" = “thanks for staying”). The past participle agrees with the person being thanked: rimasto (male), rimasta (female), restati (plural).
target_language_example: Grazie di essere venuta oggi.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming today.

additional_notes: A common, polite way to express strong gratitude. Used on its own (“Grazie mille!”), before a reason with **per** (“Grazie mille per...”), and often when saying goodbye (“Grazie mille, arrivederci”). Slightly warmer/stronger than just **grazie**.
target_language_example: Grazie mille per il tuo tempo!
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your time!

meaning: “thanks a lot for …” / “thank you very much for …”.
additional_notes: Used to thank someone warmly for a specific thing, followed by a noun or an infinitive (e.g., “Grazie mille per il regalo”, “Grazie mille per avermi aiutato”). Often appears with formal possessives like suo/suoi/sua/sue or vostro/vostra, but can also be casual (e.g., “Grazie mille per l’aiuto!”).
target_language_example: Grazie mille per avermi aspettato!
native_language_example: Thanks a lot for waiting for me!

meaning: “thanks for …” (thanking someone for an action, help, or something given).
additional_notes: Used to say what you’re thanking someone for. It’s commonly followed by: (1) an infinitive in the past (e.g., "grazie per aver…" = “thanks for having/done …”), or (2) a noun phrase ("grazie per il tuo aiuto" = “thanks for your help”). Works in formal and informal situations; you can add "Grazie per il tuo…" (informal) or "Grazie per il suo…" (formal).
target_language_example: Grazie per avermi chiamato così presto.
native_language_example: Thanks for calling me so early.

meaning: “thanks for having…” / “thanks for …-ing” (thanking someone for something they did).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a completed action in the past. Pattern: "Grazie per aver" + past participle (e.g., aiutato, portato, chiamato). With an object pronoun it becomes "Grazie per avermi/averti/averlo…" (e.g., "Grazie per avermi aiutato" = "Thanks for helping me").
target_language_example: Grazie per avermi chiamato ieri.
native_language_example: Thanks for calling me yesterday.

meaning: "thanks for having (done something) for/to us" / "thanks for + [verb] + us."
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a completed action involving “us.” It’s followed by a past participle: grazie per averci aiutato/i/e, invitato/i/e, portato/i/e, ecc. The past participle can agree with “ci” (us): aiutati (all male/mixed group), aiutate (all female). You can also add an object after it: “Grazie per averci invitati a cena.”
target_language_example: Grazie per averci accompagnati alla stazione.
native_language_example: Thanks for taking us to the station.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for an action, usually followed by a past participle (past infinitive): "grazie per avere" + participle (e.g., "aiutato", "detto"). In everyday speech you’ll also hear "grazie per" + infinitive present ("Grazie per aiutarmi") or "Grazie per aver" + participle (short for "avere"). It can be sincere or sarcastic depending on context (e.g., thanking someone for breaking your phone).
target_language_example: Grazie per avere chiamato così presto.
native_language_example: Thanks for calling so early.

meaning: “thanks for having (done something) to/for me …” (used before a past participle).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for something they did that involved you: "grazie per avermi" + past participle (e.g., dato, aiutato, salvato, ascoltato, invitato). It matches English "thanks for" + gerund/past action: "Thanks for giving me…", "Thanks for letting me…". The object pronoun "mi" (“me”) attaches to "avere" → "avermi".
target_language_example: Grazie per avermi aiutato con i compiti.
native_language_example: Thanks for helping me with my homework.

meaning: "thanks for having (done something) to/for me" / "thanks for (doing something) for me."
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for something they did involving you. It’s followed by a past infinitive (avermi + past participle): e.g., "grazie per avermi aiutato" = "thanks for helping me." The past participle can agree with "mi" when "mi" is a direct object: "chiamata/portata" (if the speaker is female) vs "chiamato/portato" (if the speaker is male).
target_language_example: Grazie per avermi aspettato fuori.
native_language_example: Thanks for waiting for me outside.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for doing something, followed by a past infinitive (essere + past participle): grazie per essere venuto/a/i/e (thanks for coming), grazie per essere rimasto/a/i/e (thanks for staying). The past participle agrees with the person being thanked: venuto (male), venuta (female), venuti (group of males/mixed), venute (group of females).
target_language_example: Grazie per essere venuti oggi.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming today.

additional_notes: Used to thank a man (or a mixed group) for coming. You can add details after it: “Grazie per essere venuto con me…” (Thanks for coming with me…). To thank a woman, say “Grazie per essere venuta”. To thank more than one person, use “Grazie per essere venuti” (men/mixed) or “Grazie per essere venute” (women only).
target_language_example: Grazie per essere venuto alla mia festa.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming to my party.

meaning: "thanks for the" (before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a specific thing or action. It’s followed by a masculine singular noun: grazie per il regalo (the gift), grazie per il collegamento (the link/connection). For other nouns you change the article: grazie per la (feminine), grazie per lo / per l’ (before certain consonant clusters or a vowel), grazie per i / per gli / per le (plural).
target_language_example: Grazie per il tuo aiuto oggi.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help today.

meaning: “thank you for your …” (formal/polite, used with Lei).
additional_notes: Used when addressing someone formally (customer, client, stranger, authority). It’s usually followed by a noun: grazie per il suo acquisto (purchase), grazie per il suo supporto (support), grazie per il suo tempo (time). With informal tu you would say: “grazie per il tuo …”.
target_language_example: Grazie per il suo tempo e la sua disponibilità.
native_language_example: Thank you for your time and your availability.

meaning: “thank you for your …” (to a man / informal “your”).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for something that belongs to them or that they did (message, purchase, support, report, etc.). It’s usually followed by a noun: “grazie per il tuo messaggio / supporto / acquisto”. Use “il tuo” when speaking to one male person you address with “tu”. For a female person: “grazie per la tua …”. For formal “you” (Lei): “grazie per il suo / la sua …”. For plural: “grazie per il vostro / la vostra …”.
target_language_example: Grazie per il tuo aiuto oggi.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help today.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for something, followed by a masculine singular noun (e.g., il vostro aiuto, il vostro messaggio, il vostro regalo). “Vostro” is the formal/plural form of “your”: it can be for addressing more than one person (“your” plural) or as the formal “your” in polite communication (often to a group/organization). For feminine singular nouns, use “grazie per la vostra …” (e.g., la vostra pazienza).
target_language_example: Grazie per il vostro aiuto.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help.

meaning: "Thanks for the …" (before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a specific thing or action. It must match the noun that follows: feminine singular = “la” (grazie per la spiegazione). For masculine singular, use “grazie per il/lo …” (e.g., grazie per il consiglio). Often followed by a noun, but it can also be followed by an infinitive: “Grazie per la/le…” vs “Grazie per avermi aiutato.”
target_language_example: Grazie per la tua pazienza.
native_language_example: Thanks for your patience.

additional_notes: Used with Lei-form (formal ‘you’) when thanking someone for a specific thing, usually followed by a noun: grazie per la sua attenzione/aiuto/ospitalità. The possessive agrees with the noun (sua = feminine singular; suo = masculine singular; sue/suoi = plural).
target_language_example: Grazie per la sua disponibilità.
native_language_example: Thank you for your availability/helpfulness.

meaning: "thanks for your..." (addressing one person; followed by a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for something they did or a quality they showed. It’s typically followed by a feminine singular noun (e.g., la tua assistenza, la tua pazienza). If the noun is masculine, use "grazie per il tuo..." (e.g., il tuo aiuto). For plural or formal "you", you may see "grazie per la vostra" / "il vostro".
target_language_example: Grazie per la tua pazienza.
native_language_example: Thanks for your patience.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for something, followed by a feminine singular noun (e.g., assistenza, attenzione, collaborazione, comprensione). “Vostra” is formal (Lei) or plural (you all). For a masculine noun, use “grazie per il vostro …” (e.g., tempo). In informal singular you’d usually say “grazie per la tua …”.
target_language_example: Grazie per la vostra comprensione.
native_language_example: Thank you for your understanding.

additional_notes: Used to ask or state a person’s blood type (A, B, AB, O), often with Rh factor (positivo/negativo). Common in medical contexts, forms, and emergencies. Typically used with the verb "avere" (to have): "Che gruppo sanguigno hai?" / formal "ha lei?".
target_language_example: Non so il mio gruppo sanguigno, devo fare un esame del sangue.
native_language_example: I don't know my blood type; I need to do a blood test.

meaning: to buy time; to stall (to get more time).
additional_notes: Used when you want to delay something so you have more time to think, prepare, or wait for something to happen. Often appears with "cercare di" (to try to): "cercare di guadagnare tempo". In sentence 3, "farò guadagnare tempo" means "I’ll save you time" (help you avoid wasting time).
target_language_example: Facciamo qualche domanda in più per guadagnare tempo.
native_language_example: Let’s ask a few more questions to buy time.

meaning: to earn a living; to make a living.
additional_notes: Used for how someone supports themselves financially (their job or way of making money). It often follows verbs like "fare" or describes an activity done "per guadagnarsi da vivere" (= in order to earn a living).
target_language_example: Lavora di notte per guadagnarsi da vivere.
native_language_example: He works nights to earn a living.

meaning: “Look how…!” / “Look at what…!” (an exclamation to draw attention).
additional_notes: Used to point something out strongly, often with surprise, admiration, or criticism: “Guarda che + noun/adjective…!” It’s common before phrases like “bello/bella/belli/belle” or to react to a mess/problem (“Guarda che casino…”). The tone depends on context; the phrase itself is neutral, but it’s often followed by emotional or even vulgar words.
target_language_example: Guarda che confusione in questa stanza!
native_language_example: Look at the mess in this room!

additional_notes: From the verb "guardare" (to watch/look at) + "la TV" (television). It’s commonly used to talk about habits or what someone is doing right now. You can change the subject and verb: "Guardo la TV" (I watch TV), "Guardi la TV?" (Do you watch TV?), "Guardiamo la TV" (We watch TV).
target_language_example: Stasera guarda la TV dopo cena.
native_language_example: Tonight he/she watches TV after dinner.

additional_notes: Direct command (imperative) meaning “look straight at me,” often to ask for honesty, seriousness, attention, or emotional connection. Commonly used in intense or personal moments; can sound firm. Literally “look at me in the eyes.”
target_language_example: Guardami negli occhi e dimmi la verità.
native_language_example: Look me in the eye and tell me the truth.

additional_notes: "Guardando" is the gerund of "guardare" (to watch/look). It’s used with "stare" to form the present continuous: "sto/stai/sta/stiamo/state/stanno guardando la TV" = "I am/you are/he is/we are/you all are/they are watching TV." You can also use it without "stare" to mean "while watching TV" (e.g., "Guardando la TV, mi addormento"). "TV" is common in Italian; you may also hear "tele".
target_language_example: Sto guardando la TV, ma posso parlare.
native_language_example: I'm watching TV, but I can talk.

meaning: to look (someone) in the face; to face (a situation/reality).
additional_notes: Literal meaning is “to look in the face.” Used both physically (making eye contact) and figuratively (“to face up to” a problem or the truth). Common in the negative form: “Non riesco a guardarlo/a in faccia” (= I can’t face/look at him/her). Also appears in fixed expressions like “non guardare in faccia a nessuno” (= to not spare anyone / to be ruthless). Note: Italian “guardare” means “to look/watch,” not “to guard/protect.”
target_language_example: È ora di guardare in faccia la realtà.
native_language_example: It’s time to face reality.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "guardare" (to watch/look at) + "la TV" (television). Common for talking about activities at home; you can also say "guardare la televisione" (same meaning, a bit more formal).
target_language_example: Stasera voglio guardare la TV con te.
native_language_example: Tonight I want to watch TV with you.

additional_notes: Commonly used after verbs like piacere ("to like") and can be used as an activity/hobby (often with other infinitives: pescare, andare in bicicletta). It’s a normal, neutral phrase: guardare = “to watch,” la televisione = “television/TV.”
target_language_example: La sera mi piace guardare la televisione con la mia famiglia.
native_language_example: In the evening I like to watch TV with my family.
