additional_notes: Definite article + holiday name: Italian usually says "il Natale" (literally "the Christmas"). Used with verbs like "passare/trascorrere il Natale" (to spend Christmas) and often followed by "con" (with): "il Natale con la famiglia". You’ll also hear it without the article in greetings: "Buon Natale!"
target_language_example: Quest'anno passiamo il Natale con i nonni.
native_language_example: This year we’re spending Christmas with our grandparents.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "con" + a person/people (Tom, la mia famiglia, i miei amici) to say who you spend Christmas with. Common with verbs like "trascorrere" or "passare": "Trascorro/Passo il Natale con...".
target_language_example: Quest'anno passo il Natale con i miei nonni.
native_language_example: This year I'm spending Christmas with my grandparents.

meaning: the Pope (head of the Catholic Church).
additional_notes: Capitalized (Papa) when referring to the Pope. Used in news, religion, and in jokes/expressions to mean “I’m the boss / I’m important” (e.g., “io sono il Papa”).
target_language_example: Il Papa vive in Vaticano.
native_language_example: The Pope lives in the Vatican.

meaning: the President (head of state or leader of an organization).
additional_notes: Used as a title before a name (Il Presidente Obama) or on its own when the context is clear (Il Presidente parlerà…). In Italian it’s capitalized when used as an official title, especially with a specific person, but can be lowercase in general references (il presidente della Repubblica). Can also refer to the president/chair of a club or company (il presidente della società).
target_language_example: Domani il Presidente incontrerà i giornalisti.
native_language_example: Tomorrow the President will meet with journalists.

additional_notes: Used with the definite article (il) as an official title. It refers to the leader of the government in a country (not the president/monarch). You can add “di + country” to specify: “il Primo Ministro della Finlandia”. Capitalization is common in news and formal writing, but you may also see “il primo ministro”.
target_language_example: Ho visto il Primo Ministro in TV ieri sera.
native_language_example: I saw the Prime Minister on TV last night.

meaning: the bathroom/restroom; the bath (act of bathing).
additional_notes: Il bagno can mean the room (bathroom/restroom): «Scusate, il bagno?» = “Excuse me, the bathroom?” It can also mean a bath as an activity, often with the verb fare: «fare il bagno» = “to take a bath” (or more generally “to bathe”). The meaning is usually clear from context (room vs. bathing).
target_language_example: Scusa, dov’è il bagno?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?

additional_notes: Bambino means a young child; it’s often understood as “boy” (especially in contrast with bambina = “girl”), but it can also be used more generally like “child/kid.” In sentences like “Il bambino sta per nascere,” it can mean “the baby” (a child about to be born).
target_language_example: Il bambino dorme già.
native_language_example: The child is already sleeping.

additional_notes: Used with the definite article il when talking about the sport in general (like il calcio, il tennis). Often appears with piacere: A Tom piace il baseball = “Tom likes baseball.”
target_language_example: Ti piace il baseball?
native_language_example: Do you like baseball?

additional_notes: A common Italian way to say the sport “basketball” (masculine singular). You may also hear the more Italian term "la pallacanestro". Don’t confuse it with English “basket” (a container): in Italian, "basket" usually refers to the sport.
target_language_example: Gioco a basket due volte a settimana.
native_language_example: I play basketball twice a week.

additional_notes: Common way to refer to a very young child. It’s masculine with the article (il bebè), and the plural is usually invariable: i bebè. You can also say il bambino / la bambina for “the child/boy/girl,” but bebè emphasizes that they’re very young.
target_language_example: Il bebè dorme nella carrozzina.
native_language_example: The baby is sleeping in the stroller.

meaning: the beak (of a bird); (figuratively, in commands) “shut up!”
additional_notes: Literal meaning is a bird’s beak ("Tutti gli uccelli hanno il becco"). In expressions like "chiudere/tenere il becco chiuso" it means “to shut up” and is rude/insulting. In "mettere il becco in tutto" it means “to stick your nose into everything” (to meddle).
target_language_example: Chiudi il becco e ascolta.
native_language_example: Shut up and listen.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like dare/dare il benvenuto (“to welcome someone”): Le do il benvenuto. It’s also used with essere (“to be welcome”): Sei/è/sarò il benvenuto qui (“You/he/I will be welcome here”). In this pattern, Italian often keeps the article: è il benvenuto/è la benvenuta (match gender), and the plural is: sono i benvenuti / sono le benvenute.
target_language_example: Siete i benvenuti a casa nostra.
native_language_example: You are welcome in our home.

additional_notes: With verbs like *studiare* (to study) and *usare* (to use), *il berbero* usually refers to the Berber language (also called *tamazight*), not a person. To refer to a person you can also say *un berbero / una berbera* (“a Berber man/woman”).
target_language_example: Sto imparando il berbero per parlare con i miei amici in Marocco.
native_language_example: I'm learning Berber to speak with my friends in Morocco.

additional_notes: Used when talking about studying/learning the Berber language as a school subject. "Berbero" is a masculine noun and here refers to the language; "a scuola" means "at school" (in school lessons).
target_language_example: Abbiamo studiato il berbero a scuola, ma ora lo parlo poco.
native_language_example: We studied Berber at school, but now I don’t speak it much.

meaning: the ticket (also: a note/message, depending on context).
additional_notes: Most commonly means a ticket for transport or an event: *il biglietto del treno* (train ticket), *il biglietto aereo* (plane ticket). It can also mean a small written note/message: *passami il biglietto* = “pass me the note.” Plural: *i biglietti*.
target_language_example: Scusi, dov’è la biglietteria per comprare il biglietto?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the ticket office to buy the ticket?

additional_notes: Refers to a person’s arm (upper limb). Often used with body-part grammar: Italian commonly uses the definite article (il) instead of a possessive (e.g., "Mi ha preso per il braccio" = "He/she grabbed me by the arm"). Common phrases: "il braccio destro/sinistro" (right/left arm), "(avere) il braccio ingessato" (to have your arm in a cast), "rompersi/bruciarsi il braccio" (to break/burn your arm).
target_language_example: Mi fa male il braccio destro.
native_language_example: My right arm hurts.

meaning: the laundry (clothes to wash / that have been washed).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like fare (to do) and ritirare (to bring in/take in, e.g., from the clothesline): fare il bucato = to do the laundry; ritirare il bucato = to bring the laundry in. It can refer both to the task and to the load of clothes.
target_language_example: Devo fare il bucato stasera.
native_language_example: I have to do the laundry tonight.

additional_notes: A common food item; used in cooking/baking and at the table. Often appears with verbs like "fare" (to make), "mescolare" (to mix), and "passare" (to pass/hand). The definite article "il" is used with this masculine singular noun.
target_language_example: Preferisco il burro sulla pasta, non la margarina.
native_language_example: I prefer butter on pasta, not margarine.

additional_notes: A food item: "burro" = butter and "arachidi" = peanuts. Usually used with the definite article "il" (e.g., "Mi piace il burro di arachidi").
target_language_example: Per colazione mangio pane con il burro di arachidi.
native_language_example: For breakfast I eat bread with peanut butter.

additional_notes: Masculine singular noun: il caffè. In Italy, “un caffè” typically means an espresso by default. Common phrases: “Prendo un caffè” (I’ll have a coffee), “Il caffè è caldo/freddo” (The coffee is hot/cold), “con/senza zucchero” (with/without sugar).
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere un caffè, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have a coffee, please?

additional_notes: Used to order or talk about a coffee that has milk added. It’s a normal noun phrase: il (the) + caffè (coffee) + con (with) + il latte (the milk). Often used with the verb bere (to drink), especially at breakfast.
target_language_example: Per colazione prendo il caffè con il latte.
native_language_example: For breakfast I have coffee with milk.

additional_notes: Used to describe the state or quality of the coffee, usually followed by an adjective (e.g., caldo = hot, forte = strong) or a past participle to describe a condition (e.g., finito = finished/there’s no coffee left). "È" is the 3rd-person singular of essere (to be).
target_language_example: Il caffè è troppo amaro.
native_language_example: The coffee is too bitter.

additional_notes: Used with the article to refer to the sport (common in phrases like guardare il calcio “watch soccer” or essere interessato al calcio “be interested in soccer”). Note: calcio can also mean “calcium” in scientific/medical contexts, and it can mean “kick” in other contexts, but in everyday conversation il calcio usually means the sport.
target_language_example: La domenica guardiamo il calcio in TV.
native_language_example: On Sundays we watch soccer on TV.

additional_notes: “Il calcio” means soccer (literally “kick”). “È” means “is”. Use “Il calcio è + noun/adjective” to give an opinion or description: Il calcio è bellissimo / noioso / uno sport popolare. Not normally used to mean the chemical “calcium” in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Il calcio è divertente, ma non lo seguo molto.
native_language_example: Soccer is fun, but I don’t follow it much.

meaning: the gate (usually a larger outdoor gate, often metal).
additional_notes: Used for a gate at an entrance (house, garden, driveway, courtyard, parking area). Common verbs: aprire/chiudere il cancello (open/close the gate), il cancello è chiuso a chiave (the gate is locked). Not the same as "porta" (door) or "cancello" meaning "I cancel" (verb: cancello).
target_language_example: Per favore, chiudi il cancello quando esci.
native_language_example: Please close the gate when you leave.

additional_notes: Definite article + noun: "il" = "the" (masculine singular) + "cane" = "dog". Used to talk about a specific dog (or dogs in general in some contexts). Plural: "i cani" (the dogs).
target_language_example: Dov'è il cane?
native_language_example: Where is the dog?

meaning: “the dog is” (Il = the, cane = dog, è = is).
additional_notes: Used to describe the dog’s state, quality, or location with the verb essere (“to be”): Il cane è stanco (tired), Il cane è in casa (in the house). In questions, the word order is usually the same and you add a question mark/intonation: Perché il cane è qui? Note: Italian cane (“dog”) is a false friend with English “cane” (walking stick).
target_language_example: Il cane è tranquillo oggi.
native_language_example: The dog is calm today.

meaning: the captain of the (team) for … / the team captain of …
additional_notes: Used to say who leads a sports team. It’s followed by the sport or the team type: "il capitano della squadra di pallacanestro" (basketball team captain), "... di wrestling/lotta" (wrestling team captain). You can also use it with a specific team: "il capitano della squadra di Milano" (captain of Milan’s team).
target_language_example: Lei è il capitano della squadra di calcio.
native_language_example: She is the captain of the soccer team.

meaning: the boss; the manager; the head (of a group/department).
additional_notes: Used for the person in charge at work (your boss/manager) or more generally the leader/head of a department, team, or organization. Common questions include “Lei è il capo?” (“Are you the boss?”).
target_language_example: Devo chiedere al capo se posso uscire prima oggi.
native_language_example: I have to ask the boss if I can leave early today.

additional_notes: Refers to a castle/fortified building or royal residence; often used with a specific name using “di” (e.g., il castello di Neuschwanstein).
target_language_example: Domani visitiamo il castello con una guida.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re visiting the castle with a guide.

additional_notes: Common in libraries, stores, and services for searching items (books, products, etc.) on the internet. It’s a noun phrase: il catalogo (catalog) + online (online). In a library context you’ll often hear it with verbs like usare/utilizzare (to use) and consultare (to look up).
target_language_example: Puoi cercare il titolo nel catalogo online della biblioteca.
native_language_example: You can search the title in the library’s online catalog.

additional_notes: Literal meaning: the organ in your head (the brain). Very often used figuratively to talk about someone’s intelligence or mental state. Common idioms in the examples: **avere il cervello di una gallina** (to be very stupid), **dare di volta il cervello** (to lose your mind / go crazy), **bruciarsi il cervello** (to rack your brain; to overthink until you’re exhausted), **bersi il cervello** (informal: to be out of your mind / have totally lost it).
target_language_example: Usa il cervello e pensaci bene prima di parlare.
native_language_example: Use your brain and think carefully before you speak.

additional_notes: Common general word for food as a thing in general (what you eat), especially in contexts like restaurants, cooking, or food quality/availability. It’s masculine singular: il cibo. For “foods” as different types/items, you’ll often see the plural i cibi.
target_language_example: Il cibo in questo ristorante è davvero buono.
native_language_example: The food in this restaurant is really good.

additional_notes: A noun phrase meaning food from Chinese cuisine. Often used with the verb "piacere" to talk about what you like (e.g., "Mi piace il cibo cinese" = "I like Chinese food"). You can add "in generale" (“in general”) or intensifiers like "molto" (“a lot”).
target_language_example: Ti piace il cibo cinese?
native_language_example: Do you like Chinese food?

additional_notes: A noun phrase meaning “Korean food/cuisine.” Used with the definite article: il cibo coreano. Common with verbs like piacere: Ti piace il cibo coreano? You can also say La cucina coreana (“Korean cuisine”), which sounds a bit more formal/restaurant-like.
target_language_example: Stasera mangiamo il cibo coreano.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re eating Korean food.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: il cibo = “the food” + giapponese = “Japanese.” Often used with piacere (“to like”) as in Ti/Le/Vi piace il cibo giapponese? (“Do you like Japanese food?”). With mancare (“to miss”), it means you will miss Japanese food: Il cibo giapponese ti mancherà (“You’ll miss Japanese food”).
target_language_example: Quando viaggio, mi manca il cibo giapponese.
native_language_example: When I travel, I miss Japanese food.

additional_notes: Used to talk about food with a “hot”/spicy flavor (like chili peppers). "Il" is the definite article (“the”); "piccante" agrees with "cibo" (masculine singular). You can also say "cibo molto piccante" for “very spicy food.”
target_language_example: Non posso mangiare il cibo piccante.
native_language_example: I can’t eat spicy food.

additional_notes: Refers to unhealthy, highly processed food (e.g., burgers, fries, chips, sweets). Often used with verbs like evitare (to avoid) or mangiare (to eat). In Italian, cibo is masculine, so you say il cibo spazzatura.
target_language_example: Dovremmo mangiare meno cibo spazzatura.
native_language_example: We should eat less junk food.

meaning: "the food is" (used to describe food or say what’s true about it).
additional_notes: Often followed by an adjective or a detail: Il cibo è buono/piccante/halal/incluso. You can use it to give an opinion (ottimo, terribile, sublime) or to state a fact (incluso). For plural, use: I cibi sono… (less common in restaurants).
target_language_example: Il cibo è buonissimo, ma un po' caro.
native_language_example: The food is very good, but a bit expensive.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “the sky” in everyday, literal contexts (weather, looking up): *Il cielo è nuvoloso/azzurro*. It can also mean “heaven” in religious or poetic contexts: *andare in cielo* (“to go to heaven”). Gender/number: masculine singular; plural *i cieli* (often poetic).
target_language_example: Oggi il cielo è molto azzurro.
native_language_example: Today the sky is very blue.

additional_notes: Used to describe the sky (weather, color, etc.). Depending on context, "il cielo" can also mean "heaven" in a religious or poetic sense (e.g., "il cielo è vuoto" = 'heaven is empty').
target_language_example: Il cielo è azzurro oggi.
native_language_example: The sky is blue today.

il cielo è pieno di stelle

target_language_multi_word_term: il cielo è pieno di stelle
additional_notes: A simple descriptive sentence you can use when talking about the night sky. "Il cielo" = "the sky"; "è pieno di" = "is full of"; "stelle" = "stars." Often paired with time words like "stanotte" (tonight) or "stasera" (this evening).
target_language_example: Qui in montagna il cielo è pieno di stelle.
native_language_example: Here in the mountains the sky is full of stars.

additional_notes: With "il" + adjective, Italian often names a language as a noun: "il cinese" = "Chinese". It’s used after verbs like "studiare" (to study), "parlare" (to speak), "scrivere" (to write), and "imparare" (to learn).
target_language_example: Sto imparando il cinese da sei mesi.
native_language_example: I’ve been learning Chinese for six months.

meaning: “the code” (a secret code, PIN/password, or program code).
additional_notes: Used with the definite article (il) to refer to a specific code already known from context. Common in situations like unlocking a phone/door (codice PIN / codice di accesso), cracking a cipher (decifrare il codice), or programming (scrivere il codice). Plural: i codici.
target_language_example: Mi dai il codice, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you give me the code, please?

meaning: the neck; the collar/neck part (of a shirt or bottle).
additional_notes: Most commonly means the body part (neck): *Mi fa male il collo* = “My neck hurts.” It can also mean the collar/neck opening of clothing or the neck of a bottle/container, depending on context (e.g., *Mettici dentro il collo* could refer to putting something into/through the neck/opening). In *prendere qualcuno per il collo*, it means “to grab someone by the neck.”
target_language_example: Ho il collo rigido stamattina.
native_language_example: My neck is stiff this morning.

additional_notes: Masculine noun (singular): il colore; plural: i colori. Used for colors in general or a specific shade: il colore rosso (the color red). Common in expressions like avere occhio per il colore (“to have an eye for color”).
target_language_example: Che colore preferisci per la maglietta?
native_language_example: What color do you prefer for the T-shirt?

additional_notes: "Coltello" is a masculine noun; the definite article is "il" (plural: "i coltelli"). Common with everyday actions like dropping it (far cadere), putting it away (mettere via), borrowing it (prestare), letting go of it (mollare), and sharpening it (affilare).
target_language_example: Puoi passarmi il coltello, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you pass me the knife, please?

additional_notes: A masculine noun with the definite article "il" (singular). Plural: "i computer" (often unchanged in Italian). Used for a PC/laptop in general; with "accendere/spegnere" (turn on/off), "lasciare acceso" (leave on), "riparare" (repair), "controllare" (check).
target_language_example: Ho lasciato il computer acceso tutta la notte.
native_language_example: I left the computer on all night.

additional_notes: A masculine singular noun phrase: *il* (the) + *concerto*. Used when talking about a specific concert; common with verbs like *andare bene* (to go well), *avere luogo* (to take place), *essere un successo* (to be a success), and *cominciare* (to start). Plural: *i concerti*.
target_language_example: A che ora finisce il concerto?
native_language_example: What time does the concert end?

meaning: "the concert is …" (used to say when it is, or that it has started/ended).
additional_notes: Use it with essere (è = “is”, past participle = “has”) to give information about a concert. With a time expression: “Il concerto è domenica/lunedì prossimo” = “The concert is next Sunday/Monday.” With a past participle: “Il concerto è cominciato/finito” = “The concert has started/ended.”
target_language_example: Il concerto è sabato sera alle otto.
native_language_example: The concert is Saturday evening at eight.

additional_notes: Often means the restaurant bill/check: "Porti il conto, per favore." It can also mean a count/number ("Ho perso il conto" = I’ve lost track of how many). In business/email contexts, "mandami il conto" can mean “send me the invoice/bill.”
target_language_example: Scusi, può portarmi il conto, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you bring me the bill, please?

meaning: 'The bill/check, please.' (asking to pay in a restaurant/café).
additional_notes: Used to ask for the bill at the end of a meal. You’ll often hear/see it with verbs like “portare” (to bring) or “dare” (to give): “Mi porta il conto, per favore?” In Italy “il conto” is the usual word; “l’assegno” is uncommon in this meaning. “Per favore” makes it polite.
target_language_example: Scusi, il conto, per favore.
native_language_example: Excuse me, the bill/check, please.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the reverse of what was said/expected (“it’s the other way around”). Often followed by **di + [noun/phrase]**: *il contrario di quello che...* (“the opposite of what…”). You can also use it alone for emphasis: *Tutto il contrario!* (“Quite the opposite!”).
target_language_example: No, è il contrario: oggi fa caldo, non freddo.
native_language_example: No, it’s the opposite: today it’s warm, not cold.

additional_notes: Used for a formal, written agreement (e.g., job, rental/lease, phone plan). Common verbs with it: firmare il contratto (to sign the contract), leggere il contratto (to read the contract), cambiare il contratto (to change/modify the contract). Gender/number: il contratto (sing.), i contratti (pl.).
target_language_example: Prima di firmare il contratto, voglio leggerlo bene.
native_language_example: Before signing the contract, I want to read it carefully.

additional_notes: Used with common verbs like: **avere il controllo (di/su)** = to have control (of/over); **prendere il controllo (di)** = to take control (of); **perdere il controllo** = to lose control (also emotionally/behaviorally); **stare perdendo il controllo** = to be losing control. With situations you often say **della situazione**; with things/people you often use **di** or **su**.
target_language_example: Devo prendere il controllo della situazione subito.
native_language_example: I need to take control of the situation right away.

additional_notes: A common noun used with the definite article (il). It can mean bravery in general (Il coraggio cresce con il pericolo) or the courage to do something, often with verbs like avere/trovare: avere il coraggio di… / trovare il coraggio di… = “to have/find the courage to…”.
target_language_example: Non ho il coraggio di dirglielo oggi.
native_language_example: I don’t have the courage to tell him/her today.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone has (or doesn’t have) the courage/bravery to do something: "avere il coraggio di..." / "non avere il coraggio di...". It can also be used more generally as "(avere) il coraggio" = "(to have) courage" without "di".
target_language_example: Non ho il coraggio di chiederglielo.
native_language_example: I don't have the courage to ask him/her.

additional_notes: A noun with the masculine singular article "il". Used in questions and statements about the virus, the illness, contagion, risk, and effects (e.g., "per il coronavirus" = "because of/from coronavirus").
target_language_example: Molte persone si preoccupano per il coronavirus.
native_language_example: Many people worry about the coronavirus.

meaning: the body; (in crime/news contexts) the corpse.
additional_notes: Usually means the physical body. In police reports or crime stories, "il corpo" often specifically means a dead body (a corpse), as in "Ha trovato il corpo" = "He/She found the body." Plural: "i corpi" (the bodies).
target_language_example: Hanno trovato il corpo vicino al fiume.
native_language_example: They found the body near the river.

additional_notes: A masculine singular noun used with the definite article "il": "il couscous". It refers to the food dish (often made from steamed semolina) and can be modified with an adjective or regional style, e.g. "il couscous cabilo" (Kabyle-style couscous).
target_language_example: Stasera mangiamo il couscous con le verdure.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re eating couscous with vegetables.

additional_notes: Very vulgar word for “butt,” common in strong idioms. Often appears in fixed expressions: “farsi/fare il culo” = to work extremely hard; “salvare il culo” = to save someone’s ass; “prendere per il culo” = to make fun of / mess with someone; “spaccare il culo (a qualcuno)” = to kick someone’s ass (threat); “leccare il culo (a qualcuno)” = to kiss someone’s ass (insult). Avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Mi hai salvato il culo, grazie!
native_language_example: You saved my ass, thanks!

additional_notes: Literally the physical heart. Very common in figurative expressions: “metterci il cuore” = to put your heart into something (do it with passion/care); “mi sanguina il cuore” = it breaks my heart / I feel deep pain or sadness about something.
target_language_example: Ha messo il cuore in questo progetto.
native_language_example: He/She put their heart into this project.

meaning: "the heart of" (the core/most important part of).
additional_notes: Used both literally (the physical heart) and very often figuratively to mean the central or most important part of something/someone: "il cuore di tutto" = "the heart of everything." You’ll also see it in fixed-style expressions like "cuore di pietra" (literally “heart of stone,” meaning a cold/unkind person). With verbs like "riempire" (to fill), Italian commonly says "riempire il cuore di + noun" = “to fill (someone’s) heart with + noun.”
target_language_example: Roma è il cuore d’Italia.
native_language_example: Rome is the heart of Italy.

additional_notes: Means “money” in a general sense, often referring to cash or an amount of funds. It’s more formal than "i soldi". Used with common verbs like avere (to have), prendere (to take/get), passare (to hand over), contare (to count).
target_language_example: Non ho il denaro per pagare adesso.
native_language_example: I don’t have the money to pay right now.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about money (il denaro = “money” as a concept; a bit more formal than i soldi). It’s followed by an adjective or noun phrase (e.g., importante, la mia priorità, un problema).
target_language_example: Il denaro è importante, ma non è tutto.
native_language_example: Money is important, but it’s not everything.

meaning: “the desire to be …” (wanting to become or be a certain way).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective or noun after essere (“to be”) to express an aspiration or goal: il desiderio di essere ricco/a (“the desire to be rich”), il desiderio di essere libero/a (“the desire to be free”). It agrees only in the following adjective/noun (ricco/ricca/ricchi/ricche), not in desiderio (which stays masculine singular here).
target_language_example: Ho il desiderio di essere più indipendente.
native_language_example: I have the desire to be more independent.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is entitled/allowed to do something, often in moral or legal contexts. It’s followed by an infinitive (e.g., "avere il diritto di sapere" = "to have the right to know"). With "non" it means someone does not have that right ("non hai il diritto di..."). Related: "diritto di voto" = "the right to vote."
target_language_example: Hai il diritto di dire di no.
native_language_example: You have the right to say no.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is entitled to receive information or an explanation (often in serious situations, e.g., privacy, personal decisions, legal/official matters). It commonly appears with verbs like "avere" (to have) and "pensare di avere" (to think you have).
target_language_example: Ho il diritto di sapere cosa sta succedendo.
native_language_example: I have the right to know what’s happening.

additional_notes: This phrase is typically used after a verb describing an accident or injury, especially with "tagliarsi" (to cut oneself): "Mi sono tagliato/a il dito con un coltello" = “I cut my finger with a knife.” Italian often uses "il" (the) where English uses "my" for body parts, and you add "mi/ti/si..." to show whose finger it is.
target_language_example: Mi sono tagliato il dito con un coltello mentre cucinavo.
native_language_example: I cut my finger with a knife while I was cooking.

additional_notes: A masculine singular noun. Use it for a book (or app/tool) you use to look up words and meanings. Often used with verbs like servire (to need), restituire (to return), and passare (to pass/hand). Plural: i dizionari.
target_language_example: Puoi prestarmi il dizionario per un momento?
native_language_example: Can you lend me the dictionary for a moment?

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to physical pain (e.g., after an injury), but it can also mean emotional pain or grief. Often used with verbs like "ignorare" (to ignore), "sopportare" (to endure/stand), and "ritornare" (to come back).
target_language_example: Non riesco più a sopportare il dolore.
native_language_example: I can’t stand the pain anymore.

additional_notes: Used to compare quantities or amounts. Common patterns: “essere il doppio di…” (to be twice as … as), “pagare il doppio” (to pay double), “il doppio del prezzo” (double the price). Often followed by “di” or “del/della/dei/degli/delle” depending on what comes next.
target_language_example: Oggi c’è il doppio della gente rispetto a ieri.
native_language_example: Today there are twice as many people as yesterday.

meaning: “Dr.” (Mr. Doctor) used before a man’s name.
additional_notes: Used as a title before a male doctor’s surname or full name (common in formal speech, hospitals, and introductions). It’s a shortened form of “il dottore.” For a woman you typically use “la dottoressa.” In Italy it can also be used for someone with a university degree, but in these examples it clearly refers to a medical doctor.
target_language_example: Mi scusi, dov’è l’ufficio del dottor Rossi?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is Dr. Rossi’s office?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male medical doctor. The feminine form is "la dottoressa". In Italy, "dottore" can also be used as a title for someone with a university degree (similar to “Dr.”), depending on context.
target_language_example: Scusi, dov'è lo studio del dottore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the doctor's office?

il dottore mi ha consigliato di

target_language_multi_word_term: il dottore mi ha consigliato di
meaning: 'the doctor advised/recommended that I...' / 'the doctor told me to...'.
additional_notes: Used to report medical advice. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (di + verb): "Il dottore mi ha consigliato di bere più acqua". The past tense "mi ha consigliato" means 'has advised'/'advised'.
target_language_example: Il dottore mi ha consigliato di riposare per qualche giorno.
native_language_example: The doctor advised me to rest for a few days.

meaning: 'the fact' (a fact/event; often used to introduce a clause: 'the fact that…').
additional_notes: Most commonly used as **il fatto che + [verb]** = “the fact that…”. It can refer to (1) an **objective fact** or **situation** (“the fact remains…”), or (2) a **specific incident/event** that can be confessed, reported, or brought to light (e.g., *confessare/denunciare il fatto*, *il fatto fu portato alla luce*). In *per il fatto che…*, it means “because/since…”.
target_language_example: Il fatto che tu sia qui oggi mi rende felice.
native_language_example: The fact that you are here today makes me happy.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause as a “fact” or reason, often after expressions like tenere in conto/accettare/negare/essere furioso per. The verb after che is frequently in the subjunctive (especially after emotions, opinions, or negation), but you may also see the indicative when stating something as objective.
target_language_example: Mi preoccupa il fatto che non risponda ai messaggi.
native_language_example: I’m worried about the fact that he/she isn’t replying to messages.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the key point or real explanation, often after a hesitation or as a correction/clarification. It’s common in spoken Italian to sound more natural or to soften what you’re about to say. It can be followed by a full sentence: “Il fatto è che + [sentence]”.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma il fatto è che oggi non posso venire.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but the fact is I can’t come today.

meaning: "the son of" (used to say who someone’s father/parent is).
additional_notes: Used to indicate family relationship or origin: "Lui è il figlio di Marco" = “He’s Marco’s son.” You’ll also commonly use it to introduce yourself: "Sono il figlio di…" or "Sono il figlio di un/una…" (with a job or description). For a daughter, use "la figlia di".
target_language_example: Ciao, sono il figlio di Laura.
native_language_example: Hi, I’m Laura’s son.

additional_notes: "Film" is a masculine noun; the singular definite article is "il". Used to talk about a specific movie already known from context. Plural: "i film" (same spelling).
target_language_example: Ti è piaciuto il film?
native_language_example: Did you like the movie?

additional_notes: Literally “the end of the week.” Used with the definite article (il) and often after prepositions like nel/il (on the weekend) or durante il (during the weekend). Common with verbs like trascorrere/passare (to spend) the weekend.
target_language_example: Cosa fai il fine settimana?
native_language_example: What do you do on the weekend?

additional_notes: Definite article + noun: il ("the") + fiume ("river"). Commonly used with expressions like lungo il fiume ("along the river") to talk about walking or places by the river. Plural: i fiumi ("the rivers").
target_language_example: Ci sediamo vicino al fiume e facciamo un picnic.
native_language_example: Let’s sit near the river and have a picnic.

additional_notes: Literal statement describing a river’s movement, often followed by where it flows: attraverso (through), tra/fra (between/among). Conjugation: scorrere → (lui/lei) scorre.
target_language_example: Il fiume scorre lentamente in primavera.
native_language_example: The river flows slowly in spring.

additional_notes: A common food noun. Uses the definite article "il" ("the") because "formaggio" is masculine singular. Often used generally (like English "cheese") or with a specific type: "il formaggio parmigiano", "il formaggio di capra".
target_language_example: Vorrei un panino con il formaggio, per favore.
native_language_example: I'd like a sandwich with cheese, please.

additional_notes: Uses the definite article (il) to talk about the language in general: Mi piace il francese (I like French). With parlare/studiare/imparare, you can say parlare/studiare/imparare il francese (“to speak/study/learn French”). Not the person from France—that’s un francese / una francese.
target_language_example: Studio il francese da sei mesi.
native_language_example: I’ve been studying French for six months.

additional_notes: Used at the end of a sentence to check/confirm something you believe is true. Here it refers to the language ("il francese" = French). Often equivalent to English "..., right?" / "..., correct?".
target_language_example: Tu parli il francese, giusto?
native_language_example: You speak French, right?

meaning: 'French at school' (as a subject you study/learn).
additional_notes: Used when talking about studying the French language as a school subject. Italian often uses the definite article with languages (il francese, l’italiano, lo spagnolo). With verbs like imparare/studiare, it means you learn/study French at school.
target_language_example: Ho studiato il francese a scuola, ma ora lo parlo poco.
native_language_example: I studied French at school, but now I don’t speak it much.

additional_notes: Basic pattern for describing a language: **Il/Lo/La + [language] + è una lingua + (adjective)**. You can add an adjective (e.g., *affascinante, difficile*) or make it a question: *Il francese è una lingua difficile da imparare?*
target_language_example: Il francese è una lingua molto utile per viaggiare.
native_language_example: French is a very useful language for traveling.

meaning: fire; a fire (flames, or a campfire).
additional_notes: Usually refers to actual flames (e.g., a fire you light with wood: accendere il fuoco). It can also be used in comparisons to mean something very dangerous or feared (temere qualcuno/qualcosa come il fuoco = to fear someone/something like fire).
target_language_example: Non avvicinarti: il fuoco è ancora acceso.
native_language_example: Don’t get close: the fire is still lit.

additional_notes: Refers to the time that will come after now. Used in general statements (Guardare verso il futuro), predictions (prevedere il futuro), or talking about what will happen later (Per il futuro...). It can also be used alone as a question (“Il futuro?” = “The future?”).
target_language_example: Dobbiamo pensare al futuro e fare un piano.
native_language_example: We have to think about the future and make a plan.

additional_notes: Masculine singular noun with the definite article: il gatto = “the (male) cat,” but it’s also the default for “the cat” in general. Plural: i gatti (“the cats”). In the idiomatic expression «Vi è morto il gatto?» it literally means “Did the cat die there?”, used humorously to suggest a place smells bad.
target_language_example: Il gatto dorme sul divano.
native_language_example: The cat is sleeping on the couch.

meaning: "the cat is" (and in some past tenses: "the cat has").
additional_notes: Uses the verb "essere" (to be): "è" = "is". It describes the cat’s state/quality/location (e.g., "Il gatto è al sicuro" = The cat is safe; "Il gatto è sulla sedia" = The cat is on the chair). With some verbs in the passato prossimo, Italian uses "essere" as the helper, so you’ll see patterns like "Il gatto è corso via" = The cat ran away (literally "is run away").
target_language_example: Il gatto è in giardino.
native_language_example: The cat is in the garden.

additional_notes: A masculine singular noun with the definite article: il gelato (“the ice cream”). Often used when talking about ice cream in general (as a category) or a specific ice cream you mean in context. Plural: i gelati (“the ice creams/ice creams”).
target_language_example: Vorrei un gelato al cioccolato, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a chocolate ice cream, please.

additional_notes: A specific flavor of gelato. Use it when saying what you like/prefer or asking someone’s preference (Mi piace…?/Ti piace…?/Vi piace…?). In Italian menus, “al + ingredient” often means “flavored with” or “made with” that ingredient.
target_language_example: Per dessert, prendo il gelato al cioccolato.
native_language_example: For dessert, I’ll have chocolate ice cream.

meaning: the Saharan cheetah (a cheetah living in the Sahara).
additional_notes: A specific animal name: *ghepardo* = “cheetah” and *sahariano* = “Saharan” (from/related to the Sahara). Used in a descriptive/scientific context, often when talking about rarity and extinction (*in via di estinzione*).
target_language_example: Il ghepardo sahariano vive nel deserto del Sahara.
native_language_example: The Saharan cheetah lives in the Sahara Desert.

additional_notes: A masculine singular noun meaning frozen water. Often used in everyday situations (e.g., asking for or bringing ice). Common simile: “freddo/a come il ghiaccio” = “as cold as ice.”
target_language_example: Puoi mettere il ghiaccio nel bicchiere, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you put ice in the glass, please?

additional_notes: Uses the definite article (il) because it refers to a language. It can also mean “the Japanese person/man” depending on context, but in these examples it clearly means the language you study/speak.
target_language_example: Parli il giapponese?
native_language_example: Do you speak Japanese?

additional_notes: Used for a game in general (board game, video game, etc.) or for a sports game/match. With sports on TV, you can say "vedere il gioco" = "watch the game". Common phrases: "Il gioco è finito" = "The game is over"; "perdere il gioco" = "to lose the game".
target_language_example: Non posso uscire: devo finire il gioco.
native_language_example: I can’t go out: I have to finish the game.

additional_notes: Usually means a daily newspaper (print or digital) you read for news. With the definite article (il), it often refers to a specific one in context (e.g., the one at home, or the one you usually read). You can also say "un giornale" for "a newspaper."
target_language_example: Ho comprato il giornale in edicola.
native_language_example: I bought the newspaper at the newsstand.

additional_notes: Literally "il" (the) + "giorno" (day). In Italian, you often use the definite article without a preposition to mean "on" a specific day/event: "il giorno di Natale" = "on Christmas Day". It can also be followed by adjectives to specify which day: "il giorno successivo" = "the following day".
target_language_example: Ci vediamo il giorno dopo.
native_language_example: See you the next day.

meaning: the next day; the day after.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the day following a specific event or a day already mentioned (often like “the next day” in a story). It can also mean “the day after” something: e.g., Il giorno dopo la festa = the day after the party.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo domani; il giorno dopo, invece, sono impegnato.
native_language_example: See you tomorrow; the next day, though, I’m busy.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that specifies which day you mean: il giorno in cui + (event/action). It can refer to a specific remembered day (Ricordo il giorno in cui...), a scheduled day (Il giorno in cui arrivo...), or a future day that will come (Arriverà il giorno in cui...). Similar to "il giorno che" in some contexts, but "in cui" is very common in standard Italian.
target_language_example: Non dimenticherò mai il giorno in cui abbiamo traslocato.
native_language_example: I’ll never forget the day we moved.

meaning: the government; also 'government' as a form/system of rule.
additional_notes: Most often means the national government/administration (the people in power). It can also refer more generally to how a country is governed (e.g., democracy as a form of government). Gender/number: masculine singular; plural is "i governi".
target_language_example: Il governo ha annunciato nuove misure economiche.
native_language_example: The government announced new economic measures.

additional_notes: Definite article + noun: *il* + *jazz* = “the jazz.” In Italian you typically use the article when talking about musical genres in general: *Mi piace il jazz* (“I like jazz”). Used with verbs like *amare* (to love) and *ascoltare* (to listen to).
target_language_example: A casa ascolto spesso il jazz.
native_language_example: At home I often listen to jazz.

additional_notes: A masculine noun used with the article (il). It’s a loanword and is usually invariable in Italian (often just "ketchup" in both singular and plural). Common in requests at the table: "Passami il ketchup" (informal, to a friend) vs. "Mi passa il ketchup?" / "Passi il ketchup" (more polite/formal).
target_language_example: Mi passi il ketchup, per favore?
native_language_example: Could you pass me the ketchup, please?

additional_notes: Masculine singular noun phrase: il ("the") + ladro ("thief"). Used for someone who steals. Plural: i ladri (the thieves). Feminine form: la ladra (the female thief). In Italian it’s common to stress identity with phrases like “Non sono io il ladro” (I’m not the thief) or “È lui il ladro!” (He’s the thief!).
target_language_example: Il ladro ha rubato il mio portafoglio.
native_language_example: The thief stole my wallet.

additional_notes: Refers to the Latin language, often in the context of studying it at school or reading Latin texts. As a language name in Italian, it usually takes the definite article: il latino.
target_language_example: Sto studiando il latino per l'esame.
native_language_example: I'm studying Latin for the exam.

additional_notes: Definite article + noun: "il" (the) + "latte" (milk). Used for milk as a food/drink, and in phrases like "con il latte" (with milk) or "senza latte" (without milk).
target_language_example: Vorrei un caffè con il latte, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a coffee with milk, please.

additional_notes: Used to describe milk or give information about it. **Il latte** = “the milk” (definite article **il** + noun **latte**). **È** is the 3rd-person singular of **essere** (“to be”): *è caldo* (it’s hot), *è liquido* (it’s liquid). Note: Italian **latte** means “milk,” which can be confusing because English “latte” usually means a coffee drink.
target_language_example: Il latte è scaduto.
native_language_example: The milk is expired.

additional_notes: Used for both (1) a specific task to do (fare il lavoro, finire il lavoro) and (2) a job/employment (trovare il lavoro, ottenere il lavoro, abbandonare il lavoro). Masculine singular with the definite article: il lavoro = “the work/the job.”
target_language_example: Devo finire il lavoro prima di cena.
native_language_example: I have to finish the work before dinner.

meaning: the “dirty work” (unpleasant, difficult, or morally questionable tasks).
additional_notes: Used when someone does the tasks others don’t want to do, often because they’re messy, risky, or unethical. Common with verbs like fare (“to do”) or lasciare fare a qualcuno (“let someone do”).
target_language_example: Non voglio farlo io: lascia che sia lui a fare il lavoro sporco.
native_language_example: I don’t want to do it: let him do the dirty work.

meaning: “the bed”; often “(to) bed” in phrases like “andare a letto” (to go to bed).
additional_notes: Literally “the bed” (masculine singular: il + letto). In everyday Italian it’s very common in expressions about sleeping/going to sleep: “andare a letto” = to go to bed, “essere pronto/a per il letto” = to be ready for bed. Can also mean the physical bed (the piece of furniture).
target_language_example: Sono stanco: vado a letto.
native_language_example: I’m tired: I’m going to bed.

additional_notes: "Il" is the masculine singular definite article (“the”), used before many masculine singular nouns. "Libro" means “book.” Used for a specific book known from context. In commands like "Chiuda il libro!" it means “Close the book!” (formal/Lei form).
target_language_example: Dov'è il libro?
native_language_example: Where is the book?

additional_notes: Used to identify/specify a particular book by adding extra information after it. "che" here means "that/which" and can be followed by a verb (e.g., "che ho comprato") or by a clause with an object pronoun (e.g., "che mi avete dato" = "that you gave me").
target_language_example: Il libro che hai consigliato è già esaurito.
native_language_example: The book that you recommended is already sold out.

additional_notes: Il = “the” (masculine singular). Libro = “book.” È is the 3rd person singular of essere (“to be”) and is used for descriptions (Il libro è fantastico.) or to ask where/with whom something is (Il libro è con te? = “Is the book with you?”). Note the accent: è (“is”) vs e (“and”).
target_language_example: Il libro è sul tavolo.
native_language_example: The book is on the table.

additional_notes: Used for legal/posted maximum driving speed. Common with verbs like rispettare (to respect/obey) and superare (to exceed): “superare il limite di velocità” = “to go over the speed limit.”
target_language_example: Non superare il limite di velocità: qui è 50 km/h.
native_language_example: Don’t exceed the speed limit: it’s 50 km/h here.

additional_notes: Used to refer to sign language as a whole (a way of communicating with hand signs), often with the verb "conoscere" (to know). In Italy you may also see "LIS" (Lingua dei Segni Italiana) for Italian Sign Language.
target_language_example: Mio fratello conosce il linguaggio dei segni.
native_language_example: My brother knows sign language.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: il loro treno (their train), il loro caffè (their coffee), il loro segreto (their secret), il loro eroe (their hero). It agrees with the noun owned, not with the owners. Other forms: la loro (fem. sing.), i loro (masc. pl.), le loro (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Ho visto il loro cane al parco.
native_language_example: I saw their dog at the park.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a dog that belongs to more than one person (e.g., a couple or a family). "Loro" is the plural possessive adjective (“their”) and it doesn’t change for gender/number of what’s owned, but the article does: il loro cane (their dog), i loro cani (their dogs).
target_language_example: Ho visto il loro cane nel giardino.
native_language_example: I saw their dog in the yard.

additional_notes: "Il" = “the” (masculine singular), "loro" = “their” (same form for masculine/feminine and singular/plural things), "lavoro" = “work/job” (singular). Used to talk about the work/job that belongs to “them” (a group). Often appears with verbs like "amare" (to love), "piacere" (to like), and "finire" (to finish).
target_language_example: Hanno fatto il loro lavoro con cura.
native_language_example: They did their work carefully.

additional_notes: Used to describe what a group of people’s job or task consists of. Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., chiamare, costruire, lavare) or sometimes by "di" + infinitive in more formal/older usage ("Il loro lavoro è di aggiungere...").
target_language_example: Il loro lavoro è controllare le prenotazioni ogni mattina.
native_language_example: Their job is to check the reservations every morning.

meaning: on Mondays; on Monday (as a regular day).
additional_notes: Used to talk about what someone usually does on Mondays (habit/routine). In Italian, days of the week often take the definite article (il, la) when you mean “on (that day) regularly.” Without the article (e.g., “lunedì”), it can refer to a specific Monday depending on context.
target_language_example: Il lunedì vado in palestra dopo lavoro.
native_language_example: On Mondays I go to the gym after work.

additional_notes: Means the specific place where people have agreed to meet. Uses the French loanword “rendez-vous,” which in Italian can sound a bit dramatic or “spy-movie-like” compared to the common words “appuntamento” or “incontro.” Often used with verbs like: sapere/dare (know/give) il luogo, trovare (find) il luogo, essere (be) lo stesso di sempre (be the same as always).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alle otto: il luogo del rendez-vous è davanti alla stazione.
native_language_example: See you at eight: the meeting place is in front of the station.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "Ho il mal di stomaco" = "I have a stomachache." Often shortened in speech to "mal di stomaco" without the article.
target_language_example: Ho il mal di stomaco da ieri sera.
native_language_example: I’ve had a stomachache since last night.

additional_notes: Literally “the pain of head.” Most often used with the verb avere (“to have”): Ho il mal di testa. You can also use venire (“to come on”): Mi viene il mal di testa (“I’m getting a headache”).
target_language_example: Ho il mal di testa, posso prendere un'aspirina?
native_language_example: I have a headache—can I take an aspirin?

additional_notes: Masculine singular noun: il mare. Used for the sea/ocean in general or the sea you can see from a place (e.g., “Vedi il mare?”). Common with adjectives to describe conditions: mare calmo (calm sea), mare agitato (rough sea).
target_language_example: D'estate andiamo spesso al mare.
native_language_example: In summer we often go to the seaside.

additional_notes: Usually means the institution/status of being married (“marriage”), but it can also refer to the wedding ceremony/celebration (“the wedding”), depending on context. Gendered noun: il matrimonio (plural: i matrimoni).
target_language_example: Quando è il matrimonio di tua sorella?
native_language_example: When is your sister’s wedding?

additional_notes: Common way to say “the doctor” in general. In specific contexts you may hear more precise phrases like “il medico di famiglia” (family doctor/GP) or “il medico legale” (forensic doctor/medical examiner). Often used with “chiamare” (to call) when someone needs medical help.
target_language_example: Se stai male, chiama il medico.
native_language_example: If you feel sick, call the doctor.

additional_notes: Used as a noun phrase. Common patterns: "Auguro a X il meglio" = "I wish X the best"; "fare il meglio di ..." = "to make the best of ..."; "essere il meglio" = "to be the best" (often about people/things you consider the best).
target_language_example: Ti auguro il meglio per il tuo nuovo lavoro.
native_language_example: I wish you the best for your new job.

additional_notes: Used before verbs like "può" (can) or "riesce" (manages/succeeds) to say someone is doing as well as possible given the circumstances: "Fare il meglio che puoi" = "Do the best you can." It often expresses effort and limitation (they’re trying hard, even if results aren’t perfect).
target_language_example: Sto facendo il meglio che posso.
native_language_example: I'm doing the best I can.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening in the month after the current one. It can go at the beginning or end of the sentence (e.g., "Il mese prossimo parto..." / "Parto... il mese prossimo").
target_language_example: Il mese prossimo iniziamo il corso di italiano.
native_language_example: Next month we start the Italian course.

additional_notes: Time expression used to say something happened in the previous month. It often comes at the end of the sentence, but it can also be placed at the beginning for emphasis (e.g., "Il mese scorso, ...").
target_language_example: Il mese scorso ho iniziato un nuovo lavoro.
native_language_example: Last month I started a new job.

additional_notes: Used for a spoken, written, or digital communication (e.g., a note, announcement, text/DM). It’s masculine singular; plural: i messaggi.
target_language_example: Ti mando il messaggio più tardi.
native_language_example: I’ll send you the message later.

meaning: the best (masculine singular, before a noun).
additional_notes: Short form of "il migliore" used before a masculine singular noun (e.g., "il miglior posto", "il miglior modo"). You can also use the fuller form "il migliore" after the noun or on its own (e.g., "Questo posto è il migliore").
target_language_example: È il miglior ristorante della città.
native_language_example: It’s the best restaurant in the city.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun: "il mio libro" = "my book". Italian possessives agree with the thing owned (not the owner): il mio (m. sing.), la mia (f. sing.), i miei (m. pl.), le mie (f. pl.). When the noun is understood, "il mio" can stand alone and mean "mine" (e.g., "Il mio è qui" = "Mine is here"). With singular family members you usually drop the article: "mio padre", "mia sorella" (but you may hear "il mio" for emphasis).
target_language_example: Dov'è il mio telefono?
native_language_example: Where is my phone?

additional_notes: Used before the platform/service name: "il mio account di Facebook/Instagram/Google". In Italian, "account" is commonly used (especially for online services). You’ll often see it with verbs like "controllare" (to check), "cancellare" (to delete), "creare" (to create), "accedere al" (to log in to).
target_language_example: Domani voglio cambiare la password del mio account di Google.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I want to change the password of my Google account.

additional_notes: Used when someone wants, asks for, or needs your help: "Vuoi il mio aiuto?" = "Do you want my help?". Note that aiuto is masculine (il), so the possessive is mio (not mia). You can also use it after verbs like chiedere (to ask for) and volere (to want).
target_language_example: Se hai bisogno, posso darti il mio aiuto.
native_language_example: If you need it, I can give you my help.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a friend who is male (or when "amico" is used as the default masculine form). It’s a noun phrase: "il" (the) + "mio" (my) + "amico" (friend). For a female friend, you usually say "la mia amica". In the plural: "i miei amici" (my friends, mixed/masculine) and "le mie amiche" (my friends, all female).
target_language_example: Domani esco con il mio amico.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going out with my friend.

additional_notes: Used to describe your (male) friend with an adjective (Il mio amico è loquace), a nationality/profession/noun (Il mio amico è indiano / medico), or a location (Il mio amico è qui). "è" is the 3rd-person singular of "essere" (to be). For a female friend: "la mia amica è"; for plural: "i miei amici sono" / "le mie amiche sono".
target_language_example: Il mio amico è molto gentile.
native_language_example: My friend is very kind.

meaning: "my love" (a term of affection; also "my love" for something).
additional_notes: Used either as (1) a romantic/affectionate way to refer to a person (similar to “my love/darling”), or (2) to talk about the love you feel for someone or something: “il mio amore per …” = “my love for …”. With a person, Italian often uses the vocative without the article: “Amore mio!” or “Mio amore!”.
target_language_example: Amore mio, mi sei mancato tanto.
native_language_example: My love, I missed you so much.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your own lawyer. Often appears with verbs like chiamare (to call) and parlare con (to speak with). In formal/polite speech you may use the imperative form with Lei: "Parli con il mio avvocato" (Speak with my lawyer).
target_language_example: Prima di firmare, voglio parlare con il mio avvocato.
native_language_example: Before signing, I want to speak with my lawyer.

additional_notes: Means “my child,” often referring to a baby or small child; grammatically masculine singular (bambino). It can also be used affectionately about someone even if they aren’t literally a baby, depending on context. For a girl, you’ll often hear “la mia bambina.”
target_language_example: Dov'è il mio bambino? Non lo trovo.
native_language_example: Where is my child? I can’t find him.

additional_notes: Literally “the my dog,” but in Italian you normally use a definite article (il/lo/la/i/gli/le) before a possessive + noun: il mio cane, la mia casa. Here it’s masculine singular (cane), so you use il mio. Plural: i miei cani (“my dogs”).
target_language_example: Non trovo il mio cane: l’hai visto?
native_language_example: I can’t find my dog—have you seen him?

additional_notes: Used to describe your dog with an adjective or phrase after è (from essere, “to be”). The adjective usually agrees with cane (masculine singular): grande, malato, pulito. You can then add more information (e.g., with con = “with” or a reason/question).
target_language_example: Il mio cane è molto amichevole con i bambini.
native_language_example: My dog is very friendly with children.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your supervisor at work. "Capo" can also mean "head" (body part) in other contexts, but with a possessive like "il mio" and in work situations it usually means "boss". To make it feminine, you can say "la mia capa" (common) or "la mia capo" (also used).
target_language_example: Devo parlarne con il mio capo prima di decidere.
native_language_example: I have to talk about it with my boss before deciding.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a hat that belongs to you. Often appears with questions like Le/A lei piace...? (“Do you like...?”) and with verbs like mettere (“to put”), perdere (“to lose”), and trovare (“to find”).
target_language_example: Non riesco a trovare il mio cappello.
native_language_example: I can’t find my hat.

additional_notes: Means you own/are responsible for the horse. "Il" is “the” (masculine singular), "mio" is “my,” and "cavallo" is “horse.” You can change the possessive: "il tuo cavallo" (your horse), "il suo cavallo" (his/her horse).
target_language_example: Dov'è il mio cavallo?
native_language_example: Where is my horse?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the date of your birthday or the day when you celebrate it. Often with "essere" for dates/time ("Il mio compleanno è a novembre") or in the past ("è stato lunedì scorso"). It can also be an object of verbs like "dimenticare/scordare" (to forget).
target_language_example: Il mio compleanno è domani, vuoi venire alla festa?
native_language_example: My birthday is tomorrow—do you want to come to the party?

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: il (the) + mio (my) + computer. Use it to talk about your own computer in everyday situations, often with verbs like funzionare (to work), rompersi (to break), smettere di funzionare (to stop working), and (informally) piantarsi (to freeze/crash).
target_language_example: Non posso lavorare: il mio computer non si accende.
native_language_example: I can’t work: my computer won’t turn on.

additional_notes: Literally “the my portable computer.” Use it to talk about your own laptop; Italian normally uses the definite article (il) with possessives before a noun (il mio, la mia, i miei, le mie). You can also just say “il mio portatile” if the context is clear.
target_language_example: Non trovo il mio computer portatile; l’ho lasciato in ufficio.
native_language_example: I can’t find my laptop; I left it at the office.

meaning: 'my computer is …' (used to describe or locate your computer).
additional_notes: Use it to start a sentence giving information about your computer. Follow with an adjective (Il mio computer è caro. = My computer is expensive), a place/ownership phrase (Il mio computer è con mio fratello. = My computer is with my brother), or other information. Often you’ll just say “Il mio computer è …” and then add what it’s like/where it is.
target_language_example: Il mio computer è in ufficio.
native_language_example: My computer is in the office.

additional_notes: Used when you’re offering your opinion on what someone should do. Common patterns: chiedere il mio consiglio (to ask for my advice), ignorare il mio consiglio (to ignore my advice), Il mio consiglio è di + infinitive / sarebbe + infinitive (My advice is/would be to…).
target_language_example: Se vuoi, il mio consiglio è di parlarne con calma.
native_language_example: If you want, my advice is to talk about it calmly.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your physical body (health, movement, age, fatigue). Often contrasts with non-physical parts like "il mio spirito" (my spirit). Can also be used in serious contexts (e.g., what happens to someone’s body after death).
target_language_example: Dopo la corsa, il mio corpo era stanchissimo.
native_language_example: After the run, my body was completely exhausted.

meaning: "my heart" (literally); often used to express feelings, love, or what you truly believe.
additional_notes: Used both literally (the physical heart) and figuratively to talk about emotions, intuition, or sincere thoughts (e.g., "follow my heart"). It can also express sympathy/solidarity ("My heart goes out to you") or loyalty to a team/cause ("my heart is green and yellow").
target_language_example: Quando sono indeciso, seguo il mio cuore.
native_language_example: When I'm unsure, I follow my heart.

meaning: "my heart forever" (a romantic way to say you’ll love someone forever).
additional_notes: Often used in emotional/romantic contexts, usually with verbs like dare (“to give”): dare il mio cuore per sempre = “to give my heart forever.” In your examples, the word before it changes depending on who you’re giving it to: darti (to you, informal singular), darle (to you, formal singular / to her), darvi (to you all / to you, formal plural).
target_language_example: Ti darò il mio cuore per sempre.
native_language_example: I’ll give you my heart forever.

additional_notes: Means money that belongs to the speaker. Often used when talking about earning money (lavorare per il mio denaro) or demanding it back (rivoglio il mio denaro). Similar alternatives: "i miei soldi" is more common in everyday speech; "denaro" can sound a bit more formal than "soldi".
target_language_example: Non voglio sprecare il mio denaro.
native_language_example: I don't want to waste my money.

additional_notes: Uses the definite article (il) with the possessive (mio): in Italian you usually say "il mio..." (not just "mio...") with singular nouns like "dizionario". It’s used to talk about your own dictionary (a book or dictionary app).
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato il mio dizionario a casa.
native_language_example: I forgot my dictionary at home.

additional_notes: Used to admit or point out that you are responsible for something done wrong. Often said as an apology or correction (similar to English “my mistake”). You can also vary it by person: il tuo errore (your mistake), il suo errore (his/her mistake), il nostro errore (our mistake).
target_language_example: Scusa, è stato il mio errore.
native_language_example: Sorry, it was my mistake.

additional_notes: "Fidanzato" is a male romantic partner. It can mean "boyfriend" or "fiancé" depending on the relationship and context (often "engaged" in more formal contexts). The feminine form is "la mia fidanzata". You can swap "mio" for other possessives: "il tuo fidanzato" (your boyfriend/fiancé), "il suo fidanzato" (her/his boyfriend/fiancé).
target_language_example: Stasera esco con il mio fidanzato.
native_language_example: Tonight I'm going out with my boyfriend/fiancé.

additional_notes: Means your brother who is younger than you. In everyday Italian, with singular family members you usually *don’t* use the article: **mio fratello minore** (not *il mio...*). **Il mio** can be used for emphasis/contrast (e.g., “*my* younger brother, not yours”). Word order: **fratello minore** = younger brother; **fratello maggiore** = older brother.
target_language_example: Mio fratello minore studia all'università.
native_language_example: My younger brother studies at university.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: il (the, masculine singular) + mio (my, masculine singular) + gatto (cat). Used when talking about your own cat; in questions like “Avete visto…?” it means you’re asking if someone has seen it.
target_language_example: Il mio gatto si chiama Leo.
native_language_example: My cat’s name is Leo.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective or description after è ("is"). Since gatto is masculine singular, adjectives usually end in -o (e.g., timido, affamato, felice). You can replace il mio gatto with another subject (e.g., "il mio cane è…").
target_language_example: Il mio gatto è stanco oggi.
native_language_example: My cat is tired today.

additional_notes: Use it to introduce something you do for fun. It’s followed by either an infinitive verb (e.g., collezionare, nuotare, suonare) or a noun with an article (e.g., la pesca, lo shopping).
target_language_example: Il mio hobby è cucinare piatti italiani.
native_language_example: My hobby is cooking Italian dishes.

additional_notes: Impiego means a job/position (employment), often a bit more formal than lavoro. It’s commonly used when talking about your job duties, requirements, or workplace situation (e.g., needing a language for work, wanting to quit).
target_language_example: Ho trovato il mio impiego tramite un annuncio online.
native_language_example: I found my job through an online ad.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male teacher you have/had. In Italian, possessives usually need the definite article: il mio insegnante. For a female teacher: la mia insegnante. Plural: i miei insegnanti (male/mixed), le mie insegnanti (female).
target_language_example: Il mio insegnante mi ha aiutato con i compiti.
native_language_example: My teacher helped me with my homework.

additional_notes: Use **insegnante di + subject** to say who teaches you a particular subject: **il mio insegnante di inglese** = “my English teacher.” **Insegnante** can be masculine or feminine; the article/possessive changes: **il mio insegnante** (male teacher), **la mia insegnante** (female teacher).
target_language_example: Il mio insegnante di matematica spiega molto bene.
native_language_example: My math teacher explains really well.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the person who teaches you French. It’s built from: il (the) + mio (my) + insegnante (teacher) + di francese (of French). You can swap the subject/possessive and the language, e.g. "il tuo insegnante di inglese" (your English teacher).
target_language_example: Il mio insegnante di francese è molto paziente.
native_language_example: My French teacher is very patient.

additional_notes: Means a laptop computer that belongs to the speaker. "Il" = "the" (masculine singular), "mio" = "my" (masculine singular). You can change the possessive (e.g., "il tuo laptop" = "your laptop").
target_language_example: Non trovo il mio laptop; l'hai visto?
native_language_example: I can’t find my laptop; have you seen it?

additional_notes: Used to talk about your occupation or the work you’re doing. Often appears with essere (Questo è il mio lavoro = This is my job) or andare (Il mio lavoro sta andando bene = My work is going well). You can also use it to mean your task/project: Il mio lavoro non è ancora completo = My work isn’t finished yet.
target_language_example: Scusa, devo finire il mio lavoro prima di uscire.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to finish my work before going out.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what your job/duty is (followed by an infinitive like "pulire") or to say the state of your work (followed by a past participle like "finito/terminato"). In conversation, Italians also commonly say "Il mio lavoro è quello di..." (My job is to...) or simply "Faccio..." (I do/I work as...).
target_language_example: Il mio lavoro è aiutare i clienti.
native_language_example: My job is to help customers.

additional_notes: Used to indicate possession: il (the) + mio (my) + libro (book). The possessive usually comes after the noun in Italian, and it normally needs the definite article (il/lo/la/i/gli/le): e.g., il mio libro, la mia borsa. In questions you may hear it with rising intonation: “È/Questo è il mio libro?”
target_language_example: Scusi, dov’è il mio libro?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is my book?

additional_notes: Used to refer to your closest friend who is male. For a female best friend, say “la mia migliore amica”. The word order is fixed: “il mio” + “migliore” + “amico”. Often used with “è” to describe who/where your best friend is (e.g., “è a Roma”, “è canadese”).
target_language_example: Il mio migliore amico vive a Milano.
native_language_example: My best friend lives in Milan.

additional_notes: Used to introduce information about your best friend (a place, nationality, adjective, or a noun): *Il mio migliore amico è a Roma / canadese / un medico.* Since **amico** is masculine, this refers to a male friend; for a female friend say **la mia migliore amica è**. You can also use plural: **i miei migliori amici sono** (“my best friends are”).
target_language_example: Il mio migliore amico è molto simpatico.
native_language_example: My best friend is very nice.

additional_notes: Used to identify yourself or refer to your own name. Often appears in common phrases like "Il mio nome è..." (My name is...), or in questions like "Come sai il mio nome?" (How do you know my name?) and "Conosci il mio nome?" (Do you know my name?).
target_language_example: Ciao, il mio nome è Marco.
native_language_example: Hi, my name is Marco.

additional_notes: Used to introduce yourself and say your name. Often followed directly by your name: “Il mio nome è + [Name].” In everyday conversation, Italians also commonly say “Mi chiamo + [Name]” (I’m called…).
target_language_example: Ciao, il mio nome è Emily.
native_language_example: Hi, my name is Emily.

meaning: "my number" (a specific number, or my phone number).
additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective mio with the definite article il: il mio + noun. In context it can mean a favorite/lucky number (e.g., "il mio numero preferito") or, very commonly, your phone number when giving contact details (often said as "Questo è il mio numero").
target_language_example: Ti mando il mio numero così mi puoi chiamare.
native_language_example: I’ll send you my number so you can call me.

meaning: "my new" (masculine singular; used before a noun).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun to say something belongs to you and is new. Word order is: article + mio + nuovo + noun (e.g., il mio nuovo cappello). If the noun is feminine, you’ll use la mia nuova; if it’s plural, i miei nuovi / le mie nuove.
target_language_example: Ti presento il mio nuovo collega.
native_language_example: Let me introduce you to my new coworker.

additional_notes: Used to state a personal aim or purpose. It’s often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., imparare, diventare, parlare, essere). You may also see: “Il mio obiettivo è quello di + infinitive” (a slightly more formal/explicit structure). Note: both “Il mio obiettivo è diventare…” and “Il mio obiettivo è di diventare…” are heard, but the most standard form is without “di”.
target_language_example: Il mio obiettivo è imparare l’italiano entro l’estate.
native_language_example: My goal is to learn Italian by the summer.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: definite article + mio + noun (masculine singular). Used when talking about your own umbrella, often in situations like losing it, leaving it somewhere, or someone else still having it. In Italian, the article (il) is normally used with possessives (il mio, la mia, i miei, le mie), except with most singular family members (e.g., mia madre).
target_language_example: Scusi, questo è il mio ombrello?
native_language_example: Excuse me, is this my umbrella?

additional_notes: Means “my timepiece.” In everyday Italian, orologio can refer to a wristwatch or a clock; context makes it clear. You often see it in phrases about keeping time, e.g. perde due minuti al giorno (“it loses two minutes a day”) and è indietro di dieci minuti (“it’s ten minutes slow/behind”).
target_language_example: Non trovo il mio orologio: l'ho lasciato a casa?
native_language_example: I can’t find my watch: did I leave it at home?

additional_notes: Paese can mean either “village/town” (often your hometown) or “country,” depending on context. Il mio paese is commonly used when talking about where you come from or the place you miss or love.
target_language_example: D'estate torno spesso nel mio paese.
native_language_example: In the summer I often go back to my hometown.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an activity you do for fun in your free time. After it, you can use an infinitive (e.g., leggere, sciare), a noun (e.g., la pesca), or a longer phrase like "quello di" + infinitive for emphasis/clarity.
target_language_example: Il mio passatempo è fare fotografie quando viaggio.
native_language_example: My hobby is taking photos when I travel.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a plan/strategy you made. With verbs like "ha funzionato" (it worked) or "sta funzionando" (it’s working) to say your plan succeeded or is succeeding. "Piano" can also mean a (floor) level in a building or a (soft/quiet) dynamic in music, but in these examples it means "plan."
target_language_example: Il mio piano non ha funzionato come speravo.
native_language_example: My plan didn’t work the way I hoped.

additional_notes: Used to say which food/dish you like the most. It often appears in sentences like “X è il mio piatto preferito” (X is my favorite dish) or “Il mio piatto preferito è X” (My favorite dish is X). You can change the possessive: il tuo / il suo / il nostro piatto preferito, etc.
target_language_example: Il mio piatto preferito è il tiramisù.
native_language_example: My favorite dish is tiramisù.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your wallet (where you keep cash, cards, ID). Often appears in questions when you can’t find it (Hai visto…? Chi ha…?) or in situations like losing it (ho perso) or having it stolen (mi hanno rubato / fu rubato).
target_language_example: Non trovo il mio portafoglio: l’hai visto?
native_language_example: I can’t find my wallet—have you seen it?

additional_notes: "Portatile" commonly means a laptop computer (short for "computer portatile"). "Il mio" = "my". Used when talking about where it is, asking someone to bring it, or describing problems (e.g., "si è bloccato" = it froze, "si è rotto" = it broke, "ha smesso di funzionare" = it stopped working).
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato il mio portatile a casa.
native_language_example: I forgot my laptop at home.

meaning: my place / my seat / my spot (also: my position or role).
additional_notes: Means a place that belongs to you: a seat in a theater/restaurant, your spot in line, or your position/role ("took my place" = replaced me). Often used with verbs like "essere" (Questo è il mio posto), "prendere" (Prende il mio posto), and "al posto mio" (in my place).
target_language_example: Scusi, credo che questo sia il mio posto.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I think this is my seat.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to say someone/something was the first (e.g., il mio primo figlio = my first son/child; il mio primo amore = my first love). It changes with gender/number: la mia prima (fem. sing.), i miei primi (masc. pl.), le mie prime (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Roma è stata il mio primo viaggio in Italia.
native_language_example: Rome was my first trip to Italy.

meaning: my first love (the first person you fell in love with).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the first person you loved romantically.
