additional_notes: Used when speaking on behalf of a group (we/us) about something you are offering: a deal in business/sales, an invitation, or help (e.g., "la nostra offerta di aiuto" = "our offer of help"). Often used with verbs like accettare (to accept) and rifiutare (to refuse).
target_language_example: Se vuoi, puoi accettare la nostra offerta di assistenza.
native_language_example: If you want, you can accept our offer of assistance.

additional_notes: Used either for a physical location (e.g., GPS coordinates, where we are) or for a viewpoint in a discussion (“our position is clear”). In Italian, it’s common to make it more specific with context: “la nostra posizione esatta” (exact location), “verso la nostra posizione” (toward our location).
target_language_example: Mandami la nostra posizione così posso raggiungervi.
native_language_example: Send me our location so I can reach you.

additional_notes: “La” = “the” (feminine singular). “Nostra” agrees with “scuola” (feminine singular) and means “our.” Used to refer to the school you and your group belong to (e.g., you and your classmates or family). Often appears as the subject of a sentence: “La nostra scuola…”
target_language_example: La nostra scuola è vicina alla stazione.
native_language_example: Our school is near the station.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a team the speaker belongs to or supports (sports, work, school, etc.). It’s a noun phrase: la (the, feminine singular) + nostra (our, feminine singular) + squadra (team). You can swap in other possessives: la mia squadra (my team), la tua squadra (your team), la loro squadra (their team).
target_language_example: La nostra squadra gioca domani alle sei.
native_language_example: Our team plays tomorrow at six.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a quality or situation of your team, followed by an adjective or phrase (e.g., "buona", "invincibile", "avanti di cinque punti"). "Squadra" is feminine singular, so adjectives usually end in -a (buona) or -e (invincibile). For plural "our teams," use "le nostre squadre sono."
target_language_example: La nostra squadra è pronta per la partita.
native_language_example: Our team is ready for the match.

additional_notes: Used to say that one person or thing is the only possible chance for success or a good outcome. You can change the possessive depending on who you mean: la mia unica speranza (my), la tua (your), la sua (his/her), la loro (their). Often followed by “di + infinitive” to say hope of doing something (e.g., di vincere = to win).
target_language_example: Un medico bravo è la nostra unica speranza di salvarlo.
native_language_example: A good doctor is our only hope to save him.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "nostra" (our) with the feminine singular noun "vita" (life). Italian often includes the definite article with possessives: "la nostra vita" = literally "the our life". It can refer to everyday life, a shared life as a couple/family, or life in general depending on context.
target_language_example: Dopo il trasloco, abbiamo iniziato la nostra vita in una nuova città.
native_language_example: After the move, we started our life in a new city.

meaning: 'the news' / 'the piece of news' (information about something that happened).
additional_notes: Used for a specific item of news or information (often something people are waiting for): *Ho una notizia!* = “I have some news!” Plural: *le notizie* (“the news”, “news items”). Often heard with verbs like *sentire* (to hear), *leggere* (to read), *dare* (to give/announce).
target_language_example: Hai già sentito la notizia?
native_language_example: Have you heard the news yet?

additional_notes: Usually refers to nighttime in general ("la notte" = "at night") or to a specific night from context (e.g., "la notte prima" = "the night before"). Common with verbs like dormire/lavorare/trascorrere: "dormo la notte" (I sleep at night), "trascorrere la notte" (to spend the night).
target_language_example: Siamo arrivati in città la notte e abbiamo trovato tutto chiuso.
native_language_example: We arrived in the city at night and found everything closed.

additional_notes: Used as a time expression meaning “yesterday night.” It can go at the end of the sentence or near the verb: “La notte scorsa ho dormito poco” / “Ho dormito poco la notte scorsa.”
target_language_example: La notte scorsa non ho dormito bene.
native_language_example: Last night I didn’t sleep well.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun: la nuova canzone (the new song), la nuova insegnante (the new teacher), la nuova divisa (the new uniform), la nuova regola (the new rule). “Nuova” must agree with the noun (feminine singular). It can also be used on its own when the noun is understood from context: Preferisco la nuova. (I prefer the new one.)
target_language_example: Preferisco la nuova versione della canzone.
native_language_example: I prefer the new version of the song.

meaning: peace (the state of no war; calm/harmony).
additional_notes: Feminine noun: pace. Often used with verbs like cercare (to look for), portare (to bring), volere (to want), trovare (to find). Common phrases: la pace nel mondo (“world peace”), la pace in casa (“peace at home”).
target_language_example: Dopo la discussione, voglio solo la pace.
native_language_example: After the argument, I just want peace.

additional_notes: Used for a physical ball in sports or games. Common with verbs like tirare/calciare (to kick), afferrare (to catch/grab), lanciare (to throw), passare (to pass), dare/ridare (to give back).
target_language_example: Puoi passarmi la palla, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you pass me the ball, please?

additional_notes: A noun used for the sport of basketball. It’s feminine singular, so it takes articles like la (the) or una (a). Often used with verbs like giocare a (to play) and guardare (to watch).
target_language_example: Giochi a pallacanestro il sabato?
native_language_example: Do you play basketball on Saturdays?

additional_notes: Most often means a single word or term ("the word" in English), especially when talking about vocabulary, pronunciation, or usage (e.g., "la parola non viene più utilizzata"). In religious contexts, "la parola di Dio" means "the Word of God." In speaking situations, "la parola a [nome]" means "[name] has the floor / over to [name]."
target_language_example: Non ricordo la parola in italiano.
native_language_example: I don’t remember the word in Italian.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the most enjoyable/important part of something (a day, an event, a story, etc.). It can also mean “the best of (someone)” in phrases like “la parte migliore di me” (“the best part of me”). You can change gender/number to match what it refers to: "il/lo/la" + "parte" (feminine) + "migliore"; plural: "le parti migliori".
target_language_example: Aspetta: la parte migliore deve ancora arrivare.
native_language_example: Wait: the best part is still to come.

additional_notes: Used for an organized game or match (soccer, rugby, etc.). Common with verbs like vincere/perdere (to win/lose) and essere annullata (to be canceled).
target_language_example: Domani guardiamo la partita in TV.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re watching the match on TV.

meaning: "the password of the" (for a masculine singular thing).
additional_notes: `password` is a common English loanword in Italian and is usually treated as feminine, so you’ll often see **la password**. **del** is the contraction of **di + il** and means “of the / for the,” used before a masculine singular noun (e.g., *del Wi‑Fi*, *del computer*).
target_language_example: Non ricordo la password del router.
native_language_example: I don't remember the router's password.

additional_notes: Used as a general, uncountable noun for pasta as a dish or ingredient (often with a sauce or other ingredients: "la pasta con...", "la pasta al..."), and also to talk about cooking it (cuocere la pasta). In Italian it typically refers to Italian pasta (spaghetti, penne, etc.), not "pastry dough" unless specified (e.g., "pasta frolla").
target_language_example: Stasera faccio la pasta al pomodoro.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m making pasta with tomato sauce.

additional_notes: Refers to a person’s or animal’s skin (color, texture, condition). Common with descriptions like “la pelle blu/scura” (blue/dark skin) or “la pelle liscia” (smooth skin).
target_language_example: Ho la pelle molto sensibile.
native_language_example: I have very sensitive skin.

meaning: “worth it / worth the effort” (in: vale la pena); also “penalty / punishment / (prison) sentence.”
additional_notes: Most commonly seen in the fixed expression **valere la pena** = “to be worth it / worth doing.” It’s often followed by an infinitive: **Vale la pena leggere…** = “It’s worth reading…”. You can also use **ne vale la pena?** = “Is it worth it?”. In legal/crime contexts, **la pena** keeps its literal meaning: “punishment/sentence” (e.g., **scontare la pena** = “to serve a sentence”).
target_language_example: Secondo me vale la pena provarci.
native_language_example: In my opinion, it’s worth trying.

meaning: the person (female noun; can refer to a man or a woman).
additional_notes: Means “the person” in general, and it can refer to someone of any gender (even though the noun is grammatically feminine). Often followed by a relative clause: “la persona che…” = “the person who…”. In expressions like “fare la persona perbene”, it means “to act like a respectable/decent person” (to behave properly).
target_language_example: Sei la persona che cercavo.
native_language_example: You’re the person I was looking for.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that describes or identifies someone. You’ll typically see it followed by a verb: "La persona che hai chiamato..." = “The person (that) you called...”. In English, “that” is often optional, but in Italian "che" is usually required here.
target_language_example: La persona che cerchi è in ufficio.
native_language_example: The person you’re looking for is in the office.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is the best/most suitable person for a task (“the right person to ask”) or a romantic match (“the right person for me/us”). Often followed by a cui + infinitive (e.g., “la persona giusta a cui chiedere”).
target_language_example: Se hai un problema con il computer, Marco è la persona giusta a cui chiedere.
native_language_example: If you have a computer problem, Marco is the right person to ask.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective after più to form a superlative about a person: la persona più + adjective (+ che/conosco, del mondo, nella mia vita, etc.). Example: la persona più importante (the most important person). Note: più agrees with nothing; persona is feminine singular, so it’s usually la persona (even if referring to a man), but you may also hear l’uomo/la donna più + adjective.
target_language_example: È la persona più gentile che conosco.
native_language_example: He/She is the kindest person I know.

additional_notes: Feminine singular noun: (la pioggia). Used to talk about rain in general or a specific period of rain. Common with verbs like piovere (to rain), fermarsi (to stop), durare (to last), distruggere (to destroy), and with adjectives like estiva (summer) or improbabile (unlikely).
target_language_example: Oggi la pioggia è stata forte, ma adesso si è fermata.
native_language_example: Today the rain was heavy, but now it has stopped.

additional_notes: Feminine singular noun: la pistola (plural: le pistole). Often used in commands in urgent situations: Abbassa la pistola! (Lower the gun!), Metti via la pistola! (Put the gun away!), Posa la pistola! (Put the gun down!).
target_language_example: Per favore, metti via la pistola.
native_language_example: Please, put the gun away.

additional_notes: Feminine singular noun with the definite article la. Use it to talk about pizza in general (Mi piace la pizza.) or a specific pizza you’re eating/ordering (Ordiniamo la pizza.). Indefinite form: una pizza.
target_language_example: Prendiamo una pizza margherita da condividere?
native_language_example: Shall we get a margherita pizza to share?

additional_notes: Used to order or talk about a pizza without meat (typically with vegetables). With "piacere" (e.g., "Ti piace...?"), it means “Do you like...?” The article "la" is often kept when naming the dish in general, but you can drop it when ordering: "Una pizza vegetariana, per favore."
target_language_example: Vorrei una pizza vegetariana, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a vegetarian pizza, please.

additional_notes: Superlative form used with feminine singular nouns (e.g., “band” is feminine: la band). It can describe physical size (“biggest”) or importance/quality (“greatest”), depending on context. Used as a stand-alone phrase, it often means “the greatest one (female/feminine thing/person)” or “the biggest one?”
target_language_example: Per me, lei è la più grande di tutte.
native_language_example: For me, she’s the greatest of all.

meaning: poetry; a poem (as a genre/art form).
additional_notes: Feminine singular noun. Often used in a general sense (“poetry” as literature/art), especially with the definite article (la). When talking about one specific poem, Italian commonly also says “la poesia” (“the poem”), and you can specify it with a relative clause: “la poesia che ha scritto…”. Related: “un poema” (a poem, sometimes longer/more formal), “poetico/a” (poetic).
target_language_example: Mi piace la poesia, ma questa poesia è difficile da capire.
native_language_example: I like poetry, but this poem is hard to understand.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "imparare" (to learn/memorize) or "sapere/conoscere" (to know) to say you’ve memorized a poem and can recite it without looking. Often said in school contexts: "imparare una poesia a memoria" / "so una poesia a memoria".
target_language_example: Devo imparare questa poesia a memoria per domani.
native_language_example: I have to memorize this poem by heart for tomorrow.

meaning: “the poem out loud” / “reading the poem aloud.”
additional_notes: Used to describe reading or reciting a poem so others can hear you. In sentences like “Ha letto la poesia ad alta voce”, “ad alta voce” means “aloud / in a loud voice,” while “la poesia” is “the poem.” Often used with verbs like leggere (to read) or recitare (to recite).
target_language_example: In classe abbiamo letto la poesia ad alta voce.
native_language_example: In class we read the poem aloud.

additional_notes: Refers to the police as an institution or the officers in general. Often used with verbs like arrivare (to arrive), chiamare (to call), avvisare (to notify), and with expressions like chiamare la polizia (call the police) and la polizia locale (local police).
target_language_example: Chiama la polizia, per favore!
native_language_example: Call the police, please!

additional_notes: Used to introduce what the police did, typically with a past participle (passato prossimo): "La polizia ha + [past participle]" (e.g., ha catturato = have/has caught). In Italian, "la polizia" is grammatically singular, so it takes "ha" even though in English we usually say "the police have" (plural).
target_language_example: La polizia ha trovato le prove.
native_language_example: The police have found the evidence.

additional_notes: Common news/police-report wording. Uses passato prossimo: "ha arrestato" (has/have arrested) often translates as simple past in English (“arrested”), especially with a specific time implied. Follow it with the person or group arrested: "la polizia ha arrestato + [person/people]". "Arrestare" is a cognate of “arrest.”
target_language_example: La polizia ha arrestato due persone ieri sera.
native_language_example: The police arrested two people last night.

meaning: “the police don’t / the police didn’t …” (police + negation).
additional_notes: “La polizia” is a singular feminine collective noun in Italian, so it usually takes a singular verb (e.g., “la polizia non ha detto nulla”). “Non” is the standard negation and normally goes right before the verb: “la polizia non crede…”, “la polizia non mi ha visto…”.
target_language_example: La polizia non vuole parlare con i giornalisti.
native_language_example: The police don’t want to talk to the journalists.

additional_notes: Used to describe an action happening now ("stare" + gerund = "are ___ing"). "Cercare" can mean "to look for" (a person/thing) or "to search for" (clues, suspects). Often followed by a direct object: "la polizia sta cercando Tom / degli indizi / dei sospetti".
target_language_example: La polizia sta cercando il ladro da ieri sera.
native_language_example: The police have been looking for the thief since last night.

additional_notes: Feminine singular noun. Used for a physical door (of a room, building, car, etc.). Common verbs with it: aprire la porta (to open the door), chiudere la porta (to close the door), sbattere la porta (to slam the door). You can specify which one: la porta sul retro (the back door).
target_language_example: Puoi chiudere la porta, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you close the door, please?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like tenere (to hold/keep) or lasciare (to leave): tenere la porta aperta = to hold/keep the door open (often for someone), lasciare la porta aperta = to leave the door open.
target_language_example: Puoi lasciare la porta aperta, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you leave the door open, please?

meaning: the door behind (oneself); i.e., the door after going through it.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like "chiudere" (to close) to say someone closes the door after entering or leaving a room: "Chiudi la porta dietro di te" = "Close the door behind you." "Di sé" means "behind himself/herself/themself" (reflexive, 3rd person). In direct address (you), it becomes "dietro di te".
target_language_example: Quando esci, chiudi la porta dietro di te.
native_language_example: When you leave, close the door behind you.

meaning: 'the door is…' (used to describe the door’s state, location, or a quality).
additional_notes: Common pattern: "La porta è" + adjective (aperta/chiusa/rossa) or + prepositional phrase for location (in fondo al corridoio = at the end of the hallway). "Porta" is feminine, so adjectives typically end in -a (aperta, chiusa, rossa).
target_language_example: Scusi, la porta è chiusa o aperta?
native_language_example: Excuse me, is the door closed or open?

additional_notes: Used to say that someone has (or doesn’t have) the chance/opportunity to do something. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., la possibilità di vedere, di incontrare). Common patterns: “avere/non avere la possibilità di…”.
target_language_example: Non abbiamo la possibilità di partire domani.
native_language_example: We don’t have the chance to leave tomorrow.

meaning: the first (feminine singular), e.g. first one / first race.
additional_notes: Feminine form used when the noun is feminine or implied (e.g., la prima gara = the first race; essere la prima = to be the first [woman/person, or first one]). Often followed by a feminine noun, or used alone when the noun is understood from context.
target_language_example: Lei è arrivata la prima alla gara.
native_language_example: She arrived first in the race.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the first action/consideration in a situation. It’s followed by a clause with **che** (a relative pronoun meaning “that/which”), e.g. **La prima cosa che ho fatto è stata...** (“The first thing I did was...”). Often appears in questions like **Qual è la prima cosa che faresti?** (“What’s the first thing you would do?”).
target_language_example: La prima cosa che ho fatto stamattina è stata preparare il caffè.
native_language_example: The first thing I did this morning was make coffee.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the first occurrence of an event. Often followed by a clause introduced by "che" (e.g., "la prima volta che..." = "the first time that...") or used on its own when the context is clear.
target_language_example: È la prima volta che vengo a Roma.
native_language_example: It’s the first time I’ve come to Rome.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s first experience doing something. It’s followed by a verb clause: often imperfect (e.g., "vedevo") when describing a past situation/background, or passato prossimo (e.g., "ho incontrato") for a completed event. You can negate it as "non è la prima volta che..." = "it’s not the first time that...".
target_language_example: È la prima volta che assaggio la carbonara.
native_language_example: It’s the first time I’m tasting carbonara.

meaning: the princess (female royal, daughter of a king/queen).
additional_notes: Used with the feminine singular definite article “la”. Common in fairy tales and royal contexts (castles, princes, wizards). The plural is “le principesse”. “Principessa madre” can mean “the princess mother” (a mother who is a princess).
target_language_example: La principessa aspetta il principe nel castello.
native_language_example: The princess is waiting for the prince in the castle.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to show possession and emphasize that it belongs to the subject: e.g., "la propria rabbia" = "her/his own anger". It agrees with the noun (la propria + noun fem. sing.). Other forms you’ll often see: "il proprio" (masc. sing.), "i propri" (masc. pl.), "le proprie" (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Devi seguire la propria strada.
native_language_example: You have to follow your own path.

additional_notes: Used as a feminine shorthand for “the next” when the noun is understood from context (e.g., la prossima stazione = the next station; la prossima storia = the next story). Often also means “next time” in phrases like “alla prossima” (“see you next time”).
target_language_example: La prossima fermata è Piazza Duomo.
native_language_example: The next stop is Piazza Duomo.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the summer that comes after the current one. Often used to discuss future plans (travel, holidays, work, etc.). You can also say "quest'estate" (this summer) or "l'estate prossima" (same meaning, a bit less common).
target_language_example: La prossima estate vorrei andare al mare con la mia famiglia.
native_language_example: Next summer I’d like to go to the seaside with my family.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the week after the current one. Often placed at the end of the sentence (like in the examples), but it can also go at the beginning for emphasis: “La prossima settimana vado a Roma.” You can also hear the shorter version “prossima settimana” without “la” in casual speech.
target_language_example: La prossima settimana ho un esame, quindi studio molto.
native_language_example: Next week I have an exam, so I’m studying a lot.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the next occasion something happens. Often used to make a promise, warning, or request about what should happen in the future (e.g., “La prossima volta, dimmelo in faccia.”). It can also be said alone (“La prossima volta.”) to mean “Next time.”
target_language_example: La prossima volta te lo dico prima.
native_language_example: Next time I’ll tell you beforehand.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that will happen on the next occasion when an action/event occurs. It introduces a clause with a verb (e.g., La prossima volta che mi chiami…). Often followed by present tense in Italian even when referring to the future.
target_language_example: La prossima volta che vieni a Roma, fammi sapere.
native_language_example: The next time you come to Rome, let me know.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you will do “next time,” often as a warning, threat, or firm promise. The pronoun “ti” means “to you” (or “you” as a direct object), and it must be followed by a verb: “La prossima volta ti chiamo” = “Next time I’ll call you.”
target_language_example: La prossima volta ti chiamo prima di arrivare.
native_language_example: Next time I’ll call you before I arrive.

meaning: "the fourth sister" (the sister who is fourth in birth order).
additional_notes: Used when siblings are numbered by age/birth order (especially in families with several children). It can work like a title or way to refer to someone (e.g., “Fourth Sister”) rather than using their name. The feminine singular article “la” agrees with “sorella.”
target_language_example: Dov'è la quarta sorella? Devo parlarle.
native_language_example: Where is the fourth sister? I need to talk to her.

meaning: the issue; the matter; the question (a problem/topic being discussed).
additional_notes: Used for a topic, problem, or point under discussion (often something to solve or decide). Common in phrases like "la questione è..." (“the issue is...”), "la questione è chiusa" (“the matter is closed/settled”), and "risolvere la questione" (“to resolve the issue”). Not usually a literal “question” you ask someone (that’s "una domanda").
target_language_example: La questione è semplice: dobbiamo decidere oggi.
native_language_example: The issue is simple: we have to decide today.

additional_notes: Feminine singular noun with the definite article: la radio. Common with verbs like ascoltare (to listen to), accendere/spegnere (to turn on/off). In context it can mean either the physical radio set or the radio as a medium/station.
target_language_example: Accendi la radio, per favore.
native_language_example: Turn on the radio, please.

additional_notes: Used in polite requests about the radio, often with verbs like accendere (to turn on) or spegnere (to turn off). Usually said as part of a full sentence (e.g., "Accenda/Spegna la radio, per favore"). "Per favore" = "please" and makes the request more polite.
target_language_example: Puoi abbassare la radio, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you turn down the radio, please?

additional_notes: Used as part of a polite request involving the radio, often with verbs like accendere (to turn on) or spegnere (to turn off). La radio = 'the radio' (feminine singular). Per piacere = 'please' and can be placed at the end of the sentence, after a comma.
target_language_example: Puoi abbassare la radio, per piacere?
native_language_example: Can you turn down the radio, please?

meaning: “the girl” (a young female; sometimes “the girlfriend” depending on context).
additional_notes: Feminine singular with the definite article: la = “the”, ragazza = “girl/young woman”. Used to refer to a specific girl already known or identified (“the new girl”, “the girl who came yesterday”). In some contexts (especially with possessives like “la mia ragazza”), it can mean “girlfriend.”
target_language_example: La ragazza che lavora qui parla inglese.
native_language_example: The girl who works here speaks English.

meaning: “the girl who/that …” (introduces a description of the girl).
additional_notes: Used to start a relative clause with **che** (“who/that”). **Che** is invariable (doesn’t change), and the verb that follows agrees with **la ragazza** (she = 3rd person singular). You can add extra information after it: *la ragazza che lavora qui* (“the girl who works here”).
target_language_example: La ragazza che parla inglese è la mia amica.
native_language_example: The girl who speaks English is my friend.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation for something that happened or a motivation for an action. Often follows questions like “Qual è la ragione per cui…?” (“What’s the reason why…?”). Similar meaning to “il motivo per cui” (a bit more common in everyday speech).
target_language_example: Questa è la ragione per cui non posso venire stasera.
native_language_example: This is the reason why I can’t come tonight.

meaning: “the queen” (a female monarch); also “queen” in a figurative sense (e.g., the queen of a dance).
additional_notes: Used for a reigning queen or a queen consort, and in set phrases like “Che Dio salvi la regina” (“God save the Queen”). It can also be used figuratively to mean the top or most admired woman in a context (e.g., “la regina del ballo” = “prom queen”).
target_language_example: Tutti aspettano la regina davanti al palazzo.
native_language_example: Everyone is waiting for the queen in front of the palace.

additional_notes: Feminine singular noun. Used for an answer to a question (often with adjectives like esatta/giusta, complicata) and for a reply/response (e.g., waiting for someone’s response). With verbs like sapere (“to know”), aspettare (“to wait for”), dare (“to give”), ricevere (“to receive”).
target_language_example: Non ho ancora ricevuto la risposta.
native_language_example: I still haven’t received the response.

additional_notes: Used for tests, quizzes, forms, or multiple-choice questions. Often with verbs like dire (to tell), segnare (to mark), scegliere (to choose). Note the agreement: risposta is feminine singular, so corretta ends in -a.
target_language_example: Non so qual è la risposta corretta.
native_language_example: I don’t know what the correct answer is.

meaning: the meeting (a scheduled gathering, often for work or planning).
additional_notes: Feminine singular noun: (la riunione). Common verbs with it: annullare (cancel), finire (end), essere (be), andare bene/male (go well/badly). In a work context it’s like “a meeting”; more generally it can also mean a gathering/reunion.
target_language_example: La riunione è alle tre, in ufficio.
native_language_example: The meeting is at three, at the office.

additional_notes: Roba is a very common informal word for “stuff/things” (objects, belongings, merchandise): La tua roba = your things. In some contexts—especially with talk of safety, deals, or exchanging—la roba can mean “the goods,” often implying drugs or illegal items. The exact meaning depends on the situation.
target_language_example: Dov'è la mia roba?
native_language_example: Where's my stuff?

additional_notes: A common feminine noun: (la) scatola, plural le scatole. Used for a physical container (cardboard, plastic, etc.). Often with verbs like aprire (to open), chiudere (to close), essere vuota/piena (to be empty/full).
target_language_example: Puoi mettere i biscotti nella scatola?
native_language_example: Can you put the cookies in the box?

additional_notes: Used to say someone chose correctly. Very common after the verb "fare" (e.g., "Hai fatto la scelta giusta" = "You made the right choice"). Agree "giusto/giusta" with the noun: "scelta" is feminine, so it’s "giusta".
target_language_example: Credo che tu abbia fatto la scelta giusta.
native_language_example: I think you made the right choice.

meaning: the scene (in a movie, play, or story).
additional_notes: Used for a specific part of a film/play (often named by location: “la scena della piscina”, “del balcone”). In filmmaking/theatre you can also use it with verbs like caricare (to upload/load), provare (to rehearse), girare (to shoot), ricostruire (to recreate). Note: “fare una scena” can also mean “to make a scene” (to cause a public fuss), depending on context.
target_language_example: Domani giriamo la scena in cucina.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re filming the kitchen scene.

additional_notes: Used for the human back. Common in health/pain contexts: “Mi fa male la schiena” = “My back hurts.” With reflexive verbs for injuries/strain: “stirarsi la schiena” (to strain/pull your back), “strappare(si) la schiena” (to hurt your back badly / throw out your back). Also used in expressions like “dietro la schiena” (behind one’s back) and “lungo la schiena” (down/along the back, e.g., a shiver).
target_language_example: Ho mal di schiena, quindi oggi non sollevo pesi.
native_language_example: I have back pain, so I’m not lifting weights today.

meaning: 'last' (referring to the previous week/month/season/year, etc., feminine).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine time word to mean the previous one: la scorsa domenica (last Sunday), la scorsa settimana (last week), la scorsa primavera (last spring), la scorsa stagione (last season). With masculine time words, use "lo scorso" (e.g., lo scorso anno = last year).
target_language_example: Siamo andati al cinema la scorsa settimana.
native_language_example: We went to the movies last week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the summer of the previous year (the summer before now). Often placed at the end of the sentence for time context: "... la scorsa estate". You can swap the noun: "la scorsa settimana" (last week), "lo scorso anno" (last year).
target_language_example: Abbiamo viaggiato molto la scorsa estate.
native_language_example: We traveled a lot last summer.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the previous night (the night before today). Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence as a time expression.
target_language_example: La scorsa notte ha piovuto molto.
native_language_example: Last night it rained a lot.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the week immediately before the current one. Often placed at the end of the sentence for time reference. You can also hear/see "scorsa settimana" without "la" in some contexts.
target_language_example: Ci siamo sentiti al telefono la scorsa settimana.
native_language_example: We talked on the phone last week.

meaning: the school; school (as a place or as studying/classes).
additional_notes: Used for the physical school building ("La scuola è di fronte a...") or for school life/classes in general ("la scuola mi tiene occupato", "è finita la scuola"). Often appears with verbs like andare a scuola (to go to school), finire la scuola (school is over/finished), lasciare la scuola (to leave school / quit school depending on context).
target_language_example: Domani non c’è scuola, quindi posso dormire di più.
native_language_example: Tomorrow there’s no school, so I can sleep more.

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns to indicate the 2nd one in order or rank (e.g., la seconda lezione = the second lesson; la seconda volta = the second time). Ordinal adjectives in Italian agree in gender and number: la seconda (fem. sing.), il secondo (masc. sing.), le seconde (fem. pl.), i secondi (masc. pl.).
target_language_example: Questa è la seconda volta che vengo qui.
native_language_example: This is the second time I’ve come here.

additional_notes: "Sedia" is a feminine noun, so it uses the article "la" (singular) and "le" (plural: "le sedie"). Commonly used with location words like "sulla sedia" (on the chair) and "sotto la sedia" (under the chair).
target_language_example: Puoi mettere la borsa sulla sedia, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you put the bag on the chair, please?

additional_notes: Used after expressions like “(avere) la sensazione che …” to introduce what you feel or suspect is true. It’s very often followed by the subjunctive (congiuntivo), because it expresses a personal impression rather than a certain fact: “Ho la sensazione che stia… / che sia… / che venga…”.
target_language_example: Ho la sensazione che oggi pioverà.
native_language_example: I have a feeling that it will rain today.

additional_notes: Used with times of day. With habitual actions it often means “in the evenings / at night” (e.g., "Lavoro la sera" = I work evenings). With a specific event it can mean “that evening” (often made clearer by context or by adding details: "la sera di Halloween" = on Halloween night).
target_language_example: La sera preferisco restare a casa.
native_language_example: In the evening, I prefer to stay at home.

additional_notes: Typically used with verbs like "passare" or "trascorrere": "passare/trascorrere la serata a + infinito" = “to spend the evening doing (something)”. Here, "a leggere" means “reading”.
target_language_example: Abbiamo passato la serata a leggere e a parlare piano.
native_language_example: We spent the evening reading and talking quietly.

meaning: the week; used to mean “per week / a week” in time expressions.
additional_notes: With numbers and “volta/e” it often means a frequency: “una/due/tre volte la settimana” = “once/twice/three times a week.” You can also use it to talk about the week in general (e.g., “questa settimana” = “this week”).
target_language_example: Lavoro da casa due giorni la settimana.
native_language_example: I work from home two days a week.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the week after the current one. Often placed at the end of the sentence (common in everyday speech). You can also say "settimana prossima" without "la" in informal conversation.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo la settimana prossima.
native_language_example: See you next week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened in the week immediately before this one. It often goes at the end of the sentence, but it can also appear earlier for emphasis (e.g., “La settimana scorsa siamo andati…”).
target_language_example: Ho visto Luca la settimana scorsa.
native_language_example: I saw Luca last week.

additional_notes: Used to criticize someone for asking for something in a shameless or disrespectful way. Often appears as: “Ha avuto la sfrontatezza di chiedere…” (= “He/She had the nerve to ask…”). “Sfrontatezza” is a strong negative word, similar to “cheek/impudence.”
target_language_example: Ha avuto la sfrontatezza di chiedere un aumento dopo una settimana di lavoro.
native_language_example: He had the nerve to ask for a raise after a week of work.

additional_notes: With verbs like "chiamare" (to call) or "mandare" (to send), it often means the security personnel (e.g., guards in a building, mall, event). In general statements, it can mean safety/security as a concept (e.g., public safety, feeling safe).
target_language_example: Se succede qualcosa, chiama subito la sicurezza.
native_language_example: If something happens, call security right away.

meaning: “the lady” / “Mrs.” (a polite way to refer to an adult woman).
additional_notes: Used as a respectful form of address for a woman. It can be followed by a last name (La signora Rossi = Mrs. Rossi) or used alone to mean “the lady.” As a title, it’s often capitalized (La Signora Rossi).
target_language_example: Scusi, la signora Bianchi è in casa?
native_language_example: Excuse me, is Mrs. Bianchi at home?

meaning: 'Miss' (a young/unmarried woman; polite title before a surname).
additional_notes: Used like a title before a woman’s last name (e.g., la signorina Miller). It can also mean “the young lady” when the name isn’t said (La signorina è occupata.). In modern Italian it can sound old-fashioned or inappropriate to stress marital status; in many situations people prefer “la signora” or just the person’s name.
target_language_example: Mi scusi, la signorina Bianchi è disponibile?
native_language_example: Excuse me, is Miss Bianchi available?

meaning: the situation; the state of affairs.
additional_notes: Common in everyday and formal contexts to refer to what is happening in a place or moment, especially when there’s a problem or something to explain. Often used with verbs like gestire (to handle), spiegare (to explain), discutere (to discuss).
target_language_example: Non capisco bene la situazione: me la puoi spiegare?
native_language_example: I don’t really understand the situation: can you explain it to me?

additional_notes: Used after verbs like pensare/credere/sperare in questions or dependent clauses. It uses the subjunctive (possa) because it expresses an opinion, doubt, or possibility. You can change the subject: che la situazione possa migliorare / che le cose possano migliorare.
target_language_example: Speri che la situazione possa migliorare presto?
native_language_example: Do you hope the situation can improve soon?

additional_notes: Used to describe or update how things are at the moment. It’s typically followed by an adjective or a set expression (e.g., "brutta" = bad/ugly, "sotto controllo" = under control, "sfuggita di mano" = gotten out of hand). You can add a time word like "ora" (now) or "qui" (here) before/after it for context.
target_language_example: In questo momento la situazione è complicata.
native_language_example: At the moment the situation is complicated.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that just one thing matters/wanted/seen, followed by a clause with a verb (e.g., “la sola cosa che voglio è …”, “la sola cosa che conta è …”). It agrees in gender/number: la sola cosa che (the only thing that), le sole cose che (the only things that).
target_language_example: La sola cosa che mi interessa è imparare l’italiano.
native_language_example: The only thing I care about is learning Italian.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a sword (a bladed weapon). Often appears with verbs like vedere (to see), mettere giù (to put down), and with adjectives describing how it’s held, e.g. più dritta (straighter/more upright).
target_language_example: Attento: quella è la spada del re.
native_language_example: Careful: that’s the king’s sword.

meaning: hope (the feeling that something good will happen).
additional_notes: A common noun used with the definite article: la speranza. Often used in expressions like perdere la speranza (“to lose hope”) and abbandonare la speranza (“to give up hope”).
target_language_example: Non perdere la speranza: domani potrebbe andare meglio.
native_language_example: Don’t lose hope: tomorrow could be better.

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to groceries you bought or to the act of grocery shopping (fare la spesa = to do the grocery shopping). In a sentence like "Dove metto la spesa?" it means the bags of groceries.
target_language_example: Devo fare la spesa dopo il lavoro.
native_language_example: I have to do the grocery shopping after work.

additional_notes: Most often refers to seasons of the year (primavera, estate, autunno, inverno), especially when talking about weather or typical temperatures. Also used for other “seasons” like the tourist season (alta/bassa stagione) or a TV series season (una stagione di una serie).
target_language_example: In estate, la stagione è molto calda qui.
native_language_example: In summer, the season is very hot here.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the part of the year when it rains a lot in a country/region. It often appears with verbs like iniziare/cominciare (“to start”) or essere iniziata/cominciata (“to have started”): Quando inizia la stagione delle piogge? / È iniziata la stagione delle piogge?
target_language_example: In Thailandia la stagione delle piogge dura da maggio a ottobre.
native_language_example: In Thailand the rainy season lasts from May to October.

additional_notes: Common for a room in a house or building. In hotels/B&Bs, it can mean a guest room and by extension the room charge (e.g., pagare la stanza = pay for the room). Feminine singular: la stanza; plural: le stanze.
target_language_example: Abbiamo prenotato la stanza per due notti.
native_language_example: We booked the room for two nights.

additional_notes: Commonly refers to the train station (stazione ferroviaria), but it can also mean other stations depending on context (e.g., bus station, police station). It’s feminine singular: la stazione; plural: le stazioni. Often used with prepositions: alla stazione (to/at the station), in stazione (at the station).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alla stazione alle otto.
native_language_example: See you at the station at eight.

additional_notes: Used to specify a station for trains (as opposed to other types of stations). Often shortened in speech to "la stazione" when it’s clear from context. "Ferroviaria" is an adjective meaning "railway" and agrees with "stazione" (feminine singular).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo davanti alla stazione ferroviaria alle otto.
native_language_example: Let’s meet in front of the train station at eight.

additional_notes: Used to say that one thing matches another in identity/quality/size, etc. It agrees with a feminine singular noun: *la stessa musica, la stessa procedura, la stessa altezza*. With *essere* it can mean “the same (as before/without someone)”: *non è stata la stessa*, *non sarebbe la stessa senza...*. For masculine use *lo stesso*; plural: *gli stessi/le stesse*.
target_language_example: Possiamo prendere la stessa strada di ieri?
native_language_example: Can we take the same road as yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to say something is identical to something else (a decision, an opinion, a question, an order, etc.). Often follows verbs like dire (to say), chiedere (to ask), decidere (to decide), ordinare (to order). You can also use it to agree: “Anch’io” / “Dico la stessa cosa” (“I say the same thing”).
target_language_example: Non voglio la stessa cosa di ieri: oggi provo qualcosa di diverso.
native_language_example: I don’t want the same thing as yesterday: today I’ll try something different.

additional_notes: Used when you repeat an identical question to someone else (or ask yourself). Often follows verbs like fare una domanda (“to ask a question”) or porre una domanda (“to pose/ask a question”). Gender/number agreement: la stessa domanda (feminine singular); le stesse domande (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Ho chiesto a tutti la stessa domanda.
native_language_example: I asked everyone the same question.

additional_notes: Used to say that two or more people (or things) are the same age. Often appears with avere (“to be [a certain age]” in Italian): avere la stessa età = “to be the same age.” You can add a comparison: la stessa età di me/te/lui/lei = “the same age as me/you/him/her.”
target_language_example: Mio fratello ed io abbiamo la stessa età.
native_language_example: My brother and I are the same age.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages. It agrees with the noun: usually feminine singular because of età (la stessa età), but you can also say lo stesso (e.g., lo stesso numero). Often used with avere: Avere la stessa età di qualcuno = to be the same age as someone. You can add words like circa (“about”) or esattamente (“exactly”) before la stessa età.
target_language_example: Io e mia sorella abbiamo la stessa età di Marco.
native_language_example: My sister and I are the same age as Marco.

additional_notes: Usually feminine singular with the definite article: la storia. It can mean the school subject or field of study (“history”), a narrative you read/tell (“story”), or an explanation/summary of a situation (“La storia è che…” = “The thing is that…”). Plural: le storie.
target_language_example: La storia è che oggi non posso venire.
native_language_example: The thing is that I can’t come today.

meaning: “the story of the …” / “the whole thing about the …”.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a story, anecdote, or explanation about something (a person, event, place, etc.). It’s followed by a noun: del = di + il (“of the” masculine singular). With other nouns you’ll see variants like: la storia della (di + la), la storia dei (di + i), la storia delle (di + le).
target_language_example: Mi racconti la storia del castello?
native_language_example: Can you tell me the story of the castle?

meaning: "the story of the" / "the history of the" (of a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what you’re talking about: a narrative (story) or past/events (history). It’s made of "la storia" + "della" (= di + la), so it’s followed by a feminine singular noun (e.g., "la storia della città"). For masculine nouns, you’ll see "la storia del" (di + il).
target_language_example: Mi puoi raccontare la storia della tua famiglia?
native_language_example: Can you tell me the story/history of your family?

additional_notes: Refers to a street or road, or to the route/directions to a place. Common with verbs like pulire (clean), aprire (open) la strada al traffico (open the road to traffic), guardare la strada (watch/look at the road), and sapere la strada (know the way). Feminine singular: la strada; plural: le strade.
target_language_example: Scusi, qual è la strada per la stazione?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what’s the way to the station?

meaning: “the road/street is …” (used to describe the condition/status of a road).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective or phrase to describe the road: La strada è ghiacciata (icy), gratuita (free of charge/toll-free), in costruzione (under construction), pericolosa (dangerous). “Strada” is often “road,” and can sometimes mean “street” depending on context.
target_language_example: La strada è chiusa oggi.
native_language_example: The road is closed today.

meaning: "his/her/its" (feminine singular); also "your" (formal, Lei) with a feminine singular noun.
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (e.g., la sua lingua, la sua malattia). The possessive agrees with the noun possessed (sua = feminine singular). Depending on context, it can mean "his", "her", "its", or "your" (formal "Lei"); Italian often relies on context to tell which one.
target_language_example: Dov'è la sua chiave?
native_language_example: Where is his/her (or your, formal) key?

additional_notes: "Sua" can mean both "his" and "her" in Italian; the context tells you which. "Amica" is a female friend (or a friend who is a woman). For a male friend, use "il suo amico". Possessives usually take the article in Italian: "la sua amica" = "his/her (female) friend".
target_language_example: Ho visto la sua amica ieri al bar.
native_language_example: I saw his/her friend yesterday at the bar.

additional_notes: “La sua” is the feminine singular possessive meaning “his/her/its/your (formal)” and it agrees with the noun: auto is feminine, so it’s “la sua auto.” It can also mean “your car” when speaking formally (e.g., to a customer): "È la sua auto?" In everyday speech, Italians often use "la sua macchina" too.
target_language_example: Dov'è la sua auto?
native_language_example: Where is his/her car?

additional_notes: Means “the car belonging to him/her,” or “your car” when speaking formally (Lei). It’s feminine singular: la automobile → usually shortened to l’automobile. Possessives in Italian usually take the article: la sua auto / la sua macchina / la sua automobile.
target_language_example: Dov’è la sua automobile?
native_language_example: Where is his/her car? / Where is your car? (formal)

additional_notes: Uses the possessive "sua" (feminine singular) because "bici" is feminine in Italian, even though it can refer to a bike owned by a man or a woman. "Sua" can mean "his", "her", or "your" (formal) depending on context. The article "la" is normally used with possessives (la mia bici, la sua bici).
target_language_example: Non toccare la sua bici: è nuova.
native_language_example: Don’t touch his/her bike: it’s new.

additional_notes: Italian often uses the definite article with possessives: "la sua bici" = "his/her bike" (also "il suo" for masculine nouns). "Sua" agrees with the noun (bicicletta = feminine singular), and can mean either "his" or "her"—context tells you which. In questions you can stress it to clarify ownership: "È la SUA bicicletta?" = "Is it HIS/HER bicycle?"
target_language_example: Non trovo la sua bicicletta da stamattina.
native_language_example: I can’t find his/her bicycle since this morning.

additional_notes: "La sua" is the polite/formal way to say "your" (to one person), and it can also mean "his" or "her" depending on context. "Biro" means a ballpoint pen (a common everyday word in Italian).
target_language_example: Scusi, è questa la sua biro?
native_language_example: Excuse me, is this your pen?

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective sua with the definite article la: la sua birra = “his/her beer” (a specific beer belonging to that person). Word order is typically article + possessive + noun. Can refer to either “his” or “her” depending on context.
target_language_example: Non bere la sua birra: è di Marco.
native_language_example: Don’t drink his beer: it’s Marco’s.

additional_notes: "Sua" agrees with the thing owned (here: "borsa" = feminine singular), not with the owner. It can mean "his", "her", or "your" (formal) depending on context. "Borsa" can mean a handbag/purse or a bag (e.g., a shopping bag); add details with "di..." (e.g., "borsa di mele" = bag of apples).
target_language_example: Ho preso la sua borsa dal tavolo.
native_language_example: I took his/her/your (formal) bag from the table.

additional_notes: "Sua" is the possessive for "he/she/you (formal)" and it agrees with the noun: "camera" (feminine singular) → "la sua". In context it often means “bedroom,” but it can also mean “room” in general. If the owner is clear, Italians often use "la sua" (his/her) rather than repeating the person’s name.
target_language_example: Marco ha lasciato i vestiti nella sua camera.
native_language_example: Marco left the clothes in his room/bedroom.

additional_notes: Means “his/her favorite song,” depending on context. In Italian, "sua" can refer to either “his” or “her,” so you usually understand it from who you’re talking about. It’s often used in questions like "Qual è la sua canzone preferita?" (“What is his/her favorite song?”).
target_language_example: Sai qual è la sua canzone preferita?
native_language_example: Do you know what his/her favorite song is?

additional_notes: Means “the person’s career” (work/professional life, or a path like a political/sports career). Note: Italian possessives agree with the thing possessed, not the owner—"la sua" matches "carriera" (feminine singular), so it can mean either “his” or “her” depending on context.
target_language_example: Dopo tanti anni, la sua carriera è decollata.
native_language_example: After many years, his/her career took off.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "suo/sua" (= his/her/its), which agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner: "casa" is feminine, so it’s "la sua casa" (even if the owner is male). Often means "home" in the sense of where someone lives.
target_language_example: Non posso venire stasera: devo tornare a la sua casa.
native_language_example: I can’t come tonight: I have to go back to his/her home.

additional_notes: Used to describe where someone’s house is or what it’s like. "Sua" is the polite/formal way to say "your" (as in Lei); it can also mean "his" or "her" depending on context. "Casa" is feminine, so adjectives after "è" agree in feminine singular (e.g., bella, grande, nuova, pulita, vicina). In informal speech to a friend, you’d often use "la tua casa è" (your house is…).
target_language_example: La sua casa è vicino al parco.
native_language_example: His/Her house is near the park.

meaning: “his/her key” (a key that belongs to him/her).
additional_notes: "Sua" is the feminine singular possessive used because "chiave" is feminine. It can mean either “his” or “her” (Italian doesn’t distinguish here); context tells you which. Often used with a specific kind of key: "la sua chiave di casa" = “his/her house key.”
target_language_example: Non trovo la sua chiave, forse è rimasta in macchina.
native_language_example: I can’t find his/her key; maybe it was left in the car.

additional_notes: Means “his guitar” or “her guitar” depending on who “sua” refers to. With the polite form Lei (you), “la sua chitarra” means “your guitar.” Italian possessives usually come with the definite article: la + sua + noun. If you mean “their guitar,” use “la loro chitarra.”
target_language_example: Dov'è la sua chitarra?
native_language_example: Where is his/her guitar?

additional_notes: Means “his decision” or “her decision”; it can also mean “your decision” when speaking formally (to Lei). Often used with verbs like prendere (“to make/take”) and annunciare/spiegare (“to announce/explain”) a decision.
target_language_example: Rispetto la sua decisione, anche se non sono d'accordo.
native_language_example: I respect his/her decision, even if I don’t agree.

additional_notes: Uses the polite possessive “suo/sua” meaning “his” or “her” (sometimes “your” in formal address). Common when talking about someone’s age in a neutral or formal way, often after expressions like “considerando” (considering) or “a” (at) + age.
target_language_example: Non dimostra la sua età.
native_language_example: He/She doesn’t look his/her age.

additional_notes: “Sua” agrees with the thing possessed (faccia = feminine singular), not with the person. Depending on context, “la sua faccia” can mean “his face,” “her face,” or “your face” (formal “Lei”). It’s also used in expressions like “mostrare la sua faccia” = “to show his/her face” (to dare to appear).
target_language_example: Non voglio più vedere la sua faccia!
native_language_example: I don’t want to see his/her face anymore!

additional_notes: “Sua” is the possessive used with the polite form “Lei” (formal ‘you’), so “la sua famiglia” can mean “your family” when speaking formally. It can also mean “his family” or “her family,” depending on context. Use the definite article: la sua famiglia (singular).
target_language_example: Come sta la sua famiglia?
native_language_example: How is your family?

additional_notes: Used to talk about “his/her family” followed by another action or person/thing introduced with **e** (“and”). **Sua** is a possessive that agrees with **famiglia** (feminine singular), not with the owner; depending on context it can mean **his**, **her**, **its**, or sometimes **your** (formal). Often used with verbs like **abbandonare** (to abandon) or in descriptions like **domina la sua famiglia** (he dominates his family).
target_language_example: Ha salutato la sua famiglia e poi è partito.
native_language_example: He said goodbye to his family and then left.

additional_notes: Fede nuziale means the wedding band (ring), usually a simple ring worn after marriage. La sua means “his/her” depending on context; you can also say la mia (my), la tua (your), la nostra (our), etc.
target_language_example: Non trovo la sua fede nuziale: forse l’ha lasciata in bagno.
native_language_example: I can’t find his/her wedding ring: maybe he/she left it in the bathroom.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the trust that belongs to a specific person. Note: in Italian, **sua** agrees with the thing owned (**fiducia**, feminine singular), not with the owner—so it can mean **his** or **her** trust depending on context. Common with verbs like **tradire** (to betray) and **guadagnare** (to earn).
target_language_example: Devi guadagnarti la sua fiducia prima di chiedergli un favore.
native_language_example: You need to earn his/her trust before asking him/her a favor.

additional_notes: Used to refer to one leg belonging to someone. "Sua" agrees with the noun (feminine singular: gamba), not with the person, so it can mean either "his" or "her". In speech, Italians often clarify with "la gamba di lui" (his) / "la gamba di lei" (hers) if needed.
target_language_example: Non riesce a camminare perché la sua gamba gli fa male.
native_language_example: He/She can’t walk because his/her leg hurts.

additional_notes: "Sua" is a possessive that can mean "his," "her," or "your" (polite/formal "Lei"); the meaning comes from context. "Gatta" is a female cat (male: "gatto"). "La" is the feminine singular "the," agreeing with "gatta."
target_language_example: Posso accarezzare la sua gatta?
native_language_example: Can I pet your cat? (formal)

additional_notes: "Sua" means "his" or "her" (and in formal address, "your"). It agrees with the noun: "idea" is feminine singular, so you say "la sua idea" (not *il suo idea*). Often used to refer back to someone’s proposal/opinion/plan: "Adottare la sua idea" = "to adopt his/her idea."
target_language_example: Non sono d'accordo con la sua idea.
native_language_example: I don't agree with his/her idea.

additional_notes: Used to state an opinion or judgment about someone’s idea. "sua" agrees with "idea" (feminine singular) and can mean "his," "her," or "your" (formal) depending on context. Common patterns: "La sua idea è buona" (good), "... è migliore della mia" (better than mine), "... è identica alla mia" (identical to mine), "... è superiore alla tua" (superior to yours).
target_language_example: La sua idea è interessante, ma costa troppo.
native_language_example: His/Her idea is interesting, but it costs too much.

additional_notes: Means “his/her imagination” (referring to someone already mentioned). Often used with verbs like usare/utilizzare (“to use”) and in phrases like “Potrebbe essere solo la sua immaginazione” = “It might just be his/her imagination,” meaning something may be imagined, not real.
target_language_example: Non è successo davvero: era solo la sua immaginazione.
native_language_example: It didn’t really happen: it was just his/her imagination.

additional_notes: "La" and "insegnante" are feminine here, so it refers to a female teacher. "Sua" means "his/her/its" (not "your"—that would be "tua"), and it agrees with the noun (insegnante), not with the owner. You may also hear "il suo insegnante" for a male teacher.
target_language_example: Marco parla spesso della sua insegnante di italiano.
native_language_example: Marco often talks about his Italian teacher.

additional_notes: “Sua” means “his/her” or “your” (formal), and the meaning depends on context. It’s polite/formal and common in letters and customer-service situations; for informal “your letter,” you usually say “la tua lettera.”
target_language_example: Ho ricevuto la sua lettera ieri.
native_language_example: I received your letter yesterday.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "sua" with the feminine singular noun "lingua" (so it’s always "la sua lingua"). In Italian, "suo/sua" can mean "his" or "her" depending on context, and it can also mean "your" when speaking formally (to "Lei").
target_language_example: Sto cercando di imparare la sua lingua.
native_language_example: I’m trying to learn his/her language.

additional_notes: Means “the car of him/her/you (formal).” Sua agrees with the noun: macchina is feminine singular, so you use la sua. It can also mean “his/her/your (formal) machine” depending on context, but in everyday speech it often means “car.”
target_language_example: Non posso usare la sua macchina oggi.
native_language_example: I can't use his/her/your (formal) car today.

additional_notes: Means “the/its camera” with a possessive: sua = “his/her/its,” or “your” in the formal address (Lei). Commonly used with verbs like prendere (to get), perdere (to lose), portare (to bring/carry), prestare (to lend), dimenticarsi di portare (to forget to bring). Often followed by con sé (“with him/her”).
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato la sua macchina fotografica in hotel.
native_language_example: I forgot his/her camera at the hotel.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s own pencil. "Sua" means "his" or "her" (it agrees with the object: matita is feminine, so "la sua matita"). Context usually tells whether it’s his or hers. Variants: "il suo ..." for masculine objects (e.g., "il suo libro").
target_language_example: Dov’è la sua matita?
native_language_example: Where is his/her pencil?

additional_notes: Means “his/her death” (death of a person previously mentioned). “Sua” can refer to either “his” or “her”; the context tells you which. Used in serious, formal, or neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Dopo la sua morte, la famiglia si è trasferita in un’altra città.
native_language_example: After his/her death, the family moved to another city.

meaning: "his/her new" (referring to a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to mean “his/her new …”: e.g., la sua nuova ragazza (his new girlfriend), la sua nuova giacca (her new jacket). In Italian, possessives are often used with the definite article (la/il/i/le), especially with ordinary nouns (clothes, objects, etc.).
target_language_example: Ho conosciuto la sua nuova collega.
native_language_example: I met his/her new colleague.

additional_notes: Means “the new car of him/her.” Used with the definite article (la) plus the possessive (sua) before the noun. It can refer to either “his” or “her” depending on context. In Italian, the possessive agrees with the thing owned: auto is feminine singular, so you say la sua (not il suo).
target_language_example: Ho visto la sua nuova auto parcheggiata davanti a casa.
native_language_example: I saw his/her new car parked in front of the house.

additional_notes: Means literally “the his/her new car.” In Italian, "sua" agrees with the thing owned (macchina = feminine singular), not with the owner. It can mean "his" or "her" (and also "your" in the formal Lei form) depending on context. Often used with verbs like "piacere" (Le piace...) and "far vedere" (Mi ha fatto vedere...).
target_language_example: Ho visto la sua nuova macchina ieri.
native_language_example: I saw his/her/your (formal) new car yesterday.

additional_notes: Uses the formal possessive "suo/sua" (often capitalized as "Suo/Sua" in very formal writing) to mean "your" when speaking politely to one person (Lei). In context, it often refers to an offer/proposal (e.g., a business offer, a price quote, or an invitation). "Offerta" can also mean a special deal/discount in shops, but in this phrase it usually means an offer someone made.
target_language_example: Grazie, accetto la sua offerta.
native_language_example: Thank you, I accept your offer.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive "sua" to mean "his" or "her" (and sometimes "your" in the formal "Lei" form). The article "la" usually stays before the possessive in Italian: "la mia opinione", "la sua opinione". Common with verbs like chiedere (to ask for) and sentire (to hear).
target_language_example: Vorrei sapere la sua opinione su questo progetto.
native_language_example: I’d like to know your opinion about this project.

meaning: "his/her word"; often "his/her promise" (as in 'give/keep your word').
additional_notes: Literally means “his/her word,” and it can refer to an actual word someone uses (e.g., “Qual è la sua parola preferita…?”). Very commonly, though, it’s used in set phrases about promises: dare la sua parola = “to give his/her word” (promise), mantenere la sua parola = “to keep his/her word” (do what was promised). You can also say “è buono/a come la sua parola” = “he/she is as good as his/her word” (trustworthy).
target_language_example: Ti do la mia parola: domani arrivo puntuale.
native_language_example: I give you my word: tomorrow I’ll arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used when speaking formally/politely to one person (Lei). Common in instructions on websites, apps, ATMs, and customer service. In informal speech to a friend you’d usually say “la tua password”.
target_language_example: Inserisca la sua password per accedere al conto.
native_language_example: Enter your password to access the account.

additional_notes: "Sua" means "his," "her," or "its" (it agrees with the thing owned: paura is feminine singular, so sua). Often used with verbs like controllare (to control), mostrare (to show), superare (to overcome). If you want to specify the owner, you can use "la paura di + name" (e.g., la paura di Mary).
target_language_example: Ha respirato a fondo per controllare la sua paura.
native_language_example: He/She took a deep breath to control his/her fear.

additional_notes: Means “the pen belonging to him/her.” With "sua" the owner can be "lui" or "lei" (it doesn’t show gender). "Sua" agrees with the thing owned: "penna" is feminine singular, so "la sua". Often used with "Lei" to be polite/formal (e.g., to a stranger, teacher, customer).
target_language_example: Scusi, è questa la sua penna?
native_language_example: Excuse me, is this your pen?

additional_notes: "La" is feminine singular (“the”). "Sua" means “his” or “her” depending on who you’re talking about. Used to indicate that the gun/pistol belongs to someone.
target_language_example: Ha preso la sua pistola dal cassetto.
native_language_example: He/She took his/her gun from the drawer.

meaning: his/her/your position (stance, view, or location; sometimes social status).
additional_notes: Literally “his/her position,” but meaning depends on context: (1) opinions/stance in a discussion ("chiarire la sua posizione" = “make his/her position clear”); (2) physical location, especially in requests like "Mi dia la sua posizione" (“Give me your location”); (3) social standing in "posizione sociale" (“social status/standing”). Note: "sua" can mean “his,” “her,” or formal “your.”
target_language_example: Può dirmi la sua posizione esatta, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you tell me your exact location, please?

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun (often omitted if it’s understood from context): e.g., "la sua prima parola" (his first word), "la sua prima moglie" (his first wife). "Sua" can mean "his," "her," or formal "your"; the gender/number matches the noun that follows (prima = feminine singular). For masculine you’d say "il suo primo" (e.g., "il suo primo lavoro").
target_language_example: È la sua prima volta in Italia.
native_language_example: It’s his/her first time in Italy.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: la (feminine singular) + sua (his/her/its) + promessa (promise). Used when referring to someone’s commitment to do (or not do) something. Common verbs with promessa: mantenere (keep), infrangere (break), dimenticare/scordare (forget).
target_language_example: Ha mantenuto la sua promessa di chiamarmi.
native_language_example: He/She kept his/her promise to call me.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something belongs specifically to that person/thing (not someone else’s). It agrees with a feminine singular noun: e.g., la sua propria esperienza/opinione/stanza/azienda/religione. Can also appear as "la propria" when the owner is understood, or "il suo/la sua/i suoi/le sue" without "propria" when you don’t need emphasis.
target_language_example: Vorrei avere la mia propria camera.
native_language_example: I’d like to have my own room.

additional_notes: Means “his/her anger” (or “your” in the formal address Lei). It’s formed by the definite article la + possessive sua + noun rabbia (feminine singular). Often used with verbs like trattenere/frenare (to hold back) or crescere (to grow).
target_language_example: Ha finalmente espresso la sua rabbia.
native_language_example: He/She finally expressed his/her anger.

additional_notes: Means “his/her girlfriend,” depending on context (sua = “his” or “her”). Used when talking about a male or female partner (ragazza = girlfriend/young woman). Often you’ll just say “la sua ragazza” without repeating the person’s name if it’s clear who you mean.
target_language_example: Ho visto Marco e la sua ragazza al cinema.
native_language_example: I saw Marco and his girlfriend at the movies.

additional_notes: Means “the reaction” of the person you’re talking about. Sua can mean “his,” “her,” or formal “your,” depending on context. Often used with a preposition: la sua reazione a/alla notizia (“his/her reaction to the news”), and you can specify the type: la sua reazione immediata (“his/her immediate reaction”).
target_language_example: Qual è stata la sua reazione alla notizia?
native_language_example: What was his/her reaction to the news?

additional_notes: "Sua" is the polite/formal possessive used with Lei (you, formal), but it can also mean "his" or "her" depending on context. "Risposta" means an answer or reply, often to a question, request, email, etc. With "aspetta(re) la sua risposta" it means "to wait for his/her/your (formal) reply."
target_language_example: Aspetto la sua risposta entro domani.
native_language_example: I’m waiting for your (formal) reply by tomorrow.

additional_notes: Means “his health” or “her health,” depending on who you’re talking about. Italian uses the possessive + noun (la sua salute) where English often uses just “his/her health.” Often used with verbs like influenzare (to affect), danneggiare (to damage), migliorare (to improve), peggiorare (to get worse).
target_language_example: È preoccupato per la sua salute.
native_language_example: He’s worried about his health.

additional_notes: “La” is feminine singular because scrivania is feminine. “Sua” agrees with the thing owned (scrivania), not with the owner. It can mean “his desk,” “her desk,” or “your desk” (formal Lei). Often used for an office/work desk; common with verbs like usare (use), pulire (clean), svuotare (empty).
target_language_example: Ho lasciato le chiavi sulla sua scrivania.
native_language_example: I left the keys on his/her/your (formal) desk.

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s team (e.g., a sports team or a work group). “Sua” agrees with the noun it describes (squadra is feminine singular), not with the owner. Without context, “sua” can mean his, her, or their (formal you).
target_language_example: È orgoglioso perché la sua squadra ha giocato benissimo.
native_language_example: He’s proud because his team played really well.

additional_notes: "Sua" is the possessive adjective for a singular feminine noun (stanza = room). The article stays: la sua stanza. In Italian, "suo/sua" can mean "his" or "her"—you usually understand which from context (or by adding a name: "la stanza di Maria").
target_language_example: Ho lasciato la valigia nella sua stanza.
native_language_example: I left the suitcase in his/her room.

meaning: “his/her story” (what he/she says happened; a story/account).
additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective sua (“his/her/its”) and agrees with the feminine noun storia (“story”). It can mean a narrative or someone’s version of events (often in contexts like believing or doubting what someone says). In Italian, sua can mean “his” or “her”; the context tells you which.
target_language_example: Non credo alla sua storia.
native_language_example: I don’t believe his/her story.

additional_notes: Uses the polite possessive “sua” to mean “his,” “her,” or “your” (formal “your”), depending on context. It agrees with the feminine singular noun “teoria,” so it stays “la sua.” Often used when talking about someone’s idea, explanation, or theoretical approach: “Dica/Gli dica la sua teoria” = “Tell them/him your theory.”
target_language_example: Può spiegarmi meglio la sua teoria?
native_language_example: Can you explain your theory to me better?

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s physical head (injuries, covering the head) and in figurative/threatening expressions where “head” can mean someone’s life or fate (e.g., “Qui è in gioco la sua testa” = “His/Her life is on the line”). Note: Italian usually uses the definite article with body parts (la testa), and "sua" agrees with the noun testa (feminine), not with the owner’s gender, so it can mean either “his” or “her” depending on context.
target_language_example: Aveva la sua testa fasciata dopo l’incidente.
native_language_example: He/She had his/her head bandaged after the accident.

additional_notes: Means “the person’s old camera.” The possessive agrees with the thing owned: macchina fotografica (feminine singular) → sua. Use it with the definite article: la sua. Context decides whose camera it is (his, her, your formal, etc.). You can change the owner: la mia (my), la tua (your), la nostra (our), la loro (their).
target_language_example: Ho trovato la sua vecchia macchina fotografica in soffitta.
native_language_example: I found his/her old camera in the attic.

additional_notes: Means “his/her life” (or “your life” when speaking politely to one person: Lei). It can refer to someone’s everyday life (Vive la sua vita) or their whole life/one’s life work (Dedicò la sua vita a…). In set phrases: “La sua vita è in pericolo” = “His/Her life is in danger”; “Ha dato la sua vita per…” = “He/She gave his/her life for…”.
target_language_example: Ha dedicato la sua vita alla famiglia.
native_language_example: He/She dedicated his/her life to the family.

meaning: "his/her life for us" (e.g., risking or sacrificing their life for our sake).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like rischiare (to risk) or sacrificare (to sacrifice) to say someone put their life in danger or gave their life for someone else. Sua agrees with the noun (la vita), not with the person, so it can mean "his" or "her". Per noi means "for us" / "on our behalf."
target_language_example: Ha dato la sua vita per noi.
native_language_example: He/She gave his/her life for us.

additional_notes: "Sua" is a possessive that agrees with the noun: "voce" (feminine singular) → "la sua". It can mean "his" or "her" (context tells you which), and also "your" in the formal "Lei" form. Used for a person’s voice, and also figuratively as "la sua voce interiore" = "his/her inner voice."
target_language_example: Non ho mai dimenticato la sua voce.
native_language_example: I have never forgotten his/her voice.

meaning: “his/hers/its” (feminine singular); also “his/hers” = “his/hers (one)” when the noun is implied.
additional_notes: Used when the possessed thing is feminine singular (e.g., “la sua decisione” = “his/her decision”). It can also stand alone as a possessive pronoun when the noun is understood from context: “La sua è migliore” = “His/Hers is better.” Which person (his vs her) depends on context; “sua” agrees with the thing owned, not the owner.
target_language_example: Preferisco la mia, ma la sua va benissimo.
native_language_example: I prefer mine, but his/hers is perfectly fine.

meaning: 'the television' (the TV; television as a medium).
additional_notes: Feminine singular noun; often shortened in speech to "la TV". Common with verbs like "accendere" (to turn on) and "guardare" (to watch): "accendere la televisione", "guardare la televisione". Use "Guardi...?" for formal 'you' and "Guarda...?" for informal.
target_language_example: Stasera non guardo la televisione.
native_language_example: Tonight I'm not watching TV.

additional_notes: Used for strong weather like heavy rain, wind, thunder, etc. Common with verbs like guardare (to watch), durare (to last), and impedire (to prevent). You can also use it figuratively (e.g., "dopo la tempesta" = after a difficult period).
target_language_example: Spero che la tempesta finisca presto.
native_language_example: I hope the storm ends soon.

meaning: a tendency to be (something); to tend to be.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a habitual trait or common behavior. It’s often followed by an adjective (e.g., distratto, smemorato) or a description. Common pattern: avere la tendenza a + infinitive (here: ad essere, before a vowel).
target_language_example: Ho la tendenza ad essere puntuale, ma oggi sono in ritardo.
native_language_example: I tend to be punctual, but today I’m late.

meaning: the earth; the ground/soil; the land (property/territory).
additional_notes: Often refers to the ground under your feet (La terra trema), the soil for farming (La terra è fertile), or land you own or control (La terra diventerebbe mia). In expressions like "baciare la terra" it means “to kiss the ground” (often figuratively: to be extremely grateful or show total respect).
target_language_example: Dopo il terremoto, la terra ha tremato per qualche secondo.
native_language_example: After the earthquake, the ground shook for a few seconds.

additional_notes: Literal meaning is the body part (head). In phrases like "usare la testa" it means using your brain/common sense. With feelings like "testa pesante" it describes a heavy head feeling (often from tiredness, a cold, or a headache).
target_language_example: Oggi ho mal di testa, quindi vado a letto presto.
