native_language_example: Today I have a headache, so I’m going to bed early.

additional_notes: A common food word. In everyday Italian, torta usually means a cake (often baked, sometimes with cream or fruit). It can also refer to certain pies/tarts; for a specifically savory pie Italians often say torta salata.
target_language_example: Per il mio compleanno voglio una torta al cioccolato.
native_language_example: For my birthday I want a chocolate cake.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun: "la tua mano" = "your hand", "la tua frase" = "your sentence". It agrees with the noun (feminine singular), and it can also be used on its own to mean "yours" when the noun is understood from context (e.g., "La tua è qui" = "Yours is here").
target_language_example: Dov'è la tua valigia?
native_language_example: Where is your suitcase?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a friend who is female (or grammatically treated as feminine). Italian possessives agree with the noun: "la" + "tua" because "amica" is feminine singular. For a male friend, say "il tuo amico".
target_language_example: Ho parlato con la tua amica ieri sera.
native_language_example: I talked with your (female) friend last night.

additional_notes: Uses the feminine singular possessive pattern: la (feminine singular) + tua (your) + auto (car). Common in questions and requests, e.g., asking to drive/borrow someone’s car. If you’re speaking formally to one person, you would say "la Sua auto" instead.
target_language_example: Dov'è parcheggiata la tua auto?
native_language_example: Where is your car parked?

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s car. “La” is the feminine singular definite article (“the”), “tua” agrees with the feminine noun “automobile.” In everyday conversation, Italians often say “la tua macchina” instead of “la tua automobile.”
target_language_example: Posso vedere la tua automobile?
native_language_example: Can I see your car?

additional_notes: Refers to a feminine noun (borsa) owned by “you” (tu). Often used for a purse/handbag, but it can also mean a bag in general depending on context (e.g., a shopping bag). Used in everyday situations like asking someone to hand it over, checking if they forgot it, or commenting that it’s heavy.
target_language_example: Aspetta, hai preso la tua borsa?
native_language_example: Wait, did you take your bag?

additional_notes: Means “your house/home” when talking to one person informally (tu). Often used with comments about someone’s home (È bella!/È pulita?), or in offers and idioms like “La mia casa è la tua casa” (“My home is your home”).
target_language_example: Posso venire a vedere la tua casa domani?
native_language_example: Can I come see your house tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to refer to how old someone is, often in comparisons or time references: “quando avevo la tua età” = “when I was your age.” It can also be used in advice/criticism like “Agisci secondo la tua età” (“Act your age”).
target_language_example: Quando avevo la tua età, studiavo già all'università.
native_language_example: When I was your age, I was already studying at university.

meaning: "your face"; sometimes used as a teasing/insulting comeback ("yeah, right!").
additional_notes: Literally means “your face” (faccia = face, tua = your). Common in direct speech: “Fammi vedere la tua faccia!” = “Let me see your face!” On its own (“La tua faccia!”) it can be an informal, childish/teasing retort, similar to “Yeah, right!” / “My foot!” depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: La tua faccia! Non ci credo nemmeno un po'.
native_language_example: Yeah, right! I don’t believe it at all.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the listener’s family. "Famiglia" is feminine singular, so it takes the feminine singular possessive: "la tua". The possessive usually comes with the definite article (la/il/i/le): "la tua famiglia", "il tuo padre", etc.
target_language_example: Conosci già la tua famiglia qui in città?
native_language_example: Do you already know your family here in the city?

additional_notes: Used when speaking directly to a friend, family member, or someone you address with tu. Often appears after verbs like ricevere (to receive), leggere (to read), scrivere (to write), and with thanks (Grazie per...). If you’re addressing someone formally (Lei), you’d say la Sua lettera.
target_language_example: Ho letto la tua lettera ieri sera.
native_language_example: I read your letter last night.

additional_notes: Means "your language" when talking about what someone speaks (e.g., "Capisco la tua lingua"). It can also mean "your tongue" (the body part), especially in the phrase "Mostrami la tua lingua" (often said to a child or at the doctor). Use "la tua" with someone you address as "tu"; for "Lei" use "la Sua lingua".
target_language_example: Sto cercando di imparare la tua lingua.
native_language_example: I'm trying to learn your language.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “your car” in everyday conversation. The possessive adjective *tua* agrees with the feminine singular noun *macchina* (la). Used to talk about something that belongs to the person you’re speaking to; in more technical contexts it can also mean “your machine” (e.g., a device).
target_language_example: Dov'è parcheggiata la tua macchina?
native_language_example: Where is your car parked?

additional_notes: Used to point out a moment or possibility for you to act or succeed. Often said as an encouragement or warning: "Questa è la tua occasione!" = "This is your chance!" You can also use it with verbs like perdere (to miss/lose): "Hai perso la tua occasione" = "You missed your chance."
target_language_example: Non sprecarla: questa è la tua occasione.
native_language_example: Don’t waste it: this is your chance.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to someone’s viewpoint/what they think. Often appears in questions like “Qual è la tua opinione?” (What’s your opinion?) or with verbs like chiedere (to ask for), sentire (to hear), and rispettare (to respect).
target_language_example: Prima di decidere, vorrei sapere la tua opinione.
native_language_example: Before deciding, I’d like to know your opinion.

additional_notes: Used when the thing being described is feminine (e.g., la moglie, la impressione, la conferenza, la visita, la missione). It often comes before the noun ("la tua prima visita"), but it can also stand alone if the noun is understood from context ("È la tua prima?" = "Is it your first time?"). For a masculine noun you’d use "il tuo primo".
target_language_example: È la tua prima volta in Italia?
native_language_example: Is it your first time in Italy?

additional_notes: In Italian, *ragazza* literally means “girl/young woman,” but with a possessive (*la mia/la tua/la sua ragazza*) it very commonly means “girlfriend.” Context can make it clear whether it’s a girlfriend or simply “your girl/your female friend.” In crude slang, *farsi (qualcuno)* can mean “to sleep with (someone),” as in the example *Mi sono fatto la tua ragazza*.
target_language_example: Stasera esci con la tua ragazza?
native_language_example: Are you going out with your girlfriend tonight?

additional_notes: Used to refer to what someone says or writes as an answer (to a question, request, email, etc.). It’s feminine singular: la risposta. Often used in phrases like Stiamo aspettando la tua risposta (“We’re waiting for your reply”). In formal situations you may see la Sua risposta (your, formal).
target_language_example: Non ho ancora ricevuto la tua risposta.
native_language_example: I still haven’t received your reply.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s physical or mental health, often in caring or concerned contexts. Common with expressions like: "Come va la tua salute?" (How’s your health?), "preoccuparsi per la tua salute" (to worry about your health), and "La tua salute è più importante" (Your health is more important). You can also drop the article and say "tua salute" in some sentences, but "la tua salute" is very common and natural.
target_language_example: Prenditi cura della tua salute.
native_language_example: Take care of your health.

additional_notes: Uses the feminine singular article and possessive: la + tua + stanza. You use it when talking to one person you address as tu. For plural “your” (to more than one person) you’d say “la vostra stanza”.
target_language_example: Puoi chiudere la porta della tua stanza, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you close the door to your room, please?

additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about someone’s life in general (their experiences, future, lifestyle) or their safety (“your life is in danger”). Often appears with verbs like cambiare (to change), rovinare (to ruin), allungare (to lengthen/extend), mettere ... nelle mani di (to put ... in someone’s hands).
target_language_example: Non lasciare che questa decisione rovini la tua vita.
native_language_example: Don’t let this decision ruin your life.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the voice of the person you’re speaking to (often when recognizing them by sound or saying you like how they sound). It’s feminine singular: la (the) + tua (your) + voce (voice).
target_language_example: Non ti vedevo, ma ho riconosciuto la tua voce.
native_language_example: I didn’t see you, but I recognized your voice.

additional_notes: Used to refer to something that belongs to “you,” when the noun is feminine and singular (often omitted because it’s understood): e.g., “la tua (auto)” = “your/yours (car).” It can stand alone in questions like “E la tua?” meaning “And yours?” (e.g., your car/your life/your sister’s, depending on context).
target_language_example: Io prendo la mia bici; tu puoi prendere la tua.
native_language_example: I’ll take my bike; you can take yours.

additional_notes: Refers to a small case/bag you carry, often for work or travel (typically a briefcase). Feminine noun: la valigetta; plural: le valigette. Common with "avere con sé" (to have with you) and "essere" + place (e.g., "è al bar").
target_language_example: Scusi, ho lasciato la valigetta sul treno.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I left my briefcase on the train.

additional_notes: Used for telling or discovering what is true. Common with verbs like dire (to tell), sapere/conoscere (to know), and scoprire (to discover): dire la verità = to tell the truth. Often used in direct requests: Dimmi la verità. You can also place it at the start for emphasis: La verità è che… (“The truth is that…”).
target_language_example: Per favore, dimmi la verità: che cosa è successo?
native_language_example: Please tell me the truth: what happened?

additional_notes: Used to introduce what the speaker considers the real or most important fact, often as a correction, clarification, or honest admission. It’s commonly followed by a full sentence; you can omit “che” in English (“The truth is, I don’t…”).
target_language_example: La verità è che non ho tempo oggi.
native_language_example: The truth is, I don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Means “life” in general (existence, a person’s life). In phrases like “perdere la vita” it means “to lose one’s life” (= to die).
target_language_example: La vita in città è più frenetica che in campagna.
native_language_example: Life in the city is more hectic than in the countryside.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s life (a person’s experiences, situation, or lifestyle): *la vita di tua sorella* (“your sister’s life”). With certain verbs it can express strong consequences or threats, e.g. *rovinare/distruggere la vita di qualcuno* (“to ruin/destroy someone’s life”), and sometimes *volere la vita di qualcuno* can mean “to be after someone’s life” (want them dead), depending on context.
target_language_example: Non voglio rovinare la vita di nessuno.
native_language_example: I don’t want to ruin anyone’s life.

additional_notes: Used to start a general statement or comment about life, often followed by an adjective (complicata, dura, pazza) or a longer description. Common in motivational, philosophical, or casual remarks.
target_language_example: La vita è breve, quindi goditela.
native_language_example: Life is short, so enjoy it.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about life, followed by a noun (usually plural) or a noun phrase: la vita è piena di sorprese/misteri. You can change the subject to something else with the same pattern: Il mondo è pieno di… / La città è piena di….
target_language_example: La vita è piena di imprevisti, ma anche di momenti felici.
native_language_example: Life is full of unexpected events, but also of happy moments.

meaning: 'life is a…' (introduces a comparison/metaphor about life).
additional_notes: Used to start a sentence where you describe life by comparing it to something (often with a noun phrase after it): *La vita è una lotteria / una strada / una ricerca…*. Because it sets up a metaphor, what follows can be positive, negative, humorous, or even vulgar depending on the speaker.
target_language_example: La vita è una sfida, ma non mollare.
native_language_example: Life is a challenge, but don’t give up.

additional_notes: Used for a person (or sometimes an animal) who has been hurt, killed, or harmed (e.g., in a crime, accident, or abuse). In news and police contexts you often hear: identificare la vittima (“identify the victim”). Feminine noun: la vittima; plural: le vittime. It can refer to a man or a woman (e.g., “La vittima è un uomo.”).
target_language_example: La polizia ha identificato la vittima.
native_language_example: The police identified the victim.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a person's voice (sound): alzare la voce = to raise your voice, abbassare la voce = to lower your voice, perdere la voce = to lose your voice. It can also mean a rumor or report (often with verbs like correre, circolare, essere vera/falsa: "la voce era vera fino a un certo punto" = the rumor was true up to a point).
target_language_example: Non alzare la voce, per favore.
native_language_example: Don’t raise your voice, please.

additional_notes: Used to refer to something that belongs to 'you' (addressing more than one person, or using polite/formal 'you') when the thing possessed is feminine singular. It agrees with the noun: la vostra cautela (your caution), la vostra casa (your house).
target_language_example: La vostra prenotazione è confermata.
native_language_example: Your reservation is confirmed.

additional_notes: Means “your friend” when the friend is a woman/girl (amica). Vostra agrees with a feminine singular noun (amica), and it’s used when speaking to more than one person (you all) or as the polite/formal “your.” Often used with questions or advice about what to do for someone.
target_language_example: Ho un regalo per la vostra amica.
native_language_example: I have a gift for your (plural/formal) female friend.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "vostro/a" with the definite article: "la vostra" + a feminine singular noun like "auto". It can address more than one person ("your" plural) or be used in formal speech as a polite "your". Compare: "la tua auto" = your car (singular, informal).
target_language_example: Scusate, dov'è parcheggiata la vostra auto?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is your car parked?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a car that belongs to more than one person (“your” plural), or as a polite/formal “your” in some contexts. Must agree with the feminine singular noun automobile, so it’s la vostra. Often used in questions about someone’s car (color, whether it’s new, fast, etc.).
target_language_example: Dov'è parcheggiata la vostra automobile?
native_language_example: Where is your car parked?

additional_notes: "Vostra" is the formal (Lei) or plural form of "your". "Biro" is a common word for a ballpoint pen in Italian; it’s feminine, so you say "la biro".
target_language_example: Scusi, posso prendere la vostra biro un attimo?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I borrow your pen for a moment?

additional_notes: Uses the feminine singular article la + vostra (“your”) + casa (“house/home”). Vostra agrees with casa. Refers to something belonging to “you” plural (voi) or to one person addressed formally (Lei), depending on context.
target_language_example: Benvenuti a la vostra casa!
native_language_example: Welcome to your home!

meaning: 'your family' (addressing more than one person, or using formal 'voi').
additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "vostra" with the feminine singular noun "famiglia". "Vostro/vostra/vostri/vostre" agrees with the noun (here: vostra). Common when speaking to a group: "La vostra famiglia è venuta con voi?" Also used with formal "voi" (less common today than "Lei" in many situations).
target_language_example: Com’è la vostra famiglia?
native_language_example: How is your family?

additional_notes: Used when addressing more than one person (plural “your”) or one person politely/formally (especially in writing). “Lettera” is feminine, so it takes “la” and “vostra.” Common in phrases like: Ecco la vostra lettera. / Ho letto la vostra lettera. / Mostratemi la vostra lettera.
target_language_example: Ho ricevuto la vostra lettera ieri.
native_language_example: I received your letter yesterday.

meaning: your language (speaking to more than one person, or as a polite “your”).
additional_notes: “Vostra” is the possessive adjective for “voi” (you plural, or formal/polite). It agrees with the feminine singular noun “lingua.” Often used when talking to a group (e.g., an audience) or in formal contexts. Informal singular would be “la tua lingua.”
target_language_example: Sto cercando di capire la vostra lingua.
native_language_example: I’m trying to understand your language.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective vostra (“your”) with a feminine singular noun (macchina). It’s used when speaking to more than one person (voi) or in formal contexts. Often refers to a car, but macchina can also mean “machine,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Dove avete parcheggiato la vostra macchina?
native_language_example: Where did you park your car?

additional_notes: Means the opinion of more than one person (you all) or of someone you address formally (e.g., customers/clients). Often used with verbs like chiedere (to ask), volere (to want), and sapere (to know). In speech you might also hear "la Sua opinione" (very formal singular) or "la tua opinione" (informal singular).
target_language_example: Vorrei conoscere la vostra opinione su questo progetto.
native_language_example: I’d like to know your opinion on this project.

meaning: "your answer" (addressing more than one person, or using formal 'you').
additional_notes: Uses the formal/plural possessive "vostra" with the feminine noun "risposta". It can refer to an answer given aloud or in writing. Common in requests like "Datemi la vostra risposta" (Give me your answer) or questions like "Quando mi darete la vostra risposta?" (When will you give me your answer?). For one person informally, you’d usually say "la tua risposta".
target_language_example: Potete mandarmi la vostra risposta entro domani?
native_language_example: Can you send me your answer by tomorrow?

meaning: "your room" (addressing more than one person, or formal 'you').
additional_notes: "La" = "the" (feminine singular), "vostra" = "your" (plural or formal), "stanza" = "room". Used when speaking to a group (e.g., children, guests) or using polite/formal address. Often appears in questions and instructions about tidying or cleaning.
target_language_example: Ecco la vostra stanza: è al secondo piano.
native_language_example: Here is your room: it's on the second floor.

additional_notes: Used to refer to soup as a dish (often served as a first course). Gender: feminine singular (la), plural: le zuppe. In conversation, saying just “La zuppa?” can mean “The soup?” (confirming or asking for clarification).
target_language_example: Per pranzo prendo la zuppa.
native_language_example: For lunch I'll have the soup.

additional_notes: A food item. Use it after verbs like piacere (Mi piace la zuppa di zucca = I like pumpkin soup) or when ordering/asking preferences. Articles may change depending on context (e.g., Vorrei una zuppa di zucca = I’d like a pumpkin soup).
target_language_example: Per cena vorrei la zuppa di zucca.
native_language_example: For dinner I’d like pumpkin soup.

meaning: I love her (also: I love it, feminine).
additional_notes: "La" is a direct object pronoun meaning "her" or "it" (feminine singular). It goes before the verb: "la amo" = "I love her/it". Used for romantic love or strong affection depending on context; for friends/family you may also hear "le voglio bene" (I care about her / I love her in a non-romantic way).
target_language_example: So che è difficile, ma la amo.
native_language_example: I know it’s difficult, but I love her.

meaning: "I know her" / "I know it" (referring to a feminine direct object).
additional_notes: "La" is the direct object pronoun for feminine singular (a woman, or a feminine noun like *la procedura*, *questa marca*). It can mean you’re familiar with someone/something or you know it well. In speech, Italians may repeat it for emphasis: *La conosco, la procedura, la conosco* (“I know it—the procedure—I know it”).
target_language_example: Tranquillo, la conosco bene, questa strada.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I know this road well.

additional_notes:
This is not the noun *faccia* (“face”) here. It’s *fare* (“to do/make”) + the direct object pronoun *la* (“it/her”): *la faccia* = “(that) you do it / do it.” You’ll see it:
- after triggers like *spero che...* where Italian uses the subjunctive: *Spero che (Lei/lui/lei) la faccia.* (“I hope you/he/she does it.”)
- as a formal command to *Lei* (polite ‘you’), often sounding like “Please do it”: *La faccia ora!* (“Do it now!”)
The verb can also mean “have/let someone do something”: *La faccia uscire* = “Have her/it taken out / let her out.”
target_language_example: Per favore, la faccia subito.
native_language_example: Please do it right away.

additional_notes: “La” is a direct-object pronoun meaning “it” (for a feminine noun, like *la cosa*, *la canzone*, *la torta*). So *la faccio* means “I do it / I make it.” The exact English translation depends on context and on the verb that may follow: for example, *Ve la faccio ascoltare* means “I’ll let you listen to it / I’ll play it for you” (literally “I make you listen to it”), where *ve* = “to you (plural).”
target_language_example: Tranquilli, la faccio io.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll do it.

additional_notes: "La" is an object pronoun meaning “it” (referring to something understood from context: a task, a challenge, a situation). So "la fai" can mean simply “you do it,” or, in many contexts, “you manage to do it / you make it.” It can also be used in causative patterns like "la fai finire" (“you make it end / you finish it”) or "la fai scegliere" (“you make (someone) choose / you let (someone) choose”). A common negative form is "non ce la fai" or "non te la fai" (“you can’t do it / you won’t make it”).
target_language_example: Dai, la fai: manca solo un ultimo sforzo!
native_language_example: Come on, you can do it: just one last effort!

meaning: 'he/she will do it' / 'he/she will make it'.
additional_notes: From the verb "fare" (to do/make) in the future tense: "farà" = "will do/make". "La" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" (referring to a feminine noun, or to an implied thing/action). Common uses: (1) "la farà" = "he/she will do it / succeed"; (2) with an infinitive: "la farà piangere" = "he/she will make her/it cry" (cause to cry). The pronoun "la" can also refer to a person (a woman) depending on context.
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: la farà anche se è difficile.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he’ll do it / he’ll make it even if it’s hard.

additional_notes: Made of the direct-object pronoun "la" (= her) + "lasci" (formal imperative for "Lei" of "lasciare"). Used to tell someone politely/formally to leave someone out of something ("La lasci fuori da...") or to let someone do something ("La lasci venire/rilassare"). In informal speech you’d often hear "Lasciala" instead.
target_language_example: Per favore, la lasci parlare.
native_language_example: Please, let her speak.

additional_notes: Used with the object pronoun **la** (“it” for a feminine noun, or **you** in formal speech = *Lei*). In Italian the pronoun comes before the verb: **la + posso + verb**. Common in polite questions like **La posso aiutare?** (“Can I help you?”).
target_language_example: La posso chiamare domani?
native_language_example: Can I call you tomorrow?

meaning: “Can I borrow it?” (referring to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask permission to borrow an object. "La" = “it/her” (feminine singular), so it refers to something like la penna (the pen), la sedia (the chair), etc. You can add a time: "per un minuto", "per un’ora", "per quanto tempo?". For politeness you can start with "Scusa" (informal, singular), "Scusate" (informal, plural), or "Scusi" (formal).
target_language_example: Scusi, la posso prendere in prestito per cinque minuti?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I borrow it for five minutes?

additional_notes: Used when speaking politely to someone with Lei (formal “you”). Literally it’s “I beg you,” and it can sound stronger or more urgent than just “per favore,” especially when pleading or insisting. You can also use it on its own as an emphatic “Please.”
target_language_example: La prego, mi ascolti un momento.
native_language_example: Please, listen to me for a moment.

additional_notes: Used to make a strong, respectful request. **La prego** literally means “I beg you” and uses the formal **Lei** form (so *la* = “you” formal). **mi** = “me/to me,” and it introduces the next verb phrase (e.g., *mi dica*, *mi accompagni*, *mi perdoni*). Common in serious or urgent situations; less common in casual everyday speech, where you’d more often hear *per favore*.
target_language_example: La prego, mi aiuti a trovare il mio telefono.
native_language_example: Please, help me find my phone.

meaning: “Please …” (formal/very polite way to ask someone to do something).
additional_notes: Used with the formal pronoun **Lei** (and object **La** = “you”), especially in polite requests, instructions, or official/customer-service contexts. It’s typically followed by an infinitive: **La prego di + infinitive** (e.g., *La prego di aspettare* = “Please wait”). With **non**: *La prego di non + infinitive* (“Please don’t …”). Can also be used to apologize politely: *La prego di scusarmi/scusarci* (“Please excuse me/us”).
target_language_example: La prego di aspettare un momento.
native_language_example: Please wait a moment.

meaning: I’ll take it (I’ll take that one).
additional_notes: Used when you offer/insist that you will take something (choose it, pick it up, carry it, take responsibility for it). **La** means “it” (feminine noun implied: e.g., *la borsa* bag, *la pizza* pizza). **Io** adds emphasis/contrast: “*I*’ll take it (not you).” For a masculine noun, you’ll often hear **lo prendo io**.
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti, la prendo io.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll take it.

additional_notes: From "smettere di" = “to stop doing.” "La" refers to the person you’re addressing with the formal "Lei" (like “sir/ma’am”), and "smetta" is the command form (“(you) stop”). It’s used to tell someone to stop an action: "La smetta di + infinitive" (La smetta di parlare / fumare). With non-people, you’ll often see "Spero che la smetta di + infinitive" = “I hope it stops …” (e.g., rain).
target_language_example: La smetta di urlare, per favore.
native_language_example: Please stop shouting.

additional_notes: A firm but formal way to tell someone to stop talking. It uses the formal address “Lei”: “smetta” is the formal imperative of *smettere* (“to stop”), and “La” is the formal pronoun referring to the person you’re addressing. You may also hear it without “La”: *Smetta di parlare.* Often combined with *per favore* to soften it.
target_language_example: Mi scusi, la smetta di parlare durante il film.
native_language_example: Excuse me, please stop talking during the movie.

additional_notes: A formal command using Lei (polite “you”). It comes from the verb "smettere di" (to stop doing) and is used with "parlare di" (to talk about). Add the topic after "di": a name, a noun, or a pronoun (e.g., "me", "lui", "lei", "sé").
target_language_example: La smetta di parlare di politica, per favore.
native_language_example: Please stop talking about politics.

meaning: "is waiting for her" / "is waiting for you" (formal).
additional_notes: Uses the present progressive: **stare + aspettando** = “to be waiting.” **La** is a direct object pronoun meaning “her,” or “you” (formal, polite). Which one it means depends on context. You can add places like **fuori** (outside), **dentro** (inside), **nel suo ufficio** (in his/her office).
target_language_example: Il direttore la sta aspettando fuori.
native_language_example: The manager is waiting for you outside.

additional_notes: “La” is a direct object pronoun meaning “her” or “it” (for a feminine noun, like *la macchina*). “Stanno aspettando” is *stare* + gerund, a common way to say “are waiting” (right now/at the moment). Word order can vary (e.g., *Tutti la stanno aspettando* = “Everyone is waiting for her”).
target_language_example: Sbrighiamoci: la stanno aspettando davanti all’ingresso.
native_language_example: Let’s hurry up: they’re waiting for her in front of the entrance.

additional_notes: "La" is a direct object pronoun meaning “her” or “it” (referring to a feminine noun, like *la faccia* “the face” or *la valigetta* “the briefcase”). It’s used when the object is already known from context: *Non la vedo* = “I don’t see it/her.” In some contexts it can also be figurative (“I see / I get it”), but often it’s literal seeing.
target_language_example: Scusi, non la vedo bene da qui.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t see it/her well from here.

meaning: tears in your eyes (about to cry).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who is crying or on the verge of crying, often because they are sad, moved, or emotional. Common with verbs like "avere" (ha le lacrime agli occhi) and "entrare/arrivare" (entrò/arrivò con le lacrime agli occhi).
target_language_example: Quando ha sentito la notizia, aveva le lacrime agli occhi.
native_language_example: When she heard the news, she had tears in her eyes.

additional_notes: Often used as an imperative with formal address (Lei): “Lasci andare…” = “Let … go / Release …”. With the reflexive form, it can mean “Relax/let yourself go” (sometimes also “lose control” or “indulge”).
target_language_example: Si lasci andare un po': oggi non deve pensare a niente.
native_language_example: Relax a bit: today you don't have to think about anything.

additional_notes: Formal/polite way to give permission or to propose that someone be allowed to do something. It uses the Lei form of "lasciare" (lasci) + "che" + the subjunctive (e.g., lasci che le aiuti, lasci che spieghi). Often translates as “let me…” / “allow me to…” when followed by a verb in the first person.
target_language_example: Lasci che le mostri la strada.
native_language_example: Let me show you the way.

additional_notes: Used to ask/tell someone to stop bothering, disturbing, or contacting someone. It’s the formal/third-person present subjunctive of "lasciare in pace" (“to leave in peace”): "Perché non mi lasci in pace?" = “Why don’t you leave me alone?” Often follows object pronouns like mi/ti/lo/la/ci/vi/li/le (e.g., "lasciami in pace", "lascialo in pace").
target_language_example: Ti prego, lasciami in pace.
native_language_example: Please, leave me alone.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop touching something or to stop bothering/interfering. Can refer to an object ("Lasci stare la cravatta" = don’t touch/leave the tie alone) or a person ("Mi lasci stare" = leave me alone). With pronouns: "Lo/La lasci stare!" = Leave him/her/it alone! Polite form uses Lei ("lasci"), but it can still sound firm.
target_language_example: Mi scusi, mi lasci stare: non mi sento bene.
native_language_example: Excuse me, leave me alone: I don’t feel well.

additional_notes: Used to give permission or allow something to happen, followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., lascia che vada, lascia che parli). It can sound like an instruction (“Let him/her…”) or an offer (“Let me…”), depending on context and who is doing the action.
target_language_example: Lascia che ti aiuti con i compiti.
native_language_example: Let me help you with your homework.

additional_notes: Used to ask permission or insist on doing something for the other person: *Lascia che ti + verb (present subjunctive)*. Common with verbs like **aiuti** (help you), **dica** (tell you), **porti** (take you/drive you), **presenti** (introduce you). Often sounds polite and supportive, like “Let me help you / Let me tell you…”.
target_language_example: Lascia che ti mostri dove si trova la stazione.
native_language_example: Let me show you where the station is.

additional_notes: Used to offer help or ask someone to allow you to help. Often followed by a + infinitive to say what you’ll help with: “Lascia che ti aiuti a pulire” (“Let me help you clean”). Can sound caring or gently insistent depending on tone.
target_language_example: Lascia che ti aiuti a portare le borse.
native_language_example: Let me help you carry the bags.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you’re about to show someone. Literally “allow that I show you,” but in natural English it’s usually “Let me show you …”. Often followed by “cosa/qualcosa/una cosa …” (what/something/a thing) and can be used on its own: “Lascia che ti mostri.”
target_language_example: Lascia che ti mostri dove si trova la stazione.
native_language_example: Let me show you where the station is.

meaning: “Let me tell you about … / Let me talk to you about …”.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a topic you want to explain. Literally “let (it be) that I speak to you about …”. After it, you add the person/thing/topic (Tom, lei, noi, una ragazza…). Often sounds like a polite but direct way to start a story or explanation.
target_language_example: Lascia che ti parli di questo posto: è davvero speciale.
native_language_example: Let me tell you about this place: it’s really special.

meaning: Leave it to me / Let me handle it.
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or to take charge of a situation. Often said as an invitation to stop worrying or to let you do the task instead. You can add a time word for emphasis (e.g., "adesso" = "now"). Tone can be friendly or firm depending on context.
target_language_example: Lascia fare a me: ci penso io.
native_language_example: Leave it to me: I’ll take care of it.

additional_notes: Common spoken imperative used to tell someone to stop trying, stop insisting, or stop talking about something (often because it’s not worth it or won’t work). It can stand alone (“Lascia perdere.”) or be followed by a topic (“Lascia perdere questa storia.”). Tone can range from friendly to impatient depending on context.
target_language_example: Volevo chiamarlo, ma lascia perdere: è meglio così.
native_language_example: I wanted to call him, but forget it: it’s better this way.

meaning: Leave it alone; forget it; drop it.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop touching/doing something (“Leave it alone!”) or to stop insisting/talking about something (“Forget it/Drop it.”). Often said as a short, firm command; can sound rude depending on tone. Common with an object: “Lascia stare + [noun/pronoun]”.
target_language_example: Lascia stare, non ne vale la pena.
native_language_example: Forget it, it’s not worth it.

additional_notes: Imperative form (to one person: “you”). Used when you want someone to stop bothering you or go away. Tone can be firm or angry depending on context; you can soften it with “per favore” (Lasciami in pace, per favore.) or strengthen it with “Basta!” / “Vattene!”
target_language_example: Lasciami in pace, per favore: ho bisogno di concentrarmi.
native_language_example: Leave me alone, please: I need to concentrate.

meaning: to leave behind; to forget to take (something).
additional_notes: Used for physically leaving a person or object behind (e.g., at home, on the bus), or more generally for not including someone (e.g., leaving someone out of a plan). Can also mean to fall behind in progress (e.g., in school or work). Often used with an object pronoun: "L'ho lasciato indietro" (I left it behind).
target_language_example: Ho lasciato indietro il telefono a casa.
native_language_example: I left my phone behind at home.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun (la + noun): lasciare la stanza/la città/la festa. It can mean (1) to leave/depart from a place or event ("leave the room/party/city"), or (2) to leave something/someone behind or in a place ("leave the plant while I take the bags"). Often interchangeable with "andare via da..." for “to go away,” but "lasciare" highlights leaving something/somewhere.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo lasciare la casa alle otto.
native_language_example: We have to leave the house at eight.

meaning: to let it go; to drop it; to forget about it.
additional_notes: Used when you decide not to continue with something (an argument, a plan, a complaint) because it’s not worth the effort. Very common in spoken Italian, especially as an imperative: “Lascia perdere!” (= “Forget it / Let it go”). It can also mean “don’t bother (with that person/thing)”.
target_language_example: Lascia perdere, non ne vale la pena.
native_language_example: Let it go, it’s not worth it.

meaning: to leave it alone; to drop it; to let it be.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop doing something or stop insisting ("Leave it alone." / "Forget it."). It can also mean not to touch or bother something/someone: "Lascia stare quel cane" (Leave that dog alone). Often used as an imperative: "Lascia stare!"
target_language_example: Dai, lascia stare: non ne vale la pena.
native_language_example: Come on, let it go: it’s not worth it.

additional_notes: Used to ask or tell someone to stop bothering you and give you privacy/space. It’s made of lasciare (to leave) + mi (me) + da solo (alone/by myself). You can change the person: lasciarti da solo (leave you alone), lasciarlo/la da solo/a (leave him/her alone).
target_language_example: Per favore, lasciami da solo per un momento.
native_language_example: Please, leave me alone for a moment.

additional_notes: Used to tell more than one person (or in formal address) to allow something to happen. It’s the imperative of "lasciare" (to let/allow) + "che" + the verb in the subjunctive: "Lasciate che parli" = "Let him speak." (Also common: "lascia che" for one person.)
target_language_example: Lasciate che finisca di parlare, per favore.
native_language_example: Please let him finish speaking.

meaning: "let me ... (for you / to you)" (addressing you all or formally).
additional_notes: Used to politely introduce what you’re about to do or say: "Lasciate che vi spieghi..." = "Let me explain...". "Lasciate" is the imperative of "lasciare" for "voi" (you plural / formal), and "vi" means "you" (plural) as an object (e.g., "tell you", "help you"). Common in speeches, presentations, or formal conversation.
target_language_example: Lasciate che vi mostri dove si trova l’uscita.
native_language_example: Let me show you where the exit is.

additional_notes: Common on voicemail/answering machines or when someone can’t answer the phone. "Lasciate" is the polite plural/formal command (voi) often used in recorded messages to address callers in general; you may also hear "Lascia un messaggio" (informal, to one person). Often followed by "per favore / per piacere".
target_language_example: Dopo il segnale, lasciate un messaggio.
native_language_example: After the beep, leave a message.

meaning: Let me go; let me leave.
additional_notes: Imperative (addressing “you” plural, or formal “you”): literally “let me go.” Used when you want permission or freedom to leave (often physically, e.g., if someone is holding you) or to go somewhere: “Lasciatemi andare a casa/in Australia.” On its own (“Lasciatemi andare!”) it’s a strong demand. With another object it can also mean “let … down/loose,” e.g., “Lasciatemi andare i capelli” = “Let my hair down/loose.”
target_language_example: Lasciatemi andare subito, per favore.
native_language_example: Let me go right now, please.

meaning: left alone; left by himself (not accompanied).
additional_notes: Past participle phrase of "lasciare" (to leave). Used after verbs like "essere" (è stato lasciato da solo = he was left alone) or "venire" (veniva lasciato da solo = he would get left alone). It agrees with the person left alone: lasciato (masc. sing.), lasciata (fem. sing.), lasciati/lasciate (plural). Often implies someone was left without supervision or company.
target_language_example: Non lasciare il bambino da solo in casa.
native_language_example: Don’t leave the child alone at home.

additional_notes: Used with the passato prossimo of **lasciare** (to leave). It’s often followed by a masculine singular noun: **lasciato il porto** (left the port), **lasciato il paese** (left the town/country). With **avere**, the past participle **lasciato** usually doesn’t change; the meaning depends on context (simple past “left” or present perfect “have left”).
target_language_example: Ho lasciato il telefono in macchina.
native_language_example: I left my phone in the car.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "lasciare" (to leave). In the past, it often appears as "(ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno) lasciato la…". It can mean leaving something somewhere ("Dove hai lasciato la tua camicia?" = where did you leave your shirt?) or leaving/quitting a place or situation ("Hanno lasciato la scuola" = they left school). "La" is the feminine singular “the”, so it must match a feminine noun (la casa, la camera, la scuola, etc.).
target_language_example: Ho lasciato la giacca in macchina.
native_language_example: I left my jacket in the car.

additional_notes: Used with the passato prossimo of "lasciare" (to leave): "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno lasciato la finestra aperta". "Aperta" agrees with "la finestra" (feminine singular). It often implies someone forgot to close it.
target_language_example: Scusa, ho lasciato la finestra aperta tutta la notte.
native_language_example: Sorry, I left the window open all night.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb "avere" to say someone forgot or intentionally left a door open: (io) ho lasciato…, (tu) hai lasciato…, (voi) avete lasciato…, (chi) ha lasciato…. Often implies it wasn’t closed when it should have been.
target_language_example: Scusa, ho lasciato la porta aperta.
native_language_example: Sorry, I left the door open.

additional_notes: Past participle of lasciare used with avere: ho/hai/ha lasciato un messaggio = “I/you/he/she left a message.” Common when talking about voicemail, a note, or a message passed through someone else. With indirect object pronouns: gli/le/ti/vi ho lasciato un messaggio = “I left him/her/you(pl.) a message.”
target_language_example: Ti ho lasciato un messaggio in segreteria ieri sera.
native_language_example: I left you a voicemail last night.

additional_notes: “Lasciò” is the passato remoto (simple past) of “lasciare” (to leave). It’s common in writing, storytelling, and in some regions in speech; in everyday conversation many speakers use “ha lasciato” instead. “Il suo / la sua / i suoi / le sue” means “his/her/its” and changes to match the noun being possessed (e.g., “il suo telefono”, “la sua borsa”). In many contexts “lasciare” can mean either “to leave (a thing somewhere)” or “to leave/quit (a job, office, relationship)”.
target_language_example: Ieri lasciò il suo zaino in macchina.
native_language_example: Yesterday he left his backpack in the car.

meaning: "(he/she) left the" (simple past; Passato Remoto of *lasciare* + *la*).
additional_notes: *Lasciò* is the Passato Remoto (a narrative/literary past tense) of *lasciare* “to leave.” It’s common in books, stories, and in some regions of Italy; in everyday speech you often hear *ha lasciato la...* instead. *La* is the feminine singular “the,” so it’s used before feminine nouns (e.g., *la scuola*, *la casa*).
target_language_example: Marco lasciò la stazione senza salutare nessuno.
native_language_example: Marco left the station without saying goodbye to anyone.

additional_notes: A drink made of milk and chocolate (or cocoa). You can use it in questions with piacere: “Ti piace il latte al cioccolato?” = “Do you like chocolate milk?” Often offered as a snack (spuntino), especially for kids.
target_language_example: Per colazione prendo un latte al cioccolato, per favore.
native_language_example: For breakfast I’ll have a chocolate milk, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about beer sold in cans. Singular: "una lattina di birra" (a can of beer). In questions you’ll often see "Quante lattine di birra...?" (How many cans of beer...?).
target_language_example: Per la festa ho comprato cinque lattine di birra.
native_language_example: For the party I bought five cans of beer.

additional_notes: "Lava" is the present tense of "lavare" (to wash): "(he/she) washes." "La sua" is a possessive meaning "his/her/its" (and sometimes "your" in the formal "Lei" form). It agrees with the thing being owned, not with the owner: "la sua automobile" (automobile is feminine), but "il suo libro" (book is masculine).
target_language_example: Lava la sua macchina ogni sabato.
native_language_example: He/She washes his/her car every Saturday.

additional_notes: "Lava" is the he/she form (and also the formal "you") of *lavare* (to wash). "La sua auto" means "his/her car" (or "your car" in formal address). In everyday speech, Italians often say *macchina* instead of *auto* (e.g., *Lava la sua macchina*).
target_language_example: Lava la sua auto il sabato mattina.
native_language_example: He/She washes his/her car on Saturday morning.

additional_notes: “Lava” is the present tense of *lavare* (“to wash”). “La sua macchina” means “his/her car” (or “your car” in the formal *Lei* form). *Sua* agrees with the thing owned (*macchina*, feminine singular), not with the owner. Often used with time expressions like *ogni mattina* (every morning) or *ogni settimana* (every week).
target_language_example: Lava la sua macchina il sabato mattina.
native_language_example: He/She washes his/her car on Saturday morning.

additional_notes: Informal singular command to one person, from the reflexive verb *lavarsi* (to wash oneself). The pronoun *ti* (“yourself”) attaches to the verb: *lava + ti → lavati*. With body parts in Italian, you often use the definite article (*i denti, la faccia, le mani*) instead of a possessive (*my/your*).
target_language_example: Prima di cena, lavati le mani.
native_language_example: Before dinner, wash your hands.

additional_notes: An informal command (imperative) meaning “wash your hands.” It uses the reflexive verb lavarsi (“to wash oneself”): lavati = “wash yourself,” le mani = “the hands.” Often used with per piacere (“please”) or with details like after the bathroom or for a certain amount of time.
target_language_example: Prima di mangiare, lavati le mani.
native_language_example: Before eating, wash your hands.

additional_notes: Used for manipulating someone’s beliefs or opinions (often in a strong/accusatory way). Common patterns: fare il lavaggio del cervello a qualcuno (to brainwash someone) and subire un lavaggio del cervello (to be brainwashed).
target_language_example: Secondo me gli hanno fatto il lavaggio del cervello.
native_language_example: I think they brainwashed him.

meaning: to brush your teeth (literally: to wash the teeth).
additional_notes: Common daily-routine phrase. In Italian it’s often used with a reflexive pronoun to mean "to brush your own teeth": mi lavo i denti (I brush my teeth), ti lavi i denti (you brush your teeth), si lava i denti (he/she brushes their teeth), ci laviamo i denti (we brush our teeth), vi lavate i denti (you all brush your teeth), si lavano i denti (they brush their teeth). You can also hear "spazzolare i denti" for a more literal "to brush the teeth."
target_language_example: Prima di andare a letto, mi lavo i denti.
native_language_example: Before going to bed, I brush my teeth.

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase used to talk about the chore in general (often after verbs like odiare, dovere, piacere, etc.). You can specify who has to do it with a + person/pronoun: “Devo lavare i piatti” (I have to wash the dishes). Literal sense: “to wash the plates/dishes.”
target_language_example: Dopo cena devo lavare i piatti.
native_language_example: After dinner I have to wash the dishes.

additional_notes: "Lavare" means "to wash." "La sua" is a polite/formal way to say "your" (to one person), but it can also mean "his" or "her" depending on context. "Auto" means "car." You’ll often see this with a name or clear context to know whose car it is.
target_language_example: Devo lavare la sua auto prima di restituirgliela.
native_language_example: I have to wash his/her car before giving it back to him/her.

additional_notes: Used to talk about washing someone’s car. In Italian, the possessive agrees with the owner (sua = his/her/its), but the article stays: la sua macchina (“the his/her car”). Often you’ll hear the more natural reflexive form for your own car: lavare la macchina / lavarsi la macchina (less common).
target_language_example: Devo lavare la mia macchina oggi.
native_language_example: I have to wash my car today.

additional_notes: Used for the everyday action of washing hands. Often appears with "(mi/ti/si/ci/vi) devo/dovrei/dovrebbe" to express necessity/advice: "Mi devo lavare le mani" (I have to wash my hands), "Ti dovresti lavare le mani" (You should wash your hands).
target_language_example: Prima di mangiare, lavati le mani.
native_language_example: Before eating, wash your hands.

additional_notes: Used when water (rain, waves, running water, etc.) removes something from a surface or carries it away. Often used with subjects like "la pioggia" (the rain) or "l’acqua" (the water): "La pioggia ha lavato via le impronte".
target_language_example: La pioggia ha lavato via la polvere dalla macchina.
native_language_example: The rain washed the dust off the car.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb: "lavarsi" = "to wash oneself." With body parts you often use the definite article: "le mani" (the hands), not "mie mani" (my hands). Common in everyday situations (before eating, after the bathroom). In the past tense it uses essere: "Mi sono lavato/a le mani."
target_language_example: Prima di mangiare, devo lavarmi le mani.
native_language_example: Before eating, I have to wash my hands.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase used with avere to form the passato prossimo of lavare i piatti (“to wash the dishes”), e.g., ho/hai/avete lavato i piatti. It often appears in questions (Avete già…? = “Have you already…?”) and to thank someone (Grazie per avere… = “Thanks for having…”).
target_language_example: Non posso uscire: non ho ancora lavato i piatti.
native_language_example: I can’t go out: I haven’t washed the dishes yet.

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s job or role: "[Persona] lavora come + professione/ruolo". You can also change the verb for other subjects and tenses (e.g., "Lavoro come...", "Lavorano come...", "Ho lavorato come...").
target_language_example: Mio fratello lavora come cuoco in un ristorante.
native_language_example: My brother works as a cook in a restaurant.

meaning: "(he/she) works in a" (used before a masculine singular workplace/place).
additional_notes: From the verb "lavorare" (to work). "in" + "un" is used with a masculine singular noun (e.g., un museo, un ospedale, un ufficio). For feminine singular, use "lavora in una" (e.g., in una banca). You can also swap the subject: "Io lavoro in un...", "Lei lavora in un...".
target_language_example: Mio padre lavora in un ristorante.
native_language_example: My dad works in a restaurant.

additional_notes: "Lavora" is the 3rd person singular of "lavorare" (to work): it can mean "he works" or "she works". Use it to say someone’s job/where they work. For other people: "lavoro" (I work), "lavori" (you work), "lavoriamo" (we work), "lavorano" (they work).
target_language_example: Mia sorella lavora in una banca in centro.
native_language_example: My sister works in a bank downtown.

meaning: '(he/she) works for' (is employed by / does work on behalf of).
additional_notes: Uses the verb *lavorare* + *per* + a person or organization. *Lavora* is 3rd person singular present (“he/she works”); you can change it: *lavoro per* (I work for), *lavori per* (you work for), *lavoriamo per* (we work for). It can mean being someone’s employee or simply doing a job/task for them.
target_language_example: Lei lavora per una grande azienda.
native_language_example: She works for a big company.

additional_notes: Used with a person or group you collaborate with: lavorare con + person (Tom, me, loro, lei). With pronouns you use the prepositional forms: con me, con te, con lui/lei, con noi, con voi, con loro. Often appears after verbs like piacere/amare (to like/love) or volere/dovere (to want/have to).
target_language_example: Domani devo lavorare con loro tutto il giorno.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have to work with them all day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about putting in a lot of effort at work or in studying. You can use it after verbs like dovere (Dobbiamo lavorare duramente = We have to work hard) or in encouragement (Continua/Continuate a lavorare duramente! = Keep working hard!). In the causative pattern far fare, it means “to make someone work hard” (ha fatto lavorare duramente le sue studentesse).
target_language_example: Se vuoi migliorare, devi lavorare duramente ogni giorno.
native_language_example: If you want to improve, you have to work hard every day.

additional_notes: Used when you continue working into the evening/night beyond the normal time. Common with time words like ieri (yesterday), stasera (tonight), domani (tomorrow), or with a specific end time: fino alle 10 (until 10).
target_language_example: Non posso uscire: devo lavorare fino a tardi.
native_language_example: I can’t go out: I have to work late.

meaning: "to work to" (in order to) or "to work for" (someone/an employer).
additional_notes:
Used in two common ways:
1) Purpose: lavorare per + infinitive = work in order to do something. Example: lavorare per salvare… (work to save…).
2) Employment/service: lavorare per + person/company = work for someone/a company (be employed by them or do work for them).
target_language_example: Sto lavorando per comprare una macchina nuova.
native_language_example: I’m working to buy a new car.

additional_notes: Used to say someone must make a strong effort, often to reach a goal or succeed. Common with verbs like "dovere" (must/have to) or in conditional phrases like "solo se" (only if).
target_language_example: Se vuoi passare l’esame, devi lavorare sodo.
native_language_example: If you want to pass the exam, you have to work hard.

meaning: work to do; tasks to get done.
additional_notes: Used to say there are tasks waiting to be done. Very common with quantities like "un sacco di" (a lot of) or "molto" (a lot of), and in questions like "Hai del lavoro da fare?" (= Do you have work to do?). Literally "work to do".
target_language_example: Scusa, non posso uscire adesso: ho ancora molto lavoro da fare.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out now: I still have a lot of work to do.

additional_notes: Used to talk about work with fewer hours than a full-time job. Common in everyday speech; you’ll often hear/see it with the English loanword “part-time” (sometimes written “part time”).
target_language_example: Sto cercando un lavoro part-time per pagare l’università.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a part-time job to pay for university.

additional_notes: Used for feminine plural nouns: either directly before a noun ("le altre ragazze" = "the other girls") or by itself when the noun is understood from context ("Prendi le altre due" = "Take the other two"). It’s the feminine plural form of "l’altro / l’altra"; for masculine plural you’d use "gli altri".
target_language_example: Non voglio queste scarpe: preferisco le altre.
native_language_example: I don’t want these shoes: I prefer the others.

additional_notes: Used to refer to other women/girls or other feminine plural nouns already known from context. It’s the feminine plural form of “l’altro/la altra” and can stand alone (“le altre”) or be followed by a noun (“le altre ragazze”). Often implies “the remaining ones” among a group.
target_language_example: Aspettiamo le altre davanti alla stazione.
native_language_example: Let’s wait for the others in front of the station.

additional_notes: "Le" is the feminine plural definite article (“the”). Singular: (l’)arancia (“orange”). Used when talking about oranges in general or specific oranges in context. Often appears with verbs like "piacere" (Mi piacciono le arance = I like oranges) and in comparisons: "Preferisco le arance alle mele" (I prefer oranges to apples).
target_language_example: Oggi compro le arance al mercato.
native_language_example: Today I’m buying oranges at the market.

additional_notes: Plural feminine noun phrase: "arma" (weapon) → "armi" (weapons). Used for weapons in general (guns, knives, etc.) and in set phrases like "Riprendete le armi!" (“Take up arms again!”). Not to be confused with "le braccia" (arms on your body).
target_language_example: La polizia ha trovato le armi nel garage.
native_language_example: The police found the weapons in the garage.

additional_notes: Definite plural feminine form: "le" = "the" (feminine plural) + "bambine" = "girls". Used to refer to a specific group of girls already known from context (e.g., your daughters). Singular is "la bambina" (the girl).
target_language_example: Le bambine stanno giocando in giardino.
native_language_example: The girls are playing in the garden.

additional_notes: Used when offering a choice between bananas that are still green (less ripe) and bananas that are mature/ripe. Often appears in preference questions with "preferire" (to prefer): "Preferisci le banane verdi o mature?". Adjectives agree with the plural feminine noun: "banane" → "verdi", "mature".
target_language_example: Al supermercato compro le banane mature, non le banane verdi.
native_language_example: At the supermarket I buy ripe bananas, not green bananas.

additional_notes: Plural of "il braccio". Common in set phrases with prepositions: "tra/fra le braccia" = "in (someone’s) arms" (holding/hugging), "mettere le braccia intorno a..." = "put one’s arms around...", "abbassare le braccia" = "lower one’s arms" (also figuratively: give up), "portare le braccia in aria" = "raise one’s arms in the air" (e.g., victory).
target_language_example: Dopo la corsa, ha portato le braccia in aria per festeggiare.
native_language_example: After the race, he raised his arms in the air to celebrate.

additional_notes: Plural of "la candela". Used for real candles you light (accendere le candele). Also commonly used for spark plugs in a car/motorbike (cambiare le candele = replace the spark plugs), depending on context.
target_language_example: Per la torta servono anche le candele.
native_language_example: For the cake we also need the candles.

additional_notes: Plural of “la carota” (a carrot). Used with the definite article “le” to mean “the carrots,” especially when talking about carrots in general or a specific batch you’re referring to.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo comprare le carote per la zuppa.
native_language_example: We need to buy the carrots for the soup.

meaning: the cards; the papers/documents; the maps (depending on context).
additional_notes: Plural of *la carta*. Often used for playing cards (*tenere/distribuire le carte* = to hold/deal the cards). It can also mean documents/ID papers (*le carte*), maps (*le carte geografiche*), or tarot/fortune-telling cards (*leggere le carte*).
target_language_example: Non ho le carte con me: le ho lasciate a casa.
native_language_example: I don’t have my documents/ID with me: I left them at home.

additional_notes: Plural of "la chiave" (key). Used for house keys, car keys, etc. Often appears with verbs like "dare" (to give), "avere" (to have), "trovare" (to find), and "mettere" (to put/place): "Dammi le chiavi" = "Give me the keys."
target_language_example: Scusa, hai visto le chiavi di casa?
native_language_example: Sorry, have you seen the house keys?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the keys for a car. Very common in everyday situations: asking where they are (Dove sono...?), looking for them (cercare le chiavi), throwing/tossing them to someone (lanciare le chiavi). You can also say "le chiavi dell’auto" (slightly more formal/neutral).
target_language_example: Non trovo le chiavi della macchina: le hai viste?
native_language_example: I can’t find the car keys—have you seen them?

additional_notes: Plural feminine noun with the definite article: singular is "la cipolla" (the onion). Common in shopping/cooking contexts (e.g., asking if someone bought onions, or talking about how they cook).
target_language_example: Per la pasta, ci servono le cipolle.
native_language_example: For the pasta, we need the onions.

additional_notes: Refers to onions that are not cooked (for example, in a salad or on a sandwich). "Le" is the feminine plural definite article (“the”), and "crude" is the feminine plural form of "crudo" (“raw”).
target_language_example: Non mi piacciono le cipolle crude nell’insalata.
native_language_example: I don’t like raw onions in salad.

meaning: the circumstances; the situation (the conditions/facts around an event).
additional_notes: Plural feminine: (le) circostanze. Used to talk about the conditions or context that explain why something happens or why someone acted a certain way. Common with verbs like capire/considerare (“understand/consider the circumstances”) and with adjectives like favorevoli/sfavorevoli (“favorable/unfavorable”) or diverse (“different”).
target_language_example: In queste circostanze, è meglio aspettare.
native_language_example: In these circumstances, it’s better to wait.

meaning: “horns”; also used in expressions about being cheated on (cuckolded).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: animal horns. Very common idiom: “mettere le corna (a qualcuno)” = to cheat on someone (be unfaithful); “dare/le mettere le corna” can also mean “to cuckold someone.” In insults/threats you may hear “rompere/spaccare le corna (a qualcuno)” = to beat someone up / ‘break your horns.’
target_language_example: Gli ha messo le corna con un collega.
native_language_example: She/He cheated on him with a coworker.

additional_notes: Very common plural of "la cosa". It can mean physical objects ("mettere le cose in una scatola"), but also "how things are/going" or a situation in general ("le cose vanno e vengono", "le cose non vanno"). Often used in set phrases like: "prendere le cose seriamente" (take things seriously), "dire le cose come stanno" (tell it like it is), and "nascondere le cose" (hide things / keep things from someone).
target_language_example: Come stanno le cose adesso?
native_language_example: How are things now?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause describing or identifying specific things: *le cose che + verb* (e.g., *le cose che meritano*, *le cose che ha detto*). Often followed by the indicative in everyday statements.
target_language_example: Non capisco le cose che mi stai chiedendo.
native_language_example: I don’t understand the things you’re asking me.

additional_notes: Used to say that the situation/reality is different from what someone thinks or expects. It’s commonly followed by a comparison or description, e.g. come… (“as…”), così… (“so…”), or quelle che… (“what/that which…”).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma le cose non sono come le immagini.
native_language_example: Sorry, but things aren’t like in the pictures.

meaning: "things" + "more" (used to say things are more/less + adjective, or you do things more often/easily, etc.).
additional_notes: Common in phrases like **rendere le cose più + aggettivo** = “to make things more + adjective” (e.g., *più facili/più difficili/più complicate*). It can also be followed by an adverb to talk about frequency or ease: **le cose più spesso** (“things more often”) or **le cose più facilmente** (“things more easily”). The adjective/adverb that comes after **più** gives the meaning.
target_language_example: Puoi rendere le cose più semplici?
native_language_example: Can you make things simpler?

additional_notes: Used to talk generally about how a situation is, often followed by an adjective (diverse, difficili, complicate) or a comparison (meglio/peggio). Common in phrases like "Adesso/Ora le cose sono..." or in questions: "Le cose sono... ?"
target_language_example: Con il nuovo lavoro, le cose sono più facili.
native_language_example: With the new job, things are easier.

additional_notes: Common way to say that the situation is different now than before. Often used with time markers like adesso/ora (“now”) or to ask why something is different (Perché le cose sono cambiate?).
target_language_example: Non possiamo fare come prima: le cose sono cambiate.
native_language_example: We can’t do it like before: things have changed.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how a situation is developing. It’s commonly followed by a verb in the gerund with "stare" (stanno + -ando/-endo): "le cose stanno cambiando" = “things are changing.” In English you often translate it with the present continuous (“are getting…/are becoming…”) rather than literally (“the things stand”).
target_language_example: Le cose stanno migliorando piano piano.
native_language_example: Things are slowly getting better.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how a situation or relationship is progressing. It’s often completed with an adverb or phrase like bene (well), male (badly), così (like this/this way), etc.: “Le cose vanno bene.” = “Things are going well.” In “Le cose vanno e vengono,” it means things come and go (change over time).
target_language_example: Non so come andrà, ma per ora le cose vanno abbastanza bene.
native_language_example: I don’t know how it will go, but for now things are going pretty well.

meaning: 'resignation' / 'resigning from a job' (often used with dare: 'to resign').
additional_notes: Used mainly in the plural in Italian. The most common expression is "dare le dimissioni" = "to hand in your resignation / to resign". You can also specify when: "dare le dimissioni oggi/ieri". Often used for public officials too: "il primo ministro dà le dimissioni".
target_language_example: Dopo dieci anni in azienda, ha dato le dimissioni.
native_language_example: After ten years at the company, he resigned (handed in his resignation).

additional_notes: Plural of *il dito* (finger). Used after body parts with possessives: *mi/ti/si è bruciato le dita* (“he burned his fingers”), *si passò le dita tra i capelli* (“she ran her fingers through her hair”). Also used for counting or skill with one’s hands: *contare con le dita*, *abile con le dita*.
target_language_example: Mi sono tagliato le dita mentre cucinavo.
native_language_example: I cut my fingers while cooking.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like tenere/tenere le dita incrociate (“to keep your fingers crossed”) or incrociare le dita (“to cross your fingers”). Often followed by per + person/thing: “Tengo le dita incrociate per te” = “I’m keeping my fingers crossed for you.”
target_language_example: Ho un colloquio domani: tieni le dita incrociate per me!
native_language_example: I have an interview tomorrow: keep your fingers crossed for me!

additional_notes: Used to refer to questions you ask in a conversation, interview, or test. Often with verbs like *fare* (to ask/make): *fare le domande* = “to ask the questions.” You can also say *domande giuste/sbagliate* (“right/wrong questions”) and *preparare le domande* (“prepare the questions”).
target_language_example: Prima dell’incontro, ho preparato le domande da fare al medico.
native_language_example: Before the appointment, I prepared the questions to ask the doctor.

additional_notes: Plural of "la donna" (woman). It’s the feminine plural form of the definite article (le) + noun (donne). Used to talk about women in general or a specific group of women depending on context.
target_language_example: Le donne sono stanche di aspettare.
native_language_example: The women are tired of waiting.

additional_notes: Literally “the women and the children.” Often used in urgent instructions or announcements to prioritize or restrict access to women and children (e.g., “Women and children first,” “Only women and children”). Can be followed by words like prima (first), davanti (in front), solo (only).
target_language_example: In caso di emergenza, prima le donne e i bambini.
native_language_example: In case of emergency, women and children first.

additional_notes: "Le" is the plural feminine form of "the". "Donne" = women, and "sono" is the "they are" form of "essere" (to be). Used to make general statements ("Le donne sono intelligenti") or to talk about specific women in context ("Le donne sono davanti alla biblioteca"). Adjectives that follow usually agree in plural feminine (e.g., "Le donne sono intelligenti").
target_language_example: Le donne sono stanche dopo il lavoro.
native_language_example: Women are tired after work.

additional_notes: This is a noun phrase usually used after verbs like *togliere*, *rimuovere*, or *strappare* to talk about weeding/removing weeds (e.g., *togliere le erbacce dal giardino* = “to pull/remove the weeds from the garden,” i.e., “to weed the garden”). *Erbacce* is plural; singular: *un’erbaccia*.
target_language_example: Oggi devo togliere le erbacce dal giardino.
native_language_example: Today I have to pull the weeds from the garden.

additional_notes: Plural feminine noun. Singular: la farfalla (“the butterfly”). Used with verbs like piacere: "Mi piacciono le farfalle" = “I like butterflies.”
target_language_example: A mia sorella piacciono le farfalle.
native_language_example: My sister likes butterflies.

additional_notes: Plural of "la festa". Most often means parties/events (e.g., birthday parties, surprise parties). It can also mean holidays/celebrations (e.g., "le feste di Natale" = the Christmas holidays). In your examples it clearly refers to parties.
target_language_example: Non mi piacciono le feste rumorose.
native_language_example: I don't like loud parties.

additional_notes: Plural feminine noun phrase (singular: la finestra). Often used with verbs like chiudere/aprire (to close/open) and with adjectives for color or description (e.g., finestre gialle). In questions, Italians often use the past tense to ask if something has been done: Avete chiuso le finestre? = Have you closed the windows?
target_language_example: Per favore, apri le finestre: fa caldo.
native_language_example: Please open the windows: it’s hot.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like tenere (“to keep”) or lasciare (“to leave”) to say that windows are kept/left open. The adjective must agree: le finestre aperte (feminine plural). You can also use commands: Tenete/Tieni/Tenga le finestre aperte (“Keep the windows open.”).
target_language_example: Per favore, non lasciare le finestre aperte quando esci.
native_language_example: Please don’t leave the windows open when you go out.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase: definite article + plural of "foglia" (leaf). Used for leaves on trees/plants; very common with seasons and weather (e.g., in autumn leaves fall; wind lifts the leaves). The singular is "la foglia".
target_language_example: In primavera le foglie sono verdi, ma in autunno diventano rosse e gialle.
native_language_example: In spring the leaves are green, but in autumn they turn red and yellow.

additional_notes: Often refers to someone’s physical energy: conservare/risparmiare/recuperare le forze (“save/recover your strength”). In expressions like unire le forze, it means “join forces” (work together). In contexts like le forze speciali, it means “special forces.”
target_language_example: Dopo l’influenza devo recuperare le forze.
native_language_example: After the flu I need to regain my strength.

additional_notes: Plural feminine with the definite article “le” (used for feminine plural nouns). Singular is “la foto” (the photo). Common with verbs like “fare” or “scattare” (to take photos) and “guardare” (to look at photos).
target_language_example: Puoi mandarmi le foto?
native_language_example: Can you send me the photos?

additional_notes: Plural feminine noun phrase: singular is "la gamba" (the leg). Used with body parts, Italian often uses a possessive pronoun (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi) plus the definite article: e.g., "Mi fanno male le gambe" = "My legs hurt" (literally, "To me hurt the legs"). In your example, "Le stava guardando le gambe?" means "Was he looking at her legs?".
target_language_example: Mi fanno male le gambe.
native_language_example: My legs hurt.

additional_notes: Plural of "la gomma." In everyday Italian it very often means vehicle tires; in sports like Formula 1 you’ll hear it a lot (e.g., "gomme dure" = hard-compound tires; "tenere vive le gomme" = keep the tires from wearing/overheating so they last). Note: "gomma" can also mean "eraser" in other contexts, but these examples point to tires.
target_language_example: Prima di partire, controlla la pressione delle gomme.
native_language_example: Before leaving, check the tire pressure.

meaning: the guards; the police/security (depending on context).
additional_notes: Plural of "la guardia". Used for people who guard a place (guards) or, in everyday speech, for law enforcement/security in general (like “the cops/the police”), especially in warnings or threats ("Chiamate le guardie!", "Ci sono le guardie!"). The exact meaning depends on the situation (a building, event, or prison vs. police officers nearby).
target_language_example: Non fare rumore: ci sono le guardie fuori.
native_language_example: Don’t make noise: the guards are outside.

additional_notes: Plural of "l’idea" (feminine). Common in expressions like "le idee chiare" (clear about what you think/what you want), "le idee giuste" (the right ideas), and "mancare le idee" (to run out of ideas). You can also use it for someone’s views/opinions (e.g., "le idee politiche").
target_language_example: Non ho le idee chiare su cosa fare stasera.
native_language_example: I’m not clear on what to do tonight.

meaning: "the information that" (introduces a relative clause about the information).
additional_notes: Used when you’re talking about specific information and then add a clause that describes it: le informazioni che avete/hai/ha richiesto (“the information (that) you (plural)/you (singular informal)/you (formal)/he/she requested”) or le informazioni che mi/le/vi servono (“the information that I/you/she/you-all need”). In Italian, "che" often equals “that/which” and is usually not omitted like in English.
target_language_example: Ecco le informazioni che mi hai chiesto.
native_language_example: Here’s the information you asked me for.

meaning: the instructions; directions (how to do/use something).
additional_notes: Feminine plural noun (singular: l’istruzione). Common with verbs like leggere (to read), seguire (to follow), dare (to give), and capire (to understand) when talking about how to use something (a device, an app, a recipe, rules for an activity).
target_language_example: Prima di montarlo, leggi bene le istruzioni.
native_language_example: Before assembling it, read the instructions carefully.

additional_notes: Plural of "la lacrima" (a tear). Very common with verbs like "asciugare" (to wipe/dry): "asciugarsi le lacrime" = to wipe away your tears. You can also say "avere le lacrime agli occhi" (to have tears in your eyes) and "le lacrime mi scendono" (tears run down).
target_language_example: Non riuscivo a trattenere le lacrime.
native_language_example: I couldn’t hold back the tears.

additional_notes: Plural feminine noun phrase. Used with verbs like indossare/portare (“to wear”) and often contrasted with gli occhiali (“glasses”). You can say: Porto le lenti a contatto (“I wear contact lenses”).
target_language_example: Oggi non porto gli occhiali: porto le lenti a contatto.
native_language_example: Today I’m not wearing glasses: I’m wearing contact lenses.

additional_notes: Used when talking about correct writing/typing (capitalization). Often appears after verbs like usare / mettere (“to use/put”) or dimenticare (“to forget”): Non dimenticare le lettere maiuscole = “Don’t forget to use capital letters.” Singular: la lettera maiuscola.
target_language_example: Nella password devi usare le lettere maiuscole e i numeri.
native_language_example: In the password you must use capital letters and numbers.

meaning: 'the lessons' (classes/lessons, especially at school or a course).
additional_notes: Plural of "la lezione". Often used to talk about school/university/course sessions (e.g., "Quando iniziano le lezioni?" = when classes start) or the lesson material you study/review (e.g., "ripassare le lezioni" = review the lessons). With "saltare le lezioni" it means to skip class.
target_language_example: Oggi non posso venire: devo prepararmi per le lezioni di domani.
native_language_example: I can’t come today: I have to get ready for tomorrow’s classes.

additional_notes: Used for languages as a subject or skill: *imparare le lingue* (to learn languages), *insegnare le lingue* (to teach languages). Note: *la lingua* can also mean “tongue” (the body part), but in these examples it means “language.”
target_language_example: Vorrei imparare le lingue per viaggiare di più.
native_language_example: I’d like to learn languages to travel more.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase: "le" = "the" (feminine plural), "lingue" = "languages" (feminine plural), "straniere" = "foreign" (feminine plural to match "lingue"). Common after verbs like "studiare" (to study) and "piacere" (to like).
target_language_example: All'università studio le lingue straniere.
native_language_example: At university I study foreign languages.

additional_notes: Possessive used with feminine plural nouns (e.g., le loro chitarre = their guitars; le loro uova = their eggs). It agrees with what is owned (feminine plural), not with who owns it. Often used with the definite article: le + loro. For masculine plural, use i loro.
target_language_example: Le loro valigie sono già in macchina.
native_language_example: Their suitcases are already in the car.

additional_notes: Feminine plural: le (the) + loro (their) + amiche (friends, female/mixed group when specified as feminine). In Italian, possessives usually take the definite article: le loro amiche = “their friends.” Loro doesn’t change form (unlike mio/mia/miei/mie) and the noun shows the feminine plural ending -e.
