additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of chiamare (“to call”). mi = “me” (object pronoun). The subject is understood from context (he/she/you formal), and you can change it: mi hanno chiamato = “they called me”; mi hai chiamato = “you called me.”
target_language_example: Mi ha chiamato mentre ero in riunione.
native_language_example: He/She called me while I was in a meeting.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "chiedere". It means someone asked you for something or asked you to do something. It’s often followed by "di" + infinitive: "mi ha chiesto di..." = "(he/she) asked me to...". The subject is understood from context (e.g., Tom / Mary / he / she).
target_language_example: Mi ha chiesto di aspettarlo davanti alla stazione.
native_language_example: He asked me to wait for him in front of the station.

meaning: "(he/she) asked me to" (requested that I do something).
additional_notes: Used to report a request in the past: *[someone]* + **mi ha chiesto di** + infinitive (e.g., *fare, andare, riscrivere*). The subject (who asked) can be stated (e.g., *Tom mi ha chiesto di...*) or left implied. Pronouns can attach to the infinitive (e.g., *di dargli*, *di portarla*).
target_language_example: Mi ha chiesto di aspettarlo fuori.
native_language_example: He/She asked me to wait for him outside.

additional_notes: Used to report a yes/no question someone asked you (indirect question). The verb is in the past: "ha chiesto" = "asked". The subject is often understood from context (he/she); you can also specify it: "Tom mi ha chiesto se...". After "se", Italian may use the subjunctive in some cases (e.g., "se pensavo che... fosse"), but beginners can focus on the overall meaning: reporting what someone asked.
target_language_example: Mi ha chiesto se avevo tempo domani.
native_language_example: He/She asked me if I had time tomorrow.

additional_notes: "Mi" = to me/for me (indirect object pronoun). "Ha comprato" is passato prossimo of "comprare" (to buy) and usually means 'bought' (recent past). Used when someone bought something for you: Mi ha comprato una bicicletta = He bought me a bike.
target_language_example: Il mio amico mi ha comprato un caffè.
native_language_example: My friend bought me a coffee.

meaning: 'he/she advised me to' / 'he/she recommended that I (do something)'.
additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo of consigliare (to advise/recommend): ha consigliato = 'advised/recommended'. mi = 'to me'. It’s typically followed by di + infinitive (e.g., di andare, di leggere, di non fumare). The subject (he/she) is often understood from context and not stated.
target_language_example: Il medico mi ha consigliato di riposare di più.
native_language_example: The doctor advised me to rest more.

additional_notes: Used when something or someone has persuaded you. It’s the passato prossimo of "convincere": "mi" = "me" + "ha convinta" = "has convinced". The past participle agrees with the (female) speaker: a man would usually say "mi ha convinto". You can add what you were convinced of with "che" (that): "mi ha convinta che...".
target_language_example: Le tue spiegazioni mi hanno convinta a provarci.
native_language_example: Your explanations convinced me to give it a try.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of “dare” (to give) with the indirect object pronoun “mi” (= to me). The subject is often understood from context (e.g., “Tom mi ha dato…” = “Tom gave me…”). Used for giving something, granting time off, offering advice, etc.
target_language_example: Mi ha dato il suo numero di telefono.
native_language_example: He/She gave me his/her phone number.

meaning: 'he/she gave me a' / 'he/she has given me a' (something masculine singular).
additional_notes: Uses the indirect object pronoun mi (“to me”) + ha dato (passato prossimo of dare, “to give”). It’s followed by a masculine singular noun: un indizio, un album, un regalo. For feminine nouns, use mi ha dato una (e.g., una mano).
target_language_example: Mi ha dato un regalo per il compleanno.
native_language_example: He/She gave me a gift for my birthday.

additional_notes: Used when someone gives you something (a gift, an object) or does an action toward you that takes an object (e.g., una pacca = a pat/slap). Grammatically: mi = “to me”, ha dato = “gave” (passato prossimo of dare), una = “a” (feminine singular). You typically need to complete it with a noun: mi ha dato una sciarpa / una bambola / una pacca.
target_language_example: Per il mio compleanno mi ha dato una maglietta.
native_language_example: For my birthday, he/she gave me a T-shirt.

additional_notes:
Passato prossimo of "dire" (to say/tell). "Mi" = to me; "ha detto" = has said/told. The subject is often understood from context (he/she/you formal, etc.). It can be followed by:
- "che" + a clause: "Mi ha detto che arriva tardi." (He told me he’s arriving late.)
- "di" + infinitive: "Mi ha detto di aspettare." (He told me to wait.)
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che non può venire oggi.
native_language_example: He/She told me that he/she can’t come today.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said. "Mi" = to me, "ha detto" = (he/she) said/told, and "che" introduces the statement that follows. The subject (who told you) is often understood from context or can be added (e.g., "Tom mi ha detto che...").
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che arriverà domani.
native_language_example: He/She told me that he/she will arrive tomorrow.

mi ha detto che a lei

target_language_multi_word_term: mi ha detto che a lei
meaning: "she told me that she..." (literally: "she told me that, to her...")
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said: "mi ha detto che..." = "she/he told me that...". The part "a lei" is a stressed indirect pronoun meaning "to her" and is very common with the verb "piacere" (a lei piace... = she likes...). It can add emphasis/contrast (e.g., "to her, (it) pleases", not to someone else).
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che a lei non piace il caffè.
native_language_example: She told me that she doesn’t like coffee.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said (reported speech). "Mi" = "to me". "Ha detto" is the past of "dire" (said/told), and "che" introduces the clause. "Aveva" (imperfect of "avere") is often used after a past reporting verb like "ha detto" to describe what the person had/was feeling/needed at that time (e.g., a cold, a problem, hunger, fear, a plan). The subject can change depending on context (he/she).
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che aveva dimenticato le chiavi.
native_language_example: He/she told me that he/she had forgotten the keys.

mi ha detto che aveva bisogno di

target_language_multi_word_term: mi ha detto che aveva bisogno di
meaning: “he/she told me that he/she needed to / needed (something).”
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said in the past: **mi ha detto** = “he/she told me,” and **aveva bisogno di** = “he/she needed / was in need of.” After **bisogno di**, you can use a **noun** (*di denaro, di tempo*) or an **infinitive verb** (*di parlare, di dormire*). The subject of **ha detto** is often omitted and understood from context.
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che aveva bisogno di aiuto con i compiti.
native_language_example: He/She told me that he/she needed help with homework.

meaning: 'he/she told me that he/she knew' (past report of what someone said).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone told you in the past. "mi ha detto" = "(he/she) told me" (passato prossimo). After "che", Italian often uses the imperfect ("conosceva") to express what was true/known at that time in the past. "conoscere" means "to know (a person/place/subject)".
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che conosceva già il professore.
native_language_example: He/She told me that he/she already knew the professor.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about themselves (or another person) in the past. "Mi" = to me, "ha detto" = said/told (passato prossimo), "che" = that, "era" = was (imperfetto). The subject is often understood from context; you can specify it (e.g., "Maria mi ha detto che era...").
target_language_example: Marco mi ha detto che era stanco dopo il lavoro.
native_language_example: Marco told me he was tired after work.

mi ha detto che era felice

target_language_multi_word_term: mi ha detto che era felice
meaning: “he/she told me that he/she was happy.”
additional_notes: Used for reporting what someone said in the past. "Mi ha detto" = "(he/she) told me" (passato prossimo). After "che" (“that”), Italian often uses the imperfect "era" (“was”) to describe an ongoing state in the past. The subject is usually understood from context (e.g., Tom/Mary); add it if needed: "Tom mi ha detto che...".
target_language_example: Luca mi ha detto che era felice del nuovo lavoro.
native_language_example: Luca told me he was happy about the new job.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said: **mi ha detto che** (“he/she told me that”) + a clause. **Eravate** is the imperfect tense of **essere** for **voi** (“you all / you plural”), often used in reported speech to describe a past state (e.g., happy, married, allergic).
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che eravate in ritardo.
native_language_example: He told me that you were late.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said (indirect speech). In the examples, **mi ha detto** is in the *passato prossimo* (“told me”), and **eri** is the imperfect of *essere* (“you were”), often used when reporting past descriptions/states: *Mi ha detto che eri stanco* (“He told me you were tired”). You can change the person: *mi ha detto che era…* (“told me that he/she was…”).
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che eri in ritardo.
native_language_example: He told me you were late.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about you. "Mi ha detto" is past tense (passato prossimo) of *dire* = “told me/said to me.” After **che**, Italian often uses the imperfect (**ero**) for reported speech about a past situation (“that I was…”). What comes after **ero** usually agrees with you (e.g., *bello/bella*, *carino/carina*).
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che ero molto gentile.
native_language_example: He/She told me that I was very kind.

meaning: "He/She told me that he…" (setting up "gli" = "to him" for verbs like *piacere/dispiacere*).
additional_notes: *Mi ha detto che…* means “he/she told me that…”. The extra **gli** is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to him,” commonly used with **piacere** and **dispiacere** (e.g., *gli piace* = “he likes it,” literally “it pleases him”; *gli dispiace* = “he’s sorry / he minds”). So *mi ha detto che gli piace…* = “he told me that he likes…”.
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che gli piace molto questo posto.
native_language_example: He told me that he really likes this place.

additional_notes: **Mi ha detto che…** means “he/she told me that…”. The **le** is an indirect object pronoun meaning **“to her”** (referring to *lei*). You often see **le** with verbs like **piacere** (“to like/appeal to”): *le piace* = “she likes it” (literally “it pleases her”), *le è piaciuto/piaciuta* = “she liked it” (past; agreement can match the thing liked: *piaciuto* masc., *piaciuta* fem.).
target_language_example: Luca mi ha detto che le piace questo ristorante.
native_language_example: Luca told me that she likes this restaurant.

mi ha detto che le piace

target_language_multi_word_term: mi ha detto che le piace
meaning: “(He/She) told me that she likes it / likes (to do it).”
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about another person’s likes. "Mi ha detto" = "(he/she) told me". "che" = "that". "le piace" literally means "it pleases her" and is used for “she likes it / she likes doing it.” The person who likes something is shown with an indirect object pronoun: le = to her (piace a lei). For “he likes,” you’d say "gli piace"; for “I like,” "mi piace." Often followed by an infinitive: "le piace nuotare" = “she likes swimming.”
target_language_example: Giulia mi ha detto che le piace la pizza.
native_language_example: Giulia told me that she likes pizza.

mi ha detto che le piaceva

target_language_multi_word_term: mi ha detto che le piaceva
meaning: "he/she told me that he/she liked it/her/him" (in the past).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said in the past: "mi ha detto" = "he/she told me" (passato prossimo). "che" introduces the clause. "le piaceva" is the imperfect of "piacere" and literally means "it was pleasing to her" → "she liked". With "piacere", the person who likes something is an indirect object: "le" = "to her" (so it means "she liked..."), "gli" would be "to him". "piaceva" (imperfect) often describes an ongoing preference/habit in the past, not just one moment.
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che le piaceva il caffè senza zucchero.
native_language_example: He/She told me that she liked coffee without sugar.

mi ha detto che non aveva

target_language_multi_word_term: mi ha detto che non aveva
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said in the past. "Mi ha detto" = "told me" (passato prossimo). After "che", Italian often uses the imperfect: "non aveva" = "didn’t have / wasn’t having" at that time. You normally add the thing that was missing after "non aveva" (e.g., soldi, bisogno, tempo).
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che non aveva tempo oggi.
native_language_example: He/She told me that he/she didn’t have time today.

mi ha detto che non era

target_language_multi_word_term: mi ha detto che non era
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said to you in the past. "Mi ha detto" = “told me” (passato prossimo). "che" introduces the reported clause. "non era" is the imperfect of essere (“wasn’t”), often used in indirect speech even when English would say “isn’t/wasn’t.” The adjective after it agrees with the person being described: convinta/sposata/ferita (female), convinto/ferito (male).
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che non era pronto a partire.
native_language_example: He told me that he wasn’t ready to leave.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone told you (indirect speech). The verb after che is in the conditional (potrebbe = “might/could”) to express possibility/uncertainty. The subject is often understood from context; you can add it for clarity (e.g., “Mi ha detto che lui/lei potrebbe…”).
target_language_example: Marco mi ha detto che potrebbe arrivare in ritardo.
native_language_example: Marco told me that he might arrive late.

mi ha detto che si sentiva

target_language_multi_word_term: mi ha detto che si sentiva
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about how they were feeling. "Mi ha detto" is the past tense of dire (to tell), and "si sentiva" is the imperfect of sentirsi (to feel), often followed by an adjective (bene/male, affamato/a, malato/a). The subject (he/she) is understood from context; the adjective must agree in gender (affamato/affamata, malato/malata).
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che si sentiva stanca e che voleva tornare a casa.
native_language_example: She told me that she felt tired and that she wanted to go home.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about an action in progress or a situation at that time. "Mi ha detto" = "(he/she) told me"; "che" = "that"; "stava" is the imperfect of "stare" and is often followed by a gerund (stava andando = was going) or by "per" + infinitive (stava per vincere = was about to win). The subject (he/she) is often understood from context.
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che stava aspettando l'autobus.
native_language_example: He told me that he was waiting for the bus.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said they wanted. It’s in the past (ha detto) and introduces an indirect statement with che (“that”). The subject is often understood from context (he/she), and voleva is the imperfect tense (“wanted/was wanting”).
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che voleva cambiare lavoro.
native_language_example: He/She told me that he/she wanted to change jobs.

meaning: 'he/she told me to' (followed by an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to report instructions or advice: "dire" + indirect object (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli) + "di" + infinitive. It can refer to a past moment (often translated as "told me to").
target_language_example: Mi ha detto di chiamarla stasera.
native_language_example: He/She told me to call her tonight.

additional_notes: Used for reported speech. Literally “to me (he/she) has said to be…”. In Italian you often use “dire + di + infinitive” to report what someone says about themselves, especially with “essere” (to be): *Mi ha detto di essere stanco* = “He told me he was tired.” The subject (he/she) is understood from context; the adjective or past participle that follows agrees with that person: *arrabbiato/stanco/sposato* (male), *sposata* (female).
target_language_example: Mi ha detto di essere pronta, quindi siamo partiti.
native_language_example: She told me she was ready, so we left.

additional_notes: Used to report a negative instruction/advice. Structure: (Subject) + ha detto a + person + di non + infinitive. Here, mi = “to me” and non goes directly before the infinitive (non perdere, non seguire, non essere, non sprecare). The subject can change (mi hanno detto di non… = “they told me not to…”).
target_language_example: Mi ha detto di non arrivare tardi.
native_language_example: He/She told me not to be late.

meaning: “he/she/it made me …” or “he/she/it did … to me”.
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of fare: mi (to me) + ha fatto (has made/done). Very commonly followed by an infinitive to mean “made me / got me to do something” (Mi ha fatto firmare… = He made me sign…). It can also be used with another verb (Mi ha fatto ridere = He made me laugh) or with a noun/adjective to mean “did/made something to me” depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi ha fatto aspettare mezz’ora.
native_language_example: He/She made me wait half an hour.

additional_notes: Used to say you enjoyed something or were pleased about an event, often with an infinitive (mi ha fatto piacere vederti = I was glad to see you). Common as a polite closing after meeting someone (Mi ha fatto piacere conoscerti/vederti = Nice to meet/see you). Past tense: literally “it made me pleasure,” but in English it’s usually “I was glad/It was a pleasure.”
target_language_example: Mi ha fatto piacere parlare con te ieri.
native_language_example: It was nice talking to you yesterday.

meaning: 'it prevented me from' / 'it stopped me from' (doing something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say that something made you unable to do an action: **[cause/thing] + mi ha impedito di + infinitive**. The cause is the subject (e.g., *la pioggia*, *la malattia*). You can swap **mi** with other object pronouns: *ti/lo/la/ci/vi/li/le ha impedito di...*.
target_language_example: Il traffico mi ha impedito di arrivare in tempo.
native_language_example: Traffic prevented me from arriving on time.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of *insegnare* (to teach): *[someone] mi ha insegnato [something]* = “someone taught me something,” and *mi ha insegnato a + infinitive* = “taught me to + verb.” The subject can be a person or a thing (e.g., *L'esperienza mi ha insegnato...* = “Experience taught me...”); the gender isn’t specified—*ha* works for both “he” and “she.”
target_language_example: Mio padre mi ha insegnato a guidare.
native_language_example: My father taught me to drive.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb to say someone taught you how to do something. "Mi" = to me, "ha insegnato" = has taught/taught, "a" introduces the infinitive (e.g., "a sciare"). You can change the object pronoun: "ti ha insegnato a" (taught you), "ci ha insegnato a" (taught us), etc., and the helper changes with the person: "mi hanno insegnato a" (they taught me).
target_language_example: Il mio amico mi ha insegnato a cucinare la pasta.
native_language_example: My friend taught me to cook pasta.

additional_notes: Used to say someone invited you to do something or to an event/place. The verb is "invitare" in the passato prossimo: "mi" = to me, "ha invitata" = has invited (agreement with a female speaker; a male speaker usually says "mi ha invitato a"). After "a" you can have an infinitive ("a partecipare") or a noun/place ("a pranzo", "a una festa", "a casa sua").
target_language_example: Marco mi ha invitata a cena domani sera.
native_language_example: Marco invited me to dinner tomorrow evening.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone invited you to a place or to do something. Structure: "mi" (me) + "ha invitato" (invited) + "a" (to). You can replace the person: "mi hanno invitato a" (they invited me to), "mi inviterà a" (will invite me to). Often followed by a noun ("a una festa") or an infinitive verb ("a entrare", "a unirsi").
target_language_example: Mi ha invitato a cena domani sera.
native_language_example: He/She invited me to dinner tomorrow evening.

meaning: “(he/she) left me” or “(he/she) left me (something)”; with an infinitive: “(he/she) let/allowed me to …”.
additional_notes:
From the verb *lasciare* (“to leave”). The meaning depends on what follows:
- **mi ha lasciato + noun** = “left me (something)” / “left (something) for me” (*Mi ha lasciato una sorpresa.*)
- **mi ha lasciato + infinitive** = “let/allowed me to …” (*Mi ha lasciato usare il suo computer.*)
- **mi ha lasciato** alone (or with context) often means “(he/she) left me” in a relationship sense.
target_language_example: Dopo cinque anni insieme, mi ha lasciato.
native_language_example: After five years together, he/she left me.

additional_notes: Used with a past participle (passato prossimo) and usually needs the main verb right after: *Mi ha mai mentito?* = “Has he ever lied to me?” In negatives, *non ... mai* means “never”: *Non mi ha mai toccato* = “He never touched me.” Here *mi* means “me” (direct object) or “to me” depending on the verb.
target_language_example: Mi ha mai chiamato dopo quella sera?
native_language_example: Has he ever called me after that evening?

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of mandare with an indirect object pronoun: mi = “to me”, ha mandato = “has sent/sent”. Used when someone sent you something (flowers, a link, a friend request, a photo, etc.). You can swap the pronoun for others: ti ha mandato (sent you), ci ha mandato (sent us), gli/le ha mandato (sent him/her).
target_language_example: Mi ha mandato un messaggio ieri sera.
native_language_example: He/She sent me a message last night.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "mordere" (to bite). The subject is often implied by context (e.g., a dog, horse, snake, insect, or a person). With body parts, Italian commonly uses the article + body part and keeps "mi" (e.g., "mi ha morso la mano" = "it bit my hand").
target_language_example: Attento: quel gatto mi ha morso!
native_language_example: Careful: that cat bit me!

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "mostrare" = "to show". "Mi" is the indirect object pronoun meaning "to me"; "ha mostrato" literally means "has shown" and often translates as simple past in English ("showed"). Use it to say someone showed you something (an object, a photo, a room) or a way/direction ("la strada").
target_language_example: Giulia mi ha mostrato dove comprare i biglietti.
native_language_example: Giulia showed me where to buy the tickets.

meaning: “he/she spoke to me” or “he/she talked to me” (also: “he/she told me about …”).
additional_notes: "Mi" = "to me" (indirect object pronoun). "Ha parlato" is the passato prossimo of "parlare" with "avere" and can mean either speaking to you (Mi ha parlato) or talking to you about someone/something (Mi ha parlato di Maria). With languages, use "in" + language: "Mi ha parlato in spagnolo" = "He/She spoke to me in Spanish."
target_language_example: Ieri mi ha parlato di questo problema.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she told me about this problem.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of *portare* with the indirect object *mi* (“to me”). Used for bringing you something (*mi ha portato il libro*, “he brought me the book”) and for taking/leading you somewhere, often with *a* or *da* (*mi ha portato a casa*, “he took me home”; *mi ha portato da te*, “he took me to you”).
target_language_example: Mi ha portato un panino e poi mi ha portato a casa.
native_language_example: He brought me a sandwich and then took me home.

meaning: “he/she introduced me to …” (spoken by a woman).
additional_notes: Used when someone introduces you to another person. The past participle agrees with the speaker if the direct object pronoun is before the verb: a woman says "mi ha presentata", a man says "mi ha presentato". You can change the pronoun for other people: "ti ha presentato/a a" (introduced you to), "ci ha presentati/e a" (introduced us to).
target_language_example: Marco mi ha presentata a sua madre.
native_language_example: Marco introduced me to his mother.

additional_notes: Past tense of *prendere* with an object pronoun (*mi* = me): literally “has taken me,” but it’s commonly used for physical contact or being caught/affected. Very often you’ll see it with an extra phrase that explains how: *mi ha preso per il braccio* (grabbed me by the arm), *mi ha preso per il collo* (by the neck). It can also be used more generally for something that “caught/got” you (e.g., a cable, a machine, an accident). Note: in *mi ha preso in giro* it becomes an idiom meaning “he/she made fun of me.”
target_language_example: Nel caos, qualcuno mi ha preso per il braccio e mi ha tirato via.
native_language_example: In the chaos, someone grabbed me by the arm and pulled me away.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of raccontare = “to tell, to recount.” Structure: mi (to me) + ha raccontato (has told). Used for stories, jokes, anecdotes, information: “Mi ha raccontato una barzelletta” (a joke), “Mi ha raccontato la storia…” (a story). The subject is understood from context (he/she/you formal).
target_language_example: Ieri Giulia mi ha raccontato cosa è successo al lavoro.
native_language_example: Yesterday Giulia told me what happened at work.

additional_notes: From the verb "rendere" (passato prossimo: "ha reso"). Very common with an adjective: "mi ha reso triste/stanco/felice" = "it made me sad/tired/happy". It can also be used in a broader sense meaning "shaped me": "mi ha reso ciò che sono" = "it made me who I am". Often you’ll see the full pattern: "Qualcosa/Qualcuno mi ha reso + adjective".
target_language_example: Quell’esperienza mi ha reso più forte.
native_language_example: That experience made me stronger.

additional_notes: Used to say someone thanked you for a specific action or reason. The past participle agrees with a direct object pronoun: you say ringraziata (female speaker) or ringraziato (male speaker). It can refer to “he/she thanked me” depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi ha ringraziata per averla aiutata con il trasloco.
native_language_example: He/She thanked me for helping her with the move.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ringraziare (“to thank”). Pattern: [person] mi ha ringraziato per + noun OR per + infinitive (often past infinitive: per aver(e) + past participle) to say what you were thanked for. The subject can be explicit (e.g., Mary) or omitted (Mi ha ringraziato...).
target_language_example: Mi ha ringraziato per avermi aiutato con i compiti.
native_language_example: He/She thanked me for helping me with the homework.

additional_notes: Used when someone stole something that belongs to you. Literally “to me” + “has” + “stolen.” In everyday Italian, the object often comes after: “Mi ha rubato la borsa” = “He/She stole my bag.” You can replace “mi” with other pronouns: “ti ha rubato” (stole from you), “ci ha rubato” (from us).
target_language_example: Mi hanno rubato il telefono in metro.
native_language_example: They stole my phone on the subway.

additional_notes: Used to say someone literally saved you from death or serious danger. It can also be used more loosely to mean “you really helped me a lot,” especially about a big favor (often with “Grazie, mi hai salvato la vita!”). Grammar: mi = “me”; ha salvato = “has saved” (passato prossimo); la vita = “the life.”
target_language_example: Grazie per il tuo aiuto: mi hai salvato la vita!
native_language_example: Thanks for your help—you saved my life!

additional_notes: Literally "has seen me" (present perfect), but in English it often translates as simple past: "saw me." It’s made of the object pronoun "mi" (me) + "ha" (has) + past participle "vista". "Vista" agrees with the gender of the person being seen: a woman says "mi ha vista"; a man says "mi ha visto." The subject is understood from context (lui/lei/Lei): "He/She/You (formal) saw me."
target_language_example: Mi ha vista uscire dal negozio.
native_language_example: He/She saw me leave the store.

additional_notes: Common past form of vedere (“to see”): ha visto = “(he/she) saw / has seen”, with mi = “me” as a direct object. Used for “when he/she saw me” (quando mi ha visto), questions (Mi ha visto? = “Did you see me?”), and with an infinitive to say someone saw you doing something: Mi ha visto correre = “He/she saw me run(ning)”.
target_language_example: Quando mi ha visto, mi ha salutato subito.
native_language_example: When he/she saw me, he/she greeted me right away.

meaning: "you have (done something) to/for me" / "you (did) ... to me".
additional_notes: Made of the indirect/direct object pronoun mi (“to me/me”) + hai (“you have,” from avere). Very common in the passato prossimo: mi hai + past participle (e.g., mi hai chiamato = “you called me,” mi hai aiutato = “you helped me”). In questions it can be mi hai mai...? (“have you ever...?”). The exact English translation depends on the verb that follows.
target_language_example: Mi hai detto la verità?
native_language_example: Did you tell me the truth?

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "chiamare" with the direct object pronoun "mi" = “me.” It can mean you called me on the phone, or you called me something (a label/insult), often followed by a noun or adjective: "Mi hai chiamato pervertito" = “You called me a pervert.” In questions you’ll often hear: "Perché mi hai chiamato?" (Why did you call me?).
target_language_example: Perché mi hai chiamato così tardi?
native_language_example: Why did you call me so late?

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "dare" (to give): "hai dato" + indirect object pronoun "mi" (to me). Used before the thing given: "Mi hai dato il libro" = "You gave me the book." It can also appear in set expressions: "mi hai dato una mano" (you gave me a hand / you helped me), "mi hai dato una buona idea" (you gave me a good idea). With "dare del + noun" it means to call someone something (often an insult): "Mi hai dato del traditore" = "You called me a traitor."
target_language_example: Perché mi hai dato il tuo numero?
native_language_example: Why did you give me your number?

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of dire: literally “you have said to me.” Used to refer back to something someone previously told you. Often followed by che + clause (mi hai detto che...) or di + infinitive (mi hai detto di fare...).
target_language_example: Mi hai detto che oggi non potevi venire.
native_language_example: You told me that you couldn’t come today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb fare in the passato prossimo (hai fatto) plus an object pronoun (mi = “me”). Very common pattern: fare + infinitive to mean “to make/let someone do something”: “Mi hai fatto ridere” = “You made me laugh.” It can also appear without an infinitive to mean “what you did to me” (“per quello che mi hai fatto”). With two verbs you may see “mi hai fatto fare + infinitive” = “you made me do + verb.”
target_language_example: Perché mi hai fatto aspettare così tanto?
native_language_example: Why did you make me wait so long?

meaning: "have you ever (to me)" (asking if something has happened at any time).
additional_notes: Used mainly in questions with the passato prossimo: "mi" = to me, "hai" = you have, "mai" = ever. It often introduces a past participle after it (detto, visto/a, sentito/a). The past participle agrees with the direct object pronoun "mi" when it means "me" (mi hai vista/sentita = you saw/heard me [female]; mi hai visto/sentito = [male]).
target_language_example: Mi hai mai chiamato dopo mezzanotte?
native_language_example: Have you ever called me after midnight?

meaning: “Did you hear me?” / “Have you heard me?”
additional_notes: Literally “you have heard me.” Commonly used as a question to check if someone heard what you just said (in person or on the phone). Depending on tone, it can also mean “Are you listening?” or “Do you understand?”
target_language_example: Ehi, mi hai sentito? Ti ho detto di chiudere la porta.
native_language_example: Hey, did you hear me? I told you to close the door.

meaning: 'they have (to me)' / 'they (did) to me' (with a past participle).
additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb avere to talk about something people did for you or to you. mi = “to me/me” (object pronoun); hanno = “they have” (3rd person plural). It’s typically followed by a past participle: mi hanno dato (they gave me), mi hanno invitato (they invited me), mi hanno chiamato (they called me), mi hanno aggredito (they attacked me), mi hanno rubato (they stole from me). In English you usually drop “have” and translate as simple past (“they gave/called/stole…”).
target_language_example: Mi hanno mandato un messaggio ieri sera.
native_language_example: They sent me a message last night.

additional_notes: Used when one or more people asked you to do an action. It’s the passato prossimo of "chiedere" with the indirect object pronoun "mi" (= to me) + "di" + infinitive (e.g., "andare", "correggere", "farlo"). You can change the pronoun: "ti hanno chiesto di" (they asked you), "gli/le hanno chiesto di" (they asked him/her).
target_language_example: Mi hanno chiesto di arrivare presto.
native_language_example: They asked me to arrive early.

additional_notes: Past tense of dare (“to give”), with mi = “to me” and hanno dato = “they gave/have given” (passato prossimo). Used for giving objects/information (Mi hanno dato i loro indirizzi), assigning something like a name or a task (Mi hanno dato il nome…, Mi hanno dato una missione), or blaming someone (Mi hanno dato la colpa = “They blamed me”). The subject (“they”) is often implied by context.
target_language_example: Mi hanno dato questo libro per il mio compleanno.
native_language_example: They gave me this book for my birthday.

additional_notes: Past tense with an indirect object pronoun: mi = “to me”. Used when the subject is “they” (often unspecified people). Usually followed by what was said: “mi hanno detto che…” (they told me that…) or “mi hanno detto di…” + infinitive (they told me to…).
target_language_example: Mi hanno detto che il negozio oggi è chiuso.
native_language_example: They told me that the store is closed today.

meaning: 'they told me that…' / 'I've been told that…'.
additional_notes: Used to report information you received from other people. Literally: “to me” (mi) + “they have said/told” (hanno detto) + “that” (che). Often introduces reported speech or news, and the speaker may or may not be naming who “they” are (it can mean “people told me”).
target_language_example: Mi hanno detto che domani il negozio è chiuso.
native_language_example: They told me that the shop is closed tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report what other people said in the past. "Mi hanno detto" is the past tense of "they told me" (passato prossimo). "Che avevano" literally means "that they had" (imperfetto of avere) and is often used after a past reporting verb to describe something that was true at that time (needs, plans, feelings, etc.).
target_language_example: Mi hanno detto che avevano già prenotato un tavolo.
native_language_example: They told me they had already booked a table.

additional_notes: Used to report information someone else gave you. "Mi" = "to me". "Hanno detto" is the passato prossimo of "dire" (they said/told). "Che" introduces the statement. "Erano" is the imperfect of "essere" (they were), often used for descriptions or states in the past (nationality, health, etc.).
target_language_example: Mi hanno detto che erano in ritardo.
native_language_example: They told me they were late.

mi hanno detto che erano molto

target_language_multi_word_term: mi hanno detto che erano molto
meaning: “they told me that they were very …”
additional_notes: Used to report what other people said to you. **Mi** = “to me,” **hanno detto** = “they told (me),” **che** = “that,” **erano** = “they were” (imperfect), **molto** = “very.” The adjective after **molto** must agree with the people being described: e.g., **molto arrabbiati** (men/mixed group), **molto arrabbiate** (women), **molto poveri/povere**, **molto affamati/affamate**.
target_language_example: Mi hanno detto che erano molto stanchi dopo il viaggio.
native_language_example: They told me they were very tired after the trip.

meaning: "they told me that they were ..." (introduces what someone told you).
additional_notes: Used for reported speech in the past: **mi hanno detto** = “they told me,” and **che** = “that.” The verb **stavano** is the imperfect of **stare** and is often followed by a gerund (**stavano andando/cercando...**) to mean “they were (in the middle of) doing …” at that time.
target_language_example: Mi hanno detto che stavano aspettando il treno.
native_language_example: They told me they were waiting for the train.

additional_notes: Used to report what other people said they wanted. Literally: mi (to me) + hanno detto (they said/told) + che (that) + volevano (they wanted; imperfect past), often implying an ongoing intention or a desire they had at the time.
target_language_example: Mi hanno detto che volevano parlare con te.
native_language_example: They told me they wanted to talk to you.

meaning: “they did to me / they made me (do/feel) …”
additional_notes: Past tense with an indirect object: *mi* = “to me,” *hanno fatto* = “they did/made.” It’s used either for something done to you (*Mi hanno fatto un torto* = “They wronged me”) or for causing a feeling/reaction (*Mi hanno fatto paura* = “They scared me”). Often followed by a noun (*una sorpresa, un torto*) or by an emotion/infinitive phrase depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi hanno fatto aspettare mezz’ora.
native_language_example: They made me wait half an hour.

meaning: “they invited me to …” / “they’ve invited me to …”.
additional_notes: Used when other people invite you ("mi" = me). "Hanno invitato" is the past tense with "avere"; the past participle can agree with you: a woman says "mi hanno invitata", a man says "mi hanno invitato". After "a" you typically use an infinitive (a mangiare, a uscire) or a place/event (a casa loro, a cena).
target_language_example: Mi hanno invitata a uscire stasera.
native_language_example: They invited me to go out tonight.

additional_notes: Used with things/people/topics to say they interest you: "X mi interessa" = "X interests me". Often used to say you do or don’t care: "non mi interessa" = "I don’t care" / "it doesn’t matter to me". You can use it alone to mean "Tell me more, I’m interested."
target_language_example: Mi interessa questo corso, ma non ho molto tempo.
native_language_example: I’m interested in this course, but I don’t have much time.

additional_notes: Uses the formal form (Lei): "lasci" = "(you) leave/let". It’s common in requests and complaints: "Mi lasci in pace" (Leave me alone), "Mi lasci sognare" (Let me dream). With nouns like "scelta" it means "leave": "Non mi lasci scelta" = "You leave me no choice." Often combined with "da solo/a" to mean "alone": "Mi lasci da solo/da sola."
target_language_example: Per favore, mi lasci in pace.
native_language_example: Please, leave me alone.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to release you or allow you to leave. It can also be followed by an infinitive to mean “let me go (do something),” e.g., “Mi lasci andare a prendere…” (“Let me go get…”). The verb is in the formal/polite form (“Lei”): “lasci” = “(you) let.”
target_language_example: Mi lasci andare a casa, per favore.
native_language_example: Please let me go home.

additional_notes: From "lasciare" (to leave) + "mi" (me) + "da solo" (alone). Used to ask someone to stop bothering you or to leave you in peace; can also mean you don’t want to be left alone with a person or in a situation. Politeness depends on tone—adding "per piacere" makes it softer.
target_language_example: Per favore, mi lasci da solo: devo lavorare.
native_language_example: Please, leave me alone: I have to work.

additional_notes: Uses the verb pattern **lasciare + (someone) + infinitive** to mean “to let/allow someone to do something.” Here **mi** = “me” (object pronoun) and **spesso** = “often.” You normally add what is being used after **usare** (e.g., *il computer*, *la macchina/la macchina = car*, *l’auto*).
target_language_example: Mio fratello mi lascia spesso usare la sua bici.
native_language_example: My brother often lets me use his bike.

meaning: I brush my teeth / I wash my teeth.
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase for tooth brushing. Italian uses the reflexive verb "lavarsi" (to wash oneself): "mi lavo" = "I wash myself," and "i denti" = "the teeth" (Italian often uses the definite article where English uses a possessive: "my teeth"). You can add time/frequency like "ogni mattina" (every morning), "dopo aver mangiato" (after eating), "due volte al giorno" (twice a day).
target_language_example: Prima di uscire, mi lavo i denti.
native_language_example: Before going out, I brush my teeth.

meaning: "I miss him/it" (literally: "he/it is missing to me").
additional_notes: Used with the verb "mancare" to say you miss someone or something. The person who misses is an indirect object (mi = to me), and what/who is missed is the subject, so you say: "Mi manca Parigi" (I miss Paris) and "Mi manca Peter" (I miss Peter). For plural things/people, use "mi mancano" (e.g., "Mi mancano i miei amici" = I miss my friends).
target_language_example: Mi manca mia sorella quando sono in viaggio.
native_language_example: I miss my sister when I’m traveling.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "mancare" to express missing someone or something. In Italian, the thing/person you miss is the grammatical subject: "Mi manca Parigi" = literally "Paris is missing to me" (not *"I miss Paris"* in structure). You can move the subject before or after: "Mi manca così tanto Parigi" / "Parigi mi manca così tanto". For a plural subject, use "mi mancano" (e.g., "Mi mancano così tanto i miei amici").
target_language_example: Mi manca così tanto la mia famiglia.
native_language_example: I miss my family so much.

additional_notes: Used to say you miss someone. Literally “you are missing to me.” The verb is "mancare": the person who is missed is the subject (tu manchi), and the person who misses is an indirect object pronoun (mi = “to me”). You can emphasize with "come" (Oh, come mi manchi! = “Oh, how I miss you!”) or "già" (Ti/tu mi manchi già = “I miss you already.”).
target_language_example: Da quando sei partita, mi manchi tantissimo.
native_language_example: Since you left, I miss you so much.

meaning: 'can you pass me the…' / 'pass me the…' (to hand something to me).
additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to hand you an object. It comes from the verb "passare" (to pass/hand). You can change the article depending on the noun: "mi passi la…", "mi passi lo…", "mi passi l’…", "mi passi i/le…". Often followed by "per favore".
target_language_example: Mi passi il sale, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you pass me the salt, please?

additional_notes: Formal, respectful way to introduce what you want to do/say, often when asking permission or making a point. Uses the formal command (Lei) form of "permettere": "mi permetta" = "please allow me". Common before verbs like chiedere, essere, finire, pensare, richiamare.
target_language_example: Mi permetta di farle una domanda.
native_language_example: Allow me to ask you a question.

additional_notes: Used with plural nouns/ideas that are the subject of the sentence: the things you like are grammatically the subject, and “mi” means “to me.” For one thing (singular), use “mi piace.” You can also like activities: “Mi piacciono scienze e matematica.”
target_language_example: Mi piacciono questi libri.
native_language_example: I like these books.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "piacere" to say you like multiple things. The structure is literally "to me are pleasing the...". Use "mi piacciono" + a plural noun. "i" is the masculine plural definite article (“the”) and is used before many plural masculine nouns (e.g., i film, i libri). For plural feminine nouns, use "mi piacciono le".
target_language_example: Mi piacciono i libri di avventura.
native_language_example: I like adventure books.

additional_notes:
Italian uses the verb piacere differently than English: it’s closer to “(something) is pleasing to me.”
- mi = “to me”
- piacciono = “(they) please/are pleasing” (plural)
- le = “the” (plural feminine)
Use it before a plural feminine noun: Mi piacciono le verdure. (I like vegetables.) For plural masculine nouns you use: Mi piacciono i/gli …
target_language_example: Mi piacciono le città italiane.
native_language_example: I like Italian cities.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere, which works differently from English: the thing you like is the grammatical subject, and mi means “to me.” Pattern: Mi piace + singular noun/infinitive (Mi piace il caffè; Mi piace studiare). For plural nouns, use Mi piacciono (Mi piacciono i film). You can add solo to mean “only/just” (Mi piace solo la carne).
target_language_example: Mi piace questo posto, ma oggi mi piace solo stare a casa.
native_language_example: I like this place, but today I only feel like staying at home.

meaning: "I really like it" / "I like it a lot."
additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that you like something. In Italian, the thing you like is the subject of the verb piacere, so it’s usually followed by a noun (Mi piace davvero questa sedia.) or by a clause/infinitive (Mi piace davvero andare lì.). The verb agrees with what you like: mi piace (singular thing) vs mi piacciono (plural things).
target_language_example: Mi piace davvero questo posto.
native_language_example: I really like this place.

meaning: “I like it more / I prefer it.”
additional_notes: Used with piacere to compare preferences. Often followed by what you’re comparing it to: di + noun/pronoun (Mi piace di più questo di quello) or che + verb/infinitive (Mi piace di più sciare che nuotare). You can also say Mi piace di più + noun when the comparison is understood from context. (Common alternative: Preferisco…)
target_language_example: Mi piace di più questa pizza di quella.
native_language_example: I like this pizza more than that one.

meaning: "I like being / I like to be."
additional_notes: Used with the verb "piacere" to say you enjoy being in a certain state or role. It’s usually followed by an adjective (e.g., "organizzata", "spontaneo") or a phrase (e.g., "da sola"). With adjectives, match gender/number to the person being described ("Mi piace essere organizzata" = a woman speaking; "organizzato" = a man speaking). The negative is "Non mi piace essere..." ("I don’t like being...").
target_language_example: Mi piace essere in ordine.
native_language_example: I like being tidy.

meaning: "I like the" (with a singular masculine noun).
additional_notes: With piacere, the thing you like is the grammatical subject: literally "the ... is pleasing to me." Use mi piace + singular (Mi piace il gelato) and mi piacciono + plural (Mi piacciono i film). "Il" is used with masculine singular nouns; for feminine singular use "mi piace la ...".
target_language_example: Mi piace il caffè.
native_language_example: I like coffee.

mi piace il modo in cui

target_language_multi_word_term: mi piace il modo in cui
additional_notes: Used to say you like how someone does something or how something is (sound, smell, etc.). It’s typically followed by a verb (e.g., canti, pensa, sorride) or by how something affects you (e.g., profuma questo fiore = how this flower smells). Often you can also say just "Mi piace come..." with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Mi piace il modo in cui parli italiano.
native_language_example: I like the way you speak Italian.

meaning: "I like his/her/its" (or "I like your" in formal speech).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: "Mi piace il suo + noun". Italian possessives agree with the thing owned (il suo avatar / la sua macchina / i suoi amici / le sue idee), not with the owner. "Suo/sua/suoi/sue" can mean "his", "her", "its", or formal "your" (Lei). "Mi piace" literally means "it is pleasing to me", so the verb often matches what you like: "Mi piacciono i suoi..." (plural).
target_language_example: Mi piace il suo stile.
native_language_example: I like his/her style.

meaning: "I like your …" (talking about something masculine singular).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun: "Mi piace il tuo + [noun]" (e.g., "Mi piace il tuo sito web"). Italian changes "tuo" to match the noun: il tuo (m. sg.), la tua (f. sg.), i tuoi (m. pl.), le tue (f. pl.). Also note the structure: literally it’s like "Your … is pleasing to me," so the thing you like is the grammatical subject.
target_language_example: Mi piace il tuo stile.
native_language_example: I like your style.

meaning: “I like your …” (addressing more than one person; masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say you like something that belongs to the people you’re speaking to (plural/formal “you”). "Mi piace" = “I like (it)” (literally “it pleases me”). "Vostro" agrees with a masculine singular noun (il caffè, il cavallo, il gatto, il maglione). For feminine singular use "la vostra" (Mi piace la vostra casa). For plural things: "Mi piacciono i/le vostri/e ...".
target_language_example: Mi piace il vostro ristorante.
native_language_example: I like your restaurant.

meaning: "I like the …" (with a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Italian uses the verb piacere literally meaning “to be pleasing.” Mi piace la + noun is used when the thing you like is feminine and singular (la cioccolata, la musica, la solitudine). The verb agrees with what is liked: mi piace la pizza (singular) but mi piacciono le pizze (plural).
target_language_example: Mi piace la musica italiana.
native_language_example: I like Italian music.

additional_notes:
Used with the verb piacere to say you like something that belongs to someone else. The thing you like is the grammatical subject: Mi piace la sua camicia = “His/Her shirt pleases me” → “I like his/her shirt.”

"Sua" is a possessive adjective meaning “his/her/your (formal)/their,” and it agrees with the noun (camicia, maglia, musica). You can also use it without repeating the noun if it’s clear from context: Mi piace la sua (camicia).
target_language_example: Mi piace la sua giacca, è molto elegante.
native_language_example: I like his/her jacket; it’s very elegant.

additional_notes: Used to say you like something that belongs to the person you’re speaking to. "Mi piace" literally means "it pleases me" (so the thing you like is the grammatical subject). "La tua" = "your" (feminine singular) and must match the noun that follows: e.g., "la tua cravatta". For masculine singular you’d say "il tuo" (e.g., "Mi piace il tuo cappello").
target_language_example: Mi piace la tua idea.
native_language_example: I like your idea.

meaning: “I like it a lot” / “I really like it.”
additional_notes: Used to express strong liking for something (or someone). Grammar note: the thing you like is the subject in Italian, so you literally say “it pleases me”: Mi piace molto questo libro. With plural things, use piacciono: Mi piacciono molto questi libri. For a person, you can say Mi piace molto Maria (I like Maria a lot).
target_language_example: Mi piace molto questa canzone.
native_language_example: I really like this song.

meaning: “I like this …” (referring to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere. The grammar is reversed compared to English: literally “this (feminine thing) pleases me.” You typically say “Mi piace questa + [feminine noun]” (e.g., camicia, musica). For masculine nouns, use “Mi piace questo …”. To like more than one thing, use “Mi piacciono queste …” (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Mi piace questa pizza.
native_language_example: I like this pizza.

additional_notes: Used to say you like something that is near you or just mentioned. With "piacere," the thing you like is the grammatical subject: "Mi piace questo colore" = "This color pleases me." For plural things, use "Mi piacciono questi/queste...". You can replace "questo" with a noun or with "quello" (that).
target_language_example: Mi piace questo ristorante.
native_language_example: I like this restaurant.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize the verb piacere (“to be pleasing to me / to like”). Veramente adds intensity (“really/truly”). It can stand alone (“Mi piace veramente.” = “I really like it.”) or be followed by a noun/person (Mi piace veramente Tom / quel tizio), or by an infinitive (Mi piace veramente leggere…). Note: with piacere, the thing you like is the grammatical subject, so it’s “Mi piace…” for singular (il pesce) and “Mi piacciono…” for plural things.
target_language_example: Mi piace veramente questa canzone.
native_language_example: I really like this song.

meaning: 'I would like' / 'I'd like' (also: 'I would love to').
additional_notes: Conditional form of "piacere" used to express a wish or polite request. Often followed by an infinitive ("mi piacerebbe avere/diventare/riposarmi") or a noun ("mi piacerebbe una tazza di caffè"). It can also introduce a desire with a limitation: "Mi piacerebbe..., però...".
target_language_example: Mi piacerebbe prenotare un tavolo per due.
native_language_example: I'd like to book a table for two.

additional_notes: From piacere (“to be pleasing”): what you like is the grammatical subject. So it literally works like “it was pleasing to me.” Use it for a finished time in the past or for a past habit/ongoing feeling. Negative: non mi piaceva (“I didn’t like it/him/her”). You can also add what you like after it: mi piaceva Boston; mi piaceva ascoltare…; mi piaceva come persona (“I liked him/her as a person”).
target_language_example: Da piccolo mi piaceva leggere prima di dormire.
native_language_example: When I was little, I used to like reading before going to sleep.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere, which works differently from English: the thing/person liked is the grammatical subject. So mi piaci is said to one person you like (often with a romantic/attraction nuance). Negative: Non mi piaci (“I don’t like you”), or Non mi piaci quando fai così (“I don’t like you when you do that”). For things you like, you’ll often use mi piace (singular) / mi piacciono (plural).
target_language_example: Mi piaci davvero, ma vorrei conoscerti meglio.
native_language_example: I really like you, but I’d like to get to know you better.

additional_notes: Literally “you bring (to) me.” It’s the present subjunctive of portare used as a polite request, common with per favore / per piacere in restaurants and shops. Used when you want someone to bring you an item (Mi porti il menù) or something to eat/drink (Mi porti da bere).
target_language_example: Scusi, mi porti un bicchiere d’acqua, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you bring me a glass of water, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask if you can trust a person (or sometimes a source). It’s the reflexive verb "fidarsi di" = "to trust" + "posso" (I can) + "mi". The person trusted comes after "di" (di lui/lei/loro, or a name): "Mi posso fidare di lui?" = "Can I trust him?" In polite/formal situations you can also use "Posso fidarmi di... ?"
target_language_example: Scusi, mi posso fidare di lei?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I trust you?

additional_notes: Polite way to ask permission to sit. Often followed by where you want to sit: accanto a… (next to…), dietro (di)… (behind…), qui/lì (here/there). You can also hear: “Posso sedermi…?” (same meaning).
target_language_example: Mi posso sedere qui vicino a te?
native_language_example: Can I sit here next to you?

meaning: “Are you kidding me?” / “Are you making fun of me?”
additional_notes: Very common, informal expression used when you think someone is joking, teasing you, or not being serious. Literally it’s like “you take me around,” but the real meaning is “you’re pulling my leg / you’re messing with me.” Can be said as a question (Mi prendi in giro?) or as an accusation (Mi prendi in giro!).
target_language_example: Dai, mi prendi in giro? Non può essere vero!
native_language_example: Come on, are you kidding me? That can’t be true!

meaning: “Are you kidding me?” / “Are you messing with me?” / “Are you making fun of me?” (vulgar).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Used when you feel someone is joking at your expense, tricking you, or not being serious. Often said as a confrontational question ("Mi prendi per il culo?") or accusation ("Mi prendi per il culo."). Avoid in polite situations; a milder alternative is "Mi stai prendendo in giro?"
target_language_example: Mi prendi per il culo? Sto parlando sul serio.
native_language_example: Are you kidding me? I’m being serious.

additional_notes: Used to express worry or concern for someone or something. It’s the verb phrase "preoccuparsi" (to worry) + "per" (about/for). You can change "mi" to match the subject: "ti preoccupi per..." (you worry), "si preoccupa per..." (he/she worries), "ci preoccupiamo per..." (we worry), etc.
target_language_example: Mi preoccupo per i miei genitori quando viaggiano.
native_language_example: I worry about my parents when they travel.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone (Lei) to lend you something. "La sua" means "yours" (formal) and often refers back to a noun mentioned right after or earlier (e.g., "la sua penna" = "your pen"). With masculine nouns it becomes "il suo" (e.g., "Mi presti il suo libro?").
target_language_example: Mi scusi, mi presti la sua penna per un attimo?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you lend me your pen for a moment?

additional_notes:
A polite way to ask someone for help. Literally 'you can help me'. Often followed by:
- "a" + infinitive to say what you need help doing: "Mi puoi aiutare a sollevare..." (Can you help me lift...)
- "ad" + infinitive before a vowel: "Mi puoi aiutare ad installare..." (help me install...)
- "con" + noun/pronoun for help with something: "Mi puoi aiutare con questo progetto?" (help me with this project)
You can make it more polite with "per favore" or "per piacere".
target_language_example: Scusa, mi puoi aiutare a trovare la stazione?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you help me find the train station?

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize a request, reminder, or warning, often like “don’t forget” or “be careful.” It can stand alone (Mi raccomando!) or be followed by an imperative: “Mi raccomando, fai attenzione.” Common in spoken Italian and can sound firm, especially with commands.
target_language_example: Mi raccomando, non dirlo a nessuno.
native_language_example: Make sure you don’t tell anyone.

additional_notes: Used with a subject (a person/thing) + rendere + indirect object pronoun (mi = me) + adjective or noun to describe the effect something has on you: "X mi rende + aggettivo" (X makes me + adjective). Often translated as "it makes me" rather than the more literal "it renders me."
target_language_example: Questo film mi rende triste.
native_language_example: This movie makes me sad.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "rendersi conto di" + a noun/pronoun: "Mi rendo conto del problema" (I realize the problem), "Mi rendo conto della tua situazione" (I understand your situation). Often used to show awareness or empathy. You can change "mi" to match the subject: "ti rendi conto" (you realize), "si rende conto" (he/she realizes), "ci rendiamo conto" (we realize), etc.
target_language_example: Mi rendo conto che hai ragione.
native_language_example: I realize you're right.

additional_notes: From the verb ricordarsi (reflexive). It’s often followed by di + person/thing: Mi ricordo di lei. It can also be used with che + clause to remember a fact: Mi ricordo che lui ama il formaggio. Common intensifiers: ancora (“still”), a malapena (“barely”), quasi non (“I hardly”).
target_language_example: Mi ricordo ancora del tuo nome, ma non mi ricordo dove ci siamo conosciuti.
native_language_example: I still remember your name, but I don’t remember where we met.

additional_notes: Used with "di" to say you remember a person/thing ("Mi ricordo di Tom", "di quel posto") or to remember having done something: "Mi ricordo di averla visto/a..." (= “I remember seeing her...”). In everyday Italian, "mi ricordo" is very common and often interchangeable with "ricordo"; in careful/formal Italian, "mi ricordo" can be felt as less formal.
target_language_example: Mi ricordo di averti chiamato ieri sera.
native_language_example: I remember calling you last night.

meaning: "I refuse to" (I won’t / I’m not willing to).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb (mi rifiuto di + verb) to say you refuse to do something. It can sound firm or confrontational, especially in disagreements. You can change the subject: ti rifiuti di (you refuse to), si rifiuta di (he/she refuses to), ci rifiutiamo di (we refuse to).
target_language_example: Mi rifiuto di firmare questo documento.
native_language_example: I refuse to sign this document.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken Italian (more informal than "penso" or "mi sembra"). Usually followed by "che" + verb: "Mi sa che hai ragione" = "I think you’re right." You can also use it alone to express doubt or a negative guess: "Mi sa di no" = "I don’t think so / I’m afraid not."
target_language_example: Mi sa che oggi piove, meglio prendere l’ombrello.
native_language_example: I think it’s going to rain today; better take an umbrella.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken Italian to express a guess, impression, or mild certainty. Literally it comes from “mi sa” (= “it is known to me / it gives me the sense”), but in practice you use it like “I think” or “I have a feeling that.” Often followed by the indicative: “Mi sa che è tardi.”
target_language_example: Mi sa che oggi pioverà, quindi prendo l’ombrello.
native_language_example: I think it’ll rain today, so I’m taking an umbrella.

meaning: “I would have …” (1st person singular conditional perfect, reflexive).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a hypothetical past or a regret. It’s the conditional form of the auxiliary verb “essere” (sarei) with the reflexive pronoun “mi” (“myself/to me”). It normally needs a past participle (mi sarei svegliato = I would have woken up) or a modal + infinitive (mi sarei dovuto fidare = I should have trusted / I shouldn’t have trusted, depending on negation).
target_language_example: Non mi sarei mai aspettato una cosa del genere.
native_language_example: I never would have expected something like that.

meaning: I was wrong / I was mistaken.
additional_notes: Used to admit a past mistake or incorrect belief. It’s the imperfect tense of the reflexive verb "sbagliarsi" (to be mistaken). Often used alone as a short correction ("Mi sbagliavo.") or with "su/a riguardo" to specify what you were wrong about.
target_language_example: Credevo che oggi fosse lunedì, ma mi sbagliavo.
native_language_example: I thought today was Monday, but I was wrong.

mi sbagliavo così tanto su di

target_language_multi_word_term: mi sbagliavo così tanto su di
additional_notes: Used when you realize your opinion or assumption about someone was very incorrect. "Mi sbagliavo" is the imperfect past of "sbagliarsi" (to be mistaken), often implying a past belief over time. "Su di" is followed by stressed pronouns like "lui" (him), "lei" (her), "loro" (them), "voi" (you plural/formal).
target_language_example: Mi sbagliavo così tanto su di te.
native_language_example: I was so wrong about you.

meaning: “I was wrong about …” / “I was mistaken about …”.
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of the reflexive verb *sbagliarsi* (*mi sbagliavo*) to talk about a past misunderstanding or wrong assumption. It’s followed by *su* (“about”): *mi sbagliavo su Tom*. With pronouns you often see *su di*: *mi sbagliavo su di loro* (“about them”), *mi sbagliavo su di me stesso* (“about myself”). For a completed/one-time mistake, you can also say *mi sono sbagliato/a su …*.
target_language_example: Mi sbagliavo su di te: eri molto più gentile di quanto pensassi.
native_language_example: I was wrong about you: you were much kinder than I thought.

additional_notes: Used with Lei (formal) to politely get someone’s attention, interrupt, or apologize (e.g., for bothering someone or for a delay). Common in shops, restaurants, and with strangers. Less formal alternatives include “scusa” (tu) or “scusate” (to a group).
target_language_example: Mi scusi, dov'è la stazione?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the station?

additional_notes: From the verb "mancare" (literally “to be missing”): in Italian you say the person “was missing to me,” so it uses "essere" + past participle. The past participle agrees with who is missed: "mi sei mancata" (female), "mi sei mancato" (male), "mi siete mancati/e" (plural). Often intensified with "molto", "tanto", or "un sacco".
target_language_example: Mi sei mancata tantissimo durante il viaggio.
native_language_example: I missed you so much during the trip.

additional_notes: Used when you felt someone’s absence. Grammar: literally “you were missing to me” (Italian uses essere + mancato). Change for gender/number: mi sei mancata (to a woman), mi siete mancati/mancate (to you all), mi è mancato (he/it), mi sono mancati (they, masc./mixed), mi sono mancate (they, fem.). Often intensified with molto/tantissimo/così tanto.
target_language_example: Scusa se non ti ho scritto: mi sei mancato davvero.
native_language_example: Sorry I didn’t write: I really missed you.

additional_notes: Used to give your opinion or impression. Often followed by a noun/adjective ("Mi sembra una cosa da poco" = It seems like a small thing to me) or by "che" + subjunctive ("Mi sembra che lei abbia ragione" = I think she’s right).
target_language_example: Mi sembra che oggi faccia più freddo del solito.
native_language_example: It seems to me that today it’s colder than usual.

meaning: "it seems to me that..." / "I feel like..." (introduces your opinion or impression).
additional_notes: Used to give a personal impression, often a bit tentative/soft: *Mi sembra che + subjunctive* (very common). In casual speech some people use the indicative, but the standard is the subjunctive (e.g., *mi sembra che sia...*, *mi sembra che stiamo...*). You can also use it to disagree gently or point something out: “from my point of view…”.
target_language_example: Mi sembra che oggi tu sia un po’ stanco.
native_language_example: It seems to me that you’re a bit tired today.

meaning: “it seems to me (that) / I feel like…”, used before an infinitive.
additional_notes: Used to express an impression, feeling, or uncertain memory/opinion. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb: “Mi sembra di capire” (I think I understand). Very common in the negative: “Non mi sembra di…” = “I don’t seem to…” / “I don’t think I…”.
target_language_example: Mi sembra di aver visto questo film, ma non ne sono sicuro.
native_language_example: I think I’ve seen this movie, but I’m not sure.

meaning: “Can you hear me?” / “Do you hear me?”
additional_notes: Used to check if someone can hear you (often on the phone, radio, or in a noisy place). Literally “you hear me” (mi = me; senti = you hear), and it can sound a bit insistent depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Mi senti bene o devo parlare più forte?
native_language_example: Can you hear me well, or do I need to speak louder?

meaning: "I felt" / "I was feeling" (about my physical or emotional state).
additional_notes: Imperfetto of "sentirsi" (to feel), used for an ongoing feeling in the past or to describe how you were at that time (emotionally or physically). Often followed by an adverb or adjective: "mi sentivo bene/male", "mi sentivo triste", "mi sentivo al sicuro". Contrast: "mi sono sentito/a" is a completed feeling at a specific moment.
target_language_example: Ieri mi sentivo stanco, quindi sono andato a letto presto.
native_language_example: Yesterday I was feeling tired, so I went to bed early.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how you felt in the past (imperfect tense of *sentirsi* = “to feel”). *Molto* intensifies the feeling (“very/a lot”). It’s followed by an adjective: *isolato/a* (isolated), *solo/a* (alone), *al sicuro* (safe), *fiero/fiera* (proud), *affamato/a* (hungry). The ending changes with gender/number (e.g., *solo* vs *sola*).
target_language_example: Ieri mi sentivo molto stanco.
native_language_example: Yesterday I felt very tired.

additional_notes: Used with adjectives to describe how you feel: mi sento bene/male (I feel good/bad), mi sento meglio (I feel better). It can also express how you feel about yourself in a situation: Mi sento stupido/a... (I feel stupid...). Agree the adjective with the speaker: mi sento rilassato (male), mi sento rilassata (female).
target_language_example: Dopo la doccia mi sento molto meglio.
native_language_example: After the shower I feel much better.

meaning: I feel well / I’m feeling good.
additional_notes: Used to talk about your physical or emotional condition. It literally means “I feel myself well,” from the verb "sentirsi" (to feel). Often used as a short answer when someone asks how you are ("Come stai?" / "Come ti senti?").
target_language_example: Dopo una buona notte di sonno, mi sento bene.
native_language_example: After a good night’s sleep, I feel good.

meaning: "I feel like" / "I feel as if" (followed by a clause).
additional_notes: Used to describe a feeling or impression by comparing it to a situation that may be real or imagined. It’s typically followed by a verb (often in the subjunctive), e.g., "mi sento come se fossi..." (I feel as if I were...). You may also hear the similar pattern "è come se..." (it’s as if...).
target_language_example: Mi sento come se stessi sognando.
native_language_example: I feel like I’m dreaming.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your emotional or physical state. "Mi sento" = "I feel" and "così" = "so/this"; it’s commonly followed by an adjective (stupida, idiota, persa, sola) or an adverbial phrase to emphasize how you feel.
target_language_example: Mi sento così stanca oggi.
native_language_example: I feel so tired today.

meaning: "I feel bad for" / "I feel sorry for" (someone); sometimes "I feel bad about" (something).
additional_notes: Used to express sympathy or compassion for a person or group (Mi sento male per loro). With a thing or situation (Mi sento male per questo), it can mean you feel upset or guilty about it. Often followed by a person (lui/lei) or people (quelle persone), or by a situation (questo).
target_language_example: Mi sento male per te: non è giusto quello che è successo.
native_language_example: I feel sorry for you: what happened isn’t fair.

additional_notes: Used to describe your current physical or emotional state, followed by an adjective: "Mi sento molto stanco/a" (very tired), "Mi sento molto felice" (very happy). The adjective usually agrees with the speaker: masculine -o (stanco, nervoso), feminine -a (stanca, nervosa).
target_language_example: Mi sento molto stanco oggi.
native_language_example: I feel very tired today.

additional_notes: Used to describe a state or emotion you experience often. It’s the reflexive verb "sentirsi" (to feel) + "sempre" (always). Typically followed by an adjective (stanco, depresso, assonnato) or sometimes a phrase like "limitato qui" (restricted here).
target_language_example: Mi sento sempre nervoso prima degli esami.
native_language_example: I always feel nervous before exams.

meaning: I need; it’s useful/necessary for me.
additional_notes: From servire (“to be useful/needed”). Used with a noun: “Mi serve + [thing]” = “I need + [thing]”. You can negate it: “Non mi serve …” = “I don’t need …”. Often interchangeable with “ho bisogno di …” (I need …), but “mi serve” sounds more like something is required or useful for a purpose.
target_language_example: Mi serve il tuo numero di telefono.
native_language_example: I need your phone number.

meaning: "I need a" / "I could use a" (for a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "servire" to express necessity: literally "a ___ is useful to me." It’s a common, natural way to ask for something you need (an object, a service, a person). Follow it with a masculine singular noun (e.g., "un letto"). For feminine singular, use "mi serve una" (e.g., "una chiave").
target_language_example: Mi serve un biglietto per domani.
native_language_example: I need a ticket for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say you need something: **mi serve + un/una + noun** = “I need a … / I could use a …”. Literally it’s closer to “it’s useful/needed for me,” so it doesn’t translate word-for-word as “serve.” Use **mi serve un** for masculine nouns (e.g., *mi serve un cavo*).
target_language_example: Mi serve una sedia in più.
native_language_example: I need an extra chair.

additional_notes: From the verb "servire" (to be needed / to be useful). "Mi" means "to me" and "servono" is plural, so it’s used with plural nouns: "Mi servono delle informazioni / più coperte". For a singular noun, use "mi serve" (e.g., "Mi serve un documento"). It’s a common, polite way to say you need something.
target_language_example: Mi servono due biglietti per Roma.
native_language_example: I need two tickets to Rome.

additional_notes: First-person singular of the reflexive verb "sedersi" (to sit down): literally "I seat myself." Often used when choosing a place to sit or making a polite request: "Ti/Le/Vi dispiace se mi siedo (qui)?" = "Do you mind if I sit (here)?" You can add location words like "qui" (here), "lì" (there), "dietro" (in the back/behind), "accanto" (next to).
target_language_example: Se è libero, mi siedo vicino alla finestra.
native_language_example: If it’s free, I’ll sit near the window.

meaning: "I have" / "I am" in the past (passato prossimo), used with reflexive verbs ("I ... myself").
additional_notes: Used to form the passato prossimo with the auxiliary verb essere + the pronoun mi. Very common with reflexive verbs: mi sono alzato/a = "I got up" (literally "I got myself up"), mi sono sbagliato/a = "I was wrong / I made a mistake". The past participle often agrees in gender/number with the subject: mi sono alzata (female), mi sono alzato (male).
target_language_example: Ieri mi sono dimenticato del tuo compleanno.
native_language_example: Yesterday I forgot your birthday.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of the reflexive verb **addormentarsi** (“to fall asleep”), so it uses **essere**: *mi sono…*. The past participle agrees with the speaker: **addormentata** (female), **addormentato** (male). Often followed by **mentre** (“while”) to say what you were doing when you fell asleep.
target_language_example: Scusa, mi sono addormentata sul divano.
native_language_example: Sorry, I fell asleep on the couch.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of addormentarsi (“to fall asleep”) with the reflexive pronoun mi (“myself”) and the auxiliary essere. Used for accidentally or naturally falling asleep (often in the middle of something). For a female speaker: mi sono addormentata.
target_language_example: Scusa, mi sono addormentato sul divano.
native_language_example: Sorry, I fell asleep on the couch.

meaning: “I got up / I stood up” (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the reflexive verb *alzarsi* (“to get up / to stand up”). *Mi* = “myself”; *sono* is the auxiliary used with reflexive verbs. *Alzata* agrees with the (female) speaker; a man would say *mi sono alzato*. Often used with times: *mi sono alzata alle sei*, *verso le sei*, *prima del solito*. Depending on context it can mean getting out of bed or standing up from a seat.
target_language_example: Mi sono alzata dal divano quando è suonato il campanello.
native_language_example: I stood up from the couch when the doorbell rang.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "alzarsi" = “to get up / to stand up,” used with the reflexive pronoun "mi" and the auxiliary "essere" (sono). "Alzato" is masculine singular; a woman would say "mi sono alzata". Often used with time adverbs like "presto" (early) or "tardi" (late).
target_language_example: Stamattina mi sono alzato tardi perché ero stanco.
native_language_example: This morning I got up late because I was tired.

additional_notes: Used with the passato prossimo of a reflexive verb to say something happened very recently. Structure: mi sono + appena + past participle (e.g., mi sono appena svegliato/a). It agrees with the subject: svegliato (male), svegliata (female). You can also use it with other reflexive verbs: mi sono appena ricordato/a, mi sono appena lavato/a.
target_language_example: Mi sono appena lavato le mani.
native_language_example: I just washed my hands.

additional_notes: Used with a reflexive past tense (passato prossimo) to say you forgot a person/thing or forgot to do something. Follow it with a noun/pronoun (mi sono dimenticata di Tom / di loro) or with an infinitive verb (mi sono dimenticata di chiamarlo). Gender/number changes with the speaker: mi sono dimenticato (male), mi sono dimenticati/e (plural).
target_language_example: Scusa, mi sono dimenticata di risponderti ieri.
native_language_example: Sorry, I forgot to reply to you yesterday.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the reflexive verb divertirsi. Use "mi sono divertita" if the speaker is female; a male speaker says "mi sono divertito". Often followed by "a" + event/place (e.g., "alla festa") and can be intensified with "molto" ("I had a lot of fun"). Uses "essere" as the auxiliary: "mi sono...".
target_language_example: Mi sono divertita tantissimo al concerto.
native_language_example: I had a great time at the concert.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo (past tense) of the reflexive verb divertirsi (“to have fun”). Used to say you had a good time at an event or in a place: mi sono divertito alla festa / a Boston. Changes with the person: mi sono divertito (male speaker), mi sono divertita (female speaker); ci siamo divertiti/e = “we had fun.”
target_language_example: Mi sono divertito tantissimo al concerto ieri sera.
native_language_example: I had a great time at the concert last night.

additional_notes: Feminine past of "mi sono fatto" (reflexive/passive-like use with essere).
