additional_notes: Uses "per" + infinitive to express purpose (“in order to”). Often follows verbs like "avere bisogno"/"servire" (to need) or describes transport and timing: "un passaggio per andare a scuola" (a ride to get to school), "l'autobus per andare a scuola" (the bus to go to school).
target_language_example: Devo prendere la metro per andare a scuola.
native_language_example: I have to take the subway to go to school.

meaning: 'for having' / 'for + past infinitive' (to explain a reason).
additional_notes: Used to give the reason for a credit, punishment, criticism, etc. It means “for having done” something (past action). Structure: per + avere (conjugated as aver before a past participle) + past participle: per aver mentito = for having lied. With verbs that use essere in the passato prossimo, you can also see “per essere + past participle” (e.g., per essere arrivato/a = for having arrived).
target_language_example: Mi hanno ringraziato per aver aiutato i miei colleghi.
native_language_example: They thanked me for having helped my coworkers.

additional_notes: Uses **per** + **avere** (infinitive) + past participle (**rubato**) to say the reason for an action, emphasizing that the stealing happened **before** the main event (e.g., being arrested/fired). In everyday English it’s often translated simply as **"for stealing"**.
target_language_example: È stato condannato per aver rubato dei soldi.
native_language_example: He was convicted for having stolen money.

meaning: for having written the book; for writing the book (as the reason).
additional_notes: Uses **per + infinitive** to express the reason why something happened (“because of / for”). Here **aver scritto** is the **past infinitive** (literally “to have written”), often used when the action happened before the main verb: *È stato messo in prigione per aver scritto il libro* = he was imprisoned because he had written the book.
target_language_example: È stato criticato per aver scritto il libro.
native_language_example: He was criticized for having written the book.

additional_notes: Used to give the reason for thanks, blame, etc.: "per" + infinitive "avere" + object pronoun "mi". It introduces a past action affecting the speaker (me), often with a past participle after it: "per avermi aiutato/a" (for having helped me). The past participle agrees with the speaker in gender/number when using "essere" or sometimes with direct-object pronouns; in common phrases like "averci/avermi aiutato" you’ll often hear agreement with the speaker ("aiutata" if the speaker is female).
target_language_example: Grazie per avermi chiamato subito.
native_language_example: Thanks for calling me right away.

additional_notes: Used after expressions like grazie (thanks), ti sono grato/a (I’m grateful), vergognarsi (to be ashamed), or ringraziare (to thank) to give the reason. It’s made of per (for) + avermi (to have + me), and it’s followed by a past participle: per avermi aiutato/a (for having helped me). The past participle can agree with the speaker if it uses essere or with a direct object pronoun in some cases; in common phrases you’ll often see aiutato/a, salvato/a, invitato/a depending on who is speaking.
target_language_example: Grazie per avermi aspettato.
native_language_example: Thanks for waiting for me.

additional_notes: Common with verbs like fare, preparare, pulire, mescolare to mean “do it properly / thoroughly” (often as an instruction). With a person (una persona/ragazza per bene), it means “a respectable/decent person,” implying good manners and good behavior.
target_language_example: Prima di uscire, chiudi la porta per bene.
native_language_example: Before going out, close the door properly.

additional_notes: Used as an exclamation to strongly refuse or deny something (often with “no”: “No, per carità!” = “No way!”). It can also add urgency to a warning or request (“Stia attento, per carità!” = “Be careful, for heaven’s sake!”). Literally it’s “for charity,” but the real meaning is idiomatic.
target_language_example: Per carità, non farlo!
native_language_example: For heaven’s sake, don’t do it!

meaning: by chance; (in questions) by any chance.
additional_notes: Used to say something happened accidentally or coincidentally (not planned): "Eravamo per caso sullo stesso treno." In questions, it often softens the request and means “by any chance…?” or “do you happen to…?” Sometimes it can sound a bit pointed or surprised depending on tone: "Vuole una banana, per caso?" (“Do you want a banana, or what?”).
target_language_example: Hai per caso visto le mie chiavi?
native_language_example: Have you by any chance seen my keys?

meaning: "By any chance, what time is it?"
additional_notes: "Per caso" is a polite, softening phrase meaning "by chance / by any chance". It’s often used in questions to sound less direct: "Sa(i/te) per caso... ?". You can use it with different forms of "sapere" depending on who you’re speaking to (Lei sa… / tu sai… / voi sapete…).
target_language_example: Scusi, sa per caso che ore sono?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you happen to know what time it is?

additional_notes: Used to talk about what someone will eat at dinner, or to invite/ask someone to stay/go out for dinner. Common with verbs like mangiare (to eat), avere (to have), restare/rimanere (to stay), uscire (to go out), invitare (to invite).
target_language_example: Hai già deciso cosa vuoi mangiare per cena?
native_language_example: Have you decided what you want to eat for dinner?

additional_notes: Used after a number to give a percentage: “dieci per cento” = 10%. You can also use it with “il/la/un … per cento (di)” to talk about a portion of a group: “il 90 per cento delle persone” = 90% of people. In writing you’ll often see the symbol “%” instead of spelling it out.
target_language_example: Solo il trenta per cento degli studenti ha finito l’esercizio.
native_language_example: Only thirty percent of the students finished the exercise.

additional_notes: Used to give the reason for a feeling or action, referring to a specific thing someone did/said or a fact (often followed by a verb in the past: per ciò che ho detto/fatto). It can also mean “for what (someone is)” in phrases like “ti amo per ciò che sei” (“I love you for who you are”). Often interchangeable with “per quello che” in everyday Italian.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace per ciò che ho detto ieri.
native_language_example: I'm sorry for what I said yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to an event that happened and is already known from context, often when apologizing or expressing concern: "Mi dispiace per ciò che è successo" (I’m sorry about what happened). Note the verb form: "è successo" = "happened" (from succedere).
target_language_example: Non è colpa tua per ciò che è successo ieri.
native_language_example: It’s not your fault for what happened yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is punished, blamed, or faces consequences because of their actions. The verb changes with the subject (ha fatto = he/she has done; hanno fatto = they have done).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace per ciò che ho fatto.
native_language_example: I'm sorry for what I did.

additional_notes: Used to say what someone eats/drinks in the morning. It often follows verbs like mangiare/bere (to eat/drink) or preparare (to prepare): “Mangio yogurt per colazione.” You can also ask about someone’s breakfast habits: “Cosa prendi per colazione?”
target_language_example: Di solito bevo un caffè e mangio un cornetto per colazione.
native_language_example: I usually drink a coffee and eat a croissant for breakfast.

additional_notes: Used to blame someone or something for a bad outcome. Very often followed by “di” + a person/thing: “per colpa di Linda” (Linda’s fault). With articles it can combine: “per colpa della tua lingua” (because of your big mouth / because of what you said). It has a negative tone; for neutral “because of,” use “a causa di” or “per via di.”
target_language_example: Siamo arrivati in ritardo per colpa del traffico.
native_language_example: We arrived late because of the traffic.

meaning: because of you; it’s your fault (blaming someone).
additional_notes: Used to assign blame or responsibility for a bad outcome. Often sounds accusatory. You can change the pronoun: per colpa mia (my fault), per colpa sua (his/her fault), per colpa nostra (our fault), etc. Commonly followed by a result: “Per colpa tua, …” / “È successo per colpa tua.”
target_language_example: Per colpa tua abbiamo perso il treno.
native_language_example: Because of you we missed the train.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something alone or without help/without involving others. It can also imply acting without permission or outside a group plan (e.g., “He acted on his own”). Don’t confuse with “per conto di (qualcuno)”, which means “on behalf of (someone)”.
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: lo farà per conto suo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he’ll do it on his own.

additional_notes: Used to soften or qualify a statement, often when you’re speaking figuratively, approximately, or using a metaphor/irony. It can be inserted between commas in a sentence (È, per così dire, ...) or said alone as a quick afterthought.
target_language_example: È un esperto, per così dire, di tutto un po'.
native_language_example: He’s an expert, so to speak, in a bit of everything.

additional_notes: Most commonly a relative phrase meaning “for which” or “that/what … for,” used to introduce the thing or reason something is done: “la ragione per cui…” (the reason why/for which), “quello per cui…” (what/that which … for). In spoken Italian it can also mean “therefore/so” to link ideas, but in your examples it’s mainly the “for which / why” use.
target_language_example: Non capisco il motivo per cui sei arrabbiato.
native_language_example: I don’t understand the reason why you’re angry.

meaning: to live for; something to live for.
additional_notes: Used after a negative/indefinite like niente/nulla to mean “no reason/purpose to keep living” (figuratively: no motivation). It refers to a goal, person, or purpose that gives meaning to life. In Italian you can also hear “un motivo per cui vivere” (“a reason to live”).
target_language_example: Dopo la nascita di sua figlia, ha finalmente qualcosa per cui vivere.
native_language_example: After his daughter was born, he finally has something to live for.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is genuine/actually happening (not a joke, not pretend). Often placed after the verb: “l’ho visto per davvero” = “I saw it for real.” Can also be used in questions to show surprise or disbelief: “Sei serio per davvero?” / “È impazzita per davvero?”
target_language_example: Pensavo stessi scherzando, ma lo dici per davvero?
native_language_example: I thought you were joking, but do you really mean it?

meaning: what’s more; moreover; on top of that.
additional_notes: Used to add an extra point (often making a situation seem even worse, more surprising, or more impressive). It can appear mid-sentence or at the start: “Per di più, …” = “What’s more, …”.
target_language_example: Non ho tempo oggi e, per di più, ho dimenticato il portafoglio.
native_language_example: I don’t have time today and, what’s more, I forgot my wallet.

additional_notes: Used with a number after "per" to indicate quantity/capacity (per dieci persone = for ten people), distance/measurement (per dieci chilometri = for ten kilometers), or duration (per dieci mesi = for ten months). It often answers “how many?” or “for how long?”.
target_language_example: Puoi tenere il tavolo per dieci persone?
native_language_example: Can you reserve the table for ten people?

additional_notes: Used to talk about something planned for tomorrow (“for tomorrow”) or a deadline that must be met no later than tomorrow (“by tomorrow”). Often placed at the beginning for emphasis: “Per domani, …”.
target_language_example: Devo consegnare il progetto per domani.
native_language_example: I have to turn in the project by tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with "per" + a duration to say how long something lasts or lasted. Common with the past tense (e.g., "ha insegnato... per due anni") and with repeated/habitual actions ("andare a scuola per due anni"). You can swap the number: "per tre anni", "per due mesi", etc.
target_language_example: Ho lavorato a Milano per due anni.
native_language_example: I worked in Milan for two years.

additional_notes: Used with a time expression after **per** to say how long something lasts (duration). Often used with the present or past to describe an activity or situation continuing for that amount of time (e.g., *Ha nevicato per due giorni*).
target_language_example: Resterò a Roma per due giorni.
native_language_example: I’ll stay in Rome for two days.

meaning: for speeding; due to driving over the speed limit.
additional_notes: Used to say the reason for an arrest or a fine. Common with verbs like "essere multato" (to be fined) and "essere arrestato" (to be arrested), and with "multa" (fine).
target_language_example: Mi hanno fermato per eccesso di velocità sull'autostrada.
native_language_example: They pulled me over for speeding on the highway.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened unintentionally (often with a verb describing an action you didn’t mean to do). Similar to “per sbaglio.” It can go at the end of the sentence or near the verb: “L’ho fatto per errore” / “Per errore ho cliccato…”.
target_language_example: Ho inviato il messaggio al contatto sbagliato per errore.
native_language_example: I sent the message to the wrong contact by mistake.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an example or illustration. It can also be used alone as a question (“Per esempio?”) to ask someone to give an example. With verbs like prendere (“to take”), it means “take … for example” (e.g., “Prendi me, per esempio.”). Often placed at the start of a sentence, but it can also come after the item being highlighted.
target_language_example: Per esempio, possiamo prendere il treno invece dell’auto.
native_language_example: For example, we can take the train instead of the car.

additional_notes: Used with *per* + infinitive to express purpose or a criterion involving "being" something. Common patterns: *troppo + aggettivo + per essere...* (“too … to be …”), and *una ragione/motivo per essere...* (“a reason to be …”). Note: in *sta per essere...* the full expression is *stare per* (“to be about to”), and *essere* is the infinitive that follows it.
target_language_example: È troppo presto per essere sicuri.
native_language_example: It’s too early to be sure.

meaning: for being late; for arriving late.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like scusarsi (to apologize) or inventare una scusa (to make up an excuse) to give the reason. Literally "in order to be late," but in these contexts it means "for being late."
target_language_example: Mi sono scusato per essere in ritardo al lavoro.
native_language_example: I apologized for being late to work.

additional_notes: Used after a main clause to say the goal/purpose of an action: e.g., "...per fare soldi" = "...to make money." Often interchangeable with "per" + infinitive (per comprare, per parlare, per aiutare). Note: don’t confuse it with "stare per" (e.g., "stiamo per fare"), which means "to be about to do"—that’s a different structure.
target_language_example: Studio italiano per fare pratica ogni giorno.
native_language_example: I study Italian to practice every day.

meaning: to do anything; to do whatever (is needed).
additional_notes: Used after adjectives/expressions like "troppo + adjective" (e.g., "troppo spaventato/a") to mean "to do anything". It can also express that something is necessary in order to do anything (e.g., needing money to be able to do things in general). "Qualsiasi cosa" = "anything/whatever" and the subject (spaventato/spaventata) changes to match the speaker.
target_language_example: Mi serve una macchina per fare qualsiasi cosa in questa città.
native_language_example: I need a car to do anything in this city.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like uscire/andare fuori/essere fuori to say you go out (or are out) with the purpose of taking a walk. Literally “in order to do a walk,” but in natural English it’s usually “to go for a walk.” You can add where: per fare una passeggiata al parco / sulla spiaggia.
target_language_example: Sono uscito per fare una passeggiata al parco.
native_language_example: I went out to go for a walk in the park.

meaning: "to do it" / "in order to do it".
additional_notes: Used after another verb to say the purpose or reason for doing something: *per* + infinitive. *Farlo* = *fare* (to do/make) + *lo* (“it”). In some contexts it can simply mean “to do it” (without strong emphasis on purpose), especially after expressions like *sto per...* (“I’m about to...”).
target_language_example: Non ho tempo per farlo oggi.
native_language_example: I don’t have time to do it today.

additional_notes: Used to make a request more polite. It can go at the end of a sentence (Mi aiuti, per favore?) or at the beginning (Per favore, ascoltami). In urgent or emotional situations it can sound like a strong plea: Per favore!
target_language_example: Può ripetere, per favore?
native_language_example: Could you repeat, please?

additional_notes:
Used to politely ask someone to call you (on the phone) or to address you by a certain name. 
- chiamami = “call me” (imperative + mi = “me”).
- If followed by a name/title ("chiamami Joe"), it means “call me Joe” (how to address you).
- If followed by a time ("più tardi", "questa sera") or a clause ("quando arrivi"), it means “call me later/this evening/when you arrive.”
target_language_example: Per favore, chiamami domani mattina.
native_language_example: Please call me tomorrow morning.

meaning: "please, give me" (asking someone to hand you something).
additional_notes: Used to make a polite request. "Dammi" is the informal (tu) command form of "dare" (to give), so it’s for friends, family, kids, or peers. With strangers or in formal situations, use "Per favore, mi dia..." or "Mi può dare...". Often followed by a noun ("il menù") or by "qualcosa da..." ("qualcosa da bere").
target_language_example: Per favore, dammi una bottiglia d’acqua.
native_language_example: Please, give me a bottle of water.

meaning: "please, give me" / "please, give us" (polite request to more than one person, or formal).
additional_notes: "Per favore" means "please." "Datemi" is the imperative of "dare" (to give) with "-mi" = "to me"; it can also mean "to us" in contexts like ordering for a group. It’s used to ask for something in shops/restaurants, or more figuratively (e.g., "datemi la vostra attenzione" = "give me your attention"). Often addressed to multiple people ("you all") or used as a polite/formal "you" (Lei), especially with staff.
target_language_example: Per favore, datemi due caffè e un cornetto.
native_language_example: Please, give me two coffees and a croissant.

meaning: "Please, tell (someone)…" (addressing you plural or a group).
additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to pass on a message: "Per favore, dite a Maria di…" = “Please tell Maria to…”. "Dite" is the imperative of "dire" for "voi" (you plural), so it’s used when speaking to more than one person (or sometimes as a polite form in some contexts). The person being told is introduced with "a" (or its combined forms: "al", "alla", "allo", etc.).
target_language_example: Per favore, dite al direttore che arrivo tra dieci minuti.
native_language_example: Please tell the manager/director that I’ll arrive in ten minutes.

additional_notes: "Per favore" means "please" and can go at the beginning, middle, or end of the sentence. "La" is a direct-object pronoun that typically comes before the verb (La chiami = call her/it; La spieghi = explain it). In polite/formal commands, you may also see "La" (often written with a capital L) meaning "you" (formal), e.g. "La smetta..." = "Please stop...".
target_language_example: Per favore, la chiami domani.
native_language_example: Please call her tomorrow.

meaning: “Please, could you … for me?” (polite request using “mi” = “to me/for me”).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a polite request when the action is directed to you or done for you. “Mi” is an indirect object pronoun (“to me/for me”) and commonly goes with verbs like comprare (buy), consigliare (advise), far sapere (let [someone] know), rispondere (reply), scrivere (write), spiegare (explain). In formal polite requests you often see the subjunctive/imperative forms like “mi compri / mi spieghi / mi faccia sapere”.
target_language_example: Per favore, mi può aiutare con questo esercizio?
native_language_example: Please, can you help me with this exercise?

additional_notes: Used to ask for something politely, especially in shops, restaurants, or when speaking to someone you don’t know well. "Mi dia" is the formal command form of "dare" (Lei form). You can follow it with an item: "mi dia un/una…", "mi dia del/della…", "mi dia due…".
target_language_example: Per favore, mi dia un biglietto per Roma.
native_language_example: Please, give me a ticket to Rome.

meaning: “please, don’t …” (a polite request not to do something).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to politely ask someone to avoid an action: “Per favore, non + verb.” The verb is in the imperative (e.g., non aggiungere/non aggiungete) or another form addressed to the person (e.g., non ti dimenticare / non vi dimenticate). In writing, a comma after “per favore” is common but optional.
target_language_example: Per favore, non parlare così forte.
native_language_example: Please, don’t speak so loudly.

additional_notes: This is just “per favore” repeated for emphasis, often to sound more pleading, emotional, or urgent (begging someone to do/stop something). Common in speech and informal writing; in more formal contexts you’d usually say “per favore” once.
target_language_example: Per favore, per favore, non andare via.
native_language_example: Please, please, don’t go away.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to bring something to you (portami + [noun]) or to take you to a person/place (portami da + [person], portami a + [place]). “Portami” is the informal (tu) command form of “portare” with the pronoun “mi” (= to me).
target_language_example: Per favore, portami un bicchiere d’acqua.
native_language_example: Please, bring me a glass of water.

meaning: "please, (formal) you…" — a polite way to give a request/instruction.
additional_notes: Used when speaking politely/formally to one person (Lei). It’s often followed by the formal command form (imperative) like: si fermi (stop), si sbrighi (hurry up), si ricordi (remember), si assicuri (make sure). In writing you may see "sì" (yes) with an accent, but here "si" is the pronoun meaning “yourself/you” in these formal commands.
target_language_example: Per favore, si accomodi.
native_language_example: Please, have a seat.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask or tell someone to come, using the formal “Lei” command form of venire: (Lei) venga. Common with invitations/requests like “venga con noi” (come with us) or with time expressions like “venga lunedì/tra tre giorni” (come on Monday/in three days). In informal speech to friends you’d usually say “per favore, vieni”.
target_language_example: Per favore, venga un attimo qui.
native_language_example: Please, come here for a moment.

meaning: "Please, come" (talking to more than one person, or using polite you).
additional_notes: "Per favore" means "please". "Venite" is the "you (plural)" command form of "venire" (to come), and it’s also used as a polite command in formal situations (like speaking to customers). It can be followed by places ("venite nel mio ufficio" = come into my office) or by a phrase describing how to come/dress ("venite vestite bene" = please come dressed well).
target_language_example: Per favore, venite qui un momento.
native_language_example: Please, come here for a moment.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone (one person) to come somewhere or come at a certain time. "Vieni" is the informal (tu) imperative of "venire" (to come); for a more formal/polite request to one person, you can use "Per favore, venga." You can add details like "con noi" (with us), a day/time ("domani", "lunedì prossimo"), or even how to come/arrive (e.g., "vestito bene" = dressed nicely).
target_language_example: Per favore, vieni qui un attimo.
native_language_example: Please, come here for a moment.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a positive outcome or relief, often contrasting with what could have gone wrong. Common at the start of a sentence (often followed by a comma) or before the verb. You can also say “per fortuna che ...” (“luckily that ...”).
target_language_example: Per fortuna abbiamo trovato un taxi subito.
native_language_example: Luckily we found a taxi right away.

meaning: (do/like/have to) no matter what; necessarily; by force.
additional_notes: Used to express obligation/inevitability (“have to”, “necessarily”) or that something happens in a forced way (“by force”). Very common with negatives: “non … per forza” = “not necessarily / doesn’t have to”.
target_language_example: Non devi venire per forza stasera.
native_language_example: You don’t necessarily have to come tonight.

meaning: just for fun; as a game (not seriously).
additional_notes: Used to say something is done playfully or without serious intent. Often appears with "solo" ("solo per gioco" = "only/just for fun").
target_language_example: Era solo per gioco: non volevo offenderti.
native_language_example: It was just for fun—I didn’t mean to offend you.

additional_notes: Combination of the preposition "per" (for) + the plural masculine article "i" (the). It’s used to say something is intended for, aimed at, or applies to a group: "per i turisti" = "for the tourists". Also common in pricing/context: "un prezzo diverso per i turisti" = "a different price for the tourists".
target_language_example: Ho preparato dei panini per i bambini.
native_language_example: I made some sandwiches for the kids.

additional_notes: Used to say something is intended for children or affects them. Common with gifts and activities (e.g., "caramelle per i bambini" = candy for the kids), suitability ("adatto per i bambini" = suitable for children), or risk/impact ("pericoloso per i bambini" = dangerous for children). Can also be used alone as a short answer to explain who something is for.
target_language_example: Ho preso dei giochi per i bambini.
native_language_example: I got some toys for the kids.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to say something is intended for you/your purposes: *per i miei gusti* (for my taste), *per i miei bambini* (for my children), *per i miei bisogni* (for my needs), *per i miei affari* (for my business), *per i miei scopi* (for my goals). *I miei* is the masculine plural form of the possessive “my” (with an implied noun if used alone: *i miei* = my family/relatives/people, depending on context).
target_language_example: Questo ristorante è troppo caro per i miei gusti.
native_language_example: This restaurant is too expensive for my taste.

additional_notes: Literally “for the money.” With verbs like dipendere (“to depend”) it often means “for money/financially” (e.g., “depend on someone for money”). With preoccuparsi (“to worry”) it means “about money.”
target_language_example: Non lo faccio per i soldi; lo faccio perché mi piace.
native_language_example: I’m not doing it for the money; I’m doing it because I like it.

additional_notes: Used with plural masculine nouns to mean “for its … / for his … / for their …” depending on context. Very common after expressions like “essere famoso per …” (to be famous for …) or “essere rispettato per …” (to be respected for …). If the noun is feminine plural, use “per le sue” (e.g., per le sue idee).
target_language_example: Questo ristorante è conosciuto per i suoi piatti di pesce.
native_language_example: This restaurant is known for its seafood dishes.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like "incolpare" (to blame) and "pagare" (to pay/suffer the consequences) to say someone is blamed or suffers because of his own mistakes. "Suoi" agrees with the thing possessed ("errori" = masculine plural), not the possessor. Swap the possessive to match the person: "per i miei/tuoi/suoi/nostri/vostri/loro errori".
target_language_example: Non incolparmi per i suoi errori.
native_language_example: Don’t blame me for his mistakes.

additional_notes: "Per" means "for" (also "to"/"in order to" in some contexts). "Il" is "the" (masculine singular). Together, "per il" is used before a masculine singular noun: per il weekend (for the weekend), per il soggiorno (for the living room), per il festival (for the festival). In polite phrases it can introduce the reason/apology or thanks: "Grazie per il tuo aiuto" / "Mi scusi per il disturbo." Often contracts to "pel" in older/literary Italian, but in modern everyday Italian you normally use "per il."
target_language_example: Grazie per il consiglio!
native_language_example: Thanks for the advice!

additional_notes: Used to say something is intended for or related to a specific concert (e.g., buying tickets, rehearsing, getting ready). Often follows a noun like "i biglietti" (the tickets) or verbs like "fare le prove" (to rehearse).
target_language_example: Ho comprato due biglietti per il concerto di stasera.
native_language_example: I bought two tickets for tonight’s concert.

meaning: (vulgar) “to make fun of / to mess with (someone)”; “to pull (someone’s) leg.”
additional_notes: Used mainly in the expression **prendere qualcuno per il culo** (“to take someone for an idiot / to mock them”). It’s common in spoken Italian but **very rude/vulgar**, so avoid in polite situations. Often said as a question to show disbelief or annoyance: **Mi stai prendendo per il culo?**
target_language_example: Dai, mi stai prendendo per il culo?
native_language_example: Come on, are you messing with me?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a reason or cause, usually followed by a clause with **che**: *per il fatto che + (subject) + verb*. It’s more formal/heavier than **perché** and is common with feelings or reactions: *essere a disagio / essere furioso per il fatto che...*. It can also be used alone in a question to mean “Because (of the fact that)?” expressing doubt or asking for the reason.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace per il fatto che non posso venire.
native_language_example: I'm sorry that I can't come.

additional_notes: Used with per + il + lavoro to say something is for work (the reason/purpose) or for the job (suitable/needed for a particular role). Often appears with adjectives like perfetto/a (perfect for the job) or with being late: in ritardo per il lavoro (late for work).
target_language_example: Mi serve un computer affidabile per il lavoro.
native_language_example: I need a reliable computer for work.

meaning: for the best; in the best possible way.
additional_notes: Common with verbs like sperare (“to hope”) and expressions like tutto va/è andato per il meglio (“everything is going/is going to be/turned out for the best”). Often implies you don’t fully control the outcome, but you hope it will end well.
target_language_example: Non possiamo fare molto: speriamo per il meglio.
native_language_example: We can’t do much: let’s hope for the best.

meaning: 'for my' (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say the reason, cause, or responsibility: e.g., apologizing or getting credit/blame for something. Grammar note: it must match the noun that follows. Masculine singular: per il mio lavoro. Feminine singular: per la mia idea. Masculine plural: per i miei amici. Feminine plural: per le mie amiche.
target_language_example: Grazie per il mio regalo!
native_language_example: Thanks for my gift!

additional_notes: Used to say something is given, done, or happens in connection with your birthday (often a gift or a phone call). It commonly follows verbs like "regalare" (to give as a gift), "ricevere" (to receive), "portare" (to bring), or "chiamare" (to call).
target_language_example: Mi hai fatto una festa sorpresa per il mio compleanno.
native_language_example: You threw me a surprise party for my birthday.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true/valid temporarily, but may change later. Common in short replies: “Per il momento no.” You can place it at the beginning or end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Per il momento resto qui, poi vediamo.
native_language_example: For now I’m staying here, then we’ll see.

additional_notes: Used to express purpose or destination: something is done/kept “for our …”. It must agree with the noun that follows: per il nostro esame (masc. sing.), per la nostra casa (fem. sing.), per i nostri amici (masc. plural), per le nostre cose (fem. plural). Often the noun comes right after it.
target_language_example: Ho preparato un riassunto per il nostro progetto.
native_language_example: I prepared a summary for our project.

meaning: 'for the gift' (as in thanking someone for it).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like ringraziare/dir(e) grazie to say what you’re thanking someone for. Often appears in phrases like “Grazie per il regalo” or “Ti ringrazio per il regalo.”
target_language_example: Ti ringrazio per il regalo, è bellissimo!
native_language_example: Thank you for the gift, it’s beautiful!

meaning: for the rest; otherwise / apart from that.
additional_notes: Common in two main uses: (1) with a noun to mean “for the rest of …”: per il resto della vita (= for the rest of your life), per il resto dei tuoi giorni (= for the rest of your days). (2) alone or set off by commas to mean “otherwise / apart from that / as for the rest,” often to contrast one point with everything else: “Ma per il resto, …”.
target_language_example: Per il resto, va tutto bene.
native_language_example: Otherwise, everything is fine.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the remaining part of a period of time. It’s followed by a feminine singular noun phrase (e.g., vita, serata, settimana). With masculine nouns, you use: "per il resto del" (e.g., per il resto del giorno).
target_language_example: Resterò qui per il resto della giornata.
native_language_example: I’ll stay here for the rest of the day.

meaning: "for his/her/its" (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with a possessive (suo = his/her/its) after a preposition: per il suo + noun. It refers back to the subject or to someone already understood from context. Changes with gender/number: per la sua (fem. sing.), per i suoi (masc. plural), per le sue (fem. plural).
target_language_example: L'ho ringraziato per il suo aiuto.
native_language_example: I thanked him for his help.

meaning: for your help / for his (or her) help.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like ringraziare (“to thank”) or essere grato/a (“to be grateful”) to say what you are thanking someone for. "Suo" is a formal "your" (to one person, with Lei) or can mean “his/her/its” depending on context; "il" may change with the noun (e.g., per la sua pazienza).
target_language_example: Grazie per il suo aiuto, signora.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help, ma’am.

additional_notes: Used with gifts or plans made for someone’s birthday. "suo" agrees with the person who has the birthday (his or her), not with the gift. You can change it to match the person: "per il mio compleanno" (for my birthday), "per il tuo compleanno" (for your birthday), "per il loro compleanno" (for their birthday).
target_language_example: Che cosa hai comprato per il suo compleanno?
native_language_example: What did you buy for his/her birthday?

additional_notes: Used to say what something relates to (e.g., an explanation) or what you feel sorry about. "Suo" can mean "his" or "her" depending on context. Often appears with verbs like "dare una spiegazione" (to give an explanation) and "essere dispiaciuto/a" (to be sorry).
target_language_example: Sono davvero dispiaciuto per il suo errore.
native_language_example: I’m really sorry about his/her mistake.

additional_notes: Used to indicate purpose/recipient ("a gift for your birthday") or cause ("if it hadn’t been for your courage"). It must agree with the noun that follows: masculine singular = "per il tuo" (per il tuo compleanno / per il tuo futuro). Feminine singular: "per la tua"; masculine plural: "per i tuoi"; feminine plural: "per le tue".
target_language_example: Ho comprato un regalo per il tuo fratello.
native_language_example: I bought a gift for your brother.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like ringraziare (to thank) or essere grato/a (to be grateful) to say what you’re thanking someone for. It agrees with the informal singular "tu" (your). In the examples, "grati" is masculine/mixed plural and "grate" is feminine plural; both mean "grateful."
target_language_example: Grazie per il tuo aiuto!
native_language_example: Thanks for your help!

meaning: for your own good; in your best interest.
additional_notes: Used to say you’re doing/saying something because you believe it will help the other person, even if they may not like it. Often said as advice or a warning, and it can sound caring or controlling depending on tone and context. You can change the possessive: per il mio bene (for my own good), per il suo bene (for his/her own good), per il nostro bene (for our own good).
target_language_example: Fidati di me: lo faccio per il tuo bene.
native_language_example: Trust me: I’m doing it for your own good.

additional_notes: Used to say something is intended as a birthday wish, gift, plan, or action. Often follows words like auguri (best wishes), regalo (gift), prendere (to get/buy), dare (to give), fare (to do).
target_language_example: Ho comprato un regalo per il tuo compleanno.
native_language_example: I bought a gift for your birthday.

additional_notes: Used to say something is intended/needed for an upcoming trip (packing, preparations, being ready). Often with verbs like preparare (to prepare), finire i preparativi (to finish the preparations), essere pronto/pronta (to be ready). Can also be used with adjectives to express how you feel about traveling, e.g., Sono morta per il viaggio! = “I’m exhausted from (all the) trip/travel.”
target_language_example: Ho comprato un adattatore per il viaggio.
native_language_example: I bought an adapter for the trip.

additional_notes: Used when addressing more than one person (your = "vostro") or when using polite/formal address (e.g., in formal writing). It often introduces what something is intended for (per il vostro esame = for your exam) or indicates benefit/purpose (per il vostro vantaggio = to your advantage). The noun that follows is typically masculine singular (il vostro + noun); for feminine singular you’d use "per la vostra" (e.g., per la vostra famiglia).
target_language_example: Ho preparato un regalo per il vostro bambino.
native_language_example: I prepared a gift for your child.

additional_notes: Used after thanks or expressions of gratitude/appreciation (e.g., "Grazie..." / "Siamo grati...") to specify what you are thanking someone for. "Vostro" is formal (to one person: "per il Suo aiuto") or plural (to multiple people: "per il vostro aiuto").
target_language_example: Grazie per il vostro aiuto, è stato davvero prezioso.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help; it was really valuable.

meaning: to learn Berber / in order to learn Berber.
additional_notes: Uses **per + infinitive** to express purpose (“in order to…”). **Imparare** = “to learn.” **Il berbero** refers to the Berber language (Tamazight); you can replace it with another language (e.g., *per imparare l’italiano*).
target_language_example: Sto seguendo un corso online per imparare il berbero.
native_language_example: I’m taking an online course to learn Berber.

additional_notes: Used to say something is whole/complete (not partial). Common with payments and amounts (pagare per intero = pay in full) and with time or duration (per intero = for the whole time). It often follows the noun or verb it refers to.
target_language_example: Preferisco pagare l'importo per intero.
native_language_example: I prefer to pay the amount in full.

additional_notes: Used to express purpose, benefit, reason, or thanks: per la nazione (for the nation), per la pittura (for painting), per la settimana prossima (for next week), grata per la gentilezza (grateful for the kindness). It can also appear in a formal relative phrase: per la quale = "for which" (feminine singular).
target_language_example: Grazie per la tua pazienza.
native_language_example: Thanks for your patience.

additional_notes: Used to say something is intended for dinner (food, plans) or that someone is ready/late for dinner. With people it often pairs with essere pronto/a (“to be ready”) or essere in ritardo (“to be late”). It refers to dinner in general, or a specific dinner everyone knows about from context.
target_language_example: Ho comprato una bottiglia di vino per la cena.
native_language_example: I bought a bottle of wine for dinner.

additional_notes: Uses **per** to say something is intended for, bought for, or done in preparation for a party or celebration: *comprare/preparare/spendere/vestirsi/noleggiare* **per la festa**. You can also specify which party: **per la festa di Halloween / di stasera**. In *Mi dispiace per la festa*, it can mean “I’m sorry about the party” (e.g., something went wrong) depending on context.
target_language_example: Ho preso delle bibite per la festa di domani.
native_language_example: I got some drinks for tomorrow’s party.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true during most of a time period or for most of a quantity. It’s often followed by a noun with an article/possessive (e.g., della giornata, della sua vita). You can also see: “per la maggior parte del” (masculine singular) and “per la maggior parte dei/degli/delle” (plural).
target_language_example: Sono rimasto a casa per la maggior parte della settimana.
native_language_example: I stayed home for most of the week.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to mean “for my …”. Common with things like la mia gente (my people), la mia lezione (my lesson), la mia reazione (my reaction), la mia salute (my health), la mia malinconia (my sadness), la mia vacanza (my vacation). The noun can be explicit or understood from context (e.g., “per la mia” meaning “for mine”/“for my [thing]”).
target_language_example: Grazie per la mia prenotazione.
native_language_example: Thank you for my reservation.

meaning: "For goodness’ sake!" / "Damn it!" (an exclamation of annoyance or frustration).
additional_notes: Used as a strong interjection when you’re irritated, surprised, or exasperated. It can stand alone ("Per la miseria!") or be followed by a name or by what you’re complaining about. It’s fairly informal and can sound like swearing, so use with care in polite situations.
target_language_example: Per la miseria, smettila di urlare!
native_language_example: For goodness’ sake, stop shouting!

meaning: for music; (having) an ear/talent for music.
additional_notes: Uses "per" to mean "for" in different senses, depending on context. Common with abilities or preferences (e.g., "avere orecchio per la musica" = to have an ear for music), and also with gratitude or appreciation ("grati/e per la musica" = grateful for the music). "La" can be generic, meaning music in general.
target_language_example: Mio fratello ha una vera passione per la musica.
native_language_example: My brother has a real passion for music.

additional_notes: Used to say something is directed toward or intended for something that belongs to “us,” followed by a feminine singular noun (e.g., *la nostra professoressa*, *la nostra casa*). *Nostra* agrees with the noun: feminine singular (*la nostra*), masculine singular (*il nostro*), feminine plural (*le nostre*), masculine plural (*i nostri*).
target_language_example: Ho comprato dei fiori per la nostra mamma.
native_language_example: I bought some flowers for our mom.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens on the first occasion (never before). Often placed at the end of the sentence or near the verb: "venne per la prima volta", "la incontrai per la prima volta".
target_language_example: Oggi guido in autostrada per la prima volta.
native_language_example: Today I’m driving on the highway for the first time.

meaning: for school (e.g., for school-related needs; to go/prepare for school).
additional_notes: Uses per (“for”) + la scuola (“school”). Common with verbs like prepararsi (“to get ready”) and essere pronto/a (“to be ready”) to mean “getting ready to go to school,” and with servire (“to be needed”) to mean something is needed for school. Agreement: pronto (m. sing.), pronta (f. sing.), pronti (m./mixed pl.), pronte (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Ho comprato un quaderno per la scuola.
native_language_example: I bought a notebook for school.

additional_notes: Used to indicate the recipient/beneficiary: *per* = “for”, and *la sua* = “his/her” agreeing with a feminine singular noun (e.g., *la sua bambina*, *la sua amica*). Often, Italian drops possessive articles in some family contexts (e.g., *mia madre*), but with other nouns you commonly use the article: *la sua…*.
target_language_example: Ho comprato dei fiori per la sua mamma.
native_language_example: I bought some flowers for his/her mom.

meaning: for his/her age; considering his/her age.
additional_notes: Used to compare someone’s appearance, height, health, etc. with what you would normally expect at that age (often meaning “surprisingly” young/tall/healthy, etc.). It agrees with the person: per la sua età (his/her), per la mia età (my), per la tua età (your), per la loro età (their).
target_language_example: È molto energica per la sua età.
native_language_example: She’s very energetic for her age.

meaning: for his/her rudeness; because of his/her bad manners.
additional_notes: Used with **per** to give the reason/cause: **arrabbiato/a per...** (“angry about/because of...”) or **scusarsi per...** (“to apologize for...”). **la sua** means “his/her/its” (you need context to know whose). **maleducazione** is “rudeness/bad manners” (not “education”).
target_language_example: Mi scuso per la sua maleducazione: non voleva essere scortese.
native_language_example: I apologize for his rudeness: he didn’t mean to be rude.

meaning: for his/her health; about his/her health (often: worried/concerned).
additional_notes: Literally “for his/her health.” Used either to say something is good/bad for someone’s health (è dannoso/terribile per la sua salute) or to express concern/worry about someone’s health (essere in ansia per la sua salute). "Sua" agrees with the person’s health (salute), not with the person; it can mean “his” or “her.”
target_language_example: Sto cercando di mangiare meglio per la sua salute.
native_language_example: I’m trying to eat better for his/her health.

meaning: for his/her safety; for his/her security.
additional_notes: Used to say an action or a worry is motivated by someone’s safety (e.g., moving somewhere, taking precautions, being anxious/concerned). "Sua" agrees with the thing owned (here, "sicurezza"), not the person, so it can mean either "his" or "her"; you choose based on context. You can also change the possessive: "per la mia/tua/nostra sicurezza" = for my/your/our safety.
target_language_example: Per la sua sicurezza, è meglio che resti qui stanotte.
native_language_example: For his/her safety, it’s better that he/she stays here tonight.

meaning: for his old age; for when he is old (for retirement).
additional_notes: Used to express saving or preparing for the time in life when someone is elderly (often linked to retirement). Literally "for his old age"; you can change the possessive: per la mia/tua/sua/nostra/vostra/loro vecchiaia.
target_language_example: Metto da un po' di soldi per la mia vecchiaia.
native_language_example: I set aside some money for my old age (for retirement).

meaning: in your head / on your mind; (with "passare") to cross your mind.
additional_notes:
Commonly used with verbs like:
- "passare per la testa" = “to cross someone’s mind” (often in questions: "Ma cosa ti passa per la testa?" = “What are you thinking?!”)
- "avere (qualcosa) per la testa" = “to have (something) on your mind,” often meaning you’re distracted or thinking about other things.
Also used in negatives: "Non mi è mai passato per la testa" = “It never crossed my mind.”
target_language_example: Non mi passa per la testa di mollare adesso.
native_language_example: It doesn’t cross my mind to give up now.

meaning: 'for your' (with a feminine singular noun); sometimes 'because of your'.
additional_notes: Made of per (“for / because of”) + la tua (“your”, feminine singular). Use it before a feminine singular noun: per la tua mamma (for your mom), per la tua gentilezza (for your kindness). With per it can express either purpose/support (“be strong for your mom”) or cause/reason (“angry because of your rudeness”).
target_language_example: Sono felice per la tua vittoria.
native_language_example: I'm happy for your victory.

additional_notes: Used to say something affects someone’s health (positively or negatively), or to express concern about someone’s health. Often follows adjectives like "buono" (good) or "dannoso" (harmful): "è buono/dannoso per la tua salute."
target_language_example: È importante dormire abbastanza per la tua salute.
native_language_example: It’s important to sleep enough for your health.

meaning: 'for your' (formal/plural), with a feminine singular noun.
additional_notes: Used with the polite/plural possessive "vostro": "vostra" agrees with a feminine singular noun (e.g., salute, amicizia, maleducazione). Often follows expressions like "grazie" / "ringrazio" (thanks for) or adjectives like "arrabbiato" (angry about/at). The full structure is typically "per la vostra + [noun]".
target_language_example: Grazie per la vostra pazienza.
native_language_example: Thank you for your patience.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun: **per** (“for”) + **le** (“the”, feminine plural). It can express purpose/recipient ("for") or what something is intended for. Examples: *per le chiamate* (for calls), *per le coppie* (for couples), *per le traduzioni* (for translations).
target_language_example: Ho comprato dei fiori per le ragazze.
native_language_example: I bought some flowers for the girls.

meaning: (to) drag on; (to) take longer than expected.
additional_notes: Used when something lasts too long or is being prolonged. Very common with verbs like **andare** (“andare per le lunghe” = to run long) and **tirare** (“tirarla per le lunghe” = to drag it out/draw it out).
target_language_example: La riunione sta andando per le lunghe, possiamo finire tra dieci minuti?
native_language_example: The meeting is dragging on—can we finish in ten minutes?

meaning: on/along the stairs; up/down the stairs.
additional_notes: Used with movement verbs to say something happens on the staircase or by using the stairs (e.g., salire/scendere per le scale = go up/down the stairs; cadere per le scale = fall down the stairs). Often paired with “su” to mean “up the stairs” (su per le scale!).
target_language_example: Siamo scesi per le scale perché l’ascensore non funzionava.
native_language_example: We went down the stairs because the elevator wasn’t working.

meaning: 'for her/its (feminine plural)' (referring to things that belong to someone).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun: per + le + sue + noun. "Sue" agrees with the noun (feminine plural), not with the owner. Depending on context, "sue" can mean her/its/their/your (formal) + feminine plural noun (e.g., "le sue scarpe" = her shoes; "le sue cascate" = its waterfalls). Common with reasons/causes too: "scusarsi per le sue azioni" (apologize for her actions).
target_language_example: Ha ringraziato tutti per le sue parole gentili.
native_language_example: She thanked everyone for her kind words.

additional_notes: Used to say what you do or where you go during a holiday/vacation period. Often followed by a specific holiday: "per le vacanze di Natale" (for the Christmas holidays). You can also use it in questions like "Dove vai per le vacanze?" (Where are you going for vacation?).
target_language_example: Quest’estate andiamo in Puglia per le vacanze.
native_language_example: This summer we’re going to Puglia for vacation.

meaning: for her; for you (formal, feminine); about her (with some verbs).
additional_notes: “Lei” is the formal “you” in Italian (used with strangers, customers, officials). So “per lei” can mean “for you, ma’am” as well as “for her,” depending on context and capitalization in writing. Common uses: doing something on someone’s behalf (“Ho lucidato le sue scarpe per lei.”), intended recipient/benefit (“Mary spera che Tom lo farà per lei.”), or with certain expressions meaning “about her”/“concerning her,” e.g. “mi dispiace per lei” = “I feel sorry for her/you (formal).” “Garantire per lei” means “to vouch for her/you (formal).”
target_language_example: Ho prenotato un taxi per lei, signora.
native_language_example: I booked a taxi for you, ma’am.

meaning: 'for them' (for their benefit / directed to them).
additional_notes: Used with "per" + the stressed pronoun "loro" to talk about doing something for someone, working for someone, being worried about someone, or addressing/sending something to someone. It can mean either 'for their benefit' (Ho fatto questo per loro) or 'intended for them' (un messaggio per loro).
target_language_example: Ho comprato dei biglietti per loro.
native_language_example: I bought some tickets for them.

meaning: for him; (with verbs like "votare") for him (= in support of him).
additional_notes: "Per" + "lui" (stressed pronoun) is used to say something is intended for, done for the benefit of, or because of a man/boy ("for him"). It can also mean "as far as he is concerned" (e.g., "Per lui è facile" = "For him, it’s easy") and with "votare" it means voting in support of someone ("Ha votato per lui" = "He voted for him").
target_language_example: Ho preparato la cena per lui.
native_language_example: I made dinner for him.

meaning: “at the hands of; by (someone)” (often in passive statements).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the person responsible for an action, especially in formal or dramatic contexts (e.g., something happens, is destroyed, or someone is killed “at the hands of” someone). It often appears with passive forms like "fu/è stato" (was/has been).
target_language_example: Il castello fu distrutto per mano del nemico.
native_language_example: The castle was destroyed at the hands of the enemy.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something done for your benefit (Puoi farlo per me? = Can you do it for me?) or something directed toward you (È preoccupata per me = She’s worried about me). It also appears in some common expressions like tenere per me (to keep to myself) and can introduce an opinion: Per me, ... (As for me / In my opinion, ...).
target_language_example: Riesci a chiamare un taxi per me?
native_language_example: Can you call a taxi for me?

meaning: “for me, it is…” / “to me, it is…”.
additional_notes: Used to give your personal opinion, judgment, or perspective about something (“in my view”). It’s often followed by an adjective or description: Per me è diverso/innocente/importante. It can also appear inside a longer sentence (e.g., “che per me è…” = “which, for me, is…”). Not the same as “il tuo amore per me è…” (“your love for me is…”), where “per me” means “for me” (the recipient).
target_language_example: Per me è un buon ristorante, ma è un po' caro.
native_language_example: For me, it’s a good restaurant, but it’s a bit expensive.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens using a tool, method, or intermediary. Common in formal/written Italian; in everyday speech you often hear alternatives like "con" (with) or "tramite" (via/through).
target_language_example: Ti contatteremo per mezzo di e-mail.
native_language_example: We’ll contact you by email.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "per" to show who something is intended for (a gift, medicine, a cake) or a dedication/toast. With singular family members in Italian, you often use the possessive without an article: "mio padre" (not *"il mio padre"* in most everyday contexts). You may also see it in formal identifications: "Per mio padre, [Name]" = "For my father, [Name]" (e.g., on a dedication or document).
target_language_example: Ho comprato un regalo per mio padre.
native_language_example: I bought a gift for my father.

meaning: for many years; for a long time.
additional_notes: Used to say how long something lasted in the past or up to the present. It often follows the verb or comes at the end of the sentence. Similar idea to "per molto tempo" (for a long time).
target_language_example: Ho studiato italiano per molti anni.
native_language_example: I studied Italian for many years.

additional_notes: Used to say that something lasts/d lasted a long period. Often placed after the verb or at the end of the sentence. As a question ("Per molto tempo?") it means "For a long time?" to confirm or show surprise.
target_language_example: Ho aspettato per molto tempo, ma non è arrivato nessuno.
native_language_example: I waited for a long time, but nobody arrived.

meaning: not at all; for nothing / in vain.
additional_notes: Often used with a negative to mean “not at all” (Non mi piace per niente. = I don’t like it at all.). It can also mean “for nothing / in vain,” especially about doing something with no result or purpose (Siamo venuti per niente. = We came for nothing.). As a standalone answer, “Per niente.” means “Not at all.” / “You’re welcome.” Depending on context, “Non per niente...” can mean “It’s no coincidence that...” / “No wonder...”
target_language_example: Ho aspettato un’ora, ma lui non è arrivato: ho perso tempo per niente.
native_language_example: I waited an hour, but he didn’t show up: I wasted my time for nothing.

meaning: 'for us' (to our benefit, for our use, or concerning us).
additional_notes: Used with verbs to say someone does something for your group (a favor, buying something, doing a task): "farlo per noi", "comprarlo per noi". It can also mean "for us" in the sense of "for people like us / in our situation" (e.g., something is difficult for us), or "for us" as support in voting/cheering: "Vota per noi!".
target_language_example: Puoi prenotare un tavolo per noi?
native_language_example: Can you book a table for us?

meaning: just in case; for any eventuality.
additional_notes: Used to say you want to be prepared if something unexpected happens. Common with doing something “extra” (bringing, writing down, preparing) as a precaution. You’ll also hear the shorter variant “per ogni evenienza” without changing the meaning.
target_language_example: Porto una batteria esterna per ogni evenienza.
native_language_example: I bring a power bank just in case.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true only at the present moment, with the idea that it may change later. It can appear at the beginning of the sentence ("Per ora, ...") or at the end ("... per ora").
target_language_example: Per ora va tutto bene, poi vediamo.
native_language_example: For now everything is fine, then we’ll see.

meaning: for hours and hours; for a very long time.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something lasted a long time (often longer than expected). Common with verbs like aspettare (to wait), piovere (to rain), parlare (to talk), camminare (to walk). The repetition "ore e ore" adds emphasis.
target_language_example: Abbiamo parlato per ore e ore al telefono.
native_language_example: We talked on the phone for hours and hours.

meaning: "to talk/speak with" (in order to talk with).
additional_notes: Uses **per + infinitive** to express purpose: *per parlare* = “to/in order to talk.” Add **con + person** for “with [someone].” Often used after verbs of coming/being somewhere (*venire*, *essere qui*) or to explain why you did something.
target_language_example: Sono qui per parlare con il dottore.
native_language_example: I'm here to talk with the doctor.

additional_notes: Used to make a request sound polite; it can come at the beginning or the end of the sentence (e.g., “Per piacere, …” / “…, per piacere.”). In very formal contexts, you may also hear “per favore.”
target_language_example: Puoi parlare più lentamente, per piacere?
native_language_example: Can you speak more slowly, please?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to hand you something or give you something. **Dammi** is the imperative of **dare** (“to give”) + **mi** (“to me”) attached: **da’ + mi = dammi**. Often followed by a noun (e.g., *dammi una penna*) or something abstract (e.g., *dammi la tua attenzione* = “give me your attention”).
target_language_example: Per piacere, dammi il menu.
native_language_example: Please, give me the menu.

meaning: "Please, give me …" (addressing "you" plural or a polite/formal "you").
additional_notes: "Datemi" is the command form of "dare" (to give) for "voi" (you all). It’s used when speaking to more than one person, or as a polite/formal way to address a single person in some contexts (e.g., in customer service). Often followed by what you want: "Per piacere, datemi il menù" / "...due hot dog".
target_language_example: Per piacere, datemi un caffè e un bicchiere d’acqua.
native_language_example: Please, give me a coffee and a glass of water.

meaning: 'Please, (to me)…' used to make a polite request (often with 'mi' + a verb).
additional_notes: Common pattern for polite requests: “Per piacere, mi + verb (Lei form)” = “Please + verb (for me).” Here “mi” is an object pronoun meaning “to me/me,” used with verbs like ascoltare (listen), passare (pass), prestare (lend), perdonare (forgive), richiamare (call back). Often paired with formal “Lei” verb forms (e.g., mi ascolti, mi passi) to be extra polite.
target_language_example: Per piacere, mi può dire dov’è la stazione?
native_language_example: Please, can you tell me where the station is?

meaning: "Please call me" (on the phone / contact me).
additional_notes: Used as a polite request. "Mi chiami" is the polite (Lei) form, like saying “please call me.” For an informal request to a friend (tu), you’d usually say "Per favore, chiamami". It can also be followed by a name (“Call me Joe”) or a time (“this evening/tonight”).
target_language_example: Per piacere, mi chiami domani mattina.
native_language_example: Please call me tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used to make a polite request, especially with strangers, in shops, restaurants, or formal situations. “Mi dia” is the formal (Lei) command form of dare (“to give”). For friends/family you’d usually say “Per favore, dammi …” or “Mi dai …?”. You can add what you want after it: “mi dia un caffè”, “mi dia la borsa”, etc.
target_language_example: Per piacere, mi dia un caffè.
native_language_example: Please, give me a coffee.

meaning: 'please, speak' (polite request to more than one person or to someone you address with 'voi').
additional_notes: "Per piacere" means "please." "Parlate" is the present-tense imperative for "you (plural) speak"; it’s used when talking to a group, or as a polite/formal address to one person in some contexts/regions. It’s often followed by "con ..." (with/to someone) or "in ..." (in a language), and can be modified with adverbs like "più forte" (louder) or "più lentamente" (more slowly).
target_language_example: Per piacere, parlate più lentamente: non capisco bene.
native_language_example: Please, speak more slowly: I don’t understand well.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to bring you something (portatemi un coltello) or to take you somewhere (portatemi da lui). “Portatemi” is the imperative for “voi” (you plural), and it includes “-mi” = “to me”. For one person in the polite form (“Lei”), you’d typically say: “Per piacere, mi porti …”.
target_language_example: Per piacere, portatemi un bicchiere d’acqua.
native_language_example: Please, bring me a glass of water.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to come somewhere, addressing them with Lei (formal “you”). Venga is the formal command form of venire (“to come”). For an informal request to a friend, you’d say: Per favore/piacere, vieni. It can also introduce polite instructions like “come tomorrow” or “come well-dressed” (venga vestito/a bene).
target_language_example: Per piacere, venga qui un momento.
native_language_example: Please, come here for a moment.

additional_notes: Commonly used to say something almost happened, often in the pattern: “Per poco non + verb” (e.g., “Per poco non cadevo” = “I almost fell”). Literally it’s “for little,” but in this usage it means “almost.”
target_language_example: Per poco non perdevo il treno.
native_language_example: I almost missed the train.

meaning: "in order to be able to" (so that someone can).
additional_notes: Used to express purpose: *per* + infinitive *potere* + another infinitive. Often followed by a verb like *fare, andare, studiare*, etc. You can use it with different subjects: *Sono venuto per poter parlare con te* (“I came so I can talk with you”). In everyday speech, *per* + infinitive is also common without *poter* when ability isn’t the focus.
target_language_example: Ho messo la sveglia per poter alzarmi presto.
native_language_example: I set an alarm so I can get up early.

additional_notes: Used to say what you eat/have at lunchtime, or to invite someone to stay for lunch ("Resta per pranzo" = "Stay for lunch"). Often answers questions like "Cosa mangi per pranzo?" (What do you eat for lunch?).
target_language_example: Oggi mangiamo pasta per pranzo.
native_language_example: Today we’re having pasta for lunch.

additional_notes: Used to say what happens first in time or what you should do first in a sequence of actions. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence as an introductory phrase: “Per prima cosa, …” It can also appear later: “Cosa faresti per prima cosa?” = “What would you do first?”
target_language_example: Per prima cosa, devo chiamare il dottore.
native_language_example: First of all, I have to call the doctor.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something before everyone else, often about taking turns (speaking, going, choosing, being served). It can refer to a person ("io/tu/lui per primo") or to order in a sequence ("porterò lui per primo" = "I’ll take him first").
target_language_example: Chi vuole parlare per primo?
native_language_example: Who wants to speak first?

meaning: for a few days; for a couple of days.
additional_notes: Used to say something lasts for a short period of several days (not exact). Common with verbs like restare/rimanere (to stay), stare (to be/stay), fermarsi (to stop/stay), or with actions done over a short span of days.
target_language_example: Resto a Roma per qualche giorno, poi torno a casa.
native_language_example: I’m staying in Rome for a few days, then I’m going home.

meaning: for a few minutes; for a little while (minutes).
additional_notes: Used to say an action or situation lasts a short, not exact amount of time (usually just several minutes). Common in requests ("Puoi aspettare/lasciarci...") and announcements ("sospese per qualche minuto").
target_language_example: Aspetta qui per qualche minuto, per favore.
native_language_example: Wait here for a few minutes, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for something, similar to “perché?” but a bit more formal/explicit. It can be a direct question (Per quale motivo mi hai chiamato?) or part of a longer sentence (Non so per quale motivo...).
target_language_example: Per quale motivo non vuoi venire con noi?
native_language_example: Why don’t you want to come with us?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason something is happening. It’s a more formal/explicit version of "perché?" and is common in careful speech or writing. Often followed by a full sentence (e.g., "Per quale ragione sei qui...?"), and you can swap "qui" and "qua" with no real change in meaning.
target_language_example: Per quale ragione non vuoi venire con noi?
native_language_example: Why don’t you want to come with us?

meaning: as much as; as far as (to the extent that).
additional_notes: Used to express extent/degree, often followed by an adjective or adverb like possibile (as much as possible), riguarda (as far as … is concerned), or ne so (as far as I know). In many cases it introduces a limit or scope: “to the extent possible.”
target_language_example: Cerco di aiutarti per quanto posso.
native_language_example: I try to help you as much as I can.

additional_notes: Used to ask about duration (the length of time something lasts), often with verbs like aspettare (wait), rimanere (stay), essere (be), prendere in prestito (borrow). In questions it’s very common at the start: Per quanto tempo...?
target_language_example: Per quanto tempo resti in Italia?
native_language_example: How long are you staying in Italy?

meaning: "How long were you...?/How long have you been...?"
additional_notes: Used to ask about the duration of a state or stay, followed by a past participle (e.g., sei stato/a, sei rimasto/a, sei restato/a, sei stata innamorata). Choose the ending to match the person’s gender/number: sei stato (male), sei stata (female). Often followed by a place or situation: a Roma, in Giappone, allo zoo, innamorato/a di qualcuno.
target_language_example: Per quanto tempo sei stato in Italia?
native_language_example: How long were you in Italy?

meaning: "How long were you (all)?" / "For how long did you (all) stay...?"
additional_notes: Used to ask about duration with "voi" (you plural) or the polite "Lei" in formal speech (same verb form: siete). It’s usually followed by a past participle (e.g., "siete rimasti/e", "siete stati/e") and/or a place: "Per quanto tempo siete rimasti a Caracas?" The past participle can agree in gender/number: "stati" (mixed/masculine plural) and "state" (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Per quanto tempo siete rimasti in Italia?
native_language_example: How long did you stay in Italy?

meaning: 'how long has/was' (asking the duration of something).
additional_notes: Used to ask about duration. It’s typically followed by a past participle with the auxiliary verb essere (è + stato/a, è rimasto/a, è restato/a, etc.). The past participle often agrees with the subject: è rimasto (he stayed) / è rimasta (she stayed). Often completed with a place or situation: Per quanto tempo è stata via? = How long was she away?
target_language_example: Per quanto tempo è stata in Italia?
native_language_example: How long was she in Italy?

meaning: for how long; for as much/as many as.
additional_notes: Used in questions about duration: "Per quanto (tempo)...?" = "For how long...?" It can also refer to an amount (less common in beginner use): "per quanto" + number/quantity = "for as much/as many as" (e.g., for six or seven months). Often paired with "tempo" (time) or a stated period.
target_language_example: Per quanto tempo resti a Roma?
native_language_example: How long are you staying in Rome?

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic you’re talking about (often followed by a noun or pronoun): per quanto riguarda il lavoro, tua sorella, me, ecc. It’s a fairly formal/neutral connector, common in speech and writing. Often interchangeable with "riguardo a" or "per quanto concerne" (more formal).
target_language_example: Per quanto riguarda la cena, possiamo mangiare alle otto.
native_language_example: As for dinner, we can eat at eight.

meaning: "as far as" (someone knows) / "for what" (e.g., "for what it's worth").
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like "sapere" to limit a statement to the information available: "Per quel che ne so" = "As far as I know." Often appears as "Per quel che ne sappiamo" (as far as we know) or in the fixed expression "Per quel che vale" = "For what it's worth."
target_language_example: Per quel che ne so, oggi il museo è chiuso.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the museum is closed today.

meaning: "for what" / "because of what" (for something that happened or was done).
additional_notes: Used to introduce the reason or cause, usually followed by a clause with **che** (e.g., *per quello che hai detto/fatto*). Common after verbs and expressions about feelings or reactions: *arrabbiarsi per...*, *essere triste/furioso per...*, *incolpare qualcuno per...*, *perdonare qualcuno per...*.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace per quello che ho detto ieri.
native_language_example: I’m sorry for what I said yesterday.

additional_notes:
Used to refer to a specific action someone did, often with the idea of consequences (e.g., being punished, paying, being blamed). The verb changes with the subject: 
- per quello che ho fatto = for what I did
- per quello che hai fatto = for what you did
- per quello che hanno fatto = for what they did
target_language_example: Mi dispiace per quello che ho fatto.
native_language_example: I'm sorry for what I did.

meaning: 'for what you did' / 'for what you have done'.
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a specific action someone did (often something already known in the conversation). Common after verbs expressing feelings or judgments like rispettare (respect), perdonare (forgive), odiare (hate), ringraziare (thank), biasimare (blame). The tense hai fatto is passato prossimo, implying a completed action with relevance now.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace per quello che hai fatto.
native_language_example: I'm sorry for what you did.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to your previous words, often in apologies or when asking if someone is upset. Common with "Mi dispiace" / "Mi scusi" and adjectives like "(essere) arrabbiato". You can change the subject: "per quello che hai detto" (you said), "per quello che abbiamo detto" (we said), "per quello che ha detto" (he/she said).
target_language_example: Non volevo offenderti per quello che ho detto.
native_language_example: I didn’t mean to offend you with what I said.

meaning: for what happened; because of what happened.
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a specific event that has occurred. Often follows expressions of blame, apology, explanations, or consequences (e.g., "I blame myself...", "the lines are busy..."). In speech it can also be shortened to "per quello che è successo" as a standalone answer ("Yes, about what happened"). Note: "successo" here means "happened/occurred," not "success."
target_language_example: Mi dispiace per quello che è successo.
native_language_example: I’m sorry for what happened.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a reason or purpose mentioned or understood from context. It can mean (1) cause: “because of this/for this reason” (Per questo devo essere cauto.) or (2) purpose: “for this/for this purpose” (Sono qui per questo.). Often matches English “that’s why” when it introduces a consequence.
target_language_example: Non abbiamo abbastanza tempo; per questo dobbiamo partire subito.
native_language_example: We don’t have enough time; that’s why we have to leave right away.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the reason or explanation for what was just said. Very common with "è": "(Ed) è per questo che…" = "And that's why…". It can also appear in negative questions: "Non è per questo che…?" = "Isn't that why…?".
target_language_example: È per questo che dobbiamo partire adesso.
native_language_example: That's why we have to leave now.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened unintentionally or due to an error. It commonly goes with verbs like prendere (to take), fare (to do), dire (to say), and can be placed after the verb or near the action it describes (e.g., "Ho preso per sbaglio...", "Per sbaglio ho...", "L'ho fatto per sbaglio").
target_language_example: Scusa, ho chiamato per sbaglio il numero sbagliato.
native_language_example: Sorry, I accidentally called the wrong number.

meaning: for himself; for his own benefit / for himself alone.
additional_notes: Used to say that a man does something for his own benefit or keeps something for himself (not for others). It changes with the person: per se stessa (for herself), per se stessi / per se stesse (for themselves). Often used after verbs like volere (to want), tenere (to keep), fare (to do).
target_language_example: Ha comprato il biglietto per se stesso, non per gli altri.
native_language_example: He bought the ticket for himself, not for the others.

additional_notes: Used to say something lasts without end, or that someone/something is gone permanently. Common in emotional phrases like "Addio per sempre!" and with future/intentions ("Voglio essere con te per sempre").
target_language_example: Non voglio perdere questa foto: la terrò per sempre.
native_language_example: I don’t want to lose this photo: I’ll keep it forever.

meaning: on the street; out in the street (sometimes: homeless).
additional_notes: Often means being/meeting someone outside while walking or passing by (“in the street”). In contexts like vivere/dormire per strada, it means living/sleeping on the street (without a home).
target_language_example: L'ho visto per strada mentre andavo al lavoro.
native_language_example: I saw him on the street while I was going to work.

meaning: 'to study French' / 'in order to study French'.
additional_notes: Uses **per + infinitive** to express purpose (“in order to…”). The verb stays in the infinitive (**studiare**). You can replace **il francese** with another subject: *per studiare l’italiano / per studiare la matematica*.
target_language_example: Ho scaricato un’app per studiare il francese.
native_language_example: I downloaded an app to study French.

additional_notes: Used to say something is intended for one person (a gift, an idea, help, etc.). Often appears with verbs like fare (to do/make) or with è (is) to indicate who something is for: "È per te" = "It’s for you." Uses te (informal singular); for formal singular use "per Lei", and for plural use "per voi".
target_language_example: Questo regalo è per te.
native_language_example: This gift is for you.

meaning: in time; early enough (before it’s too late).
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens with enough time to spare, often to avoid missing a deadline, train, appointment, etc. Common with verbs like arrivare (to arrive), essere (to be), finire (to finish), and in phrases like: “Siamo arrivati per tempo” (We arrived in time/early enough).
target_language_example: Siamo partiti per tempo per non perdere il treno.
native_language_example: We left early enough so we wouldn’t miss the train.

meaning: on the ground; onto the ground.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of putting/throwing to mean “onto the ground” (e.g., gettare/posare per terra). With verbs describing position it means “on the ground” (e.g., stare/steso per terra). In some contexts it implies “on the floor” indoors. Common in set phrases like "dormire per terra" (sleep on the floor/ground) and actions done downward like "sputare per terra" (spit on the ground).
target_language_example: Ho lasciato le chiavi per terra vicino alla porta.
