The thing liked is the subject: "giocare a calcio" (to play soccer) + "piace" (singular, because an activity counts as one thing). You can turn it into a question by raising your intonation: "A te piace...?"
target_language_example: A loro piace giocare a calcio dopo scuola.
native_language_example: They like to play soccer after school.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere: the thing being watched is the grammatical subject. Common patterns: “Mi piace guardare…” = “I like to watch…”, “Ti piace guardare…?” = “Do you like to watch…?”, “A Tom piace guardare…” = “Tom likes to watch…”. You can also use “piace guardare + noun” (e.g., “piace guardare le serie TV”).
target_language_example: A me piace guardare film in italiano con i sottotitoli.
native_language_example: I like watching movies in Italian with subtitles.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere: the thing liked is the subject (guardare la TV), and the person who likes it is introduced with a + pronoun/name (a me, a lui, a Felicja). Example patterns: A me piace guardare la TV. / A loro piace guardare la TV mentre mangiano. With a plural thing liked, use piacciono (e.g., Mi piacciono i film).
target_language_example: A me piace guardare la TV la sera.
native_language_example: I like to watch TV in the evening.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere: the thing liked is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with a + name/pronoun (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli). With il, it refers to a masculine singular noun (piace il gelato). For a plural thing: piacciono i/le; for feminine singular: piace la; with an infinitive: piace + verb (Mi piace nuotare).
target_language_example: Mi piace il gelato, ma non mi piace il caffè.
native_language_example: I like ice cream, but I don’t like coffee.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere: the thing liked (il basket) is the subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with a + pronoun/name (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli + a Tom). So it’s literally “basketball is pleasing to (someone),” even though in English we say “(someone) likes basketball.” Questions are often formed just with intonation: A Tom piace il basket?
target_language_example: Ti piace il basket o preferisci il calcio?
native_language_example: Do you like basketball, or do you prefer soccer?

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to say someone likes something. The person who likes it is introduced with a + name/pronoun (A Tom…, A loro…). With singular thing: piace; with plural things: piacciono. Common forms: mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli piace il caffè.
target_language_example: Mi piace il caffè, ma non mi piace il tè.
native_language_example: I like coffee, but I don't like tea.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to say someone likes something. The person who likes it is introduced with a + indirect object (a me, a te, a Tom, a tutte le mie amiche). Because calcio is singular, you use piace (not piacciono). Word order is flexible: A Tom piace il calcio / Il calcio piace a Tom.
target_language_example: A me piace il calcio, ma a mio fratello piace il basket.
native_language_example: I like soccer, but my brother likes basketball.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing”). The person who likes something is introduced with a + name/pronoun (A Tom, A me, A tutti), and the thing liked is the grammatical subject: A Tom piace il cibo = “Tom likes food” (literally: “Food is pleasing to Tom”). With plural things, use piacciono: A Tom piacciono i dolci (“Tom likes sweets”).
target_language_example: A me piace il cibo italiano.
native_language_example: I like Italian food.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing”). The person who likes something is introduced with an indirect object (often with a + pronoun/noun): a me/mi (I), a te/ti (you), a lui/gli (he), a lei/le (she), a noi/ci (we), a voi/vi (you all), a loro/gli. The thing liked is the grammatical subject, so with a singular noun you use piace; with plural nouns you use piacciono.
target_language_example: Mi piace il cibo cinese, ma oggi preferisco la pizza.
native_language_example: I like Chinese food, but today I prefer pizza.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to say someone likes something. The thing liked (il gelato) is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with an indirect object pronoun or phrase: mi piace il gelato (I like ice cream), ti piace...? (do you like...?), le piace...? (formal you), a chi piace...? (who likes...?). With plural things, use piacciono (e.g., Mi piacciono i gelati).
target_language_example: Mi piace il gelato al cioccolato, ma non mi piace quello alla vaniglia.
native_language_example: I like chocolate ice cream, but I don’t like vanilla one.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "piacere" (to be pleasing). The person who likes something is introduced with "a" (A me/ a te/ a lui/ a lei/ a Tom...), and the verb agrees with what is liked: "piace" + singular thing (il jazz), "piacciono" + plural things (i film).
target_language_example: A me piace il jazz, ma a mio fratello no.
native_language_example: I like jazz, but my brother doesn't.

additional_notes: Used to say you like (or don’t like) someone’s behavior/style of doing something. Italian often uses the structure "A + person + piace" (e.g., "A Maria piace...") or "Mi piace / Non mi piace...". "il modo" = “the way/manner,” and "in cui" = “in which/that.” You can also use the plural: "Mi piacciono i modi in cui..." (“I like the ways (that) ...”).
target_language_example: Mi piace il modo in cui parli italiano.
native_language_example: I like the way you speak Italian.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing”), so the person who likes something is marked with an indirect object (a me/mi, a te/ti, a lei/le, etc.). The thing liked (il purè) is the grammatical subject, so the verb is usually singular here: mi piace il purè (“I like mashed potatoes”). You can form a question with intonation or a question mark: Ti piace il purè?
target_language_example: A noi piace il purè, ma a loro no.
native_language_example: We like mashed potatoes, but they don’t.

additional_notes: Used with piacere: the thing liked (il riso) is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with a + pronoun/name (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli piace...). Common pattern: (A me/Marco) piace il riso; (A noi) piace il riso.
target_language_example: A me piace il riso, ma non mi piace la pasta.
native_language_example: I like rice, but I don’t like pasta.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere: the person who likes something is introduced with a + pronoun/name (A me piace il tennis = I like tennis; A Tom piace il tennis? = Does Tom like tennis?). Negative: non piace. You can swap order: Il tennis mi piace.
target_language_example: A te piace il tennis?
native_language_example: Do you like tennis?

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (to be pleasing): the thing liked (il tè) is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with an indirect object (a/ad + pronoun/name), e.g., Mi piace il tè = I like tea; A lui piace il tè = He likes tea; Ti piace il tè? = Do you like tea?
target_language_example: Mi piace il tè, ma preferisco il caffè.
native_language_example: I like tea, but I prefer coffee.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "piacere" to express liking. The person who likes something is introduced with "a" (or a pronoun like "mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli"). The thing liked is the grammatical subject, so you use "piace" for singular ("la ...") and "piacciono" for plural. Example: "A Maria piace la macchina" = "Maria likes the car" (literally: "To Maria, the car is pleasing").
target_language_example: A me piace la pizza.
native_language_example: I like pizza.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere, where the thing liked (la birra) is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with a + indirect pronoun: mi (to me), ti (to you), gli/le (to him/her), ci (to us), vi (to you all), gli (to them). Often: A me piace la birra / Mi piace la birra. With plural things: Mi piacciono le birre artigianali.
target_language_example: A noi piace la birra, ma non ci piace il vino.
native_language_example: We like beer, but we don’t like wine.

additional_notes: With piacere, the thing liked (here, la cioccolata) is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is expressed with an indirect object pronoun or with a + name/pronoun: mi piace... (I like...), ti piace...? (Do you like...?), a Paul piace... (Paul likes...). Use piace (singular) with one thing; use piacciono with plural things (e.g., Mi piacciono i biscotti).
target_language_example: Ti piace la cioccolata fondente?
native_language_example: Do you like dark chocolate?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "piacere" (literally “to be pleasing”). The person who likes something is introduced with "a" (indirect object): "A Nancy piace la musica" = “Nancy likes music.” The thing liked (“la musica”) is the grammatical subject, so the verb is singular (piace). With pronouns you’ll often hear: "Mi piace la musica" (I like music), "Ti piace la musica" (Do you like music?).
target_language_example: A Marco piace la musica classica.
native_language_example: Marco likes classical music.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing”). The person who likes it is introduced with a + indirect object: A Tom piace la musica classica = “Tom likes classical music” (literally, “Classical music is pleasing to Tom”). Question form: A te piace la musica classica? (“Do you like classical music?”).
target_language_example: A mia sorella piace la musica classica, ma a me piace il rock.
native_language_example: My sister likes classical music, but I like rock.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "piacere": the thing liked ("la pasta") is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with "a" (often combined with an article: "a + il = al"). So "A Tom piace la pasta" is literally “To Tom, pasta is pleasing.” For more than one person, use "piacciono" (e.g., "A Tom e Maria piacciono i film").
target_language_example: A me piace la pasta, ma a mia sorella piace il riso.
native_language_example: I like pasta, but my sister likes rice.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere, which works differently from English “to like.” The person who likes something is introduced with a + name/pronoun (or an indirect object pronoun: mi, ti, gli/le, ci, vi, gli). The thing that is liked is the grammatical subject: piace with singular nouns (la pizza), and piacciono with plural nouns (Le pizze mi piacciono). Common pattern: A Marco piace la pizza / A loro piace la pizza.
target_language_example: A me piace la pizza, ma a mia sorella piacciono gli hamburger.
native_language_example: I like pizza, but my sister likes hamburgers.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere: the thing liked (la root beer) is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with a + pronoun/name (mi, ti, gli/le, ci, vi, gli; e.g., A me piace..., A te piace...?). Often used as a question: Ti piace la root beer? = “Do you like root beer?”
target_language_example: A me piace la root beer, ma a lui non piace.
native_language_example: I like root beer, but he doesn’t like it.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "piacere" (literally "to be pleasing"), so the person who likes something is marked with "a" (A me/A te/A Tom) or with an indirect object pronoun (mi/ti/le/gli). The thing liked is the subject: "leggere" (to read) or what you read ("Mi piace leggere romanzi"). Common forms: "Mi piace leggere" = I like reading; "Ti piace leggere...?" = Do you like reading...?; "Le piace leggere" (polite) = You like reading.
target_language_example: Ti piace leggere prima di dormire?
native_language_example: Do you like reading before going to sleep?

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing”), so the person who likes something is introduced with a + name/pronoun: A Maria piace… (“Maria likes…”). With pronouns you often use indirect object forms: mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli piace… (“I/you/he/she/we/you(pl)/they like…”). Example: Gli piace leggere… = “He likes reading…”. You can add an adjective for the type of literature: la letteratura inglese/francese.
target_language_example: A me piace leggere la letteratura italiana.
native_language_example: I like reading Italian literature.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing”). The person who likes something is introduced with a + pronoun/name: A Tom piace leggere libri = “Tom likes reading books” (literally: “Reading books is pleasing to Tom”). The thing liked is the subject (here: leggere libri). Question form is the same word order, with rising intonation or a question mark in writing.
target_language_example: Ti piace leggere libri in italiano?
native_language_example: Do you like reading books in Italian?

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to say someone likes doing an activity. The person who likes it is an indirect object: mi piace mangiare (I like to eat), ti piace mangiare? (Do you like to eat?), a Marco piace mangiare… (Marco likes to eat…), ai conigli piace mangiare… (Rabbits like to eat…). Use piace (singular) because the thing liked is the action “mangiare.”
target_language_example: Ti piace mangiare la pizza?
native_language_example: Do you like eating pizza?

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere. The person who likes something is introduced with an indirect object (mi, ti, gli/le, ci, vi, gli) or with "a + name" (e.g., A Tom). The thing liked is the grammatical subject: "Mi piace la pizza" (singular) vs. "Mi piacciono i libri" (plural). "Molto" intensifies the liking: "really/very much".
target_language_example: Mi piace molto questa canzone.
native_language_example: I really like this song.

meaning: to like talking / to enjoy talking.
additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere: the person who likes something is introduced with "a" (e.g., "A me piace...") or as an indirect object pronoun ("Mi piace..."). "Parlare" is an infinitive, so the thing you like is the action of talking. You can add what you like talking about with "di" ("parlare di...") and who you like talking to with "con" ("parlare con...") or sometimes "a" ("parlare a qualcuno" = talk to someone).
target_language_example: Mi piace parlare con i miei colleghi durante la pausa.
native_language_example: I like talking with my colleagues during the break.

meaning: “to like to go for a walk / to like strolling.”
additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere + infinitive: literally “(it) is pleasing to (someone) to stroll.” The person who likes it is shown with an indirect object pronoun: mi piace… (I like…), ti piace… (you like…), le piace… (you like…, formal or “she likes…”), gli piace… (he likes…). You can also specify with A me / A lei / A Marco, etc.: A lei piace passeggiare? = Do you (formal) like to go for a walk? Note: piace looks like English “please” but it doesn’t mean “please!” here.
target_language_example: Ti piace passeggiare in centro la sera?
native_language_example: Do you like strolling downtown in the evening?

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to ask/say that someone likes something. The person who likes it is expressed with an indirect object pronoun (mi, ti, gli/le, ci, vi, gli) or with 'a + name/pronoun' (A me, A Tom). The thing liked is the grammatical subject, so you use 'piace' with singular nouns (questo colore) and 'piacciono' with plural nouns (queste scarpe). Often used in questions: 'Ti piace questo...?' = 'Do you like this...?'
target_language_example: Ti piace questo ristorante?
native_language_example: Do you like this restaurant?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "piacere" (to be pleasing). The person who likes it is an indirect object: "Mi piace studiare" = "I like studying" (literally: "Studying is pleasing to me"). For questions: "Ti piace studiare?" (Do you like studying?), "Vi piace studiare?" (Do you all like studying?), "A voi piace studiare?" (Do you like studying?—emphasizing "you").
target_language_example: Non mi piace studiare la sera, preferisco la mattina.
native_language_example: I don’t like studying in the evening; I prefer the morning.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to emphasize a strong liking. Remember the structure: A + person + piace + thing/activity (literally “To [someone], [thing] is pleasing”). With pronouns: mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi piace veramente… (e.g., Gli piace veramente = He really likes it).
target_language_example: Mi piace veramente questa pizza.
native_language_example: I really like this pizza.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere: the thing you like (here, viaggiare = “to travel”) is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with a + pronoun/name: A me piace viaggiare (I like traveling), A Tom piace viaggiare (Tom likes traveling). With an infinitive like viaggiare, you typically use piace (singular).
target_language_example: Ti piace viaggiare in treno?
native_language_example: Do you like traveling by train?

additional_notes: Used when you meet someone for the first time in a formal/polite context. It uses the formal object pronoun “La” (= you), so you say it to someone you would address with “Lei” (e.g., a stranger, a boss, an older person). Less formal: “piacere di conoscerti”. Often said on its own as “Piacere.”
target_language_example: Buongiorno, piacere di conoscerla, dottore.
native_language_example: Good morning, nice to meet you, doctor.

additional_notes: A common greeting when you meet someone for the first time. Often said after exchanging names. You’ll also hear variations: “piacere di conoscerla” (formal, to someone you address as Lei), “piacere di conoscerti” (informal, to someone you address as tu), or simply “Piacere!” (“Nice to meet you!”).
target_language_example: Ciao, sono Emma. Piacere di conoscerti!
native_language_example: Hi, I'm Emma. Nice to meet you!

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere in the imperfect tense. The person who likes something is introduced with "a" (e.g., "A Fadil..."), and the thing liked is grammatically the subject. "Piaceva" is for singular things; for plural things use "piacevano". It agrees with the noun after it (here "la" + a feminine singular noun). Often translates to English as "liked" in the past.
target_language_example: Da bambino, a me piaceva la pizza.
native_language_example: As a child, I liked pizza.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere in the imperfect tense (piaceva) to talk about liking in the past, often in reported speech after che (e.g., Ha detto che...). Remember the structure: the thing liked is the subject (la mia idea), and the person who likes it is an indirect object pronoun (gli/le/mi) or a + pronoun (a lui/a loro).
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che le piaceva la mia idea.
native_language_example: He/She told me that she liked my idea.

meaning: "(Someone) liked the snow" (in the past / used to like the snow).
additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere, which works like “to be pleasing”: a lei piaceva la neve = “she liked the snow” (literally, “the snow was pleasing to her”). Piaceva is the imperfect tense, common in reported speech after ha detto che… and for describing past preferences/habits. The person who likes something is shown with an indirect object (mi, ti, gli/le, ci, vi, gli) or with a + pronoun (a me, a lei, a loro).
target_language_example: Da bambino, mi piaceva la neve, ma ora preferisco il sole.
native_language_example: As a child, I liked the snow, but now I prefer the sun.

meaning: “(he/she) liked the rain” / “(he/she) used to like the rain.”
additional_notes: Imperfect of piacere (“to be pleasing”). The person who likes something is expressed with an indirect object: mi (to me), ti (to you), gli (to him), le (to her), ci (to us), vi (to you all), gli (to them). So “A lui piaceva la pioggia” literally means “To him, the rain was pleasing,” i.e., “He liked the rain,” often describing a past habit or ongoing feeling.
target_language_example: Da bambino, gli piaceva la pioggia perché poteva saltare nelle pozzanghere.
native_language_example: As a child, he liked the rain because he could jump in puddles.

meaning: “(someone) liked pizza” / “pizza was pleasing to (someone)” (past, imperfect).
additional_notes: With piacere, the thing liked is the grammatical subject (la pizza), and the person who likes it is introduced with an indirect object: a Ziri, a lei, mi, gli, le, etc. Piaceva is the imperfect tense, used for a past state or habitual liking (“used to like,” “liked (back then)”). Word order can vary: A lei piaceva la pizza / La pizza le piaceva.
target_language_example: Quando era bambina, a Marta piaceva la pizza margherita.
native_language_example: When she was a child, Marta liked margherita pizza.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere in the past: the thing that is liked is the grammatical subject, so you say Mi è piaciuta la cena (“The dinner pleased me” = “I liked the dinner”). Piaciuta agrees with a feminine singular noun (la cena, la scuola, la minestra). Often appears with an indirect object pronoun or phrase: mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli, or a + person (A me, a te).
target_language_example: Ti è piaciuta la mostra?
native_language_example: Did you like the exhibition?

additional_notes: Used with the verb **piacere** (“to be pleasing/liked”), which works differently from English: the thing that is liked is the grammatical subject (**il mio libro**), and the person who likes it is introduced with **a + person** (e.g., **a lei**, **a loro**). In the past tense (**è piaciuto**), the verb agrees with what is liked: **è piaciuto** (masc. singular, for **il libro**), **è piaciuta** (fem. singular), **sono piaciuti/piaciute** (plural).
target_language_example: Ti è piaciuto il mio libro?
native_language_example: Did you like my book?

additional_notes: Used to indicate the position of a planet when you count outward starting from a reference point (usually the Sun): “il quarto pianeta a partire dal Sole” = “the fourth planet from the Sun.” The pattern is: [number + pianeta] a partire da/dal + [starting point]. Use “dal” before masculine singular nouns like “il Sole” (a partire dal Sole) and “dalla” before feminine singular nouns (a partire dalla Terra).
target_language_example: Giove è il quinto pianeta a partire dal Sole.
native_language_example: Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens repeatedly whenever a certain situation occurs. “Ogni volta che” (“every time that/whenever”) is followed by a verb (often in the present tense for a general habit): e.g., “piango ogni volta che lo vedo” = “I cry every time I see it/him.”
target_language_example: Piango ogni volta che penso a quei giorni.
native_language_example: I cry every time I think about those days.

additional_notes: Used with a noun (piani per un picnic = plans for a picnic) or with an infinitive (piani per andare = plans to go). Common with "avere": "Ho dei piani per..." = "I have plans to/for...".
target_language_example: Hai già dei piani per il weekend?
native_language_example: Do you already have plans for the weekend?

additional_notes: Common in spoken Italian. It can mean doing something carefully/softly (often with verbs like sedersi, parlare, andare) or that something happens gradually over time (“little by little”).
target_language_example: Cammina piano piano: la strada è scivolosa.
native_language_example: Walk slowly/carefully: the road is slippery.

meaning: the upstairs floor; the floor above.
additional_notes: Used to refer to an upper level in a building (often in a house). Common with verbs of movement like andare/salire (to go up) or with sounds coming from above (sentire qualcuno al piano di sopra).
target_language_example: Il bagno è al piano di sopra, a destra.
native_language_example: The bathroom is upstairs, on the right.

meaning: the floor downstairs; the lower floor.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the level below where you are (often the ground floor from an upstairs room). It can be used with verbs of movement (andare/tornare/scendere al piano di sotto) or location (essere/aspettare al piano di sotto).
target_language_example: Vado al piano di sotto a prendere un bicchiere d'acqua.
native_language_example: I'm going downstairs to get a glass of water.

additional_notes: Used with the subjunctive verb form "sia" (from "essere" = to be), typically after expressions like "penso che..." (I think that...) to give an opinion. "Piuttosto" often means "rather/pretty" (a bit, fairly). Note: "piano" here means "plan" (not the musical instrument).
target_language_example: Penso che questo piano sia piuttosto stupido, ma possiamo discuterne.
native_language_example: I think this plan is rather stupid, but we can discuss it.

additional_notes: A simple, literal phrase: **pianta** (verb, from *piantare*) means “(he/she) plants,” and **una pianta** means “a plant” (e.g., a tree, flower, rose bush). Used for actions like planting something in a garden, or ceremonially planting in someone’s memory (often with *in memoria di...*).
target_language_example: Ogni primavera, mio nonno pianta una pianta nuova sul balcone.
native_language_example: Every spring, my grandfather plants a new plant on the balcony.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase used with the auxiliary avere to form the passato prossimo: ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno piantato un albero. In Italian, piantare means “to plant” (a tree, flowers, seeds) and also “to stick/drive in” something (like a pole), so context helps. The phrase can be used literally or in a humorous/angry way (“Who the hell planted a tree on my ship?”).
target_language_example: L'anno scorso abbiamo piantato un albero in giardino.
native_language_example: Last year we planted a tree in the garden.

additional_notes: Used for a meal eaten outside (often in a park or countryside). In Italian it’s commonly written as one word ("picnic") or two ("pic nic"). Plural: "i picnic" / "i pic nic".
target_language_example: Domani facciamo un pic nic al parco.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re having a picnic in the park.

additional_notes: Used to describe a village that is small in size/population. Often follows a preposition like "in" ("in the small village"). "Piccolo" agrees with the noun: "piccolo villaggio" (masc. sing.), "piccoli villaggi" (masc. plural).
target_language_example: In quel piccolo villaggio tutti si conoscono.
native_language_example: In that small village everyone knows each other.

meaning: pickup truck (a small truck with an open cargo bed).
additional_notes: In Italian, "pick-up" is a loanword used for the vehicle type (often masculine: *il pick-up*; plural usually *i pick-up*). It’s common when talking about cars/vehicles (e.g., *pick-up o SUV*).
target_language_example: Abbiamo noleggiato un pick-up per trasportare i mobili.
native_language_example: We rented a pickup truck to transport the furniture.

additional_notes: A tool used to pry things open or pull out nails. Literally “pig’s foot,” but in Italian it means the tool, not an animal body part. It’s masculine: un/il piede di porco.
target_language_example: Puoi passarmi il piede di porco?
native_language_example: Can you pass me the crowbar?

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns/adjectives (e.g., una scatola/stanza/persona è piena di...). With masculine nouns use "pieno di"; plural: "pieni di" (masc.) / "piene di" (fem.). Can describe something literally filled ("una scatola piena di mele") or figuratively ("piena di energia/curiosità").
target_language_example: Sono piena di impegni questa settimana.
native_language_example: I'm full of commitments this week.

additional_notes: Used mostly about women/girls (piena is feminine). For a man/boy, say pieno di energia. Common with verbs like essere (“to be”) and sembrare (“to seem”): Sono/Lei sembra piena di energia.
target_language_example: Dopo il caffè, sono piena di energia.
native_language_example: After coffee, I’m full of energy.

additional_notes: Used to say something is filled with something else. It agrees with what’s “full”: pieno di (masc. singular), piena di (fem. singular), pieni di (masc. plural), piene di (fem. plural). Often used with body parts or expressions: occhi pieni di lacrime/speranza (“eyes full of tears/hope”). With slang nouns it can mean “loaded with”: pieni di grana (“loaded with money”).
target_language_example: La sala era piena di gente.
native_language_example: The room was full of people.

additional_notes: Used to say something contains a lot of something (physical or abstract): "pieno di sale" (filled with salt), "pieno di rabbia" (full of anger). With people it can describe an attitude: "pieno di sé" means "full of oneself" → conceited/very self-important.
target_language_example: La stanza è piena di gente.
native_language_example: The room is full of people.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who has an inflated opinion of themselves and acts smug or conceited. In standard Italian it’s written with the accent: “pieno di sé” (meaning “of himself/herself/themself”). It agrees with the person described: pieno (m.), piena (f.), pieni (m. pl.), piene (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Da quando ha avuto quella promozione, è sempre più pieno di sé.
native_language_example: Since he got that promotion, he’s more and more full of himself.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like riuscire a (manage to), sapere (know how to), and potere (can) to talk about having the ability to operate and fly a helicopter. In everyday English you’d usually say “fly a helicopter,” while Italian commonly uses pilotare (“to pilot/operate”) for aircraft and other vehicles.
target_language_example: Non so pilotare un elicottero, ma so pilotare un aereo.
native_language_example: I can’t fly a helicopter, but I can fly a plane.

additional_notes: A loanword used for the sport played on a table with small paddles and a light ball. Very common in everyday Italian; often used interchangeably with "tennis da tavolo" (more formal/official). With "giocare": "giocare a ping-pong" = to play ping-pong.
target_language_example: Giochiamo a ping-pong dopo cena?
native_language_example: Shall we play ping-pong after dinner?

additional_notes: Common noun for the sport (same as "tennis da tavolo"). Often used with verbs like "giocare a ping pong" (to play ping-pong) and "fare ping pong" (to play ping-pong). In casual speech it can also be used as a quick question or suggestion: "Ping pong?" = "Ping-pong?" / "Want to play?".
target_language_example: Domani pomeriggio giochiamo a ping pong al parco.
native_language_example: Tomorrow afternoon we’ll play ping-pong at the park.

meaning: To rain very heavily; to pour down ("to rain cats and dogs").
additional_notes: Common idiom used to emphasize intense rain. You can use it in any tense (e.g., "ha piovuto a catinelle"). Often appears with weather phrases like "Oggi piove a catinelle".
target_language_example: Oggi piove a catinelle, meglio prendere l’ombrello.
native_language_example: It’s pouring down today, better take an umbrella.

additional_notes: Commonly used with the auxiliary verb "avere" in the passato prossimo: "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno pitturato" + "le pareti" (the walls). You can add a color with "di" + color: "pitturare le pareti di bianco" = "to paint the walls white".
target_language_example: Abbiamo pitturato le pareti di grigio chiaro.
native_language_example: We painted the walls light gray.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something fairly well (often better than expected, but not necessarily perfectly). It can sound a bit modest/understated. Position: usually after the verb (e.g., parlare piuttosto bene).
target_language_example: Me la cavo piuttosto bene in italiano.
native_language_example: I get by pretty well in Italian.

additional_notes: Used when ordering or talking about a specific pizza topping. "Salame piccante" is spicy salami (often like pepperoni), and "con" means "with." In questions like "Le piace...?" and "Vi piace...?" it means "Do you like...?" (formal singular / plural).
target_language_example: Vorrei una pizza con il salame piccante, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a spicy salami pizza, please.

meaning: Sal’s pizzeria (a pizzeria owned by/associated with Sal).
additional_notes: In Italian, **di + name** is a common way to show possession or association, like **“Sal’s …”** in English. You’ll also see it with businesses and shops: *il bar di Marco* (Marco’s bar), *la farmacia di Anna* (Anna’s pharmacy). In the examples, *la famosa pizzeria di Sal (e figli)* means “the famous pizzeria of Sal (and sons).”
target_language_example: Prendiamo una pizza alla pizzeria di Sal stasera?
native_language_example: Shall we get a pizza at Sal’s pizzeria tonight?

additional_notes: Used to compare duration ("more long"), often with verbs like vivere, restare/rimanere, parlare, aspettare. It can be followed by "di/che" to compare two durations: "più a lungo di/che...".
target_language_example: Possiamo restare qui più a lungo?
native_language_example: Can we stay here longer?

additional_notes: Comparative form of "alta" (feminine singular), used when comparing two things or people: "più alta di..." = "higher/taller than...". Use it with feminine nouns (e.g., "una montagna più alta") or a woman/girl ("Lei è più alta"). For masculine, use "più alto"; for plural, "più alti/alte". Related superlative: "la più alta" = "the tallest/highest" (feminine).
target_language_example: Questa torre è più alta di quella.
native_language_example: This tower is taller/higher than that one.

additional_notes: Used for comparisons with di: più alto di me = taller than me. With il/la/i/le + più alto it forms the superlative: il ragazzo più alto = the tallest boy. You can strengthen it with molto (much) or ancora (even): molto più alto, ancora più alto. "Alto" can describe people (tall) and things/positions (high).
target_language_example: Questa sedia è più alta di quella.
native_language_example: This chair is higher than that one.

additional_notes: Comparative form: più + adjective + di. Use it to compare height (people) or level/height (objects). Often intensified with molto (much) or only slightly with soltanto leggermente. After di you can use a noun or pronoun (e.g., di Mary, di lui). Superlative pattern: il più alto di tutti = “the tallest of all”.
target_language_example: Questo edificio è più alto di quello.
native_language_example: This building is taller/higher than that one.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages or how old someone looks. It agrees in gender/number with the person described: più anziano di (male singular), più anziana di (female singular), più anziani di / più anziane di (plural). You can use it with a person or with “quel che/di quanto” to mean “than (what/how much)”: più anziano di quel che sembra = older than he seems.
target_language_example: Mia sorella è più anziana di me di tre anni.
native_language_example: My sister is three years older than me.

additional_notes: Used to compare: **più bella di + noun/pronoun** = “prettier than…”. With **la/le + più bella** it becomes a superlative: **la più bella** = “the most beautiful (one)”. Feminine singular form, so it describes a feminine noun/person (e.g., *ragazza, spiaggia*).
target_language_example: Secondo me, questa foto è più bella dell’altra.
native_language_example: In my opinion, this photo is prettier than the other one.

meaning: more beautiful / nicer; (with articles) the most beautiful.
additional_notes: Used to compare: "più bello di ..." = "more beautiful/nicer than ...". With a superlative: "il/la/i/le posto più bello" = "the most beautiful place". It can also be used emphatically to mean "even nicer/better" (e.g., "ancora più bello" = "even more beautiful").
target_language_example: Questo parco è più bello di quello vicino a casa mia.
native_language_example: This park is more beautiful than the one near my house.

meaning: mostly; more than anything else; rather.
additional_notes: Used to highlight the main thing among several possibilities, often to correct/nuance what you just said (“not so much X, but mainly Y”). Common with verbs like ricordare, cercare, volere, essere/sembrare.
target_language_example: Non è che mi dispiace: più che altro sono stanco.
native_language_example: It’s not that I mind; I’m mostly just tired.

meaning: more than ever (now more than at any other time).
additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that something is true/important especially now, compared to any time in the past. Often follows the idea it intensifies ("ne ho bisogno più che mai") or can stand alone as a short emphatic reply ("Più che mai!").
target_language_example: In questo periodo, abbiamo bisogno di restare uniti più che mai.
native_language_example: In this period, we need to stick together more than ever.

additional_notes: Used for comparisons and quantities: "più di + number/amount" = "more than/over" (Più di 30 miglia). You can also use it to compare actions or amounts with someone/something: "più di suo padre" = "more than her father." Often followed by a number, a noun, or a pronoun (me/te/lui/lei/noi/voi/loro).
target_language_example: Ho lavorato qui per più di cinque anni.
native_language_example: I’ve worked here for more than five years.

più di cinque fette di pizza al mese

target_language_multi_word_term: più di cinque fette di pizza al mese
meaning: more than five slices of pizza per month.
additional_notes: A quantity phrase used to talk about frequency/amount over a month. Structure: "più di" (more than) + number + noun ("fette di pizza") + time period ("al mese" = per month). Often used in questions with "Di solito" or "Solitamente" (usually).
target_language_example: Non mangio più di cinque fette di pizza al mese.
native_language_example: I don't eat more than five slices of pizza per month.

additional_notes: Used in comparisons with "più" (more) + "di" (than) + the stressed pronoun "me" (me). It can refer to quantity, frequency, or degree: "lavora più di me" (works more than me), "ama più di me" (loves more than me). After "di" you use "me" (not "io").
target_language_example: Parli italiano meglio di me.
native_language_example: You speak Italian better than me.

meaning: more than anything else; above all (else).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is the top priority or the strongest preference (or dislike) compared to everything else. It can be placed after the verb/object, or set off by commas in the middle of the sentence for emphasis.
target_language_example: Desidero, più di ogni altra cosa, passare del tempo con la mia famiglia.
native_language_example: More than anything else, I want to spend time with my family.

additional_notes: Used to compare quantities/degree: “more than” + a clause (often with the subjunctive in formal Italian), meaning “more than I thought/expected/wanted/should.” You may also see “più di quanto non …” where “non” doesn’t negate; it’s just an idiomatic/formal extra often used with comparisons.
target_language_example: Ho speso più di quanto pensassi.
native_language_example: I spent more than I thought.

additional_notes: Used to compare degrees/amounts with a clause: più di quanto + verb (often in the subjunctive), meaning “more than I/you/he thought/expected/believed.” You may also see the optional "non" in the following clause (più di quanto non...), which doesn’t make it negative; it’s a common expletive "non" in comparisons.
target_language_example: Mi piace questo posto più di quanto pensassi.
native_language_example: I like this place more than I thought.

meaning: more than a year; over a year.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration of time that exceeds one year. Often follows expressions like "da" (for/since) to say how long something has been happening: "da più di un anno" = "for more than a year."
target_language_example: Studio italiano da più di un anno.
native_language_example: I've been studying Italian for more than a year.

additional_notes: Used with verbs to say someone should increase their effort or intensity (e.g., cercare/guardare più duramente = look/search more thoroughly; lavorare/provare più duramente = work/try harder). Common in advice or commands. In everyday Italian you may also hear "più forte" (especially for physical effort) or "di più" (more in general).
target_language_example: Se vuoi passare l’esame, devi studiare più duramente.
native_language_example: If you want to pass the exam, you have to study harder.

additional_notes: Comparative form: più + adjective (facile) = “more …”. Used to compare things (più facile di … = “easier than …”) or to say something becomes easier (diventare più facile). With object pronouns: lo/la rende più facile = “it makes it easier.”
target_language_example: Con questo metodo, è più facile imparare l'italiano.
native_language_example: With this method, it’s easier to learn Italian.

additional_notes: Comparative form of "forte" (strong, intense, loud). Used for physical strength (rendere più forte = make stronger), effects (a stronger drink/medicine: qualcosa di più forte), or sound (parla più forte! = speak louder). Often translates as "stronger," but in context it can mean "stronger (effect)," or "louder" for volume.
target_language_example: Hai qualcosa di più forte per il mal di testa?
native_language_example: Do you have something stronger for a headache?

additional_notes: Used to compare strength or power: "più" (more) + "forte" (strong/strongly) + "di" (than). Often appears with intensifiers like "molto" (much): "molto più forte di...". You can use it literally for physical strength or more generally for power, influence, or effect.
target_language_example: Questa squadra è molto più forte di quella dell’anno scorso.
native_language_example: This team is much stronger than last year’s one.

additional_notes: Used to compare intensity. Very common with speaking/volume: "Parla più forte" = "Speak louder." With actions or forces it means "more strongly/harder" (wind, blow, hit, push). You can intensify it with words like "ancora" (even) or "possibile" (as possible): "il più forte possibile" = "as loud/strong as possible."
target_language_example: Puoi mettere la musica più forte, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you turn the music up louder, please?

additional_notes: Used to compare ages, often with "di" (più giovane di lui = younger than him) and can add the difference: "di due anni". With "il/la ... più giovane" it means "the youngest" (e.g., il figlio più giovane). "Non è più giovane" usually means "He/She isn’t young anymore" (no longer young).
target_language_example: Mia sorella è più giovane di me di cinque anni.
native_language_example: My sister is five years younger than me.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages (or how old someone looks). It follows the common comparative pattern "più + adjective + di" (= "more + adjective + than"). It can also be followed by a clause: "più giovane di quel che pensi" = "younger than you think."
target_language_example: Mio fratello è più giovane di me, ma sembra più grande.
native_language_example: My brother is younger than me, but he looks older.

additional_notes: Used for comparisons: "più grande di" = "bigger/larger/older than." With a noun phrase, it can mean "the biggest/largest": "il/la + noun + più grande" (often with "della/del" = "in the/of the"). For age, Italians commonly say "più grande" rather than "più vecchio" in neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Mio fratello è più grande di me.
native_language_example: My brother is older than me.

additional_notes: Used to make comparisons: più + adjective + di/che. With grande you usually use di, which combines with the definite article: di + la = della, di + il = del, di + lo = dello, di + i = dei, di + gli = degli, di + le = delle. You can also use di + pronoun: più grande di te/lui/lei. Often the noun is omitted when it’s clear: La mia (casa) è più grande della tua.
target_language_example: Questo zaino è più grande del tuo.
native_language_example: This backpack is bigger than yours.

additional_notes: Used for comparisons: X è più grande di Y. With people, it often refers to age (older). You can intensify with numbers/expressions (e.g., tre volte più grande di = three times bigger than) or make it negative: non più grande di = no bigger than.
target_language_example: Questo appartamento è più grande di quello, ma è più caro.
native_language_example: This apartment is bigger than that one, but it's more expensive.

additional_notes: Comparative/superlative of "grande" (big/great). Use it to compare size: "più grandi di ..." = "bigger than ...". With family members, it commonly means older: "sorelle più grandi" = "older sisters". It can also be part of a superlative: "una delle più grandi" = "one of the biggest".
target_language_example: Questo zaino è più grande del mio.
native_language_example: This backpack is bigger than mine.

additional_notes: Used with comparisons and superlatives. With "più" + adjective you get a comparison: "A è più importante di B" (A is more important than B). With an article + "più" you often get a superlative: "la cosa più importante" (the most important thing). In phrases like "cosa ancora più importante" it means "something even more important".
target_language_example: Per me, la cosa più importante è stare bene.
native_language_example: For me, the most important thing is to be well.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a higher position or level (physically or sometimes figuratively). Often used with nouns like "la mensola più in alto" (“the highest shelf / the shelf up higher”) or with comparisons like "due piani più in alto" (“two floors higher”). You can also say it alone as a direction: "Più in alto!" (“Higher up!”).
target_language_example: Puoi mettere la scatola più in alto, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you put the box higher up, please?

additional_notes: Used to say you want to reach the maximum height you can. Often appears with verbs like volare (to fly) and saltare (to jump). You’ll also commonly see it with the article: il più in alto possibile (“as high as possible”).
target_language_example: Metti la valigia più in alto possibile.
native_language_example: Put the suitcase as high up as possible.

additional_notes: Used to compare speed or to urge doing something with more speed. Often follows a verb (e.g., "andare più in fretta" = "to go faster"), and it can be reinforced with "possibile" ("più in fretta possibile" = "as fast as possible").
target_language_example: Dobbiamo finire più in fretta, altrimenti perdiamo il treno.
native_language_example: We have to finish faster, otherwise we’ll miss the train.

additional_notes: Used to make a comparison. It’s built with the comparative pattern “più + adjective + di” (more + adjective + than). With a clause, you often see “di quanto …” or “di quel che …” (e.g., “più intelligente di quanto sembri” = “more intelligent than you seem”).
target_language_example: Secondo me, questo esercizio è più intelligente di quello di ieri.
native_language_example: In my opinion, this exercise is more intelligent than yesterday’s one.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to slow down (walking, talking, driving, etc.). Often appears in polite requests with "Per favore/Per piacere". With commands you may see either informal "Parla/Cammina" (to a friend) or formal "Parli/Camini" (to a stranger). You can also compare speeds with "più lentamente di ..." (more slowly than ...).
target_language_example: Mi puoi spiegare più lentamente, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you explain it to me more slowly, please?

additional_notes: Used to say something is not exact or only partially true/known. Common after numbers and times ("le quattro, più o meno" = "around four"), and also to mean "kind of / sort of" with verbs like sapere/capire ("lo capisco più o meno" = "I kind of understand"). It can sound vague; in some contexts it may be criticized ("Più o meno non è abbastanza!").
target_language_example: Arrivo tra dieci minuti, più o meno.
native_language_example: I’ll arrive in about ten minutes, more or less.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens after a certain time. Often with a time expression: qualche minuto/giorno più tardi (“a few minutes/days later”). Common in everyday plans: Lo faccio più tardi (“I’ll do it later”).
target_language_example: Ci sentiamo più tardi.
native_language_example: We’ll talk later.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages: "più + adjective + di" = "more + adjective + than". With age, Italians often also say "più grande di". It agrees with the person described: "più vecchio" (masc.), "più vecchia" (fem.). "Di" is used before a noun or pronoun (di Maria, di noi).
target_language_example: Lei è più vecchia di me.
native_language_example: She is older than me.

additional_notes: Comparative: più veloce = faster (often followed by “di …” for “than …”). Superlative: il/la più veloce = the fastest (e.g., Tu sei la più veloce). Common in commands and encouragement: “Più veloce!” = “Faster!” With “possibile/che puoi” it means “as fast as possible / as fast as you can.”
target_language_example: Possiamo andare più veloce, ma non troppo.
native_language_example: We can go faster, but not too fast.

additional_notes: Used to compare speed: più + adjective/adverb (veloce) + di + person/thing. With verbs, it often appears as "correre più veloce di..." (to run faster than...). You can also use it with nouns: "un corridore più veloce di..." (a faster runner than...).
target_language_example: Questo treno è più veloce di quello.
native_language_example: This train is faster than that one.

additional_notes: Comparative adverb used to say someone does something at a higher speed than before or than someone else. Often followed by a comparison: "più velocemente di..." (faster than...).
target_language_example: Puoi parlare più velocemente, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you speak faster, please?

additional_notes: Used to compare amounts of money or to say someone wants/has/earns a larger amount. Often followed by a comparison: “più soldi di me/dei suoi genitori” (more money than me/his parents). With verbs like “fare” it commonly means “to earn”: “fare più soldi” = “to make/earn more money.”
target_language_example: Vorrei più soldi per comprare un computer nuovo.
native_language_example: I’d like more money to buy a new computer.

additional_notes: Used to say you need additional time to finish something or to ask someone to wait longer. Often appears with verbs like "avere" (to have), "dare" (to give), "servire" (to need), and "bisognare" (to be needed): "Mi serve più tempo" = "I need more time."
target_language_example: Possiamo parlarne domani? Ho bisogno di più tempo.
native_language_example: Can we talk about it tomorrow? I need more time.

più tempo a casa o al lavoro

target_language_multi_word_term: più tempo a casa o al lavoro
meaning: more time at home or at work.
additional_notes: Used to compare where someone spends the larger share of their time (often with verbs like passare/trascorrere = “to spend (time)”). You can change the places: “più tempo in ufficio o in viaggio?”
target_language_example: In questo periodo passo più tempo a casa che al lavoro.
native_language_example: These days I spend more time at home than at work.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened repeatedly or on multiple occasions. Often placed after the verb (è successo più volte) or before an infinitive (ho pensato più volte di...).
target_language_example: Te l’ho detto più volte: non lasciare la porta aperta.
native_language_example: I’ve told you several times: don’t leave the door open.

additional_notes: Used to say a small number of people (not many). It can be the subject or object of the sentence: “Poche persone…” = “Few people…”, “ci sono poche persone” = “there are few people.” Often contrasts with “molte persone” (many people).
target_language_example: Oggi al museo ci sono poche persone.
native_language_example: Today there are few people at the museum.

additional_notes: Means a small number of days. Often used with time expressions like "entro pochi giorni" (within a few days) or "pochi giorni più tardi" (a few days later).
target_language_example: Ritorno tra pochi giorni.
native_language_example: I'll be back in a few days.

additional_notes: Used to say you have only a short amount of time, or that something will happen soon (e.g., “in a few minutes,” “a few minutes later”). With distances/travel time, it can mean “a few minutes away” (Siamo a pochi minuti = We’re a few minutes away).
target_language_example: Aspettami: arrivo tra pochi minuti.
native_language_example: Wait for me: I’ll be there in a few minutes.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that improves, grows, or changes slowly over time, often step by step. Common with verbs like migliorare (to improve), crescere (to grow), riprendersi (to recover), and can go at the end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: andrà meglio poco a poco.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it will get better little by little.

meaning: a short while ago; just now.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened recently (a few minutes or a little time ago). It can go at the end of the sentence (common) or near the verb: “Mi ha chiamato poco fa” / “Poco fa mi ha chiamato”.
target_language_example: Sono arrivato poco fa, scusa il ritardo.
native_language_example: I arrived a short while ago, sorry I’m late.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t have much time available, or that something lasts only a short time. Common patterns: "in poco tempo" = "in a short time"; "per poco tempo" = "for a short time"; "(mi) resta/rimane poco tempo" = "I have little time left"; "poco tempo fa" = "a short time ago".
target_language_example: Scusa, ho poco tempo: possiamo parlare domani?
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have much time: can we talk tomorrow?

additional_notes: Usually written as one word: **poiché**. It introduces a reason or explanation (similar to *perché*, but often a bit more formal). Typically followed by the indicative: *Poiché piove, restiamo a casa.*
target_language_example: Poiché non ho tempo, lo faccio domani.
native_language_example: Since I don't have time, I'll do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: A food item. Often used with an article: "il pollo fritto" (the fried chicken). You can also use it on its own as an answer/order: "Pollo fritto!"
target_language_example: Per cena prendo il pollo fritto.
native_language_example: For dinner I’ll have fried chicken.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the business that handles funerals (the company/office that organizes the funeral and related services). Often used with a place word like “casa di pompe funebri” (funeral home).
target_language_example: Dobbiamo chiamare le pompe funebri per organizzare il funerale.
native_language_example: We have to call the funeral home to arrange the funeral.

meaning: “Fuck!” / “For fuck’s sake!” (a very strong swear word).
additional_notes: Very vulgar Italian exclamation used to show sudden anger, frustration, shock, or emphasis—similar to English “fuck!” or “for fuck’s sake!”. It can be shouted on its own ("Porca puttana!") or added at the end of a sentence for emphasis. Avoid in polite situations, with strangers, at work, or around children.
target_language_example: Porca puttana, ho perso le chiavi!
native_language_example: Fuck, I lost my keys!

meaning: a very strong, vulgar swear word (like “for fuck’s sake!” / “goddamn it!”).
additional_notes: Used to express strong anger, frustration, or emphasis, either on its own ("Porca troia!") or added to a sentence. It’s offensive/vulgar and should be avoided in polite situations; it can sound aggressive if directed at someone.
target_language_example: Porca troia, ho perso le chiavi!
native_language_example: For fuck’s sake, I lost my keys!

meaning: to put an end to; to end (something).
additional_notes: Used in formal or serious contexts to mean ending a situation, activity, conflict, or relationship. It’s often followed by "a" + noun/infinitive: "porre fine a una guerra" (end a war), "porre fine agli insulti" (put an end to the insults). Less common in casual speech than "finire" or "mettere fine a".
target_language_example: È ora di porre fine a questa discussione.
native_language_example: It’s time to put an end to this discussion.

additional_notes: Used to politely refer to the door when making a request, most commonly in phrases like “Apri la porta, per favore.” The comma shows a pause: you’re adding “please” to soften the request. “Porta” here is the noun “door” (not the verb “he/she brings”).
target_language_example: Chiudi la porta, per favore.
native_language_example: Close the door, please.

meaning: an open door; (left) the door open.
additional_notes: Used literally to describe a door that is open or has been left open. Often appears with verbs like lasciare (to leave): "Hai lasciato la porta aperta?" = "Did you leave the door open?".
target_language_example: Per favore, non lasciare la porta aperta.
native_language_example: Please, don’t leave the door open.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "portare" to talk about wearing items like glasses, contact lenses, clothes, etc. It describes a usual or current characteristic (often with "solitamente" = usually). In questions, subject pronouns are often omitted: "Porta gli occhiali?" = "Do you wear glasses?"
target_language_example: Mio padre porta gli occhiali da lettura.
native_language_example: My father wears reading glasses.

meaning: "always carries (it) with him/her" / "always keeps (it) on them".
additional_notes: Used to say someone habitually has an object with them. The item usually follows the phrase: "Porta sempre con sé + [object]". "Con sé" literally means "with oneself" and refers back to the subject (so you can change it: "porto sempre con me" = I always carry with me; "porta sempre con te" = you always carry with you).
target_language_example: Lei porta sempre con sé un ombrello, anche quando c'è il sole.
native_language_example: She always carries an umbrella with her, even when it’s sunny.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **portare via**. It’s used when something is removed from a place or when something (like wind) carries something off. In the imperative (**Porta via…**), it’s a direct command meaning “Take … away.”
target_language_example: Per favore, porta via questi piatti dal tavolo.
native_language_example: Please take these plates away from the table.

additional_notes: Common with direct object pronouns (ti, lo, la, li, le): "Ti porto a casa" = "I’ll take you home." It can mean either taking someone home (e.g., giving them a ride) or bringing something back home; context tells you which. In the passato prossimo it uses "avere": "Ti ho portato/a a casa".
target_language_example: Se vuoi, ti porto a casa dopo la festa.
native_language_example: If you want, I’ll take you home after the party.

meaning: to finish; to carry through to completion.
additional_notes: Used for completing a task, project, plan, or goal. It often implies seeing something through until the end (sometimes despite difficulty). In contexts like pregnancy ("portare a termine la gravidanza"), it means carrying it to full term.
target_language_example: Sono stanco, ma voglio portare a termine questo lavoro entro stasera.
native_language_example: I'm tired, but I want to finish this work by tonight.

meaning: to carry on; to continue; to pursue (a project/plan).
additional_notes: Used with activities, work, plans, or projects: “portare avanti un progetto/il lavoro/le trattative” = keep it going and make progress. It can also mean “to carry forward” in a more literal sense, and in some contexts “portare avanti una gravidanza” = to carry a pregnancy to term.
target_language_example: Non è facile, ma dobbiamo portare avanti il progetto.
native_language_example: It’s not easy, but we have to carry on with the project.

additional_notes: Common household chore meaning to bring the garbage outside (often to the bins/curb). You may also hear: "buttare la spazzatura" (throw away the trash) or "portare giù la spazzatura" (take the trash down, e.g., to the building’s dumpster).
target_language_example: Puoi portare fuori la spazzatura prima di uscire?
native_language_example: Can you take out the trash before you go out?

meaning: to take away; to carry off; to take (someone) away.
additional_notes: Used for removing or taking something from a place (often ‘away from here’), or taking a person away from someone/somewhere. With direct objects: portare via il pacco = take the package away. With a person: portare via qualcuno = take someone away (sometimes in the sense of being taken from someone’s care). In polite requests you may see it with ‘mi’: Mi può portare via…? = Can you take me away/with you?
target_language_example: Può portare via questi piatti, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you take these dishes away, please?

meaning: taken away; carried off (sometimes: swept away, figuratively).
additional_notes: Past participle of **portare via** (“to take/carry away”). Often used for someone being removed or taken somewhere (e.g., by force), for stealing (“He took it away”), and in the passive: **è stato portato via** (“he was taken away”). It can also be figurative: **portato via dalla passione** = “carried/swept away by passion.” You may see it with pronouns: **se lo sono portato via** = “they took him/it away (with them).”
target_language_example: La polizia lo ha portato via in ambulanza.
native_language_example: The police took him away in an ambulance.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **portare a casa** (“to take/bring home”). **Porti** is the present tense used with **Lei** (polite “you”) and is also used as a formal imperative: **Mi porti a casa** = “Take me home, please.” With **tu**, you’ll often hear **mi porti a casa** (informal present) or **portami a casa** (informal command). It can also mean “take someone home” in a dating/romantic sense: **Scegli meglio chi ti porti a casa** = “Be more careful about who you bring home (with you).”
target_language_example: Può portarmi a casa, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you take me home, please?

additional_notes: "Possiamo" is the 1st-person plural of "potere" (can/to be able to). Used to offer help (often as a question: "Come possiamo aiutare?"), or to say you’re able/willing to help ("Possiamo aiutare."). With pronouns, it becomes more specific/polite: "La/Le possiamo aiutare?" = “Can we help you?” (formal; La = you singular, Le = you plural or polite singular in some contexts).
target_language_example: Se vuoi, possiamo aiutare con i bagagli.
native_language_example: If you want, we can help with the luggage.

meaning: "we can go" / "can we go?" (permission or possibility).
additional_notes: Used to talk about being able to go somewhere, or asking for permission to leave/go. Often followed by a destination with "a" (possiamo andare a casa/a scuola) or "in/nel" (possiamo andare nel cortile). In questions, intonation (or a question mark in writing) makes it mean “Can we go?”; as a statement it means “We can go.” Related: "ce ne possiamo andare" = “we can leave / we can go away.”
target_language_example: Se hai finito, possiamo andare.
native_language_example: If you’re done, we can go.

additional_notes: Formed by possiamo (we can) + fare (to do/make). Used to say what is possible/feasible (“we can do this”) or to ask about options (“Possiamo fare qualcosa?”). Often followed by an object (qualcosa, questo) or an activity (un passo, una pausa). In contexts like “non possiamo fare più niente”, it means “there’s nothing more we can do.”
target_language_example: Possiamo fare una pausa adesso?
native_language_example: Can we take a break now?

meaning: "can we do to ...?" / "what can we do to ...?"
additional_notes: Used to ask what actions are possible in order to achieve a goal. It’s often followed by an infinitive (per aiutare, per fermare, per risolvere) or a noun (per te, per il problema). In questions, it commonly appears as: Che cosa possiamo fare per...? / Come possiamo fare per...?
target_language_example: Che cosa possiamo fare per risolvere questo problema?
native_language_example: What can we do to solve this problem?

additional_notes: From the verb "fidarsi" = "to trust." It’s used with "di" before a person/pronoun/thing you trust: "fidarsi di qualcuno/qualcosa". "Possiamo" means "we can" (also "can we" in questions). With a pronoun, use: "possiamo fidarci di lui/lei/loro"; often "di" + name: "possiamo fidarci di Maria".
target_language_example: Possiamo fidarci di questo sito?
native_language_example: Can we trust this website?

additional_notes: Used to ask for permission or possibility to talk, often meaning “Can we talk (for a moment/in private)?” If you add an object, you specify who you want to talk to: "Possiamo parlare con lui/lei/loro?" (= Can we talk to him/her/them?). With "di" you specify the topic: "Possiamo parlare di..." (= Can we talk about...?).
target_language_example: Scusa, possiamo parlare un attimo?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can we talk for a moment?

additional_notes: Used to talk about how likely something is to happen. Often followed by a noun (possibilità di successo = chance of success) or by an infinitive verb (possibilità di vincere/essere eletto/salvarsi = chance of winning/being elected/saving oneself). Common with negatives and quantifiers: nessuna/alcuna possibilità di (no chance of), qualche possibilità di (some chance of), una possibilità di (a chance of).
target_language_example: Abbiamo ancora una possibilità di finire in tempo.
native_language_example: We still have a chance of finishing on time.

additional_notes: Used to offer help or say you’re able to help. In questions, you’ll often hear it as **Posso aiutare?** (“Can I help?”). With the formal polite object pronoun, **La posso aiutare?** means “Can I help you?” (to a stranger/customer). With an informal person you can say **Ti posso aiutare?**.
target_language_example: Posso aiutare con le valigie?
native_language_example: Can I help with the suitcases?

meaning: “Can I help you?” (formal, to a woman / using polite ‘Lei’).
additional_notes: Used in customer service, phone calls, or when speaking politely to someone you don’t know well. It literally means “I can help you,” but in questions like “Come posso aiutarla?” it’s the standard formal way to offer help. The pronoun “-la” refers to “her/you (formal).” For a man you can also hear “posso aiutarla?” (still Lei), and informally with friends you’d usually say “posso aiutarti?”
target_language_example: Buongiorno, posso aiutarla?
native_language_example: Good morning, can I help you?

meaning: "Can I go?" / "May I go?" or "I can go."
additional_notes: Used to ask for permission or possibility to go somewhere or do something (often as a question: "Posso andare...?"), and it can also state ability/possibility ("Posso andare in treno" = "I can go by train"). With a destination it often uses a preposition: "a" + place (Posso andare al bagno?), "in" + means of transport (Posso andare in treno). For "to leave" (go away), you’ll often hear "posso andarmene" or "me ne posso andare".
target_language_example: Scusi, posso andare via un momento?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I step out for a moment?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask for something (information or an item). Very common in cafés, shops, and service situations. Often followed by a noun: “Posso avere un caffè?” You can add “per favore/per piacere” to sound more polite.
target_language_example: Posso avere un bicchiere d’acqua, per favore?
native_language_example: Can I have a glass of water, please?

meaning: “Can I have a …?” (polite way to ask for something).
additional_notes: Used to request an item or a serving (often in cafés, restaurants, shops, or at an event). It’s a polite, common formula; you can also use it with feminine nouns: “Posso avere una…?” (e.g., una bottiglia). Often preceded by “Scusi/Scusami/Scusatemi” to be extra polite.
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere un bicchiere d’acqua, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have a glass of water, please?

meaning: “Can I have a…?” / “May I have a…?” (polite request).
additional_notes: Used to ask for something you want to receive (a drink, an item, a document, an opinion). It’s often followed by a noun: “Posso avere una birra…?”, “Posso avere una lista…?”, “Posso avere una seconda opinione?”. Add “per favore” or “per piacere” to be extra polite. The “una” changes with gender/number: “un” (masc. singular), “una” (fem. singular), “due” + plural (e.g., “Posso avere due biglietti?”).
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere una bottiglia d’acqua?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have a bottle of water?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone is reliable or willing to help. It’s the verb phrase “contare su” (to count on / rely on) with “posso” (can I). Often followed by a person (su Tom, su di lei) or by an action: “Posso contare su di te per…” (Can I count on you to…). “su di lei” is formal (“you” = Lei).
target_language_example: Posso contare su di te domani mattina?
native_language_example: Can I count on you tomorrow morning?

additional_notes: Used when you’ll see someone and want to relay a message to them for another person. Very common with an indirect object pronoun: gli posso dare un messaggio? (to him), le posso dare un messaggio? (to her). You can also name the person: Posso dare un messaggio a Tom?
target_language_example: Certo, posso dargli un messaggio quando lo vedo.
native_language_example: Sure, I can pass him a message when I see him.

meaning: "can I give you" / "I can give you" (offering to give someone something).
additional_notes: Used to offer something to someone (an object, information, help, or even a ride: "posso darti un passaggio"). It can be a question ("Posso darti...?" = "Can I give you...?") or a statement ("Posso darti..." = "I can give you..."). The pronoun "-ti" means "to you" (informal singular).
target_language_example: Se vuoi, posso darti una mano con i compiti.
native_language_example: If you want, I can give you a hand with your homework.

meaning: “can I say?” / “I can say” / “what can I say?”
additional_notes: From the verb *potere* (“can/to be able to”) + *dire* (“to say”). Used to ask for permission or possibility to say something (*Posso dire una cosa?*), to express uncertainty about whether you should say something (*Non so se posso dire…*), or in the fixed, common expression *Cosa posso dire?* meaning “What can I say?” (often implying “there’s not much to add”). In negatives, it often becomes *non posso dire…* (“I can’t say…”).
target_language_example: Non so se posso dire la verità, ma ci proverò.
native_language_example: I don’t know if I can tell the truth, but I’ll try.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "potere" (posso = I can) + "fare" (to do/make). Used to talk about ability or possibility ("Lo posso fare più tardi" = I can do it later) and also to ask permission/offers ("Posso fare una doccia?" = Can I take a shower?; "Posso fare qualsiasi cosa per te?" = Can I do anything for you?). Often followed by a noun (fare una doccia) or by a direct object pronoun (lo/la) in front of "posso" ("Lo posso fare"). In "Ce la posso fare", it means "I can manage / I can make it."
target_language_example: Posso fare una domanda?
native_language_example: Can I ask a question?

meaning: 'what can I do to/for …?' (asking how to help or achieve something).
additional_notes: Used when asking what action you can take to help someone or to reach a goal, usually followed by an infinitive (e.g., "aiutare", "migliorare") or by a person/pronoun ("te", "Lei"). Very common in polite help-offers: "Che cosa posso fare per aiutarla?" (formal).
target_language_example: Che cosa posso fare per aiutarti?
native_language_example: What can I do to help you?

meaning: "can I do for you?" / "what can I do for you?" (offering help).
additional_notes: Used to offer help or ask what someone needs. With "per te" it’s the informal "you" (tu). In polite/formal situations, you’ll often hear "Cosa posso fare per Lei?". The phrase can sound neutral and helpful in customer service, but tone and extra words (e.g., swearing) can make it aggressive.
target_language_example: Buongiorno, cosa posso fare per te?
native_language_example: Good morning, what can I do for you?

meaning: May I ask you a question? (formal)
additional_notes: Used to politely ask permission to ask a question in formal situations. "farle" = "fare" (to ask/make) + "Le" (to you, formal). You can add an adjective to specify the type: "una domanda personale" (a personal question), "indiscreta" (nosy), etc. Informal version: "Posso farti una domanda?"
target_language_example: Mi scusi, posso farle una domanda?
native_language_example: Excuse me, may I ask you a question?

meaning: “Can I do it?” / “I can do it.”
additional_notes: From the verb phrase “potere + fare” (“to be able to do”). It can be a question asking for permission or possibility (“Posso farlo?” = “Can I do it?/May I do it?”) or a statement of ability (“Posso farlo oggi.” = “I can do it today.”). The pronoun “lo” means “it” (a previously mentioned thing). You can add a time or method: “oggi”, “adesso”, “in modo diverso”.
target_language_example: Non posso farlo adesso, ma posso farlo più tardi.
native_language_example: I can’t do it now, but I can do it later.

additional_notes: Used to offer instruction: posso = “I can”, insegnare = “to teach”, come = “how”. It’s normally followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., come guidare = “how to drive”). Often includes an object pronoun before posso (e.g., Le posso… = “I can teach you…” formal; vi posso… = “I can teach you all…”).
target_language_example: Ti posso insegnare come cucinare la pasta.
native_language_example: I can teach you how to cook pasta.

meaning: “I can teach you (formal) to …” / “I can teach her to …”.
additional_notes: Used to offer or say you are able to teach someone how to do something. The pronoun **-le** means “to her” or “to you” when speaking formally with **Lei** (it can also be used formally for “to him”). It’s followed by **a + infinitive** (e.g., *a cantare* = “to sing”).
target_language_example: Posso insegnarle a cucinare un piatto semplice.
native_language_example: I can teach you (formal) to cook a simple dish.

additional_notes: Used to offer to teach a skill. "posso" = I can; "insegnarvi" = teach you (to you all / to you in formal "voi"); followed by "a" + an infinitive verb (e.g., scrivere, tradurre, cantare). In everyday modern Italian, for one person you’ll more often hear "posso insegnarti a…" (informal "tu") or "posso insegnarle a…" (formal "Lei").
target_language_example: Se vuoi, posso insegnarvi a cucinare piatti semplici.
native_language_example: If you want, I can teach you to cook simple dishes.

meaning: “Can I speak?” / “May I speak?” (also: “I can speak.”).
additional_notes: Most often used to ask permission to speak or to speak with someone (Posso parlare con…?). Add polite words like “per favore / per piacere”. “Non posso parlare ora” means “I can’t talk right now.” Without “con + person”, it can mean you’re able/allowed to speak (e.g., “Posso parlare.” = “I can speak.”).
target_language_example: Scusi, posso parlare con lei un momento?
native_language_example: Excuse me, may I speak with you for a moment?

additional_notes: Used to ask permission to speak with someone, especially on the phone or in a polite request. Follow with a name or a person: "Posso parlare con Mike?" / "Posso parlare con il direttore?". With pronouns it changes: "con lei" (formal you/her), "con te" (informal you), "con voi" (you all or formal you in some regions). Often paired with "per favore".
target_language_example: Buongiorno, posso parlare con la responsabile, per favore?
native_language_example: Good morning, can I speak to the manager, please?

additional_notes: "Posso" = "I can" (also used to ask "Can I...?"), and "portare" = "to bring/carry/take". Use it for bringing objects ("Posso portare un messaggio"), taking something somewhere ("Lo posso portare al parco"), or taking someone somewhere ("Ti posso portare da lei" = "I can take you to her"). Common patterns: "Posso portare X?" (Can I bring X?), "Posso portare X a casa?" (Can I bring X home?), "Posso portare X a lui/lei?" (Can I bring X to him/her?), "Posso portarti..." (Can I take you...).
target_language_example: Posso portare il vino alla cena?
native_language_example: Can I bring the wine to dinner?

meaning: “Can I bring you…?” / “Can I take you…?”
additional_notes: "Posso" = "can I". "portarti" is "to bring/take you" (to you / with you), so the exact meaning depends on context: (1) offering to bring someone something: "Posso portarti qualcosa/altro?" (2) offering to take someone somewhere: "Posso portarti al parco/da loro." Common in everyday speech when offering help, like a waiter asking what to bring.
target_language_example: Posso portarti un bicchiere d’acqua?
native_language_example: Can I bring you a glass of water?

additional_notes: Used to ask permission or possibility to take/get something. In cafés/restaurants it often means “May I have…?” (ordering). With extra words it can form common expressions like “prendere cura di” = “take care of.”
target_language_example: Scusi, posso prendere un caffè e un cornetto?
native_language_example: Excuse me, may I have a coffee and a croissant?

additional_notes: Used to ask permission to borrow something temporarily. Very common in polite requests; you can make it more formal by using Lei forms (e.g., i suoi / il suo). Often followed by an object and a time expression (per un minuto, per un momento, per oggi).
target_language_example: Scusa, posso prendere in prestito la tua penna per un attimo?
native_language_example: Sorry, can I borrow your pen for a moment?

posso prendere in prestito il vostro

target_language_multi_word_term: posso prendere in prestito il vostro
additional_notes: Used to politely ask to borrow something from the person you’re addressing. “Prendere in prestito” = “to borrow.” “Il vostro” agrees with a masculine singular noun (il coltello, il computer, il laptop); for feminine singular use “la vostra” (la penna), masculine plural “i vostri,” feminine plural “le vostre.” You can add the item after it: “Posso prendere in prestito il vostro coltello?”
target_language_example: Scusi, posso prendere in prestito il vostro caricabatterie?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I borrow your charger?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask to borrow an object. Literally “can I take it on loan.” Often followed by a time limit: “per un secondo/un minuto/per quanto tempo…”. Use “Scusa” (informal) or “Scusi” (formal) to sound more polite.
target_language_example: Posso prenderlo in prestito per un attimo?
native_language_example: Can I borrow it for a moment?

additional_notes: Used to ask for something that belongs to you to be returned. You normally add the noun after it (e.g., “Posso riavere il mio telefono?”). If the item is feminine, change it to “la mia” (e.g., “Posso riavere la mia borsa?”).
target_language_example: Scusi, posso riavere il mio passaporto?
