native_language_example: After work, she washed her hands and changed clothes.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the reflexive verb "lavarsi" (to wash oneself). It uses "essere" as the helper verb: "si è" + past participle "lavato" (masculine singular; for a woman: "si è lavata"). Often used with body parts using the definite article: "si è lavato le mani/i denti" = "he washed his hands/ brushed his teeth." You may also see "si è lavato via ..." meaning "he washed ... off".
target_language_example: Dopo il lavoro si è lavato le mani.
native_language_example: After work he washed his hands.

additional_notes: Used with the passato prossimo (auxiliary essere) plus "mai". Very common in negatives: "non si è mai ..." = "(someone) never ... / has never ...". In questions it often means "Have you ever ...?". "Si" can be reflexive (talking about a specific person: "Lui non si è mai preoccupato") or impersonal/passive-like (general/unspecified subject: "Non si è mai fatto male" = "No one ever got hurt").
target_language_example: Ti si è mai perso il passaporto?
native_language_example: Have you ever lost your passport?

meaning: “she put on / she put (herself)”, past tense of mettersi.
additional_notes: Feminine singular form (for “lei/she”) in the passato prossimo. Commonly used with clothing: si è messa le calze = “she put on her socks.” Also appears in set phrases like si è messa in contatto con… = “she got in touch with…”. (Masculine: si è messo; plural: si sono messi/messe.)
target_language_example: Si è messa la giacca perché faceva freddo.
native_language_example: She put on her jacket because it was cold.

meaning: "he/she put on" (clothes) or "he/she put" (something on/into something).
additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the reflexive verb "mettersi". Very common with clothing: "si è messo i pantaloni / gli stivali" = "he put on his pants/boots". It’s also used for placing things on/into somewhere, often with pockets: "si è messo le mani in tasca" = "he put his hands in his pockets"; "si è messo la macchina fotografica in tasca" = "he put the camera in his pocket". For other subjects: "mi sono messo" (I put on), "ti sei messo" (you put on), "ci siamo messi" (we put on).
target_language_example: Si è messo il cappotto prima di uscire.
native_language_example: He put on his coat before going out.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the reflexive verb **nascondersi** = “to hide (oneself)”. Used when a female subject (lei) hid somewhere: *Si è nascosta dietro la mamma.* It can also mean “she hid/covered” a body part from view: *Si è nascosta il volto* = “She hid/covered her face.” (With a male subject you’d say **si è nascosto**.)
target_language_example: Quando ha sentito il rumore, si è nascosta sotto il tavolo.
native_language_example: When she heard the noise, she hid under the table.

meaning: "he hid" / "he has hidden" (past tense of "to hide").
additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "nascondersi" = "to hide oneself". Used with "essere" as the helper verb: (lui) si è nascosto; (lei) si è nascosta; (loro) si sono nascosti/nascoste. Often followed by a place with prepositions like "dietro" (behind), "tra" (among), "nel/nel/la" (in the).
target_language_example: Quando ha sentito un rumore, si è nascosto dietro la porta.
native_language_example: When he heard a noise, he hid behind the door.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "offrirsi di" = to offer oneself/volunteer to do something. It’s used with a verb in the infinitive after "di": "si è offerto di aiutare". The subject changes the helper verb and ending: "mi sono offerto/a di..." (I offered), "ti sei offerto/a" (you), "si è offerto" (he), "si è offerta" (she), "ci siamo offerti/e" (we). You can also use it in questions and negatives: "Si è offerto di...?" / "Non si è offerto di...".
target_language_example: Giulia si è offerta di accompagnarmi alla stazione.
native_language_example: Giulia offered to take me to the station.

meaning: "(he/she/it) got lost" or "(he/she/it) is lost"; also "(he/she/it) was lost" (depending on context).
additional_notes: Past tense of "perdersi" (to get lost). It uses "essere" as the auxiliary verb: "si è perso/a". The ending agrees with the person: "si è perso" (male), "si è persa" (female). Can be literal (physically lost: in a forest, desert) or figurative (something like "a part of him/her was lost").
target_language_example: Mi sa che Luca si è perso: non trova più la strada per tornare a casa.
native_language_example: I think Luca got lost: he can’t find the way back home.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the reflexive verb "prendersi". It’s used when someone takes something for themselves or assumes responsibility: "si è preso la colpa" (he took the blame), "si è preso una giornata libera" (he took a day off), "si è preso il tempo" (he took the time). It can also appear in set expressions like "si è preso gioco di..." = "he made fun of..." (idiomatic).
target_language_example: Marco si è preso la responsabilità dell’errore.
native_language_example: Marco took responsibility for the mistake.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the verb phrase “prendersi cura di” = “to take care of”. It’s reflexive and uses “essere”, so the past participle agrees with the subject: si è preso (male), si è presa (female), si sono presi/e (plural). Followed by “di” + a person/thing: “si è preso cura di suo nonno” = “he took care of his grandfather”.
target_language_example: Dopo l’operazione, si è presa cura di sua madre per due settimane.
native_language_example: After the operation, she took care of her mother for two weeks.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of the reflexive verb "rifiutarsi di" + infinitive. It’s used to say someone would not do something (often a firm decision). It changes with the subject: "mi sono rifiutato/a di" (I refused to), "si è rifiutato di" (he refused to), "si sono rifiutati/e di" (they refused to).
target_language_example: Si è rifiutata di rispondere alle domande.
native_language_example: She refused to answer the questions.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the reflexive verb "rifiutarsi di" = “to refuse to.” It’s used with a following infinitive (di + verb), e.g. "si è rifiutato di parlare". Change the ending to match the subject: "mi sono rifiutato/a" (I refused), "ti sei rifiutato/a" (you refused), "si è rifiutato/a" (he/she refused), "ci siamo rifiutati/e" (we refused), "si sono rifiutati/e" (they refused). In compound tenses with "essere," the past participle agrees in gender/number (rifiutato/rifiutata/rifiutati/rifiutate).
target_language_example: Si è rifiutato di rispondere alle domande.
native_language_example: He refused to answer the questions.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of rompersi (to break). Used for a feminine subject: a woman (lei) or a feminine noun like la tazza, la coppa. With body parts it means someone broke a bone (e.g., si è rotta una gamba = she broke her leg). The masculine version is si è rotto.
target_language_example: La sedia si è rotta mentre mi sedevo.
native_language_example: The chair broke while I was sitting down.

additional_notes: Uses the reflexive verb "rompersi" (to break a body part) with "essere" in the passato prossimo. The past participle agrees with the person: "si è rotta" (female), "si è rotto" (male). With body parts, Italian usually uses the definite article: "il braccio" (= the arm) instead of a possessive ("my/her").
target_language_example: Si è rotta il braccio giocando a calcio.
native_language_example: She broke her arm playing soccer.

meaning: "the ... broke" / "the ... is broken" (for a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb *rompersi* (“to break”) in the *passato prossimo*: *si è rotta* agrees with a feminine singular thing (*la teiera, la videocamera*). It can describe something that stopped working or got damaged. With body parts you’ll often see it like: *Si è rotta la caviglia* = “She/He broke her/his ankle” (Italian commonly uses the body part with *la/il* instead of a possessive).
target_language_example: Si è rotta la stampante.
native_language_example: The printer broke / is broken.

additional_notes: Past tense of rompersi (to break). Used with the auxiliary essere and often refers to something that broke on its own (especially machines/things): Il computer si è rotto. With body parts it means “to break (a bone)”: Si è rotto una costola (“He broke a rib”). The subject can come after the verb: Si è rotto il computer.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, si è rotto l’ascensore.
native_language_example: Sorry, the elevator is broken.

additional_notes: Common way to say someone has broken an arm. It uses the past tense with essere (si è rotto/si è rotta). The reflexive pronoun si is used with body parts in Italian: literally “broke the arm (to himself/herself)”, meaning “broke his/her arm.” For a named person: “Tom si è rotto il braccio.” For a woman: “Si è rotta il braccio.”
target_language_example: Marta è caduta e si è rotta il braccio.
native_language_example: Marta fell and broke her arm.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the reflexive verb *rompersi* (“to break [a body part]”). Used when someone breaks a part of their own body in an accident. You can change the person: *mi sono rotto/a la gamba* (I broke my leg), *ti sei rotto/a la gamba* (you broke your leg), *si sono rotti/e la gamba* (they broke their leg).
target_language_example: Luca si è rotto la gamba giocando a calcio.
native_language_example: Luca broke his leg playing soccer.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the reflexive expression “schiarirsi la gola” = “to clear one’s throat,” often said when someone does it before starting to speak. It changes with the subject: mi sono schiarito/a la gola (I), si è schiarito/a la gola (he/she), ci siamo schiariti/e la gola (we), si sono schiariti/e la gola (they). The past participle agrees with the person (schiarito = masculine, schiarita = feminine).
target_language_example: Mi sono schiarito la gola e ho iniziato a parlare.
native_language_example: I cleared my throat and started speaking.

meaning: “he forgot to …” (he didn’t remember to do something).
additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the verb scordarsi di (“to forget to”). Used when someone fails to do an action: si è scordato di + infinitive (e.g., chiudere, lavarsi, venire, invitare). Often interchangeable with si è dimenticato di.
target_language_example: Mi sono scordato di chiamarti ieri sera.
native_language_example: I forgot to call you last night.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the reflexive verb scusarsi (“to apologize”). Used for a male subject (lui): si è scusato. For a female subject: si è scusata. Often followed by con + person (si è scusato con loro = he apologized to them) or per + reason (si è scusato per essere in ritardo = he apologized for being late).
target_language_example: Marco si è scusato con me per il suo errore.
native_language_example: Marco apologized to me for his mistake.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "scusarsi" (to apologize), used with "per" to introduce what the person is apologizing for (a noun or an action). You can change the subject and auxiliary: "mi sono scusato/a per" (I apologized for), "ti sei scusato/a per" (you apologized for), "si è scusato" (he), "si è scusata" (she), "ci siamo scusati/e" (we), "si sono scusati/e" (they). Before a verb, Italian often uses an infinitive: "per essere..." / "per non essere...".
target_language_example: Mi sono scusato per l’errore.
native_language_example: I apologized for the mistake.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "sedersi" (to sit down), used with "essere": "(lui) si è seduto". Often followed by "per" + infinitive to say why someone sat down (e.g., "si è seduto per leggere"). You can add where someone sat with "su" (on), "davanti a" (in front of), or "al" (at the).
target_language_example: Si è seduto al tavolo per mangiare.
native_language_example: He sat down at the table to eat.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of the reflexive verb "sposarsi" (to get married), 3rd person singular feminine. Use "a" for place or age/time (e.g., "si è sposata a Roma", "a diciassette anni") and "con" for the person (e.g., "si è sposata con un americano").
target_language_example: Si è sposata con Luca l'anno scorso.
native_language_example: She got married to Luca last year.

meaning: “he got married to a …” / “(he) married a …” (past).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "sposarsi" (to get married). "Si è sposato" is the passato prossimo (past) and usually refers to a man: “he got married.” It’s followed by "con" + a noun phrase (often introduced by "una" = “a”), e.g., "con una ragazza" (to a girl), "con una canadese" (to a Canadian woman), "con una vedova" (to a widow). For a woman you’d say "si è sposata con un/una...".
target_language_example: Marco si è sposato con una dottoressa italiana.
native_language_example: Marco got married to an Italian doctor.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the reflexive verb *suicidarsi* (“to commit suicide”). Uses *essere* as the auxiliary: *si è suicidata* (female), *si è suicidato* (male). Often followed by *ieri* (“yesterday”) or by a gerund describing how: *impiccandosi* (“by hanging herself”), *prendendo del veleno* (“by taking poison”). You can also add a cause with *a causa di…* (“because of…”).
target_language_example: Maria si è suicidata la settimana scorsa.
native_language_example: Maria committed suicide last week.

additional_notes: Past tense of the reflexive verb *suicidarsi* (“to commit suicide”), formed with *essere*: *si è suicidato*. The past participle agrees with the subject: masculine *si è suicidato*; feminine *si è suicidata*. You can add a reason with *per* (“because of”): *si è suicidato per la depressione*.
target_language_example: Marco si è suicidato l'anno scorso.
native_language_example: Marco killed himself last year.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the reflexive verb "svegliarsi" (to wake up). "Si" is the reflexive pronoun and "è" is the auxiliary used with reflexive verbs. "Svegliata" agrees with a feminine subject (lei / a feminine noun like "la gatta"). For a masculine subject: "si è svegliato"; plural: "si è svegliata/e" (f.), "si sono svegliati" (m./mixed). Often used with time expressions like "a che ora" or "nel bel mezzo della notte".
target_language_example: Si è svegliata presto perché doveva andare al lavoro.
native_language_example: She woke up early because she had to go to work.

meaning: “he woke up / he has woken up.”
additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of svegliarsi = “to wake up,” used for a male subject. It’s a reflexive verb, so it uses essere as the helping verb (si + è + past participle). For a female subject: si è svegliata. You can also use it without naming the subject if it’s clear from context.
target_language_example: Quando ho chiamato, si è svegliato subito.
native_language_example: When I called, he woke up right away.

additional_notes: Reflexive past tense of tagliarsi (“to cut oneself”), using essere as the auxiliary: si + è + tagliata (feminine singular). Often followed by a body part: si è tagliata il dito/la mano/la gamba. You can add the cause/instrument with con: si è tagliata con un coltello.
target_language_example: Si è tagliata il dito mentre cucinava.
native_language_example: She cut her finger while she was cooking.

meaning: “she took off / removed” (something she was wearing or had on).
additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the reflexive verb *togliersi* (“to take off” clothes/accessories). Used for things you remove from yourself: *si è tolta la giacca*, *si è tolta gli occhiali*. The feminine ending *-a* shows the subject is a woman/girl; for a man you’d say *si è tolto*.
target_language_example: Quando è entrata in casa, si è tolta il cappotto.
native_language_example: When she came into the house, she took off her coat.

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb **togliersi** (“to take off/remove from oneself”). In the **passato prossimo**, it uses **essere**: *si è tolta* (for a female subject). The past participle agrees with the subject: *si è tolta* (she), *si è tolto* (he), *si sono tolti/e* (they). The article changes with the noun: *si è tolta il casco*, *si è tolta la giacca*, *si è tolti i vestiti* (plural).
target_language_example: Dopo il lavoro, si è tolta la giacca.
native_language_example: After work, she took off her jacket.

meaning: “he took off / removed (something)” (about himself, e.g., clothes).
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of the reflexive verb "togliersi" (to take off). Used when someone removes something they are wearing (helmet, clothes, hat, shirt, etc.). It agrees with the item removed: "si è tolto" (masc. sing.), "si è tolta" (fem. sing.), "si è tolti" (masc. plural), "si è tolte" (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Dopo l’allenamento, si è tolto le scarpe.
native_language_example: After training, he took off his shoes.

meaning: "(he/she) took off" (an item of clothing or something worn).
additional_notes: Past tense with the reflexive verb "togliersi" (to take off from oneself). It’s used before a masculine singular noun with "il" (e.g., il casco, il cappello, il cappotto). For feminine nouns you change the article: "si è tolta la giacca". In the passato prossimo it agrees with the subject: "si è tolto" (he), "si è tolta" (she), "si sono tolti/e" (they).
target_language_example: Appena entrato in casa, si è tolto il cappotto.
native_language_example: As soon as he came into the house, he took off his coat.

additional_notes: Used with body-worn items in the passato prossimo. It’s the verb "togliersi" (to take off something you’re wearing), so it takes "essere" as the auxiliary and agrees with the subject: "si è tolto" (he took off), "si è tolta" (she took off), "si sono tolti/e" (they took off). The thing removed follows, usually plural with an article (e.g., le calze, le cuffie).
target_language_example: Dopo il lavoro, si è tolto le scarpe.
native_language_example: After work, he took off his shoes.

meaning: “(he) moved” / “(he) has moved” (to a new home/city).
additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the reflexive verb trasferirsi (“to move/relocate”). Used with essere: si è trasferito = “he moved”; si è trasferita = “she moved”; mi sono trasferito/a = “I moved”. Often followed by a place with a: si è trasferito a Boston, or into an area with in: si è trasferito nel mio quartiere.
target_language_example: Marco si è trasferito a Milano l'anno scorso.
native_language_example: Marco moved to Milan last year.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the reflexive verb *trasferirsi* = “to move/relocate.” Use it with a place introduced by *a* (typically cities/countries): *si è trasferito a Boston*. For a woman: *si è trasferita a…*. Plural: *si sono trasferiti/e a…*.
target_language_example: Marco si è trasferito a Milano per lavoro.
native_language_example: Marco moved to Milan for work.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the reflexive verb trasformarsi in (“to transform into”). It uses essere as the helping verb, so the past participle agrees with the subject: si è trasformato (masc. sg.), si è trasformata (fem. sg.), si sono trasformati (masc. pl.), si sono trasformate (fem. pl.). Used for both literal changes (snow into water) and figurative ones (something became a trend).
target_language_example: Con il caldo, il ghiaccio si è trasformato in acqua.
native_language_example: With the heat, the ice turned into water.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the reflexive verb *ubriacarsi* (“to get drunk”). It changes with the subject: *mi sono ubriacato/a* (I got drunk), *ti sei ubriacato/a* (you got drunk), *si è ubriacato* (he got drunk), *si è ubriacata* (she got drunk), *ci siamo ubriacati/e* (we got drunk), *si sono ubriacati/e* (they got drunk). The past participle agrees in gender/number (*ubriacato/ubriacata/ubriacati/ubriacate*). You can add what they drank with *di*: *si è ubriacato di tequila* (“he got drunk on tequila”).
target_language_example: Marco si è ubriacato alla festa.
native_language_example: Marco got drunk at the party.

additional_notes: Reflexive form of **uccidersi** (“to kill oneself”), in the **passato prossimo**. **Si** = “herself,” and **è** is used because reflexive verbs take *essere* as the auxiliary. **Uccisa** agrees with a female subject (for a man: **si è ucciso**). Often used as a factual statement; you may also hear **si è suicidata** (“she committed suicide”).
target_language_example: Dicono che si è uccisa perché era disperata.
native_language_example: They say she killed herself because she was desperate.

meaning: 'he joined the' / 'he became part of the'.
additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "unirsi a" = "to join". It agrees with the subject: mi sono unito/a, ti sei unito/a, si è unito (male) / si è unita (female), ci siamo uniti/e, vi siete uniti/e, si sono uniti/e. Used with groups/organizations/events (a team, church, revolt, family). You’ll often see it with "a" + article: "alla" (a+la), "al" (a+il), "ai" (a+i), "alle" (a+le).
target_language_example: Marco si è unito alla squadra ieri.
native_language_example: Marco joined the team yesterday.

meaning: 'he dressed up as' / 'he was dressed as' (a costume).
additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb *vestirsi* + *da* to say someone wore a costume or disguised themselves as something/someone, especially for events like Halloween or Carnival. It changes with the subject and tense (e.g., *mi sono vestito/a da…*, *si sono vestiti/e da…*).
target_language_example: Per la festa, si è vestito da pirata.
native_language_example: For the party, he dressed up as a pirate.

additional_notes: Used with the verb essere in the present subjunctive (sia) + ancora (“still”) after triggers like che / se, especially after verbs and expressions of opinion, doubt, wondering, or probability (e.g., penso che…, mi chiedo se…, è probabile che…). It refers to something continuing up to now.
target_language_example: Non credo che sia ancora aperto.
native_language_example: I don’t think it’s still open.

additional_notes: Used in clauses introduced by **che** after verbs like *pensare* (to think), *dubitare* (to doubt), or in questions: **che [someone] sia ancora in [place]**. **Sia** is the present subjunctive of *essere* (to be), often used when the main verb expresses uncertainty, opinion, or a question. It changes with the subject (e.g., *che io sia*, *che tu sia*, *che loro siano*).
target_language_example: Dubito che Maria sia ancora in ufficio.
native_language_example: I doubt that Maria is still in the office.

meaning: “(that she/you) had fun at the party.”
additional_notes: This is the past subjunctive (congiuntivo passato) of the reflexive verb divertirsi (“to have fun / enjoy oneself”). It’s commonly used after expressions like spero che… (“I hope that…”). Divertita is feminine singular (speaking to/about a woman); for a man you’d say sia divertito. With “tu” you often see the full form ti sia divertita; with “lei” it’s si sia divertita.
target_language_example: Spero che Maria si sia divertita alla festa.
native_language_example: I hope Maria had fun at the party.

additional_notes: Used with the present subjunctive (sia = 'be') after expressions like "voglio che..." (I want that...), "spero che..." (I hope that...), and questions/uncertainty like "mi chiedo se..." (I wonder if...). It typically refers to someone else’s happiness (lui/lei), not 'I am happy' (which is "sono felice").
target_language_example: Spero che tua sorella sia felice a scuola.
native_language_example: I hope your sister is happy at school.

meaning: "is innocent" (in the subjunctive, used after expressions of belief/opinion/doubt).
additional_notes: Used in sentences like "Credo/Penso che..." or questions like "Pensi che...?" to express an opinion, uncertainty, or belief: "che [someone] sia innocente" = "that [someone] is innocent". "sia" is the present subjunctive of "essere" (to be), triggered by verbs like credere/pensare (to believe/think).
target_language_example: Non credo che sia innocente.
native_language_example: I don’t think he/she is innocent.

additional_notes: Fixed, formal/exclamatory religious-style phrase using the subjunctive of essere (“sia” = “may it/he be”) + past participle “lodato” (“praised”). Commonly follows “Che …” (“May …”): “Che Dio sia lodato!” = “Praise be to God!” You can also invert it: “Sia lodato il Signore!”
target_language_example: Che il cielo sia lodato, siamo arrivati in tempo!
native_language_example: Thank heaven, we arrived on time!

meaning: “(that) he/she/it is dead” / “(that) he/she/it has died” (subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used after expressions that trigger the subjunctive, especially opinions, doubts, reactions, or reports: credo che…, pare che…, penso che…, non posso accettare che…. It refers to a third person singular (lui/lei/esso/ella). With a plural subject you’d use “siano morti/e”.
target_language_example: Spero che non sia morto.
native_language_example: I hope he isn’t dead.

additional_notes: Used mainly with the present subjunctive of *essere* (sia) after verbs like *pensare*, *credere*, *chiedersi* and expressions of doubt/opinion: *Pensi che Tom sia onesto?* = “Do you think Tom is honest?” It can also be a polite/formal command with *Lei*: *Per favore, sia onesto.* = “Please, be honest.”
target_language_example: Non credo che sia onesto con me.
native_language_example: I don't think he's being honest with me.

meaning: “has been / was” (subjunctive past of *essere*), used after “I think/it seems/people say that…”.
additional_notes: *Sia stato* is the **passato congiuntivo** of *essere* (formed with *sia* + *stato*). It appears in dependent clauses introduced by **che** after expressions of doubt, opinion, uncertainty, or report, like *credo/penso che…*, *sembra che…*, *si pensa che…*. In English it often becomes “was” or “has been,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Non credo che sia stato lui a rompere il vaso.
native_language_example: I don’t think it was him who broke the vase.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "succedere" (to happen) in the past subjunctive: "sia" + past participle "successo". It commonly appears after expressions like "non so / mi chiedo / nessuno sa" and question words like "cosa / quando / perché" to talk about something that happened (often with uncertainty). Don’t confuse "successo" here (happened) with the noun "il successo" (success).
target_language_example: Dimmi cosa sia successo ieri sera.
native_language_example: Tell me what happened last night.

meaning: “is too …” (subjunctive), used after expressions like “I think that…”.
additional_notes: It’s made of **sia** (present subjunctive of *essere*, “to be”, for *lui/lei/Lei*) + **troppo** (“too”). You typically see it after **che** with verbs of opinion or doubt: *penso che…, credo che…, non penso che…* followed by an adjective or adverb (e.g., *sia troppo stanco/lenta/caro*).
target_language_example: Credo che questo sia troppo difficile per me.
native_language_example: I think this is too difficult for me.

sia troppo grassa per essere una cheerleader

target_language_multi_word_term: sia troppo grassa per essere una cheerleader
meaning: “is too fat to be a cheerleader.”
additional_notes: This is a clause often used after verbs like “pensare che…” (“to think that…”). After “pensare che”, Italian commonly uses the subjunctive, so you get “sia” (subjunctive of “essere”) instead of “è”. Structure: “troppo + adjective + per + infinitive” = “too + adjective + to + verb” (“too fat to be…”). Note: “grassa” (“fat”) can sound insulting depending on context.
target_language_example: Non credo che Maria sia troppo grassa per essere una cheerleader.
native_language_example: I don’t think Maria is too fat to be a cheerleader.

meaning: “(that) … be a …” (present subjunctive of essere) or “Be a …” (formal command).
additional_notes: Used with verbs/expressions that introduce uncertainty, opinion, or appearance, often after che: Credo che…, Sembra che…, Sei convinto che…. Here sia is the present subjunctive of essere (to be) for lui/lei/Lei. It can also be a formal imperative (Lei): Sia un po’ più paziente. (Note: with a vowel you’ll see sia un’: sia un’idea brillante.)
target_language_example: Penso che sia un buon ristorante.
native_language_example: I think it’s a good restaurant.

meaning: 'is a bounty hunter' (subjunctive: 'be a bounty hunter').
additional_notes: Used inside a clause introduced by che, especially after expressions of doubt/uncertainty or in questions/negatives (e.g., Sei sicuro che…?, Non sono sicuro che…). Sia is the present subjunctive of essere (to be); un cacciatore di taglie means “a bounty hunter.”
target_language_example: Non sono sicuro che lui sia un cacciatore di taglie.
native_language_example: I'm not sure that he is a bounty hunter.

meaning: 'is a' (subjunctive), used after phrases like 'they say that…'.
additional_notes: 'Sia' is the present subjunctive of *essere* (to be). You often use it after verbs/expressions that introduce reported information, opinion, or uncertainty (e.g., *dicono che…*, *penso che…*, *sembra che…*). 'Una' agrees with a feminine singular noun that follows (e.g., *una stilista*).
target_language_example: Dicono che sia una brava insegnante.
native_language_example: They say she’s a good teacher.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like credere/pensare in sentences expressing opinion or doubt, especially with che (often optional in speech): Credo (che) sia una buona idea. With negation, Italian commonly uses the subjunctive: Non credo (che) sia una buona idea. On its own, sia is the present subjunctive of essere (“to be”) for lui/lei/Lei.
target_language_example: Non penso sia una buona idea uscire adesso.
native_language_example: I don’t think it’s a good idea to go out now.

meaning: "be that as it may" / "whatever it is".
additional_notes: Fixed, idiomatic expression used to move on from an uncertain or disputed detail: you acknowledge that something is unknown or doesn’t matter, then continue with the main point. It uses the subjunctive (sia) and often appears at the start of a sentence or between commas.
target_language_example: Sia quel che sia, dobbiamo prendere una decisione oggi.
native_language_example: Be that as it may, we have to make a decision today.

meaning: "both I and..." / "me and..." (together with someone else).
additional_notes: Used in the correlative construction "sia X che Y" meaning "both X and Y". It often comes at the start of the sentence: "Sia io che Tom...". The verb is usually plural because it refers to two subjects (io + someone else).
target_language_example: Sia io che mia sorella lavoriamo domani.
native_language_example: Both my sister and I are working tomorrow.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of “andare” (to go), formed with the auxiliary “essere”: siamo + andate. “Andate” agrees with the subject: use “siamo andate” for a group of women (or an all-female group); use “siamo andati” for men or mixed groups. Common with destinations, often followed by “a/in” (e.g., a scuola, in macchina) or “nel/al” (e.g., nel parco).
target_language_example: Dopo cena siamo andate al cinema.
native_language_example: After dinner we went to the cinema.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "andare" with "essere". "Andate" agrees with an all-female group (or a group referred to as feminine); for a mixed/all-male group you usually say "siamo andati a". Used before a destination (city, place): "siamo andate a Roma / al museo".
target_language_example: Ieri siamo andate a Roma per il weekend.
native_language_example: Yesterday we went to Rome for the weekend.

additional_notes: Used to say that a group of females went somewhere. Italian uses "essere" with the verb "andare" in the passato prossimo: "siamo andate". The past participle agrees with the subject: andate (feminine plural); for a mixed/masculine group you’d say "siamo andati". "al" = "a + il" and is used before a masculine singular noun (al museo, al castello, al ballo).
target_language_example: Dopo cena siamo andate al cinema.
native_language_example: After dinner we went to the cinema.

additional_notes: Used when the subject is a group of women/girls (or an all-female group) talking about going somewhere. Italian uses the auxiliary “essere” in the past: “siamo” + past participle “andate” (feminine plural). It’s commonly followed by “in” + a country/region or an activity/place (e.g., in Italia, in campeggio, in gita). If the group is mixed or all men, you usually say “siamo andati in”.
target_language_example: Siamo andate in Italia per una settimana.
native_language_example: We (women) went to Italy for a week.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of andare with essere: siamo (we are) + andati (gone). It agrees with the subject: siamo andati (mixed or all-male group), siamo andate (all-female group). Often followed by a place with a (a Roma), in (in spiaggia), or da (dal medico).
target_language_example: Ieri sera siamo andati al cinema.
native_language_example: Last night we went to the cinema.

meaning: “we went to / we went (in order) to …”
additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of “andare” with “essere”: siamo andati/e = “we went.” Used before a destination or event with “a” (siamo andati a Roma / a teatro / a una partita) and before an infinitive to express purpose: “siamo andati a + verb” = “we went to (do something)” (e.g., siamo andati a fare una passeggiata). Agree the ending with the group: andati (all male or mixed group), andate (all female).
target_language_example: Siamo andati a cena e poi siamo tornati a casa.
native_language_example: We went out to dinner and then we went back home.

meaning: 'we went to the' (masculine singular place, e.g., al museo/al teatro).
additional_notes: "Siamo andati" is the passato prossimo of "andare" for "noi" (we). Use it when talking about a completed trip/visit in the past. "Al" = "a" + "il" and is used before masculine singular nouns; for feminine singular you’d say "siamo andati alla" (e.g., alla stazione). Often used with places you visit or go to.
target_language_example: Ieri sera siamo andati al ristorante.
native_language_example: Last night we went to the restaurant.

additional_notes: Past tense with essere: "andare" forms the passato prossimo with "essere" → "siamo andati/e". Use "andati" for a group of all males or mixed genders; "andate" for all females. "In" is used with many destinations/contexts: countries and regions (in Belgio, in Australia), places/activities (in montagna, in terapia), and some set phrases like "andare in soccorso (di qualcuno)" = "to go to someone’s aid".
target_language_example: Ieri siamo andati in centro a fare una passeggiata.
native_language_example: Yesterday we went downtown to take a walk.

meaning: "we just…" / "we have just…" (used with the past tense).
additional_notes: Used with the passato prossimo to say something happened very recently. With many verbs, especially movement verbs, Italian uses essere as the auxiliary, so you’ll often see: siamo appena + past participle (e.g., siamo appena arrivati = we’ve just arrived). "Appena" typically goes between the auxiliary (siamo) and the past participle.
target_language_example: Siamo appena usciti di casa.
native_language_example: We’ve just left the house.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of arrivare: essere + arrivati. Used for reaching a place or arriving at an event. Agreement: arrivati (mixed/masculine plural); if the group is all female, say siamo arrivate.
target_language_example: Siamo arrivati in stazione in tempo.
native_language_example: We arrived at the station on time.

meaning: “we arrived at / we got to” (a place, a point in time, or a result).
additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "arrivare": "siamo" + "arrivati" (plural masculine/mixed; use "siamo arrivate" for an all-female group). Common with places ("siamo arrivati a Londra"), and figuratively for reaching an understanding/decision ("siamo arrivati a capirci", "siamo arrivati a un compromesso"). For cities you typically use "a"; for countries/regions you usually use "in" ("siamo arrivati in Italia").
target_language_example: Finalmente siamo arrivati a una decisione.
native_language_example: We finally reached a decision.

meaning: we met; we got to know each other.
additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the reflexive verb "conoscersi" = "to meet / to get to know each other." It’s often used with "ci" ("ci siamo conosciuti") and with a place or time: "a Boston", "ieri sera". You can also use it to mean you’ve been introduced and now know each other: "Ora ci siamo conosciuti".
target_language_example: Ci siamo conosciuti all’università e siamo diventati amici.
native_language_example: We met at university and became friends.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "entrare" for "noi". Used for entering a place (a building, a room, a city, a tunnel, etc.). It uses the auxiliary "essere", so the past participle agrees with the group: "siamo entrati" (mixed/men), "siamo entrate" (all women). Often followed by "in" or "nel/nella" + place: "siamo entrati in biblioteca", "siamo entrati nel tunnel". You can add how you entered: "siamo entrati gratis / gratuitamente" (we got in for free).
target_language_example: Siamo entrati in casa senza fare rumore.
native_language_example: We came into the house without making any noise.

meaning: “we are in / we’re on” (in a situation/mode), or “there are (number of us)” in a group.
additional_notes: Common pattern with essere: **siamo in + noun** to say you’re in a certain condition or mode (e.g., *in vivavoce* = on speakerphone, *in ritardo* = late, *in riunione* = in a meeting). It’s also used with numbers to say how many people are present: **siamo in otto** = there are eight of us / we’re eight (in total).
target_language_example: Parla piano: siamo in vivavoce.
native_language_example: Speak softly: we’re on speakerphone.

meaning: "we are annoyed/bothered by the noise of the ..."
additional_notes: Used to complain about a nuisance. "Siamo" = "we are"; "infastiditi" = "annoyed/bothered"; "dal" = "by the"; "rumore" = "noise"; "delle" = "of the" (feminine plural), so it’s followed by a feminine plural noun like "auto", "macchine", "automobili".
target_language_example: Siamo infastiditi dal rumore delle auto di notte.
native_language_example: We’re bothered by the noise of the cars at night.

additional_notes: Used to say that a group (including the speaker) is ready to do something, or to ask if everyone is ready. Often followed by “per” + infinitive (e.g., “per cominciare”, “per mangiare”). “Pronti” agrees with the group: mixed/all-male group “pronti”, all-female group “pronte”.
target_language_example: Ok, siamo pronti per andare!
native_language_example: OK, we’re ready to go!

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb (e.g., "fare", "partire") to say that a group is prepared or willing to do something. You can change "siamo" for other people: "sono pronti a" (they’re ready to), "sei pronto/a a" (you’re ready to), "sono pronta a" (I’m ready, feminine). Often implies both readiness and willingness; with "a tutto" it means “ready for anything / to do anything.”
target_language_example: Siamo pronti a partire quando vuoi.
native_language_example: We’re ready to leave whenever you want.

additional_notes: Used to say why you are present (purpose: "to...") or who/what you are supporting or dealing with ("for..."). In the sentences, it can mean being there to help someone ("per lei"), for a reason ("per questo"), or to do something like an appointment/visit ("per vedere..."). You can change the subject: "sono qui per" (I’m here to/for), "sei qui per" (you’re here to/for), "siamo qui per" (we’re here to/for).
target_language_example: Siamo qui per aiutarti.
native_language_example: We’re here to help you.

meaning: "we have been" (said by/for a group of women).
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of *essere* for **1st person plural** with a **feminine plural** past participle (*state*). Used when the speakers are all female, or when the group is grammatically feminine. Often followed by an adjective (*siamo state fortunate*), a place (*siamo state a Roma*), or in expressions like *siamo state in grado di...* (“we were able to...”). It can also be used in passive constructions (*siamo state citate* = “we were cited”).
target_language_example: Ieri siamo state molto occupate.
native_language_example: Yesterday we were very busy.

meaning: "we were" / "we have been"; also "we were" in the passive voice (="we were + past participle").
additional_notes: Form of the verb "essere" (to be): present "siamo" + past participle "stati". Used (1) as the past of "we are" ("We were/We have been...") and (2) to form the passive voice with another past participle: "siamo stati invitati" = "we were invited". Agreement: "stati" (masculine plural/mixed group) and "state" (feminine plural): "Siamo state pagate" = "We (women) were paid."
target_language_example: Siamo stati molto fortunati quel giorno.
native_language_example: We were very lucky that day.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of *tornare*: **essere** + past participle. It’s used when a group including the speaker has returned, often with places (**siamo tornati al motel**) or a reason (**siamo tornati per chiedere aiuto**). It agrees in gender/number: **siamo tornati** (mixed group or all men), **siamo tornate** (all women).
target_language_example: Scusa il ritardo: siamo tornati tardi a casa.
native_language_example: Sorry we’re late: we got back home late.

additional_notes: Used to say that something applies to everyone in a group. It’s often followed by an adjective or noun (e.g., “siamo tutti felici” = “we’re all happy”), but it can also stand alone (“Siamo tutti.” = “We’re all here / We’re all present,” depending on context).
target_language_example: Siamo tutti pronti?
native_language_example: Are we all ready?

meaning: we came; we have come (we arrived).
additional_notes: Past tense of "venire" (to come): "siamo" + past participle "venuti". Used for a completed action in the past ("we came") or for something connected to the present ("we have come / we’re here now"). You’ll often hear it with a purpose: "siamo venuti a..." = "we came to..." or with emphasis like "fin qui" (all the way here) and "apposta" (on purpose). "Venuti" is masculine plural; a group of only women would say "siamo venute".
target_language_example: Siamo venuti a prendere i biglietti.
native_language_example: We came to pick up the tickets.

meaning: "we came here to / we came here in order to".
additional_notes: Used to explain your purpose for coming somewhere. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., comprare, costruire, divertirci). Italian uses the past tense with essere: "siamo venuti" (masculine/mixed group) or "siamo venute" (all-female group). Often you can also say "sono venuto/a qui per" (I came here to).
target_language_example: Siamo venuti qui per chiedere informazioni.
native_language_example: We came here to ask for information.

additional_notes: Used after expressions like "voglio che…" (I want that…), "spero che…" (I hope that…), or questions/doubts, which typically trigger the present subjunctive in Italian. "Al sicuro" means "safe / out of danger."
target_language_example: È importante che i bambini siano al sicuro.
native_language_example: It’s important that the children are safe.

additional_notes: "Siano" is the present subjunctive of "essere" for "they" (loro). It’s commonly used after expressions like "penso che..." / "credi che..." / "è importante che..." where Italian often requires the subjunctive. "In salute" means “healthy / in good health.”
target_language_example: Spero che i nonni siano in salute.
native_language_example: I hope the grandparents are in good health.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *essere*: *sono/è sicura che…* (“I’m/she’s sure that…”). *Sicura* agrees with the speaker/subject: *sicuro* (masc. sing.), *sicura* (fem. sing.), *sicuri/sicure* (plural). After *che*, Italian often uses the subjunctive, especially for opinions/uncertainty: *Sono sicura che Tom sia…* (“I’m sure Tom is…”). Don’t confuse *sicuro/sicura* with “secure” in English: it usually means “sure/certain” here (though it can also mean “safe”).
target_language_example: Sei sicura che sia la strada giusta?
native_language_example: Are you sure this is the right road?

additional_notes: Used to describe a (female) person who feels confident and comfortable with herself. It often appears with “essere” (è sicura di sé) or “sembrare” (sembra sicura di sé). For a male person: “sicuro di sé”.
target_language_example: Dopo il colloquio, mi sento più sicura di me.
native_language_example: After the interview, I feel more confident.

meaning: "(are you) sure you want to...?" (female person).
additional_notes: Used to check or double-check someone’s decision. It agrees with the person you’re talking about: sicura (female), sicuro (male), sicuri/sicure (plural). With polite/formal "Lei", you often see: "È sicura di volere...". It’s usually followed by an infinitive (volere andare, volere fare) or by "che" + subjunctive (volere che ti aiuti...).
target_language_example: Sei sicura di volere partire adesso?
native_language_example: Are you sure you want to leave now?

additional_notes: Used with the verb essere (e.g., sono sicuro/a che…, sei sicuro/a che…) to say you’re confident something is true or will happen. It’s often followed by the subjunctive (sia, fosse, andrà, ritornerà), especially when expressing certainty about someone else or something not directly confirmed. You can also use it in questions: Sei sicuro che…? = Are you sure that…?
target_language_example: Sei sicuro che lui abbia capito?
native_language_example: Are you sure he understood?

meaning: (be) sure that it is / that it’s really…
additional_notes: Used after **(essere) sicuro** to introduce what you’re certain about. Italian typically uses the **subjunctive** here: **sia** = “(it) is” (subjunctive of *essere*). Often appears as a question to double-check or challenge: **Sicuro che sia…?** = “Are you sure it’s…?” You can also change the person: **sono/siete/è sicuro che sia…**
target_language_example: Sei sicuro che sia la strada giusta?
native_language_example: Are you sure this is the right road?

additional_notes: Used to say you are confident about something or that something will happen. Common patterns: (1) **essere sicuro di + infinitive**: *Sono sicuro di riuscire* = “I’m sure I’ll manage.” (2) **non essere sicuro di + question word (cosa/come/…)**: *Non ero sicuro di cosa fare* = “I wasn’t sure what to do.” In questions it often means **“Are you sure…?”**: *Sicuro di non volere…?*
target_language_example: Sei sicuro di voler uscire stasera?
native_language_example: Are you sure you want to go out tonight?

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who feels confident in themselves (their abilities, choices, or how they act). It agrees with the person: sicuro di sé (male), sicura di sé (female); plural: sicuri di sé / sicure di sé.
target_language_example: Nonostante l'esame, Marta era molto sicura di sé.
native_language_example: Despite the exam, Marta was very self-confident.

meaning: 'are you still...?' (addressing more than one person).
additional_notes: Used to ask if a situation/state continues. It’s the present tense of "essere" for "voi" (you plural / you all) + "ancora" = still/yet. Often followed by an adjective or phrase: "amici" (friends), "arrabbiati/e" (angry), "qui" (here), "single" (single), "con + name" (with someone), "assieme" (together).
target_language_example: Siete ancora in ufficio?
native_language_example: Are you still at the office?

additional_notes: Past tense with "essere" (passato prossimo) of "andare" for a group addressed as all female (or mixed gender in some contexts). Used to talk about where people went/have gone; often followed by a destination with "a" or "in" (e.g., "siete andate in Italia").
target_language_example: Dove siete andate ieri sera?
native_language_example: Where did you (all) go last night?

meaning: 'you (plural, feminine) went to' / 'you (plural, feminine) went to (do)'.
additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "andare" used with "essere": "siete andate" = "you went" when speaking to a group of women/girls (or a mixed group treated as feminine). "Andate" agrees in gender/number with the subject. Followed by a place ("a Boston") or by an infinitive to express purpose ("a vederlo" = "to see him/it").
target_language_example: Siete andate a mangiare fuori ieri sera?
native_language_example: Did you (all, feminine) go out to eat last night?

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "andare" with "essere": "siete" (you are) + past participle "andati". Used with "voi" (you all) or polite "Lei" in older/formal contexts when addressing more than one person. The past participle agrees with the subject: "siete andati" (male/mixed group), "siete andate" (all female). Often followed by a destination: "siete andati a casa / al lavoro / in chiesa".
target_language_example: Dove siete andati dopo la cena?
native_language_example: Where did you go after dinner?

additional_notes: Second-person plural of passato prossimo of arrivare (“to arrive”), used to talk about an arrival in the past with a present result (“you’re here now”). It’s also the polite/formal form for one person (Lei): “(have) you arrived?” Agreement: use arrivati for a group of all men or mixed; arrivate for a group of all women.
target_language_example: Siete arrivati in hotel?
native_language_example: Have you arrived at the hotel?

additional_notes: Used to comment on a quality or characteristic of more than one person (voi): “Siete” = “you are” (plural), and “così” intensifies the following adjective (“so”). The adjective agrees in gender/number with the people you’re talking to (alte/coraggiosi/fortunate, etc.).
target_language_example: Siete così gentili!
native_language_example: You’re so kind!

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of women (or an all-female group) if they are willing/ready to do something. It’s the present tense of *essere* + *disposte a* + infinitive. Use **siete disposti a** when speaking to men or a mixed group. **ad** is used before a vowel sound (e.g., *ad aiutare*, *ad imparare*), while **a** is used before most consonants.
target_language_example: Siete disposte ad aspettarmi cinque minuti?
native_language_example: Are you (women) willing to wait for me five minutes?

additional_notes: Used to ask if a group of people (or someone you address as “voi” for formality) is willing/ready to do something. It’s followed by a verb in the infinitive: "Siete disposti ad aiutare?". "Disposti" agrees with the group (mixed/men plural); for an all-female group you’ll often hear "Siete disposte a …".
target_language_example: Siete disposti ad aspettare cinque minuti?
native_language_example: Are you willing to wait five minutes?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s position on a proposal/idea/policy. Commonly followed by “a” + something: “Siete favorevoli o contrari a + [noun/idea]?” Here “siete” is 2nd person plural (“you all are”) and can also be used as the formal “you” in some contexts.
target_language_example: Siete favorevoli o contrari a questa proposta?
native_language_example: Are you in favor or against this proposal?

meaning: "Are you in favor or against (it)?" (addressing a group of women).
additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion/position on a proposal, idea, rule, etc. "Siete" = "you (plural) are". "Favorevoli" means "in favor" (same for mixed/all-male groups too). "Contrarie" is the feminine plural form of "contrario"; if you’re speaking to men or a mixed group, you usually say "siete favorevoli o contrari". It’s normally followed by "a" or "a + article" (a ciò, al/alla piano/idea, etc.).
target_language_example: Siete favorevoli o contrarie a questa proposta?
native_language_example: Are you in favor of this proposal or against it?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (voi) if they have visited a place before. It’s the present of essere (siete) + past participle (stati) with the adverb già (“already”). Use a + city names; with countries you usually say in (e.g., Siete già stati in Italia?). For an all-female group, you can say: siete già state a/in.
target_language_example: Siete già stati a Roma?
native_language_example: Have you already been to Rome?

meaning: “you are free to go” / “you can leave (if you want)”.
additional_notes: Polite/neutral way to tell more than one person (or one person formally: “Lei”) they may leave; implies permission or that there’s no obligation to stay. Often used by a teacher/host/official at the end of something. Can be followed by a destination (e.g., “a casa”) or paired with alternatives (“andare o restare/rimanere”).
target_language_example: La riunione è finita: siete liberi di andare.
native_language_example: The meeting is over: you’re free to go.

meaning: "have you ever" (asking if something has ever happened).
additional_notes: Used mainly in questions with the passato prossimo: "Siete mai stati/e... ?" (= Have you ever been...?). "Siete" is the 2nd-person plural of "essere" (you all are / you are, polite plural), and it agrees with the subject: "stati" (masc./mixed) or "state" (fem.). "mai" means "ever" in questions (and often "never" in negative sentences: "non ... mai").
target_language_example: Siete mai stati a Roma?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Rome?

meaning: "Have you (all) ever been to…?" (addressing a group of women).
additional_notes: Used to ask about past experience visiting a place or attending an event. It’s the verb "essere" (siete) + past participle "state" (feminine plural) + "mai" (“ever”). Use "siete mai stati a" for a group of men or a mixed group. With one person: "Sei mai stato a…?" (male) / "Sei mai stata a…?" (female). Often followed by a city/country or an event: "a Londra", "a un matrimonio".
target_language_example: Siete mai state a Roma in primavera?
native_language_example: Have you (all) ever been to Rome in the spring?

meaning: "Have you (all) ever been to/in…?" (addressing a group of women).
additional_notes: Used to ask about past experience visiting a place. It’s feminine plural because it’s said to a group of women (state). For a mixed/men’s group you usually say: “Siete mai stati in…?” For one woman: “Sei mai stata in…?” For one man: “Sei mai stato in…?”
target_language_example: Siete mai state in Italia?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Italy?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (voi) or in formal address (Voi) whether they have ever been somewhere. It’s the present perfect of "essere" (siete stati) plus "mai" = "ever"; it’s usually followed by a place with a preposition (a/alle, in, su, nel/allo).
target_language_example: Siete mai stati in Italia?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Italy?

meaning: “Have you ever been to…?” (to a place, addressing you all / you plural).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone (plural “you”) has ever visited a place. It’s built from essere in the passato prossimo: siete (you are) + mai (ever) + stati/state (been, masculine/feminine plural) + a (to/in). You may also hear the formal singular version: “È mai stato/a a…?”
target_language_example: Siete mai stati a Roma?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Rome?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people, or someone you address with the formal 'voi', whether they have ever been to a country/city/place. Literally 'are you ever been in', but in English it’s expressed as 'have you ever been to'. Often followed by a place name (e.g., in Australia/in Cina).
target_language_example: Siete mai stati in Italia?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Italy?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s position in a debate or decision. It’s the 2nd-person plural form (addressing a group, or used as formal singular "Lei" in some contexts). Often followed by a noun or pronoun: "Siete pro o contro il piano?". You can also say "Sei pro o contro...?" (informal singular) or "È pro o contro...?" (he/she/it).
target_language_example: Siete pro o contro la nuova regola?
native_language_example: Are you for or against the new rule?

meaning: "are you (all) ready for …?" (addressing a female group).
additional_notes: Used to ask if a group of two or more people is prepared for something. "Siete" is 2nd-person plural (you all). "Pronte" is feminine plural; for a male or mixed group use "Siete pronti per". Often followed by a noun ("per il viaggio") or by an infinitive verb ("per parlarne"). You can also use it as a statement: "Siete pronte per partire" = "You’re ready to leave."
target_language_example: Siete pronte per partire?
native_language_example: Are you all ready to leave?

additional_notes:
Uses the verb essere (to be): siete = “you are” (plural, also used formally for one person as “Lei”), pronti = “ready” (masculine plural; change to pronte for a group of women). Often followed by:
- a + infinitive: Siete pronti a partire? (ready to leave)
- per + noun: Siete pronti per la notizia? (ready for the news)
- al + noun (a + il): Siete pronti al peggio? (ready for the worst)
It can be a question (with rising intonation or a question mark) or a statement.
target_language_example: Siete pronti a cominciare?
native_language_example: Are you ready to start?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people if they are ready to do something; it’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., iniziare, partire) or by “+ verb + si” (e.g., divertirsi → divertirvi). Singular: “sei pronto/a a …?”. Formal plural: “siete pronti/e a …?”.
target_language_example: Siete pronti a partire?
native_language_example: Are you ready to leave?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people if they are prepared for something (an event, news, a meal) or ready to do something. The verb agrees with the subject: use "sei pronto/a per" (you singular), "siete pronti/e per" (you plural). With a noun: "per la cena". With an infinitive: "per cominciare" / "per parlarne". End it with a question mark when it’s a question.
target_language_example: Siete pronti per uscire?
native_language_example: Are you ready to go out?

additional_notes: Used to ask for confirmation or express doubt. "Siete" is the plural "you are" (addressing more than one person). "Sicure" is feminine plural, so it’s used when speaking to a group of women (or an all-female group). For a mixed/masculine group, use "siete sicuri che".
target_language_example: Siete sicure che sia una buona idea uscire adesso?
native_language_example: Are you (plural, women) sure it’s a good idea to go out now?

meaning: "are you sure that...?" (to a group / formal "you").
additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (or one person using polite "voi") to confirm something. It’s often followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., "riesca", "stia arrivando", "sia"). Singular is "sei sicuro/a che..."; formal singular is "è sicuro/a che...".
target_language_example: Siete sicuri che sia la strada giusta?
native_language_example: Are you sure this is the right road?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (or to be formal with one person, using "voi") if they’re sure about something. It’s typically followed by an infinitive (e.g., "voler/volere") or by a noun/pronoun: "Siete sicuri di voler partire?" / "Siete sicuri di questa scelta?".
target_language_example: Siete sicuri di voler uscire adesso?
native_language_example: Are you sure you want to go out now?

meaning: "were you able to" / "have you been able to" (to do something).
additional_notes: Second-person plural, feminine (addressing a group of women). Used to ask whether someone managed to do something. Tense depends on context: often passato prossimo ("have you been able to"), but it can translate naturally as simple past in English ("were you able to"). Followed by an infinitive (e.g., "contattare", "parlare").
target_language_example: Siete state in grado di finire il lavoro in tempo?
native_language_example: Were you able to finish the work on time?

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "essere" for "voi" (you all). It’s used with adjectives ("siete stati fantastici" = you were fantastic), states/conditions ("siete stati felici" = you were happy), or with "stati" + place/structure ("siete stati in Portogallo" = you have been to/in Portugal; "siete stati in grado di..." = you were able to...). Agreement: use "siete state" if the group is all female.
target_language_example: Siete stati in Italia l'anno scorso?
native_language_example: Have you (all) been to Italy last year? / Were you in Italy last year?

additional_notes: Past tense of venire (“to come”) in the passato prossimo: siete (you are) + venute (come). Used when speaking to two or more women/girls; for a mixed or all-male group, use "siete venuti". Common in questions about who someone came with, why they came, or when they arrived. Literal structure is “you are come,” but English translates as “you came / you have come.”
target_language_example: A che ora siete venute?
native_language_example: What time did you (plural, female) come?

meaning: “you (plural) came / have come” (past; informal also used as “you guys came”).
additional_notes: Second-person plural (voi) past tense of venire (“to come”), used when speaking to more than one person. It’s most often understood as “you came” or “you have come” depending on context. With a female-only group, it becomes “siete venute.” Often appears in questions like “Perché siete venuti…?” (“Why did you come…?”).
target_language_example: Siete venuti in macchina o in treno?
native_language_example: Did you come by car or by train?

meaning: “you (plural) came to / have come to” (to do something or to a place).
additional_notes: Used with “voi” (2nd person plural) and the verb “venire” in the past (passato prossimo): “siete venuti/venute”. It often introduces a purpose with an infinitive (“siete venuti a salvarci” = you came to save us) or a destination with a place (“siete venuti a Deressa” = you came to Deressa). Use “venuti” for a group of men or mixed group; “venute” for a group of women.
target_language_example: Siete venuti a parlare con il direttore?
native_language_example: Did you come to talk to the director?

meaning: “you came here” / “have you come here?” (to more than one person, or formal).
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of venire (to come): siete (you are) + venuti (come, masc. plural) + qui (here). It’s used with "voi" (you all) or as a formal "you" in some contexts. If the group is all/mostly female, you’ll hear "siete venute qui".
target_language_example: Perché siete venuti qui così tardi?
native_language_example: Why did you come here so late?

additional_notes: Used to explain the meaning or consequence of something. In statements, it introduces what something implies (often followed by the subjunctive after expressions like “non significa che …”). In questions, “Significa che …?” asks for clarification (“Does that mean that…?”).
target_language_example: Se non risponde, significa che è occupato.
native_language_example: If he doesn’t reply, it means that he’s busy.

additional_notes: Used to explain the consequence or interpretation of something, followed by a verb in the present tense (e.g., non riesci, non vedrete). Common in explanations/definitions: “X significa che non …” = “X means you can’t/don’t …”. The subject can be implied or stated later in the sentence.
target_language_example: Se non risponde, significa che non ha visto il messaggio.
native_language_example: If he doesn’t reply, it means he hasn’t seen the message.

additional_notes: Used to express that something is emotionally important or valuable to you (a gesture, presence, knowledge, or even a person). You can swap the subject before it (e.g., La tua presenza / Quello / Sapere che… / Tom) or use it alone after someone says something kind.
target_language_example: Grazie per essere venuto: significa molto per me.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming: it means a lot to me.

meaning: “Officer” / “Mr. prison guard” (a very formal way to address a correctional officer).
additional_notes: Used when speaking politely (or sometimes sarcastically) to an officer responsible for guarding detainees/prisoners. "Signor" = "Mr."; "agente" = "officer/agent"; "di custodia" specifies they work in custody (a prison/jail guard). In many real situations you may also hear "agente" or "agente di polizia penitenziaria".
target_language_example: Mi scusi, signor agente di custodia, posso fare una telefonata?
native_language_example: Excuse me, officer, can I make a phone call?

meaning: "Sir, don't…" / "Sir, you can't…" (polite way to address a man and say 'not').
additional_notes: Used when speaking politely/formally to an adult man (e.g., a customer, stranger, older man). “Signore,” is a direct address (“Sir,”) and is often followed by a negative sentence starting with “non…”. You’ll commonly hear it in requests, warnings, or refusals: “Signore, non può…”, “Signore, non così…”.
target_language_example: Signore, non può entrare qui.
native_language_example: Sir, you can’t come in here.

additional_notes: Used to address an audience in a formal or public setting (speeches, announcements, introductions). Often comes at the start of a sentence and may be followed by a pause/comma. Note: singular forms are "signore" (sir) and "signora" (madam).
target_language_example: Signore e signori, vi do il benvenuto alla cerimonia.
native_language_example: Ladies and gentlemen, I welcome you to the ceremony.

additional_notes: Imperative (command) form of essere (tu): sii = “be”. Used to tell someone to treat a person politely or kindly. The person comes after con (with): Sii gentile con lui/lei; with names: Sii gentile con Maria. For more than one person: Siate gentili con…; formal singular: Sia gentile con….
target_language_example: Per favore, sii gentile con i tuoi compagni di classe.
native_language_example: Please, be kind to your classmates.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a website (a web page or online presence). It’s masculine: il sito web / un sito web. Common with verbs like avere (to have) and visitare (to visit).
target_language_example: Puoi mandarmi il link del tuo sito web?
native_language_example: Can you send me the link to your website?

additional_notes: Used with the passato prossimo of "smettere": "ho/hai/ha… smesso di" + infinitive to say you stopped doing an activity (often meaning you stopped and didn’t continue). Common in questions: "Perché avete smesso di…?" = "Why did you stop…?".
target_language_example: Ho smesso di fumare l'anno scorso.
native_language_example: I quit smoking last year.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "smettere" + "di" + infinitive. "Ho smesso di fumare" is past (passato prossimo) = “I quit/I stopped smoking.” You can also use the imperfect: "Smettevo di fumare" = “I was quitting/used to stop smoking.” With another subject: "ha smesso di fumare" = “he/she quit smoking.”
target_language_example: Mio padre ha smesso di fumare l'anno scorso.
native_language_example: My dad quit smoking last year.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "smettere di" + infinitive = "to stop doing (something)". "Smesso" is the past participle used with "avere" (hai smesso, avete smesso). Often appears in questions with "Perché...?" (Why...?).
target_language_example: Ho smesso di studiare il francese perché non avevo tempo.
native_language_example: I stopped studying French because I didn’t have time.

additional_notes: Formal imperative (Lei form) of "smettere di" + infinitive, used to tell someone politely but firmly to stop doing something: "Smetta di parlare" (Stop talking). For an informal "tu" command, you’ll often hear "smetti di".
target_language_example: Smetta di parlare, per favore.
native_language_example: Please stop talking.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say you stop an action or habit: smettere di + infinitive (e.g., smettere di parlare = to stop talking). It can be a request/order after chiedere/dire: mi ha chiesto di smettere di… (“asked me to stop…”). Often used in the imperative: Smetti di! (Stop!).
target_language_example: Puoi smettere di fare rumore, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you stop making noise, please?

additional_notes: Uses the verb pattern “smettere di + infinitive” = “to stop doing (something)”. Here, “bere” means “to drink” and in this context usually refers to drinking alcohol (often in the sense of quitting/reducing). Often used after verbs like “consigliare” (to advise) or “dovere” (should).
target_language_example: Ha deciso di smettere di bere per la sua salute.
native_language_example: He decided to stop drinking for his health.

meaning: "to stop calling me that / like that."
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop using a certain name, nickname, label, or way of addressing you. "Chiamarmi" = "call me"; "così" means "like that/that way" and refers to what they’ve just called you. You’ll often see it with different object pronouns depending on who you’re speaking to: "Ti ho detto..." (I told you, informal singular), "Le ho detto..." (I told you, formal), "Vi ho detto..." (I told you, plural/formal).
target_language_example: Per favore, smetti di chiamarmi così: mi dà fastidio.
native_language_example: Please, stop calling me that: it bothers me.

meaning: to quit smoking; to stop smoking.
additional_notes: Uses the verb pattern “smettere di + infinitive” (to stop doing something). Here it’s “fumare” (to smoke). Often used with advice or necessity: “devi/dovresti smettere di fumare” (you must/should quit smoking). In the past: “ha deciso di smettere di fumare” (he decided to quit). With someone causing another person to stop: “far smettere qualcuno di fumare” (to make someone quit smoking).
target_language_example: Ho smesso di fumare l'anno scorso.
native_language_example: I quit smoking last year.

additional_notes: Imperative used to tell people to stop an action: **smetterla di + infinitive**. **Smettetela** is addressed to **more than one person** (voi) or can sound like a **polite/formal** “you (plural)”. For one person you often hear **Smettila di…**. The **la** is part of the fixed expression **smetterla** (“to stop it/knock it off”).
target_language_example: Smettetela di urlare, per favore.
native_language_example: Stop shouting, please.

meaning: “stop (doing) …” (used to tell someone to quit an action).
additional_notes: From the verb *smettere* (“to stop/quit”) + *di* + infinitive: *smetti di fumare* (“stop smoking”). Often used as an imperative, and it can sound strong/annoyed depending on tone and context. In vulgar expressions like *rompere i coglioni*, it becomes very rude.
target_language_example: Smetti di parlare e ascolta un attimo.
native_language_example: Stop talking and listen for a moment.

additional_notes: Imperative form of "smetterla" used to tell someone to stop an action. It’s often direct and can sound rude unless softened with "per favore" or said in a gentle tone. It’s normally followed by an infinitive: "smettila di parlare / urlare / toccarmi". You can add pronouns after the infinitive: "smettila di dirmi...".
target_language_example: Smettila di guardare il telefono mentre guidi.
native_language_example: Stop looking at your phone while you’re driving.

additional_notes: Past historic (passato remoto) form of "smettere di" (to stop doing something), used mostly in written narratives or storytelling. It’s followed by an infinitive: "smise di" + verb (e.g., "smise di suonare" = it stopped ringing). In everyday spoken Italian you’ll more often hear "ha smesso di".
target_language_example: A un certo punto, smise di parlare e uscì dalla stanza.
native_language_example: At a certain point, he stopped talking and left the room.

additional_notes: Used as a common pattern with a pause (often written with a comma) to introduce a contrast or add something despite what was just said. Most often you’ll see it as **lo so, ma…** (“I know, but…”) to acknowledge someone’s point and then disagree or explain; or **non so, ma…** (“I don’t know, but…”) to express uncertainty and then offer an idea or reaction.
target_language_example: Lo so, ma oggi non posso venire.
native_language_example: I know, but I can’t come today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "sapere" (to know). "So" is the 1st-person singular present tense (“I know”), and "che" introduces a following clause (“that …”): "So che + [sentence]". In questions/negatives, note that "che" can also mean “what” (e.g., "Non so che cosa fare" = “I don’t know what to do”), but "so che" is typically the statement “I know that …”.
target_language_example: So che oggi non hai tempo.
native_language_example: I know that you don’t have time today.

meaning: “I know that …” (with **ci** meaning “there / us / about it,” depending on context).
additional_notes:
**So che** = “I know that.” The little word **ci** changes meaning based on what comes next:
- **ci sei** = “you’re there” (ci = “there”)
- **ci divertiremo** = “we’ll have fun” (ci is part of the verb *divertirsi*)
- **ci avete aiutato / assunto** = “you helped / hired us” (ci = “us”)
- **ci provi** = “you’re trying (at it)” (ci = “at it / there,” depending on context)
target_language_example: So che ci sei: rispondi, per favore!
native_language_example: I know you’re there: answer, please!

meaning: “I know that … me” (I know that someone is doing something to/for me).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause starting with **che** (“that”). **So** = “I know” (from *sapere*). **Mi** is an object pronoun meaning “me” and can mean “to me” or “me” depending on the verb: *So che mi ama* = “I know (that) he/she loves me”; *So che mi ha assunto* = “I know (that) he/she hired me”; *So che mi state ascoltando* = “I know you’re listening to me.” Common potential confusion: Italian **so** does **not** mean English “so” (= *così / quindi*).
target_language_example: So che mi stai dicendo la verità.
native_language_example: I know you’re telling me the truth.

meaning: “I know that … not / I know that … don’t …”
additional_notes: Used to state you’re sure about a negative fact: **so** = “I know”, **che** = “that”, **non** = “not”. In Italian, **non** comes before the verb: *So che non vieni* = “I know you’re not coming.”
target_language_example: So che non hai tempo oggi.
native_language_example: I know you don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to state that you know a fact about the other person (identity, location, profession, etc.). Often followed by a noun or adjective (e.g., "Sarah", "un insegnante") or by an adverb/phrase (e.g., "lì"). If what follows is feminine past participle, you may also see "so che sei stata..." (“I know you went/you have been...”, speaking to a woman).
target_language_example: So che sei stanco, ma dobbiamo andare.
native_language_example: I know you’re tired, but we have to go.

additional_notes: Used to state certainty about a fact or situation. It’s made of: “so” = “I know” (from the verb *sapere*), “che” = “that”, and “è” = “is” (from *essere*). Very common before an adjective or noun (“so che è intelligente”, “so che è tuo padre”) or a clause describing what something is like (“so che è necessario”). Note: Italian “so” can look like English “so,” but it means “I know.”
target_language_example: So che è tardi, ma devo finire questo lavoro.
native_language_example: I know it’s late, but I have to finish this work.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "sapere" ("to know"), where "so" means "I know" and "chi" means "who". Often followed by a clause: "So chi è" (I know who it is), "So chi ha fatto questo" (I know who did this). The negative form is common too: "Non so chi sia" (I don’t know who he/she is).
target_language_example: So chi ti ha chiamato ieri.
native_language_example: I know who called you yesterday.

meaning: “I know how …” / “I know what … is like.”
additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question with **come** (“how”), describing that you understand the way something works, happened, ends, etc.: *So come funziona / so come ha fatto*. With people, it can mean you know someone’s character or habits: *So come sei* (“I know what you’re like”). Often you’ll also see **lo so, come...** but **so come...** is common in speech.
target_language_example: Tranquillo, so come si fa.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I know how to do it.

additional_notes: Used to say you know the way/method to do something. It’s often followed by an infinitive ("So come farlo" = “I know how to do it”) or by a clause with "come si" ("So come si fa" = “I know how it’s done / how to do it”). Note: Italian "come" means “how,” not the English verb “come.”
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti, so come risolvere il problema.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I know how to solve the problem.

additional_notes: Used to say you know what someone did/said/thought, often followed by a verb clause: "So cosa hai fatto" (I know what you did). In many cases you’ll also hear "So che..." for "I know that..."; use "so cosa" when the unknown/known thing is "what".
target_language_example: So cosa hai detto ieri.
native_language_example: I know what you said yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say you know the location of something or where someone is/does something. Often followed by a verb (e.g., *so dove cercarlo* = “I know where to look for it”) or by a clause (e.g., *so dove lavora* = “I know where he/she works”). You may also hear *non so dove…* (“I don’t know where…”).
target_language_example: Tranquillo, so dove parcheggiare.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I know where to park.

meaning: “I know if/whether …” (often used as **non so se** = “I don’t know if/whether …”).
additional_notes: **So** is the 1st-person singular of *sapere* (“to know”). It’s most commonly used in the pattern **(non) so se + clause** to introduce uncertainty: **Non so se posso venire** (“I don’t know if I can come”). In everyday speech you may hear **non lo so se…** (“I don’t know if…”) with **lo** referring to the whole idea.
target_language_example: Non so se domani ho tempo.
native_language_example: I don’t know if I’ll have time tomorrow.

meaning: (I am) satisfied with my new house. (female speaker)
additional_notes: Used with the verb "essere" (to be): "Sono soddisfatta...". "Soddisfatta" agrees with the speaker: a man would say "soddisfatto". Italian uses "di" + article to mean “with/about”: "di + la" → "della" ("satisfied with the...").
target_language_example: Sono davvero soddisfatta della mia nuova casa.
native_language_example: I’m really satisfied with my new house.

additional_notes: “Soffrire di” is used to say someone suffers from (or has) an illness/health condition. In everyday English you often translate it as “has” or “suffers from.” You can change the subject: “Io soffro di… / Lei soffre di…”.
target_language_example: Mia madre soffre di osteoporosi da anni.
native_language_example: My mom has (suffers from) osteoporosis and has had it for years.
