additional_notes: Used as a direct command telling someone to return to a previous place or to stop and reverse direction. It can be literal (walk/drive back) or figurative (go back to the previous step/page). From the verb "tornare" (to return) + "indietro" (back).
target_language_example: Aspetta, torna indietro: hai dimenticato le chiavi!
native_language_example: Wait, come back: you forgot your keys!

meaning: 'to go back/return to' (a place), or 'to go back to' doing something.
additional_notes: Used with a destination (often a city/place): tornare a Boston = return to Boston. With an infinitive, it means resuming a previous action: tornare a studiare = go back to studying. In the past, you often see it with essere: è tornato/a a casa (he/she went back home).
target_language_example: Dopo pranzo devo tornare a lavorare.
native_language_example: After lunch I have to go back to work.

meaning: to go back home; to return home.
additional_notes: Used to talk about returning to your home/house from somewhere else. You can conjugate it for time: deve tornare (has to return), doveva tornare (had to return). Often used with an indirect object to say whose home: Tornare a casa mia/tuA/suA (go back to my/your/his/her home).
target_language_example: Devo tornare a casa presto.
native_language_example: I have to go back home early.

meaning: to go back; to return (to a previous place).
additional_notes: Used when you need to turn around or return to where you were before (e.g., because you forgot something or to get someone). It can also be used in a more abstract sense to mean that you can’t undo the past (“Non si può tornare indietro” = “You can’t go back / there’s no going back”).
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato le chiavi: devo tornare indietro.
native_language_example: I forgot my keys: I have to go back.

additional_notes: Used for talking about time travel or, more commonly, imagining going back to a past moment to change something (often introduced by "se" = "if"). It’s built from tornare (to return) + indietro (back) + nel tempo (in time).
target_language_example: Se potessi tornare indietro nel tempo, cambierei quella scelta.
native_language_example: If I could go back in time, I would change that choice.

additional_notes: Past participle feminine singular of "tornare a casa" (to go/come back home). Used with the auxiliary "essere": "sono tornata a casa" (I came back home, said by a woman) / "è tornata a casa" (she came back home). For a man: "tornato a casa".
target_language_example: Dopo il lavoro sono tornata a casa e ho cenato.
native_language_example: After work I came back home and had dinner.

additional_notes: Past participle of "tornare" used with "essere" (e.g., "sono tornato/a a casa" = "I came back home"). Change the ending for gender/number: tornato (male singular), tornata (female singular), tornati (male/mixed plural), tornate (female plural). Often used with time words like "appena" (just) or to emphasize being safely home.
target_language_example: Siamo tornati a casa tardi dopo il concerto.
native_language_example: We got back home late after the concert.

additional_notes: Future tense (3rd person singular) of tornare + a casa. Used to talk about when someone will come back home. Often appears in questions (A che ora tornerà a casa?) or with time expressions like alle sette (“at seven”) or non appena (“as soon as”).
target_language_example: Se finisce presto, tornerà a casa prima delle otto.
native_language_example: If he finishes early, he’ll come back home before eight.

additional_notes: Uses the Lei form (third-person singular) to address someone politely: it can be a request/command ("Per piacere, torni a casa.") or a question ("Torni a casa?"). In casual speech with friends you’d usually say "torna a casa" (tu) or "tornate a casa" (voi).
target_language_example: Scusi, torni a casa adesso?
native_language_example: Excuse me, are you going home now?

additional_notes: From the verb tornare (to return) + indietro (back). It’s most often used as an order or request addressed to one person using the formal Lei form: "Torni indietro!" = "Go back!" With "per piacere" it becomes a polite request. For the informal singular (to a friend), you’d say: "Torna indietro!"
target_language_example: Torni indietro subito, per favore!
native_language_example: Go back right away, please!

meaning: "let’s go back home" / "we’re going back home."
additional_notes: "Torniamo" is the 1st-person plural of "tornare" (to return). With "a casa" it means returning home. Depending on context and tone, it can be a simple statement ("We’re going home") or a suggestion/decision ("Let’s go home"). Often used with time words like "ora" (now) or urgency like "prima che sia troppo tardi" (before it’s too late).
target_language_example: È tardi: torniamo a casa.
native_language_example: It’s late: let’s go home.

additional_notes: Used when speaking as a group (“we”): it can mean physically going back to a place, or figuratively going back to an earlier point (in a story, plan, conversation) to start again or reconsider. It can be a suggestion (“Why don’t we go back?”) or an urgent instruction (“Let’s go back!”).
target_language_example: Aspetta, torniamo indietro: ho dimenticato le chiavi.
native_language_example: Wait, let’s go back: I forgot the keys.

additional_notes: Used to say you return to your home (often after being out). The verb is tornare (to return); “torno” is the 1st-person singular present (“I return”). You can add time expressions like “la sera” (in the evening) or “presto” (early/soon).
target_language_example: Dopo il lavoro, torno a casa e preparo la cena.
native_language_example: After work, I go home and make dinner.

meaning: "I’ll be right back" / "I’ll be back soon."
additional_notes: Used when you’re leaving briefly and want someone to wait, stay put, or keep an eye on something (e.g., a shop/bar). Often said on its own as a quick reassurance. Polite versions include “Torno subito, signora/signore.”
target_language_example: Aspettami qui: torno subito.
native_language_example: Wait for me here: I’ll be right back.

additional_notes: A common food phrase meaning a cake made with chocolate. In everyday conversation you’ll often see it with piacere (e.g., Mi piace la torta al cioccolato. / Ti piace la torta al cioccolato?).
target_language_example: Per il mio compleanno vorrei una torta al cioccolato.
native_language_example: For my birthday I’d like a chocolate cake.

additional_notes: A common dessert. Usually used with the verb piacere to say you like it (e.g., Mi piace la torta di mele). You can also say fare una torta di mele (“to make an apple pie”) or avere della torta di mele (“to have/some apple pie”).
target_language_example: Mi piace la torta di mele, soprattutto quando è calda.
native_language_example: I like apple pie, especially when it’s warm.

meaning: in five minutes (five minutes from now).
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen after five minutes from the present moment. Common with future time references: "comincia/inizia tra cinque minuti" (it starts in five minutes), "sarà qui tra cinque minuti" (it will be here in five minutes). "Tra" can often be swapped with "fra" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo tra cinque minuti davanti al bar.
native_language_example: See you in five minutes in front of the café.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something shared or happening within a group that includes the speaker (noi). With two people it often means “between us”; with a larger group it can mean “among us.” Common with verbs like dividere (to split/share), and in phrases like Non ci sono segreti tra di noi (“There are no secrets between us”). It can also refer to a relationship: tra di noi = “between us (as a couple/friends).”
target_language_example: Teniamolo tra di noi, per favore.
native_language_example: Let’s keep it between us, please.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen after a time interval counted from the present moment. Common with future actions: "Arrivo tra dieci minuti". You can also hear "fra dieci minuti" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Scusa, sono in ritardo: arrivo tra dieci minuti.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m running late: I’ll be there in ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used to describe a position, relationship, or choice involving exactly two items. Common with nouns: “tra due mondi” (between two worlds), “tra due paesi” (between two countries), “scegliere tra due…” (to choose between two…). “Tra” can also mean “in” (time) in other contexts (e.g., “tra due ore” = in two hours), but in these examples it means “between.”
target_language_example: Devo scegliere tra due opzioni.
native_language_example: I have to choose between two options.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen after two days have passed from the current moment. You can replace the number: tra tre giorni (in three days), tra una settimana (in a week). Contrast: "due giorni fa" = two days ago; "fra due giorni" means the same as "tra due giorni".
target_language_example: Ci vediamo tra due giorni davanti alla stazione.
native_language_example: See you in two days in front of the station.

meaning: "among the" / "between the" (before a plural masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to indicate being in the middle of people/things (physical or figurative), or to express choice/comparison within a group. It’s the preposition "tra" + the plural masculine article "i". Typical uses: "tra i migliori/peggiori" (among the best/worst), "tra i pasti" (between meals), "scegli tra i due" (choose between the two).
target_language_example: Questo ristorante è tra i più economici del quartiere.
native_language_example: This restaurant is among the cheapest in the neighborhood.

meaning: underfoot; in the way (getting in the way).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically in your way or, more generally, is an annoyance because they keep interfering or hanging around where they shouldn’t. Often appears with verbs like "essere" (è sempre tra i piedi) or "venire/mettersi tra i piedi" (to come/get in the way). Slightly colloquial in tone.
target_language_example: Scusa, mi stai sempre tra i piedi: posso passare?
native_language_example: Sorry, you’re always underfoot/in the way—can I get through?

additional_notes: Used with feminine plural nouns after "tra" (same meaning as "fra"). Common for: position between two things (Tra le due città), space separating things (tra le righe), being in a group/among (tra le migliori; tra le varie cose), and ranges/repetition (tra le cinque e le sei volte = between five and six times).
target_language_example: Il mio posto è tra le due finestre.
native_language_example: My seat is between the two windows.

additional_notes: Used to say something is physically being held (often with verbs like tenere/avere/prendere/nascondere), or more figuratively that you have something available or to deal with (e.g., "troppo tempo tra le mani" = lots of free time on your hands). The possessive is often implied by context: "tra le mani" can mean "between his/her hands" as well.
target_language_example: Ho il telefono tra le mani, ma non trovo il numero.
native_language_example: I have the phone in my hands, but I can’t find the number.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically in your embrace. Common with verbs like "addormentarsi" (to fall asleep) or "morire" (to die), often in emotional contexts. "Tra" here means "between/among," but the natural English translation is usually "in my arms."
target_language_example: È rimasta tra le mie braccia per un po'.
native_language_example: She stayed in my arms for a while.

additional_notes: Literal: used for something physically in or among clouds (e.g., flying, mountains, the sun appearing between clouds: “fa capolino tra le nuvole”). It can also be used figuratively to mean someone is dreamy or not paying attention (“avere la testa tra le nuvole”), but that usually includes “la testa.”
target_language_example: Durante il volo eravamo tra le nuvole.
native_language_example: During the flight we were in the clouds.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone being physically held by another person (often romantic or comforting). With "morire" it can mean someone died while being held by the other person. The possessive "sue" agrees with "braccia" (feminine plural) and can refer to either "his" or "her" depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi sento al sicuro tra le sue braccia.
native_language_example: I feel safe in his/her arms.

meaning: to myself; in my head (said privately).
additional_notes: Usually used with verbs like pensare/dire/parlare to show you’re thinking or speaking quietly to yourself. Very often you’ll hear the fuller expression “tra me e me” (= to myself). On its own, “tra me” sounds incomplete unless the context implies the rest.
target_language_example: Ho pensato tra me e me: "Meglio andare a casa".
native_language_example: I thought to myself, “Better go home.”

meaning: "between me and..." (involving only me and another person/thing).
additional_notes: Used to say there is a relationship, difference, issue, or agreement involving only you and someone/something else: "tra me e te" (between you and me), "tra me e lui/lei" (between me and him/her). Often implies privacy/exclusivity: "È una cosa tra me e lui" = it’s between me and him (no one else’s business).
target_language_example: È una questione tra me e te.
native_language_example: It’s a matter between you and me.

meaning: "between us" (between you and me; between us in a relationship).
additional_notes: Used for (1) something private/secret that should stay only between the people involved ("just between us"), and (2) the state of a relationship: "How are things between us?" It can also be more literal/physical: something (or someone) is "between us" or "standing between us".
target_language_example: Tra noi è finita, ma ti auguro il meglio.
native_language_example: It's over between us, but I wish you the best.

meaning: “in parentheses”; also “as an aside / by the way.”
additional_notes: Used literally for writing: put something inside brackets/parentheses ( ). It’s also used figuratively to add an extra comment that’s not central to what you’re saying, similar to “as an aside” or “by the way.” Often appears at the start of a sentence (“Tra parentesi, …”) or inserted mid-sentence (“…, tra parentesi, …”).
target_language_example: Tra parentesi, domani non posso venire.
native_language_example: By the way, I can’t come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen after a short time from now. Common in everyday speech for plans, arrivals, or immediate future changes (e.g., getting dark, time to eat). Similar to "fra poco".
target_language_example: Aspetta qui: torno tra poco.
native_language_example: Wait here: I’ll be back soon.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen after a short amount of time (minutes, not hours). Common with the future tense or present used for the near future: "Arrivo tra poco". Similar to "fra poco". Can also mean "shortly" when talking about the immediate future ("Tra poco inizia").
target_language_example: Arrivo tra poco, sto finendo una cosa.
native_language_example: I'll be there in a little while; I'm just finishing something.

additional_notes: Used when asking someone to translate a specific sentence. Often followed by a target language with "in" (e.g., "in inglese", "in esperanto"). In requests you may see it with "puoi... ?" (informal), "può... ?" (formal), or "mi potrebbe... ?" (very polite).
target_language_example: Mi puoi tradurre questa frase in inglese, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you translate this sentence into English for me, please?

additional_notes: Used to say that someone spends a lot of time doing something (often followed by “a” + infinitive, e.g., “a studiare”) or with someone/at a place (often with “con” or “a/in”). The subject can be omitted in Italian when it’s clear from context.
target_language_example: Trascorro molto tempo a studiare l'italiano.
native_language_example: I spend a lot of time studying Italian.

additional_notes: Used with a person or group after con (e.g., con lei/lui, con gli amici). Trascorrere is a fairly formal/common verb for “to spend (time)”; in everyday speech you may also hear passare del tempo con. Pronoun reminders: con lui = with him, con lei = with her, con me = with me, con te = with you.
target_language_example: Questo weekend voglio trascorrere del tempo con la mia famiglia.
native_language_example: This weekend I want to spend time with my family.

additional_notes: Used when you want to say you’d like to be with someone more often/for longer. Very common with verbs like "vorrei" (I’d like) and "voglio" (I want). In the present tense: (io) trascorro, (tu) trascorri, (lui/lei) trascorre, (noi) trascorriamo, (voi) trascorrete, (loro) trascorrono.
target_language_example: Dovremmo trascorrere più tempo con i nostri amici.
native_language_example: We should spend more time with our friends.

trascorrere più tempo fuori e meno tempo dentro

target_language_multi_word_term: trascorrere più tempo fuori e meno tempo dentro
meaning: to spend more time outside and less time inside.
additional_notes: Used as advice or a recommendation, often with "dovresti/dovrebbe/dovreste" (you should / he-she should / you all should). "Trascorrere" means "to spend" (time). "Fuori" = outside; "dentro" = inside.
target_language_example: Per stare meglio, dovresti trascorrere più tempo fuori e meno tempo dentro.
native_language_example: To feel better, you should spend more time outside and less time inside.

additional_notes: Uses the verb *trascorrere* (“to spend” time) in the *passato remoto* (simple past), common in writing and in some regions of Italy. You’ll often see other forms like *ho trascorso il Natale* (I spent Christmas) or *ha trascorso il Natale* (he/she spent Christmas). It’s typically followed by a place (*a Boston/in Australia*) or company (*con la sua famiglia*).
target_language_example: L'anno scorso trascorse il Natale da solo.
native_language_example: Last year he spent Christmas alone.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *trascorrere* (“to spend” time), usually in the *passato prossimo*: *ho/ha/abbiamo/avete trascorso...*. It’s commonly followed by **con** + people (*con loro* = with them) or **a/in** + place, and can also be followed by **a** + infinitive to say what you spent time doing (*ha trascorso molto tempo a studiare* = she spent a lot of time studying).
target_language_example: Ho trascorso molto tempo a studiare per l’esame.
native_language_example: I spent a lot of time studying for the exam.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **trascorrere** (“to spend” time) in the **passato prossimo**: *ho/abbiamo trascorso tutta la giornata…* It’s commonly followed by **in + place** (*in spiaggia, in biblioteca*) or **con + person** (*con lei, con loro*) to say where/with whom you spent the entire day.
target_language_example: Ieri abbiamo trascorso tutta la giornata a Roma.
native_language_example: Yesterday we spent the whole day in Rome.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "trascorrere" (to spend/pass time). It usually takes "avere" as the helping verb: "ho/ha/hai trascorso". The past participle "trascorso" agrees only in gender/number when used with a direct object pronoun (e.g., "l’ho trascorsa"), but in this phrase it typically stays "trascorso". Often followed by a person: "con Tom", "con Maria".
target_language_example: Ho trascorso tutta la mattinata con mia sorella.
native_language_example: I spent the whole morning with my sister.

additional_notes: Used to count down right before starting an action (like “3, 2, 1!”). Often said with an exclamation point, or with extra words like “via!” (go!) or “tra...” (“in...” as in “in 3, 2, 1!”). You can also hear it when giving timing/instruction cues (e.g., before turning, jumping, starting a game, recording, etc.).
target_language_example: Tre, due, uno… via!
native_language_example: Three, two, one… go!

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (how long something lasts) or a point in the past. Common patterns: "da tre anni" = "for three years" (continuing up to now), "tre anni fa" = "three years ago", "per tre anni" = "for three years" (duration, not necessarily continuing), "in tre anni" = "in/within three years".
target_language_example: Studio italiano da tre anni.
native_language_example: I've been studying Italian for three years.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It usually comes at the end of the sentence (or right after the time expression). You can replace the number: "due anni fa" (two years ago), "dieci anni fa" (ten years ago).
target_language_example: Ho cambiato lavoro tre anni fa.
native_language_example: I changed jobs three years ago.

additional_notes: Used to state the length of time someone was incarcerated, often with verbs like "passare" or "trascorrere" (to spend): "Ha passato/trascorso tre anni in prigione".
target_language_example: Mio cugino ha passato tre anni in prigione.
native_language_example: My cousin spent three years in prison.

additional_notes: Used to talk about amounts of money in dollars, often with verbs like costare (to cost), venire (to come to/cost), spendere (to spend), and dovere (to owe). You can also say it on its own to state how much money you have: Ho solo tre dollari.
target_language_example: Quanto costa? Tre dollari.
native_language_example: How much does it cost? Three dollars.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has (or had) three children. In Italian, "figli" is the plural of "figlio" and can mean “children” in general (not only “sons”), especially when talking about a parent’s kids. Common with verbs like "avere" (to have), "crescere" (to raise), and "perdere" (to lose).
target_language_example: Hanno tre figli e vivono a Milano.
native_language_example: They have three children and live in Milan.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (for three days: "per tre giorni"), or about time relative to another moment (three days before/after: "tre giorni prima/dopo"). It can also describe something that lasts three days ("un viaggio di tre giorni").
target_language_example: Resto a Roma per tre giorni.
native_language_example: I'm staying in Rome for three days.

meaning: “three days in/at …”, “three days until …”, or “three days a/per …” (depending on context).
additional_notes: Common patterns: (1) With places (especially cities): “tre giorni a Roma” = three days in/at Rome. (2) With “mancano … a …”: “mancano tre giorni a Natale” = there are three days until Christmas. (3) With time-frequency expressions: “tre giorni a settimana” = three days a/per week.
target_language_example: Siamo stati tre giorni a Milano.
native_language_example: We were in Milan for three days.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened three days before now. It typically comes after the verb or at the end of the sentence (e.g., “È successo tre giorni fa”). With other numbers you can swap out “tre” (e.g., “due giorni fa” = two days ago).
target_language_example: Ho iniziato questo corso tre giorni fa.
native_language_example: I started this course three days ago.

additional_notes: Used to indicate an exact quantity: the number 3 + the plural noun "libri" (books). "Tre" stays the same regardless of gender; "libro" → "libri" is the plural. Often appears after a verb (e.g., "Ho portato tre libri" = "I brought three books").
target_language_example: Devo comprare tre libri per la scuola.
native_language_example: I have to buy three books for school.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration of time or a period, often with verbs like "trascorrere" (to spend): "Ho trascorso tre mesi..." = "I spent three months...". "Tre" agrees with "mesi" (plural of "mese").
target_language_example: Resterò in Italia per tre mesi.
native_language_example: I will stay in Italy for three months.

additional_notes: Used to say when something happened in the past. The time expression usually comes at the end of the sentence (as in the examples), but it can also be placed at the beginning for emphasis: “Tre mesi fa, …”. “Fa” means “ago” in these expressions (e.g., due giorni fa = two days ago).
target_language_example: Ho iniziato a studiare italiano tre mesi fa.
native_language_example: I started studying Italian three months ago.

additional_notes: A simple time expression used for duration (“for three minutes”), a deadline (“in/within three minutes”: entro tre minuti), or distance in time (“in three minutes”: tra tre minuti). It’s also used to talk about being early/late by a small amount: “con tre minuti di anticipo” (three minutes early) or “per tre minuti” (by three minutes, e.g., missing a train by three minutes).
target_language_example: Aspettami tre minuti, per favore.
native_language_example: Wait for me three minutes, please.

meaning: three or four; about three or four.
additional_notes: Used to give an approximate number (not exact). Often followed by a plural noun (tre o quattro libri) or by a time expression like “volte” (tre o quattro volte al mese = three or four times a month).
target_language_example: Restiamo qui tre o quattro giorni.
native_language_example: We’ll stay here for three or four days.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration or time needed. Common patterns: **in tre ore** = “in three hours” (time it takes to finish something); **a tre ore (e mezzo) da qui** / **a tre ore di macchina** = “three hours (and a half) from here” / “three hours away by car” (travel time).
target_language_example: Ci vogliono tre ore per arrivare a Firenze in treno.
native_language_example: It takes three hours to get to Florence by train.

additional_notes: A quantity of time (3 weeks). Use it with time expressions like "per tre settimane" (for three weeks) and with recurring events like "ogni tre settimane" (every three weeks). With "passare/trascorrere", it means spending three weeks somewhere or doing something.
target_language_example: Rimango a Roma per tre settimane.
native_language_example: I’m staying in Rome for three weeks.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened three weeks before now. "Fa" comes after the time expression (e.g., "due giorni fa", "un mese fa"). You can place it at the end of the sentence or after the verb for emphasis.
target_language_example: Ci siamo trasferiti qui tre settimane fa.
native_language_example: We moved here three weeks ago.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens on three occasions. Often with frequency expressions like "tre volte la settimana" (three times a week). You can also hear it in requests like "ripetilo tre volte" (repeat it three times).
target_language_example: L'ho controllato tre volte, ma non ho trovato errori.
native_language_example: I checked it three times, but I didn’t find any mistakes.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens in one day (meals, medicine, routines). Common in instructions, especially medical ones: "Prenda/Devi prendere ... tre volte al giorno".
target_language_example: Devo prendere queste gocce tre volte al giorno.
native_language_example: I have to take these drops three times a day.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens in one month. It usually comes after the verb or at the end of the sentence. You can swap the number: "due volte al mese" (twice a month), "una volta al mese" (once a month).
target_language_example: Faccio palestra tre volte al mese.
native_language_example: I work out three times a month.

additional_notes: A specific amount of money (300 USD). Used after verbs like guadagnare (to earn), vendere (to sell), vincere (to win), prendere una multa (to get a fine), and dovere (to owe). The number comes before the currency name: trecento dollari.
target_language_example: Il biglietto costa trecento dollari.
native_language_example: The ticket costs three hundred dollars.

additional_notes: Used to state someone’s age. In Italian you say someone "has" an age with avere: "Ho tredici anni" = "I’m thirteen." Often used with "solo/soltanto" to mean "only" (emphasizing how young someone is).
target_language_example: Mia sorella ha tredici anni.
native_language_example: My sister is thirteen years old.

additional_notes: Used to say a train arrived or departed later than scheduled. Often appears with an article or possessive: “Il treno era in ritardo” (The train was late), “Il mio/tuo/suo treno era in ritardo” (My/your/his-her train was late). Note: “in ritardo” means “late/delayed,” not the English insult “retarded.”
target_language_example: Il treno era in ritardo di venti minuti.
native_language_example: The train was twenty minutes late.

additional_notes: A quantity of money. Used with verbs like dare (to give), prestare (to lend), dovere (to owe), rimanere (to have left). Word order is number + currency; in Italian the currency name stays plural here (dollari).
target_language_example: Non ho che trenta dollari con me.
native_language_example: I only have thirty dollars on me.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration or time interval ("for/in 30 minutes"), how long something takes ("it takes 30 minutes"), how often something happens ("every 30 minutes"), or a delay ("30 minutes late"). Common patterns: "ci vogliono trenta minuti" (it takes thirty minutes), "fra/tra trenta minuti" (in thirty minutes), "ogni trenta minuti" (every thirty minutes), "in trenta minuti" (in/within thirty minutes), "in ritardo di trenta minuti" (thirty minutes late).
target_language_example: L'appuntamento è fra trenta minuti.
native_language_example: The appointment is in thirty minutes.

additional_notes: Used to say that something lasted longer than it should have. Often placed after the verb (e.g., "Ho aspettato troppo a lungo"), but it can also come at the start for emphasis ("Troppo a lungo hai...").
target_language_example: Abbiamo aspettato troppo a lungo per comprare i biglietti.
native_language_example: We waited too long to buy the tickets.

additional_notes: Used to say the price is higher than you think is acceptable or affordable. It can describe something (Questo è troppo costoso.) or someone’s service (Quel dentista era troppo costoso.). Agreement: costoso (masc. sing.); costosa (fem. sing.); costosi (masc. pl.); costose (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Vorrei comprarlo, ma è troppo costoso per me.
native_language_example: I’d like to buy it, but it’s too expensive for me.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is not old enough to do something. Very often followed by an infinitive verb: “troppo giovane per + infinitive” (e.g., troppo giovane per guidare = too young to drive).
target_language_example: Sei troppo giovane per andare in discoteca da solo.
native_language_example: You’re too young to go to the club by yourself.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t have enough time/availability to do something. It’s followed by an infinitive (e.g., per aiutare, per scriverle). "Impegnata" is feminine singular; masculine is "troppo impegnato per", plural "troppo impegnati/e per".
target_language_example: Sono troppo impegnata per venire stasera.
native_language_example: I'm too busy to come tonight.

additional_notes: Used with "essere" (to be): "Sono/Sei/È/Siamo... troppo in ritardo". "In ritardo" means "late"; adding "troppo" stresses it’s excessively late—so late that you’ll likely miss something or it’s no longer acceptable.
target_language_example: Siamo troppo in ritardo per prendere il treno.
native_language_example: We’re too late to catch the train.

additional_notes: Used to say something doesn’t fit because it’s smaller than needed. It agrees with the noun: troppo piccolo per (masc. sing.), troppo piccola per (fem. sing.), troppo piccoli per (masc. pl.), troppo piccole per (fem. pl.). The pronoun after per changes: per me/te/lui/lei/noi/voi/loro.
target_language_example: Queste magliette sono troppo piccole per i bambini.
native_language_example: These T-shirts are too small for the kids.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened earlier than appropriate or expected. It can refer to time (arriving/coming) or to doing something before you should: "È troppo presto per andare" (It’s too early to go).
target_language_example: Siamo arrivati troppo presto, il negozio è ancora chiuso.
native_language_example: We arrived too early; the shop is still closed.

meaning: “too tired to / for (doing something)” (said about a woman/girl).
additional_notes: Used to say someone doesn’t have enough energy to do an action: “troppo stanca per + infinitive” (e.g., per studiare, per ballare). Change gender/number as needed: troppo stanco (male), troppo stanchi/stanche (plural).
target_language_example: Oggi sono troppo stanca per uscire.
native_language_example: Today I’m too tired to go out.

additional_notes: Used to say someone doesn’t have enough energy to do an action. Follow with an infinitive verb (e.g., ballare, camminare, aiutare). You can change stanco to match the person: stanca (fem. singular), stanchi (masc./mixed plural), stanche (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Siamo troppo stanchi per uscire stasera.
native_language_example: We’re too tired to go out tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say something is happening after the right time or after an opportunity has passed. Often used with "È" ("È troppo tardi!" = "It’s too late!") or after a verb to mean you realized/arrived/acted too late ("L'ho scoperto troppo tardi" = "I found out too late").
target_language_example: Siamo arrivati troppo tardi per il treno.
native_language_example: We arrived too late for the train.

meaning: "too late to / for" (not enough time left to do something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (per + verb) to say someone missed the chance/time to do something: "È troppo tardi per + infinitive". With "non" it can reassure that there’s still time: "Non è troppo tardi per...". You can also use it to describe arriving after an event: "Sono arrivato troppo tardi per...".
target_language_example: Siamo ancora in tempo o è troppo tardi per prenotare un tavolo?
native_language_example: Are we still in time, or is it too late to book a table?

additional_notes: Used to say someone is so shy that they can’t or don’t manage to do an action. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., dire, guardare, ammettere, fare). You can change the adjective for gender/number: troppo timido per (male), troppo timidi per (plural).
target_language_example: Ero troppo timida per chiedere aiuto.
native_language_example: I was too shy to ask for help.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is so shy that they can’t/won’t do an action. Structure: "troppo" + adjective + "per" + infinitive. Example pattern: "Sono troppo timido per parlare" = "I'm too shy to speak."
target_language_example: Sono troppo timido per chiedere aiuto.
native_language_example: I'm too shy to ask for help.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is older than is appropriate or possible for an action or situation. Often followed by an infinitive: “troppo vecchio per + verb” (e.g., “per lavorare” = to work). It can also be followed by a noun/pronoun to express suitability (e.g., “troppo vecchio per te” = too old for you, in a dating/relationship sense). Agreement: “vecchio/vecchia/vecchi/vecchie” matches the person being described.
target_language_example: Sono troppo vecchio per uscire stasera.
native_language_example: I’m too old to go out tonight.

additional_notes: Most often means “too much time” when talking about how long you spend doing something (passare/spendere/trascorrere troppo tempo a + infinitive / con / su qualcosa). In the pattern “non troppo tempo fa,” it means “not too long ago.”
target_language_example: Ho aspettato troppo tempo per chiamarti.
native_language_example: I waited too long to call you.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun (un + noun): *trovare un marito / un cellulare / un compratore / un modo*. In the common phrase **andare a trovare (qualcuno)** it means “to go visit (someone)” (e.g., *Vado a trovare un amico* = “I’m going to visit a friend”).
target_language_example: Devo trovare un regalo per mio padre.
native_language_example: I have to find a gift for my dad.

meaning: to find a job (to get a job).
additional_notes: Used for successfully obtaining employment (not just spotting a job posting). Often follows verbs like suggerire (“to suggest”) or riuscire a (“to manage to”). You can change the article: trovare lavoro (more general), trovare un lavoro (a job).
target_language_example: Dopo mesi di ricerca, ho finalmente trovato un lavoro.
native_language_example: After months of searching, I finally found a job.

additional_notes: Used when you need to look for and choose another babysitter (for example because the old one quit or isn’t available). Common with verbs like "avere bisogno di" (to need) and "dovere" (must/should). "Babysitter" is a common loanword in Italian; the article is usually feminine: "una babysitter".
target_language_example: Dobbiamo trovare una nuova babysitter per sabato sera.
native_language_example: We have to find a new babysitter for Saturday night.

additional_notes: Used when talking about solving a problem or situation (often with "a" + the problem: "trovare una soluzione a un problema"). It can refer to practical fixes, agreements/compromises, or any way out of a difficulty.
target_language_example: Se restiamo calmi, possiamo trovare una soluzione.
native_language_example: If we stay calm, we can find a solution.

additional_notes: Used with the passato prossimo of *trovare* (to find): *ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno trovato il ...* + a masculine singular noun (e.g., *il libro, il cane, il Graal*). In some contexts, *trovare* can also mean “to find (something) + adjective,” i.e., to think/consider it a certain way: *Ho trovato il teatro affollato* = “I found the theater crowded.”
target_language_example: Ho trovato il tuo telefono sul tavolo.
native_language_example: I found your phone on the table.

additional_notes: Usually used with the auxiliary verb in the passato prossimo: “ha trovato le sue chiavi” = “he/she found / has found his/her keys.” “Sue” agrees with the plural feminine noun “chiavi” (keys), and it can mean either “his” or “her” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ho trovato le mie chiavi sotto il divano.
native_language_example: I found my keys under the couch.

additional_notes: Uses the past participle of *trovare* (“to find”) in the *passato prossimo*: *ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno trovato qualcosa* = “I/you/he… found something / have found something.” With *avere*, *trovato* usually doesn’t change form (no agreement) when followed by *qualcosa*.
target_language_example: Ho trovato qualcosa di interessante nel cassetto.
native_language_example: I found something interesting in the drawer.

additional_notes: From the verb **trovare** (“to find”), used with **passato prossimo**: **(avere) trovato un + noun**. With a reflexive pronoun it often means “found yourself a / got yourself a”: **Ti sei trovato un fidanzato?** = “Did you get yourself a boyfriend?” The noun after **un** is masculine singular (e.g., *un telefono, un fidanzato*).
target_language_example: Ho trovato un ristorante vicino all’hotel.
native_language_example: I found a restaurant near the hotel.

additional_notes: Used with the passato prossimo of *trovare* (“to find”): *ho/ha/hanno trovato un lavoro* = “I/he/they found a job” / “have found a job.” *Trovato* is the past participle; with *avere* it doesn’t change for gender/number here.
target_language_example: Finalmente ho trovato un lavoro.
native_language_example: I finally found a job.

additional_notes: Used with the passato prossimo of *trovare* (to find): **ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno trovato** + **una soluzione**. Commonly followed by **a/al/alla** to say what the solution is for: *una soluzione al problema* (“a solution to the problem”).
target_language_example: Finalmente abbiamo trovato una soluzione al problema.
native_language_example: Finally we found a solution to the problem.

additional_notes: "Trovò" is the passato remoto (a narrative past tense, common in books/stories and in some regions in speech) of "trovare" = “to find.” It’s used with a masculine singular noun starting with a consonant: "trovò un lavoro" (found a job), "trovò un pelo" (found a hair). For feminine nouns you use "una" (e.g., "trovò una soluzione" = found a solution).
target_language_example: Alla fine, trovò un appartamento economico.
native_language_example: In the end, he/she found an inexpensive apartment.

meaning: “that you have” (present subjunctive of avere, used after che / expressions of opinion, doubt, etc.).
additional_notes: Used when the subject is “you” and the verb needs the present subjunctive, often after phrases like “penso che…/credo che…/non penso che…/è possibile che…”. It typically expresses opinion, uncertainty, or judgment rather than a simple statement of fact. In the indicative (a straightforward fact), you’d use “tu hai”.
target_language_example: Non credo che tu abbia tempo oggi.
native_language_example: I don’t think you have time today.

meaning: 'and you, what…?' (used to ask what YOU think/do/say).
additional_notes: Used in questions to put emphasis on *tu* (“you”), often to contrast with someone else or to turn the question back to the other person (similar to “what about you?”). Very common with verbs like *dire* (to say), *pensare* (to think), *fare* (to do). You may also hear it as *e tu, che cosa…?*
target_language_example: Io sono d’accordo; tu che cosa ne pensi?
native_language_example: I agree; what do you think?

meaning: “do you know” (are you familiar with / do you know personally).
additional_notes: Uses conoscere (to know someone, or to be familiar with a place/thing). It’s commonly used for knowing people (“Tu conosci Tom?”) and being familiar with places/things/rules (“Tu conosci questo quartiere/le regole?”). For ‘know a fact’ or ‘know how to’, Italian often uses sapere instead.
target_language_example: Tu conosci questo ristorante?
native_language_example: Do you know this restaurant?

meaning: 'and you, what…?' (directly asking the other person).
additional_notes: Used in questions to put emphasis on *you* and ask for the other person’s opinion, answer, or reaction. It’s common in spoken Italian and often appears after a short lead-in like **E tu, cosa…?** (“And you, what…?”). Word order is flexible (you may also hear **Cosa fai tu?**), but **Tu cosa…?** sounds very direct.
target_language_example: E tu cosa ne pensi?
native_language_example: And what do you think?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s opinion. Very often followed by “di + [person/thing]” (Tu cosa ne pensi di Tom? = What do you think of Tom?). “Ne” refers back to the topic already mentioned (“about it/about them”). You can add emphasis with words like “veramente” (really). In everyday speech you may also hear “E tu, cosa ne pensi?”
target_language_example: Ho un dubbio su questo progetto: tu cosa ne pensi?
native_language_example: I’m not sure about this project—what do you think?

meaning: "you must / you have to" (addressing one person).
additional_notes: Used to state an obligation or strong necessity for the person you’re speaking to. It’s the subject pronoun tu (“you”, informal singular) + devi (present tense of dovere, “to have to/must”). In Italian, tu is often omitted; saying it (Tu devi...) adds emphasis and can sound more direct/forceful (like “You have to…”). For polite/formal address, use Lei deve.
target_language_example: Tu devi finire i compiti prima di uscire.
native_language_example: You have to finish your homework before going out.

meaning: "you must/you have to go" (you need to go).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is obligated or strongly expected to go somewhere or leave. It can be followed by a place: a scuola (to school), ad/al + city/neighborhood, dal + person/professional (e.g., dal dentista = to the dentist). As a question (Tu devi andare?) it means “Do you have to go?”
target_language_example: Tu devi andare via adesso.
native_language_example: You have to leave now.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone there is a necessity or strong obligation to be a certain way (often followed by an adjective: onesta, pronto, aggressiva). It’s quite direct; for softer advice you often hear "tu dovresti essere" ('you should be').
target_language_example: Tu devi essere paziente con i bambini.
native_language_example: You must be patient with the kids.

additional_notes: "Tu" is the informal singular "you." "Dovresti" is the conditional form of "dovere" (to have to), used to give advice, recommendations, or a mild obligation. It’s commonly followed by an infinitive (e.g., "studiare", "entrare").
target_language_example: Tu dovresti parlare con il tuo insegnante.
native_language_example: You should talk with your teacher.

meaning: “you and your …” (usually followed by a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Literally a coordination: “you and your …”. Grammatically it’s normal and can be neutral (e.g., “tu e la tua famiglia…”), but in real speech it’s often used with a blaming/hostile tone, especially in insults (as in the examples). It’s typically followed by a feminine singular noun (la tua amica, la tua libertà, la tua banda, etc.). For a masculine noun, you’d say “tu e il tuo …”.
target_language_example: Tu e la tua famiglia siete i benvenuti a cena.
native_language_example: You and your family are welcome to dinner.

meaning: “you were” / “you used to be” (imperfect tense of essere).
additional_notes: Used to describe a past state, condition, or ongoing situation (age, feelings, being alone, being drunk, etc.), often as background information or for habits in the past. It’s the 2nd-person singular (“tu”).
target_language_example: Tu eri sempre molto gentile con me.
native_language_example: You were always very kind to me.

meaning: 'you were' (subjunctive; often in 'that you were' / 'if you were').
additional_notes: “Tu fossi” is the imperfect subjunctive of essere (to be) for “tu” (you). It’s used in dependent clauses, especially after expressions like non sapere / non pensare / non avere idea che… (“not to know/think/have any idea that…”), and in hypothetical sentences (often with se: “se tu fossi…” = “if you were…”). In English it usually translates simply as “you were,” even though Italian uses the subjunctive mood.
target_language_example: Pensavo che tu fossi già a casa.
native_language_example: I thought you were already at home.

additional_notes: Used with "tu" (informal singular "you") + "hai" (2nd person singular of *avere*, "to have"). It can mean possession ("You have...") or be an auxiliary to form the *passato prossimo* (e.g., *tu hai preso* = "you took/you have taken"). Not used for formal "you" (*Lei ha*).
target_language_example: Tu hai già finito i compiti?
native_language_example: Have you already finished your homework?

additional_notes: Used with the present perfect (passato prossimo) to ask or say that something has happened already. In questions it often implies surprise or checking if it’s done yet. Word-by-word: tu (you) + hai (have) + già (already). Often in real conversation, Italians drop 'tu' and just say 'Hai già...?'
target_language_example: Tu hai già mangiato?
native_language_example: Have you already eaten?

meaning: 'have you ever...?' (asking if someone has done something at least once).
additional_notes: Used to ask about life experiences. It’s formed with the present tense of avere (tu hai) + mai, usually followed by a past participle: “Tu hai mai visto...?” In everyday speech, Italian often drops the subject pronoun: “Hai mai visto...?” A negative answer often uses “mai” too: “Non ho mai...” (“I’ve never...”).
target_language_example: Tu hai mai provato la cucina giapponese?
native_language_example: Have you ever tried Japanese food?

meaning: "have you ever seen" (asking if someone has seen something at any time up to now).
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s experience. It’s built from: tu (you) + hai (you have) + mai (ever) + visto (seen). Often followed by a noun or by an infinitive to describe an action (e.g., “Tu hai mai visto Tom piangere?” = “Have you ever seen Tom cry?”). In conversation, Italians may drop “tu” and just say “Hai mai visto…?”.
target_language_example: Tu hai mai visto questo film?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen this movie?

additional_notes: Uses the verb vedere (to see) in the passato prossimo: hai visto = “have you seen / did you see”. Tu is often omitted in Italian (Hai visto Tom?). Used to ask if someone has seen a person or thing recently; can also mean “Did you see…?” depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu hai visto le mie chiavi?
native_language_example: Have you seen my keys?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "avere" (to have) with the subject pronoun "tu" + "hai" (you have). Italian often drops subject pronouns, so you’ll also hear just "Hai...?"; using "tu" adds emphasis or contrast ("you, specifically"). Used for possession ("Tu hai i miei soldi?"), relationships ("Tu hai figli?"), and many common expressions with "avere" like "avere paura" (to be afraid) and "avere fiducia" (to trust).
target_language_example: Tu hai tempo stasera?
native_language_example: Do you have time tonight?

additional_notes: Used to say that the listener still has something (often time) left. In questions, it checks if that’s still true (e.g., “Do you still have time?”). Often followed by a noun: tempo, soldi, pazienza, etc.
target_language_example: Tu hai ancora un biglietto per me?
native_language_example: Do you still have a ticket for me?

meaning: you need (to); you have need of.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone needs something or needs to do something. It’s the informal singular “you” (tu). Structure: “tu hai bisogno di + noun” (Tu hai bisogno di tempo.) or “tu hai bisogno di + infinitive” (Tu hai bisogno di studiare di più.). Often you can also just say “hai bisogno di …” without “tu”.
target_language_example: Tu hai bisogno di un po' di riposo.
native_language_example: You need a bit of rest.

additional_notes: Used with a plural noun to mean you have an unspecified number of something. Here, "dei" is the plural partitive article (di + i) and often corresponds to “some” in statements and “any” in questions. In questions you may also hear "Hai dei... ?" without "tu" (subject pronouns are often dropped).
target_language_example: Tu hai dei minuti per parlare?
native_language_example: Do you have a few minutes to talk?

additional_notes: Used before a plural feminine noun (e.g., delle allergie, delle amiche, delle informazioni, delle responsabilità). "Delle" is the partitive article (di + le) and often translates as “some”; in questions/negatives it can feel like “any.”
target_language_example: Tu hai delle domande per me?
native_language_example: Do you have any questions for me?

meaning: “are you planning to / do you intend to”.
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s intention or plan. It’s followed by an infinitive (e.g., aiutare, andare, restare). You can make it more polite by using “Lei ha intenzione di…?” with formal “Lei”.
target_language_example: Tu hai intenzione di studiare stasera?
native_language_example: Are you planning to study tonight?

additional_notes: Used with the verb avere (to have) in the present tense: tu hai = you have. In many situations Italian drops the subject pronoun, so you’ll often hear just Hai un…? (Do you have a…?). Choose the right form of the indefinite article: un (masc. before most consonants), uno (masc. before s+consonant, z, gn, ps, etc.), una (fem.), un’ (fem. before a vowel).
target_language_example: Hai un biglietto per il concerto?
native_language_example: Do you have a ticket for the concert?

meaning: "you have a" (addressing one person; before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb avere (to have) + una (a/an) when the thing is feminine singular: Tu hai una sorella? = Do you have a sister? In speech, it’s often dropped because Italian can omit the subject: Hai una sorella? Also used in statements (Tu hai una macchina.) or questions (Tu hai una rivista?).
target_language_example: Tu hai una penna?
native_language_example: Do you have a pen?

additional_notes: Used when the subject is explicitly "tu" (you) and the direct object is "lo" (= him/it). In Italian, object pronouns like "lo" usually go BEFORE the conjugated verb: "tu lo chiami" = "you call him". Saying "tu" is often for emphasis/contrast (because the verb ending already implies "you"). "Lo" can refer to a person (him) or a masculine thing (it), depending on context.
target_language_example: Sei sicuro? Tu lo sai meglio di me.
native_language_example: Are you sure? You know it better than I do.

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone is familiar with a person or something. Here, "tu" is usually added for emphasis (like “you, do you...?”). "lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning “him” (or sometimes “it,” depending on context). For a woman you’d say "tu la conosci?"; for plural: "tu li/le conosci?". You can also add a name: "Tu lo conosci, Tom?"
target_language_example: Tu lo conosci già?
native_language_example: Do you already know him?

additional_notes: Used to say someone already knows something, or to ask if they know something. "Lo" literally means "it" and can refer to a specific thing already mentioned (e.g., a fact), or it can stand in for the idea in a following clause/question (common in spoken Italian). Often said with emphasis: "Tu lo sai" = "You know."
target_language_example: Tu lo sai che domani non lavoro, vero?
native_language_example: You know I’m not working tomorrow, right?

additional_notes: Used when the subject is explicitly "tu" (you) and the object pronoun is "mi" (me). It often adds emphasis/contrast: "Tu mi..." = "YOU ... me" (not someone else). "Mi" can mean either "to me" (indirect object: Tu mi devi tre dollari) or "me" (direct object: Tu mi intimidisci), depending on the verb.
target_language_example: Tu mi hai detto la verità?
native_language_example: Did you tell me the truth?

additional_notes: Used with a past participle to form the passato prossimo (present perfect): "Tu mi hai + participle" = "You have + past participle" / often "You + past tense" in English. Common with verbs that take "avere" as the helping verb. Word order: subject (tu) + object pronoun (mi) + auxiliary (hai) + past participle (arrestato/ingannato/usata).
target_language_example: Tu mi hai chiamato ieri sera.
native_language_example: You called me last night.

meaning: "you don't / you do not" (often with emphasis on "you").
additional_notes: Used to negate a verb with an explicit subject pronoun "tu". In Italian, the subject pronoun is often omitted (e.g., "Non capisci"), but adding "tu" can add emphasis or contrast ("you, not someone else"). "Non" normally comes right before the verb: "Tu non capisci".
target_language_example: Tu non puoi entrare qui.
native_language_example: You can't come in here.

meaning: “you don’t have” / “you haven’t” (negated form of *avere* for “you”).
additional_notes: Used to say that “you” (singular) do not have something: *Tu non hai soldi.* It’s also used with a past participle to make the negative *passato prossimo*: *tu non hai fatto…* = “you didn’t / you haven’t done…”. Often followed by words like *niente/nulla* (“anything/nothing”) or *mai* (“ever/never”).
target_language_example: Tu non hai detto la verità.
native_language_example: You didn’t tell the truth.

additional_notes: Literally “you (singular) don’t know.” Used to tell someone they lack knowledge or understanding, often in a confrontational or emphatic way. With an infinitive it can mean “you can’t” (e.g., "Tu non sai leggere" = “You can’t read”). Often followed by: chi (who), cosa (what), con chi (who/whom), di cosa (what), quello che (what/that which).
target_language_example: Tu non sai quanto mi dispiace.
native_language_example: You don’t know how sorry I am.

additional_notes: Direct statement addressed to “you” (tu). Often used to accuse someone of ignorance or of not understanding a situation (it can sound harsh). Commonly followed by “di … / del … / della …” to say what the person doesn’t know: “Tu non sai niente di me” = “You don’t know anything about me.”
target_language_example: Tu non sai niente di quello che è successo.
native_language_example: You don’t know anything about what happened.

additional_notes: Used to say what someone is not (identity, role, or quality): "Tu non sei Thia" / "Tu non sei affidabile". Often followed by a noun or an adjective. With "più" it means "no longer": "Tu non sei più il benvenuto" = "You’re no longer welcome." In everyday speech Italian often drops the subject pronoun: "Non sei..." instead of "Tu non sei...".
target_language_example: Tu non sei in ritardo, sei in anticipo.
native_language_example: You’re not late, you’re early.

additional_notes: Present tense of "parlare" used with "tu" (you). Often used to ask if someone speaks a language: "Tu parli inglese?". With a direct object you can say "parli italiano/il cinese" (you speak Italian/Chinese). To mean “talk about (a topic)”, use "parlare di": "Tu parli di...".
target_language_example: Tu parli italiano?
native_language_example: Do you speak Italian?

additional_notes: From the verb *pensare* (“to think”). In Italian, questions often use the same word order as statements, with rising intonation: *Tu pensi in francese?* (“Do you think in French?”). The subject pronoun *tu* is often omitted: *Pensi che sia vero?* (“Do you think it’s true?”). On its own, *Tu pensi?* can mean “Do you think so?” or “You really think that?” (often skeptical).
target_language_example: Tu pensi che sia una buona idea?
native_language_example: Do you think it’s a good idea?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s opinion or guess before a clause. Very often followed by the subjunctive (congiuntivo), especially when you’re unsure or asking a question: "Tu pensi che sia…?" (= Do you think he is…?). In everyday speech you may also hear the indicative, but beginners will commonly meet it with the subjunctive.
target_language_example: Tu pensi che sia una buona idea?
native_language_example: Do you think it’s a good idea?

additional_notes: Used to question or express doubt/surprise about what the other person believes. It’s followed by a clause introduced by che; often the verb in that clause is in the subjunctive (e.g., sia, siano, funzioni). You can drop the subject pronoun for a more natural sound: Pensi davvero che…?
target_language_example: Pensi davvero che sia una buona idea?
native_language_example: Do you really think it’s a good idea?

meaning: “you can / you’re able to” (addressing one person).
additional_notes: Used with the pronoun *tu* (informal singular “you”) + *puoi* (you can). Often adds emphasis or contrast (e.g., “*you* can…” / “even *you* can’t…”). It can express ability (“you’re able to”), permission (“you may”), or possibility depending on context. In everyday speech Italian often drops the subject pronoun, so you’ll also hear just *puoi*.
target_language_example: Tu puoi venire con noi, se vuoi.
native_language_example: You can come with us, if you want.

meaning: “can you…?” / “are you able to…?” (speaking to one person).
additional_notes: Used to ask someone if they manage/are able to do something (ability, possibility, or whether they can handle something). It’s followed by an infinitive (e.g., capire, distinguere, vedere). Often similar to “puoi…?”, but “riesci a…?” stresses success/being able to manage.
target_language_example: Tu riesci a venire domani mattina?
native_language_example: Can you make it tomorrow morning?

meaning: "do you know" / "can you" (asking if someone has a skill).
additional_notes: Literally "you know." Used in questions to ask if someone knows how to do something (a learned skill), often followed by an infinitive: "Tu sai + verb" (Tu sai nuotare?). In statements it can mean "you know" (Tu sai che...). In everyday speech, Italians often drop the subject pronoun and just say "Sai...?"
target_language_example: Tu sai cucinare la pasta?
native_language_example: Can you cook pasta?

meaning: “you know” (you are aware / you have the information).
additional_notes: Used to state that the listener already knows something or to ask if they know something. Often followed by "già" (already), "troppo" (too much), a question word ("tu sai qual è...?" = do you know what...?), or "qualcosa di..." ("tu sai qualcosa della sua famiglia?" = do you know anything about his/her family?).
target_language_example: Tu sai dove è la stazione?
native_language_example: Do you know where the station is?

meaning: “you know that …” (used to introduce something the speaker assumes you already know or should realize).
additional_notes: Often used to remind someone of a fact, point out something obvious, or emphasize what follows. In speech it can sound accusatory or emotional depending on tone (e.g., “Tu sai che mi hai fatto piangere.”). It’s also common as a filler like English “you know …,” especially in conversation.
target_language_example: Tu sai che domani abbiamo un esame, vero?
native_language_example: You know we have an exam tomorrow, right?

additional_notes: Used with "tu" (informal singular "you") + "sei" (2nd-person singular of "essere", "to be"). Often appears in questions ("Tu sei...?") or for emphasis/contrast; in Italian you can often drop "tu" and just say "Sei...".
target_language_example: Tu sei pronto?
native_language_example: Are you ready?

meaning: “are you still…?” (asking if something is still true).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to check if someone remains in the same state/situation. Pattern: “Tu sei ancora + adjective/place/status?” Example: “Tu sei ancora a casa?” = “Are you still at home?” In everyday speech, Italians often drop “tu”: “Sei ancora a casa?”
target_language_example: Tu sei ancora in ufficio?
native_language_example: Are you still at the office?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s position/opinion. It’s typically followed by **a** + something: **a questo/ciò**, or **a + article**: **al** (a + il), **alla** (a + la), etc. You can also use it with *essere favorevole/contrario a* + an idea, plan, proposal, law, etc.
target_language_example: Tu sei favorevole o contrario a questa proposta?
native_language_example: Are you in favor of or against this proposal?

meaning: 'you are the' (addressing a male person or a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used with "tu" (informal singular "you"). "Il" is masculine singular and is typically followed by a masculine noun or superlative: "Tu sei il massimo" (you’re the best), "Tu sei il migliore amico" (you’re the best friend). For a female person/ feminine noun use "tu sei la"; for plural use "voi siete i/le".
target_language_example: Tu sei il migliore della squadra!
native_language_example: You’re the best on the team!

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to say someone is “my …” (friend, son, savior, etc.). In Italian, the definite article often appears before possessives (il mio/la mia/i miei/le mie), especially for emphasis or with adjectives like unico (“only”): “il mio unico amico”. Without extra emphasis, you’ll also often hear “tu sei mio” (“you’re mine”) or “mio amico” (“my friend”). For feminine singular, use “tu sei la mia …”.
target_language_example: Tu sei il mio eroe.
native_language_example: You are my hero.

meaning: "Have you ever been to…?" (to a woman).
additional_notes: Used to ask a woman if she has ever visited a place. It uses the present tense of essere + past participle (sei stata) to talk about life experience. "mai" means "ever" in questions. For a man: "tu sei mai stato in…?" You can add a place after "in" (continents, countries, cities).
target_language_example: Tu sei mai stata in Italia?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Italy?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has ever been somewhere, usually followed by a place introduced by a/alle/in/nel, etc. It uses the present perfect: "sei stato" (literally "you have been") + "mai" (ever). Often the subject pronoun "tu" is omitted: "Sei mai stato...?" If you’re speaking to a woman, it becomes "tu sei mai stata".
target_language_example: Sei mai stato a Roma?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Rome?

meaning: "Have you ever been to…?" (asked to a man).
additional_notes: Uses the present tense of essere + stato (past participle) to ask about life experience. Common with countries/cities: “Tu sei mai stato in + place?” For a woman: “Tu sei mai stata in…?” For “you (plural)”: “Siete mai stati/e in…?”
target_language_example: Tu sei mai stato in Spagna?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Spain?

additional_notes: Used with the informal singular subject pronoun “tu” (“you” to one person) + “sei” (you are) + “molto” (very/a lot). It’s typically followed by an adjective: “Tu sei molto timido/a” = “You are very shy.” The adjective usually agrees with the person: -o (male), -a (female).
target_language_example: Tu sei molto gentile con tutti.
native_language_example: You are very kind to everyone.

meaning: "you are a" (addressing one person, with a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used with "tu" (informal singular "you") to say what someone is: "Tu sei un + [masculine singular noun/adjective used as a noun]". With feminine nouns use "tu sei una" (e.g., "Tu sei una studentessa"). In formal speech, Italians often use "Lei è un/una..." instead of "Tu sei...".
target_language_example: Tu sei un bravo insegnante.
native_language_example: You are a good teacher.

meaning: "you are a" (addressing a woman/girl; before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify or describe someone with a feminine singular noun (or a feminine adjective used like a noun): "Tu sei una giornalista/nerd/testimone." For a man/boy, use "tu sei un..." (before most masculine nouns) or "tu sei uno..." (before s+consonant, z, gn, ps, etc.). It can be a question with rising intonation: "Tu sei una giornalista?"
target_language_example: Tu sei una studentessa?
native_language_example: Are you a (female) student?

additional_notes: Used to say the speaker’s impression about someone. Very common with an adjective (Tu sembri stanco/a = You look tired) or with “di” + infinitive (Tu sembri di fretta = You seem to be in a hurry). “Sembrare” can refer to looks, mood, or behavior—not a confirmed fact, just how it appears.
target_language_example: Tu sembri un po' preoccupato oggi.
native_language_example: You seem a bit worried today.

meaning: "that you are" / "that you may be" (subjunctive of *essere*, used in dependent clauses).
additional_notes: *Tu sia* uses the **congiuntivo presente** (present subjunctive) of **essere** for **tu**. It commonly appears after expressions of opinion, doubt, feelings, or wishes (e.g., *penso che tu sia…*, *spero che tu sia…*) and after some commands/requirements (e.g., *che tu sia sul posto* = “make sure you’re there”). It’s also used in clauses like **ovunque tu sia** (“wherever you are”).
target_language_example: Spero che tu sia felice qui.
native_language_example: I hope you’re happy here.

additional_notes: Used when the subject is "tu" and the verb is reflexive (or uses "ti" as an object pronoun). Common with daily-routine verbs like "alzarsi" (to get up), and with modal verbs: "Tu ti devi..." + infinitive (You have to...). In Italian, the subject pronoun "tu" is often omitted because the verb ending already shows it: "Ti alzi...?"
target_language_example: Tu ti senti meglio oggi?
native_language_example: Do you feel better today?

meaning: "you" + reflexive pronoun + "have" (passato prossimo with reflexive verbs).
additional_notes: Used with reflexive verbs in the passato prossimo (present perfect/past). Structure: "Tu ti sei" + past participle. It uses "essere" as the auxiliary, and the past participle agrees with the subject: "Tu ti sei divertito" (male) / "Tu ti sei divertita" (female). Common with verbs like divertirsi (to have fun), svegliarsi (to wake up), vestirsi (to get dressed), ritirarsi (to retire/withdraw).
target_language_example: Tu ti sei svegliato presto stamattina?
native_language_example: Did you wake up early this morning?

additional_notes: Uses the verb volere (to want) with the subject pronoun tu (you, singular). In Italian, the subject pronoun is often omitted, so you’ll very commonly hear just vuoi…? in questions. "Tu vuoi…?" can sound more emphatic ("you—do you want…?") or contrastive. Used to offer something (Tu vuoi una birra?), ask about desire/intention (Tu vuoi venire?), or challenge/confirm (Tu vuoi vincere?).
target_language_example: Tu vuoi che ti aiuti?
native_language_example: Do you want me to help you?

additional_notes: Used when talking to or about someone’s friend who is a woman/girl. It can mean “your friend” when the friend is female, or when the speaker is female and is offering friendship (“I want to be your friend”). Agreement: tua (feminine singular) + amica (female friend). For a male friend: tuo amico. Plural: tua amica → le tue amiche.
target_language_example: Domani esco con la tua amica.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I'm going out with your (female) friend.

additional_notes: Often used in phrases like “alla tua età” (“at your age”) and “della tua età” (“your age / the same age as you”) to compare ages or talk about what’s typical/expected for someone your age.
target_language_example: Alla tua età, non avevo ancora la patente.
native_language_example: At your age, I didn’t have my driver’s license yet.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the listener’s family. It’s feminine singular: la tua famiglia. In questions you’ll often see it with prepositions: alla tua famiglia (about/to your family), con la tua famiglia (with your family), della tua famiglia (about your family).
target_language_example: Come sta la tua famiglia?
native_language_example: How is your family?

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective **tua** (feminine singular) + **figlia** (daughter). With close family members, Italian often **drops the article**: *tua figlia* (your daughter). You may also hear **la tua figlia** to add emphasis/contrast (e.g., “your daughter, not mine”).
target_language_example: Dov'è tua figlia?
native_language_example: Where is your daughter?

additional_notes: Means “your car” when speaking to one person you address as tu. Agree the possessive with the noun: la tua macchina (feminine singular). Often used with a preposition: sulla tua macchina (“on your car”), alla tua macchina (“compared to your car”).
target_language_example: Posso usare la tua macchina oggi?
native_language_example: Can I use your car today?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the listener’s mother. It’s feminine singular: tua (your) + madre (mother). For a question you might also hear/see "È tua madre?" (Is she your mother?).
target_language_example: Ho parlato con tua madre ieri sera.
native_language_example: I spoke with your mother last night.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s mother with the verb *essere* (“to be”). In Italian you usually don’t use an article here: *tua madre è…* (not *la tua madre è…*). It can also be used in a question with rising intonation, e.g. *Tua madre è a casa?* (“Is your mother at home?”).
target_language_example: Tua madre è stanca oggi.
native_language_example: Your mother is tired today.

additional_notes: "Mamma" is the common, familiar word for “mom” (more informal/affectionate than "madre"). "Tua" means “your” and agrees with the feminine singular noun "mamma". You’ll often also hear it with the article: "la tua mamma" (“your mom”). Depending on tone and context, it can be neutral/affectionate or used in insults (e.g., "tua mamma..." in an argument).
target_language_example: Tua mamma è a casa stasera?
native_language_example: Is your mom at home tonight?

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "tua" (your) with the feminine singular noun "moglie" (wife). Italian possessives agree with the noun: e.g., "tuo marito" (your husband), "tua moglie" (your wife). In phrases like "a casa da tua moglie", "da" can mean “at/to (someone’s place)”—literally “at your wife’s home.”
target_language_example: Puoi chiamare tua moglie, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you call your wife, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about your wife (feminine singular): **tua moglie** = “your wife” and **è** is the 3rd-person singular of **essere** (“to be”). It’s commonly followed by a place (e.g., **a casa**, **in ufficio**) or an adjective (e.g., **alta**), and can be used in questions (**...?**) or statements.
target_language_example: Tua moglie è al lavoro oggi?
native_language_example: Is your wife at work today?

additional_notes: Used when speaking to one person informally (tu) to ask for or refer to their personal view. Often appears after verbs like dare (give), chiedere (ask), or with expressions like avere diritto a (to have the right to): "Dammi la tua opinione" = "Give me your opinion."
target_language_example: Vorrei sapere la tua opinione su questo ristorante.
native_language_example: I’d like to know your opinion about this restaurant.

meaning: “your health” (used in a toast: “to your health!”).
additional_notes: Commonly said as **Alla tua salute!** when clinking glasses (a toast). You can also hear **Alla nostra salute!** (“to our health!”). In the examples, it’s used to drink in someone’s honor, often with their name (e.g., *Alla tua salute, Gosha!*).
target_language_example: Alla tua salute! Cin cin!
native_language_example: To your health! Cheers!

additional_notes: Used to refer to the listener’s sister. It’s feminine singular: tua (your, f.) + sorella (sister). If speaking politely to one person (Lei), you’d say "Sua sorella". In some contexts, "Tua sorella!" can be used as a rude/ironic retort (informal).
target_language_example: Ho visto tua sorella ieri al supermercato.
native_language_example: I saw your sister yesterday at the supermarket.

additional_notes: Means “your room,” usually addressed to one person using tu (family, friends, children). It’s feminine singular: la tua stanza. With a specific item in the room, Italian often uses di + possessive: la finestra della tua stanza (“the window of your room”).
target_language_example: Puoi mettere in ordine la tua stanza prima di uscire?
native_language_example: Can you tidy up your room before going out?

additional_notes: Uses the informal singular possessive "tua" (feminine singular) with "vita". Often used both literally (your life in general) and figuratively to mean the people/things that are part of your life: "nella tua vita" (in your life), "fare parte della tua vita" (to be part of your life). "È la tua vita" can also mean "It’s your life" (your choice/responsibility).
target_language_example: Non voglio più stress nella tua vita.
native_language_example: I don’t want any more stress in your life.

additional_notes: Feminine plural: use when the friends are women/girls (mixed group usually takes masculine: “i tuoi amici”). In real sentences it’s most often used with an article: “le tue amiche” = “your friends”. “Tue” agrees with the noun “amiche” (plural feminine).
target_language_example: Esci spesso con le tue amiche?
native_language_example: Do you often go out with your (female) friends?

additional_notes: Plural of "tua mano" (your hand). The possessive adjective must agree with the noun: tua (feminine singular), tue (feminine plural). Very often you’ll also see it with the definite article: "le tue mani" = "your hands" (common in Italian).
target_language_example: Lavati le tue mani prima di mangiare.
native_language_example: Wash your hands before eating.

additional_notes: "Tuo" means "your" (informal singular, used with tu). It’s commonly used after prepositions like: "conto sul tuo aiuto" (I’m counting on your help), "ho bisogno del tuo aiuto" (I need your help), and with expressions like "ringraziarti per tutto il tuo aiuto" (to thank you for all your help) or "devo il mio successo al tuo aiuto" (I owe my success to your help).
target_language_example: Grazie per il tuo aiuto!
native_language_example: Thanks for your help!

additional_notes: Used to refer to a friend of the person you’re speaking to (tu = you, informal singular). With a masculine singular noun like amico, it’s tuo amico (no article). If you use an article, it becomes il tuo amico (“your friend”). For a female friend: tua amica / la tua amica. For formal “you” (Lei): Suo amico / il Suo amico.
target_language_example: È tuo amico o è solo un collega?
native_language_example: Is he your friend, or just a colleague?

meaning: your love (your beloved person, or the love you feel).
additional_notes: Usually refers either to (1) the person you love (your partner/crush) or (2) the feeling of love you have. Common in emotional/romantic contexts: “combattere/lotta per il tuo amore” = fight for your relationship or for the person you love; “dichiarare il tuo amore” = declare your love.
target_language_example: Non smettere di credere nel tuo amore.
native_language_example: Don’t stop believing in your love.

additional_notes: "Tuo" is the masculine singular form of "your" and it usually comes before the noun: tuo cane. Use it when speaking to one person (informal singular "tu"). For a female dog, you can say "tua cagna" (often avoided because it can sound insulting); many people still say "il mio/tuo cane" even for a female dog. For formal "you" (Lei), use "il Suo cane".
target_language_example: Dov'è il tuo cane adesso?
native_language_example: Where is your dog now?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the listener’s birthday. In Italian, possessives like "tuo" usually go with the definite article: "il tuo compleanno" = "your birthday". You can also say "È il tuo compleanno?" (Is it your birthday?).
target_language_example: Auguri! Oggi è il tuo compleanno?
native_language_example: Happy birthday! Is today your birthday?

additional_notes: Uses the informal singular possessive "tuo" (for someone you call "tu"); with "computer" (masculine singular) it becomes "il tuo computer" = "your computer." In questions you’ll often hear it without the article, but the article is common in Italian.
target_language_example: Posso controllare un attimo il tuo computer?
native_language_example: Can I check your computer for a moment?

meaning: "your body" (talking to one person you address as tu).
additional_notes: Uses the informal singular possessive: tuo = “your” (for a masculine singular noun), corpo = “body.” Often used in health/feelings contexts (“listen to your body”), but it can also be metaphorical (“this building is your body”). For a more formal/polite “your body,” you’d typically say il Suo corpo.
target_language_example: Ascolta il tuo corpo e riposati se ne hai bisogno.
native_language_example: Listen to your body and rest if you need to.

additional_notes: Means the physical heart, but very often it’s used figuratively to talk about emotions, love, inner feelings, compassion, or conscience. Common in expressions like “nel tuo cuore” (“in your heart”) and “fidati del tuo cuore” (“trust your heart”).
target_language_example: Ascolta il tuo cuore e fai la scelta giusta.
native_language_example: Listen to your heart and make the right choice.
