additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective tuo (“your”) + the noun figlio (“son”). In Italian, possessives usually need the definite article (il tuo figlio), but with family members in the singular you typically omit the article: tuo figlio, tua madre, tuo fratello. When speaking formally (Lei), you’d say suo figlio (“your son”).
target_language_example: Quanti anni ha tuo figlio?
native_language_example: How old is your son?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the person who is the listener’s brother. Often appears as "di tuo fratello" (“of your brother / your brother’s”). If you address more than one person, use "vostro fratello" (“your (plural) brother”).
target_language_example: Dov'è tuo fratello adesso?
native_language_example: Where is your brother now?

additional_notes: Means the job/work that belongs to the person you’re talking to (tu). It’s made of tuo (“your”, informal singular) + lavoro (“work/job”). Often used after prepositions like con/col (“with”): con il tuo lavoro / col tuo lavoro. In some contexts it can imply “your career/position” (e.g., if you care about keeping your job).
target_language_example: Come va col tuo lavoro ultimamente?
native_language_example: How’s your job going lately?

additional_notes: "Tuo" is the informal singular possessive "your" and agrees with the noun: "libro" is masculine singular, so it’s "tuo". In Italian, possessives are usually used with an article: "il tuo libro" = "your book". Without the article it can sound more like a direct address or emphasis, but with "libro" you’ll most often hear "il tuo libro".
target_language_example: Scusa, dov’è il tuo libro?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is your book?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the husband of the person you’re speaking to. With close family members in the singular (marito, moglie, padre, madre, etc.), Italian often drops the definite article: "tuo marito" (not *"il tuo marito"*). You may hear the article in some contexts (e.g., with emphasis, in some regional usage, or with adjectives: "il tuo caro marito").
target_language_example: Tuo marito lavora oggi?
native_language_example: Is your husband working today?

additional_notes: Uses the informal singular possessive "tuo" (used with "tu"). Often appears with prepositions like "col tuo nome" (with your name) or "del tuo nome" (of your name). In polite/formal situations, you’ll usually hear "il suo nome" (your name, formal) instead.
target_language_example: Scusi, qual è il tuo nome?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what’s your name?

additional_notes: Uses the informal possessive "tuo" (for "tu"). With family members, Italian typically uses the definite article: "il tuo padre" is unusual; you normally say "tuo padre". In direct speech it can be used as a subject or object (e.g., "Smettila di disturbare tuo padre").
target_language_example: Tuo padre è a casa?
native_language_example: Is your father at home?

additional_notes:
Used at the start of a sentence when addressing someone about their father and then immediately using the pronoun ti before the verb. In Italian, object pronouns like ti usually come before the verb: 
- tuo padre ti aspetta = your father is waiting for you
- tuo padre ti vuole bene = your father loves you/cares about you
Depending on the verb, ti can mean either "you" (direct object) or "to you" (indirect object).
target_language_example: Tuo padre ti chiama in cucina.
native_language_example: Your father is calling you into the kitchen.

additional_notes: Used to describe your dad (identity, profession, qualities, or where he is). Often followed by an adjective (forte), a noun with an article (un prete), or a place/status phrase (al lavoro = “at work”). Note: Italian padre means “father,” but English “padre” can mean a priest/chaplain, so don’t confuse them.
target_language_example: Tuo padre è a casa oggi?
native_language_example: Is your father at home today?

additional_notes: "Tuoi" is the plural masculine possessive for "your" used with a plural noun; it agrees with "amici". Use "tue amiche" for a female-only group (your female friends). Common after prepositions: "con i tuoi amici" (with your friends), "dei tuoi amici" (some of your friends).
target_language_example: Stasera esci con i tuoi amici?
native_language_example: Are you going out with your friends tonight?

additional_notes: "Tuoi" is the plural masculine form of "your" and agrees with "figli" (literally "sons"), but in everyday Italian "i tuoi figli" often means "your children" in general (sons and/or daughters). Used with the article: "i tuoi figli" = "your children."
target_language_example: Come stanno i tuoi figli?
native_language_example: How are your children?

additional_notes: "Tuoi" is the plural possessive adjective for "tu" (you, informal singular). It agrees with the plural noun "genitori". Often used with the article: "i tuoi genitori" = "your parents." For formal "you" (Lei), use "i Suoi genitori."
target_language_example: I tuoi genitori vengono a prenderti dopo scuola?
native_language_example: Are your parents coming to pick you up after school?

additional_notes: Means “your eyes” when speaking to one person you address as tu. Tuoi is the masculine plural possessive adjective used with occhi (plural). With prepositions you may see contractions like coi tuoi occhi (= con i tuoi occhi, “with your eyes”).
target_language_example: Nei tuoi occhi vedo una grande tristezza.
native_language_example: In your eyes I see a great sadness.

additional_notes: Used to put full blame on a person or thing. Often followed by a possessive (tutta colpa mia/sua/nostra = entirely my/his/our fault) or by "di" + noun/pronoun (tutta colpa di Marco = all Marco’s fault; tutta colpa di questo vaso = all because of this vase). You may also hear it with "è": "È tutta colpa tua".
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, è tutta colpa mia.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, it’s entirely my fault.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to mean the entire amount/thing/time period: tutta la mela (the whole apple), tutta la settimana (the whole week). It agrees with the noun: tutto il (masc. sing.), tutti i / tutte le (plural). Often followed by a possessive: tutta la sua paghetta (all of her allowance).
target_language_example: Sono rimasto a casa tutta la giornata.
native_language_example: I stayed home all day.

additional_notes: Means the entire city and everyone/everything in it. It can be the subject (“Tutta la città lo sa” = the whole city knows it) or, with prepositions like in/per, it often means “throughout/all over the city” (“in tutta la città”).
target_language_example: C'è un blackout in tutta la città.
native_language_example: There’s a blackout all over the city.

meaning: the whole family; everyone in the family.
additional_notes: Used to include every member of a family as a group (not just close relatives). Common with verbs like salutare/mandare saluti (“send greetings”), preparare (“prepare”) or when talking about responsibility/support for everyone in the household.
target_language_example: A Natale viene a cena tutta la famiglia.
native_language_example: At Christmas the whole family comes for dinner.

additional_notes:
Refers to the entire day from start to finish. Common with:
- "per tutta la giornata" = "throughout the whole day"
- "passare/trascorrere tutta la giornata a + infinitive" = "to spend the whole day doing (something)"
- "passare/trascorrere tutta la giornata con + person" = "to spend the whole day with (someone)"
target_language_example: Abbiamo lavorato tutta la giornata.
native_language_example: We worked all day.

meaning: the whole day in the library.
additional_notes: Used to say someone spent the entire day at the library (often with verbs like "passare" or "trascorrere"). "Tutta la giornata" = "all day / the whole day"; "in biblioteca" = "in/at the library."
target_language_example: Oggi ho studiato tutta la giornata in biblioteca.
native_language_example: Today I studied the whole day in the library.

additional_notes: Used to say something lasted for the entire morning. Often with verbs like essere (è stato), lavorare, continuare, rimanere. You can also say "per tutta la mattina" with the same meaning; "tutta la mattina" is also common without "per".
target_language_example: Sono rimasto in ufficio tutta la mattina.
native_language_example: I stayed at the office all morning.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your entire life up to now ("all my life") or your life as a whole ("my whole life"). The word order can vary (e.g., "per tutta la mia vita" = "for my whole life"). Often used for emphasis about long duration or deep importance.
target_language_example: Ho aspettato questo momento tutta la mia vita.
native_language_example: I’ve waited for this moment my whole life.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens for the entire duration of the night. It can emphasize that it lasted a long time or continuously. Often paired with verbs like dormire (sleep), piangere (cry), studiare (study), lavorare (work), fare festa (party).
target_language_example: Abbiamo studiato tutta la notte per l'esame.
native_language_example: We studied all night for the exam.

additional_notes: Used to say something lasts for the entire evening. Often interchangeable with **per tutta la sera** (“for the whole evening”). In the pattern **È tutta la sera che + verb**, it means “I/we have been … all evening” (ongoing action).
target_language_example: Ho lavorato tutta la sera.
native_language_example: I worked all evening.

additional_notes: Means the entire duration of the week. Often used with time expressions like "sono stato occupato tutta la settimana" (I’ve been busy all week). With "per" ("per tutta la settimana") it emphasizes the full length of time (“for the whole week”), but in many sentences both versions sound natural.
target_language_example: Lavoro tutta la settimana, quindi esco solo nel weekend.
native_language_example: I work all week, so I only go out on the weekend.

meaning: the whole story; the full story.
additional_notes: Used when you want the complete account of what happened (all the details), or to say you already know everything about a situation. In contexts like "inventò tutta la storia," it can mean someone made up the entire story.
target_language_example: Raccontami tutta la storia, per favore.
native_language_example: Tell me the whole story, please.

meaning: “all of his/her” (referring to a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to mean the entire amount/extent of something belonging to someone: “tutta la sua + [noun]” (e.g., tutta la sua esperienza = all his experience). Often appears after words like “nonostante” (“despite”) or in expressions like “È tutta la sua …” to say someone is exactly like a female relative (“She’s just like her mom”). For masculine nouns: “tutto il suo”; for plural: “tutti/e i/le suoi/sue”.
target_language_example: Ha usato tutta la sua pazienza per spiegare tutto.
native_language_example: He used all his patience to explain everything.

additional_notes: Means someone’s entire lifetime, or from birth up to the present point being discussed. Often used with verbs like vivere (to live), passare/trascorrere (to spend), dedicare/dare (to devote/give). You can change the possessive to match the person: tutta la mia vita (all my life), tutta la tua vita, tutta la nostra vita, etc.
target_language_example: Ho lavorato in questo negozio per tutta la mia vita.
native_language_example: I’ve worked in this shop my whole life.

additional_notes: Often used with **per** to mean “for (your) whole life” (**per tutta la vita**). Without **per**, it can refer to “life as a whole” in a general, philosophical way (e.g., talking about what life is).
target_language_example: Ho vissuto in questa città per tutta la vita.
native_language_example: I’ve lived in this city my whole life.

meaning: “all this” (referring to a feminine singular thing).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to mean “all this/this whole (thing)” and often adds emphasis (amount, effort, etc.): tutta questa acqua = “all this water,” tutta questa fatica = “all this effort.” It agrees with the noun: tutto questo (masc. sing.), tutti questi (masc. pl.), tutte queste (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Non posso credere di aver speso tutta questa energia per niente.
native_language_example: I can’t believe I spent all this energy for nothing.

meaning: all these people; all this crowd.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of people you can see or are talking about, often emphasizing that there are many of them. It can sound a bit dramatic or rhetorical in questions/exclamations (like “all these people…?”).
target_language_example: Non capisco perché tutta questa gente sia qui così presto.
native_language_example: I don’t understand why all these people are here so early.

meaning: all this stuff / all these things.
additional_notes: "Roba" is a very common, informal way to say “stuff/things” (objects, belongings, or even information). "Tutta questa" emphasizes quantity (“all this”), sometimes with a tone of surprise or annoyance: "Dove metto tutta questa roba?" = “Where do I put all this stuff?”
target_language_example: Non so dove mettere tutta questa roba in casa.
native_language_example: I don’t know where to put all this stuff in the house.

meaning: 'all the' (feminine plural) / 'every' with feminine plural nouns.
additional_notes: Used with feminine plural nouns: tutte le carte (all the cards), tutte le mele (all the apples). In time expressions, it can mean “every”: tutte le mattine (every morning), tutte le sere (every evening). The masculine plural is tutti i / tutti gli.
target_language_example: Vado in palestra tutte le settimane.
native_language_example: I go to the gym every week.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of other people/things that are feminine plural (or treated as feminine plural), often in comparisons ("più ... di tutte le altre" = "more ... than all the others") or when talking about the rest of a group ("contro tutte le altre" = "against all the other [teams]"). For mixed-gender groups in Italian, you typically use masculine: "tutti gli altri".
target_language_example: Questo vestito costa meno di tutte le altre opzioni.
native_language_example: This dress costs less than all the other options.

additional_notes: Means “all the things” in a general sense, often in serious or reflective statements (e.g., about life ending, mistakes, or the end of everything). You’ll also see it followed by an adjective or a relative clause: “tutte le cose brutte…”, “tutte le cose che…”.
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato tutte le cose che dovevo comprare.
native_language_example: I forgot everything I had to buy.

additional_notes: Plural feminine: "tutte" (all) + "le donne" (the women). Used to refer to every woman in a group or in general (sometimes as a generalization: "Tutte le donne..." = "All women..."). You’ll also see it with a relative clause: "tutte le donne che..." (all the women who...).
target_language_example: Tutte le donne del gruppo hanno ricevuto un messaggio.
native_language_example: All the women in the group received a message.

additional_notes: Used to refer to every window in a room/building. Often appears with verbs like chiudere (to close) or aprire (to open). Agreement: tutte (feminine plural) matches finestre (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Per favore, chiudi tutte le finestre prima di uscire.
native_language_example: Please close all the windows before going out.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause describing “the letters.” After this phrase, you typically add a verb like *hai scritto* (you wrote), *avete scritto* (you all wrote), or *ha mandato* (he/she sent). *Che* = “that/which,” and *mi* = “to me.”
target_language_example: Ho conservato tutte le lettere che mi hai scritto.
native_language_example: I kept all the letters you wrote to me.

additional_notes: Uses the feminine plural: *tutte* (all, fem. pl.) + *le* (the, fem. pl.) + *luci* (lights). Common with verbs like *accendere* (to turn on) and *spegnere* (to turn off): *Accendi/Spegni tutte le luci*. It can refer to the lights in a room/house, or more generally to every light in a place.
target_language_example: Prima di uscire, spegni tutte le luci.
native_language_example: Before you go out, turn off all the lights.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a repeated habit or routine that happens each morning. Often placed at the end of the sentence (common in Italian), but it can also come at the beginning for emphasis.
target_language_example: Vado al lavoro in autobus tutte le mattine.
native_language_example: I go to work by bus every morning.

additional_notes: "Tutte" is the feminine plural form of "tutto" (“all”). It agrees with the noun: "mele" (apples) is feminine plural, so you say "tutte le mele." Used to refer to the complete set of apples being talked about (e.g., all of them here/on the table/in the basket).
target_language_example: Non comprare altre mele: abbiamo già tutte le mele che ci servono.
native_language_example: Don’t buy more apples: we already have all the apples we need.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun to mean “all of my …”. It agrees in gender/number: tutte (feminine plural) + le (plural) + mie (feminine plural). For masculine plural nouns, use “tutti i miei” (e.g., tutti i miei libri = all my books).
target_language_example: Ho perso tutte le mie chiavi.
native_language_example: I lost all my keys.

additional_notes: "Tutte" agrees with a feminine plural noun: "amiche" (female friends). It can be the subject ("Tutte le mie amiche abitano qui") or follow an indirect-object pattern with piacere/mancare: "A tutte le mie amiche piace..." = "All my friends like..." and "A me mancano tutte le mie amiche" = "I miss all my friends."
target_language_example: Tutte le mie amiche vengono alla festa stasera.
native_language_example: All my (female) friends are coming to the party tonight.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun to mean “all of our …”. It agrees with the noun: tutte (feminine plural) + le (the, feminine plural) + nostre (our, feminine plural). For masculine plural you’d use “tutti i nostri” (e.g., tutti i nostri amici).
target_language_example: Abbiamo salutato tutte le nostre colleghe prima di andare via.
native_language_example: We said hello to all our (female) colleagues before leaving.

additional_notes: Means the whole group of people being talked about. Often followed by a verb in the plural (e.g., “tutte le persone hanno…”). With “non” it can mean “not everyone” or “not all people,” depending on context: “Non a tutte le persone…” = “Not everyone…” / “Not all people…”.
target_language_example: In questa città, tutte le persone parlano italiano.
native_language_example: In this city, everyone speaks Italian.

additional_notes: Used to refer to every door in a place (house, building, rooms). Often appears in commands with verbs like "chiudere" (to close) or "chiudere a chiave" (to lock): "Chiudi/Chiudete/Chiuda tutte le porte". Agreement: feminine plural "tutte" + "le porte".
target_language_example: Prima di uscire, controlla che tutte le porte siano chiuse.
native_language_example: Before leaving, check that all the doors are closed.

additional_notes: Means having/knowing every answer or solution. Often used with verbs like avere (to have), conoscere (to know), cancellare (to delete), especially in contexts like tests, quizzes, or problem-solving. Can also be used figuratively: non avere tutte le risposte = not to have everything figured out.
target_language_example: Non ho tutte le risposte, ma posso informarmi e richiamarti.
native_language_example: I don’t have all the answers, but I can find out and call you back.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens regularly each evening. Often paired with a habitual action (e.g., "Lavoro tutte le sere"). With "quasi" it becomes "almost every evening" ("quasi tutte le sere"). You can also use it as an exclamation meaning "every single night, same thing!" ("Tutte le sere...").
target_language_example: Studio italiano tutte le sere dopo cena.
native_language_example: I study Italian every evening after dinner.

meaning: all his/her (feminine plural things), meaning “all of his/hers” with a feminine plural noun.
additional_notes: Used with a feminine plural noun owned by a person (sue = “his/her” feminine plural). It agrees with what follows: tutte le sue feste = “all his/her parties,” tutte le sue cose = “all his/her things.” With masculine plural it becomes “tutti i suoi…”. Often translated as “all his/her …” rather than literally “all the his/her.”
target_language_example: Ha cancellato tutte le sue prenotazioni.
native_language_example: He/She canceled all his/her bookings.

additional_notes: “Tutte” = “all” (feminine plural), “le” = “the” (feminine plural), “sue” = “his/her/your (formal)” depending on context, and “amiche” = “female friends.” Use “tutti i suoi amici” for “all his/her male friends,” and “tutti i suoi amici” can also mean “all his/her friends” in a mixed-gender group.
target_language_example: È uscita con tutte le sue amiche dopo scuola.
native_language_example: She went out with all her (female) friends after school.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun to mean you include everything that belongs to the person you’re talking to: tutte le tue risorse (all your resources), tutte le tue domande (all your questions), tutte le tue energie (all your energy/efforts). It agrees with the noun: masc. plural would be tutti i tuoi (e.g., tutti i tuoi libri). Often used for emphasis with words like energie/forze (“with all your strength”).
target_language_example: Devi usare tutte le tue energie per finire oggi.
native_language_example: You have to use all your energy to finish today.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens on every occasion. Often followed by a clause with "che" (e.g., "tutte le volte che...") or used alone for emphasis ("Tutte le volte la stessa storia!" = "Same story every time!"). It can also mean "for all the times" when referring back to repeated past actions (e.g., "per tutte le volte che...").
target_language_example: Tutte le volte che piove, dimentico l'ombrello.
native_language_example: Every time it rains, I forget my umbrella.

additional_notes: Used when the speakers/group are all women or the group is treated as feminine (e.g., in some contexts with mixed groups you may still hear masculine: “tutti noi”). Often appears after a preposition, especially “a tutte noi” (“to all of us”): “Mancava a tutte noi” = “We all missed him/her.” The masculine equivalent is “tutti noi.”
target_language_example: È importante per tutte noi.
native_language_example: It’s important for all of us (women).

meaning: all of them / every single one (feminine plural, emphatic).
additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that you mean the whole group. It agrees in gender/number: tutte quante refers to an all-female group or feminine plural nouns (e.g., le ragazze, le cose, le chiavi). The masculine/mixed form is tutti quanti. Often placed after the noun or pronoun it refers to (e.g., loro tutte quante; le ho viste tutte quante).
target_language_example: Le ho invitate tutte quante alla festa.
native_language_example: I invited all of them to the party.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun (explicit or implied) to refer to a specific set of things that are not here/near the speaker, or that have been mentioned/are obvious from context. Often conveys “so many of those” depending on tone/context. With a noun: “tutte quelle + [noun]” (e.g., tutte quelle chiavi). Without a noun it can stand alone when the noun is understood (e.g., “Tutte quelle cose…”).
target_language_example: Perché hai comprato tutte quelle scarpe?
native_language_example: Why did you buy all those shoes?

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun to refer to a whole group of things close to the speaker/context: tutte queste lingue (all these languages), tutte queste storie (all these stories). It can sound slightly emphatic/complaining depending on tone (e.g., “all these questions!”). For masculine plural, use “tutti questi”.
target_language_example: Perché hai comprato tutte queste cose?
native_language_example: Why did you buy all these things?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a set of things just mentioned or understood from context. Often expresses surprise, emphasis, or a broad/general idea (e.g., opinions, topics, actions).
target_language_example: Non capisco perché devi comprare tutte queste cose.
native_language_example: I don’t understand why you have to buy all these things.

meaning: "all the" (plural masculine before a vowel/s + consonant/z/gn/ps/x/y).
additional_notes: Used to mean “all the” with masculine plural nouns that take the article "gli" (e.g., autobus, esseri, insegnanti). It agrees with the noun: tutti + gli. For feminine plural, use "tutte le"; for masculine plural with "i" (most consonant-starting nouns), use "tutti i".
target_language_example: Tutti gli studenti sono qui.
native_language_example: All the students are here.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the rest of the people/things in a group, excluding the person/thing already mentioned or implied (often “us/me/you”). It can be a pronoun phrase by itself (“Dove sono andati tutti gli altri?”) or used in comparisons like “come tutti gli altri” (“like everyone else”). You may also see it agree in gender/number: “tutte le altre” (all the others, feminine plural).
target_language_example: Io resto qui; tutti gli altri vanno al bar.
native_language_example: I'm staying here; everyone else is going to the café.

additional_notes: Means the entire group of animals being talked about (general statement). It’s the plural of "tutto" (all) + "gli animali" (the animals). Used with "sono" (are) and often with "non" to say "not all the animals" ("non tutti gli animali").
target_language_example: Nel parco non tutti gli animali si possono toccare.
native_language_example: In the park, not all the animals can be touched.

additional_notes: Means the entire group of students. Often used with negation as "non tutti gli studenti..." = "not all the students..." (some, but not everyone).
target_language_example: Tutti gli studenti devono portare un quaderno.
native_language_example: All the students have to bring a notebook.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the entire group of birds in general statements. "Tutti" = "all"; "gli" is the plural masculine article meaning "the" (used before certain consonant clusters like z, s+consonant, gn, ps); "uccelli" = "birds". Often used in sentences like "Non tutti gli uccelli..." (Not all birds...).
target_language_example: Tutti gli uccelli costruiscono un nido?
native_language_example: Do all birds build a nest?

additional_notes: Literally “all the men.” Often used in general statements about people/humanity (sometimes meaning “everyone”), not just a specific group of men. Agreement: plural masculine. You can also say “tutte le persone” for a more gender-neutral “everyone/all people.”
target_language_example: Tutti gli uomini nascono liberi e uguali in dignità e diritti.
native_language_example: All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.

meaning: 'all men are / all human beings are' (a general statement).
additional_notes: Used to make broad, general statements about people. Often followed by an adjective or noun phrase (e.g., uguali, mortali, fratelli). With non: "Non tutti gli uomini sono..." = "Not all men are...". In many contexts it’s understood as "all people/humans," not only males; you may also hear "tutte le persone sono..." for a more gender-neutral wording.
target_language_example: Non tutti gli uomini sono d'accordo su questo punto.
native_language_example: Not all people agree on this point.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to mean “all the …” or “every …” (general statement). With feminine plural nouns, use "tutte le" instead. Example: "tutti i giorni" = "every day" / "all the days".
target_language_example: Tutti i negozi sono chiusi la domenica.
native_language_example: All the shops are closed on Sundays.

additional_notes: Usually refers to the Catholic holiday (also called "Ognissanti"). You may see it in date/time expressions like "a/il giorno di Tutti i Santi" (on All Saints’ Day) or "vacanze di Tutti i Santi" (All Saints’ break). In exclamations like "per tutti i santi!" it means something like "for heaven’s sake!", but that’s a different fixed expression.
target_language_example: Il primo novembre è la festa di Tutti i Santi.
native_language_example: November 1st is All Saints’ Day.

additional_notes: "Tutti" means "all" and "i cani" means "the dogs" (plural). Used to talk about the entire group of dogs. It can be the subject (Tutti i cani sono...) or the object (Voglio tutti i cani).
target_language_example: Tutti i cani del rifugio meritano una casa.
native_language_example: All the dogs at the shelter deserve a home.

additional_notes: Used when you want complete, specific information about something (a story, a case, a plan, an event). Often follows verbs like dire (to tell), sapere/conoscere (to know), contenere (to contain), svelare (to reveal), and can be followed by “di/del/della …” to say what the details are about (e.g., tutti i dettagli della storia).
target_language_example: Puoi spiegarmi tutti i dettagli del progetto?
native_language_example: Can you explain all the details of the project?

additional_notes: Used to describe a daily habit or something that happens each day. Often goes at the end of the sentence, but it can also appear earlier for emphasis. Literal meaning: “all the days.”
target_language_example: Prendo un caffè tutti i giorni prima di andare al lavoro.
native_language_example: I have a coffee every day before going to work.

additional_notes: Means every book in a given group or place. Often followed by a specification with “di …” (e.g., “tutti i libri di questa biblioteca” = “all the books in this library”). Uses masculine plural “tutti” + plural article “i” + “libri.”
target_language_example: Devo sistemare tutti i libri sullo scaffale.
native_language_example: I have to put away all the books on the shelf.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to mean “all of their …”. It agrees with the noun that follows: tutti i loro amici (m. pl.), tutte le loro cose (f. pl.). The stressed form “loro” is often used instead of the unstressed possessive “i suoi/le sue” when you want to be extra clear about whose things they are.
target_language_example: Hanno venduto tutti i loro mobili prima di traslocare.
native_language_example: They sold all their furniture before moving.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to mean “all of my …”: tutti i miei piani/esami/libri. With people, it refers to “all my (boys/guys/kids/people)”: tutti i miei ragazzi. For feminine plural nouns, use “tutte le mie” (e.g., tutte le mie amiche).
target_language_example: Ho perso tutti i miei documenti.
native_language_example: I lost all my documents.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your entire group of friends. Agreement matters: with people, use plural verbs/adjectives (e.g., “sono”, “parlano”). Word order is typically “tutti i/le miei/mie + noun” (e.g., tutti i miei amici; tutte le mie amiche). Often used for general statements (“All my friends do it”) or to emphasize inclusion (“All my friends are invited”).
target_language_example: Stasera esco con tutti i miei amici.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m going out with all my friends.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that none of your money is left or that you gave/lent/spent your entire amount. Often appears after the verb (e.g., Ho speso tutti i miei soldi) but can also be placed earlier for emphasis. In speech you might also hear "tutti i soldi" (all the money) or "tutti i miei" with the noun understood from context.
target_language_example: Non posso uscire stasera: ho già speso tutti i miei soldi.
native_language_example: I can’t go out tonight: I’ve already spent all my money.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to mean “all our …”: tutti i nostri amici/nomi/libri. For feminine plural, use “tutte le nostre” (e.g., tutte le nostre amiche). You can also use it more generally for “all of our” when the noun is understood (e.g., Erano tutti i nostri soldi! = It was all our money!).
target_language_example: Dobbiamo proteggere tutti i nostri dati.
native_language_example: We have to protect all of our data.

meaning: all the boys; all the kids/guys (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literally “all the boys.” In many everyday contexts, especially when talking about a group of children or teens, ragazzi can also mean “kids” or “guys” (sometimes mixed gender, depending on the speaker and situation). Common structure: tutti + i + plural noun. For “all the girls,” use tutte le ragazze.
target_language_example: A scuola, tutti i ragazzi devono rispettare le regole.
native_language_example: At school, all the kids have to follow the rules.

additional_notes: Used to mean the entire amount of money being talked about (not just some of it). Common in questions about where money went ("Dove vanno tutti i soldi?") and with verbs like dare (to give), prendere (to take), avere (to have), spendere (to spend). You can add details: "tutti i soldi che avevo" (all the money I had), "tutti i soldi di cui avevo bisogno" (all the money I needed).
target_language_example: Ha speso tutti i soldi per il viaggio.
native_language_example: He spent all the money on the trip.

additional_notes: Uses the relative clause "che aveva" (= “that he/she had”) to specify the total amount of money someone possessed at that time. Often followed by who received it ("a Mary") or clarified with "con sé" (= “on him/her, with him/her”).
target_language_example: Ho speso tutti i soldi che avevo in un giorno.
native_language_example: I spent all the money I had in one day.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to mean “all of his.” Italian possessives usually take the definite article: i suoi libri = “his books.” It changes with gender/number: tutto il suo (all his + masc. sing.), tutta la sua (all his + fem. sing.), tutte le sue (all his + fem. plural). Can also mean “all of her/its” depending on context (suoi/sue agree with the thing owned, not the owner).
target_language_example: Ha venduto tutti i suoi CD.
native_language_example: He sold all his CDs.

additional_notes: Means a male person's entire group of friends. It uses the possessive "suoi" (his) with a plural noun "amici" (friends). In Italian the possessive agrees with the noun (amici), not with the owner; for a female owner you’d say "tutte le sue amiche" (all her friends) or "tutti i suoi amici" depending on whether the friends are female-only or mixed/masculine plural.
target_language_example: Parla sempre con tutti i suoi amici dopo il lavoro.
native_language_example: He always talks to all his friends after work.

additional_notes: Means “all of his problems” or “all of her problems,” depending on who "suo/suoi" refers to in the sentence. Used for blaming someone (incolpare qualcuno per tutti i suoi problemi) or talking about solving them (la soluzione a tutti i suoi problemi; tutti i suoi problemi sono stati risolti).
target_language_example: Non puoi dare la colpa agli altri per tutti i suoi problemi.
native_language_example: You can’t blame others for all his/her problems.

additional_notes: Means the entire amount of money belonging to someone (a man or a woman). It often appears with verbs like dare (to give), spendere (to spend), rubare (to steal), and can be used with prepositions like in/per (e.g., in vestiti = on clothes; per una moto = for a motorbike). Note: suoi changes with the owner: tutti i miei soldi (all my money), tutti i tuoi soldi (all your money), tutti i nostri/vostri/loro soldi.
target_language_example: Non voglio spendere tutti i suoi soldi.
native_language_example: I don’t want to spend all his/her money.

meaning: all kinds of / all types of.
additional_notes: Used before a noun to say there is a wide variety (without listing them). It agrees in number and gender with "tipo" here: plural masculine "tutti i tipi di" ("all the types of"). Often followed by a plural noun, e.g. "tutti i tipi di sport".
target_language_example: Nel negozio vendono tutti i tipi di frutta.
native_language_example: In the shop they sell all kinds of fruit.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to mean “all of your …”: tutti i tuoi fratelli / sogni / problemi. It agrees with the noun (tutte le tue = feminine plural; tutto il tuo = masculine singular; tutta la tua = feminine singular). Often followed directly by the noun.
target_language_example: Ho letto tutti i tuoi messaggi.
native_language_example: I read all your messages.

meaning: all of your (plural/with a masculine plural noun).
additional_notes: Used with a plural noun to mean “all the … that belong to you (you all / you plural / formal you).” It agrees in gender/number with the noun: tutti i vostri commenti/album/dottori (masc. plural); tutte le vostre foto (fem. plural). With a masculine singular noun: tutto il vostro tempo (“all your time”).
target_language_example: Ho letto tutti i vostri messaggi.
native_language_example: I read all of your messages.

additional_notes: Used to include the speaker in a group (“we, everyone in our group”). It can be the subject (“Tutti noi parliamo…”) or an object after a verb/preposition (“…a tutti noi” = “to all of us”).
target_language_example: Tutti noi vogliamo aiutarti.
native_language_example: All of us want to help you.

additional_notes: Used for emphasis to mean the whole group, without exceptions. It can refer to people in general ("everyone") or, in commands, to a group you’re addressing ("all of you"). Often placed after the verb or set off by commas in spoken Italian: "Andate tutti quanti" / "Tutti quanti, ascoltate!"
target_language_example: Venite tutti quanti alla riunione alle sei.
native_language_example: All of you come to the meeting at six.

meaning: "all that money" (a large amount of money).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the amount of money is surprisingly big or noteworthy. Often appears in questions or with verbs like dare (to give), prendere (to take/get), guadagnare (to earn), servire (to need/be useful). "Quei" = "those" (plural), referring to money that’s already known from context.
target_language_example: Non capisco perché hai speso tutti quei soldi per un telefono.
native_language_example: I don’t understand why you spent all that money on a phone.

additional_notes: Used to refer to every person or thing in a group that matches a description, followed by a clause with **che** ("who/that"). For people you can also hear **tutti coloro che** (more formal). For feminine plural: **tutte quelle che**.
target_language_example: Ringrazio tutti quelli che mi hanno aiutato.
native_language_example: I thank everyone who helped me.

additional_notes: Means “all those (people) that I know.” It’s a relative clause: quelli = “those (people)” + che conosco = “that I know.” You can change it for gender/number: tutti quelli… (masc. or mixed group), tutte quelle… (all women). Often used to make general statements about your acquaintances.
target_language_example: Tutti quelli che conosco vivono in questa città.
native_language_example: Everyone I know lives in this city.

additional_notes: Used with plural nouns to point to a specific group of items/people already known or visible in the context: *tutti questi film/rumori/funghi*. It can also refer to a period of time: *in tutti questi anni* (“in all these years”). The masculine plural *questi* is also used for mixed-gender groups; for feminine plural use *tutte queste*.
target_language_example: Perché hai comprato tutti questi libri?
native_language_example: Why did you buy all these books?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the whole period of time up to now (often with surprise or emphasis), like English “all these years” or “for all these years.” You’ll often see it after a preposition: “in tutti questi anni” = “in all these years / over all these years.”
target_language_example: Non ci posso credere: in tutti questi anni non l’ho mai saputo.
native_language_example: I can’t believe it: all these years I never knew.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of books that are present/visible or already mentioned. Often expresses surprise or emphasis in conversation (e.g., noticing someone has many books). Agreement: "tutti" (masc. plural) + "questi" (masc. plural) + plural noun "libri".
target_language_example: Perché hai tutti questi libri sul tavolo?
native_language_example: Why do you have all these books on the table?

additional_notes: Used to address or refer to a group of people directly, often for emphasis. Common in commands or exclamations (e.g., "Ascoltate, tutti voi!") and can also be used after a preposition: "a tutti voi" = "to all of you," "senza tutti voi" = "without all of you."
target_language_example: Grazie a tutti voi per l’aiuto.
native_language_example: Thank you all for the help.

meaning: “all (of them) and …” / used with a number: “all three/two/etc.”
additional_notes: Used before adding another clause with **e** (“and”) to mean “everyone/all of them”: *Tutti e tutti odiano me.* It’s also very common in the pattern **tutti e + number** to mean “all + number (together)”: *tutti e tre* = “all three,” *tutti e due* = “both.” It agrees for gender/number when needed: **tutti** (masc./mixed), **tutte** (fem.).
target_language_example: Vorrei parlare con loro tutti e tre dopo la lezione.
native_language_example: I’d like to talk to all three of them after class.

additional_notes: Used to refer to two people or two things together (emphasizing that it’s both, not just one). Often answers a choice question ("Which one?" → "Tutti e due!"). With people, it can mean "both of you" ("Uscite tutti e due" = "You two, get out"). For objects you also commonly hear "tutti e due" or "tutte e due" depending on gender, though in everyday speech many speakers use "tutti e due" broadly.
target_language_example: Vuoi il caffè o il tè? Tutti e due, grazie.
native_language_example: Do you want coffee or tea? Both, thanks.

additional_notes: Used with a plural subject (“tutti” = everyone/all) + “hanno” (they have). It introduces a general statement about what people have/need/think. You can also say “tutti hanno + noun” (Tutti hanno paura = Everyone is afraid) or “tutti hanno bisogno di + noun” (Everyone needs…).
target_language_example: Tutti hanno diritto a una pausa.
native_language_example: Everyone has the right to a break.

additional_notes: Used to say that a whole group does something as one (in the same place or at the same time). Often comes after the subject (e.g., “andiamo tutti insieme”) or can be said alone as an encouraging call (“Tutti insieme!”).
target_language_example: Facciamo una foto tutti insieme.
native_language_example: Let’s take a photo all together.

meaning: all of you / all of them; everyone (emphatic).
additional_notes: An emphatic way to say "tutti" (“everyone/all”), often used when calling to or including the whole group. Common with commands and invitations: "Tutti quanti fuori!" = “Everybody out!” Can stand alone as an answer to mean “all of them/all of you.”
target_language_example: Venite tutti quanti, così partiamo insieme.
native_language_example: Come all of you, so we can leave together.

additional_notes: Used to say that all the people in a place/group are present or included. Often in statements like “Siamo tutti qui” (we’re all here) or “Tutti qui sanno…” (everyone here knows…). It can also be used as a call/command: “Venite tutti qui” = “Everyone come here.”
target_language_example: Siamo tutti qui, possiamo iniziare.
native_language_example: We’re all here, we can start.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement presented as common knowledge or something widely believed. Often followed by a full clause (subject + verb): “Tutti sanno che + [sentence]”. You can also use it sarcastically to suggest that something is obvious (or supposedly obvious).
target_language_example: Tutti sanno che domani è festa.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that tomorrow is a holiday.

additional_notes: Used to exclude one or more people from a group. Often followed by a person/pronoun (tutti tranne me/te/lui/lei/noi/voi/loro) or a noun phrase (tutti tranne Marco). You may also hear the singular form: "tutto tranne" = "anything but".
target_language_example: Vengono tutti tranne Luca.
native_language_example: Everyone is coming except Luca.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re the only exception in a group. Often comes after a statement ("Hanno riso tutti tranne me") or at the start for emphasis ("Tutti tranne me sono occupati"). You can swap in other pronouns: "tutti tranne te" (everyone except you), "tutti tranne lui/lei" (everyone except him/her), "tutti tranne noi" (everyone except us).
target_language_example: Sono venuti tutti tranne me.
native_language_example: Everyone came except me.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the whole of something already mentioned or understood. Very common in the pattern "tutto ciò che + verb" = "everything that ..." (e.g., "tutto ciò che voglio" = "everything I want"). It can also stand alone: "Tutto ciò è cambiato" = "All that has changed".
target_language_example: Non dimenticare tutto ciò che ti ho detto.
native_language_example: Don’t forget everything I told you.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the totality of things within a relative clause (followed by a verb), often meaning “everything that …”. Very common with verbs like vedere, fare, volere, rimanere, avere: e.g., "Tutto ciò che voglio è..." = “All I want is…”.
target_language_example: Tutto ciò che posso fare adesso è aspettare.
native_language_example: All I can do now is wait.

tutto ciò che devi fare è

target_language_multi_word_term: tutto ciò che devi fare è
additional_notes: Used to introduce a simple action or requirement. It’s often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., chiedere, ascoltare, aspettare) or by a longer phrase explaining what is required.
target_language_example: Tutto ciò che devi fare è premere questo pulsante.
native_language_example: All you have to do is press this button.

additional_notes: Used to refer to all of someone’s belongings/possessions in the past. It’s often used with verbs like perdere (to lose) or vendere (to sell). The verb possedeva is the imperfect tense (he/she used to own / owned), which fits when talking about what someone had at that time.
target_language_example: Dopo il fallimento, ha dovuto vendere tutto ciò che possedeva.
native_language_example: After the bankruptcy, he had to sell everything he owned.

meaning: "All I want is" / "All I want to do is".
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you have one main desire or request. It’s often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., andare, parlare) or by a noun phrase (e.g., la libertà, il vostro amore). You can also say "tutto quello che voglio è" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Tutto ciò che voglio è riposarmi un po'.
native_language_example: All I want is to rest a bit.

meaning: “everything that (someone) needs” / “all that (someone) needs” (introduces the thing needed).
additional_notes: Used to introduce the object of a verb like avere bisogno di (“to need”) or parlare di (“to talk about”). Pattern: tutto ciò di cui + subject + verb + (di) + ... Example with need: tutto ciò di cui ho bisogno = “everything that I need” (literally: “all that of which I have need”). Often followed by a clause (ho bisogno, avete bisogno, avevano bisogno).
target_language_example: Qui trovi tutto ciò di cui hai bisogno per cucinare.
native_language_example: Here you’ll find everything you need to cook.

meaning: all the; the whole (masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to mean “all the” or “the entire/whole.” The noun is often a thing or amount (tutto il tempo, tutto il vino) but can also be a collective/group treated as singular (tutto il paese = the whole town/country). Changes with gender/number: tutta la, tutti i, tutte le.
target_language_example: Ho passato tutto il giorno a casa.
native_language_example: I spent the whole day at home.

additional_notes: Used to say something lasts for the whole day, from morning to night. It often goes at the end of the sentence after the verb: "Ho lavorato tutto il giorno." You can also change the article for other days: "tutta la notte" (all night), "tutta la mattina" (all morning).
target_language_example: Sono rimasto a casa tutto il giorno.
native_language_example: I stayed home all day.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened for the entire day on the previous day. Often you’ll also hear (and many speakers prefer) the order “ieri tutto il giorno”. You can add “per” to emphasize duration: “(per) tutto il giorno ieri”.
target_language_example: Ieri ho studiato tutto il giorno.
native_language_example: Yesterday I studied all day.

additional_notes: Usually means “the whole world” in a global sense: di tutto il mondo (“from all over the world”), in tutto il mondo (“all over the world”). In some contexts it can also mean “everyone” (“tutto il mondo lo sa” = “everyone knows it”). Note the common proverb: Tutto il mondo è paese (“people are the same everywhere”).
target_language_example: Ci sono turisti da tutto il mondo qui in estate.
native_language_example: There are tourists from all over the world here in the summer.

meaning: the whole country; everyone in town (the whole town).
additional_notes: Means “all of the country” when talking about something nationwide (e.g., news known everywhere). It can also mean “the whole town/village” (i.e., all the people there) when the context is a local community: “È venuto tutto il paese” = “Everyone in town came.” Word order can change with the same meaning: “in tutto il paese” = “throughout the country.”
target_language_example: La notizia si è diffusa in tutto il paese.
native_language_example: The news spread throughout the whole country.

additional_notes: Used to say an activity lasted for the entire afternoon (from after lunch until evening). Often used with verbs like aspettare (to wait), passare/trascorrere (to spend), and can be followed by: a + infinitive (a cucinare = cooking) or in + place (in biblioteca = at the library).
target_language_example: Ho lavorato tutto il pomeriggio.
native_language_example: I worked all afternoon.

additional_notes: Used to say that you’ve done (or are doing) as much as possible, often in difficult situations or to reassure someone. Common with verbs like "fare" and "stare" (stiamo facendo tutto il possibile = we’re doing everything we can).
target_language_example: Farò tutto il possibile per aiutarti.
native_language_example: I’ll do everything I can to help you.

meaning: “everything possible to / in order to” (to do your best to achieve something).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to say you did all you could to reach a goal: “fare tutto il possibile per + infinitive.” Often implies effort and trying hard (similar to “do everything you can to…”).
target_language_example: Farò tutto il possibile per arrivare in orario.
native_language_example: I’ll do everything possible to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to refer to all the remaining things not already mentioned. Often follows a list ("X e tutto il resto" = “X and everything else”) or stands alone as the subject ("Tutto il resto è..." = “Everything else is…”).
target_language_example: Ho preso i documenti; tu occupati di tutto il resto.
native_language_example: I got the documents; you take care of everything else.

additional_notes: "Tutto" means "all/everything" and "il suo" means "his/its" (masculine singular). Used before a masculine singular noun: "tutto il suo lavoro" = "all his work"; "tutto il suo capitale" = "all his capital". With other nouns, it changes: feminine singular "tutta la sua...", masculine plural "tutti i suoi...", feminine plural "tutte le sue...". Often "suo" can also mean "your" (formal), but in these examples it’s "his/its" because it refers to "lui/Tom".
target_language_example: Ha perso tutto il suo denaro in un giorno.
native_language_example: He lost all his money in one day.

additional_notes: Means the entire amount of money that belongs to someone. "suo" agrees with the owner (his/her), while "denaro" is masculine singular, so it’s "il suo". You can swap in other possessives: "tutto il mio denaro" (all my money), "tutto il nostro denaro" (all our money). Often used with verbs like "dare" (to give), "perdere" (to lose), and "spendere" (to spend).
target_language_example: Ho speso tutto il suo denaro per il biglietto.
native_language_example: I spent all his/her money on the ticket.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens/was true during the entire period in question (“the whole time”). It can also mean “constantly/always” depending on context (“all the time”). Often appears with "per" (per tutto il tempo = for the whole time) or alone (tutto il tempo = the whole time).
target_language_example: Sono rimasto in casa tutto il tempo perché pioveva.
native_language_example: I stayed at home the whole time because it was raining.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb *essere*: *Sono tutto orecchie!* You say it to show you’re ready to listen attentively to what someone is about to say.
target_language_example: Dimmi pure: sono tutto orecchie!
native_language_example: Go ahead and tell me—I’m all ears!

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause referring to the totality of things or information. Commonly followed by a verb (e.g., "tutto quel che so"). It’s similar in meaning to "tutto ciò che" and often interchangeable with it.
target_language_example: Ti dirò tutto quel che so.
native_language_example: I’ll tell you everything that I know.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the whole of something already mentioned or understood from context. Very often followed by a relative clause with che: "tutto quello che..." = "everything that...". It can also be used alone when the thing is clear: "Perché vuole tutto quello?" = "Why does he want all that?"
target_language_example: Prendo tutto quello che mi serve e poi vado.
native_language_example: I’ll take everything I need and then I’ll go.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause describing the totality of things/actions/information. Often followed by a verb: "tutto quello che + verb" (e.g., "tutto quello che ha fatto" = everything that he/she did). It can refer to things someone asks for, knows, says, finds, etc.
target_language_example: Ho perso tutto quello che avevo nello zaino.
native_language_example: I lost everything I had in my backpack.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the total of someone’s possessions/resources, often followed by more detail (e.g., what was on a plate). "Aveva" is the imperfect of *avere* (“to have”), so it often describes what someone had at that time. You can change the verb to match the person/tense: *tutto quello che ho / hai / hanno* (everything that I/you/they have).
target_language_example: Ha venduto tutto quello che aveva per comprare una casa.
native_language_example: He sold everything he had to buy a house.

tutto quello che deve fare è

target_language_multi_word_term: tutto quello che deve fare è
additional_notes: Used to say that something is the only necessary step, often to make instructions sound simple. Uses the formal “Lei” form: deve (you must) + fare (to do). In informal speech to a friend you’d often hear: “Tutto quello che devi fare è …”.
target_language_example: Tutto quello che deve fare è compilare questo modulo e firmare qui.
native_language_example: All you have to do is fill out this form and sign here.

tutto quello che devi fare è

target_language_multi_word_term: tutto quello che devi fare è
meaning: "all you have to do is" ("all you need to do is").
additional_notes: Used to say something is easy/simple: after è you typically use an infinitive (e.g., è chiamare, è aspettare). You can change the person: tutto quello che devo fare è... (I), tutto quello che dobbiamo fare è... (we), etc.
target_language_example: Tutto quello che devi fare è aspettare cinque minuti.
native_language_example: All you have to do is wait five minutes.

tutto quello che dovete fare è

target_language_multi_word_term: tutto quello che dovete fare è
meaning: “all you have to do is …” (addressing multiple people or formal “you”).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a simple instruction or the only necessary action. "dovete" is the present tense of dovere (“must/have to”) for voi (you all) or formal plural (e.g., customers). Often followed by an infinitive (aspettare, premere, scusarvi, seguire). For one person/informal singular: "Tutto quello che devi fare è..."; for formal singular: "Tutto quello che deve fare è...".
target_language_example: Tutto quello che dovete fare è compilare questo modulo e firmarlo.
native_language_example: All you have to do is fill out this form and sign it.

meaning: "everything (that) he/she does"; sometimes "all he/she does is...".
additional_notes: Refers to all of someone’s actions. The subject is often understood from context (he/she/it). It can be followed by more information (e.g., "per me" = for me). In sentences like "Tutto quello che fa è...", it means "All he/she does is..." and is often used to criticize or describe a repeated behavior.
target_language_example: Tutto quello che fa è lavorare, anche nei weekend.
native_language_example: All he does is work, even on weekends.

meaning: "everything that (to) him…" / "all that he…" (referring to a male person).
additional_notes:
Used to introduce a relative clause about a man/boy (gli = “to him”). It often appears with verbs like dire (“to tell”) or servire (“to need”):
- tutto quello che gli diciamo = everything we tell him
- tutto quello che gli serve/serviva = everything he needs/needed (literally “everything that is necessary to him”).
If it’s a woman, you usually use: tutto quello che le…
target_language_example: Ho comprato tutto quello che gli serviva per il viaggio.
native_language_example: I bought everything he needed for the trip.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the full content of what someone said. Literally “all that which (he/she) has said,” with a relative clause introduced by che. ha detto is passato prossimo of dire (“to say”) and can refer to either “he said” or “she said” depending on context. You can change the start for gender/number: tutta quella che… (everything she said, referring to a feminine thing), tutti quelli che… (all those who/that…).
target_language_example: Non ricordo tutto quello che ha detto durante la riunione.
native_language_example: I don’t remember everything he said during the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to talk about all your possessions/resources, or sometimes the only person/thing you rely on (emotional sense): "Sei tutto quello che ho" = "You’re all I have." Often appears with "è" (it’s all I have) or as the object of another verb (e.g., "portarmi via" = take away from me).
target_language_example: Non posso perderlo: è tutto quello che ho.
native_language_example: I can’t lose it: it’s all I have.

additional_notes: Used before a verb like dice/dico/ho detto (“say/tell”) to mean “everything that (someone) says/tells to her.” **le** is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to her” (or “to you” in the polite/formal form). It must match who receives the information (e.g., le dice = “says to her/you”).
target_language_example: Non credere a tutto quello che le dicono.
native_language_example: Don’t believe everything they tell you/her.

meaning: "everything that (someone) … to me" / "all that … to me".
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause meaning “everything that …,” followed by the indirect object pronoun mi (“to me”). It’s typically followed by a verb: tutto quello che mi dice (“everything he says to me”), tutto quello che mi rimane (“everything that remains to me”), tutto quello che mi serviva (“everything I needed”). You can change mi to other pronouns (ti, gli/le, ci, vi, gli).
target_language_example: Ho capito tutto quello che mi hai spiegato.
native_language_example: I understood everything you explained to me.

meaning: everything (that) he/she owned; all (that) he/she possessed.
additional_notes: A relative clause meaning “all that … owned.” It’s often used with verbs like dare (to give), perdere (to lose), vendere (to sell). The verb possedeva is the imperfect (“owned/used to own”), describing what someone had up to that point; in the present you’d say tutto quello che possiede (“everything he/she owns”).
target_language_example: Dopo l’incendio, ha perso tutto quello che possedeva.
native_language_example: After the fire, he lost everything he owned.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is doing as much as possible, often implying they’re trying their best. The subject can change: tutto quello che posso (I can), può (he/she can), possiamo (we can), potete (you all can), possono (they can). It’s often followed by a purpose phrase with “per” + infinitive: “tutto quello che può per + verb” (everything (they) can to do something).
target_language_example: Sto facendo tutto quello che posso per aiutarti.
native_language_example: I’m doing everything I can to help you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause meaning “everything that someone does/says to you” or “everything that I can do/tell you.” It’s often followed by a verb like dice (says/tells you), fa (does), posso dire (I can tell you). The pronoun ti means “to you” (informal singular).
target_language_example: Ho fatto tutto quello che ti ho promesso.
native_language_example: I did everything I promised you.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the one thing (or everything) you desire. It’s built from: tutto (“everything/all”) + quello che (“what/that which”) + voglio (“I want”). It can be the subject or object of the sentence: Tutto quello che voglio è... (“All I want is...”). With “to be,” Italian agrees with what comes after: Tutto quello che voglio sei tu (“All I want is you”)—using sei because tu is “you (singular).”
target_language_example: In vacanza, tutto quello che voglio è rilassarmi.
native_language_example: On vacation, all I want is to relax.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the one thing (or main things) someone desires or asks for. It’s often followed by a noun (il tuo amore), a phrase (pace e tranquillità), or an infinitive action (sedermi qui e bere...). In speech you’ll also hear: "Tutto quello che voglio è che..." (All I want is that...).
target_language_example: Tutto quello che voglio è un po' di tempo per riposarmi.
native_language_example: All I want is a bit of time to rest.

additional_notes: Literally “all that (he/she) wanted.” Uses the imperfect tense of volere (voleva = “wanted/was wanting”), often to talk about what someone wanted at that time in the past. It can refer to things someone received, bought, had, or was given. You can change the verb to match the person: volevo (I), volevi (you), voleva (he/she), volevamo (we), volevate (you plural), volevano (they).
target_language_example: Alla fine, ha ottenuto tutto quello che voleva.
native_language_example: In the end, he got everything he wanted.

meaning: whatever you want; anything you want.
additional_notes: Used to give someone freedom of choice: after a verb it often means “as much/as many as you want” (e.g., eat/watch as much as you want). Said on its own, it can mean “anything you like/whatever you want,” sometimes with a tone of indifference (“fine, whatever you want”).
target_language_example: Scegli tutto quello che vuoi dal menu.
native_language_example: Choose whatever you want from the menu.

meaning: “everything (that) he/she wants” or “all that he/she wants.”
additional_notes: Used to talk about having/being able to get whatever someone wants. It’s a relative clause: tutto (“everything”) + quello che (“that which”) + vuole (“he/she wants”). The verb changes with the person: tutto quello che vuoi (you want), tutto quello che vogliono (they want). In a question it can also mean “Is that all you want (to know)?”
target_language_example: Se ha soldi, può comprare tutto quello che vuole.
native_language_example: If he has money, he can buy everything he wants.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause with di cui (“of which/that”), very common with avere bisogno di (“to need”). Pattern: tutto quello di cui + subject + verb (often: ho bisogno) = “everything that … needs”. You can also replace tutto with only what fits: quello di cui (“what/that which … needs”), or add a noun: tutte le cose di cui… (“all the things that…”).
target_language_example: Ho comprato tutto quello di cui avevo bisogno per il viaggio.
native_language_example: I bought everything I needed for the trip.

meaning: all this time; this whole time.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize how long something has been happening or how much time has passed. Often appears with prepositions: "per tutto questo tempo" = "for all this time" (duration up to now or up to a point), "dopo tutto questo tempo" = "after all this time" (after a long period).
target_language_example: Non posso credere che tu lo sapessi da tutto questo tempo.
native_language_example: I can’t believe you’ve known all this time.

additional_notes: Refers to the entire situation, set of events, or group of things being discussed. Often used to talk about a problem or scenario (“Come finirà tutto questo?”), to thank someone for handling something (“occuperarsi di tutto questo”), or to point to a collection of items (“Tutto questo appartiene a…”). Can also be used with a verb to mean “to know all of this” (“sapere tutto questo”).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace per tutto questo, non volevo creare problemi.
native_language_example: I’m sorry about all this; I didn’t mean to cause problems.

additional_notes: Common, everyday phrase used to ask if someone is okay or if everything is fine, and to answer that things are fine. Often said as a quick check-in (like “You good?”) or to confirm there’s no problem. Can also appear as “È tutto a posto.”
target_language_example: Hai trovato le chiavi? Tutto a posto?
native_language_example: Did you find the keys? Everything okay?

additional_notes: Common, friendly check-in question, often used on its own as a greeting. You can answer with “Tutto bene.” (All good.) or “Sì, tutto bene.”; if not, you can say “Non molto.” (Not really.) or briefly explain what’s wrong.
target_language_example: Ciao! Tutto bene?
native_language_example: Hi! Everything okay?

meaning: “all by myself” (said by a female speaker).
additional_notes: Used to say you did everything on your own, without help. The form changes with gender/number: tutto da solo (male), tutto da soli (group of males/mixed), tutto da sole (group of females). Often used with verbs like fare (“to do”).
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: posso farlo tutto da sola.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I can do it all by myself.

meaning: all by yourself; on your own (without help).
additional_notes: Used to say someone did something without anyone’s help or company. With people, it agrees in gender/number: tutto da solo (male singular), tutta da sola (female singular), tutti da soli (male/mixed plural), tutte da sole (female plural). Often used with verbs like fare (to do) or andare (to go).
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti, posso farlo tutto da solo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I can do it all by myself.

additional_notes: Used to say that something has completely ended (a situation, a relationship, a problem, an event). Very common with the verb essere: “È tutto finito” = “It’s all over.” It can sound final or dramatic depending on context.
target_language_example: Tranquillo, è tutto finito: possiamo andare a casa.
native_language_example: Relax, it’s all over: we can go home.

meaning: “everything in terms of (…); with (something) as the main way of thinking/measuring.”
additional_notes: Used to say someone interprets or evaluates everything using one main criterion (often money, profit, etc.). Common with verbs like pensare a / vedere: “pensa a tutto in termini di denaro” = “she thinks about everything in terms of money.” Also works with other nouns (tempo, costi, vantaggi).
target_language_example: Non pensare a tutto in termini di soldi: conta anche il tempo.
native_language_example: Don’t think about everything in terms of money: time matters too.

additional_notes: Very common informal way to ask if things are fine or to reassure someone that there’s no problem. Often used as a short reply on its own (no verb needed): "Tutto ok." It can also be a question: "Tutto ok?" Tone depends on context and can be sarcastic or aggressive if paired with an insult (e.g., "stronzetto").
target_language_example: Ehi, tutto ok? Ti vedo un po' stanco.
native_language_example: Hey, everything OK? You look a bit tired.

meaning: "that's all / that's it"; sometimes literally "everything here".
additional_notes: Common in conversation to downplay or conclude: it means “nothing more than that” or “that’s it” (often after an explanation). It can also be used literally to mean “everything here/right here,” especially with gestures or when telling someone where to put things (e.g., "Metti tutto qua" = "Put everything here"). Often said as a short standalone comment: "Tutto qua." / "Tutto qua?" ("Is that it?").
target_language_example: Volevo solo farti una domanda, tutto qua.
native_language_example: I just wanted to ask you a question, that's all.

additional_notes: Used to say that a situation is managed and going as planned, or to ask for reassurance (often as a short question: “Tutto sotto controllo?”). Common with avere/essere: “Ho tutto sotto controllo” / “È tutto sotto controllo.”
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: è tutto sotto controllo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everything is under control.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone that there are no problems (“Everything’s fine”). With *se* (“if”), it means “if all goes well” and introduces a condition about the future. *Tutto* = “everything”, *va* (andare) = “goes”, *bene* = “well”.
target_language_example: Non ti preoccupare: tutto va bene.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everything is fine.

additional_notes: Used to offer or ask someone to choose between tea and coffee (informal "vuoi" or formal "vuole"). You’ll often hear it as a quick choice question: "Tè o caffè?"
target_language_example: Per colazione preferisci tè o caffè?
native_language_example: For breakfast, do you prefer tea or coffee?

additional_notes: A type of tea. Often used with an article (il tè verde = the green tea) or without one when speaking generally (Bevo tè verde = I drink green tea). You can contrast it with “tè nero” (black tea).
target_language_example: Preferisco il tè verde al tè nero.
native_language_example: I prefer green tea to black tea.

meaning: the last word; the final say (final decision).
additional_notes: Literally “last word.” Often used in the expression “avere l’ultima parola” = “to have the final say” (the person who makes the final decision). Can also mean the last thing someone says in a conversation or argument.
target_language_example: In questa scelta, i miei genitori hanno l’ultima parola.
native_language_example: In this decision, my parents have the final say.

additional_notes: Used with the verb dare (“to give”): dare un abbraccio a qualcuno = “to give someone a hug.” You’ll also hear it as a greeting/closing in messages: Un abbraccio! (“Hugs!” / “A hug!”).
target_language_example: Quando l'ho vista, le ho dato un abbraccio.
native_language_example: When I saw her, I gave her a hug.

additional_notes: Used for an arrangement or deal between people, companies, or countries. Common with verbs like fare/raggiungere (make/reach), avere (have), and firmare (sign). It can be formal (a contract or treaty) or informal (a personal deal).
target_language_example: Possiamo raggiungere un accordo entro domani?
native_language_example: Can we reach an agreement by tomorrow?

additional_notes: Indefinite article + noun: used to talk about any one airplane (not a specific one). In questions it often means “a/any plane?” (e.g., “a private plane?”). The plural is “degli aerei” = “some airplanes/planes.”
target_language_example: Devo prendere un aereo domani mattina.
native_language_example: I have to catch a plane tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used when talking about finding/booking a place to stay. After the verb "essere" it means "a hotel" (e.g., "Questa casa è un albergo?"). "Albergo" is masculine, so it takes "un" in the singular; plural: "degli alberghi".
target_language_example: Cerco un albergo vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a hotel near the station.

additional_notes: Used for a single (unspecified) tree. The article changes with gender/number: un albero (a tree), l’albero (the tree), gli alberi (the trees). Common with verbs like piantare (to plant) and with places like sotto un albero (under a tree).
target_language_example: C’è un albero grande davanti a casa.
native_language_example: There is a big tree in front of the house.

meaning: an alibi (proof/excuse that you were somewhere else).
additional_notes: Used especially in crime/police contexts to mean evidence or a story that shows you couldn’t have done something because you were elsewhere. It can also be used more generally as a “pretext/excuse” (often with a negative tone).
target_language_example: Se hai un alibi, dillo subito alla polizia.
native_language_example: If you have an alibi, tell the police right away.

meaning: an alien (a non-human being from another planet).
additional_notes: Used both literally (in sci‑fi: “I saw an alien”) and figuratively to mean “I’m not a weirdo/stranger; I’m normal like you.” Singular masculine; feminine: "un'aliena". Plural: "gli alieni".
target_language_example: Tranquillo, non sono un alieno: lavoro qui da anni.
native_language_example: Relax, I’m not an alien: I’ve worked here for years.

additional_notes: Used to say someone coaches a particular sport. Put the sport after di: un allenatore di basket/tennis. Feminine: un’allenatrice di.
target_language_example: Mia sorella è un’allenatrice di nuoto.
native_language_example: My sister is a swimming coach.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun (un altro vantaggio, un altro test). It can mean an additional one (“one more”) or a different one (“another/different”). For feminine singular, use “un’altra” (un’altra volta). For plural, use “altri/altre” (altri nomi, altre persone).
target_language_example: Vuoi un altro caffè o preferisci un’altra bevanda?
native_language_example: Do you want another coffee, or would you prefer a different drink?

additional_notes: Used when you want to change how you do something or how you say something (e.g., try a different method, rephrase). Often appears with verbs like provare (to try) and dire (to say): "in un altro modo" = "in another way".
target_language_example: Possiamo farlo in un altro modo?
native_language_example: Can we do it another way?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a different man than the one already mentioned or expected. In relationship contexts it can imply “someone else/a lover” (e.g., “She has another man in her life”), but it can also be neutral (“Another man is coming”). Often contrasts with a specific man: “non… che un altro uomo…” = “not… that another man…”.
target_language_example: Non voglio vedere un altro uomo con lei.
native_language_example: I don’t want to see another man with her.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun (or alone) to mean an additional or different one of the same kind: un altro libro (another book), un altro bicchiere (another glass). For feminine nouns use "un'altra" (e.g., un'altra volta = another time).
target_language_example: Possiamo prendere un altro caffè?
native_language_example: Can we have another coffee?

additional_notes: Used when you want one more serving of wine (after already having one). In a polite offer or request you’ll often hear: “Vorrebbe un altro bicchiere di vino?” (formal singular) or “Vorrebbe...” / “Vorresti...” depending on how formal you want to be. "Bicchiere" = glass (the container/serving), "un altro" = another/one more.
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere un altro bicchiere di vino, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have another glass of wine, please?

additional_notes: Used when referring to an additional or different item/person, often replacing a noun already understood: "Ne voglio un altro" = "I want another one." It agrees in gender/number: "un altro" (masc. sing.), "un'altra" (fem. sing.), "altri/altre" (plural). Common fixed expression: "in un modo o in un altro" = "one way or another."
target_language_example: Non mi piace questo caffè: ne prendo un altro.
native_language_example: I don’t like this coffee: I’ll have another one.

additional_notes: "Un amante" can mean (1) a romantic/sexual partner, often implying a secret affair (like “a lover” in English), or (2) someone who really loves something (“an enthusiast/fan”), often used with "di": "un amante del vino rosso" = “a red-wine lover.” Feminine: "un'amante" (a lover / a female lover).
target_language_example: Marco è un amante della musica jazz.
native_language_example: Marco is a jazz music lover.

additional_notes: Indefinite article + noun: "un" = "a" before a masculine singular noun. Used to introduce someone as a friend ("Sono un amico di...") or to mention one friend in general ("Ho chiesto a un amico..."). For a female friend: "un'amica".
target_language_example: Ho incontrato un amico al bar.
native_language_example: I met a friend at the bar.

meaning: “a friend who …” (introduces a description of a friend).
additional_notes: Used to add more information about a friend using a relative clause with che (“who/that”). With a specific friend, you’ll often use the indicative: Avevo un amico che si chiamava Tom. With an unknown or hypothetical friend (often in questions), Italian commonly uses the subjunctive: Hai un amico che possa aiutarti?
target_language_example: Cerco un amico che parli inglese.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a friend who speaks English.

additional_notes: Literally means an angel (the spiritual/religious being). Very often used figuratively as a compliment: "È un angelo" = he/she is so kind, patient, helpful. Common comparisons: "come un angelo" (like an angel), especially about singing/voice, and "sembra un angelo" (he/she looks like an angel), sometimes referring to wearing white.
target_language_example: Sei un angelo, grazie per l'aiuto!
native_language_example: You’re an angel—thanks for the help!

additional_notes: Basic noun phrase using the indefinite article (un). Used literally for an animal, and sometimes figuratively about a person behaving in a rough/violent or out-of-control way ("He’s not an animal!"). The plural is "animali".
