additional_notes: Imperfetto (past imperfect) of "volere" + "essere": it describes a past desire/aspiration (often ongoing or habitual). The subject can be understood from context (lui/lei). The article changes with gender/number: "un" (masc.), "una" (fem.), "un'" (before a vowel), "dei/delle" (plural).
target_language_example: Da bambino voleva essere un pilota.
native_language_example: As a child, he wanted to be a pilot.

meaning: "(he/she) wanted to do" / "was wanting to do".
additional_notes: Imperfect tense of "volere" + infinitive "fare". Used to talk about a desire/plan in the past (often ongoing, repeated, or background to another action). The subject is understood from context ("lui" or "lei"); for other people: "volevo fare" (I), "volevi fare" (you), "volevamo fare" (we), "volevano fare" (they).
target_language_example: Ieri sera voleva fare una passeggiata, ma pioveva.
native_language_example: Last night he/she wanted to go for a walk, but it was raining.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone wanted to talk with someone else. "Voleva" is the imperfect past of "volere" (to want), often used for an ongoing or background desire in the past. After "con" you use a person or a pronoun: con me (with me), con te (with you), con lei/lui (with her/him), con loro (with them).
target_language_example: Ieri voleva parlare con me, ma ero occupato.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she wanted to talk with me, but I was busy.

additional_notes: Used to soften what you’re saying, often to sound polite, modest, or to reassure someone that your intention is simple (e.g., no big deal, no pressure). It’s the imperfect tense of "volere" (volevo = I wanted) + "solo" (only/just), usually followed by an infinitive: "volevo solo + verb".
target_language_example: Scusa, volevo solo chiederti un favore.
native_language_example: Sorry, I just wanted to ask you a favor.

additional_notes: Used to express a desire or intention in the past. It’s the imperfect of "volere" (to want) + "che", and it’s typically followed by the subjunctive (congiuntivo): "Volevo che lui venisse" (I wanted him to come). In English, this is usually translated with an infinitive (“to…”) rather than “that…”.
target_language_example: Volevo che mi chiamassi prima di arrivare.
native_language_example: I wanted you to call me before arriving.

additional_notes:
Used to soften what you’re saying or to emphasize that your request/goal is limited. Often followed by:
- "che" + imperfect subjunctive to express a wish about someone/something ("Volevo solo che tu fossi..." = "I just wanted you to be...").
- a noun to express a simple request ("Volevo solo una tazza di caffè" = "I just wanted a cup of coffee").
target_language_example: Scusa, volevo solo chiederti un favore.
native_language_example: Sorry, I just wanted to ask you a favor.

additional_notes: Used with volta (“time/occasion”) + che to introduce a clause describing what happened. Very common in phrases like: la prima volta che… (the first time that…), la seconda volta che… (the second time that…), quella volta che… (that time when…).
target_language_example: È la prima volta che vengo in Italia.
native_language_example: It’s the first time I’ve come to Italy.

meaning: to turn one’s back (on); to abandon/ignore.
additional_notes: Literally “to turn the back.” Used both physically (turning so your back faces someone) and figuratively (refusing to help, abandoning, or ignoring someone/something). Often followed by “a” + person/thing: “voltare le spalle a qualcuno/a qualcosa”.
target_language_example: Non posso voltarti le spalle proprio adesso.
native_language_example: I can’t turn my back on you right now.

additional_notes: Used after a number to say how many times something happens each day (e.g., una volta al giorno = once a day; due/tre/cinque volte al giorno = two/three/five times a day). “Volta” is singular; “volte” is plural.
target_language_example: Prendo questo medicinale due volte al giorno.
native_language_example: I take this medicine twice a day.

meaning: "I would like to have" / "I'd like to have".
additional_notes: Used to express a desire or request in a polite, softer way than "voglio avere" (“I want to have”). It can refer to having something physically (“with me”) or more generally (“some proof”, “your luck”, “a brother”). Often followed by a noun ("vorrei avere un caffè") or by "che" + verb ("vorrei avere che tu mi aiuti" is less common; usually "vorrei che tu mi aiutassi").
target_language_example: Vorrei avere un po' di tempo per pensarci.
native_language_example: I'd like to have a bit of time to think about it.

additional_notes: Polite way to ask to speak with someone (in person or on the phone). Uses the conditional of volere (vorrei = “I would like”), so it sounds softer than “voglio”. Add a person’s name (“con Bill”), a title (“con il signor Alexandre”), or a pronoun (“con lei” = formal “with you/her”). You can add details like “in privato” (in private) or “a fondo” (in depth).
target_language_example: Buongiorno, vorrei parlare con il direttore, per favore.
native_language_example: Good morning, I’d like to speak with the manager/director, please.

meaning: 'I wish (that)…' / 'I would like (it) if…' (followed by the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express a wish, desire, or preference about a situation (often hypothetical or not currently true). It’s followed by a verb in the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., fosse, potessimo, smettesse).
target_language_example: Vorrei che tu venissi con noi.
native_language_example: I wish you would come with us.

meaning: “I’d like there to be …” / “I wish there were …”
additional_notes: Used to express a desire/wish about a situation. It combines vorrei (“I would like”) with che + the congiuntivo imperfetto (fossero, “were”) because it refers to something you want, not a fact. ci here means “there” (as in “there are”). You normally continue with a plural noun (e.g., più persone, meno compiti).
target_language_example: Vorrei che ci fossero più posti a sedere.
native_language_example: I’d like there to be more seats.

meaning: "I would like you to..." (introduces a wish/request).
additional_notes: Used to express what you want someone else to do, so it’s followed by the subjunctive (congiuntivo): e.g., fossi, parlassi, potessi, venissi. It can sound polite and somewhat formal; for a more direct request you might also hear "voglio che tu" (I want you to).
target_language_example: Vorrei che tu mi aiutassi domani.
native_language_example: I would like you to help me tomorrow.

meaning: “I would like to be” / “I wish I were.”
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of volere (vorrei = “I would like”) + essere (“to be”) to express a wish, a hypothetical situation, or a polite desire. Often followed by a place (“vorrei essere a…”), a role/identity (“vorrei essere un…”), or an adjective (“vorrei essere più…”).
target_language_example: Vorrei essere più organizzato.
native_language_example: I would like to be more organized.

meaning: "Your Majesty" (very formal way to address a king or queen).
additional_notes: Used when speaking directly to a monarch, often in historical, ceremonial, or very formal contexts. In Italian it’s written with a capital letter (Maestà) and often paired with formal pronouns/verb forms like "vi" and sometimes a respectful plural verb (e.g., "guardate").
target_language_example: Vostra Maestà, posso parlarvi un momento?
native_language_example: Your Majesty, may I speak to you for a moment?

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "vostra" (your) with a feminine singular noun ("amica"). It can refer to "your" in the plural (voi = you all) or as a formal/polite "your" (especially in more formal contexts). For a male friend: "vostro amico".
target_language_example: Posso parlare con vostra amica un momento?
native_language_example: Can I talk to your (female) friend for a moment?

meaning: your family (addressing more than one person, or using formal “voi”).
additional_notes: “Vostra” is the possessive for “voi” and agrees with the noun: vostra famiglia (singular), vostre famiglie (plural). Used when speaking to a group (“you all”) or in formal/old-fashioned contexts where “voi” is used instead of “Lei”. In everyday singular polite speech, you more often hear “la Sua famiglia”.
target_language_example: Come sta la vostra famiglia?
native_language_example: How is your family?

additional_notes: “Vostra” is the feminine singular form of “vostro” and agrees with “figlia” (daughter). Use it when speaking politely to one person (formal “you”) or when addressing more than one person (plural “your”). In casual speech to one person you usually say “tua figlia”.
target_language_example: Vostra figlia ha già finito la scuola?
native_language_example: Has your daughter already finished school?

meaning: "your mother" (addressing more than one person, or using formal "you").
additional_notes: Uses the possessive "vostra" with "voi" (you plural) or formal "voi" in some regions/older style. In everyday informal speech to one person, you’ll more often hear "tua madre" (your mom). It can also be used in insults depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Vostra madre sta bene?
native_language_example: Is your mother doing well?

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "vostra" (your) with the feminine singular noun "sorella" (sister). "Vostra" is typically used when speaking to more than one person (voi = you all), or in very formal/older-style address. In everyday speech to one person, you’ll often hear "tua sorella" (your sister).
target_language_example: Vostra sorella viene con voi stasera?
native_language_example: Is your sister coming with you tonight?

additional_notes: "Vostre" is the plural feminine form of "vostro" and agrees with "amiche" (female friends). It’s used when speaking to more than one person (voi): "le vostre amiche" = "your friends" (addressing you all). If talking to one person (tu), you’d usually say "le tue amiche".
target_language_example: Potete invitare le vostre amiche alla festa?
native_language_example: Can you all invite your (female) friends to the party?

additional_notes: "Vostri" is the possessive for "voi" (you plural) and also used as a polite/formal "you" (like addressing a group or using formal speech). It must match the noun in gender and number: "amici" = masculine plural (or mixed group). For an all-female group you’d say "vostre amiche". Often used after prepositions like "con" (with) or "da" (from/at someone’s place): "con i vostri amici", "dai vostri amici".
target_language_example: Potete venire con i vostri amici stasera?
native_language_example: Can you come with your friends tonight?

meaning: your parents (addressing more than one person).
additional_notes: “Vostri” is the plural possessive (“your”) that agrees with the plural noun “genitori” (parents). It’s used when talking to two or more people (voi): e.g., “i vostri genitori” = “your parents.” When speaking to one person formally (Lei), Italian more often uses “i Suoi genitori.”
target_language_example: Quando arrivano i vostri genitori?
native_language_example: When are your parents arriving?

meaning: "your help" (addressing more than one person, or being formal/polite).
additional_notes: Uses the possessive "vostro" to mean "your" when speaking to a group (voi) or in formal contexts. It often appears after prepositions like "grazie al" (thanks to) or "per" (for): "Grazie al vostro aiuto..." / "per tutto il vostro aiuto". For one person informally you’d say "il tuo aiuto"; for one person formally, "il suo aiuto".
target_language_example: Non ce la faccio senza il vostro aiuto.
native_language_example: I can’t do it without your help.

meaning: 'your friend' (addressing more than one person, or using formal 'you').
additional_notes: "Vostro" is the possessive for "voi" (you plural) and is also used with the formal "voi" in some contexts. With one male friend: "vostro amico"; one female friend: "vostra amica"; more than one male/mixed group: "vostri amici"; more than one female group: "vostre amiche".
target_language_example: È vostro amico?
native_language_example: Is he your friend?

meaning: “your brother” (addressing more than one person, or speaking formally to one person).
additional_notes: Uses the possessive "vostro" with "fratello" (brother). "Vostro" is used with "voi" (you plural) and also as a formal way to address one person (less common than "suo/sua" today). Often said without the article: "Vostro fratello è qui?"
target_language_example: Potete chiamare vostro fratello, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you call your brother, please?

meaning: your father (addressing more than one person).
additional_notes: Uses the possessive "vostro" (your, plural) with "padre" (father). It’s used when speaking to a group (voi): "vostro padre" = "your (all) father." With close family terms like "padre," Italian often omits the article: "vostro padre" (not *"il vostro padre"*), though an article may appear in some contexts (e.g., with an adjective).
target_language_example: Vostro padre viene a prendervi alle sei.
native_language_example: Your father is coming to pick you up at six.

meaning: “your country” (addressing more than one person, or formally).
additional_notes: Uses the possessive vostro (“your”) with paese (“country” or sometimes “town/village,” depending on context). In the examples it clearly means “your country.” Agree it with what is owned: vostro paese (masc. sing.), vostra città (fem. sing.), vostri paesi (masc. pl.), vostre città (fem. pl.). Often used when talking to a group or in formal speech; for one person informally you’d usually say il tuo paese.
target_language_example: Com’è il vostro paese in inverno?
native_language_example: What is your country like in winter?

meaning: (dated, often offensive) a street vendor (often an immigrant), especially selling goods to tourists.
additional_notes: Originally a slang/eye-dialect rendering of vendors calling out "Vuoi comprare?" (“Do you want to buy?”). In modern Italian it’s widely considered derogatory/racist and is best avoided; use neutral options like "venditore ambulante" (street vendor) or "venditore".
target_language_example: Alcuni turisti usano ancora il termine "vu cumprà", ma è considerato offensivo.
native_language_example: Some tourists still use the term "vu cumprà", but it’s considered offensive.

additional_notes: Uses the informal singular "tu" form: vuoi (you want) + andare (to go). Often used as a question, with rising intonation or a question mark. The destination is commonly introduced by: a + place (Vuoi andare a casa?), in + country/region (Vuoi andare in Germania?), da + a person’s place / to someone (Vuoi andare da Hagrid?).
target_language_example: Vuoi andare al cinema con me?
native_language_example: Do you want to go to the movies with me?

additional_notes: Used to ask for clarification or to check you understood correctly. Often followed by **che + a clause** (*Vuoi dire che…?* = “Are you saying that…?”) or by a noun/pronoun (*Vuoi dire questo?* = “Do you mean this?”).
target_language_example: Scusa, vuoi dire che domani non vieni?
native_language_example: Sorry, do you mean you're not coming tomorrow?

meaning: “Do you mean that…?” / “Are you saying that…?”
additional_notes: Used to check or clarify what someone means, often showing surprise or disbelief. Literally “you want to say that…?”, but it’s normally understood as “do you mean…?”. You can change the person: “vuol dire che…” (does it mean that…?), “volevo dire che…” (I meant that…).
target_language_example: Vuoi dire che non vieni più?
native_language_example: Do you mean you’re not coming anymore?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone wants to do something: "Vuoi fare + noun/infinitive?". With "fare" it can mean either "do" or "make" depending on the noun (e.g., "fare un patto" = make a deal). In some contexts it can sound challenging/accusatory, like "Are you trying to…?" (e.g., "Vuoi fare lo stronzo?" = Are you trying to be an asshole?).
target_language_example: Vuoi fare una pausa?
native_language_example: Do you want to take a break?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone wants information, often introducing an indirect question (chi, che/cosa, come, quanti, etc.). It can be a genuine question or a lead-in before telling something (“Vuoi sapere una cosa?”). Literally “you want to know.”
target_language_example: Vuoi sapere dove siamo stati ieri sera?
native_language_example: Do you want to know where we went last night?

meaning: "Do you want to see?" / "Want to see?" (sometimes: "You’ll see.")
additional_notes: Literally a question using the verb "volere" (you want) + "vedere" (to see). It’s used to invite someone to look at something: "Vuoi vedere la mia camera?" = "Do you want to see my room?". Said on its own ("Vuoi vedere?") it can be rhetorical, meaning "You’ll see" / "Just wait and see"—often when you’re about to show something or prove a point.
target_language_example: Vuoi vedere come funziona?
native_language_example: Do you want to see how it works?

meaning: “Do you want me/us to…?” (asking what someone wants).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., vuoi che vada, vuoi che lo facciamo) to ask if someone wants you/you all to do something, or wants something to happen. In everyday English it’s often translated with “Do you want me to…?” / “Should I…?” / “Do you want us to…?”.
target_language_example: Vuoi che ti aiuti con i compiti?
native_language_example: Do you want me to help you with your homework?

meaning: "Do you want me to do (it)?" / "Do you want me to…?"
additional_notes: Used to ask what action someone wants you to take. It’s built with "vuoi che" + the subjunctive: "faccia" is the present subjunctive of "fare" (to do/make). Often followed by what you should do: "Vuoi che faccia delle copie?" You can change the verb depending on the action: "Vuoi che ti chiami?" (Do you want me to call you?).
target_language_example: Vuoi che faccia una prenotazione per stasera?
native_language_example: Do you want me to make a reservation for tonight?

additional_notes: Common structure to ask for instructions or offer help: "Vuoi che + (lo/la/li/le) + verb (subjunctive)?" The verb is usually in the present subjunctive (e.g., apra, beva, chiami, dica/diciamo, legga, tenga, uccidiamo). "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" (sometimes "him," depending on context). You can add a subject for emphasis: "io" (me) or "noi" (us).
target_language_example: Vuoi che lo faccia io?
native_language_example: Do you want me to do it?

additional_notes: Used to offer to do something for someone. It’s usually followed by the subjunctive (congiuntivo) of another verb: "Vuoi che ti + [verb]?". "Ti" is an object pronoun meaning "to you/for you" (or sometimes just "you"), depending on the verb.
target_language_example: Vuoi che ti chiami un taxi?
native_language_example: Do you want me to call you a taxi?

additional_notes: Used with **volere + che + subjunctive**: *vuoi che + venga* (from **venire**, “to come”). The person who should come depends on context: **vuoi che venga** can mean “do you want **me** to come?” or “do you want **him/her** to come?”. Negative: **non vuoi che venga** (“you don’t want me/him/her to come”).
target_language_example: Vuoi che venga a prenderti alla stazione?
native_language_example: Do you want me to come pick you up at the station?

meaning: “do you mean…?” / “are you saying…?” (also: “you want to say/tell”).
additional_notes: From the verb phrase *volere* (“to want”) + *dire* (“to say”). Commonly used to ask for clarification or the intended meaning: *Cosa/Che cosa/Che vuoi dire?* = “What do you mean?” It can also introduce a rephrasing or guess: *Di gente nuda, vuoi dire?* = “Naked people, you mean?”
target_language_example: Non capisco: cosa vuoi dire esattamente?
native_language_example: I don’t understand: what exactly do you mean?

meaning: "do you want to do" / "what do you want to do?"
additional_notes: Literally "(you) want to do" (volere + fare). Used to ask what someone intends or wants to do next: "Che cosa vuoi fare?" / "Ora che vuoi fare?". In the fixed expression "(E) che cosa ci vuoi fare?", it often means "what can you do about it?" / "there’s nothing you can do," with a resigned tone; "ci" refers to the situation/problem.
target_language_example: Che cosa vuoi fare stasera, restiamo a casa o usciamo?
native_language_example: What do you want to do tonight, should we stay home or go out?

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "volere dire" (literally “to want to say”), used to explain the meaning of a word or to clarify what a fact implies. Very common in spoken Italian. Often used in negative form: "non vuol dire (niente)" = “that doesn’t mean (anything)” / “that doesn’t necessarily mean…”.
target_language_example: Se non risponde, non vuol dire che sia arrabbiato.
native_language_example: If he doesn’t reply, it doesn’t mean he’s angry.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the explanation or consequence of something (often after a fact or situation). It can also be used to clarify what something implies: "X... vuol dire che Y" = "X... which means that Y". In speech and writing, you may also see the fuller form "vuole dire che" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Se non risponde, vuol dire che è occupato.
native_language_example: If he’s not answering, that means he’s busy.

meaning: “(it) means”; “to mean” (to have a meaning / imply).
additional_notes: From the verb "volere" ("vuole") + "dire" (to say): literally “wants to say,” but it’s used as the normal way to ask/give a meaning in Italian. Common patterns: "Che vuol dire?" = "What does it mean?"; "Questo vuol dire che..." = "This means that..."; "Non vuol dire (che)..." = "It doesn’t mean (that)..." (often used to correct a misunderstanding: "Essere X non vuol dire essere Y").
target_language_example: Scusa, che vuol dire "scontrino"?
native_language_example: Sorry, what does "scontrino" mean?

additional_notes: Used to explain the consequence or implication of what was just said (often after a fact, number, or condition). Very common in both speech and writing. Often appears in negatives: "non vuol dire che…" = "it doesn’t mean that…".
target_language_example: Hai detto che non puoi venire: vuol dire che sei ancora al lavoro.
native_language_example: You said you can’t come: that means you’re still at work.

additional_notes: "Vuole" is the present tense of volere (to want) for lui/lei/Lei. It’s commonly followed by an infinitive like "andare" (to go): volere + infinitive. The subject is often understood from context (e.g., "(lui/lei) vuole andare").
target_language_example: Vuole andare al cinema stasera.
native_language_example: He/She wants to go to the movies tonight.

meaning: '(he/she/you polite) wants to do' (sometimes: 'wants to be' as a job).
additional_notes: Formed from "volere" (to want) + "fare" (to do/make). "Vuole" can refer to "he/she wants" or the polite "you want" (Lei). It’s used to ask what someone intends/plans to do ("Cosa vuole fare adesso?"), to express intentions ("vuole fare un passo in più" = wants to take a step further), or with a role/job to mean "wants to be" ("vuole fare il pilota" = wants to be a pilot).
target_language_example: Che cosa vuole fare dopo la cena?
native_language_example: What do you (polite) want to do after dinner?

additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase "vuole" (wants) + "parlare" (to talk) + "con" (with). "Vuole" can mean "he/she wants" or the polite form "you want" (Lei). Often followed by a person/pronoun: con me (with me), con te (with you informal), con lei (with you/her), con loro (with them), con voi (with you all).
target_language_example: Vuole parlare con me adesso?
native_language_example: Do you want to talk with me now?

meaning: (He/She) wants to speak with you (formal) / with her.
additional_notes: "Vuole" is the polite/formal form of "vuoi" (you want). "Con lei" can mean "with you" when addressing someone formally (Lei = formal "you"), or "with her" depending on context. Often used in polite questions like "Vuole parlare con lei?" = "Do you want to speak with her/with you (formal)?"
target_language_example: Il dottore vuole parlare con lei dopo la visita.
native_language_example: The doctor wants to speak with you after the appointment.

meaning: “(he/she) wants to know” / “do you want to know?”
additional_notes: Used with an indirect question: vuole sapere + che/cosa/il perché/dove/se/qual è… (“wants to know…” / “do you want to know…?”). In the fixed expression **non ne vuole sapere (di …)** it becomes idiomatic and means “(she/he) wants nothing to do with …” or “refuses to have anything to do with …,” not simply “doesn’t want to know.”
target_language_example: Vuole sapere che ora è la riunione?
native_language_example: Do you want to know what time the meeting is?

meaning: "(he/she) wants to see" / "(he/she) wants to meet (someone)".
additional_notes: Used with the verb "volere" + infinitive: "vuole" (he/she wants) + "vedere" (to see). It can mean wanting to watch something (a game, a movie), or wanting to see/meet a person. Very common with object pronouns: "mi/ti/lo/la/ci/vi/li/le vuole vedere" = "he/she wants to see me/you/him/her/us/you/them".
target_language_example: Il dottore la vuole vedere oggi.
native_language_example: The doctor wants to see her today.

meaning: "(he/she) wants" + "that..." (used to express what someone wants someone else to do).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a request/desire about another person’s action. It’s the 3rd-person singular of *volere* (wants) + *che*. In Italian it’s typically followed by the subjunctive (e.g., *vuole che tu vada*, *vuole che andiate*). The subject is often omitted when clear: *Vuole che...* = “He/She wants (that) ...”.
target_language_example: Vuole che tu venga domani.
native_language_example: He/She wants you to come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone wants you to do something. It’s followed by the subjunctive (congiuntivo): vuole che io vada / venga / faccia, etc. The subject after che is explicitly "io" (I), so it focuses on what *I* should do.
target_language_example: Vuole che io venga con voi stasera.
native_language_example: He/She wants me to come with you tonight.

additional_notes: Used when someone wants another person to do something, followed by a verb in the subjunctive (congiuntivo): vuole che + [subjunctive]. The “la” is a direct object pronoun meaning “her” or “it” (feminine singular), placed before the verb in the dependent clause (e.g., vuole che la aiuti = he wants you to help her).
target_language_example: Il professore vuole che la leggiate entro domani.
native_language_example: The professor wants you to read it by tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone wants you to do something. After "vuole che" Italian normally uses the present subjunctive: "aiuti" (from "aiutare"). "La" is an object pronoun meaning “her” (help her). Often the subject is understood from context: "(Lui/Lei) vuole..."
target_language_example: Marco vuole che la aiuti a portare le valigie.
native_language_example: Marco wants me to help her carry the suitcases.

additional_notes: Used to express what someone wants another person to do. After "vuole che" you normally use the subjunctive (e.g., "lo faccia", "lo chiami", "lo prenda"). "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning "him" or "it" (masculine), referring to something already known from context. The subject is often implied ("(lui/lei) vuole che...").
target_language_example: Vuole che lo aspetti qui?
native_language_example: Does he/she want me to wait for him/it here?

additional_notes: "Vuole" = "(he/she) wants" (from volere). "che" introduces what someone wants/asks. "lo" = "him" (direct object pronoun). "aiuti" = "you/me help" (present subjunctive of aiutare), used after expressions of wanting (volere che...). You can add time or details: "domani" (tomorrow), "con/coi" (with) "i suoi compiti" (his homework).
target_language_example: Vuole che lo aiuti a preparare la cena stasera.
native_language_example: He wants me to help him prepare dinner tonight.

meaning: “(Do you) want me to leave?” / “(Do you) want me to go away?”
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone wants you to leave. Literally it’s “(he/she/you formal) wants that I leave,” so Italian uses the subjunctive: vuole che + (io) me ne vada. “Me ne vada” is from the verb “andarsene” (to go away/leave), often implying leaving from here/this situation. “Vuole” can mean “you (formal) want” or “he/she wants,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Se la disturbo, vuole che me ne vada?
native_language_example: If I’m bothering you, do you want me to leave?

additional_notes: Used with the partitive article to offer/ask for an unspecified quantity of something, especially food or drink. "del" changes depending on the noun: del (m. sing.), dello (m. sing. before s+consonant/z/gn/etc.), della (f. sing.), dei/degli/delle (plural). In questions like "Vuole del…?" it’s often the polite form (Lei) meaning "Would you like some…?"
target_language_example: Vuole del pane o del formaggio?
native_language_example: Would you like some bread or some cheese?

additional_notes: Formed by the verb "volere" (to want) + "essere" (to be). Used to express someone’s desire to be in a certain state or to be something/someone. Subject is often understood from context (lui/lei/Lei). For the polite "you" (Lei), it can also mean "Do you want to be…?" in questions (e.g., "Vuole essere famoso?").
target_language_example: Non vuole essere disturbato.
native_language_example: He doesn't want to be disturbed.

meaning: “(he/she/you formal) wants to be a …” (with a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s desired job/role in the future. It’s made of "vuole" (wants) + "essere" (to be) + "un" (a/an, masculine). Change "un" to "uno" before s+consonant/z/gn/ps (e.g., "vuole essere uno studente"), or to "una" for feminine nouns (e.g., "vuole essere una dottoressa"). Often follows a subject like "Lui/Lei" or a name.
target_language_example: Mio fratello vuole essere un insegnante.
native_language_example: My brother wants to be a teacher.

additional_notes: "Vuole" is the present tense of *volere* (to want) for **lui/lei** and **Lei** (formal you). It’s followed by an infinitive like *fare* (to do/make): *Che cosa vuole fare?* = “What do you want to do?” Often implies intention/plan; can be made more polite with *Vorrei fare...* (“I’d like to do...”).
target_language_example: Che cosa vuole fare dopo?
native_language_example: What do you want to do afterward?

additional_notes: From volere (to want) + sapere (to know). Used to ask what information someone wants, or to say that someone wants to know a fact, a reason (il perché), the truth (la verità), a place (dove...), or an amount (quanto...). The subject can be implied in context; "vuole" can refer to "lei" (you, formal) or "lui/lei" (he/she).
target_language_example: Buongiorno, cosa vuole sapere esattamente?
native_language_example: Good morning, what exactly do you want to know?

additional_notes: "Vuole" is the 3rd-person singular of "volere" (to want): it refers to "he/she" or the polite "you" (Lei). "Un" is the masculine singular indefinite article (before many masculine nouns, e.g., "un divorzio", "un frigorifero"). In questions, "Vuole un…?" can be a polite offer meaning "Would you like a…?".
target_language_example: Vuole un caffè?
native_language_example: Would you like a coffee?

additional_notes: Common loanword (also written “weekend”). Often used with “questo” or “il” (e.g., “questo week-end” = “this weekend”; “nei week-end” = “on weekends”). In Italian you’ll also hear “fine settimana” as a more standard alternative.
target_language_example: Questo week-end non lavoro, quindi possiamo vederci.
native_language_example: This weekend I’m not working, so we can see each other.

meaning: An informal exclamation like “hey!” / “yo!” (used to get attention or as a shout).
additional_notes: Used as a stand-alone shout or repeated for emphasis ("Ya-sho! Ya-sho!"). It can also be used at the start of a sentence to address someone, similar to “hey,” and with rising intonation ("Ya-sho?") to show surprise or to check if someone heard you.
target_language_example: Ya-sho, vieni qui un attimo!
native_language_example: Hey, come here a second!

additional_notes: Used for sugar made from sugarcane. In everyday shopping/cooking contexts it usually refers to brown cane sugar (granulated). You’ll often see it on ingredient lists or when talking about sweetening drinks: “Io uso solo lo zucchero di canna.”
target_language_example: Per il caffè preferisco lo zucchero di canna.
native_language_example: For coffee, I prefer cane sugar.

additional_notes: Used when saying you add/put sugar into a specific drink or container. "Nel" is a contraction of "in + il" (= "in the"), and it changes with gender/number: "nel tè", "nello zucchero" (in the sugar bowl), "nella tazza" (in the cup), "nei bicchieri" (in the glasses), "nelle tazze" (in the cups). Often appears with verbs like "mettere" (to put/add): "mettere zucchero nel tè".
target_language_example: Preferisci poco zucchero nel caffè?
native_language_example: Do you prefer little sugar in your coffee?

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is at home (at their house). With people, it often implies they are home/available (e.g., you can ask to speak to them). With objects, it means the item is at home. The base expression is “essere a casa” (to be at home); “è” is the he/she/it form.
target_language_example: Non posso uscire stasera: mia madre è a casa.
native_language_example: I can’t go out tonight: my mom is at home.

additional_notes: Used with two common meanings depending on context: (1) to say something is sufficient: "È abbastanza, grazie" = "That’s enough, thanks." (2) to say something is fairly/quite a lot or fairly good: "È abbastanza difficile" = "It’s quite difficult." With an adjective it usually means “quite/fairly”; on its own it often means “enough.”
target_language_example: È abbastanza difficile, ma ce la faccio.
native_language_example: It’s quite difficult, but I can do it.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has reached the necessary age, size, or maturity to do something. Common pattern: (subject) + è + abbastanza + adjective + per + infinitive (e.g., è abbastanza grande per guidare). You can make it a question by raising intonation: È abbastanza grande per…?
target_language_example: Non è abbastanza grande per andare da solo.
native_language_example: He/She isn’t old enough to go alone.

meaning: “is allergic to” (followed by a feminine plural noun).
additional_notes: Used to say someone has an allergy to something. It agrees with the person: è allergico (male) / è allergica (female). “Alle” = a + le (“to the”) and is used before feminine plural nouns (le uova, le noccioline, le arachidi). Other common forms: al (a + il), alla (a + la), all’ (a + l’), ai (a + i), agli (a + gli). It can also be used jokingly/figuratively (e.g., “allergic to girls” = really dislikes/avoids).
target_language_example: Mia sorella è allergica alle fragole.
native_language_example: My sister is allergic to strawberries.

meaning: 'she is as tall as' (used to compare height).
additional_notes: Used to compare a female person's height with someone else. It agrees with the subject: è alto come (male), sono alta come / sono alto come (I am), etc. Often followed by a person/pronoun: come me/te/lui/lei/voi/loro.
target_language_example: Giulia è alta come sua sorella.
native_language_example: Giulia is as tall as her sister.

meaning: “She is as tall as her mother.”
additional_notes: Used to compare height: **alta** = “tall” (feminine), and **come** means “as” in comparisons (**X è ... come Y** = “X is ... like/as Y”). **sua madre** means “her mother” (or “his mother,” depending on context). You can swap in other adjectives: *è intelligente come sua madre* (“as smart as her mother”).
target_language_example: A quindici anni, è alta come sua madre.
native_language_example: At fifteen, she’s as tall as her mother.

additional_notes: Used with the verb essere (to be) to describe a person’s height (tall) or the height of something like a building (high). It agrees with gender/number: lui è alto, lei è alta; loro sono alti/alte. In questions you’ll often hear: Quanto è alto/a…? (How tall/high is…?). Note: English “alto” (a voice type) is a false friend—Italian alto usually means “tall/high.”
target_language_example: Quanto è alto questo muro?
native_language_example: How high is this wall?

additional_notes: Used to compare height with someone else. It agrees with the subject: for a female you would say "è alta come". Often followed by a person or pronoun (e.g., "come sua madre", "come lei"). In negatives: "non è alto/alta come...".
target_language_example: Mio fratello è alto come me.
native_language_example: My brother is as tall as me.

meaning: "He is as tall as his father."
additional_notes: Used to compare height. The pattern is: (subject) + essere + alto/alta + come + (person/thing). Example: "Lei è alta come sua madre" = "She is as tall as her mother." In Italian you can also use "quanto" with comparisons (e.g., "è alto quanto suo padre").
target_language_example: Mio fratello è alto come suo padre.
native_language_example: My brother is as tall as his father.

additional_notes: Used to say a state, feeling, situation, or action continues up to now. Very common with emotions (è ancora arrabbiato), locations (è ancora in macchina/lì), and ongoing actions (è ancora lì che ti aspetta). In questions, it means “Is it still…?” (È ancora vero?).
target_language_example: Scusa il ritardo: il treno è ancora fermo.
native_language_example: Sorry for the delay: the train is still stopped.

meaning: “is still in / is still (in a state of)”
additional_notes: Used with a place or condition to say someone remains there/in that state. Very common with locations (“in Germania”) and with states like health (“in buona salute”). For other subjects, change the verb: “sono ancora in…”, “sei ancora in…”, “siamo ancora in…”.
target_language_example: Lei è ancora in ufficio.
native_language_example: She’s still at the office.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone (or an animal) is still alive at the present moment, often implying there was doubt or danger. For a man you can also hear/see “È ancora vivo”; for a woman: “È ancora viva”. You can specify the subject: “Lui/Lei è ancora vivo/a”, or use a name: “Ursua è ancora vivo”.
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: il cane è ancora vivo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: the dog is still alive.

meaning: 'she went / has gone'; also '(it) went' (talking about how something turned out).
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of andare with essere. The past participle agrees with the subject: è andata (she), è andato (he/it), sono andati/andate (they). You’ll often hear it with an implied subject to mean “it went,” especially in: È andata bene. = “It went well.” In questions it can mean “Did she go…?” (È andata con il suo ragazzo? = “Did she go with her boyfriend?”).
target_language_example: Com'è andata? È andata bene!
native_language_example: How did it go? It went well!

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of **andare** used with **essere**. **Andata** agrees with the subject: *è andato a* (he), *sono andati/e a* (they). Usually followed by a destination after **a** (cities, events) or **in** (countries/regions).
target_language_example: È andata a Milano ieri.
native_language_example: She went to Milan yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say that an event, situation, or attempt had a good outcome (meeting, exam, trip, etc.). It’s the past tense with "essere" + "andare" ("to go") and agrees with what “went” (feminine singular here: "andata"; you may also hear "è andato bene" for masculine singular). With an indirect object pronoun, it means “it went well for someone”: "Ti è andata bene" = “It went well for you” (sometimes implying you were lucky). Can be a question: "È andata bene?" = “Did it go well?”
target_language_example: L'esame è andato bene, grazie.
native_language_example: The exam went well, thanks.

meaning: 'she went to' (a country) / 'she has gone to'.
additional_notes: Feminine singular of the past tense of "andare" (to go): "è" (auxiliary) + "andata" (gone/went). Used with "in" for countries and some destinations (e.g., in Canada, in Italia). The male form is "è andato in"; plural: "sono andati/e in". Often followed by a reason/purpose with "a" + infinitive (e.g., "a studiare").
target_language_example: Mia sorella è andata in Spagna per lavoro.
native_language_example: My sister went to Spain for work.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of *andare* (to go), formed with **essere**: *è andato* (masc. singular). It agrees with the subject: *è andata* (she went), *sono andati* (they went, masc./mixed), *sono andate* (they went, fem.). Often used when the subject is understood from context.
target_language_example: Marco è andato al supermercato.
native_language_example: Marco went to the supermarket.

meaning: "he went to" (did something) / "he went to" (a place).
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of andare (auxiliary essere): è andato (he), è andata (she), sono andati/e (they). Often followed by a + infinitive to mean “went to do something” (è andato a comprare = he went to buy). It can also be followed by a place: è andato a Roma = he went to Rome.
target_language_example: Marco è andato a prendere i bambini a scuola.
native_language_example: Marco went to pick up the kids at school.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "andare a casa" = to go home. Uses the auxiliary "essere" with agreement: è andato (he), è andata (she), sono andati/e (they). Can mean a completed past action ("he went home yesterday") or that he is now at home ("he has gone home"). Often followed by details like who with (con lei), when (ieri, tre ore dopo), or how (in bici).
target_language_example: Dopo la festa, è andato a casa molto tardi.
native_language_example: After the party, he went home very late.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "andare a letto" = "to go to bed" (i.e., to go to sleep/turn in for the night). It uses the auxiliary "essere" and the past participle agrees with the subject: è andato (he), è andata (she), sono andati/andate (they). Often used after saying you were tired or finished something.
target_language_example: Dopo cena, è andato a letto presto.
native_language_example: After dinner, he went to bed early.

additional_notes: Used with essere + andare (past tense) to say that someone went to fish as an activity. It refers to a male subject (lui); for a female, say: "è andata a pescare". You can add time words (oggi, lo scorso weekend) or a place (in un fiume, al lago).
target_language_example: Marco è andato a pescare al lago stamattina.
native_language_example: Marco went fishing at the lake this morning.

meaning: “he went to school” / “he has gone to school.”
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of andare (uses essere). The past participle agrees with the subject: è andato (he), è andata (she). You can add details: a scuola di legge (“to law school”), a scuola con me (“to school with me”), and an adjective to describe how he went: È andato a scuola triste (“He went to school sad”).
target_language_example: Oggi è andato a scuola con suo fratello.
native_language_example: Today he went to school with his brother.

additional_notes: Past tense with essere (passato prossimo) of andare: è andato = “he went/has gone.” Used for a male subject; for a female, say è andata. In questions you can use rising intonation or add a question mark in writing: È andato ad una festa?
target_language_example: Marco è andato ad una festa ieri sera.
native_language_example: Marco went to a party last night.

meaning: "he went to the" / "he has gone to the".
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "andare" (to go): "è" (auxiliary essere) + "andato" (past participle). Used with a masculine singular destination introduced by "al" (= a + il), e.g., al villaggio, al parco, al negozio. It changes with the subject: "è andata al" (she went), "sono andati al" (they went, masc./mixed), "sono andate al" (they went, fem.).
target_language_example: Marco è andato al supermercato stamattina.
native_language_example: Marco went to the supermarket this morning.

meaning: "he went to the park" / "he has gone to the park."
additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo of andare (to go): è andato = “he went/has gone” (literally “is gone”), used for completed past actions or recent past. al = a + il, meaning “to the” before masculine singular nouns like parco. Change the ending to match the subject: è andata (she), sono andati (they m./mixed), sono andate (they f.).
target_language_example: Mio fratello è andato al parco dopo scuola.
native_language_example: My brother went to the park after school.

meaning: "he went to the" / "he has gone to the" (past of *andare a* + *al*).
additional_notes: Uses *passato prossimo*: **è andato** = “he went/has gone” (masculine singular). For a woman: **è andata al...**. **al** = *a* + *il* (“to the” before masculine singular nouns). Other forms: **allo** (a+lo), **alla** (a+la), **ai** (a+i), **alle** (a+le). Often followed by places like *al museo*, *al teatro*, *al centro commerciale*.
target_language_example: Marco è andato al supermercato dopo il lavoro.
native_language_example: Marco went to the supermarket after work.

meaning: 'he went to' (a place), using the verb 'andare' in the past.
additional_notes: Masculine singular passato prossimo of 'andare' (to go): 'è andato' = 'he went/has gone'. It commonly uses 'in' before many countries, continents, and certain places/buildings (e.g., in Africa, in America, in Italia, in farmacia). For a woman you’d say 'è andata in'.
target_language_example: Dopo il lavoro, è andato in centro per comprare un regalo.
native_language_example: After work, he went downtown to buy a gift.

meaning: he retired / he has gone into retirement.
additional_notes: Used to say someone has stopped working because they reached retirement. It’s the past tense (passato prossimo) of “andare in pensione” (to retire). Change it by person/gender: “è andata in pensione” (she retired), “sono andati/e in pensione” (they retired). Often followed by a time expression: “a ottobre”, “di recente”.
target_language_example: La mia insegnante è andata in pensione l'anno scorso.
native_language_example: My teacher retired last year.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "andare via" (to leave/go away). "È" is the auxiliary used with movement verbs, and "andato" agrees with the subject (masculine singular). Often the subject is implied from context; for a woman you’d say "è andata via". Used for leaving a place or departing (sometimes also in the sense of being gone).
target_language_example: Quando sono arrivato, era già andato via.
native_language_example: When I arrived, he had already left.

meaning: "he/she is passionate about" / "he/she is really into" (something).
additional_notes: Used with a subject (often omitted in Italian) + "è" + "appassionato" (masculine) / "appassionata" (feminine) + "di" + noun or activity. Common for hobbies and interests: "È appassionato di cinema" = He’s really into movies.
target_language_example: Mia sorella è appassionata di fotografia.
native_language_example: My sister is passionate about photography.

additional_notes: Used with a past participle (passato prossimo or passive) to say something happened a very short time ago: "è appena successo" = "it has just happened", "è appena stato eletto" = "he has just been elected". You can also use it with other persons: "ho appena finito" (I’ve just finished), "sono appena arrivato/a" (I’ve just arrived).
target_language_example: È appena arrivata a casa.
native_language_example: She has just arrived home.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something arrived very recently. With the verb *arrivare*, Italian uses *essere* in the past tense: *è arrivato*. The past participle agrees with the subject: *è appena arrivata* (she), *sono appena arrivati* (they, masc./mixed), *sono appena arrivate* (they, fem.). You can add where/from where: *a casa*, *qui*, *a Roma*, *da scuola*.
target_language_example: Il pacco è appena arrivato.
native_language_example: The package has just arrived.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is mad/angry at a person or group. It agrees with the subject: è arrabbiato (he is angry), è arrabbiata (she is angry), sono arrabbiati/e (they are angry). You can also ask questions: È arrabbiato con me? ('Is he angry with me?').
target_language_example: Lei è arrabbiata con me perché sono in ritardo.
native_language_example: She’s angry with me because I’m late.

meaning: 'she/it has arrived' / 'it arrived' (feminine singular); also used in 'there arrived...' (a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Past of arrivare with essere: è arrivata is used with a feminine subject (lei, la polizia, la primavera, una macchina, etc.). In questions, the subject can come after the verb: Quando è arrivata la tua famiglia? It can also introduce something happening/appearing: È arrivata una macchina = 'A car arrived' / 'A car has arrived.'
target_language_example: È arrivata mia sorella alle otto.
native_language_example: My sister arrived at eight.

additional_notes: Past tense of arrivare used with essere. It can mean a completed past event (“he arrived”) or a recent/connected-to-now event (“he has arrived”). You can add where/how/when with phrases like "a Kyoto" (to/in Kyoto), "su un taxi" (by taxi), or "giusto stamattina" (just this morning). It’s also used for rankings/results: "È arrivato quinto" = "He came/finished fifth".
target_language_example: È arrivato in ritardo perché c’era traffico.
native_language_example: He arrived late because there was traffic.

additional_notes: Used with a destination (city, place, address). With cities/countries you usually use the preposition “a” (è arrivato a Roma / a Londra), while with some places/regions you may use “in” instead (è arrivato in Italia / in Toscana). Changes for person/number: sono arrivato/a, sei arrivato/a, è arrivato/a, siamo arrivati/e, siete arrivati/e, sono arrivati/e.
target_language_example: Siamo arrivati a Milano alle otto.
native_language_example: We arrived in Milan at eight.

meaning: “he has arrived home / he got home.”
additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of “arrivare” used with “essere”. It usually refers to a male subject (è arrivato); for a female subject, use “è arrivata a casa”. Often used to say someone has just gotten home.
target_language_example: È arrivato a casa tardi ieri sera.
native_language_example: He got home late last night.

additional_notes: Past tense of arrivare (to arrive): è (present of essere) + arrivato (past participle) + qui (here). Used with times like ora (now), prima di… (before…), il mese scorso (last month), troppo presto (too early). The subject can be a person or something like a train; for a female subject you say è arrivata qui.
target_language_example: Mio fratello è arrivato qui alle otto.
native_language_example: My brother arrived here at eight.

additional_notes: Used to describe a female person or any feminine noun (e.g., la città, la casa). Italian often drops the subject, so it can mean “she is beautiful” or “it’s beautiful,” depending on context. In questions like “Vero che è bella?”, it’s a way to seek agreement: “It’s beautiful, right?”
target_language_example: Questa foto è bella, vero?
native_language_example: This photo is beautiful, right?

additional_notes: Used to describe a person, thing, animal, or weather as beautiful/nice: "X è bello". With an infinitive, it’s an impersonal comment meaning “It’s nice/great to …”: "È bello vederla!" = “It’s nice to see her!” You can also intensify it: "Com’è bello!" = “How beautiful!”
target_language_example: È bello passeggiare qui la sera.
native_language_example: It’s nice to take a walk here in the evening.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has skill or is talented at an activity. After "a" you can use: (1) a noun for a sport/game (e.g., "a tennis", "a mahjong"), or (2) an infinitive verb for an action (e.g., "a guidare", "a insegnare", "a imitare"). You can change the subject and verb: "sono bravo/a a" (I am good at), "sei bravo/a a" (you are), "è brava a" (she is). "Bravo" agrees with the person (bravo = male, brava = female).
target_language_example: Mia sorella è brava a cucinare.
native_language_example: My sister is good at cooking.

meaning: “it/he is good” (kind, nice) or “it is good” (tasty, good quality).
additional_notes: Used with the verb essere (“to be”) + buono (“good”). The meaning depends on context: with people it often means “kind/good-hearted” (Il prete è buono), while with food/places/products it usually means “good/tasty” or “good quality” (Questo ristorante è buono). The expression “È buono come il pane” literally “He’s as good as bread” means someone is very kind.
target_language_example: Questo gelato è buono, ma quello è ancora meglio.
native_language_example: This ice cream is good, but that one is even better.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "cadere" (to fall), formed with "essere". It can mean a completed past action (“fell”) or a recent past action (“has fallen”), depending on context. The past participle agrees with the subject: "è caduto" (male/it), "è caduta" (female), "sono caduti/cadute" (plural). Often used for accidents (falling down) or things dropping/falling.
target_language_example: Attento: il bicchiere è caduto per terra.
native_language_example: Careful: the glass fell on the floor.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "capitare" (to happen/occur). Very often used with an indirect object meaning “to happen to someone”: "Mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli è capitato..." = “It happened to me/you/him/her/us/you/them...”. With "a" + person: "È capitato al mio amico". The past participle agrees with the subject: "È capitato qualcosa" (masc. sing.), "È capitata una cosa" (fem. sing.), "Sono capitate delle cose" (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Mi è capitato di perdere il treno due volte questa settimana.
native_language_example: I happened to miss the train twice this week.

meaning: 'it’s clear' / 'obviously' (often to emphasize that something is obvious).
additional_notes: Used to state that something is evident ("Allora tutto è chiaro!" = “So everything is clear!”). It can also be used as a forceful tag question to demand agreement or check understanding ("Non è chiaro?" = “Isn’t it clear?” / “Is that clear?”). In arguments it can sound bossy or threatening depending on tone and context (especially with insults).
target_language_example: È chiaro che non possiamo entrare senza biglietto.
native_language_example: It’s clear that we can’t go in without a ticket.

additional_notes: Used to say something is not open or accessible. Common for shops, bars, offices, etc. ("Il negozio è chiuso" = the store isn’t open). It can also mean something is physically shut/closed, like a door, lid, valve, or tank ("Il serbatoio è chiuso" = the tank is closed/sealed). For plural objects/places: "sono chiusi" (masc.) / "sono chiuse" (fem.).
target_language_example: Scusi, oggi è chiuso?
native_language_example: Excuse me, is it closed today?

additional_notes: Used with essere to say something is locked: è/sono chiuso/a/i/e a chiave. Common for doors, gates, cars, trunks (bagagliaio), garages, etc. Can also describe a person being locked inside somewhere: È chiuso a chiave dentro (= He’s locked in).
target_language_example: La porta è chiusa a chiave, non possiamo entrare.
native_language_example: The door is locked; we can’t go in.

additional_notes: Used to identify or emphasize the thing that something is (often like an English cleft sentence): “X è ciò che + verb/phrase” = “X is what + verb/phrase.” Often followed by a verb (e.g., “è ciò che conta” = “is what matters”) or by a clause (e.g., “È ciò che penso?” = “Is it what I think?”).
target_language_example: La pazienza è ciò che serve in questo lavoro.
native_language_example: Patience is what you need in this job.

additional_notes:
Used to assign responsibility or blame. Very often followed by:
- "è colpa mia/tua/sua/nostra/vostra/loro" = it’s my/your/his-her/our/your/their fault
- "è colpa di + person/thing" = it’s the fault of / it’s because of
Often appears in the negative: "non è colpa di..." = it’s not ...’s fault.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace: è colpa mia.
native_language_example: I’m sorry: it’s my fault.

additional_notes: Used to take responsibility for a problem or mistake. Very common with negation: “Non è colpa mia” = “It’s not my fault.” You can change the person: “è colpa tua” (your fault), “è colpa sua” (his/her fault), “è colpa nostra” (our fault). Often follows “Mi dispiace…” to apologize or express regret.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, è colpa mia: ho dimenticato di chiamarti.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, it’s my fault: I forgot to call you.

additional_notes: Used to blame someone for something. Often followed by **se** (“if/that”) to explain the reason: **È colpa sua se...** = “It’s his/her fault that...”. **Sua** refers to a third person (his/her/its) and agrees with **colpa** (feminine).
target_language_example: È colpa sua se siamo in ritardo.
native_language_example: It’s his/her fault that we’re late.

additional_notes: Used to blame someone for a problem or mistake. Often appears with negation: “non è colpa tua” = “it’s not your fault.” You can intensify it with “Sì, è colpa tua” or “Sì che è colpa tua” (“Yes, it is your fault”).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma è colpa tua se siamo in ritardo.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but it’s your fault if we’re late.

meaning: “is like a …” (used to compare someone/something to something else).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to make a comparison (often metaphorical): *X è come un Y* = “X is like a Y.” The noun that follows agrees in gender/number: *è come una madre*, *è come un fratello*; plural: *sono come dei fratelli / delle sorelle*.
target_language_example: Per me, questo posto è come una seconda casa.
native_language_example: For me, this place is like a second home.

meaning: “it’s like a …” (comparison with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to make a comparison or metaphor: “X is like a Y.” Since it ends with “una,” it’s followed by a feminine singular noun (una pietra, una spalla, una giornata, una vasca). With a masculine noun, you use “è come un …” (e.g., è come un sogno).
target_language_example: Questo posto è come una casa per me.
native_language_example: This place is like a home to me.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something that feels or seems true, often as a comparison rather than a literal fact. It’s very commonly followed by the imperfect subjunctive (e.g.,   come se fossi/stessi/andassi	).
target_language_example: È come se non mi ascoltassi.
native_language_example: It’s as if you weren’t listening to me.

additional_notes: Used with the verb essere (“to be”) to intensify what comes next (an adjective or past participle): è completamente vuoto (completely empty), è completamente impazzita (has gone completely crazy). It often adds emphasis, similar to “totally” in English but neutral in tone. In phrases like È completamente escluso, it means “It’s completely out of the question / absolutely not.”
target_language_example: Il museo è completamente chiuso oggi.
native_language_example: The museum is completely closed today.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone is and who they are with. Refers to a male person (lui). For a female person, say: "è con i suoi amici" (same if the group is mixed or all male) or "è con le sue amiche" (all female friends). You can add an adverb like "di solito" or "solitamente" to mean "usually".
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: è con i suoi amici.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he’s with his friends.

meaning: “is so / is like that” (used to emphasize an adjective or describe how something is).
additional_notes: Most often used before an adjective to mean “so” (very/that much): “è così + adjective” (è così tranquillo = he’s so calm). It can also mean “it’s like that / that’s the way it is,” depending on context, but in these examples it’s the intensifier “so.”
target_language_example: Sei così gentile!
native_language_example: You’re so kind!

additional_notes: Used to introduce or emphasize the way something is done (“it’s like this that…”). Often appears in negatives like “non è così che…” = “that’s not how…”.
target_language_example: Non è così che si parla a un amico.
native_language_example: That’s not how you talk to a friend.

additional_notes: Used to say something is very hard, often with emphasis (così = “so/that”). It can be a statement (È così difficile.) or appear in questions (Perché è così difficile...?) and comparisons (Non è così difficile come pensi = “It’s not as difficult as you think”).
target_language_example: Non è così difficile imparare l’italiano se studi un po’ ogni giorno.
native_language_example: It’s not so difficult to learn Italian if you study a little every day.

meaning: "it is really" / "is it really?" (used for emphasis).
additional_notes: Used with adjectives, adverbs, or whole statements to intensify them ("really", "truly"). In questions it often expresses surprise or doubt: "È davvero...?" = "Is it really...?". It’s the verb "è" ("is") + "davvero" ("really").
target_language_example: È davvero una buona idea?
native_language_example: Is it really a good idea?

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that something is fully true or fully the case. It’s often followed by an adjective or past participle (e.g., è del tutto naturale/vero/finito). You can also use "del tutto" without "è" as an adverb meaning “completely”.
target_language_example: È del tutto impossibile arrivare in tempo.
native_language_example: It’s completely impossible to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used with essere (“to be”) to say someone/something has returned to a previous state, condition, place, or situation. Often followed by an adjective (è di nuovo felice), a past participle/adjective (è di nuovo rotto), or a place expression (è di nuovo a casa).
target_language_example: Dopo la vacanza, sono di nuovo al lavoro.
native_language_example: After the vacation, I’m back at work.

additional_notes: Used to say something is hard to do or understand. Often followed by an infinitive: “Imparare l’italiano è difficile” (“Learning Italian is hard”). You can also add a person with an indirect object pronoun: “Mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi è difficile” = “It’s difficult for me/you/him/her/us/you (pl.).”
target_language_example: Per me è difficile svegliarmi presto.
native_language_example: For me, it’s hard to wake up early.

additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive to say something is difficult to do: “X è difficile da + infinitive” (e.g., imparare, capire, tradurre). The subject can be a thing (“questa parola”) or a person (“il capo”), and then it often means they’re hard to please/satisfy (“difficile da accontentare/soddisfare”).
target_language_example: Questo esercizio è difficile da fare senza aiuto.
native_language_example: This exercise is hard to do without help.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is hard for you personally. Often followed by an infinitive with or without “da”: “È difficile per me capire…” (to understand), “Questo è difficile per me da fare” (to do). You can also replace “per me” with another person: “per te” (for you), “per lui/lei” (for him/her).
target_language_example: È difficile per me parlare italiano velocemente.
native_language_example: It’s difficult for me to speak Italian quickly.

meaning: "is available" (can be gotten/used; or free/not busy).
additional_notes: Used for availability of things (in stock, accessible, ready to use) and of people (free/not busy). Often followed by time expressions like "al momento" (at the moment) or "stasera" (tonight).
target_language_example: La camera è disponibile da domani.
native_language_example: The room is available starting tomorrow.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "diventare" with "essere": "(lei/essa) è diventata". Used for a change of state or becoming something/someone. It agrees in gender/number: masculine "è diventato", plural "sono diventati/diventate". Often followed by a noun/adjective: "è diventata famosa" (became famous), "è diventata una ballerina" (became a dancer).
target_language_example: Con il tempo, la città è diventata più tranquilla.
native_language_example: Over time, the city has become quieter.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **diventare** (“to become”) in the **passato prossimo**: **essere + diventato/a**. **È diventata** agrees with a **female** subject (a man would be **è diventato**). **Una** is the feminine singular indefinite article; with a masculine noun you’d use **un** (or **uno**). Common with jobs/roles/relationships: *è diventata una dottoressa / una vera amica*.
target_language_example: Dopo l’università, è diventata una insegnante.
native_language_example: After university, she became a teacher.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "diventare" = "to become", formed with "essere". It agrees with the subject: "è diventato" (masc. sing.), "è diventata" (fem. sing.), "sono diventati" (masc. plural/mixed), "sono diventate" (fem. plural). Often used for changes/status changes: becoming rich, busy, a leader, a favorite place, etc.
target_language_example: Con il tempo è diventato più sicuro di sé.
native_language_example: Over time, he became more confident.

meaning: "he has become" / "he became" (followed by a masculine noun).
additional_notes: From the verb "diventare" = "to become." Used to say someone changed into a new role/status/identity: "È diventato un pastore" = "He became a shepherd." For a feminine noun, use "è diventata una" (she became a...). Tense depends on context: it can mean "became" (completed past) or "has become" (result up to now).
target_language_example: Dopo anni di studio, è diventato un medico.
native_language_example: After years of studying, he became a doctor.

additional_notes: Used to say that an activity, thing, or situation is enjoyable or entertaining. It’s the verb essere (è = “is”) + the adjective divertente (“fun/entertaining”). You can add an infinitive to explain in what way it’s fun: è divertente da guardare (“it’s fun to watch”), è divertente da fare (“it’s fun to do”).
target_language_example: Questo gioco è divertente da fare con gli amici.
native_language_example: This game is fun to play with friends.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of entrare for a male subject: essere + entrato. Used for going into a place (nel/nella = into the). For a female subject: è entrata; for plural: sono entrati/entrate.
target_language_example: Marco è entrato in casa e ha chiuso la porta.
native_language_example: Marco went into the house and closed the door.

meaning: "he entered" / "he went into" (followed by a feminine singular place: "in the").
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "entrare" for a male subject ("he"): "è entrato". It’s typically used with a place you go inside. "nella" = "in" + "la" (feminine singular), so you’ll also see: "nel" (in+il), "nei" (in+i), "nelle" (in+le), etc. For a female subject: "è entrata nella".
target_language_example: Lui è entrato nella farmacia per comprare delle medicine.
native_language_example: He went into the pharmacy to buy some medicine.

meaning: “is extremely / is very (to an extreme degree)”
additional_notes: Used with essere ("è" = "is") + the adverb estremamente (“extremely”) to intensify an adjective: è estremamente + aggettivo (e.g., è estremamente piccolo/veloce). For plural subjects, use sono: Sono estremamente stanchi.
target_language_example: Questo ristorante è estremamente caro.
native_language_example: This restaurant is extremely expensive.

additional_notes: Used to say something is easy. It often introduces an infinitive: "È facile + verb" (È facile capire) or takes "per me/te/lui..." to mean "for me/you/him..." (È facile per me). You can also use it with a noun: "La lezione è facile" (The lesson is easy).
target_language_example: È facile arrivare qui in metro.
native_language_example: It’s easy to get here by subway.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say something/someone is easy to do/use/learn/reach, etc.: "[Subject] è facile da + infinitive". You can change tense/person: "era facile da...", "sarà facile da..."; and use plural: "sono facili da...".
target_language_example: Questo esercizio è facile da fare.
native_language_example: This exercise is easy to do.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is easy for you to do. Often followed by an infinitive (È facile per me leggere...) or used with a subject clause (Parlare francese è facile per me). You can swap the pronoun: è facile per te/lui/lei/noi/voi/loro. The opposite is "è difficile per me".
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: è facile per me spiegartelo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it’s easy for me to explain it to you.

meaning: “is famous for its/her” (talking about something a place/thing is known for).
additional_notes: Used to say what someone/something is known for. It agrees with the subject: è famoso per il… (masc.), è famosa per la… (fem.); plural: sono famosi/e per… . After this you typically name a feature/product/activity: per la sua industria, per il suo vino, per le sue spiagge. With a person it can mean “her”: Maria è famosa per la sua voce.
target_language_example: Napoli è famosa per la sua pizza.
native_language_example: Naples is famous for its pizza.

additional_notes: From essere + fatta (past participle of fare). Used (1) to talk about what something is made of: “È fatta di…” = “It’s made of…”. Used (2) on its own as a reassuring statement/exclamation meaning “It’s done”, “All set”, “We did it” (often after completing something).
target_language_example: Ok, ho inviato l’email: è fatta.
native_language_example: Okay, I sent the email: it’s done.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s position/opinion about a proposal, idea, plan, etc. It’s feminine singular (contraria) and is typically said to a woman (Lei) or about a feminine subject; for a man you’d say "è favorevole o contrario". Often followed by "a" + the thing you’re discussing: "a questo", "al piano", "alla sua idea".
target_language_example: È favorevole o contraria a questa proposta?
native_language_example: Are you in favor of or against this proposal?

additional_notes:
Used to ask someone’s position on a proposal, idea, law, etc. It’s usually followed by "a/al/alla/alle" + the topic: 
- "È favorevole o contrario al piano?" (al = a + il)
- "È favorevole o contrario alla pena di morte?" (alla = a + la)
You can also say: "Sei favorevole o contrario...?" when speaking informally to someone you address with "tu".
target_language_example: È favorevole o contrario a questa proposta?
native_language_example: Are you in favor of or against this proposal?

additional_notes: Used to say that a situation/event is finished. Literally “it is finished,” with finita (feminine) agreeing with an implied feminine noun like la storia, la guerra, etc. In some contexts with a pronoun + on/to (e.g., “Mi è finita sui capelli?”), finire means “to end up,” so it means “Did it end up on my hair?”
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma è finita.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but it’s over.

additional_notes: Used to say something is completely impossible, unacceptable, or not allowed. It can stand alone (È fuori questione.) or be followed by a clause with che + subjunctive: È fuori questione che tu vada… (“There’s no way you’re going…”). Often stronger than “non è possibile” and can sound firm/strict depending on tone.
target_language_example: Per me, saltare la riunione è fuori questione.
native_language_example: For me, skipping the meeting is out of the question.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a key point or the start of something important (an event, a decision, a reveal). Slightly formal/dramatic; in everyday speech you can also say "è arrivato il momento" or "è ora".
target_language_example: È giunto il momento di andare.
native_language_example: The time has come to go.

meaning: “is already” / “has already” (depending on the verb tense).
additional_notes: Used to say something has happened sooner than expected or is already true. Often appears as “è già + past participle” (passato prossimo passive: “è già stato risolto?” = “has it already been solved?”) or “è già + adjective/past participle” (“Tom è già morto” = “Tom is already dead”). In questions, it can suggest surprise or checking status (“È già arrivata la lettera?”).
target_language_example: Siamo già pronti, possiamo partire.
native_language_example: We’re already ready; we can leave.

additional_notes: Used with masculine singular nouns to identify/define something: "X è il Y" = “X is the Y.” Very common with superlatives and comparisons: "è il meno/più + adjective" = “is the least/most + adjective.” (For feminine: "è la"; masculine plural: "sono i"; feminine plural: "sono le".)
target_language_example: Questo è il ristorante migliore del quartiere.
native_language_example: This is the best restaurant in the neighborhood.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is the leader or person in charge of a group, organization, or situation. Often followed by a phrase like “di/del/della …” (e.g., è il capo del partito) or can stand alone (“è il capo lì” = he’s the one in charge there). “capo” can mean boss/leader/head; in family contexts “capo famiglia” means “head of the family.”
target_language_example: Non discutere con lui: è il capo del reparto.
native_language_example: Don’t argue with him: he’s the head of the department.

meaning: “it’s the day when” (the day on which).
additional_notes: Used to define or explain what a particular day is, followed by an event or situation. It introduces a relative clause with "in cui" = "in which/on which" (often equivalent to English "when"). You can change the verb and noun: "è la settimana in cui" (it’s the week when), "è il momento in cui" (it’s the moment when).
target_language_example: Oggi è il giorno in cui firmiamo il contratto.
native_language_example: Today is the day when we sign the contract.

meaning: "is the best that (you/they) can do" / "is this the best that…"
additional_notes: Used to say that something is the maximum possible result or effort. Often appears as a rhetorical/critical question: "È il meglio che sai fare?" (= "Is that the best you can do?"). It’s usually followed by a verb (e.g., sai fare, puoi ottenere, sapete fare).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma è il meglio che posso fare oggi.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but it’s the best I can do today.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something (masculine singular) is the best. The subject can be a person (“He is the best”) or a thing (“It’s the best”), often understood from context. For a woman, use “è la migliore”; for plural, “sono i/le migliori.” You can add comparisons like “tra di noi” (“among us”).
target_language_example: Secondo me questo ristorante è il migliore della città.
native_language_example: In my opinion this restaurant is the best in the city.

additional_notes: Used with essere (to be) + a possessive to say something belongs to you or is associated with you: "È il mio libro" = "It’s my book." The possessive agrees with the noun that follows (il mio / la mia / i miei / le mie). You can also use it alone to mean "It’s mine" when the noun is understood from context: "Di chi è questo? È il mio."
target_language_example: Scusa, è il mio posto.
native_language_example: Sorry, that’s my seat.

additional_notes: Used to say that today (or a specified time) is your birthday. You can swap the time word/phrase before it: Oggi/Domani/Tra dieci giorni è il mio compleanno. Also common: È il tuo/suo compleanno (It’s your/his/her birthday).
target_language_example: Scusa, oggi è il mio compleanno: possiamo festeggiare stasera?
native_language_example: Sorry, today is my birthday: can we celebrate tonight?

additional_notes: Used to explain that something is part of your job or responsibility. You can say it as a simple answer ("Certo, è il mio lavoro.") or add details before it ("Vendere macchine è il mio lavoro."). It can also imply obligation or lack of choice ("È il mio lavoro, non ho scelta.").
target_language_example: Non ti preoccupare: è il mio lavoro.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it’s my job.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone (or sometimes something, jokingly) is your best friend. The subject can be a person name or a thing: "Il mio computer è il mio migliore amico." In speech you can drop the subject pronoun (Italian often does), so "È..." can mean "He/She/It is...". For a woman you’d say: "è la mia migliore amica".
target_language_example: È il mio migliore amico da quando eravamo bambini.
native_language_example: He’s been my best friend since we were kids.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the last one in a series for you (last day, last interview, last project, etc.). Often followed by a noun: “È il mio ultimo giorno/colloquio/progetto.” You can also leave the noun implied if it’s clear from context: “È il mio ultimo.” Note agreement: ultimo (masc. sing.), ultima (fem. sing.), ultimi (masc. pl.), ultime (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Domani è il mio ultimo giorno di lavoro.
native_language_example: Tomorrow is my last day of work.

additional_notes: Used to say that the right (or wrong) time has arrived to do something. Often followed by a phrase like “di + infinitive” (È il momento di andare.) or “per + infinitive” (Non è il momento per discutere.), or by “del/della + noun” to mean “it’s time for …” (È il momento del discorso.). Can also be said alone to mean “Now!” or “This is it.”
target_language_example: È il momento di andare a casa.
native_language_example: It’s time to go home.

meaning: "is our" (referring to a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify someone/something as belonging to “us” or connected to “us,” usually followed by a noun: “È il nostro insegnante / autista / leader.” The possessive agrees with the noun (nostro = masculine singular). Variations: è la nostra (feminine singular), è i nostri (masculine plural), è le nostre (feminine plural). Italian often uses the article (il/la/i/le) before a possessive + noun.
target_language_example: Luca è il nostro vicino di casa.
native_language_example: Luca is our neighbor.

additional_notes: Used to form the relative superlative: **è il più + adjective** (“he/it is the most …”). It’s often followed by **di/tra/fra + group**: *È il più vecchio dei tre* (“the oldest of the three”). For feminine, use **è la più**; for plural, **sono i/le più**.
target_language_example: Questo ristorante è il più economico della zona.
native_language_example: This restaurant is the cheapest in the area.

additional_notes: Used to compare people or things and say one has the greatest height in a group.
